¶ Here the pedigree of the Chełmskis breaks off, so that it cannot be said with certainty from whom the members of the family given below descend. In an old pedigree I find that Mikołaj, son of Marcyan II, had a son Jerzy, who signed the election of Jan Kazimierz with the province of Kalisz. By Urszula Cielecka he is said to have had sons: Klemens Stefan and Mikołaj, who left no issue, and Krzysztof Ścibor and Andrzej Ścibor. The by-name Ścibor, borne by Jan, Master of the Hunt of Kraków, and then by Krzysztof, Master of the Hunt of Kraków, Andrzej, Standard-bearer of Sandomierz, and Marcyan, Camp Master, suggests rather that they were sons of Jan, and not of the Jerzy above.
boniecki1900/c02:
2.976.177-182

¶ Krzysztof Ścibor made a deed of life interest with his wife, Teofila Ossowska, daughter of Aleksander and of Katarzyna née Koniecpolska, before the municipal court of Nowy Korczyn in 1676. He was the owner of Śladków, in the district of Wiślica, and of part of Łukomia in the province of Kalisz. In the acts he was called Master of the Hunt of Kraków and royal colonel. His widow entered a protest in the municipal court of Kraków in 1703 against her husband's brother Andrzej, that he alone held the estate of Łukomia in the province of Kalisz, half of which ought to belong to her son.

¶ Andrzej Ścibor Chełmski signed the election of Augustus II with the province of Kraków; he was called in the acts in 1690 Vice-Steward of Sandomierz and colonel of the Crown army, and in 1692 Standard-bearer of Sandomierz. He died in 1697, and Morsztyn became Standard-bearer after him. By his wife, née Pałuska, he had sons, Franciszek, who left no issue, and Józef, married to Helena Zielonacka, and daughters, Anna, wife of Józef Tworzyański, and Teresa, wife of Jan Czarnocki, Master of the Hunt of Chełm. A judgment of the Tribunal at Piotrków of 1748, given in the suit over the estate of Łukomia, shows us this.

breyer1935gaue/35:
V. THE WARTHE MARSHES

Landscape

The Berlin-Warsaw glacial valley (Urstromtal), in which the Warthe now rolls its waters sluggishly, is in places hardly wider than 3 kilometres. The river valley is mostly open. Only in the area between the towns of Koło and Konin do dense stands of alder and poplar cover the valley floor, which is fertile, though in places also sandy. As little as 150 years ago the glacial valley was ground hostile to settlement. Backwaters, bogs and high sandbanks, covered with impenetrable bushes and climbing plants, teemed with water birds. Then as now, in spring murky floods poured over the whole valley, though not with such devastating effect as on the Vistula. Here as there the spring water leaves behind the silt that is wanted for the growth of the meadows. So the wanderer today sees splendid meadows in the "Bruch", as the landscape of the Warthe valley is generally called. The cheerful twittering of the rich bird life enlivens the stillness of this peculiar landscape.

Settlements

Over a stretch of 130 kilometres, from the former Prussian border to Leśnik south of the town of Uniejów, 63 larger German villages, with a population of 7000 souls, are strung one after another, with greater and smaller breaks. In addition, some 4000 Germans live in 105 Polish marsh villages or in isolated small German settlements. As little as 40 years ago some villages still had their old German names, such as Sophiental, Friedrichsfeld, Ludwigslust, Ingelfingen, Adelhof.

The conditions of ownership are good in most of the marsh villages. The most prosperous German settlements lie west of the town of Konin. In the foreground of farming are the raising of cattle and poultry. Large pieces of meadow are let for good money. On the higher-lying fields grain and potatoes are grown, and there too, mostly scattered, the farmsteads stand. Sometimes the villages take a position along the bank, as in Daniszew, Leszcze, Paprot Hol., Młyny, Piekarskie and Stawki. The silt soil, or "Letten" (clay), as the "Brücher" (the marsh people, also called in mockery "Wasserpatscher", water-splashers) call it, needs strong horses for ploughing. The yields of the harvest are high accordingly. The cattle are grazed here in "Koppeln" (fenced pastures) and not in "Hocken", as the Vistula German would say.
breyer1935gaue/36:
In the building of houses, brick has lately gained the upper hand. The half-timbered barns of the Leśnik language island bear witness, together with the dialect, to the Pomeranian origin of the settlers. The villages near Konin have old barns of planks or modern board cladding.

History of Settlement

The German settlement of the Warthe marshes of central Poland began around 1750. The first marsh settlement that can be shown by documents is Wenglewer Holland, which was laid out in 1767 on the lands of the estate of Sławsk, whose owner was the district judge (Landrichter) S. Leszczyc-Zielonawski. At the same time the Holländereien (Olęder colonies) of Rumin, Kolno and Sławsk arose within the lordship of Sławsk. The marsh villages lying further east, Briesener Hol., Paprot Hol., Drążyn Hol. and Tury Hol., were founded around 1775. In 1781 King Stanislaus Augustus Poniatowski confirmed the rights of the Holländerei of Majdany, lying in the Chełmno estate group (Schlüssel), the property of the Archbishop of Gniezno. The German villages opposite Majdany, Police, Daniszew and Leszcze, arose around 1785. The great Leśnik language island south of Uniejów was founded, according to its charter, in 1796. On taking over 10 Hufen of forest land the colonists paid the estate owner Milewski 189 Thaler of ground money. In 1792 German farmers settled in Czyste, Kaczka and Machnówka.

In 1845 the German villages of Józefow, Młyny, Łęg, Nowa Kaczka and Rosengarten arose in the Leśnik language island on swampy, sandy soil. All the villages were "laid out in the forest, on overgrown places, on moor soil, pastures and waste land", as a court judgement puts it. In the 19th century new villages were founded now and then, such as Neu-Czarkow in 1835. The emigration to Volhynia depopulated many villages, especially those set on poor soil.

The cloth-makers and weavers who came into the towns of Zagórów, Konin and Koło after 1818, and who managed to hold their own after a fashion until 1870, went over to other trades under the pressure of circumstances. Most of them have wholly shed their inherited nationality (Volksart), and have at times become eager standard-bearers of Polishness, so carrying a deep split into what decades ago was a closed community of church and people.
breyer1935gaue/37:
[Picture: German farmhouse from Timmingen, Koło county - Photo: Breyer]

Origin

The settlers of the Warthe marshes of central Poland came chiefly from the marshes of the Oder, the Netze and the western Warthe. The country round Landsberg an der Warthe, Sonnenburg and Driesen is often named in the church books. The "Brücher" were therefore people who knew how to deal with swamp forest and marshy meadow land, men "skilled in water works". Before the war there were among them experienced boatmen and boat-builders, who carried Polish grain from the area of Koło and Konin to Germany in Oder barges. Even now they speak a Low German (Platt) coloured by the Mark. In many villages a popular High German has already taken hold.

The inhabitants of the Leśnik language island come from the Netze district and speak the Pomeranian dialect.
breyer1935gaue/38:
Schools

The old marsh villages had German elementary schools from the beginning. When land was taken, a set piece of land was always given over to the school.

| Year | Number of German elementary schools and cantorates |
|---|---|
| 1800 | 10 |
| 1865 | 22 |
| 1898 | 24 |
| 1919 | 24 |
| 1925 | 4 |

Churches

The first Evangelical parish was founded in Konin in 1826, after long negotiations with the government offices. Brave Lutherans of Konin turned for legal support even to the then viceroy of Poland, Grand Duke Konstantin Konstantinowitsch. The first preacher, A. Kegler, came from Eckartsberg in Thuringia. The congregation of Zagórów was raised in 1858 from a branch (Filial) founded in 1833 to an independent parish. The branch of Lissewo-Peisern, lying in the Warthe marshes, arose in 1858. The congregation of Koło, at first a branch of Turek, became independent in 1903. It has had its own church since 1882.
breyer1935gaue/39:
VI. THE KALISZ COUNTRY

Landscape

South of the towns of Zagórów and Konin stretches a swampy, sandy plain, broken in strips by meagre pine woods. Alder carrs and rows of pollard willows along drainage ditches surround thin, peaty meadows. Sand hills, poor fields and stretches of drifting sand alternate. The field of view in this half-open landscape is narrow. Light, fine-grained sand is the most striking mark of this secluded, quiet, dreamy country. The names of the villages also point to the sandy nature of the landscape: Białe Błoto, Bielawki, Biała, Biała Panieńska, Białobrzegi, Łazy, Borowiec, Grądy, Mokre, Bagno. In earlier centuries the wealth of forest gave rise to glassworks and iron hammers, as can be seen from the village names Huta Stara, Huta Nowa, Huta Trąbczyńska, Huta Lukomska, Huta, Prażuchy, Kużnica, Huta bei Prażuchy.

20 kilometres north of Kalisz the picture of the landscape changes almost suddenly. A fertile plain, thickly set with manor farms and wholly without forest, opens before the wanderer's eyes. Here, apart from two villages that arose in the 20th century, we find no trace of German settlements.

Settlements

The German villages of the Kalisz country lie over an area of a good 1000 km². They form a relatively closed area of settlement, in which some 25,000 Germans of Silesian stock live. Unlike other regions, we find here some large villages with a population of over 500 souls. The village of Łazińsk has 757 souls, Borowiec 668, Obory 635, Białobłoty 588. 9500 Germans live in 26 large villages, some 8000 in a further 74 smaller ones.

The quality of the soil, as already said, is far below middling. In dry years the yields of grain and root crops are small. It is said then that bread is eaten only at Christmas. On market days the German farmers bring, instead of

 Białe Błoto = white swamp, Bielawki = the white one, Białobrzegi = white banks, Łazy = Brücher (marsh people), Borowiec = peaty soil, (Grądy, Mokre, Bagno) = swamps
breyer1935gaue/40:
sacks filled with grain, sacks of pine cones. To enlarge the area of tillage, the drifting sand is carted load by load into the lower-lying marshy meadows.

[Picture: German farmer's wife of Pomeranian stock from Gawrony, Konin county - Photo: Breyer]

Over-population is heavy. In most cases it leads to the division of farms among heirs (Realteilung) and to the growth of a large rural proletariat. Seasonal work in Germany (Sachsengängerei) was widespread for many decades before the war. Even after the war hundreds of young men and girls went to Germany in spring for farm work. For three years this almost only source of earnings has run dry. Economic need has therefore reached an unbearable degree
breyer1935gaue/41:
in many German villages. The conditions of ownership are fairly dismal. Of the 805 who pay church dues in the congregation of Grodziec, 101 families, or 13 in a hundred, are landless; 183 families, or 23 in a hundred, have typical dwarf holdings of 1 to 6 Morgen. In the congregations of Zagórów, Stawiszyn and Prażuchy things are by no means better.

In house building building with planks prevails everywhere, which is natural given the great wealth of forest. Since the shallow peaty meadows hold bog iron ore in most cases, this stone is much used for building farm buildings, even dwelling houses. Lately Jewish traders have been buying up these "iron stones" and taking them to the factories of Upper Silesia, where artificial fertiliser is made from them. In the Silesian settlements the dwelling house always stands apart. The farm buildings are often surrounded by birch groves and patches of wood. Because of the marshy, sandy ground, scattered settlement prevails with only few exceptions. The farmsteads lie off the village street, each with its own access road.

Now and then the last traces of the old folk costume are still to be met. Folk art is well kept among the Silesians. Only among them are the finely carved and tastefully decorated grave boards to be seen. Folk dance and folk song are still alive. Folk life always received new impulses from the seasonal work in Germany, though not always in a good sense. There is almost no link with the Łódź industrial area.

History of Settlement

Around 1740 the German settler made his way with axe and spade into the tracts of the Kalisz country, remote from men and untilled since time immemorial. In 1746 the owner of the estate of Trąbczyn, Paul von Kolno-Prusiński, concluded with honest Hollanders a contract of hereditary lease (Erbpachtvertrag), by which the woods and waste lands south of the estate of Trąbczyn were given over to be brought under cultivation. The village of Łazińsk Holland arose. The castellan of Sieradz, J. Wężyk, settled four German villages on his estates at Grodziec in 1772: Borowiec, Konary, Grunde and Wielołęka. On the lands of the estate of Ceków a whole series of Holländereien arose after 1770, among them the large village of Prażuchy, which by 1799 already counted 34 farmers on 24 Hufen; in 1775 Poroże was founded; in 1775 Zbiersk Holland and Ciświca-Holland, in 1778 Lipnica and Jarantów, in 1780 Jaszczury and Zakrzyn. The owner of the landed estates of Piegonisko and Stoki, the steward (Truchsess) of Smolensk, M. Wągrowski, who had extensive woods at his disposal, laid out in 1782 the Hollän-
breyer1935gaue/42:
dereien of Piegonisko, Sobiesęki and Stoki. The German village of Kazimierka-Stara has a founding charter of 1782; eight years later Kazimierka-Nowa arose. In 1784 the lord of Biskupice settled the village of Adlerholland, or Orlin, in his woods lying west of the estate. The owner of the lordship of Gadow, the noble Peter von Sokoła-Gałczyński, concluded a contract with worthy Hollanders in 1784, since his woods "promise no use whatever, neither now nor in the future, the same with regard to the proven uses which Hauländer bring to all hereditary estates". The new village is called Gadow-Holland. In 1786 Zamęty and Danowiec were founded. The starost of Odolanów (Adelnau), F. Stadnicki, settled the Holländerei of Białobłoty "on the green forest" in 1787. The hereditary lord of the estate of Chocz, the prelate K. Lipski, in 1790 gave the hard-working George Müller forest for Holländereien on the boundary of Obory, granting seven free years. The taker bound himself to settle twenty Hollanders in the new colony of Józefów. So, even before the last partition of Poland, the whole forest area north of Kalisz between the Prosna and the Teleszyna had been opened up by German settlers. Numerous clearing islands, larger and smaller, studded the forest land thickly.

In the 19th century the work of clearing went on. Around the old villages a ring of daughter settlements arose here and there. So near Prażuchy the German villages of Celestyny, Feliksów, Kotwasice, Niedżwiady, Annopol, Wygoda; in the neighbourhood of Grodziec in 1845, from the estate of Grabieniec, the colony of Wojciechowo, later Wycinki, Boberfeld, Michalinów, Łagiewniki, Sołomina. From the emancipation of the peasants on, the work of settlement rested entirely. The space free for settlement [sielungsfreie] is now used up. The nearness of the Prussian border gave the young people of the villages chances of earning in the Reich; seasonal work in Germany slowly developed, which in summer wholly emptied many German settlements. The emigration to Volhynia did not reshape the Kalisz country as strongly as other German areas. No village was noticeably weakened by it.

In the Kalisz country lies the first and oldest German industrial town in central Poland. The castellan (Burgherr) of Gniezno, M. H. von Górowo-Górowski, founded the town of Władysławow in 1738. In the same year arose "the praiseworthy craft of the ticking-weavers, fustian-weavers and linen-weavers in Władysławow". To the present day the German community, though small in numbers, has held out bravely in spite of every economic hardship.
breyer1935gaue/43:
[Picture: Evangelical church in Babiak, Koło county, built 1823 - Photo: Schindler]

German Catholic weavers from Bohemia came to Turek around 1826, for whose religious needs a Catholic priest from Bohemia was even appointed. At the same time weavers came from Saxony, West Prussia and Silesia. In all, 56 in a hundred came from German Bohemia, 26 in a hundred from Saxony, 12 in a hundred from West Prussia and 6 in a hundred from Prussian Silesia. In 1828 a weavers' guild was founded in Turek, which exists to the present, although the German members of the guild are already very much in the minority.
breyer1935gaue/44:
The town of Kalisz was rebuilt by the Prussian government after the fire of 1793 and settled with many Prussian officials. German craftsmen, merchants and tradesmen joined them. After 1831 many German entrepreneurs left Kalisz; even so it counted 2405 Germans in 1860, 2500 Evangelicals in 1913, and in 1921 only 1297 Evangelicals. The Kalisz cloth factory of Repphahn, founded in 1816, was known far beyond the borders of central Poland. Not far from Kalisz, in Opatówek, Fiedler founded a fine-cloth factory in 1823.

Origin

Apart from the villages of Józefów, Wielopole and part of Białobłoty, in which Pomeranian farmers settled, the German population of the Kalisz country is of Silesian origin. The Silesian dialect, with certain gradations, prevails without exception. Custom and usage, folk art and folk song are of a truly Silesian stamp. In the church books of the Evangelical congregations of Grodziec, Stawiszyn and Zagórów the places of origin given for the immigrants are above all villages in the neighbourhood of: Bentschen, Neutomischl, Grätz, Wollstein, Tirschtiegel, Zduny, Wreschen, Pudewitz, Krotoschin, Kirch-Boruj, Militsch, Heinzenburg, Parchwitz, Wohlau, Brieg. All these places lie within the area of the Silesian dialect, in southern Posen and the neighbouring Lower Silesia. The settlers came from the new settlements that had arisen in the 17th and 18th centuries. In the wooded, swampy areas of the Kalisz country they found soil like the soil they were used to at home around Grätz, Neutomischl and Wollstein. The growing of hops, carried on in many Kalisz colonies until the World War, also points to the Neutomischl area.

Only a few of the stated origins point to other dialect areas. Only from the neighbouring Oder marshes did a limited number of immigrants come, from the neighbourhood of Landsberg an der Warthe, Sonnenburg and Driesen.

Schools

A report written in 1797 by Pastor Grimm of Stawiszyn for the consistory in Posen gives German elementary schools in the following Hollander villages: Zbiersk, Prażuchy, Kosmowo, Dannowitz, Zamenty, Zakrzyń, Przespolew, Czachulec, Grojetz and Mycielin. With the schools in Obory, Łazińsk, Białobłoty, Gadowskie Hol. and Wierzchy, which also already existed then, this gives a total of 15 German elementary schools. The way of working and the conditions of pay
breyer1935gaue/45:
of the "school-keepers" (Schulhalter) were like those in other German areas of settlement. Some schools, as in Adler-Holland, Łazińsk and Obory, had 15, 18 and 22 Morgen of land respectively. Besides teaching, the teacher's most important duties were reading the sermon every Sunday, baptising and burying. In the first half of the 19th century religious schools were founded in the newly laid-out daughter settlements. The teachers' level of education remained very low as before. Around 1870, after the German teachers' seminary in Warsaw put its pupils at the disposal of the German elementary schools, the state of the elementary schools slowly began to rise. Even so, in 1898 the cantorate schools made up 74 in a hundred of all German schools.

| Year | Number of German elementary schools and cantorates |
|---|---|
| 1797 | 15 |
| 1865 | 42 |
| 1898 | 37 |
| 1919 | 45 |
| 1925 | 24 |

The large number of inhabitants of the single German villages helped to keep the schools going.

Churches

The mother congregation of the Kalisz country is that of Władysławow, founded in 1776. The first pastor, Martin Marggraf, travelled from Władysławow not only through the Kalisz country but through almost the whole of Kuyavia. Four years later the parish of Stawiszyn was founded. In 1795 the Lutherans of Kalisz asked the town authorities to appoint an Evangelical preacher. Pastor Karl Michael Sinell, who took up the office in the same year, became the real founder of the congregation. In Prussian times the congregation of Grodziec arose, with the lively part of the lord of the manor, Count Stadnicki. The first pastor, D. Bergmann, came from Fraustadt. In Prażuchy, which Pastor Grimm of Stawiszyn had served until then, a parish of its own arose in 1808 with the active help of the lord of the manor, Celiński, owner of the lordship of Ceków. In Iwanowice the estate owner Wężyk founded an Evangelical congregation in 1808. In 1818, since lightning had burnt down the church in Iwanowice, it was moved to Sobiesęki. In the weavers' town of Turek a branch was founded in 1827, followed in 1845 by an independent congregation. That the great landowners took a direct part in the founding of four Evangelical congregations shows how important the German settlers in town and country were to the Polish nobility.

breyer1935mutterland/2:
The Polish researcher H. Wiercieński, in a treatise on German immigration devoted to the Germans of Congress Poland, says the following:

> "The German settlements on Polish soil are as old as Poland itself. Numerous names of places and castles bear witness to this; the history of the country, too, and that of many Polish families speaks of it. The German settlers were bound to the native economic circles by common economic interests. Marriage strengthened the mutual relationship. From this the adopted homeland gained many deserving citizens, who often stood out from the sameness of the mass of the people and who knew how to win names of historical importance for themselves and their descendants. To this day we find many bearers of German names among the outstanding minds of the country."

Over the centuries German people streamed continually, with greater or lesser interruptions, into the lands beyond the Oder. Dr. Lück, in his epoch-making work "Deutsche Aufbaukräfte in der Entwicklung Polens" (German constructive forces in the development of Poland), has shed light on this German question of fate in the East and has often given us quite bitter insights. His research covers the whole territory of the Polish state and all the centuries of the Polish nation's existence as a state. My task is not drawn so wide in space and time. I want to show that the greater part of the Germans who immigrated into central Poland in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries came from the neighbouring eastern provinces of Germany, the old ones and above all West Prussia and Posen, acquired later through the partitions. From there German farmers, craftsmen, teachers, pastors, scholars and artists streamed to the culturally undeveloped lands of the East, to find new places to work here and to do good German work.

 "Ekonomista", year 1908, vol. II
breyer1935mutterland/4:
In what follows, the origin of three groups of the Germans of central Poland, by their station, is to be proved:

> 1. the rural settlers;

> 2. the German burghers and the German craftsmen;

> 3. the Lutheran clergy, the German teachers and the members of the free professions.

The first rural settlement on the soil of central Poland is, to our present knowledge, the Vistula village of Słońsk, founded in 1605 and called Schlonske in the popular speech, not far from the well-known salt-water spa of Ciechocinek. In quick succession a whole series of new foundations followed up the Vistula, such as Alt-Bogpomoż, Lentzen, Neu-Bogpomoż, Woluszewo. The Polish historian J. Baranowski says in his treatise "Wsie holenderskie na ziemiach polskich" (Dutch villages in the Polish lands):

> "In this way at the beginning of the 17th century both banks between Thorn and Breslau [sic - probably meant is Leslau/Włocławek - JD] were sown with Dutch colonies."

The settlers of these lowland villages, who are also called "Holländer" at Lentzen, at Wolluschewo and so on in the 17th-century church books of the Lutheran congregation at Thorn, came for the greater part from the Vistula villages around Thorn, Kulm, Graudenz and Schwetz. Schmidt says in his "Deutschtum des Landes Posen" (The Germans of the Posen country) that as early as about 1600 numerous Lutheran "Holländer" were settled below and above Thorn, in the villages of Gurske, Nessau, Silno and Dybow, because the strictly orthodox town government of Thorn did not like Mennonites as settlers. The Thorn lowland villages were mostly daughter settlements of the Holländereien (the Dutch-law settlements) lower down the Vistula, which had arisen about the middle of the 16th century. The inmates of the Holländereien were by no means Dutch by stock. In this respect we agree with Schmidt's view that real Dutchmen took part only in the first decades of the clearing of the Danzig Werder. In the course of time the

 The name Schlonske misled some writers of almanacs and newspapers before the war, in a few cases, into the view that the lowland farmers who had moved from Schlonske into other German lowland villages came from Silesia (Schlesien).

 "Przegląd Hist." year 1915, vol. 19, no. 1.
breyer1935mutterland/5:
German farmers of the neighbouring marsh areas also took over the Dutch way of farming. So the name "Holländer" passed to them in the legal and technical sense.

According to the Thorn church books, a small number of settlers from eastern Pomerania, from the neighbourhood of Christenberg, Schifelbein, Kolberg and Latzken, also lived in the new Vistula villages.

A comparison of the present family names with those of the old Thorn church books convinces us of the likeness of the names; a proof that the Vistula Germans have long been settled. Names such as Leuschner, Heise, Milke, Kersten, Gollnig, Moltzahn, Netzel, Kröning, Raths and so on bear witness to this. After 1700 the description "Holländer" disappears from the Thorn church books; it is replaced by farmers' names from Slonske, Woluschewo and so on.

About 1740 settlement in the lowland villages began to quicken. One after another numerous villages arose, up to the mouth of the river Wieprz, 100 km south of Warsaw. Of the origin of these settlers we receive reliable information from the church books of the Lutheran congregations of Gombin, Iłow, Plozk and Neuhof. Most came from the surplus population of the old settlements between Thorn and Wlozlawek. But settlers from the lowland villages below Thorn, Bromberg and Graudenz also took part in the clearing of the Vistula meadows; some even came from East Prussia.

Going through five years of the registers of the congregation of Gombin, founded in 1832, gave 45 statements of origin for the lowland villages. Of these West Prussia had 30, the old Vistula villages of central Poland 15; in detail, the neighbourhood of Thorn 12, Slonske 9, Graudenz 5, Schwetz 4, Bogpomoż and Dembe 3, Bromberg 2, and Fordon, Neuenburg, Straßburg, Riesenburg, Mewe, Mehlsack, Braunsberg and Driesen on the Warthe one family each.

The church books of the Lutheran parish of Iłow, founded in 1775, contain for the period 1779 to 1840 the following 80 places of origin, which we list going up the Vistula: Danzig Werder, Baldrum near Marienwerder, Neuenburg, Montau 1 settler each, Graudenz 4, the Kulm lowland 2, Bromberg, Flötenau 1 each; from Neidenburg, Amt Schoden, Bergbruch, Neuenort, Altretz 1 settler each, Altendorf (3), the neighbourhood of Thorn (11), Nischewke 19, Deutsch-Glinne 9, Slonske 9, Neu-Ciechocinek (2), Woluschewo and Rybit (1), Bogpomoż 5, Witoschiner Lengde, Liciszewo near Lipno 1 family each.
breyer1935mutterland/6:
In the civil registers of the congregation at Neuhof (Nowydwór), which arose in 1780, we find for 1782 to 1806 the following places of origin: Danzig 1, Langenau 6, Bromberg 2, Straßburg in East Prussia 2, the neighbourhood of Rypin 5, the neighbourhood of Thorn 4, Slonske and Rybit 1 each, Bogpomoż and Osieker Lengden 2.

If we sum up the statements on the origin of the German farmers in the Vistula lowland, it follows that 95 in a hundred of the first settlers came from the Vistula country around Thorn and down the Vistula. 5 in a hundred came from the Dobrzyń country (Dobriner Land), related by stock. The Vistula villages that arose after 1750 are mainly daughter settlements; they formed a widely branched, one might say, great family of one stock. Characteristic of the Vistula lowland, too, is the exclusive use of the Thorn and Rogal (Königsberg) hymn books. The Mennonites of our area, whose number has now greatly shrunk, came after 1760 mostly from the lowland south of Thorn.

The German country people of the Dobrzyń country, who began to immigrate about 1700, came from the neighbouring counties of West Prussia, and to a lesser part also of East Prussia. Part of the town population of Lipno and Rypin also came from the Netze district (Netzegau) and from the Reich.

The baptism, marriage and death registers of the congregation of Rypin, 1785 to 1854, give 127 statements of origin: of these Straßburg county 41 or 31 in a hundred, Graudenz county 11 or 8 in a hundred, Thorn county 8 statements, Briesen 7, Marienwerder and Kulm 4 each, Schwetz, Soldau, Bromberg, Osterode, Königsberg 3 each, Mohrungen, Mewe, Rosenberg in West Prussia, Pr.-Holland 2 each, Angerburg, Goldap, Darkehmen, Lyck, Gilgenburg, Kalminnen, Insterburg, Pr.-Eylau, Riesenburg, Johannisburg, Hammerstein, Wohlsin 1 statement each. The townspeople came from Konitz, Tuchel, Filehne, Nakel, Lobsens, Labischin, Schubin; from the Reich came craftsmen from Berlin and Hamburg, 2 each, and from Mühlhausen in Alsace, Stuttgart and Reichenbach in Silesia, 1 each.

The church books of the Lutheran congregation of Lipno in the Dobrzyń country give for the period 1799 to 1815 the following places of origin: Thorn county 5 persons, Mohrungen county 4, the counties of Graudenz, Labischin and Kolmar 2 each, Osterrode, Soldau, Briesen, Schwetz, Schubin and Konitz 1 each; 2 came from Saxony and one craftsman from Silesia to Lipno. Of 26 place names, then, 13 fall to the counties neighbouring the Dobrzyń country, much as in the parish of Rypin.

The dialect of the Dobrzyń country is also spoken in the Vistula lowland, around Danzig and in the western strip of present-day East Prussia. The folklore of the colo-
breyer1935mutterland/7:
nists leans strongly on these areas, and the family names agree too. Finally, here as there the Rogal and in part the Thorn hymn book was in use. Characteristic of the settlement history of the Dobrzyń country is the additional name "Räumungen" (clearings) for most German villages. It is also found in Straßburg county. All these facts speak for it that the Germans of the Dobrzyń country come from neighbouring West Prussia and the western counties of East Prussia.

Research into the origin of the Germans has gone furthest on the Kuyavian lake plateau (Kujawische Seenplatte). This was treated at length in Heft 2 of the "Deutsche Monatshefte in Polen". Therefore only a short summary is to be given here. The dialect, the family names, the Alt-Stettin hymn books and prayer books, the way the houses and barns are built, and the folklore point beyond doubt to eastern Pomerania as the country of origin. The place names from the church books of the Lutheran congregations of Sompolno, Babiak, Koło, Chodecz, Przedecz and Maślaki carry special weight as proof. The 529 places of origin found for the period 1800 to 1860 are divided among the counties of the former province of Posen as follows: Mogilno 129 (27 in a hundred), Strelno 89 (19 in a hundred), Obornik 40 (8.4 in a hundred), Kolmar 24 (5 in a hundred), Witkowo 21 (4.4 in a hundred), Schubin 20 (4.1 in a hundred), Hohensalza 17 (3.6 in a hundred), Posen 15 (3.1 in a hundred), Schroda 13 (2.7 in a hundred), Bromberg 12 (2.5 in a hundred), Znin 10, Wreschen 8, Wirsitz 7, Jarocin, Kempen, Filehne 4 each, Schmiegel, Samter and Adelnau 3 each, Wollstein, Lissa, Krotoschin, Grätz, Pleschen, Neu-Tomischel, Rawitsch, Ostrowo, Fraustadt 2 each, Kosten, Gostin, Czarnikau, Meseritz and Samotschin 1 place name each. By stock, 90 in a hundred fall to the Pomeranians, 10 in a hundred to the Silesians. This proportion shifts still further in favour of the Pomeranians if we add the rural, and in part urban, settlers who came directly from eastern Pomerania. From Jastrow came 3, and 1 settler each from: Berlinchen, Pasewalk, Alt-Stettin, Flatau, Damlug in Pomerania, Stolp in Pomerania, Bublitz, Saba in Pomerania, Alt-Glebsow, Neugardt, Sandow, Gollnow, Hammerstein; further, one each from Tiefenau in Old Prussia, Perleberg in the Prignitz, Schwerin on the Warthe, Bachwinkel, Altstadt, Stieglitz near Grünfier and from Schneidemühl.

Into the Kalisz country (Kalischer Land) the Germans immigrated from the areas around Neutomischel, Kirchplatz Boruj, Grätz and the western Warthe marshes [Wartebruch]. Once again the

 These findings agree, happily, with the map of the Posen Holländereien drawn by Dr. Maas in the special issue for the fiftieth anniversary.
breyer1935mutterland/8:
Silesian dialect, the way of farming (the growing of hops), the customs, the dress, the way the houses are built, the hymn books, mostly of Züllichau and Breslau, and the family names give a convincing pointer to Lower Silesia, in part to the Warthe marshes [Wartebruch]. Special importance in this case, too, falls to the registers of the Lutheran congregations of Zagorow, Grodziec, Stawiszyn, Turek and Władysławow, which contain statements of origin, though not always in the number one would wish. Some of the writers of the church books gave no information at all on the place of origin for years. Sometimes, too, in the death entries, the relatives did not know the place of birth; this was mostly the case with retired farmers (Ausgedinger).

Going through the marriage and death registers of the congregation of Zagorow from 1843 to 1847 gave 18 place names, divided as follows: Wollstein county 1, the western Warthe marshes, Lower Silesia 1, the Silesian dialect area west of Posen, in Posen county, 2; the Netze marshes 2, the counties east of Posen 2, from the rest of the Reich 5.

From the church books of the Lutheran congregation of Grodziec we take for the period 1797 to 1826 137 place names: the neighbourhood of Neutomischel county 36, Meseritz 3, Wollstein 5; the western Warthe marshes 20, the Oder marshes 3; Lower Silesia 18, the Silesian dialect area in Posen county 16, the Pomeranian dialect area in the same county 8, the Netze district 15, Pomerania 8, the rest of the Reich 5.

For the colonists of the congregation of Stawischin we found for the period 1780 to 1830 70 statements of place; of these Neutomischel county had 16, Meseritz 1, Wollstein 3; Lower Silesia 7, the Silesian dialect area in Posen county 5, the Pomeranian one in the same county 5; the western Warthe marshes 17, the Netze district 8, the rest of the Reich 8.

The church books of the congregation of Turek supply for 1837 to 1847 42 statements of place: Neutomischel county 6, Lower Silesia 14, Silesian dialect areas in Posen county 3, the Pomeranian area east of Posen 7, the Netze marshes 10, the Reich 2.

For Władysławow, the mother congregation of the Kalisz country, we found for 1775 to 1800 the following 15 statements of place: Neutomischel county 2, Lower Silesia 5, the Silesian dialect area in Posen county 3, the eastern, Pomeranian part of the same county 2, the Netze marshes 1, from Pomerania 2.
breyer1935mutterland/9:
If we sum up the statements of origin for the Kalisz country, we obtain the following distribution: Silesians 54 in a hundred, Pomeranians 21 in a hundred, people of the Mark (Brandenburg) 12 in a hundred; to the rest of the Reich fall 10 in a hundred.

This provisional reckoning is unfair to the Silesians in so far as the statements of the congregations of Prażuchy and Sobiesęki near Kalisch are still missing; they are inhabited almost exclusively by Silesian farmers. The strong showing of the Pomeranians and the people of the Mark comes from the fact that our reckoning took in mainly the northern congregations, neighbouring the Pomeranian dialect. It is natural to suppose that in the parishes lying further south the number of Pomeranians and people of the Mark will be comparatively small.

With few exceptions all the German villages of the Łódź industrial area are daughter settlements, mainly of the German colonies on the Kuyavian lake plateau and in the Kalisz country. On the whole, in the Łódź area the two stocks of the Silesians and the Pomeranians balance each other. The Swabian villages make up a certain percentage only in the neighbourhood of Łódź and in the Gostynin country. In the Gostynin country, about 1800, the wholesale merchant v. Treskow settled farmers from the western Warthe marshes, from the neighbourhood of Landsberg on the Warthe and from Driesen on his extensive woods, as we have been able to establish from the Gostynin church books.

In conclusion we state: the German rural population in central Poland comes in each case from the German areas neighbouring it to the west. In the great majority the German villages of central Poland are daughter settlements of the mother provinces of Silesia, Posen, West and East Prussia. This finding also holds for the German farmers of the Chełm and Lublin country, and likewise of Volhynia. For the settlers of these areas come, with few exceptions, from the German districts (Gaue) of central Poland. They moved away from here between 1855 and 1885; many thousands of colonists from central Poland found their way overseas after 1890.

The urban Germans of central Poland look back on a history of a good 200 years. The immigrants of the 18th century, it is true, as shows most starkly in Warsaw, were lost in the host people; only small groups have kept their nationality (Volkstum), for example in the town of Władysławów, founded in 1738. As everywhere, the urban Germans who arose from single immigrants have here too a far smaller national (völkisch) power of resistance than the German farmers settled together. In the time of the Polish kings of the
breyer1935mutterland/10:
Saxon house, many officials, craftsmen and soldiers came from Saxony to Warsaw. The Treaty of Warsaw of 1768, which guaranteed freedom of belief to the Dissenters, brought a stronger stream of German craftsmen and members of the free professions. In 1781 the splendid Lutheran church in Warsaw was consecrated. Among the Germans of that time many came from the neighbouring Prussian areas. It would go beyond the bounds of a short lecture to list all the names. Some outstanding representatives shall nonetheless be named. The well-known coach-maker Thomas Michael Dangel, raised to the Polish nobility in 1792, came from Pasewalk in Pomerania. The outstanding Warsaw architect Ephraim von Schröger was born in Thorn; he too was ennobled, in 1775. Another important architect, Theodor Gottlieb Seyfried, was born in Buk near Posen. Of the forebears of the leading Polish booksellers' firm Gebethner and Wolff, Gebethner came in 1727 from Krotoschin and Wolff from Brätz. The family of the well-known Warsaw wholesale merchant Herse comes from Schwiebus. About 1776 the forebears of the Warsaw factory owners Schlenker came from Thorn. The dyer Werner in Warsaw, whose descendants now own extensive landed estates [Goßgrundbesitz] in the neighbourhood of Łęczyca, came from Obersitzko. The list could, as I said, be continued at will.

Let us now turn to the urban Germans who arose from settlement in closed groups. The second German town settlement after Władysławów, which the Germans called Rostarschütz, is the small craftsmen's town of Neuhof, laid out in 1782 by the Archbishop of Gniezno. According to the church books of the local Lutheran congregation, the cloth-makers came from Schwersenz, Czarnikau, Schönlanke, Bütow in Pomerania, Braunsberg [Brausnsberg] in Silesia, Fraustadt, Neudamm and Gilgenburg in East Prussia. The stocking-knitters, shoemakers, locksmiths and tailors came from Sonnenburg, Jastrow, Pasewalk, Johannisburg in East Prussia, Löbau, Thorn, Straßburg in West Prussia, Bischofswerder and from Ohlau in Silesia, all of them, then, from the neighbouring Prussian provinces.

When, by the second and third partitions of Poland, considerable territories of the Polish Republic fell to Prussia, German craftsmen and merchants streamed into the depopulated Polish towns together with the Prussian officials. A fine example of this is the voivodeship town of Kalisch, which had fallen victim to a terrible fire in 1793. The first concern of the Prussian authorities was the rebuilding of the town, which lay well placed for trade and administration. From the neighbouring areas of Silesia numerous building craftsmen immigrated, who within a few years raised the town out of rubble and
breyer1935mutterland/11:
ruins. As early as 1795 the Prussian authorities installed the first Lutheran preacher, Karl Michael Christian Sinell, from Stolzenhagen in Pomerania. From his entries of the couples married in the period 1795 to 1815 we take the following places of origin: of 298, the Silesian dialect area has 192, the Pomeranian dialect area 36, East Prussia 14, the rest of the Reich 36. That gives 69.3 per cent Silesians, 13 per cent Pomeranians, 5 per cent East Prussians and 13 per cent from the rest of the Reich. Among the Silesian towns Zduny stands first with 30 immigrants; there follow Breslau with 14, Ostrowo 12, Groß-Wartenberg 11, Rawitsch and Militsch 7 each, Kempen, Suhlau and Namslau 5, Festenberg, Krotoschin, Guhrau and Oels 4. From Bromberg came 8 persons, from Saxony 20, from Württemberg 8. By trade there were: bakers 17, joiners and masons 15 each, tailors 12, carpenters 9, hatters and shoemakers 8 each, windmillers and coachmen 6 each, merchants 5, saddlers and butchers 4 each, doctors, teachers, printers and soap-boilers 3 each, hairdressers, glaziers, girdlers, rope-makers, innkeepers, turners, confectioners, gardeners, wheelwrights and coopers 2 each. Of trades certainly new to the town life of that time may be named: a maker of sealing wax, a glove-maker, a stuff-maker, a fulling-miller, a maker of musical instruments, a bookbinder, a dyer, a furrier.

If the border town of Kalisch naturally received the strongest increase of German settlers from the neighbouring Silesian areas, at the county town of Gostynin, in the north of Congress Poland on the left bank of the Vistula, we find above all an inflow from the neighbouring Low German area. Here cloth-makers were settled from 1821 to 1828. Beside the old town a new cloth-makers' settlement grew up. On the strength of the notes of origin in the church books of the Lutheran congregation at Gostynin for the period 1825 to 1850, and of the records in the happily preserved guild books of the German cloth-makers' guild, it follows: of 88 statements of place, 68 or 78 in a hundred fall to the Netze district, the remaining 22 in a hundred to the Silesian areas. From the separate cloth-making towns of the Netze district there came: Radolin 15, Samotschin 13, Labischin 11, Schönlanke 9, neighbouring Jastrow 7, Margonin 4, Zielenzig 4, Lobsens and Rogasen 3 each, Wirsitz, Althütte, Kolmar, Ritschenwalde 1 each. From Bojanowo, Rawitsch, Breslau, Schwiebus, Schwersentz, Palmburg, Neudeck, Landeck and Schulitz came one cloth-maker each. In the first German cloth-makers' town in central Poland, in Dombie, 61 per cent of the cloth-makers came from the Netze district, 39 per cent from Silesia.

The statements on the origin of the cloth-makers in Zgierz, Alexandrow and Blendow are in my contribution to Lück's book "Die Aufbaukräfte". The en-
breyer1935mutterland/12:
tries in the church books of the congregations of Zduńska Wola, Konstantynow, Brzeziny and Pabjanice give, on the whole, the same picture. In the northern towns of central Poland the cloth-makers from the Netze district are in the majority, in those lying further south those from Silesia. On the strength of the 685 place names gathered so far, the statements from Ozorkow and in part from Tomaschow being unfortunately still missing, it follows that 66 in a hundred of the immigrant cloth-makers came from Silesia and 34 in a hundred from the Netze district.

With the cloth-makers, German craftsmen of every kind also appeared in the newly laid-out cloth-making towns. Manifold personal and economic ties meant that they left their old home towns at the same time and sought new places of work together.

In the time that followed a strong regrouping took place in some cloth-making towns. Many have lost all their inhabitants by migration to the great industrial centres of the Łódź area, such as Dombie, Przedecz, Chodecz and Poddębice. The surrounding German villages, too, gave up their surplus population to the rising industrial towns. Their make-up by stock was thereby hardly changed much, since west and south of Łódź, Pabjanice and Zgierz the village population is mainly Silesian, while east of Łódź and south of Ozorkow live farmers of Pomeranian stock. New elements among the urban Germans are the proletarianised Swabians, who immigrated from the colonies founded in the Prussian period and in the decades after. Some towns, especially Tomaschow and Łódź, also have immigrants from Bielitz and Biala, mostly cloth-makers and weavers. So the Tomaschow cloth manufacturer Piesch is a man of Bielitz, and others.

Now something more about the origin of the Lutheran clergy in central Poland. The first German Lutheran congregation in central Poland is Wengrow, founded in 1650 by Prince Radziwiłł, who was himself a Protestant. A series of pastors from Greater Poland, such as Tyräus, Rosentreter, Bachstrom, served this congregation, lying lonely and much cut off, in the first century of its existence.

After the death of the first pastor of the newly founded Warsaw congregation, Johann Jakob Scheidemantel, a Silesian by birth, Pastor Gottlieb Ringeltaube was elected; he came from Gramtschen near Thorn, where his father was the Lutheran preacher. The afternoon preacher Friedrich Cerulli, whom the congregation had elected in 1779, came from Königsberg.
breyer1935mutterland/13:
Particular credit for the growth of the Lutheran congregation of Warsaw was earned by Pastor Karl Heinrich Wilhelm Schmidt, in office from 1790 to 1813, who was born in Karge. For many years he was guardian of the German Lutheran school in Warsaw and president of the Consistory. His greatest merit, however, is that in 1803 he published the first hymn book for the Lutheran church in the Kingdom of Poland, whose improved edition appeared only 40 years later. From the Polish national hero Th. Kościuszko Pastor Schmidt received a letter in his own hand for exemplary care of the sick and truly patriotic feeling, which he had shown in the war year 1795.

The later superintendent and pastor of the Warsaw congregation, Karl Lauber, whom the South Prussian consistory installed as preacher in 1803, came from Schmiegel; he was the eldest son of the pastor there. The first pastor of the congregation of Michalke, founded in 1779, Albert Bocianowski, was born in Lötzen in East Prussia. The first pastor of the congregation of Neuhof, founded in 1775, Gottfried Leske, came from Rastenburg in East Prussia; he was also active as a writer. The pastor of the congregation of Stawischin, Karl Callmann, was born in Bojanowo and died in Stawischin in 1794.

In the Prussian period eleven new Lutheran congregations arose in central Poland. In the mother congregation of the Vistula lowland, in Iłow, Pastor Wittold, born in Schadewalde near Marienburg, held office. In the congregation of Grodziec [Grodzierc] the first pastor, Bergemann, came from Fraustadt, where his father was a cloth manufacturer. Pastor Herzberg in Kalisch came from Schweidnitz. Pastor Grimm in Stawiszyn was born in Großstrelitz in Silesia.

In the time of the Duchy of Warsaw there immigrated: Pastor Gieser in Babiak, born at Wronke; Pastor Hewelke, later superintendent of the Płock diocese, an uncommonly able organiser of the parishes under him. On his gravestone is to be read:

> "Death is not death, only the ennobling of mortal nature. Resting place of Johann Karl Hewelke, pastor of the Lutheran congregation at Plozk, superintendent of the Plozk diocese, born at Thorn in the year 1771, died at Plozk 1836."

The long-serving pastor and president of the Reformed consistory in Warsaw, the court preacher Karl Diehl, was born in Lissa in 1765. The deserving pastor of Władysławów, the mother congregation in the Kalisz country, Karl Gottlieb Bartsch, who held office in that congregation from 1810 to 1852, came from Michelsdorf in Silesia.
breyer1935mutterland/14:
The immigration of German Lutheran cloth-makers, weavers and other "Professionisten" (tradesmen) between 1818 and 1828, which led to the founding of eleven Lutheran parishes, also brought a number of Lutheran clergymen into the country, in most cases young candidates of theology. Of the pastors appointed at that time, seven called the Silesian lands of their stock their home: Pastor Benni from Lissa, whose descendants were well-known linguists, Biedermann from Zduny, Gerbling and Rother from Breslau, Hayn from Oels, Rüdiger from Schawone and Sachs from Rawitsch. The fathers of some were cloth-makers. Pastors Modl, Berkau and Jaeckel were from Posen, Thorn and Filehne respectively. Of the pastors who came into the country after 1830: Stiller from Rawitsch [Rawisch], a cloth-maker's son, Wilhelm from Birnbaum, a pastor's son, Jeute from Bojanowo, a cloth-maker's son, Kattein from Beuthen, a burgher's son, Hinz from Wilhelmsburg in East Prussia, where his father was superintendent, Sray from Postelwitz in Silesia. After 1840 these were newly appointed: Pastor Häßner, born in Hermersdorf near Görlitz, Jarnecki from Klein-Ellgut near Oels; Cotta from Winzig in Silesia; Modl from Herrnstadt in Silesia; Menzmann from Langenau in Prussia; Kruschwitz from Jaulitz in Lusatia. Pastor Lemon was born in Posen, the son of a privy councillor; he is the last in time of the pastors who immigrated into Poland from the neighbouring Prussian areas. He worked in Ozorkow from 1880 to 1910.

After 1850 sons of the native German burghers and craftsmen were already choosing to study theology. In the last decades of the past century the Russian government made insuperable difficulties over confirming foreign pastors. In the Warsaw Lutheran consistorial district there was a great shortage of clergymen before the World War, which can be regarded as remedied only today, now that the Warsaw theological faculty has been working at full stretch.

In sum we state that in the period 1780 to 1850 41 pastors immigrated into central Poland from Silesia and the Posen country. If we add the pastors whose fathers came into the country as Prussian officials, namely Schwarz, Hermes, Lembke and Börner, the number comes to 45. To these brave German Lutheran men the founding and building up of the Lutheran church and school system is owed without reserve. This, unfortunately, is all too often knowingly passed over in silence by the present Lutheran clergy.
breyer1935mutterland/15:
Beside the clergyman, German elementary schoolteachers came into the newly arisen towns and villages, for the greater part from the neighbouring German provinces. Numerous school lists in the church archives bear witness to this.

After 1870 the stream of teachers from Germany ebbed away completely, since in 1866 the Russian authorities in Warsaw had opened a teachers' seminary, German at first and completely Russified after a few years.

It should not go unmentioned that the creator of the Polish dictionary, Samuel Gottlieb Linde, for many years director of the Royal Lyceum at Warsaw, founded by the Prussian authorities in 1805 as a model school, was born in Thorn in 1771. The music teacher of the well-known Polish composer Moniuszko was Joseph Xawer Elsner, born in Grottkau in Silesia. The outstanding Warsaw doctor Aug. Ferdin. Wolff, for whose fiftieth year of service the Polish doctors' association had a medal struck, was born in Lissa in 1768. Similar examples are listed in numbers in Lück's book.

With that I am at the end of my report. It is a first attempt to work new ground in scholarship. A great part of the work, admittedly, remains to be done. On the strength of what has been done so far, it may be estimated that of the 325,000 Germans in central Poland, the 20,000 of the Chełm and Lublin country and the 50,000 of Volhynia, at least 85 in a hundred immigrated over a good 300 years from the neighbouring Prussian provinces. In the old Polish time these settlers were already Germans abroad (Auslanddeutsche), who had lived for centuries in the western areas of Poland, had faithfully kept their nationality, and kept up schools and churches from their own means.

If the migration of the rural settlers went on quietly, unnoticed and evenly, that cannot be said of the immigration of the cloth-makers. The removal of 10,000 families to Congress Poland was a terrible bloodletting for the German border areas, from which they have hardly been able to recover. The empty houses in the former cloth-making towns had to be pulled down by order of the police, in Rawitsch for example some 55, as H. Barten reports in his work "Siedlung in Südwestposen" (Settlement in south-western Posen). But this by the way.

The guiding idea of our work is to establish as exactly as possible the make-up of the Germans by stock. Only this sure foundation makes possible, taking into account the very different colonising abilities, strengths and weaknesses of the individual stocks, a full understanding of the historical development and of the prospects of the Germans of central Poland.

breyer1938/1:
I. Landscape

From the former border town of Peisern to below the archbishop's little town of Uniejow — a stretch of 130 km — some hundred German villages line the valley of the Warthe, some of them on the very edge of its banks. The Berlin-Warsaw glacial valley, at times up to 5 km wide, in which the Warthe rolls its waters sluggishly along its winding course, is varied in its scenery. By the towns of Zagórow and Konin lush green cattle pastures spread out, broken here and there by gleaming sand hills. In general, however, the river meadows form a half-open landscape in which picturesque clumps of alder, willow and poplar prevail, and in places wind-torn pines.

Into the tranquil quiet of the marsh landscape comes no noise of raftsmen, no pounding of steamers. Silently the mirroring waters glide by. Gulls and lapwings now and then bring some life into the dreamy seclusion of these river meadows. It also happens that here and there fishermen glide downstream in a rocking boat, laying out their nets. Mostly hidden in the thickets of alder and willow, as cattle breeders and farmers, the German people of this region lead their quiet yet busy life far from the bustle of the world, but faithful to the ways and manner of life of their fathers and bound to their traditions.

A hundred and eighty years ago the marsh was an impassable region, truly "broken" ground. Between primeval undergrowth and huge oaks and maples lay, by turns, still backwaters thick with marsh and water plants, which in places were beginning to break up into smaller and larger, eerily overgrown pools. Swamp and mire everywhere fought for mastery, where today profitable peat cuttings and lush meadowland spread out, but where even today there are enough "mouldering meadows" ("Moderwiesen"). Then as now, at the spring thaw, turbid floods poured over the glacial valley and made every unevenness of the ground disappear. An all-embracing, boundless realm of water formed, out of which the bare crowns of the huge marsh trees broke helplessly. Gradually the turbid masses of water fell, leaving behind a rich silt, the fertile "Letten", as the present German inhabitant, the "Brücher" (marsh-dweller), or in mockery the "Wasserpatscher" (water-splasher), calls it. For the meadows the spring flood is a welcome manuring. If the spring water is low, the marsh farmer is dissatisfied: his meadows and fields lack the strength to grow in summer. It is the raging floods, too, that are to blame for the large
breyer1938/2:
sand hills and the wide sand fields, and that now bury valuable farmland under sand for many years. For months and years the evil floods give the marsh farmer work of clearing. Cartload after cartload of drift sand is carried off to the swampy spots of the meadows, so that new bread-land may arise. Tough and untiring, the German goes about this honourable work of cultivation. In proud awareness he treads here in the footsteps of his forefathers, who often, in far harder conditions, set foot in this swamp wilderness with courage and resolve to fight.

> "They knew but toil and meagre bread,
> Mire and wasteland breathed fever's death,
> The foul waters welling at the spade
> Their will forced sudden into ditch and drain,
> And ever deeper into the wild drove
> The hoe; slowly the sown field rose..."
> (Maria Kahle)

These proud memories the sight of the neat villages of the Warthe marshes calls up in the ethnic German (volksdeutsch) wanderer. And confident hopes that the strength of the people will last fill him as he comes to know better the splendid German stock of this still, dreamy Warthe landscape.

[Picture: German farmstead in Janow, Koło county]
breyer1938/3:
II. The German Settlements

Like links of a long chain the German villages of the Warthe marshes follow one another. Only by the towns of Konin, Koło and Uniejów are there, strangely, gaps in the settlement, which might be explained by early settlement near the towns. In four large language islands, the Wenglew, Paprot, Politz and Leśnik islands, live some 10,000 Germans, all of them members of the Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confession, belonging to the parishes of Zagórow, Konin, Koło, Władysławow-Rosterschütz and Turek. Living conditions in the German marsh villages may be called satisfactory, it being noted that the villages around Zagórow and Konin are more prosperous than the others. This is caused by the quality of the soil in each place. The Wenglew and in part the Paprot language island have in some places fertile silt soil, here simply called "Lett", on which wheat and clover can be grown. There are also meadows with a good growth of grass. Certainly the fields have their fair share of waste land and sand, or of mouldering, sour meadows, since the quality of the soil is spread like a mosaic over the marsh. The other marsh villages, further up the Warthe, mostly have very sandy soil, which is especially striking in the settlements on the edge of the valley. In the Leśnik language island most meadows bear only a poor growth because their soil is shallow. In dry years this shows strikingly. Everywhere cattle breeding and dairy farming stand first in farming, and in the lower part of the Warthe marshes goose breeding. The cattle graze here in "Koppeln", meadows fenced with willow hurdles. Some holdings consist mostly of meadow, which gives the owner a good income. German farmers from the neighbouring villages of the upland rent sizeable meadows in the marsh every year. The "Brücher" also brings hay to the town market. In some marsh villages bee-keeping is practised too, and here we find without exception "bee skeps" woven of straw, a special form that only German bee-keepers prefer. Among the most widespread side occupations, which for poorer farmers even becomes the main one, is basket-weaving. The basket rods, called "Wieten", grow abundantly on the sandy river islands and on the edges of the "Altwasser" (backwaters) and "Laken" (pools). With the products of basket-weaving, white wickerwork and green-woven baskets, the markets of the marsh towns are
breyer1938/4:
supplied; indeed, large wagonloads are sent even to Łódź and Kalisz. In some German villages live professional fishermen, who fish the Warthe with all sorts of gear and sell their catch in the small towns and the cities. That the "Brücher" are skilful boatmen and boat-builders goes without saying. Most of them, especially the less well-off, "went on the barge" in their young years or took up "Flötterei", that is, timber rafting, travelling long stretches of river, as far as Küstrin and Stettin, and indeed by the Oder to Breslau. Up to the World War the timber trade and the timber industry flourished in the Warthe region. Many found paying work sawing boards and cutting stave wood, just as since the beginnings of the immigration many German beam-hewers and "wood-cutters" were to be found in the forests of the Warthe meadows. In the church books we find signs that around 1830 German boat-builders lived in the Warthe village of Piersk, building Berlin barges and similar craft.

[Picture: Former German school house in Drożynek-Holl., Konin county. It now serves as a prayer house.]

The yield of grain and potatoes is mostly enough for the household's own use. The rich stands of alder and pollard willow give the marsh farmer the fuel he needs, the more so as peat is also cut in many places. In building houses, wood used to prevail, and in places bog iron ore, the "ironstone". Today most new buildings are put up of fired or sand bricks. For the woodwork of houses and barns the abundant poplar is used. Characteristic of the marsh dwellers are the wagon baskets woven of willow rods,
breyer1938/5:
called "Wasung". The well-kept horses are likewise the marsh farmer's pride. Working the loamy soil needs a strong team, and for the farmer himself ploughing is hard work that costs much sweat. So it is said in mockery that a "Brücher" ploughing on the sandy fields of the upland can be known by the loud cursing and swearing with which he means to urge his horses on. Orchards are found only in the rarest cases. The only exception are the sour-cherry gardens, which thrive on the light, shallow soil. In recent years the local authorities have set about regulating the Warthe. In places dikes have been built which keep the neighbouring villages from flooding, so that the "drowning" of the grain fields can now be counted as remedied. On the other hand, some of the "Brücher" are not quite content with the new state of things. The yearly floods, by leaving silt and mud, gave the fields, and the meadows in particular, an abundant manuring.

The most widespread form of settlement in the Warthe marshes is the scattered settlement, in a particularly marked form of its own. Every new settler sought to build his farmstead on the edge of a meadow, from where he could most easily keep watch over the grazing cattle, the "Geziefer". Since on any given area of settlement the pieces of meadow lay jumbled together without order, the holdings had of necessity to stand on the edges of the meadows. In the marsh the edges of the meadows mostly run in a winding line; so a kind of zigzag came about, along which the single holdings were strung. In the marsh villages a village street, mostly straight, serves as the common road, and an access way leads to it from each farmstead. This manner of settlement, which takes account of the natural conditions of the marsh, might be called the marsh-edge village (Bruchranddorf), since it is found only in the swampy ground of the Warthe marshes and in part in the Kalisz country. Besides this predominant form of village we also come upon peculiar line villages lying along the boundary between the river valley and the valley slope. Here the farmsteads turn the house side toward the meadows and pastures, while the barns stretch along the village street. Finally it should be pointed out that, except for the villages of the Wenglew language island and in part of the Paprot language island, the settlements lie out of danger of flooding. So there is no need here to build the houses on
breyer1938/6:
artificially raised mounds (Wurten). The German village of Neu-Czarkow alone is an exception. It happens that in a very high flood the whole field area is covered by the waters, or as the marsh farmer says, "by the bare water", and traffic can be kept up only by boat. The members of the cantorate then come to the service by boat; funerals likewise go by water. All this vividly recalls the roads of the Spreewald. In some respects economic life in the Warthe marshes resembles that of the Vistula lowland. On the whole, however, the Warthe marshes are a landscape rich in peculiarities of their own, which stands out markedly from the area of settlement of central Poland. The "Brücher" are loath to marry up to the "Höhe" (the height), the Silesian or Pomeranian villages on the upland. They cling with all their heart to their green home. It should be stressed that the marsh dwellers of Brandenburg (Mark) stock in particular are distinguished by a sober and straightforward mind. Here we have never found sects, which cannot be said of the Pomeranians in the Leśnik language island. The Pomeranian farmer is more open to religious enthusiasm.

[Picture: German farmhouse in Genowefa, Konin county - Photo: A. Breyer]
breyer1938/7:
III. The History of Settlement

Early Times and the Middle Ages

The valley of the Warthe has always by its nature been hostile to settlement. Even today the Warthe marshes deter a settler "unskilled in water works" from settling there. The floods at the spring thaw, and sometimes at St John's (24 June), do their damage year in, year out, and rob the marsh farmer of his harvest.

In the grey past the river was an important route of communication for the neighbouring regions. The river kept this importance, of course, only in the formerly Prussian territory. In the former Russian partition the wild, untamed river is still, as before, closed to shipping. The fisherman and hunter has since time immemorial pushed into the swampy thicket and found his living there after a fashion. On steep banks he would put up his hut if need be; he also liked to take possession of single islands of higher ground (Werder; ostrowy) rising above the swamp, from which he could go about his hunting. Such dwelling places might be the islands of Spicimierz, Koło, Ochle, Swięte, Ostrów near Sławsk and Ratyń. That these "Kämpen" may have been well settled in prehistoric times appears from the many finds of urn sherds that one comes upon everywhere on these sand hills. In 1855, not far from the village of Powiercie south of Koło, two statues of heathen idols were found in the bed of the Warthe. The names of some islands, such as Swięte, Swięciec, and likewise Modlica and Modla, also speak of heathen places of worship. The place names Grójec and Grodzisko point to refuge forts.

In the following centuries the fertile banks of the valley may have been chosen for villages because of the good meadows beside them. This is true especially of the Warthe villages on the right bank.

Fishing held its place then, as now, as an occupation of its own, as may be seen from the grant of the fishing village of Rybaki west of

 Rawita-Gawroński, Wielkopolskie miasto Koło, Petrikau 1912, p. 5.
breyer1938/8:
Konin to the Cistercian monastery at Lond in 1145. The charters of that time speak of fishermen further, as in the villages of Dobrow and Czarkow, where they say "cum piscatoribus" (with the fishermen). In 1232 a charter of the village of Dobrow noted that fishing and the taking of beaver in the rivers Warthe and Ner were released to the inhabitants ("piscatio et castores in fluviis Wartha et Ner"). Moreover, the riverside villages were obliged to the monastery at Lond "to draw the net in fishing on the Warthe". In the same charter we also read of the wealth of grass of the Warthe marshes; at one place it says: "the rent-paying villages are obliged, at the time of the hay harvest, to bring three cartloads of hay each into the monastery's barns".

In the 12th and 13th centuries Polish provincial princes began to give single Warthe villages to church dignitaries. Thus around 1136 the Archbishop of Gniezno owned the villages of Chełmno, Uniejów, Kwiatków, Dombie and Jankowice, to which Rzuchów, Leszno, Grabina and Szadow were added in 1284. Towards the end of the 13th century the archbishop acquired, in the land between the Warthe and the Ner, the villages of Cechmiany, Grodziska, Orzeszków, Ostrowsko and Zbylczyce. The archbishop's property grew considerably south of the town of Uniejów, where the following villages were acquired or founded: Spicimierz, Wiejszcze, Kościelnica, Zielenin, Ubysław, Lubiszewice, Niemysłów, Boleszczyn, Smólsko and Popów. Downstream he acquired the villages of Skobielice and Trzęśniew, which bordered on his property. All the archbishop's villages together made up a wide property stretching a good 50 km along the course of the Warthe.

The Bishop of Poznań received from the ruling prince the village of Ciążeń in 1251 and Ratyń in 1261. West of the town of Koło lay the only property of the ruling prince, the village of Gozdów, since in 1362 the prince's villages of Bliżna and Nagórna Wieś were incorporated into the newly founded town of Koło. Among the archbishop's possessions a few noble villages are scattered, such as Balin, Białków, Powiercie, Grójec, Wola Podłężna, Daniszew and others.
