chodyla2015/front:
Zbigniew Chodyła

Outline of the Earliest History of the Olęder Settlements in the Pyzdry Forest, 1746 – 1793

Pyzdry 2015
chodyla2015/5:
The Near Unknown

The Pyzdry Forest (Puszcza Pyzdrska) is a large forest complex that owes its name to the fact that nearly one sixth of its area belonged to the town of Pyzdry from 1387 to 1793. The natural boundaries of this geographical region are formed on the west, north and east by the rivers Prosna, Warta and Powa. The southern boundary of the Pyzdry Forest is set by the extent of the continuous woods stretching north of Brudzew, Stawiszyn and Ceków Kolonia. Centuries of agricultural colonisation, which consisted in cutting down the forest, reduced its area considerably. A continuous forest complex of 16,500 ha has nevertheless survived to our day, together with three other complexes close by of 1,100 to 1,400 ha. In their neighbourhood there are, besides, more than 300 smaller woods.

We owe the breaking up of the forest chiefly to the Olęder settlers, who in the eighteenth, but also in the nineteenth century cleared about 50% of its area, creating in the years 1746-1793 alone, that is in less than half a century, 58 settlements with their own churches, schools and cemeteries. These were not colonists settled in the time of the Prussian partition by the Prussian occupying authorities. The Olęder settlers came at the invitation of Polish landowners at the end of the First Commonwealth, migrating to Poland for their bread. Settlers of the Protestant confessions (chiefly the Lutheran), of German and sometimes of Polish nationality, made up the greater part of this movement, but Catholics and Poles took part in it too, in more than a third. Besides settlements whose people were of one confession and one nation there were also settlements mixed in both respects.

After the Second World War, when the descendants of the Protestant German Olęders were expelled, many of these villages were emptied. On land that until recently had been worked intensively, cleared and drained for farming, natural succession set in, and the abandoned meadows turned into marsh. Locally the forest began to be called "the Bieszczady of Greater Poland", a name that sums up the character of the region.

To the north the Pyzdry Forest borders on an area farmed just as extensively, the valley of the Middle Warta, protected within the Nadwarciański Landscape Park, which includes two areas of the NATURA 2000 network. Together the two regions form an area with a clear
chodyla2015/6:
geographical, natural and cultural unity that sets it apart from the more urbanised areas around it. Its geographical and cultural unity is made by clear boundaries shaped by nature and by the Olęder landscape, a mosaic of woods, fields and meadows with lone farmsteads scattered among them and set into the landscape. Its natural unity comes from the large share of woodland and the great quantity of extensively used fields and meadows. There are many marshy wilds and high dunes within the woods, but also corners of villages full of colour, warmth and quiet. In the frequent floods the Warta valley turns into a vast expanse of water, a refuge of wetland birds of European importance. The cultural unity that sets the whole area apart from its neighbours is made above all by the rich heritage of Olęder architecture. Many inhabited traditional farmsteads, found elsewhere only in open-air museums, have survived to our day. A particular feature are the "houses of iron", that is, houses built of bog iron ore. The forest has the largest number in Poland of buildings built of this interesting material. Architectural surveys made in 2009 made it possible to pick out the common features of the building here. This is the basis for gradually defining a style of architecture of its own, which will lastingly and favourably distinguish this region in Poland and in the world. The isolation of the forest from the surrounding areas favoured the survival of old trades and ways of farming. The old crafts are represented by the potter's workshop in Czarny Bród, the only one in Greater Poland. Old ways of animal husbandry and the customs that go with them are also kept up to this day, such as the free grazing of the geese of Zagórów and the meadow communities in the Warta valley, unchanged since 1864.

The unity of the area, and at the same time its difference from the neighbouring areas, was noticed by local volunteers, gathered chiefly in the Cultural Society "Echo Pyzdr". In 2009 the long-forgotten name "Puszcza Pyzdrska" was restored. Thanks to grants won in competitions for non-governmental organisations, the first research in history on the cultural heritage of the area (architecture, design), which had until then seemed uninteresting, was begun. Its results were very fruitful and were partly presented in public, among other places in the Ethnographic Museum in Poznań, at the exhibition "Puszcza Pyzdrska. Olędrzy i ich domy z żelaza" (The Pyzdry Forest. The Olęders and their houses of iron). Workshops in old building techniques were held, teaching materials were prepared for teachers and teachers were trained in using them in lessons, and the first tourist map of the forest was made and published, with the publication "Puszcza Pyzdrska – olęderskie dziedzictwo" (The Pyzdry Forest – the Olęder heritage). In 2013 the first tourist guide to the Pyzdry Forest was prepared and published, and together with the map it received a distinction at the Tour Salon tourism fair in Poznań. A demonstration outcrop of bog iron ore at Wierzchy was opened, and the building of stops – museums was begun. In 2014 the first documentary film about the people of the Pyzdry Forest, "Ludzie z żelaznych domów" (People of the houses of iron), was made. Those who revived the name "Puszcza Pyzdrska" realised the size of what they had set in motion. The forest turned out to cover, as a reasonably compact area, 15 and in a wider
chodyla2015/7:
sense even 17 communes in 6 districts, which until then had practically not worked together. To meet this challenge the Local Tourist Organisation "Puszcza Pyzdrska" was founded as early as 2012, a coalition of all the local forces and authorities with an interest in building the identity and the tourist potential of this large area. The Board of the Landscape Parks of the Greater Poland Voivodeship also took an active part in the revival of the Pyzdry Forest. Since 2014 the two institutions have together been carrying out the plan of an Ecomuseum of the Warta Valley and the Pyzdry Forest. Its purpose is to protect the natural, cultural and landscape values of the Nadwarciański Landscape Park and the Pyzdry Forest, treated as one region, and to make them accessible to residents and visitors. The Ecomuseum is a museum without staff, walls or display cases. It is a network of sites scattered across the land, which together form a collection showing the attractions of the region. It takes in monuments, valuable natural sites, traditional farmsteads, craft workshops and pieces of tourist infrastructure. By an Ecomuseum is meant an active, not a passive, way of saving the whole natural, cultural and landscape heritage, as three inseparable parts.

The publication "Zarys najstarszych dziejów osad olęderskich w Puszczy Pyzdrskiej (1746-1793)" by Dr Zbigniew Chodyła fits perfectly into the educational work carried on among the inhabitants of the Ecomuseum. It is the first publication on the history of the founding and the workings of the 58 Olęder villages of the Pyzdry Forest, based chiefly on archival material not known until now. This and other educational work will aim to strengthen among the people of the forest a sense of pride in living in a remarkable region, and this will make them more responsible for the state of the local heritage. The goal is an attractive tourist product centred on outstanding natural attractions (the unregulated river Warta, rare species of birds, the natural landscape, traditional farming) and cultural ones (old settlements, archaeological sites, "ghost" places, a style of architecture of its own, folklore, battlefields, cemeteries, regional shops and cooking) found within one geographically coherent area. All these attractions must be well described and marked on the ground and attractively promoted. But it is not worth waiting until the Ecomuseum is fully realised. I invite you now to immerse yourselves in the Pyzdry Forest. Following the trail of the Olęders by bicycle, we will discover a world full of secrets, until recently condemned to oblivion. We will come across abandoned fields and farmsteads, or only traces of them, such as old pear trees, chestnuts or lilac bushes. In secluded places we will come upon mysterious Protestant cemeteries. Paddling a canoe down the Warta or the Prosna we can admire the beauty of these rivers and the richness of their plants and animals.

President of the Local Tourist Organisation "Puszcza Pyzdrska"
chodyla2015/8:
Ladies and Gentlemen!

It is with great pleasure that we hand you a publication on the earliest history of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest. The forest, running through the communes of the District of Kalisz – Blizanów, Stawiszyn, Mycielin and Ceków Kolonia – is threaded with field tracks and canals, with dunes overgrown by woods, and with clearings cut long ago by the first settlers. We are sure that the beauty of this land and the hospitality of its people will stay in the memory of everyone who decides to visit us.

Caring for the heritage of our ancestors, we are also undertaking a number of measures for the development and the future of the district. The Kalisz land is a region open to new economic ventures and to cooperation with potential investors. All this, together with its many assets in culture and tourism, means that our district is ready for further development in many areas of life.

We warmly invite everyone to read this book and to visit the District of Kalisz. We hope that after a first visit you will want to come back to us many times.

Krzysztof Nosal, Starost of the District of Kalisz
chodyla2015/9:
Introduction

One of the most important types of rural rent-paying settlement in the Polish lands in the years 1547-1864 was Olęder settlement, which took its name from its pioneers, the Dutch, called in Old Polish olędrzy, olendrzy or holędrzy. What decided its nature, however, was not the settlers' ethnic origin, the kind of land (wet or dry) or the way it was taken in (by draining or by clearing), but the Dutch or Olęder law, brought by the Dutch and applied by those who came after them, chiefly Germans and Poles, together with the economic function carried out under it: for the most part, taking in land that was hard to bring into use, farming the land in one piece, and a large place for stock-raising. Under this law the Olęders, holędrzy, so called even when they were no longer of Dutch nationality, were personally free and held their land by emphyteusis: at first a lease for many years, a long term, and later (especially in Greater Poland) a perpetual lease, a perpetual rent tenure for what was called entry money (okupne), with the right to pass the farm on to their heirs or to sell it after informing the owner of the land. When the free years allowed for setting up the farm had run out, they owed the feudal lord only rents (in money and in kind) and, to a very limited extent (though not always), labour. They had a limited freedom of the land, answered jointly, as a whole commune, for meeting their obligations to the lord on time, had an elected commune self-government, which among other things saw to it that these obligations were met, and kept a limited judicial freedom, being subject to their own village court and only partly (in criminal cases and on appeal) to the lord's jurisdiction. They paid, besides, dues to the Catholic Church and taxes to the state, as a rule had freedom of trade, and enjoyed freedom of religion and the right to found their own schools, which were most often also houses of prayer. Of these principles it was above all the collective solidarity of the Olęder commune towards the lord, which guaranteed him a sure and steady income (especially from the money rents), the equality of rights and the mutual help of neighbours within the commune that followed from it, and the particular organisation and functions of the village (commune) self-government that

made up the legal distinctness and the greater attraction of Olęder settlement compared with other forms of colonisation under German law, such as settlement under a sołtys (village mayor), in which the settlers received their holdings (farms) for perpetual use, but not, like the Olęders, on the strength of foundation contracts made with the whole commune: by individual charters.

According to research so far, at least about 1,700 Olęder settlements in all were founded in the years 1547-1864 in the lands of the First Commonwealth and, after 1795, in the lands of its three partitions, at least 350 of them with an exclusive or partial share of ethnic Dutch of the Mennonite confession and their descendants, some of them by then turned Lutheran. At least about 925 of these settlements arose in Greater Poland proper, which in the Old Polish period consisted of two voivodeships, of Poznań and of Kalisz, and from 1768, after a third voivodeship, that of Gniezno, was formed from part of the second, of three such administrative units. In the years 1597-1793 alone, that is from the year the oldest settlement was founded until the whole of Greater Poland proper had been brought within the borders of Prussia in the Second Partition of Poland, 758 Olęder settlements in the wider sense were created in 8 of its 10 districts (Poznań, Kościan, Kalisz, Konin, Nakło, Pyzdry, Gniezno and Kcynia), at least 711 of them (with 8 ephemeral ones) certain, 22 of a transitional type and 25 whose legal and constitutional character is unclearly documented in the sources.  The certain settlements had a sure legal and constitutional character, confirmed in the sources, and above all in their foundation charters, issued to whole communes. The transitional settlements, whose legal constitution is not quite certain, could develop towards settlements that were certainly Olęder, or towards sołtys or emphyteutic ones. The settlements whose legal status is unclearly stated in the sources had an elected self-government or a sołtys appointed by the lord, but did not always keep complete equality and solidarity towards the lord, and, besides, because of the sometimes small number of hearths – farms (2-3) – and of inhabitants, they raise the doubt whether an Olęder self-government could have been organised and could have worked in them. Since, however, 1) before and in the years 1789-1793, and later, they were very consistently described as olędry and showed other secondary features of Olęder settlements, 2) they were probably for the most part tied administratively and judicially to larger Olęder settlements or formed communes of two or more villages, and 3) by the end of the eighteenth century and the first quarter of the nineteenth they had grown, and their legal status had on the whole probably settled, and most often they had gained a separate administrative and judicial organisation, we count them as such.

In the Greater Poland region they were inhabited by people who had come in: Dutch of the Mennonite confession and their descendants (in about 0.8%); in the great majority (about 54%) by Protestants who had come in, chiefly Lutheran, with relatively few Reformed, chiefly ethnic Germans, though in part also Poles); and in a large percentage (about 38%) by Catholic, Polish people, and in part also by people mixed in confession and ethnicity, that is Protestant-Catholic and German-Polish (in about 7.2%).

An area of Greater Poland in which Olęder settlement also developed fairly vigorously in the eighteenth century was the Pyzdry (or Pyzderska) Forest, from the early Middle Ages to the present day one of the still fairly large forest complexes, which has kept the features of a natural landscape to a considerable degree. It lay and lies, broadly, on the west, east and north between stretches of the river Warta and its tributaries, the Prosna and the Powa, and on the south it reaches a line running roughly through the places Brudzewek, Brudzew, Lipe, Jarantów, Stawiszyn, Ceków Kolonia, Zbiersk, Mycielin, Stropieszyn, Kosmów, Ceków Kolonia, Przespolew Kościelny, Poroże, Smaszew, Gadów, Nowy Świat, Lisiec Nowy and Kowalewek, which partly follows the course of small streams flowing into the Prosna, the Czarna Struga and the Powa, tributaries of the Warta.

This forest area, a part of which has now been set apart as the Nadwarciański Landscape Park (which takes in a part of the Pyzdry Forest in its southern part, but also land north of the Warta), measured, as it stood in the middle of the eighteenth century, about 44,000 ha, that is 440 km². Of this, more than 7,000 ha belonged to the town of Pyzdry. In the Pyzdry Forest the watersheds, the sandy soils and the dunes were the most heavily wooded. Pine predominated among the trees, with some birch, and on wet ground oak and alder. Along the western edge of the forest, parallel to the Prosna, ran the road from Kalisz through Pyzdry to Poznań and Gniezno, and its eastern edge was served by the route joining Kalisz and Kruszwica through Konin. The middle of the forest was crossed by the Stawiszyn-Lądek road along the Czarna Struga, from which above all the economic penetration was made, by settlement going deep into the Pyzdry Forest and gradually reducing its area. This settlement went on in several phases: in the Middle Ages (twelfth/thirteenth to fifteenth century), in early modern times (1501-1793), in modern times (1794/1796-1918), in recent times (to 1945) and in the present, up to today, and within them in several periods. Its growth or its halting were tied to the booms and slumps of social and economic life, deepened by political events, by wars (above all the Swedish "Deluge" (1655-1659/60), the Great Northern War (1700-1721), and the First and Second World Wars) and by natural disasters, among them above all epidemics. The shrinking of the network of settlements was also furthered by the extensive system of farming then in general use, the communal three-field system, which exhausted the soil and produced what are called settlement deserts, that is, the disappearance of settlements as they

The decline in the number of settlements was overcome gradually, on a wider scale, only from the 1720s, by the founding of rent-paying settlements, which from the second half of the 1740s were founded above all under Olęder law. As a result the number of places grew, in absolute and in relative terms, through the founding of entirely new villages and hamlets on what was called raw root (surowy korzeń, untouched land) and through the rebuilding of old ones, but on other legal terms and mostly with new inhabitants.

In following the development of the earliest settlement, Olęder settlement included, in the Pyzdry Forest on the basis of Old Polish sources, one has to remember that, in the old administrative divisions, its area lay within a single voivodeship, that of Kalisz, but within three of its districts, namely those of Pyzdry, Konin and Kalisz. Today the area of the Pyzdry Forest lies within a single voivodeship, that of Greater Poland, six districts (Kalisz, Konin, Pleszew, Słupca, Turek and Września) and fifteen communes: Blizanów, Ceków-Kolonia, Chocz, Gizałki, Grodziec, Lądek, Malanów, Mycielin, Pyzdry, Rychwał, Rzgów, Stare Miasto, Stawiszyn, Tuliszków and Zagórów.

The most important of them survive in the series of the municipal court books (księgi grodzkie), especially those of Pyzdry, Konin and Kalisz, but also in a valuable collection of originals and copies of such documents and records called the Papers of Albert Breyer (Spuścizna Alberta Breyera), kept in the State Archive in Poznań (cited below as APP). For questions of the same kind, but also others, concerning above all the number and structure of the farms, the population and the social and economic life of the Olęder settlements, of fundamental importance are: the surveys of the crown estates of 1789, the tables of hearths, of hearth tax and of population and the tax of the offering of 10 and 20 groszy of the years 1789-1790, and the so-called grain levy (zsypka zbożowa) of 1791. Written sources (in originals and copies) concerning above all the founding of the Olęder settlements and their internal administrative and judicial organisation, together with parts of cartographic sources showing where the Olęders were and portraits of their founders, are reproduced in the text of this study, with an explanation of each there and in the list of illustrations.

At the end of this study, besides the conclusions that follow from the account of these questions, we show very briefly, in outline, chiefly from the literature (and above all from the studies of A. Breyer mentioned above, from the cartographic sources and from the communes' development plans), some of the most important facts of the later history of rural settlement (Olęder settlement included) in the Pyzdry Forest, in the period from 1794 to recent years. The range of subjects and of time, the large holdings and different character of the sources and their scattering over many different archives mean that the history of this settlement in the years 1794-1864, and the later fortunes of the Olęder settlements, require a separate study.

In its construction the study consists of an introduction; six separate chapters, which present the questions named above in an essentially scholarly manner and are furnished with notes, bibliographical and sometimes on points of substance, numbered throughout; a conclusion; a Glossary of Old Polish terms that appear often in the text and are not understood today and need explaining; and a list of illustrations.

The oldest Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest, founded in 1746 in the district of Konin, in the parish and on the estate of Trąbczyn, were the Trąbczyńskie Stare Ol. and the Luśnie Ol. They were founded, on half of the wood Ostrowiec, half of the wood or rather marsh Stawisko, and on the woods Miąsykąt, Dziadulin and Luśnie, stretching from Stawisko towards Czarny Bród, by the married couple Paweł and Katarzyna née Rozdrażewska Prusimski, the owners of the estate at the time, by a charter of theirs that has not survived. This is known from the decree of the boundary commission court of 1776 on fixing the boundaries between the estates of Trąbczyn and Łukom. According to it, a part of the Trąbczyn estate together with the Olęder villages, which in 1771 had been wrongly adjudged by the boundary commission court and tradowana, that is officially handed over, to Stanisław Chełmski, the owner of the estate of Łukomia or Łomów, was to be restored (together with the income unlawfully drawn from it for 4 years) to the nephew and heir of the founder, Antoni Prusimski, owner of Trąbczyn Mały or Nowa Wieś, starost of Niszczewice [so called from the village of Niszczewice, the seat of a non-castle starosty in the district and voivodeship of Inowrocław]. On the strength of what this source says about the names, the Lutheran school and the cemetery, it can be said that the settlers placed in these Olęder villages were German peasants of the Lutheran, Evangelical-Augsburg, confession (Ill. 4). Since they were settled on wooded and marshy land, which needed clearing and draining, they probably received 7-8 free years to make the land fit for tillage and to put up their buildings. The inspection [description] of the Trąbczyn estate of 1754, eight years later, says that 15 Olęders lived in these settlements. Of these, 12 Olęders and an inn were in the wood Lusina, that is in the Luśnie Ol., which was taken to be the greater part of the Trąbczyńskie Stare Ol. in the wider sense, but was later also called the Łukomskie Ol. The Trąbczyńskie Nowe Ol. probably arose after 1754 and before 1767. This seems to follow, indirectly, from two inspections, of the fields and of the boundaries of the Trąbczyn estate, both of 1767. According to the inspection of the fields, water flowing from the Stawisko had flooded the farms of the Olęders settled in the Trąbczyn woods with ploughland measured out for tillage, and meadows..., through the fault of people from the village of Łukom, acting on their owner's orders; and according to the inspection of the boundaries, the meadows of 4 Trąbczyn Olęders had been flooded, so far that they could not be mown, because the flowing water had been dammed in the pond by the throwing up of a dike. In 1791 Catholics and Lutherans lived in the Trąbczyńskie St. and Nw. Ol., and they then had 31 "self-tilling" (samorolne) hearths (farms), that is, farming ones.

Before 1750 and in 1772 the Przespolewskie Ol. arose in the district of Kalisz, in the parish of Przespolew Kościelny, on the noble estate of Przespolew Pański; they took in a part of Przespolew Pański and Poroże Wielkie. The approximate date of the founding of their oldest part can be fixed from the mention of the rents of the "olendrzy" in the act of tradition of 1750 to Leon Bielecki, posesor, that is the holder, of a part of the Przespolew estate. The founder, or rather the co-founder, of the second part of the Przespolewskie Ol., the settlement of Poroże Wielkie Ol., founded in 1772, was Marcin Stanisław Zaremba, Adjutant General of His Royal Majesty, owner of the property of Przespolew. On the strength of the foundation charter he issued that year to the "industrious Olęders" Marcin Schmarschel and Fryderyk Jakobcek, Marcin Lehmann and others, at least several German settlers, Lutherans, settled in the place. They were settled on wooded land, that is most probably in the forest, since they received 7 free years for setting up their farms and buildings. In the decree of the commission court of 1779 on the tradition of a part of the Przespolew estate in payment of a debt of its owner, Tadeusz Zaremba, to the creditor Tomasz Moraczewski, 3 Olęders living at Poroże are named (two of them probably the same as those named above in the charter of 1772), who paid, among other things, rent, and of the others it is said that they give no rent since they still enjoy the freedom under their contracts for a time, except the innkeeper, handed over [officially transferred] to His Honour Pan Wolski [probably yet another creditor]. After 1754, and certainly before 1789 or by 1793, Łazy (Olędry) arose in the district of Konin, in the parish and on the noble estate of Trąbczyn, probably founded by those already mentioned above: Katarzyna née Rozdrażewska Prusimska, widow, or Antoni Prusimski, starost of Niszczewice. In the sources of the Old Polish period (as, for instance, in the inspection of the Trąbczyn estate of 1754) they are recorded without the addition Olędry, with which they appear only in the Prussian register of houses and population of 1796, which, however, gives them the same number of houses/hearths as the table of "self-tilling", that is farming, hearths of 1791. In 1791 they were inhabited by Catholics, 48 persons in all. It seems that, as an Olęder settlement, they arose through the transfer of their existing inhabitants, who had owed labour service, to Olęder law.

After 1765, and before 1793, the settlement of the Lisewskie Ol. (Olsz) was founded in the starosty and district of Pyzdry, in the parish of Szymanowice (whose centre lay in the district of Kalisz), by Michał Drogosław Skórzewski, then starost of Pyzdry in the years 1751-1789 (Ill. 5). Its founding can be linked, indirectly, with the conversion to rent of the village of Lisewo, until then a labour-service village, carried out after 1751 by the same starost. north-west of Lisewo, the new settlement of the Lisewskie Ol., also called Olsz or Olszowiec. The information of two surveys of the starosty of Pyzdry, that of 1765 on the entry-fine village of Lisewo paying rents, and that of 1789 on the farmers and the rent-paying cottagers in Lisewo and on four contract settlers on isolated holdings (pustkowianie kontraktowi) by the village of Lisewo, does not undermine the view that this second settlement was Olęder in its legal character, even though its inhabitants are not expressly called Olęders. Some doubt on this point can be raised only by the fact that its inhabitants were on individual contracts (agreements). This, however, seems to have been temporary, and they seem to have obtained a collective (though to us unknown) foundation charter, since in the later sources too the addition Olędry was consistently used in the name of this village. In the registers of the parish of Szymanowice of the years 1775-1780 there are entries on inhabitants of the "Lisewskie Olędry alias [otherwise] Olszowiec", probably mixed in nation and confession. This settlement also appears as Holendry Lisewskie on the map of K. Perthées. The village now called Kolonia Lisewo, on the other hand, was not an Olęder settlement (at least not an Old Polish one). It was founded with German and Lutheran settlers in the so-called Frederician colonisation in the period of so-called South Prussia, in its Poznań department, on the state domain of Pyzdry, as a colony by the demesne farm of Lisewo, which in 1804 numbered 20 families, 99 persons, with an area of 23 łany and 13 morgen.

Before 1755-1756 the Ciemierowa/Tomickie/Szymanowickie Stare Olędry were founded, situated in the district of Kalisz and the parish of Szymanowice, and recorded on Gilly's map. Their founder was probably Ignacy Samek Glis[z]czyński, starost of Pasierby, so called from the village of Pasierby, the seat of a non-castle starosty, in the district of Gostynin, in the voivodeship of Rawa, owner of the estate of Tomice. From the form of the names of the Olęders written in the baptismal registers of the parish of Szymanowice in those years it can be inferred that Catholics, Germans and Poles, lived in this settlement, though it is not out of the question that some of them were Protestant Lutherans, who were also often forced to receive this sacrament at the hands of Catholic priests.

In 1761 the Zbierskie Olędry were founded in the district of Kalisz, in the parish of Zbiersk, on the noble estate of that name. Their founder was Stanisław Dzik Kożuchowski, land judge of Wieluń. According to the emphyteutic-perpetual foundation charter he issued at Zbiersk on 16 December 1761, the colonists were settled in the forest, and received 8 free years for clearing and setting up their farms

Under the oblata (official copy) of the text of the foundation charter the Olęders are named, in the number given above, settled in the years 1761-1778, partly the same as the first ones of 1761 but partly others, probably among other things because farms were sold and bought. This charter laid down that from the beginning and the choosing of his huba every inhabitant is to take a card to remember his free years and to go to his lord, so that their first names and surnames be written down (Ill. 6). From these two premises it can be inferred that the founding of the whole village took as long as 17 years. The inventory of the Zbiersk estate, which was then held by Leon Gąsiorowski, royal chamberlain (szambelan), drawn up in 1771 by the lessees, the married couple Jakub and Franciszka Przespolewski, names 6 Olęders in this settlement (the sołtys among them) and their dues, and 3 Olęders not yet paying them. The inventory of the Zbiersk estate drawn up in 1775 found, among other things, that there were still 14 farmers in the Zbierskie Ol..

Before or in 1767 Wielołęka was founded as an Olęder settlement in the district of Konin, in the parish of Grodziec, on the noble estate of Królików. In a protest lodged in 1767 with the Crown Tribunal at Bydgoszcz by Piotr Kurcewski, owner of the estate of Kuchary Borowe, against Józef Wężyk, sword-bearer and judge of the land of Wieluń, owner of the estates of Grójec (Grodziec) and Królikowo, there is already mention of the deserta [empty land] Łęka, now called Wielołęka with Olędry. This village was founded first by a collective foundation charter issued by Józef Wężyk, castellan of Konary and of Sieradz, given at the castle of Grodziec on 6 September 1770. A copy of this charter in German shows that the settlers had earlier received separate, individual foundation charters, from the issuing of which their seven free years, meant for clearing and setting up their farms on the deserted village overgrown with forest, were to be counted. This village was in a way re-founded and enlarged by his son-in-law Count Franciszek Stadnicki, starost of Ostrzeszów, owner of the estates of Grójec (Grodziec), Królików and Biskupice, by his emphyteutic-perpetual charter, issued at Biskupice on 3 February 1791. He did so... to increase the population and multiply the intrats [income] from useless woods, moved by the requests [!] of free incomers, partly already settled and partly still to settle..., who have already paid the gruntgielt [entry money]. The free years were probably 7, or at least 5. In this charter the founder also assigned the village half a huba free of charge for a little school, and laid on the settlers, who were of mixed confession, Catholics and dissenters (Protestants), the obligation to pay fees for baptisms, weddings and funerals to the parish priest of the parish church at Grodziec; the dissenters too were to hold their baptisms and weddings in that church.

In 1768 the Cekowskie Stare Ol. arose in the district of Kalisz, on the royal estates, in the lease (dzierżawa) of Ceków, in the parish of Kosmów. Their founder was Jan Bezan, captain of the Front Guard of the Crown of His Royal Majesty and the Commonwealth, and the foundation charter he issued at Ceków on 18 April 1768 was confirmed on 26 January ("tycznia") 1774 by their next lessee, Franciszek Byszewski. 9 honest men of the Olęder estate (2 with Polish and 7 with German names), Lutherans and Catholics, were settled in the settlement. They settled "in the thickets of the Ceków estate", that is in woodland that needed rudunek (clearing), for which, and for setting up their farms, they received 7 free years. They were also bound to pay tithe to the parish priest of the parish church at Kosmów. The settlers declared that they were ready to pay for the "contract", that is the collective charter, a minted thaler each, having already paid for it one red złoty, that is a ducat. According to the inventory of the Ceków estate of 1774 there were then 5 Olęder farmers here, newly brought in, settled under a contract, that is under the foundation charter described above. "They have put up huts for themselves, by which they want to bind themselves further according to the measuring out of the hubas [łany, włóki], only that His Honour Pan [Antoni] Kawecki, owner [of neighbouring] Kuszyn, forbids them, maintaining that it is his own ground; where the lands were allotted them by the late His Honour Pan Jan Bezan, holder of the estate of the village of Ceków, and for that reason they do not want to bind themselves by these".

In the years 1770-1772 six more Olęder settlements were founded in the district of Konin, in the parishes of Królików and partly Grodziec and Królików, on the noble estates of Grodziec and Królików.

They included, first, Konary or the Konarskie Olędry, which their owner, Józef Wężyk, already mentioned, founded on the Grodziec estate by a charter that was in effect shared with, and in any case identical in content to, that of the Wielołęka Ol., issued on 6 September 1770. Lutheran Olęders settled there, as is shown by the mention in this charter of an agreement with the parish priest of Grodziec about the fees for weddings and funerals (Ill. 8). The founding of this settlement was formally confirmed and extended by Count Franciszek Stadnicki by his charter, shared by them and the Borowieckie Ol., issued in Polish at the castle of Grójec (Grodziec) on 25 August 1785. The settlement was founded in the Grójec forests, which were a part of the Pyzdry Forest. The settlers were granted 7 free years ...to those now already settled, and these [the Grójec forests] ...granting to each from his entering and paying the gruntgielt...". According to this charter the settlers were Protestants and Catholics. This last piece of information can, however, apply only to the Borowieckie Ol., since in Konary, as information from another contemporary source cited below shows, only Lutherans lived.

Probably in 1770 the Grójeckie or Grodzieckie Olędry (today a part of Grodziec, or perhaps Janowo?) were founded on the Grodziec and Królików estates, by an unknown charter, also issued by Józef Wężyk. The settlers were placed in the forest. This follows from the inspection of the estates of Grodziec and Królików with their appurtenances of 1771, made at the request of Helena née Jordan, widow of Józef Wężyk, pani oprawna (that is, holding a life settlement on this property), in which they are described as: the Hollendry of Grudziec, newly settled on ten hubas, who are only now clearing [them] for building themselves.

Probably in the same year 1770 the Białobłockie (Białe, Białogłowy, otherwise Królikowskie) Olędry arose on the Królików estate, founded by an unknown charter issued by the owner of this estate, Józef Wężyk, named above. Their existence in 1775 is confirmed by a deed of purchase and sale of land, dated 10 March 1775 and signed by the sołtys and the assessors of this commune. They were re-founded and enlarged by a charter of 17 October 1787, issued by his son-in-law and heir, the Count Franciszek Stadnicki already mentioned. He did so to multiply the intrats [income] from an increased population, moved by the request of free incomers wishing to settle in the Królików forests... Probably as early as about 1770 the Borowieckie Stare Ol. also arose on the same estates, founded by an unknown charter issued by Józef Wężyk. This is confirmed by a deed of purchase of land of 1770, signed by the sołtys and the assessors of this commune. According to the table of hearths of 1775 this settlement, described as "Olędry Borowiec i Huta", had 29 farms. The inventory of the properties of Grodziec and Królików of 1779 found 27 farmers living in the Borowieckie Ol., named with their first names and surnames (4 of them Polish), on holdings that differed in area. The existence of this settlement was confirmed by Wężyk's son-in-law and heir, Count Franciszek Stadnicki, also already mentioned, in the joint foundation charter for the Konarskie Ol. and for them of 25 August 1785, founding at the same time, it seems, the Borowieckie Nowe Ol. This charter contains the statement: All these points and descriptions set out above, in keeping with the customary Dutch laws, the whole settlement of the Borowieckie Holendry most solemnly promises, and is bound, to observe. The settlers, who were then settled in an unknown number, were Lutherans and Catholics by confession (Ill. 9).

Before and in 1771, and in 1791, the Grądy Stare and Nowe Ol. were also founded on the same property. The former were probably founded by Józef Wężyk himself. Their founding was confirmed, and extended to the Grądy Nw. Ol. as well, by Count Franciszek Stadnicki in an emphyteutic-perpetual foundation charter of 1791, meant for the Olęders on the Grądy, who have already paid the grontgielt; he declared that he did so ...to increase the population and multiply the intrats from useless woods, moved by the request of free incomers, partly already settled and partly still to settle..., that is with a motive like the one he gave in the charters for the Konarskie Ol. and the Białobłockie Ol. (Ill. 10). The settlers, Catholics and Protestant Lutherans (judging from the mention of a little school and of the obligations to the parish priest of the Catholic parish church of Grodziec), were settled in the forest, and received probably 7 free years. This charter stated that: The farmers newly settled not long ago on poorer lands [probably in the Grądy Nw. Ol. – Z.Ch.] after their rudowanie [clearing], when they are recognised as such by the commune office and the manor's jurisdiction [authority], would have relief in their dues to the manor (Ill. 11).

About 1771 the Gliny Olędry were founded in the district of Konin, in the parish of Dzierzbin (whose centre lay in the district of Kalisz), on the estate of Biała (Panieńska) of the convent of the Order of St Clare (the Franciscan nuns) of Kalisz. The inhabitants of this village were probably Catholics and Poles.

Not much later, in 1774 and 1780, the Cekowskie Nowe [Ol.] or Prażuchy were set up in the district of Kalisz, on the royal estates, in the lease of Ceków. The founders of this settlement were first Arnold Byszewski, colonel of the Front Guard, later major general of the Crown army, and Krzysztof Celiński, holder [from or after 1775] by the right he acquired, both of life tenure and of emphyteusis for fifty years, which... serves him by inheritance. At least 8 settlers (6 with German and 2 with Polish names), Lutherans, settled there. They took up the ground in Ceków beyond the pond called Prażuchy, which was undoubtedly wooded, since in the contract (foundation charter) of 1780 they received 7 free years for clearing the ground and the meadows. This contract was made with four honest free men of the Dutch estate, named by their surnames, who (...) had settled earlier under the contract of the former holder, the Most Illustrious and Magnificent His Honour Pan Arnold Byszewski, major general in the Crown army, and also with other men of the Dutch estate, whoever signs this contract. The list of Olęders included in the charter shows that the founding of the village was still going on in the years 1780-1782, and that some farms changed owners later, in 1785 and 1787 (Ill. 12).

In the years 1775 and 1784, in the same district, on the noble estate of Kosmów, in the parish of that name, the Kosmowskie or Szadokierskie Olędry were founded. Their founder was Antoni Kawiecki, owner of the estates of Kosmów [Kuszyn and Gostynie]. The settlement agreement (foundation charter) of 1775 was made between him and two colonists settled in the Kosmów forest called Szadykierz, with Polish names, Marcin Kapliński and Jan Droga/Droże, ...who make the contract in their own name and that of others..., acting as the locators, that is the establishers, of this village. In this agreement ...all who, together with those making the contract, wish to come and build were given 7 free years. The colonists were Protestant Lutherans, as is confirmed by the mention in the charter of an agreement with the parish priest of Kosmów about their obligations to him. Two further settlers, "honest", that is personally free, also with Polish names, were settled under Olęder law by a foundation charter of 1784, receiving the same free years.

Next, in the years 1776-1781, in the same district, on the same estates and in the same parish, and by the same founder, Antoni Kawiecki, owner of the estates of Kuszyn, Kosmów and Plewnie, the settlement of the Kuszyńskie or Jaszczurowo Olędry was founded. 7 colonists (4 with German and 3 with Polish names), Lutherans, settled there. two representatives of the settlers, Michał Gesse and Krzysztof Malus, and then in the years 1776-1781 a further 5 Olęders were added to it. According to this charter the settlement, because the place was so small, had a little school and a cemetery in common with the neighbouring Kosmowskie Ol..

In 1776 the Lubieńskie (Lubień) or Biała Olędry were set up in the district of Konin, in the parish of Dzierzbin, on the estate of Biała (Panieńska) belonging to the convent of the Order of St Clare (the Franciscan nuns) of Kalisz. Their foundress was Anna Chlebowska, prioress of that convent, who together with other members of its governing body issued two emphyteutic-perpetual foundation charters on 10 November 1776. According to them the village was founded at the urgent requests of the Holędrzy. The settlers, personally free, Catholics and Poles, settled by the right of free purchase on the deserta [empty land] Lubień, and received 7 free years (counted from 10 XI 1776), but their years of freedom were to run out according to their separate contracts, that is agreements (Ill. 13). This last piece of information seems to show that they settled in woodland that needed rudunek (clearing), at first under individual agreements.

Probably as early as about 1770, and in 1781, two settlements were founded in the district of Pyzdry, in the parish of Zagórów, in the starosty of Pietrzyków: Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol. Their earlier origin is confirmed by two konotacje (memoranda) issued to the Olęders by I. Gałęski, the plenipotentiary of Szczepan Turno, starost of Pietrzyków. In the first, of 23 July 1776, the manorial dues from 12 hubas (włóki) of farms were set for the industrious people of Rąmpczyn, that is for the inhabitants of Wrąbczynek, who still owed labour service (after the old konotacja had been lost). In the second, of 30 September 1777, a confirmation was issued of the measuring of the lands by the sworn surveyor Bogusław, which had found only 11 hubas, and accordingly the inhabitants of Wrąbczynek were let off the rent of 1 huba. It also contained the statements that on that day the community was to choose a sołtys and 2 assessors with the manor's consent, and that a royal law would be issued for them, that is a confirmation of the foundation charter by the monarch. This konotacja also contained the information: Since the Rąbczynek Holendry, their free years for the rumunek being out, have today received the law under which they are to remain in their dues, so that these too [that is the Olęders in Wrąbczynek], settled together with them, are not raised to higher dues than the Holędrzy, they are ascribed an equalisation with those, so that they [belong] to the dues set out here. It follows that the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol. were founded on overgrown, probably wooded, land, and that the two settlements were founded at the same time. of 19 June 1781, issued by Krystyna née Szembek Turnowa, wife of the stolnik of Poznań, the mother, and Stefan/Szczepan Turno, starost of Pietrzyków, the son, to Ignacy Dobrski, the description of the village of Wrąbczynek contains the information that there are handed over to him the Olędry both on the Budy and the Nowe Olędry, whose freedom runs out this very year, with all their dues and rents.... The inspection of 1776 of the place (land) Benefickie beyond the river Warta, belonging to the estates of the town of Pyzdry, tells of its being taken over, together with a part of the old road from Pyzdry to Konin, by an Olęder recently settled by Stefan (Szczepan) Turno, and that in the wood Spławie the Olęders of the said Pan Turno are clearing, cutting the wood down to the stump and destroying the building timber. According to the joint, collective and final emphyteutic-perpetual foundation charter for both settlements, issued at Pietrzyków on 20 October 1781 by the said Szczepan Turno, they were founded to bring the ruined royal estates of the starosty of Pietrzyków, and precisely the villages of Rąpczyno, into good condition. The founder therefore granted to Jakub Krysa [Kriese], sołtys, and to Wojciech Kurtz and Krzysztof Szultz, assessors, ...the demesne farm with all its lands and the village thickets in the existing village of Wrąbczynek, with a total area of 11 hubas measured by the surveyor, besides the gardens and village plots, and the pastures; and to the Rąpczyn Hollendry [that is the inhabitants of the Wrąbczynkowskie Olędry], 9 ½ hubas cleared by them from the deserta [empty land] in the forest, having earlier set up in them a sołtys and 2 assessors, named with their first names and surnames. They received their free years, that is the time for building and setting up their farms, according to the individual contracts they had obtained earlier. They received, besides, 16 morgen of meadows they had cleared. The provisions of the charter applied to both settlements, as the phrase in it confirmed: By this present law [the collective one], long promised them, I secure both the village commune and the Dutch commune...". Settlers with German and Polish names settled in both settlements. Most of them were probably Lutherans, as is shown by the grant to both settlements of land for a teacher and for a burial ground, although the visitation of the deanery of Konin of 1792 shows only Catholics in Wrąbczynek and only Protestants in the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol.. In an asekuracja (written assurance) of 20 XI 1781, issued by S. Dobrski, plenipotentiary of Turno, starost of Pietrzyków, besides confirming that the labour services had been done, the Olęders were promised that they would obtain the royal law (that is, the king's confirmation of the foundation charter issued by the starost-tenant) once they had paid a contribution for the purpose, and it is stated that the Germans, who have been measured out on the lord's demesne farm, will be bound to pay the remaining half of the grungielt". The confirmation of this charter by King Stanisław August Poniatowski, however, came only on 2 February 1787.

In 1777, and then before and in 1784, the Gadowskie Stare and Nowe [Ol.] (today Gadowskie Holendry) were set up in the district of Konin, in the parish of Dzierzbin. Their founders were Piotr Sokół Gałczyński and Agnieszka née Sieroszewska Gałczyńska, his widow, life holder of the estates of Gadów, Smuszew and others with their appurtenances. She justified the founding of the settlement on economic grounds in her foundation charter issued at Gadów on 1 November 1784: Since the extent and abundance of the woods on the estates of Gadów with their appurtenances... bring no use, neither now nor later, taking the example practised in this country until now in setting up Holędrzy, on hereditary estates and on estates held for life, seeing the need to strengthen the revenues [income] of Gadów, weakened by various accidents to the land, and wishing to keep their condition at its best for my most beloved children in my lifetime [that is, to keep these estates in the best possible condition for the children], and also to hand [pass] on to them the intrats of these estates increased later [the profits of these estates increased later], I have resolved ... to give emphyteutic law to the Gadowskie Holendry, to free people subject to no subjection, brought in while my husband was still alive... and coming in during my possession ... according to separate contracts [agreements]. This charter names 3 settlers with German names, the sołtys and the assessors, but there were also others with German and Polish names, Protestant Lutherans and Catholics. They were settled in the forest called "Zielony Las" (the Green Wood). Its text also shows that they settled gradually and received free years fixed individually, set earlier by separate contracts. According to a protest of 23 VIII 1787 against A. Gałczyńska, lodged by Bogumił Leszczyc Dobrzycki, royal chamberlain, owner of the estate of Rychwał and of the deserta of Sokołowo with their appurtenances, which bordered on the Gadów estates, A. Gałczyńska settled some dozen Olęders on the Rychwał forests and the deserta [empty land] of Sokołowo, which she had seized by force and unlawfully, having cut down the trees and sold them, and besides she is carrying off by force the hay from meadows she has appropriated. In the inspection of the Gadów estates of 10 June 1780, A. In 1778 the Pyzdrskie Olędry were founded. They were founded by the council of the town of Pyzdry (the president Karol Ogrodowicz and 5 councillors) in order to protect the forests belonging to the town. The settlers were Poles and Catholics, partly burghers of Pyzdry and partly peasants of the surrounding area. They settled in the Pyzdry forests and received 7 free years for clearing their holdings (Ill. 14). The issuing of their foundation charter on ordinary paper and not on stamped paper, as the law required, became the cause of long lawsuits between the Olęders and the town authorities. The Pyzdrskie Olędry were the only Olęder settlement in Greater Poland that arose on the estates of a royal town. Today, as was said above, 9 settlements or parts of them correspond to it (cf. Tab. 1).

In the same year 1778 the Jarantowskie (Jaruntowskie) or Jarantów Olędry were founded in the district of Kalisz, in the parish of Lipe, on a noble estate. From the remains of a Protestant cemetery it can be said that only, or also, Protestants lived there.

In 1781 Wierzchy, or the Tomickie Nowe Olędry, were created in the district of Kalisz, in the parish of Szymanowice, on the noble estate of Tomice. Their founders, by an emphyteutic-perpetual foundation charter issued at Tomice on 23 September of that year, were Jan Samek Glis[z]czyński, chamberlain (podkomorzy) of His Royal Majesty, owner of the estates of Tomice and Wierzchy, and his wife K. Glis[z]czyńska. 12 settlers with Polish (8) and German (4) names settled in the settlement, most probably Lutherans, since remains of a Protestant cemetery have survived in the village, or mixed in confession and nation, given the German and Polish names of its inhabitants recorded for this village in the

In the years 1782 the Kazimierskie or Niniewskie Stare Ol. were founded, and in 1790 the Kazimierskie Nowe Olędry, situated in the district of Kalisz, in the parish and on the estate of Chocz. For the first of them the foundation charter of 1782 is unknown. The second received a charter issued on 9 November 1790 by the Rev. Kazimierz Lipski, mitred provost of Chocz, abbot of Lubin. It shows that the locator of this settlement was Georg [Jerzy] Müller. The settlers, who were Germans and Lutherans, received 7 free years (counted from 9 XI 1790), running out in 1797. This last piece of information shows that the village arose on wooded land, which needed so long a time for clearing and setting up the farms. It seems that the Kazimierskie St. Ol. were founded earlier on land of a similar character, and that their founder too was the said Kazimierz Lipski (Ill. 15), from whose first name both settlements took their names.

Kazimierz Poraj Biernacki, wojski of the district of Ostrzeszów, owner of the estate of Siąszyce, which was set down in one joint collective emphyteutic-perpetual foundation charter, issued at Kalisz on 25 June 1783, Dzierzbin and the property of Sul[i]szew. The founder justified their creation by saying that he did so having so many woods beyond his need, and at the request of the Olęders. The recipients of this charter were Marcin Szynwald, Jan Fitz and other settlers not named, mostly, if not exclusively, Lutherans.

They were given the woods called Zdanowiec and Zamęty to settle. The first settlers received holdings of one włóka each. The two villages formed separate communes, with separate sołtyses and assessors. The charter stated that: They are allowed freedom for as many years as they have agreed in their separate contracts, which will be entered in the wilkierz or inventory, making them free of all dues and labour during these free years (Ill. 16). From this last piece of information it can be inferred that settlers had settled in this settlement under individual agreements earlier, that is before 1783. Later, further settlers were brought into both villages and farms were divided through inheritance, since rent in the years 1791-1792 and taxes in the years 1789-1795 were paid, or were to be paid, from different numbers of hubas, as is shown by the entries in a village book common to both settlements.

Also before 1783 the Plewińskie (Stare) Olędry were founded in the district of Kalisz, in the parish of Kosmów, and in 1793 the Plewińskie Nowe or Kuźnickie Olędry. Their founder was Antoni Kawiecki, owner of the estates of Kuszyn, Kosmów and Plewnie. The first, also called Stara Huta, whose foundation charter is unknown to us, are recorded in the years 1783-1784, and in 1789 they had 7-8 hearths. From the foundation charter issued by A. In 1783 two settlements were founded by one charter in the district of Kalisz, in the parish of Brudzew and on the estate of Lipe: the Piskory Ol., founded in the Lipe wood on the land of Bi[e]lawy, and Dębniałki, or the Bolimowskie or Brudzewskie Olędry, founded "on the Brudzew land called Rosocha and Dębianki [!]", with separate sołtyses and assessors. In the charter, issued at Tymianka on 17 VII 1783, only 3 are named (2 with German names and 1 with a Polish name), Catholics and Lutherans ...who ...have settled and will settle; they took up the Lipe wood and forest and meadows, ground long useless, which needed rudunek, and accordingly received 7 free years counted from the time each settler settled; there were, however, more settlers (6 Olęders received free years to 1791 and 2 to 1792). The dissenters were also to receive plots for a burial ground and for a school, common to both settlements. The issuers of the charter and founders of both settlements were Wawrzyniec Antoni Łodzia Czarnecki, stolnik of the district of Inowłódz, deputy castle starost of the voivodeship of Łęczyca, owner of the little town of Stryków with the villages of Smolice Górne and Dolne, Lipe, Cesarka, Dobra and Kiełmina in the voivodeship of Łęczyca, district of Brzeziny, and in the voivodeship and district of Kalisz of the villages of Brudzew and Bolimów and of the former little town of Korab, and his wife Ewa née Nowowiejska Czarnecka, owners of the village of Lipe in the latter district and voivodeship (Ill. 18 and 19). In the second charter, issued by Ewa Czarnecka as a widow on 10 September 1790 at Lipe, the Piskory Ol. received free pasture in the forests and pastures, and the use of the pond at Piskory, in return for each of the 16 farmers ploughing within the year

Their founders were the owners of the village and demesne farm of Obory, the married couple Jan and Marianna née Rożnowska Szarzyński, treasurer of Latyczów and his wife. The settlers, whose number and confession the charter does not give, were, as the remains of a separate Protestant cemetery show, only or also Lutherans.

Before and in 1784 the settlements of the Orlińskie (Orlina) Duże and Małe Olędry were created in the district of Konin, on the estate and in the parish of Królików(o). Their founder, and the issuer of the preliminary charter, issued at Królików on 5 May 1784, was the owner of this estate, Count Franciszek Stadnicki, starost of Ostrzeszów, and directly his plenipotentiary Józef Koźmiński, and the locators were Bogusław Krol, sołtys, and Michał Arent. This charter contains the phrase ... in future all the present and the earlier ones [settlers] will have one law, which justifies the supposition that one of the two settlements, that is the Orlińskie Duże Ol., arose earlier, and the second, the Orlińskie Małe Ol., was founded later, in 1784. The founder also stated in it: I allow this sołtys free clearing and rudowanie with his co-samsiads [!] [neighbours], whose first names and surnames will be written on this contract. In 1784, 20 settlers settled (most of them with Polish names and some with German), Catholics and Lutherans.

After 1783-1784 and before 1789 the Lisieckie [Ol.], or Lisiec, were founded on the river Powa, in the district of Konin, in the parish of Lisiec Wielki, in the Lisiec key (group of estates) of the starosty of Konin. In 1791 they had only 2 self-tilling hearths, inhabited by dissenters (perhaps Reformed Protestants, attached to the church at Żychlin, as another name of this settlement, the Żychlińskie Ol., would seem to show), and in 1796, 4 houses in all. Their founder was probably Józef Mycielski, starost of Konin, lieutenant general of the Lithuanian army, voivode of Inowrocław, owner of the estate of Szamotuły.

Perhaps as early as about 1777, and certainly in the years 1785-1789, the settlement of Stara Huta-Grójeckie Olędry (today Stara Huta) arose in the same district, in the parish and on the noble estate of Grodziec ("Grojec"). Its founder was probably Count Franciszek Stadnicki, judicial starost of Ostrzeszów, then owner of the estates of Grodziec, Królików and Biskupice. The settlement was founded on empty land overgrown with forest. The inhabitants of this village were Catholics and Poles.

About 1786, and certainly before 1790, the Siąszyckie or Złotkowskie Olędry were founded in the district of Konin, in the parish of Grochowy, on the noble estate of Siąszyce. Their founder was most probably the then owner of the Siąszyce estate, Kazimierz Biernacki, mentioned above, by then styled stolnik of Piotrków. According to the manifestacja (protest) of his plenipotentiary of 1790, Onufry Gałczyński, a towarzysz of the National Cavalry, with a few of his men and 2 privates, attacked in December 1789 the Olęders settled on the manor land of the village of Siąszyce, took the cattle of two of them, Łukasz and Bernard, and carried off one Olęder, Łukasz Łyszkowski, to Konin, forcing him to enter military service in the squadron in which he served, although he was a farmer and an immigrant and the new law of the Diet forbade it (Ill. 20). In 1791 this settlement had 9 "self-tilling" hearths.

In 1787 the Mycielińskie Stare and Nowe Olędry (today Kazala St. and Nw.) were founded in the district of Kalisz, in the parish of Kościelec, on the noble estate of Mycielin, by two charters, in fact settlement agreements, made at Mycielin on the same day, 30 March 1787. Their founder was Maciej Łuczycki, owner of the estate of Mycielin. He made one preliminary agreement with 2 "honest", that is personally free, peasants with German names, who, being unable to write, put crosses under it. The settlers were settled on land partly wyrudowany [cleared], partly overgrown with various trees, called Kazalnia, towards the boundary of the village of Korzeniew, and received 6 free years for setting up their farms (Ill. 21). The second agreement, also a preliminary one, was made between Maciej Łuczycki and 6 Olęders, also "honest" (3 of them with Polish names, 1 with a German one, 1 named only by his first name and 1 whose surname is not given). They were settled on a part of the ground, that is of the thickets dense with various trees, called Krzewina, on land called Rusiny, by the boundary of the lands of the village of Słuszków, which needed rudunek. They were guaranteed 7 free years. Should there not be enough land for the sixth of these settlers, he was to be settled on another part of the ground called Kazale [Kazalnia] and to clear his holding there. The agreement was signed by the founder and the Olęders, in the case of the latter, who could not write, with crosses.

In the years 1787 and 1791 the Stropieszyńskie, or Radzany and Gostynie, Olędry were founded in the district of Kalisz, in the parish of Kościelec. Their founder, and the issuer of the emphyteutic-perpetual foundation charters, was Ignacy Skarbek Kozietulski, treasurer and later wojski of the land of Czersk, owner of the village and demesne farm of Stropieszyn. According to the first charter, which he issued on 6 December 1787 at Stropieszyn, the settlers took up "Stropieszyn" land (of the village of Stropieszyn) that was ready, meadows, and overgrown land "under Bugaj and in Radzanów by the ponds", receiving 3 free years for setting up their farms (counted from 11 XI 1787). The village also received land for a school and for a burial ground (Ill. 22). From this last piece of information it may be inferred that the Olęders were Lutherans and Germans. The second charter, issued on 22 November 1791 at Stropieszyn, mentions an earlier agreement of 27 November 1787, and by it the issuer at the same time confirmed and supplemented the first charter for this village, adding to it also the married couple Józef and Elżbieta Gierecki, servants, settled under a separate charter on ½ huba of ploughland.

Before 1789 the following arose in the district of Konin, in the parish of Zagórów, on the noble estates of Łukom and Łomowo, on the initiative of their owners of the time: the settlements of Bukowo/Bukowe or the Łomowskie Olędry, Imielno Olędry, and a village mixed in its legal constitution, "Myszaków with the Olędry", or more exactly Myszakówko, and Stara Huta with the Olędry, or the Zagórowskie Ol. (today Huta Łukomska). The people who settled in them were of various confessions and nations.

In the same district, in the parishes and on the estates of Sławsk and Grodziec, there were founded: before 1789, the Kowalewskie Olędry, and before 1792 the Jaroszewickie Olędry (today Jaroszewice Grodzieckie). Their founders were the owners of these estates at the time, Stefan Zielonacki and Count Franciszek Stadnicki, who were also the largest landowners in the district of Konin in the years 1789-1791.

In 1790 the settlement of Świdle Nowa Kolonia, or the Świdle Olędry, was founded in the district of Kalisz, in the parish and on the noble estate of Przespolew(o). Its founder was Ignacy Zaremba, son of the starost of Prośniatów, civil and military commissary for order of Kalisz, holder of this estate. According to the table of the grain levy from the self-tilling hearths of the district of Kalisz of 1791, the Świdle Ol. were "newly set up in the year 1790", and they then had 3 "self-tilling" hearths.

Summing up and supplementing the detailed information given above on the distribution, time, causes, conditions and organisation of the founding of the 58 Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest in the years 1746-1793, the following more general conclusions can be drawn, which, to make them easier to read, we set out in several points. 1) Of the 58 Olęder settlements founded in the years 1746-1793 in the Pyzdry Forest in 3 districts of the voivodeship of Kalisz, in 21 parishes (4 of which lay on the border of two districts), 5 were founded in the district of Pyzdry, in 4 parishes: Ciążeń (1), Pyzdry (1), Szymanowice (2) and Zagórów (2); 28 in the district of Konin, in 8 parishes: Dzierzbin, whose centre lay in the district of Kalisz (6), Grochowy (1), Grodziec (5), Królików (2), partly lying in both of the last two parishes (4), Lisiec Wielki (1), Trąbczyn (3), Sławsk (1), Zagórów (5); and 25 in the district of Kalisz, in 10 parishes: Brudzew (1), Chocz (2), Dzierzbin (2), Kościelec (5), Kosmów (5), Lipe (2), Przespolew Kościelny (3), Rzegocin (2), Szymanowice (2), Zbiersk (1). Of these 58 Olęder settlements, 7 were founded on royal estates (1 in the starosty of Pyzdry and 2 in the starosty of Pietrzyków in the district of Pyzdry, 1 in the starosty and district of Konin, 2 in the lease of Ceków in the district of Kalisz, 1 on the estates of the royal town of Pyzdry), 3 on church estates (1 on secular church estates, in the Ciążeń key of the latifundium of the bishopric of Poznań, in the district of Pyzdry, and 2 on the monastic estates of the convent of the Order of St Clare, the Franciscan nuns, in Kalisz, in the district of Konin), and the majority, 48 settlements, on noble estates (25 of them in the district of Konin and 23 in the district of Kalisz), mostly on such estates as Gadów, Grodziec-Królików and Trąbczyn, Łukom and Łomowo in the district of Konin, and Dzierzbin, Chocz, Kosmów and Lipe in the district of Kalisz. Of these, two villages (the Kazimierskie Stare and Nowe Olędry) in the parish and on the estate of Chocz, which formed the endowment of a noble foundation of the chapter of the collegiate church of Chocz (created in 1620 on the condition that it be presided over by a clergyman of the Lipski family, with the dignity of a mitred prelate), are sometimes classed in the sources as villages that were church property2) The date of origin of more than half (31) of the 58 Olęder settlements that arose in the Pyzdry Forest in the eighteenth century is fixed exactly by their foundation charters; for the rest it can be established exactly or approximately from the first mentions in other kinds of sources, such as inspections, inventories, court decrees and tax tables. The chronology of their founding, certain and hypothetical, falls within the periodisation we have adopted for the history of Olęder settlement

in Poland and Greater Poland, within their second phase (1660-1793/1795) and third period (1721-1793/95). Of these 58 settlements, 3 arose in the first sub-period (1721-1750), 11 in the second (1751-1772) and 44 in the third (1773-1793) of this period. This order in time of the founding of the Olęder settlements is not wholly clear-cut, however, since some of them were re-founded or had further settlers brought in during different sub-periods.

3) The cause of the founding of the settlements for the feudal founders was the wish to increase their income by settling and bringing into use the reserves of land they held, especially woodland not settled until then, or settled but long deserted, depopulated and overgrown again with forest, and, exceptionally, land that was ready, already tilled. The settling of Olęders, who answered jointly, in accordance with one of the basic principles of Olęder law, for paying money rents to the lords, assured these of a steady and regular income. This is also shown, indirectly, by the founding of some Olęder settlements on usurped land, that is land that was the subject of lawsuits between the owners of neighbouring estates. For the Olęders the motive for settling were favourable legal and economic conditions of life, far better than in the country and the place of their origin or their earlier residence in Poland, and the assurance of religious toleration and freedom of worship, guaranteed to the settlers in the foundation charters in accordance with the principles of Olęder law, which will be discussed in detail below. The foundation charters for the settlements in the Pyzdry Forest (apart from five, for Wielołęka, the Białobłockie, Konarskie, Grądy St. and Nw. and Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol.) do not speak directly of these mutual economic advantages, since they were, so to speak, obvious.

4\. The character of the land on which Olęder settlements were founded in the Pyzdry Forest in the years 1746-1793 varied. Most of them were founded on wooded land or on land that had become overgrown again. In the light of the source information given above, at least 37 of the 58 settlements were founded on woodland. Of these, at least 27 Olęder villages were founded on raw root, 5 were founded on the site of settlements or parts of settlements that had existed earlier under the same names, even since the Middle Ages, and had been deserted and overgrown with forest at the end of the sixteenth and the beginning of the seventeenth century, and 5 on land partly tilled and ready, 1 of them (the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol.) also on the lands of a demesne farm. In the light of the source information on the character of the land where the settlements were founded, and of the data of modern soil maps, it can be said that of the 58 settlements, 27 were founded on podzolic soils (Cekowskie Nw. Ol., Gadowskie St. and Nw. So half of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest were founded on fertile and moderately fertile soils, half on infertile soils, and 4 on mixed soils, though with infertile soils predominating.

5) The Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest were founded by the founders, the owners or holders of the landed estates, in agreement with the locators, the representatives, and perhaps also the recruiters, of the settlers, acting on behalf of the whole future commune, or with whole communes; they often issued to them first individual or collective but preliminary charters (which were in fact agreements between the two parties), and only later (for instance once the necessary number of settlers had gathered) collective and final ones, which settled the Olęder character of the village. On the royal estates they were founded by their tenants (lessees) of the time, on the church estates by the bishop and by the superior and other members of the governing body of the convent of the Franciscan nuns in Kalisz, on the town estates by the magistrate of Pyzdry, and on the noble estates chiefly by the rich and middling nobility. The co-founders or founders of the largest number on a single noble property, that of Grodziec-Królików, no fewer than 8, were its successive owners, Józef Wężyk and Count Franciszek Stadnicki. On the few other properties at most 3-2 were founded, or only 1. Most of them were founded on so-called raw root, that is on places not settled before, in forests or woods, and in a few cases also on the sites of old villages dating back to the Middle Ages but deserted, that is overgrown again with forest, which is also shown by the long free years, 7, meant for clearing, setting up and building the settlements. These settlements were settled by people often described in the foundation charters as "honest" (uczciwi), that is personally free (at least once they had crossed the Polish border). They also had to have – as we shall show below – cash (needed to pay the entry money for the holdings of land they received, which guaranteed them the acquisition of the perpetual rent tenure of the land) and the basic live and dead stock (tools), which allowed them

chodyla2015/77:
to take up, build on and bring into use the holdings of land they received. The settlers undoubtedly took part in founding the settlements, which, as the text of many foundation charters shows, also took place at their request. In the founding of a few settlements one may guess at the presence of a locator or locators (osadźca, zasadźca), founding entrepreneurs acting on the authority of the whole commune, but for the most part whole groups (communities) of settlers acted in this capacity. The settlers of most settlements were Protestants by confession (chiefly Lutherans), some of them Catholics, and by nation Germans and Poles, who in some settlements also settled together. The settlements were founded on the strength of charters, which had to be paid for. The process of founding the Olęder settlements lasted at least through the free years (that is mostly several years), but often, as the information quoted above shows, even longer, probably mainly because of the difficulty of finding enough settlers and their coming and going. That is why settlers sometimes received individual contracts, sometimes collective but preliminary ones, replaced only in time, after the free years of all the settlers had run out, by collective, final, emphyteutic-perpetual foundation charters guaranteeing the perpetual rent tenure of the farms they held. The way, that is the technique, of founding the settlements, by clearing and/or by draining, which consisted in digging or deepening drainage ditches, depended on the character of the land taken up. Both sides bore the costs of the founding. The manor not only gave land for founding the settlements but probably organised part of the transport of the colonists, granted them building timber free of charge (allowing them to sell what was left over after the buildings were put up, in order to raise cash), and sometimes helped financially with putting up the buildings, which we discuss in detail below.

An important cultural aspect of Olęder settlement in the area of the Pyzdry Forest was the toponymy of the settlements. Of the 58 villages, most had, beside their name proper, the additional element (H)olędry or (H)olendry, used to mark the legal and economic character and the spatial layout of the place (like the terms folwark, kolonia and so on). As a component of the name of a settlement, this element served at the same time to identify it and to distinguish it.

Most of the settlements, founded sometimes on raw root, but mostly near old mother settlements, centres and estates and on their lands, received names that were:

1) possessive, that is, such as: Lisewskie, Pyzdrskie, Wrąbczynkowskie, Gadowskie St. and Nowe; Grodzieckie/Grójeckie, Jaroszewickie, Kowalewskie, Lisieckie, Siąszyckie or Złotkowskie, Smuszewskie, Trąbczyńskie Stare and Nowe; Ciemierowskie/Szymanowickie Stare, Cekowskie Stare and Nowe, Jarantowskie, Oborskie Nowe, Plewińskie Stare and Nowe, Zbierskie – Olędry.

2) topographical, derived from local names: of woods, thickets, forests and wilds, such as: Borowiec/Borowieckie Stare and Nowe, Dębniałki, (Dzierzbińskie)
