chodyla2015/78:
– Zdanowiec and Zamęty, Grądy, Luśnie, Orlińskie (Orlina) Duże and Małe, Piskory, Poroże Małe, Wierzchy – Olędry; of marshes and bogs, such as: Białebłota Olędry; names of industrial sites, such as: Stara Huta Grójeckie and Stara Huta Zagórowskie – (Olędry); 3) characteristic, formed independently of the naming of old settlements, that is, among others, personal names, derived from the first names and surnames of the founders and members of their families, such as: Kazimierskie (Stare and Nowe) Olędry.

There were also combinations of two types of name, namely possessive and topographical, such as: Ciążeńskie or Zarzeczne, (Kosmowskie) or Szadokierskie (Szadykierz), Kuszyńskie or Jaszczurowo, Lisewskie or Olsz/Olszowiec, Obory Stare or Wronów, Przespolewskie-Przespolewa (Pańskiego) and Poroża Wielkiego, Mycielińskie or Kazala Stara and Nowa, Stropieszyńskie or Radzany and Gostynie – Olędry.

Some settlements, on the other hand, bore names inherited from settlements long deserted (overgrown with forest and bushes), or from settlements that had changed their legal situation, that is had been turned from labour-service villages into Olęder ones.

These were names that were:

1\. topographical, such as: Bukowa/-e, Gliny, Imielno, Konary, Łazy, Lubień, Świdle Nowe, Wielołęka, Wrąbczynek

2\. possessive, such as: Myszakówek Olędry (written with or without the element Olędry).

The names of these settlements were also often written in both forms, interchangeably, as Konary or Konarskie, Lubień or Lubieńskie – Olędry.

Because of the changes in the meaning and function of the term (H)olędry, the names of Olęder settlements containing this element, but not only these, were transformed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. This happened above all by dropping the element Olędry (Olendry/Holendry). It also happened that in the names of Olęder settlements the distinguishing elements Kolonia or Pustkowie were used in place of (H)olędry, (H)olendry (in such forms as Świdle Nowa Kolonia, Pyzdrskie Pustkowie for the Pyzdrskie Ol.), applied to the Olęder villages because of their scattered spatial form and their small size. Several other factors also affected the transformation of the names of Olęder settlements, namely: 1) the persistence of the earlier tendency in the evolution of naming, connected with the settlers' own interchangeable use of the names of settlements, and with their changing forms in official records and lists of places (soon after their founding); 2) the parcelling and consolidation of land as a result of the regulation and the enfranchisement reforms, which brought back names used earlier, which in the case of the Pyzdrskie Ol. meant that one collective name was replaced by nine names of scattered settlements that had probably been moved to Olęder law together (Baraniec, Glinianki, Dolne and Górne Grądy, Królewiny, Kruszyny, Tłoczyzna, Trzcianki, Zapowiednia); 3) decisions of the administrative authorities at various levels, following a tendency to shorten and simplify the written forms of place names, as a result of which the adjectival elements of the names of Olęder settlements were changed into noun forms, for example Borowieckie St. and Nowe Ol. into Borowiec Stary and Nowy.

As a result of the structural and linguistic transformations of most of the old names of Olęder settlements with the element (H)olędry, (H)olendry, caused by the factors mentioned

chodyla2015/80:
2. The area and layout of the Olęder settlements, their size and types by the number and structure of hearths, and their social and functional-economic organisation

The area of the Olęder settlements that arose in the years 1746-1793 in the Pyzdry Forest, at the time of their founding, is not exactly known for all 58. For the greater part of them (37) it can be fixed approximately from the foundation charters and other records giving the number and/or size of the holdings of land (farms) received or held by the settlers not long after the founding. For the remaining settlements one can try to fix it only probably, from the information on the number and character of the hearths in general and of the farming hearths (farms) in these settlements in the years 1789 and 1791. Multiplying these numbers by hypothetical holdings of one huba or half a huba makes it possible to fix the lower and upper limits of the area of their arable land.

In the sources on the Olęder settlements in Greater Poland the area of the holdings of land assigned to the settlers was mostly given in włóki (łany), mostly called hubas (from German Hufe), or more rarely ślady. The włóka, as a unit of measure of arable land, was the basis for fixing the amount of rents (in money and in kind) and of labour services. It was identified with the area of a full, economically independent farm. Hubas (włóki, łany), however, varied, and their area also depended on the measure by which they were laid out. Usually this was the Chełmno włóka (earlier also called the Flemish or the Środa łan), used in four variants of different area. This włóka was divided into 30 morgen, the morgen = 300 (30x10) square rods. The rod, also called in the sources laska or rózga, often varied in size, however; it ranged from 7½ ells (the rod of the new or Warsaw measure of 1764) to 9 ells (the margrave's rod). The sources mention ells of the Chełmno, Polish (old), German and Poznań measure, but do not define these measures more closely. Besides, the ell itself, used within the same measure of area, such as the various kinds of włóka, also often varied in size. The constitution of the Diet of 1764 unifying measures fixed the Warsaw ell, as a measure of length, at 24 inches (59.55 cm). A włóka of 30 morgen, each of 300 square rods measured with this ell, would equal 17.95 ha, that is 179,550 m² After 1764, in spite of this unification, ploughland was still mostly measured with the Chełmno rod, which moreover varied, most often of 8 and 9 ells, most rarely of 7½ ells. The Chełmno ell,
chodyla2015/81:
probably the same as the old Polish or the German ell named in the sources, was somewhat shorter than the Crown ell of the new measure of 1764 and came to 57.6 cm. The area of a włóka measured with a rod of 7½ ells comes to 16.80 (more exactly 16.7962) ha, with one of 8 ells to 19.20, with one of 8½ ells to 21.60, and with one of 9 ells to as much as 24.20 ha. Exceptionally, measures of area other (at least in name) than the Chełmno włóka were used in Olęder settlements. One Warsaw ell as a measure of area, in turn, came to 0.354666 m². Land was sometimes measured in ślady identical with the Chełmno włóka (huba), but also sometimes equal to almost or exactly two such włóki (that is, of 50–60 Chełmno morgen). In isolated cases the sources mention land being measured with the Magdeburg rod, but there is no information on how many ells it contained. In the second half of the eighteenth century, in the districts of Kalisz, Konin and Pyzdry, land was often measured in the "rydlandska" measure, that is probably the Rhenish (the name probably comes from the word Reihnland), with a rod of 7½ ells. The Rhenish rod, from 1816 also called the Magdeburg rod (and so probably the same as the one mentioned earlier) or the Prussian rod (equal to about 3.766 m), was the measure generally in force (by a royal order of 1750) and the most widely used in Prussia, and from 1775 it was in force in all the provinces of the country except Silesia and the Polish lands newly annexed in the First Partition. In settlements founded with settlers coming from Silesia, especially up to 1740, holdings were also measured, at the settlers' wish, with the Imperial rod, probably equal to 8½ ells.

Here is a survey of the Olęder settlements founded in the Pyzdry Forest by their area, especially their arable land, in the measures given in the sources, by their district and in alphabetical order.

In the district of Pyzdry, then, the area can be grasped for only 3 of the 5 Olęder settlements.

In the Ciążeńskie or Zarzeczne Ol., in the Ciążeń key of the estates of the bishopric of Poznań, 4 settlers received 3 włóki in all, probably of the Chełmno measure, so that on average each of them would have had a farm of 22½ morgen.

The data quoted above for the greater part of the Olęder settlements that arose in the Pyzdry Forest show that their land was given in włóki laid out mostly in the Crown measure, that is measured with the rod of 8½ ells, and in the rydlandska (Rhenish) measure, in which the morgen were laid out with the rod of 7½ ells. The number and sizes of the holdings (farms) in 37 of the 58 Olęder settlements founded in the Pyzdry Forest, as they stood at the founding and sometimes also later, do not give a full statistical picture of their size at one time common to them all. This can be created only from the data of the tables of hearths and of hearth tax of 1789, drawn up in the course of the first census of population in Poland and the second in Europe and checked in 1790, and from the tables of farming hearths of 1791, drawn up in connection with the grain levy that the Diet voted on them. Since these are sometimes given jointly for one or even more settlements belonging to the same landed estate, and are sometimes even missing, their state in some settlements has to be established indirectly and by estimate (resorting to other sources, in the form of information from the foundation charters, the tables of hearths and hearth tax of 1775 (with suitable corrections), the survey of the royal estates of 1789, and the inventories and revisions of church estates of the years 1791-1793). Moreover, detailed tables of hearths, which make it possible to grasp their functional-economic structure, survive only for some of the Olęder settlements that concern us here, those in the districts of Pyzdry and Kalisz. For the district of Konin they have to be established indirectly from the table of the hearth tax of 1789 or the table of the grain levy of 1791. Before we proceed, however, to set out the numbers of hearths in general and of farming hearths of all the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest, taken from the sources named or estimated on the basis of them, and to interpret their numbers and in part the structure mentioned, some explanations are needed.

First, it should be said that in the census tables (protocols, sheets) of hearths of 1789, by a hearth in general (dym), treated as the unit of account of the tax called the hearth tax (podymne), was understood, in the countryside but also in the towns, above all, but not only, a farm with its dwelling and farm buildings, or, more exactly, a farmstead. For this term covered cottages in the village and in the futory [outlying farmsteads] and (or) distant from the village – with one farmer, but sometimes also with two farmers, and also the garden (ogrodowe) – smallholders' – ones (with land and garden or without land and garden), craftsmen's, manufacturing, and manor and church hearths, mills (water and wind), breweries, inns and Jewish hearths. The manor and parsonage buildings, on the other hand, of which there were none in the purely Olęder villages, and which in the mixed ones belonged legally to their labour-service parts and not to their Olęder rent-paying parts, were counted as one hearth.

Second, it should be said that by the Diet's resolution, in accordance with the text of the constitution of the Diet of 1791, every hearth whose holder or inhabitant sowed land with grain, regardless of the nature of the estate and of whether he paid the offering of 10 or 20 gr., was to be considered a farming hearth subject to the grain levy for the army (in the amount of 2 korzec of rye and 4 korzec of oats). Because of the differences in the size of their land, farming hearths were allowed to be burdened with the tax in different amounts,

So on average there would have been 11.224 hearths to a settlement. For the greater part of these settlements the number of farms showed a certain constancy compared with the initial state of the period of their founding, shown above; for the smaller part, however, it varied, most often upwards, because further settlers were brought in, or because of the increasingly varied social and economic structure of the villages, through the division of farms by inheritance.

There was a wide range in the number of farms among the Olęder villages. It can be grasped directly for the 38 settlements given separately. Among them there were: very small settlements, of 2-5 hearths – 9; small ones, of 6-10 hearths – 11; middling ones, of 11-15 hearths – 5; larger than middling, of 16-20 hearths – 8; large, of 21-25 hearths, only 2; and very large, of 26 hearths, only 1. The number of their hearths ranged from 6 to 33, so that on average one of them would have had from 3 to 16.5 hearths.

we leave aside 2 breweries, 6 inns and 2 craftsmen's hearths, hearths with 1 farmer decidedly predominated, found in all 15 Olęder villages, 636 in all. Hearths with 2 farmers, 37 in all, were found in only 5 settlements, garden hearths with land and garden, 16 in number, in 3 settlements, and those without land and garden, 2 in number, in 1 settlement. Unfortunately there are no data on the structure of the other 43 Olęder villages. It may be supposed, however, among other things from the social structure of the inhabitants, that not only in these 16 settlements but also in most of the Olęder settlements that concern us, hearths-farms with one farmer predominated, that is of one or half a włóka (full and half peasant farms, kmiece, rolnicze and półkmiece, półrolnicze), and only a very small part of them were smaller ones, with two farmers, and smallholders' ones with land and garden, and rather rarely lodgers' ones.

According to the tables of the grain levy (in rye and oats) for the army of 1791 for the districts of Pyzdry, Konin and Kalisz, there were 662 "self-tilling", that is farming, hearths in the 58 Olęder villages of the Pyzdry Forest. A comparison of the data on the farming hearths of 1791 with the information on the total numbers of hearths of 1789 shows that in all there were 1.662% more farming hearths two years later. Since, however, the numbers of hearths for 34 settlements are estimates, the totals of hearths of both categories need correcting. We do this by raising the total of 662 farming hearths by 6.34%, that is by 42 hearths, since that was the difference between farming hearths and hearths in general shown by the complete statistical data surviving for a representative sample of rural settlements of the districts of Kalisz, Pyzdry and Kościan. As a result of this addition we obtain 704 hearths. By adding this sum of 42 hearths to the 649 hearths in general (since most of the estimated numbers in the first column of the table repeat the number of farming hearths as a minimum), we obtain the number of 691 hearths in general, which should be taken as more realistic for the year 1789. By 1791 their number, in keeping with a slightly higher annual rate of natural increase, could have grown by at least 1%, that is by 6 persons, that is to about 699 persons in all. The literature shows, however, that more than 98% of the inhabitants of the Olęder settlements were occupied in farming. This will be discussed further below. So probably almost the same, or a similar, percentage of the hearths in the 58 Olęder settlements founded in the Pyzdry Forest were farming hearths (farms) in 1789. For the farms of innkeepers and teachers, which were the main source of their holders' living, were not counted as farming hearths.

The settlement charters of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest contain, in principle, no information on their layout and the character of their buildings. Only in the foundation charters cited above, for the Orlińskie D. and M. Ol. of 1784 and the Białobłockie Ol. of 1787, is it said that their inhabitants are "...to build properly and on a line", that is to create a village in the form of a street village. chodyla2015/93:
founded in other areas of Greater Poland, however, their layout was of three kinds: 1) mostly spontaneous (sometimes growing gradually), 2) planned, made at one stroke on the initiative of the feudal lord, or 3) inherited (as in the case of Wrąbczynek). Within each of these ways of founding Olęder villages, mostly according to their form on the ground, shaped chiefly by factors of the geographical environment, there were three types of spatial form: 1) the lowland settlement adapted to the relief and the water conditions of the land, the row village (rzędówka), a village with compact, more concentrated (a regular street village) or looser (an irregular street village) buildings; 2) the loose, scattered settlement (in the form of larger or smaller irregular clusters of farmsteads, sometimes with a green or a pond); and 3) the mixed settlement, combining some elements of the first two types. The more or less compact settlement, that is the row village (also called the marsh row village), and the loose, scattered settlement were, in principle, two new types of village layout brought by Olęder settlement into Greater Poland, and the most widespread in it. Row villages – street villages with strips of land holding various kinds of farmland (fields, meadows, pastures and others) – formed in the conditions of Greater Poland one, two, but sometimes three straight, bent or broken rows, lines of farmsteads (farms), placed in various ways in relation to each other (parallel and perpendicular), more or less concentrated and of various lengths (mostly 1–1.5 km), much less, however, than in Royal Prussia.

The layout of most Olęder settlements in the period closest to their founding can be established only from the later Map of the Quartermaster General's staff of the Army of the Kingdom of Poland of 1839, and from the modern Map of Poland of the Surveyor General of the Country at a scale of 1:100,000 and the tourist map of the Pyzdry Forest at 1:55,000. From an analysis of these maps, taking into account the fact that as a result of the enfranchisement reform of 1864 the layout of these rent-paying villages without a demesne farm did not change fundamentally, it can be said that of the 58 Old Polish Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest, 9 settlements were marsh row villages, founded where marshy and dry land met, on mixed ground, with rows of buildings in various arrangements, sometimes partly scattered (Białobłockie Ol., Cekowskie St. Ol., Gadowskie Ol., Kazimierskie St. and Nw. Ol., Lisewskie Ol., Luśnie Ol., Myszakowskie Ol., Piskory Ol.); 2 settlements were regular and irregular street villages founded on mixed ground (Dębniałki Ol., Grodziec Ol.); as many as 40 settlements were loose, scattered settlements; and 7 were mixed (Białobłockie Ol., Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol., Orlińskie St. and Nw. Ol., Wierzchy Ol. and Wrąbczynek).

The layout of the Olęder settlements (made at the founding on raw root, or taken over from older settlements), the network of roads, the arrangement and system of the land, and sometimes the placing of the buildings, shaped their geometric forms. Accordingly, from the point of view of their physiognomy, the Olęder villages represented various types and subtypes of form.

Burszta, Od osady słowiańskiej do wsi współczesnej [From the Slavic settlement to the modern village], pp. 108–109, 114–118; the same, Osadnictwo i kształty wsi [Settlement and the forms of villages], [in:] Kultura ludowa Wielkopolski [The folk culture of Greater Poland], ed. the same, vol. I, Poznań 1960, pp. 31- 105; Z. Chodyła, Osadnictwo olęderskie w Wielkopolsce (1597-1793).
chodyla2015/94:
The form of these villages was also affected by the layout of the fields (arable land, meadows, pastures) and the system of tilling them. As to the latter, the three-field system in the Olęder villages was, to a far smaller degree than in the labour-service villages, a communal three-field system, that is one tied to the so-called compulsion of the field (przymus polny or niwowy) for the whole village, under which each peasant had in a given year to sow, on one of the fields of his farm, lying in one line with and next to the like fields of other farms, particular crops (winter or spring crops) or to leave that field fallow, according to the decision of the whole village community. In the compact Olęder settlements, in the regular and irregular row villages, but also in those of various other forms, often, and in the scattered, loose ones generally, the individual three-field system was used. This followed from the predominance in them of the łan (strip) layout. With such a layout of the land each settler had his field in one piece (block), usually on a long strip of land (a rectangle), and tilled it as he saw fit, independently of his neighbours. These strips lay parallel to each other and ran from the middle of the village to its boundary. A characteristic feature of the łan layout, which distinguished the villages in which it was found from those with the niwa (open-field) layout, was also that each farm had its own field road running the length of its whole strip of land. The łan layout of many Olęder villages came about because they were founded on forest clearings, where the land lay in just such a way and the soils varied, or on so-called pustkowia (isolated holdings), where the land was brought into use gradually. In the latter case settlement most often began with one, two or a few scattered farms, distant from each other, which of course had no conditions for the communal three-field system.

The layout of the Olęder villages, especially their internal layout, was affected by the types of their homesteads, their farmsteads. Of the four types of farmstead – sets of buildings (distinguished by the placing of the masses of the dwelling and farm buildings, and by their position in relation to the roads, the watercourses and each other) – proper to the traditions of the country and place the settlers came from, the most widespread in Greater Poland, including the settlements founded in the eighteenth century in the Pyzdry Forest, was the fourth type: the scattered farmstead, most often with an arcaded cottage (in time this type of building disappeared and is not found today), set with its gable or its wall to the road, and with free-standing farm buildings, put up of wooden logs, in post-and-plank or, more rarely, log construction, and also, in large numbers, of clay and bog iron ore. In general people built with the material that was most readily available and cheapest. All the buildings (house, cowshed-pigsty, stable, barn, granary) were put up separately, scattered, most often on a quadrangular plan; barns were sometimes placed apart, beyond the road. The commonest pattern was one of two or three buildings: the cottage, the barn, and a livestock building (made up of pigsty, stable, cowshed and cart shed). At the same time, though more rarely, there were free-standing buildings such as sheepfolds, sheds and cart sheds.

O tworzeniu się krajobrazu osadniczego ziem polskich i rozplanowań wsi [From the Slavic settlement to the modern village. On the making of the settlement landscape of the Polish lands and of village layouts], Wrocław 1958.

chodyla2015/95:
At the beginning of the clearing of wooded and overgrown land, the inhabitants of the Olęder settlements put up temporary huts (budy) to live in, and then, still within the free years, they were bound to put up cottages. Huts are mentioned in the foundation charters and other sources for the Cekowskie St. Ol., the Przespolewskie Ol., Świdle Nowa Kolonia and the Trąbczyńskie St. Ol.. The charters for some settlements stated that the settlers were to put up their buildings before their free years ran out (Gadowskie St. Ol.), within a set time of two or four years (Białobłockie Ol., Orlińskie D. and M., Lubieńskie Ol.), properly (Cekowskie Nw. Ol.), as quickly as possible, properly and "on a line" (that is keeping to the layout of a street village), in the first case under the supervision of the sołtys and assessor (Grądy St. and Nw. Ol.), within a set time of several years under threat of inspection and a money fine (Grądy St. and Nw. Ol., Borowieckie St. and Nw. and Konarskie Ol.). Such orders arose from the dawdling or laziness, or the limited means for investment, of some Olęders, as the case of the Trąbczyńskie St. and Nw. Ol. confirms. The area of the land assigned for the homestead, that is for the buildings of a farm, was stated only once, in the charter for the Mycielińskie Ol., at 1 morgen (Magdeburg?).

In the buildings and layout of the Olęder villages in the Pyzdry Forest, most of which were wholly or partly inhabited by people of the Protestant confession, important elements were the buildings for worship that were also educational (schools – houses of prayer, later churches), and the burial grounds, which lay on the whole on the edges of the villages, on hilly, wooded or poor land, and which will be discussed more fully in the last chapter of this study.

In keeping with the differences in the size of the 58 Olęder villages in the Pyzdry Forest by the number of hearths in the years 1789-1791, their population too differed at this time. Only for some of them do we know, from foundation charters or other sources, the numbers of the settler farmers (the "heads" of families) at the time of their founding or in the following years. For most of them (50) these numbers, with their structure, can be established at one time on the basis of the data of the detailed tables of population of 1789 and the record of the visitation of the deanery of Konin of 1790-1791, and for the remaining 8 settlements (1 in the district of Kalisz and 7 in the district of Konin) approximately, by multiplying the previously estimated numbers of their hearths by the population index we have established, 6.05 persons per hearth.

Tab. 3c shows that the population of 20 of the 28 Olęder settlements in the district of Konin, 1,337 persons in all, was made up demographically of 654 males and 683 females. Adults numbered 782 persons, and children and young people (described as boys and girls without division by age) 482 persons. By confession, the 1,337 inhabitants of 20 of the 28 settlements were as follows: there were 6 settlements with an exclusively dissenting population, 385 in all (Lutheran, and perhaps to a small degree Reformed), 4 with a Catholic population, 210 in all, and 10 settlements with a mixed population, Catholic and Protestant (almost exclusively Lutheran), with 365 Catholics and 377 dissenters in all. So in all these settlements there would have lived 575 Catholics and 762 dissenters in all, that is Protestants – Lutherans, and perhaps in two or three of these settlements also Reformed. The former would thus have made up 43.01% and the latter 56.99% of their whole population. In the remaining 8 settlements of the district of Konin, for which the demographic and confessional composition is not known from the sources, there lived, according to estimates made in the same way as for such settlements in the districts of Pyzdry and Kalisz, 522 persons. In all, 1,859 persons would have lived in all 28 Olęder villages of this district.

Summing up the results of the calculations given in Tab. 3a, b, c, it must be said that about 3,815 persons in all lived in the 58 Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest in the years 1789–1790, of whom 469 in 5 settlements in the district of Pyzdry, 1,457 in 25 settlements in the district of Kalisz, and 1,859 in 28 settlements in the district of Konin. The statistical average number of inhabitants per settlement would have been 65.77 persons. In the 45 settlements for which the demographic structure of their inhabitants is known there lived 3,154 persons, 1,707 (50.32%) of them male and 1,685 (49.68%) female. Of these 3,154 persons, 449 (234 male and 215 female) lived in 3 settlements of the district of Pyzdry, 1,368 persons (691 male and 677 female) lived in 22 settlements of the district of Kalisz, and 1,337 persons (654 male and 683 female) lived in 20 settlements of the district of Konin. For 13 settlements (2 in the district of Pyzdry, 8 in the district of Konin and 3 in the district of Kalisz) the structure by sex is not shown in the sources that survive and are available to us. The demographic structure of 25 Olęder settlements (3 in the district of Pyzdry and 22 in the district of Kalisz) looked different again by the criteria adopted in the census of 1789, with the population divided into men, married men and widowers; sons (that is boys of pre-conscription age, under 15, and those subject to the conscription register, aged 15 and over); białogłowy (married women and widows); and daughters, that is girls, in the sense, it seems, not only of persons young in age but of unmarried women in general, from infancy to old age. Thus in 3 of the 5 Olęder villages in the district of Pyzdry, of a total of 449 inhabitants, 88 were men, 108 sons under 15, 38 sons aged 15 and over,

In 22 of the 25 Olęder villages of the district of Kalisz, with a total population of 1,368 persons, 309 were men, then 304 sons under 15, then 78 sons aged 15 and over, then 282 women, and 395 daughters. So in the 25 Olęder settlements of the districts of Pyzdry and Kalisz, of a total of 1,817 persons of their population, 397 were men, 412 sons under 15, 116 sons aged 15 and over, 371 women and 521 daughters. Among these five categories of the demographic composition of the population the category of sons aged 15 and over was undoubtedly understated, probably because of the threat of conscription into the army. Perhaps some of them were counted among the sons under 15, whose number seems somewhat too high, especially given the high mortality of children under 5 in former times. In a somewhat simplified form (without dividing the boys into age groups) the demographic composition of the population of 20 of the 28 Olęder settlements in the district of Konin can be grasped; according to the lists of 1790-1791 it is given in the records of the visitation of the parishes of the deanery of Konin already mentioned above. In these lists the population of the settlements was divided into four categories: men, women, boys and girls. Adding up the data in this source for the 20 Olęder settlements that concern us, it can be said that of the total of 1,337 inhabitants (in this case probably covering only the Olęder farmers with the members of their families, leaving out the farm servants and servants and other categories of landless people) men numbered 427 persons, women 428, boys 227 and girls 255. Summing up the information above on the numerical relation of the four demographic categories of the population of 45 Olęder settlements in the three districts of Pyzdry, Konin and Kalisz, leaving aside the differences of age among the boys, it can be said that of their 3,124 inhabitants for whom such a division is known, 824 persons were men, 598 women, 956 boys and 756 daughters (girls and unmarried women of various ages).

While the size of the population of each, and of all, of the 58 Olęder villages in the Pyzdry Forest, and the demographic structure of most of them, 45, can be established exactly or by estimate, it is harder to give exact statistics of their social, property and occupational structure. It can be grasped in the detailed census tables for only 25 of them (3 in the district of Pyzdry and 22 in the district of Kalisz). There were in all in them 1,518 farmers, that is Olęders proper with the members of their families, farmers and rent-paying cottagers, who can in principle be regarded as one and the same social and occupational category, 50 lodgers, 7 craftsmen, 13 innkeepers and tapsters, 102 farm servants and servants, 68 luźni (landless people) and 59 "other" persons. The village community of the settlements, as far as the Olęder farmers were concerned, was internally differentiated in property already at the founding, according to the size of the holdings received, and still more so a dozen or several dozen years after it, when farms were sometimes divided into smaller ones through inheritance. The differences of property were also tied to the financial means of the settlers themselves, in the form of the size of the entry money they had to, and could, pay for the holdings of land of a given size that they received for perpetual use.

As to the confessional and ethnic composition of the inhabitants of the 58 Olęder settlements founded in the years 1746-1791 in the Pyzdry Forest, it must be said that it was

This follows from the statistical data for 22 Olęder villages (2 in the district of Pyzdry and 20 in the district of Konin), already given above in Tab. 3a and 3c, contained in the records of the church visitation of the deanery of Konin of 1790-1791, and also from the direct and indirect information on this question in the foundation charters of these settlements and other sources concerning them, especially such as inspections, inventories and revisions, and sometimes also the census tables of 1789, which have partly been given above and will partly be presented below.

Thus it is known that in the three oldest settlements, neighbours of one another, in the district of Konin – the Trąbczyńskie St. and Nw. Ol. and the Luśnie Ol. (founded in 1746 and 1754) – Catholics and Lutherans settled, the latter predominating. This follows from the names given in the commission decree, Kinos and Meller, and from the list of population of 1790-1791 in the record of the visitation of the deanery of Konin. In the Łazy Ol., probably also founded about 1754, and certainly before 1789, only Catholics lived in 1790.

In the Przespolewskie Ol. in the district of Kalisz at least several German settlers, Lutherans, settled before 1750 and in 1772, 3 of them known by name: Marcin Schmarschel, Fryderyk Jakobeck, Marcin Lehmann The decree of the commission court of 1779 on the tradition (judicial handing over) of a part of the Przespolew estate in payment of a debt of its owner, Tadeusz Zaremba, to the creditor Tomasz Moraczewski names 3 Olęders living in a part of this settlement, Poroże Wielkie: Marcin Smaża, Andrzej Szuldz and Frydrych Jakopczyk; two of them probably the same as those named above in the charter of 1772. The inventory of (a part of) the Przespolewskie Ol. of 1785 names 22 Olęders with names that are (except perhaps for one Polish one) undoubtedly German. Here they are, with their first names, in the forms written in this source: Krystian Lekner, Krystian Werner, Mateusz Bruchajzer, Wawrzyniec Fagen, Balcer Gotfryd, Krystian Szulc, Józef Kubs, Kr[z]ysztof Mager, Henryk Draier, Adam Walkier, Krystjan Macanka, Jan Raych, Wojciech Walle, Jan Walkier, Bernard Caydler, Gotfryd Daubyc, Jan Perszel, Jan Caydler, Wojciech Frank, Kasper Waber, Marcin Leyman, Bogusław Geerszling. Marcin Schmarschel and Fryderyk Jakobeck/Jakubek/Jakobczyk, named above, are not among them.

In the Lisewskie Ol. (Olsz), in the district of Pyzdry, founded after 1751 and before 1765, the existing Polish and Catholic population probably lived, though in one or two cases also, it seems, German people. The names and first names of the inhabitants of the Lisewskie Ol. are given only in the registers of the parish of Szymanowice. As living in this settlement there were first entered there, under the year 1775, in turn: Weronika Pankowska, Wojciech Panek, and Stanisław and Maria Krzywiński. In 1776 the names of Elżbieta Pankow, Gertruda Panek and Jan Łamek were entered in them, in 1779 Agnieszka and Łukasz Nowacki, in 1780 Grzegorz

and Maria Dąbrowski, later, in 1793, Feliks and Mara Koźlak were recorded in them, and in 1794 Józef and Maria Broniarczyk. The form of the names seems to show that the population of this settlement was mixed, Polish-German, the German part, being in the minority, becoming assimilated fairly quickly, to judge from the change of a name (Pankow to Pankowski).

In the Ciemierowa/Tomickie/Szymanowickie Stare Ol., in the district of Kalisz, which arose before 1755-1756, it can be inferred from the form of the names (Cyft, Rotenberg(er), Dresler, Klim, Sypniewski, Vaber and others) and from the baptismal registers of the settlers' children that they were Catholics, but perhaps partly also Protestant Lutherans, mostly Germans, but also Poles.

In the Zbierskie Ol., in the district of Kalisz (founded in 1761), 14 settlers with German and Polish names, Lutherans, were settled. Under the text of the foundation charter of that year the following settlers are named: Andrzej Hert, Bogusław Cherman (Herman), Marcin Krol, Krzysztof Szulc, Maciej Góra, Marcin Szulc, Krystian Kurtz, Paweł Hauman (or Hawman), Krzysztof Bonig, Marcin Weys, Marcin Reszka, Godfri(e)d(t) Wuntrach, Jędrzej Kamyszek, Krystian Ryska, the widow of Maciej Tak, settled in the years 1761-1769, three of them only temporarily. The inventory of the Zbiersk estate belonging to Gąsiorowski, royal chamberlain, drawn up in 1771 by the married couple Przespolewski, names 6 Olęders (Marcin Szulc, Marcin Krol, Maciej Góra, Maciejowa Takowa, Krzysztof Szulc and Jan Krzysztof Wajstak) and the amount of their dues, and 3 Olęders not yet paying them. The inventory of the same estate of 1775 found, among other things, 14 farmers in the Zbierskie Ol. By confession they were Protestants, perhaps even Reformed, since, as was mentioned above, they used the Reformed church at Żychlin, though it is not out of the question that they were Lutherans going to that church because it was close to them.

In the Wielołęka Ol. in the district of Konin, founded before or in 1767, there settled, according to the charters of 1770, Jan Czarneski, Sebastian Rest, Walenty Ginter, Bogusław Sztruma, Wojciech August Ralcer, Arnold Jan Kimel, Krzysztof Fryze, Bogumił Wondrak, Krystian Kiejzer. According to the inventory of the properties of Grodziec and Królików of 1779, 15 farmers lived in this settlement (14 of them named with first names and surnames of German sound, 1 innkeeper and 1 szkolny, that is teacher, not named). In 1790, 168 dissenters, that is Lutherans, lived in this village.

In the royal Cekowskie St. Ol. in the district of Kalisz, 9 settlers were settled in 1768 (2 with Polish names – Kazimierz Kuczka, wójt, and Andrzej Warmiński – and 7 with German names), Lutherans and Catholics, described as people "of the Olęder estate"; some of them most probably came from abroad, since the foundation charter guaranteed them the right to sell the farms granted them ...should any of them not like it in this country.

chodyla2015/108:
In the Cekowskie Nowe Ol., or Prażuchy, their neighbours, which arose on the same royal lease of Ceków in 1774 and 1780, at least 8 Lutheran colonists, with German and Polish names, settled according to the settlement contract, namely: Wojciech Pruchno, Krzysztof Stefan (sołtys), Gotfryd Reszka, Krystian Kurc, Krystian Heinc, Frydrych Heinc, Gotfryd Szwander, Jan Paszkowski. Later, in the years 1782, 1785 and 1787, there were settled: Kups, Hertel, Puntzler, Krzysztof Kowal, Gajzler and Grynberg.

In the 6 Olęder settlements founded before 1770 and in 1771-1772 (and re-founded in 1787 and 1789) in the district of Konin, on the noble estates of Grodziec and Królików, the population was mixed in nation and confession. In the Białobłockie Ol. at least several colonists settled, Lutherans with German names. The number, names, nationality and confession of those brought in to settle in 1787 are unknown. In 1790, 157 Catholics and 48 dissenters lived here. In 1792 the Olęders Józef and Jakub Hersa, brothers, and Andrzej Langa/Lange lived in this village.

In the Borowieckie St. and Nw. Ol., the settlers, settled in an unknown number, bore German and Polish names and were Lutherans and Catholics by confession. According to the inventory of the properties of Grodziec and Królików of 1779, 27 farmers lived in the Borowieckie Ol., named with their first names and surnames (4 of them of Polish sound). In 1790 there were 52 Catholics and 42 dissenters in this settlement.

In the Grójeckie or Grodzieckie Olędry there settled, in an unknown number, probably 10 farmers, Germans – Lutherans.

In the Grądy Stare and Nowe lived settlers with German and Polish names, in 1790 exclusively Lutherans, 100 in number.

In Konary Ol., in turn, whose locator, that is establisher, was Jan Kimel, mentioned above, sołtys of the Wielołęka Ol., settlers with German and Polish names were settled, in 1790 exclusively Lutherans, 81 in number).

In two settlements founded in the district of Konin about 1771 and in 1776, but on the church estates of the convent of the Order of St Clare (the Franciscan nuns) of Kalisz, namely in the Gliny Olędry and the Lubieńskie Ol., lived Poles and Catholics. In the foundation charter for the latter settlement the settlers are described as honest Olęders ...of the honest faith and rites of the Roman Catholic church..., being Poles now and hereafter..

In Poroże Małe, in the district of Kalisz, which arose in or before 1775, settled settlers whose names and confession are unknown.

In the Kuszyńskie or Jaszczurowo Olędry, in turn, also in the district of Kalisz, 7 colonists settled, 4 with German and 3 with Polish names, Protestant Lutherans. They took up "the forest or deserta" (empty land) Jaszczurowo, belonging to Kosmów. The settlement agreement was first made with the founder in 1776 by two representatives of the colonists, Michał Gesse and Krzysztof Malus (Mikosz?), and then in the years 1776-1781 3 more settlers were added to it: Marcin Makosz, Paweł Dysza and Piotr Jering.

In the years 1776 and 1781 Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol. were founded. In Wrąbczynek at least 4 settlers settled (3 with German names and 1 with a Polish one), Protestant Lutherans. The settlers of the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol., Jakub Krysa/Kriese (sołtys), Wojciech Kurtz and Krzysztof Szultz (assessors), were settled on overgrown, probably wooded, land, since the second konotacja contained the information: Since the Rąbczynek Holendry, their free years for the rumunek being out, have today received the law under which they are to remain in their dues, so that these too, settled together with them, are not raised to higher dues than the Holędrzy, they are ascribed an equalisation with those, so that they [belong] to the dues set out here.

In the asekuracja of 20 XI 1781 of S. Dobrski, plenipotentiary of Turno, starost of Pietrzyków, besides confirming that the labour services had been done, the Olęders are promised that they will obtain the royal law (that is the king's confirmation of the foundation charter issued by the starost-tenant) once they have paid a contribution for the purpose, and it is stated that the Germans, who have been measured out on the lord's demesne farm, will be bound to pay the remaining half of the grungielt. In the Wrąbczyńskie Ol. 3 settlers settled, with German and Polish names, Protestant Lutherans. Settled on the Wrąpczyn wood, three new inhabitants give fl. [silver złoty] 32; according to the charter of 1776, and also the Rąbczyn Holendry, who hold half of the tenth [9½] huba cleared from the deserta in the forest, with Bogusław Szeyder, sołtys, Jakub Wróbel and Michał Szpryngier, assessors.

In the charter for the Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol., set up in 1777 and then before and in 1784 in the district of Konin, 3 settlers with German names are named: Walenty Ginter (probably the same as the Olęder who had settled earlier, in the years 1767-1770, in Wielołęka), Bogusław Gryger and Jonat Zamer, the sołtys and assessors; but others with German and Polish names, Lutherans and Catholics, also lived there.

In the Kazimierskie or Niniewskie St. and Nw. Ol., founded in the same district in the years 1782 and 1790, lived Germans, Lutherans, who left behind a church and a cemetery. The locator of the latter was Georg [Jerzy] Müller.

Settlers of the same nation and confession settled in the Dzierzbińskie – Zamęty and Zdanowiec Olędry, also founded in the district of Kalisz, in 1783, by one foundation charter, but forming separate communes. Two settlers, with names of German sound, are known from the charter: Marcin Szynwald and Jan Fitz, Lutherans. Their confession is also shown by the grant in the charter of land for the bakałarze (teachers/schools) and for a common cemetery "for the dissenters".

In the Plewińskie (Stare) and Nowe, or Kuźnickie, Olędry (founded before 1783 and in 1793), in the district of Kalisz, 19 settlers settled (14 with German and 5 with Polish names), Lutherans. They included Bogusłw Werner and Paweł Pus, who made the foundation agreement with the founder, Antoni Kawiecki, on behalf of the whole commune, and Krystian Hek, Rejmand Gaysler, Marcin Nyps, Jędrzej Fire, Bogumił Konczak, Krystian Vizur (?), Marcin Tulik (or Talik), Jan Reska, Bogusław Lang, Bogusław Litman, Samuel Bigiel, Jan Gierat, Bogusław Stary Werner, Maciej Piwecki, Jan Ściernisko, Bogusław Glapa and Krzysztof Figa. Their Protestant confession is confirmed by the village's receiving land for a szkolny (teacher).

In the settlements set up in 1783, Dębniałki or the Bolimowskie/Brudzewskie Ol. and the Piskory Olędry, in the district of Kalisz, the first joint settlement charter of 1784 names only these settlers: 2 with German names (Mikołaj Hayschler, sołtys, and Michał Helman, assessor) and 1 with a Polish name (Franciszek Borowy, assessor), Catholics and Lutherans. There were, however, more settlers (6 Olęders received free years to 1791 and 2 to 1792); the dissenters were also to receive plots for a burial ground and for a teacher (school), common to both settlements. It is also known that 11 settlers with German and Polish names, Catholics and Protestant Lutherans, were settled in the Piskory or Lipeckie Olędry.

chodyla2015/111:
In the Oborskie Stare Ol., or Wronów, and the Nowe Ol., which arose in 1783 and before 1788 in the district of Kalisz, Protestants, Germans, also or exclusively lived.

In the settlements of the Orlińskie (Orlina) Małe and Duże Olędry, in the district of Konin, 19 settlers settled in 1784 (most with Polish names), Germans and Poles, Catholics and Lutherans. They included among others: Bogusław Krol, Michał Arent, Franciszek Maciejowski, Maciej Walczak, Maciej Jarmuszkiewicz, Wawrzyniec Kośmicki, Micha Wynt, Krystian Tenus, Johannn Samuel Weychnert(?), Franciszek Organiściak, Grzegorz Gojak (?) with their families. In 1790 there were 29 Catholics and 36 Protestants.

In the Lisieckie Ol., in the starosty of Konin, in the Lisiec key (founded in 1783-1784 and before 1789), lived Germans, dissenters (20 in number in 1791), perhaps of the Reformed confession.

The inhabitants of Stara Huta – the Grójeckie Olędry (founded perhaps as early as about 1777, and certainly in the years 1785 and 1789), in the same district, were Germans and probably also Poles, Catholics, 51 persons in 1790.

In the Siąszyckie or Złotowskie Olędry, which arose probably about 1786, and certainly before 1790, one of the two settlers known from the sources, Łukasz Łyszkowski, was an emigrant who had come back from abroad. Both settlers were probably Catholics.

In the Mycielińskie Stare and Nowe Olędry (today Kazala St. and Nw.), founded in the years 1786-1788 in the district of Kalisz, in the parish of Kościelec, on the noble estate of Mycielin, whose locators were Jakub Tonka and Godfryd Legner, 6 settlers in all settled (1 with a German name, 3-4 with Polish names and 1 whose name is unknown), most probably Protestants, since they were to receive land for a school.

In the Stropieszyńskie, or Radzany and Gostynie, Olędry, in the district of Kalisz (founded in the years 1787 and 1791), the settlers were Germans and Protestant Lutherans. They were expressly described as Germans in the foundation charter. Their nationality is also confirmed, indirectly, by a separate charter for the honest Marcin Werner and his successors for the Bugaj inn, which lay on the Kalisz road, binding him, should the property be sold, to present as purchaser a man who knew the Polish language. The Protestant confession of the inhabitants of these settlements is shown by the assignment in the foundation charter of 6 XII 1787 of land for the szkolny (the teacher). The foundation charter of 1791, which at the same time confirmed and supplemented the first, also added to the commune the married couple Józef and Elżbieta Gierecki, manor servants, settled under a separate charter on ½ huba of ploughland [most probably Catholics and Poles]. In granting the Olęders at the same time land for a school and a cemetery, the charter confirmed their German nationality and Protestant confession.

chodyla2015/112:
In the Ciążeńskie Olędry, on the other hand, created before 1788-1789 in the district of Pyzdry, in the Ciążeń key of the mensal estates of the bishopric of Poznań, there lived, according to the revision of the Ciążeń key of 1793, 4 Olęders (3 with Polish names: Jan Macieje[w]ski, Mateusz Czajka, Marcin Ławicki, and 1 with a German name: Augustyn Maytler), Poles, Catholics.

The inhabitants of 8 smaller Olęder settlements that arose before 1789, and at the latest before 1792, in the district of Konin, varied in confession and nation. In 1791 in Bukowa/Bukowe (Bukowe Budy), or the Łomowskie Olędry, lived only Catholics, 74 in number; in Imielno lived 21 Catholics and 42 dissenters; in the Myszakówko Olędry 16 dissenters; in Stara Huta – the Zagórowskie Ol. 37 Catholics. In 1790, in turn, 21 Catholics and 20 dissenters lived in the Kowalewskie Olędry, and the Jaroszewskie Olędry were probably inhabited by Catholics and Lutherans, Poles and Germans.

In the three hearths of the Olęder settlement of Świdle Nowa Kolonia, founded in 1790 in the district of Kalisz by the old village of Świdle, there lived, it seems, people of the Protestant and the Catholic confession, of German and Polish nationality.

Summing up the information above on the confession, nationality and origin of the inhabitants of the 58 Olęder settlements that arose in the years 1746-1789 and 1791 in the Pyzdry Forest, it must be said that information stating directly the ethnic belonging of the Olęders occurs in the sources only three times. There are, however, indirect indications of the ethnic composition. One of them, besides confession, is their first names and surnames, often distorted by being Polonised (first names) and written as they sounded (surnames). In some cases, from the form of the names, Polish Protestants or German Catholics, or Polonised Germans, may be guessed at among the settlers. However, if not all of the colonists, then certainly a fair number of them also understood Polish, as is shown, indirectly, by the fact that most of the foundation charters and other documents or records were written in Polish. Other indications pointing indirectly to the nationality of the Olęders are the dialect of German they used (known chiefly from the pre-war research on part of the German minority in Poland) and the kind and size of the measures of land (rods), which also point to their place of origin, though not in the sense of a locality but of a region or country.

For the localities from which the Olęder settlers came are, for the period that concerns us, with very few exceptions, unknown. In 16 of the 28 Olęder settlements in the district of Konin, inhabited exclusively or partly by dissenters, in the light of the information on their confession, and also of the dialect of Low German (plattdeutsch) they used and the kind and size of their measures of land (rods), emigrants may be guessed at from the borderland of Greater Poland and Silesia and from the older Olęder settlements that had arisen in western Greater Poland, that is in the voivodeship of Poznań (from the area of Zbąszyń

and Nowy Tomyśl). From these lands, chiefly from the districts of the voivodeship of Kalisz (from towns and villages), came the Catholic and Polish settlers who lived, exclusively or partly, in a dozen or so settlements, especially those that were church property, but in a few cases also on noble ones. It seems that already in the first decades after the settlements were founded the confessional and ethnic composition of the villages changed, though to a very limited extent, as their inhabitants moved, because, among other things, of their personal freedom and the sales of land, and through marriages with women and men of neighbouring villages, especially rent-paying or Olęder ones. They were inhabited, at least half of them, wholly or partly, by German Protestant settlers, and afterwards, until 1945, by their descendants, who sometimes (especially in the settlements mixed in confession and nation) adopted Catholicism and in time became Polonised.

In three Olęder settlements, besides peasants, petty nobles also lived, though mostly on special terms, not being part of the peasant communes of the Olęder settlements and not subject to their self-government, or not willing to submit to it. Thus in 1791 one Różański lived under Olęder law on the land of the village of Ceków, a royal property. In 1792 there lived in the Białobłockie or Królikowskie Ol. Mikołaj Mąkowski, who then summoned before the landowners' court Count F. Stadnicki, the owner, the Olęders Józef and Jakub Hersa, brothers, Andrzej Langa, former sołtys, and Józef Koźmiński, commissary of the Królików estate, and other persons, for damage to his sown crops and pastures, for verbal and physical insult and for being treated like a peasant by the sołtys, and for the violent taking of his oxen. In reply Count F. Stadnicki summoned the same M. Mąkowski before the landowners' court, holding that by his marriage to an Olęder widow he was subject (like her previous husband) to Olęder law in matters with the sołtys and assessor and the persons of the commune, with the threat of a money fine for summoning them wrongly before the landowners' court. In Świdle, in turn, but not in the Świdle Ol., in the years 1789-1792, the noble Hieronim Nieszkowski held under a contract, that is under Olęder law, 5½ hubas and 3 morgen of land measured with the rod of 7½ ells. He remained, however, outside the Olęder commune created in 1790.

4. The legal status and the administrative and judicial organisation of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest

In the Olęder settlements founded in the Pyzdry Forest, the legal relation of the first settlers and of the later inhabitants of the Olęder settlements to the feudal lord (the founder of the settlement and his successors), the rules of the Olęders' life together in the settlements, the organisation and functions of their self-government, and finally their obligations to institutions and third persons (among them the state and the Church) were set by the foundation charters of the settlements, also called laws (prawa), consents (konsensy) and letters (listy). Formally they were unilateral acts, issued and signed by the lords, the founders of the settlements; in fact they were agreements made between them and the locators acting on behalf of whole communes as their representatives, or, mostly, with the settlers as a body. Sometimes they could also be oral, or written but preliminary, or individual, and only in time were they replaced by final written documents common to the whole commune. So it was in Wielołęka, Konary, the Lubieńskie Ol., the Przespolewskie Ol., Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol., the Gadowskie St. and Nw., and the Dzierzbińskie-Zdanowiec and Zamęty Ol., where the settlers, settling gradually, first obtained individual contracts fixing their free years, or, as in the Mycielińskie St. and Nw. Ol., preliminary charters, which were replaced only later by collective charters (agreements) of a final character. The Olęder commune had to pay for the issue of a collective charter; the foundation charter for the Cekowskie St. Ol. of 1768 states that the settlers "declare they will give for the contract a minted thaler each, and have already given one red złoty towards it".

The Olęders, unlike the peasants owing labour service, were always personally free. This was expressly confirmed in the collective foundation charter for the Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol. (I have resolved... to give emphyteutic law to the Gadowskie Holendry, to free people subject to no subjection, brought in while my husband was still alive... and coming in during my possession... according to its contracts). That those who settled in the Olęder settlements that concern us were people

Ol. and Lubieńskie Ol., Cekowskie Nw. Ol., Kosmowskie Ol., Plewińskie Nw. Ol., and the Stropieszyńskie, or Radzany and Gostynie, Ol.

The Olęders' subjection as to the land showed itself in their rights in rem to the land, through the definition of the forms of holding it and the conditions of the freedom to alienate and sell farms, in their rights of use on the lord's land (the so-called servitudes), and in their dependence on the manor's monopolies (chiefly that of propination). The most important of them, the right to the land, took in Greater Poland in the eighteenth century (apart from a few exceptions of emphyteusis in the sense of a short-term lease of land, for several decades) in principle the form of emphyteusis in the sense of a lease unlimited in time, perpetual, tied to the requirement that the holding of land first be bought by entry money, which once the entry money was paid turned in practice into a perpetual rent tenure (German Erbzinsrecht). This was guaranteed by the emphyteutic-perpetual charters, tied to the prior payment to the manor of entry money (grundgeld) for the land received. The sources show that the following settlements enjoyed perpetual rent tenure: the Pyzdrskie Ol. (in which, according to the census of 1789, lived entry-fine holders, rent-payers [settled] on the forests of the town of His [Royal] Majesty, Pyzdry), Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczyńskie/Wrąbczynkowskie Ol., the Białobłockie Ol. (and in them at least the brothers Józef and Jakub Hersa), the Borowieckie St. and Nw. Ol. (which, however, had not paid the grundgeld by 1789), the Lubieńskie or Biała Ol. (where the Olęders settled by the right of free purchase), the Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol. (who had still to pay the grungielt customary among the Holendry), the Grądy St. and Nw. Ol., Konary or the Konarskie Ol., Wielołęka (where in 1791 the settlers received a second emphyteutic-perpetual foundation charter), the (Ciemierowskie) Stare Ol. (described as a rent-paying, entry-fine village), the Cekowskie St. and Nw. Ol., the Dębniałki and Piskory Ol., the Dzierzbińskie – Zamęty and Zdanowiec Ol. (whose inhabitants had earlier obtained individual charters), and at least partly the Jarantowskie Ol., the Kazimierskie St. and Nw. The foundation charters for some settlements give the amount of the entry money. In the Cekowskie St. Olędry and the Mycielińskie St. and Nw. chodyla2015/116:
Under a law of 1775, emphyteutic charters were to be issued on stamped paper, with a fiscal fee of 1 grosz. If this condition was not met, the official validity of the charter could be legally questioned, even by its issuer himself. This was what happened in the Pyzdrskie Ol., and it became the cause of a long lawsuit between their inhabitants and the magistrate of the town of Pyzdry, which had perhaps deliberately issued the settlers a charter on ordinary paper.

Be that as it may, the ownership of the land assigned to the Olęders was not full but usufructuary and divided, since its legal owner was still the lord, who, however, had no right to remove an Olęder from it as long as he used it in accordance with the provisions of the charter. The Olęder was bound to take such care of the land as if it were his property, and could dispose of it freely as long as he paid the lord the dues owed and paid the entry money mentioned. In Greater Poland this was paid only once, on obtaining the right of perpetual possession of the land, in a lump sum, exceptionally in instalments. It was a payment for the land allotted. For this reason the peasants – Olęders who had paid the entry money also obtained freedom of alienation: of transferring the ownership of the land by gift to their natural heirs, and by transactions of sale and purchase to other persons, on condition of obtaining the manor's consent and paying the lord a fee (wadium) of one grosz in ten of the sale price of the farm. This was stated expressly in the charters for: the Pyzdrskie Ol. (freedom to sell farms with the magistrate's consent, on payment of a vadium of one grosz in ten), Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol. (the Olęders may sell, give or exchange the lands they have paid entry money for, cleared and built on, after informing the manor), the Lubieńskie Ol., the Orlińskie D. and M. Ol., the Cekowskie St. Ol. (the buildings and live stock belong to the farmers, who may sell them ...should any of them not like it in this country), the Cekowskie Nw. Ol. (permission to sell farms with the manor's consent, on giving it one grosz in ten of the sale price,

 In the complaint of the Olęders Mateusz Konieczny, sołtys, and Józef Baranowski and Jakub Bończyk, assessors and plenipotentiaries of the commune, against the magistrate of the town of Pyzdry, there is the information that the magistrate, taking advantage of the fact that they, "..not being enlightened, as unlearned little peasants", had received from the town council an improperly written foundation charter, since it was not on stamped paper, and for that reason the chancery of the municipal court of Pyzdry would not accept it for entry (oblata), gave them, in place of the old charter they had handed in, one on stamped paper, but with the signatures of its own members and without the signatures of the commonalty [the guild elders], and demanded a second payment for it. Now, they said, it wanted to abolish this law and take it away from them by deceit, spreading it about that this was because of the objection of the commonalty, which "knew everything", although they had already paid the town the entry money for the holdings of land they had received, acquiring a perpetual rent tenure of them. To this end it informed the Olęders that it had once obtained a decree of the starost's court abolishing this foundation charter, which had, after all, earlier been confirmed by the king. Besides, attempts were made in various other ways to drive the Olęders out of their farms, among others by cutting the deeds of sale of farms out of the sołtys's record and taking from them the original law kept in that record, and by a raid of citizens of Pyzdry with 15 horses, acts of violence committed under the pretext of taking recruits, and other abuses. Accordingly, the Olęders declared they would pursue the matter before the Referendary Court. That proceeding, which ended in a just judgment, is the subject of other records (a royal letter of safe-conduct for the Olęders, complaints of the Olęders, powers of attorney for the court from the Olęder commune, summonses, decrees, correspondence and others, of 1790), with their call numbers, titles and the pages of the edition of the Ks. RKor., in: Z. Chodyła, Osadnictwo olęderskie w Wielkopolsce (1597-1793), Annex I/5.

(whoever wishes to move away is to settle another Olęder on his farm with the knowledge of the sołtys and the assessors, and of the whole commune), the Plewińskie Nw. Ol. (whoever moves away is to settle another Olęder on his farm with the knowledge of the sołtys and the assessors and of the whole commune, otherwise the others will answer for him), the Wierzchy Ol. (freedom to sell farms after informing the manor) and the Zbierskie Ol..

The settlement charters for the Olęders limited the circle of buyers of farms to people of equal condition (that is above all personally free peasants): in the Lubieńskie Ol. (a farm may be sold after informing the manor, without reducing the sowing on the huba and without ruining or carrying away the buildings..., on payment of one grosz in ten to the manor, ...to one equal in his estate..., to burghers, but not to nobles), and in the Zbierskie Ol. (they may sell the lands to people of equal condition, give, donate or exchange them without any claim of the lord). Transactions in farms, with the sellers and buyers and the conditions and prices of the sales, are confirmed by their entries in the village (sołtys) books of the Pyzdrskie and the Dzierzbińskie – Zdanowiec and Zamęty Ol.

The right of inheritance in the emphyteutic settlements in the Olęder villages of the Pyzdry Forest was probably held – as in the Olęder settlements in the districts of Poznań, Kościan and Gniezno, for which the relevant data survive in the foundation charters – by all the natural heirs of a deceased farmer, women included (in an order set by the degree of kinship). If an Olęder had no offspring or nearest relatives (brother and sister), the farm he tilled, with all its equipment, was to return to the disposal of the manor.

In the foundation charters surviving for 37 of the 58 Olęder settlements founded in the Pyzdry Forest, with the exception of those for 2 settlements, the principle of the Olęders' solidarity and their collective responsibility for the dues to the manor is not stressed. In the charter for the Stropieszyńskie, or Radzany and Gostynie, Ol., this principle is expressed in general terms by the stress on the punctual payment of the rents and other dues. For a dozen or so of the other settlements, however, it appears implicitly in statements that speak of the joint payment of the manor's dues through the sołtys, or the sołtys and the assessors, who were made responsible for their collective payment, which will be discussed in detail below.

The law in rem also included, as confirmed in the charter: 1) rights of use on the lord's land – that is servitudes of pasture (the basis

Under the servitudes of pasture the inhabitants – farmers in the Olęder settlements could graze cattle or pigs on the lord's land, on condition of making a certain payment or giving a due in grain. In the Dębniałki Ol. and the Piskory Ol. the settlers received in a separate charter pasture in the forests and the use of the pond at Piskory, in return for each of the 16 farmers ploughing within the year 10, and in all 150, laski (rods) of the manor's ploughland on the Bilawy "for fallow, spring crop and strip".

The lords' occasional economic help for the Olęders took the form of material and non-material benefits, temporary or long-term, which they received from them. During their free years they could use free of charge, freely or to a set degree and extent, every kind of building and firewood on the land taken up for their farms. In the Cekowskie Nw. Ol. they obtained in the foundation charter help in firewood and building timber on their own huba, and after fires they were to receive timber for rebuilding from the Ceków forest; they could also dig clay on land set aside for it. In the Stropieszyńskie, or Radzany and Gostynie, Ol. they were granted timber for building a school. In the Orlińskie D. and M. Ol., and also in the Wierzchy Ol., they obtained help in the building timber cleared from their holding. In the Grądy St. and Nw. "Every Olęder, before selling off the timber, is to build himself properly and in line with the others within four years...".

The regular and joint payment of the dues to the lord, the state and the Church, the carrying out of other administrative and judicial tasks, and the keeping of the peace in the Olęder settlements of the Pyzdry Forest were ensured, as in other Olęder villages, by an elected self-government. It consisted of the sołtys and the assessors, elected by the commune assembly of all the farmers (sometimes called the gmin or gromada). In administrative matters the sołtys and the assessors were, as was said above, to see that the settlers built as quickly as possible, properly and on a line (Orlińskie D. and M. Ol.), and to watch that ...every discipline and obedience of the said Dutch communes was kept (Gadowskie St. and Nw. and probably the Smuszewskie Ol.).

The existence of a sołtys, and often also of assessors, is clearly confirmed in the foundation charters or other records in 21 of the 58 Olęder settlements that concern us. Namely: in the district of Pyzdry in the Ciążeńskie Ol. (sołtys), Wrąbczynek (sołtys and assessors) and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol. (sołtys and assessors); in the district of Konin in the Białobłockie Ol. (sołtys and assessors), the Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol. (sołtys and assessors), the Grądy St. and Nw. Ol., Konary Ol. The sołtys and the assessors were on the whole elected every year by the commune assembly and confirmed by the manor, though there were sometimes departures from this rule, on the whole short-lived. In Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol. the sołtys and the assessors were elected, with the manor's consent, by the commune assemblies (meetings of the Olęder farmers) of both villages; in the Pyzdrskie Ol., according to the foundation charter of 1778, the farmers were to elect from among themselves every 3 years, on the first Monday after St Adalbert (23 IV), a sołtys and 2 assessors, confirmed by the magistrate; in the Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol. and the Grądy St. and Nw. Ol. the sołtys and two assessors were elected by the gromada, that is the gmin, in the Stropieszyńskie or Gostynie and Radzany Ol. by the commune assembly, and the manor had to confirm them for a year. In the Orlińskie M. and D. Ol. the sołtys Bogusław Krol, who had permission for "...free clearing and rudowanie with his co-samsiads [!]..." [neighbours], was given Michał Arent to help him, probably as an assessor, which suggests seeing the two of them as the locators of one of these settlements.

In Konary Ol., in turn, the sołtys was elected from 3 candidates put forward by the community; the two of them not elected to the office probably then served as assessors. In the Dzierzbińskie – Zamęty and Zdanowiec Ol. there were separate sołtyses and assessors, elected every year on 11 XI; in the Kosmowskie Ol., the Plewińskie St. and Nw. Ol., the Stropieszyńskie or Radzany and Gostynie Ol. and the Wierzchy Ol. the sołtys was also elected every year and approved by the manor; in the last of these, in the first year, the sołtys Daniel was chosen by the manor (probably because he was the locator), and the assessors by the commune, that is by the commune assembly made up of the farmers.

For his work the sołtys often received an additional endowment in land or other remuneration. Thus in Wrąbczynek, for his labours for the commune, the sołtys received an ostrów [allotment, island, part] of five morgen in each field [that is the spring, the winter and the fallow field]; in the Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol. and the Grądy St. and Nw. Ol. half a quarter of a huba in addition, free of dues.

As the commune court, the sołtys and the assessors were to keep internal peace and order in the settlements and to settle quarrels and disputes. They judged by Olęder law, whose terms were set by the foundation charters of the individual settlements and, for some of them, also by the wilkierze (village ordinances). The wilkierze were collections of legal rules issued formally by the feudal owners – the founders of the settlements or their successors – but in fact formulated by the commune assembly

Such a wilkierz, a very extensive one (of 41 points), written in German, undated, but most probably from before 1793, survives for the Wielołęka Ol. Because of the limited size of this study its content cannot be discussed in detail. It is worth saying, however, that it regulates such matters as the role of the commune self-government in ensuring harmonious life among neighbours and order and peace in the village, among other things by controlling the movement of persons coming into it from outside; the organisation and working of the commune court; the keeping and watching over of honesty (also by imposing penalties); it set the rules of trade in cattle, horses and other goods, of neighbourly help in rebuilding after fires, the conditions for returning neighbours' livestock seized for damage, help for widows and persons over 70, and the inhabitants' share in founding and maintaining a church and a school after the free years had run out. A wilkierz is also mentioned in the foundation charters for the Zbierskie Ol. and the Dzierzbińskie – Zamęty and Zdanowiec Ol. The first states of it: They are to be judged by the sołtys according to their law for good conduct, which they will give, alias the wilkier, and from him the wronged party is to have appeal to the manor. The second contains this information about it: They are given a wilkir, which will belong to the charter, and the charter to the wilkir; this, however, is the most principal [the first] point in the wilkir: that when there is need they should be ready with their whole heart, with whatever proper weapons they can have, for a sudden need, that is should an enemy break in, for defence, and also for defence [against] fire, should the forest catch fire by some chance.

From the judgments of the commune court the Olęders had the right of appeal to the manor, that is the lord's court (in the Pyzdrskie Ol. to the court of the magistrate, in the Cekowskie Nw. Ol. and the Zbierskie Ol. to the dominium court, that is the lord's), for which the right to judge in criminal cases of robbery, arson, homicide and serious bodily harm, and of course all offences against the lord, was also reserved. Court fines went half to the manor and half to the court (Cekowskie Nowe Ol.), or to the manor alone.

The lords also guaranteed the Olęders their protection, and promised them and their descendants, in their own name and that of their heirs, to keep the terms of the foundation charters. They sometimes also bound the Olęders not to seek anyone else's protection against them, stating that should anyone make use of it, he cannot claim payment for his plot.

Among the members of the self-government the main burden of administrative duties lay on the sołtys. He was above all bound to see to order and good husbandry in the commune, and that the whole commune met its obligations to the manor – rents, labour services and payments to the manor and the Church, and taxes to the state treasury – punctually and in full. It was for him and the assessors to collect these dues (recorded for the Stropieszyńskie or Gostynie and Radzany Ol.). Since the commune was usually jointly responsible for the manor's dues, the commune self-government was bound to remove an Olęder who farmed badly and to put another on the farm (Cekowskie Nw. Ol., Plewińskie St. and Nw. Ol.). The sołtys probably also, with the lord's support, carried out the judgments of the commune court.

Most of the 58 eighteenth-century Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest, of various sizes in their area of land (especially arable), their number of hearths and their population, were independent spatial-economic and administrative-judicial units (communes). They formed separate one-village communes with their own self-government, a sołtys and assessors. Some of them, however, 14 (the Borowieckie St. and Nw., the Grądy St. and Nw. Ol., the Orlińskie D. and M. Ol., the Trąbczyńskie St. and Nw. Ol., the Mycielińskie St. and Nw. Ol., the Plewińskie St. and Nw. Ol., the Stropieszyńskie – Radzany and Gostynie Ol.), formed two-village communes, and in one case the Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol. and probably the Smuszewskie Ol. formed a three-village commune, with a common sołtys and assessors.

Perhaps some of the Olęder villages or communes founded in the Pyzdry Forest had their own seal as a mark of their self-government, with which its organs – the office and the court (or rather the office-court) – sealed their letters and documents, which, as originals or copies, were entered in their own commune books – sołtys books, sometimes town books – and were also sent to other communes. Commune and sołtys books (containing, among other things, copies of foundation charters, registers of rents and labour services, transactions of sale and purchase of farms, inventories of movables and the Olęders' wills), kept by the commune clerk, who was probably most often the teacher, survive for only three Olęder communes, the Pyzdrskie Ol. and the Dzierzbińskie – Zamęty and Zdanowiec Ol., one common book for the last two.
