chodyla2015/123:
5. The economic and social life of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest in the years 1746-1793

The technique of tilling the land in the lowland settlements consisted in draining the land by digging, and keeping in good order, a system of large and smaller drainage ditches, and in keeping the arable land, once drained, fit for tillage. In the settlements that lay higher, on dry forest land, tillage consisted in clearing the forests and thickets and then raising the fertility of the soil by manuring (chiefly with dung, provided by well-developed cattle-raising). Sometimes the Olęders took up ploughland already in use, even with buildings and sown crops. Settlements founded on the ready or partly overgrown land of former villages kept the communal three-field layout, tied to the system of tillage then general. With the scattered layout of the farms in the great majority of the settlements, however, the three-field system was individualised, and there was, on the whole, no compulsion to till in common in the individual settlements. The varied and often low fertility of the soils, partly wet, partly (after the forest was cleared) sandy, together with the extensive grain-and-fallow three-field system and moderate manuring (in spite of fairly well-developed stock-raising, especially of cattle), made for rather low yields.

The basic branches of farming in the Olęder settlements of the Pyzdry Forest were crop-growing and stock-raising. In the former, grain predominated. Among the grains rye predominated; oats and barley were also grown, more rarely buckwheat, and among other crops peas and flax. Because of the low fertility of the soils, most farms obtained yields of grain of 3-3½ grains for 1 sown. Meadows and pastures were of great importance, as places for grazing cattle but also for getting fodder for them for the winter in the form of hay. Garden crops were of secondary, supplementary importance: hops, tobacco, potatoes and carrots, chiefly for the household's own use. The sources we have used allow conclusions about the character of crop-growing only to a very limited extent, only from the dues in kind set out below and the information on meadows and pastures. The data given above have been formulated by analogy with other Olęder settlements in Greater Poland for which the relevant concrete data survive.

 They are given by W. Rusiński, Osady tzw. olędrów, pp. 71-72.
chodyla2015/124:
The second important branch of the economy of the inhabitants of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest was the raising of animals: cattle, sheep and pigs, and also horses and poultry. This is shown by direct information about permission to keep sheep and cattle, and by indirect information about meadows and pastures, given in the charters for settlements already named and others, namely for: Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol. (where the settlers received 16 morgen of land cleared for meadows, and Jakub Wróbel one and a half morgen for keeping sheep and cattle), the Pyzdrskie Ol. (free pasture for livestock in the forests), the Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol. (permission to raise cattle and other livestock, but without damage to the manor's pastures), Wielołęka (permission to fatten hogs, free pasture for cattle in places set aside), the Cekowskie St. Ol., the Dzierzbińskie – Zamęty and Zdanowiec Ol. (they may keep as many horned cattle as they wish), the Przespolewskie Ol. and the Zbierskie Ol. The charters for the Cekowskie St. and Cekowskie Nw. Ol. set limits on the number of stock kept. The first allowed the raising of 25 sheep, and the second the keeping on a huba of 7 cows, 4 horses, 4 oxen, 10 pigs and 30 sheep. In the Ciążeńskie Ol. there were fees for pasture: for a cow 1 zł, for a head of young stock, not counting calves, 18 gr. In the Dębniałki and Piskory Ol. the settlers received free pasture in the forests and pastures in return for each of the 16 farmers ploughing within the year 10, and in all 150, laski (rods) of the manor's ploughland on the Bilawy, for fallow, spring crop and strip. The raising of poultry also played a significant part. This is confirmed indirectly by the information quoted below about dues in kind: in geese, capons and eggs.

The people of the Olęder settlements founded in the Pyzdry Forest drew additional income from non-farming occupations: from bee-keeping, which was allowed by the settlement charters for the Pyzdrskie Ol., Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol., and Wielołęka.

The people of the Olęder settlements founded in the Pyzdry Forest in the years 1746-1792 also most probably took an active part in trade, mostly local and retail, selling chiefly the surplus of their crops (grain) and their stock (cattle, horses, pigs, poultry and dairy produce) and of what they made or obtained in their non-farming occupations (for instance crafts and bee-keeping), and buying in return grain and other foodstuffs, timber, or tools at the markets and fairs in the towns and little towns. The foundation charter for the Cekowskie St. Ol. (allowed trade in salt and bread), and that for the Cekowskie Nw. Ol. of 1774, guaranteed the settlers freedom to trade in hogs, horses, cattle and sheep, and forbade trade in salt and iron. None of the foundation charters for the other Olęder villages states this expressly, but there is no doubt that the Olęders were guaranteed freedom of trade, since it was chiefly in this way that they could obtain the money to meet their financial obligations to the manor, the state and the Church. Jews were often the intermediaries in the trade in farm produce.

Gross income was reduced by the unknown costs of the household's own consumption and of investment, and above all by the obligations to the manor, the Church and the state, which decisively determined the value of the net income.

On account of the perpetual, hereditary use of the land, the Olęders settled in the Pyzdry Forest on private estates were bound to render to the lords – the founders of the settlements and their heirs – money rents for the land, dues in kind and labour (the repair of roads, and tłoki, seasonal labour service at harvest and haymaking, and other services, set on a yearly basis after the free years had run out), and to buy the manor's drink under the compulsion of propination. They also bore some administrative fees, for instance on the sale of land, mentioned above.

The charters and other records show that the most important burden was the money rent to the manor, paid on the whole once a year, on a set date (mostly 11 XI), and in an amount according to the size of the holding (farm). It was collected from the individual farmers and handed over jointly by the sołtys of the village, against a receipt, to the feudal lord or his representative. Such receipts for rents received, of the years 1769-1783, are known for the Ciemierowskie/Szymanowickie or Stare Ol. and in the Pyzdrskie Ol. (in their commune or sołtys book).

For the Cekowskie Nw. Ol. there is an exact list of the payments and the amounts of rent for the individual farmers, named by their surnames: Krzysztof Stefan, in whose place now Grymberk, from 1 huba 80 zł; Gotfryd Reszka from 1 huba 9 morgen 105 złp 10 gr; Wojciech Pruchno from ½ h. and 5 morgen 46 złp. 20 gr, from 6 I 1782; Krystian Kurcz, in whose place Kups, from 6 I 1785; the rest of the Olęders settled on 1 and ½ h., from 6 I 1787; Hertel from 1 h. 80 złp; Puntzler from 1½ h. 120 złp; Heinc from ¾ h. 60 złp; Szwander from 1¼ h. 100 złp.; Kups from 1 h. 80 złp.; Krzysztof Kowal from ¾ h. 60 złp.; Gajzler from ¾ h. 60 złp.; Jan Paszkowski from 1 h. 80 zł; Grynberg from 2 h. taken up in 1782, 160 zł.. A register of rents paid and labour done, and of fines imposed for various offences, together with transactions of purchase and sale of farms, of the years 1792-1813, is known from the village (sołtys) book of the Dzierzbińskie [-Zamęty] Ol..

The annual rates of rent per huba varied, but were mostly close to one another. Thus it is known that they came to: in the Dębniałki and Piskory Ol. 72 złp; in the Gadowskie St. and Nw. O., the Konarskie Ol., Wielołęka, the Cekowskie St. Ol. and the Oborskie Ol. 76 złp.; in the Lubieńskie Ol. 78 złp.; in the Kazimierskie Nw. Ol. 45 złp., but per half-huba; in Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol. and the Cekowskie Nw. Ol. 80 złp.; in the Grądy St. and Nw. Ol. 90 złp. In the Dzierzbińskie – Zamęty and Zdanowiec Ol., the Kosmowskie Ol., the Kuszyńskie Ol. and the Plewińskie Ol., on the other hand, they were set at 60 tynfs per huba, and in the Wierzchy Ol. at 30 tynfs per half-huba. Further: the farmers were bound to give 4 wiertele of oats, of the new royal measure, and 4 capons or 2 geese once a year in the Lubieńskie Ol., 4 capons or 2 ganders in the Dębniałki and Piskory Ol., and 2 wiertele of oats, 2 hens and 1 goose, and 2 mendle of eggs in the Dzierzbińskie-Zamęty and Zdanowiec Ol.

Labour services were of secondary importance in the Old Polish Olęder settlements of the Pyzdry Forest. They are indeed named in the foundation charters of many of them, on a yearly basis per huba (or per half-huba), in the form of manual work, varying in kind and in the number of days, chiefly seasonal (the so-called tłoki), and of journeys (carting, podwody), but often with the possibility of commuting them into money at a set rate.

Labour services are known for: the Ciążeńskie Ol. (6 manual tłoki at harvest), Wrąbczynek and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol. (to plough 3 morgen, to cart dung 2 days and at harvest to work 3 manual days). Another serious burden to the manor was the complete compulsion of propination, in force in all the Olęder settlements of the Pyzdry Forest. The Olęders were forbidden, under penalty, to make any drink or to take it from anyone but the manor. This was stated expressly, either in general terms or with the penalties for breaking this ban, by the foundation charters for the Pyzdrskie Ol., the Gadowskie St. and Nw. Ol., the Lubieńskie Ol., the Orlińskie D. and M. Ol., Wielołęka, the Cekowskie St. Ol., the Cekowskie Nw. Ol. (with the threat of a fine of 40 zł for a garniec of beer and 80 zł for a garniec of vodka), the Oborskie St. and Nw. Ol., the Dębniałki and Piskory Ol. (with the threat of a fine of 2 thalers), the Kosmowskie Ol. (with a fine of the price of 1 "dry barrel" and 3 garniec of vodka), the Kuszyńskie Ol., the Mycielińskie Ol. (under threat of paying a "dry barrel"), the Plewińskie Ol., the Przespolewskie Ol. and the Wierzchy Ol. On such occasions too as christenings, weddings and parties, the Olęders were always bound to drink the lord's drink. Different from the compulsion of propination, under which buying drink depended on the settlers' will, was the compulsion to buy a certain amount of drink, and so, indirectly, a compulsion to consume. It was rarely met with in the Olęder villages, but it did occur. So it was in the Oborskie St. and Nw. Ol. and the Wierzchy Ol., whose farmers were bound to buy ½ and 1 barrel of beer at the election of the sołtys.

In some Olęder settlements there was also a compulsion to buy other goods at the inn in a set amount, for instance in the Lubieńskie Ol. ("the lord's herrings" during Lent) and in the Stropieszyńskie – Radzany and Gostynie Ol. (20 herrings for each hearth).

The inhabitants of all the Olęder settlements founded in the eighteenth century in the Pyzdry Forest were also bound, like the inhabitants of non-Olęder villages, to render to the state taxes in money, paid every year in two instalments (March and September) – the poll tax (pogłówne), set in the tariffs for 1775 and 1789-1790, the hiberna in the settlements on royal estates in the tariff of 1775, and the tax of the offering (from 1789) of 10 gr. (on noble estates) and 20 gr. (on church estates) – and a tax in kind, the so-called levy (zsypka) from the "self-tilling" hearths (in the form of korzec of rye and oats per hearth, varying in the individual charters). Their payment is confirmed in the sources for the royal Cekowskie St. Ol. in 1775 (hearth tax of 126 złp from 18 hearths at a rate of 7 zł per hearth, and 56 for the hiberna together with Ceków), the noble Zbierskie Ol. (which paid 36 złp. of poll tax in 1775), the Ciemierowskie St. Ol., which in 1790 were in arrears with the payment of 112 złp. of hearth tax in the September instalment,

The annual rate of the tax of the offering was set for most of the 58 settlements on the basis of the average income of their owners over the last three (exceptionally two) years. According to the data surviving in the table of the tax of the offering of 10 or 20 groszy of 1789, this tax was paid on the annual rent, on the propination of beer and vodka, and on the dues in rye (counting the korzec at 6 zł).

The grain levy from the self-tilling hearths was fixed in 1791 and served the needs of the army.

Besides, all the inhabitants of many Olęder settlements, Catholics but also, to a large extent, Protestants, were bound to render to the Roman Catholic Church dues in the form of fees jura stolae (that is for baptisms, weddings and funerals), meszne (mass dues) and kolęda (Christmas offering). The Protestants paid them until 1768, as they often did after the toleration law of that year too, especially when they settled on land formerly settled and later deserted, in Olęder villages that arose on the site of medieval settlements assigned in this respect to Catholic parishes, which was sometimes contained in their foundation deeds (akty erekcyjne). The foundation charters set out these obligations in general terms, saying that they would be fixed in separate agreements made between the settlers and the parish priests through the manor (that is the feudal founder of the settlement), or else they gave conditions already agreed earlier. Thus it is known that in the Białobłockie Ol. the Olęders paid the parish priest at Królików 4 zł each for a funeral and a wedding and 1 zł 6 gr for a baptism, while in the Borowieckie St. and Nw. chodyla2015/132:
6. The material and spiritual culture and the daily life of the inhabitants of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest in the years 1746-1793

The manifestations of the material and spiritual culture and the daily life of the inhabitants of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest in the years 1746-1793 can for the most part be grasped only to a very modest extent in the written Old Polish sources, or there is no information about them at all. No objects of the second half of the eighteenth century illustrating them have survived to our day either, so that most of the questions connected with them, especially in the case of material culture, can be described only on the basis of objects (for instance buildings, pieces of the furnishing of houses, farm tools) of the nineteenth and first half of the twentieth century, their museum photographs, and the ethnographic and other literature, mostly by the method of retrogression.

The written sources hand down only a dozen or so pieces of information about dwelling and farm buildings. According to them, the farmsteads of the Olęders in the Pyzdry Forest had, besides the cottage, that is the dwelling house, farm buildings: barns, cowsheds, stables and pigsties for the livestock. As was said above (in Chap. 2), according to the detailed tables of hearths surviving for the Olęder settlements that concern us in the districts of Pyzdry and Kalisz, most of them had "cottages with one farmer". The foundation charters surviving for 31 settlements show that the dwelling and farm buildings were put up of timber given by the founder (chiefly pine), mostly standing on the Olęders' holdings and cleared by them. The charters for a few settlements contained recommendations to put them up "as carefully as possible", or orders to build them within a set time of several years under threat of a money fine or even removal from the settlement. The dwelling and farm buildings were probably put up by carpenters and masons from the Olęder settlements or neighbouring ones. Among the former, the arcaded cottages proper to the villages of the time, and not only the Olęder ones, most probably predominated, set on the whole with their gable and not their ridge to the road, while the farm buildings were put up round the yard, so that together with the cottage they formed a quadrangle. Unfortunately, in the Old Polish Olęder settlements of the Pyzdry Forest, with a few exceptions, no buildings of the eighteenth century have survived. Far more of the farm buildings and cottages surviving to our day date from the nineteenth century. An inspection of them, together with an analysis of the archival photographs
chodyla2015/133:
of the folk buildings in these villages kept in the District Museum in Konin and reproduced in the book of I. F. Tłoczek, and the information in the ethnographic literature, have made it possible to establish that these houses had elements also proper to eighteenth-century building. Buildings were then put up of wood, in post-and-plank, log and half-timbered (frame) construction. Clay and bog iron ore were also commonly used building materials. Buildings of wood and of bog iron ore were insulated inside with a daub of clay. The architecture of the dwelling houses of the Pyzdry Forest area, as architectural research of the years 2009 – 2011 has shown, has recurring features common to the whole area of the forest. They are: symmetrical pitched roofs at an angle of 45 degrees; gables boarded vertically; rafters resting on decorated ceiling beams projecting beyond the face of the wall; box windows, "standing rectangles", of one or two casements; divided windows, with panes of the same size or larger below and smaller above; outer doors of ledged or frame-and-panel construction, mostly decorated, most often double. The features of the farm buildings are close to those of the dwellings. The visible differences concern the following features: rectangular or square windows; additional small window openings without glass, in the shape of an equilateral triangle; doors of boards set vertically.

The houses usually had wide chimneys, joined at the bottom to bread ovens. The latter, which also served for drying flax, were built by the Olęders of the Pyzdry Forest, as a precaution against fire, in the yard or the garden. The house ovens were inspected every year by the sołtys and the assessors, who collected fines for the manor for the forbidden drying of flax in the cottages.

Because the surviving houses have been rebuilt many times, the original layout of their interiors cannot be established exactly. According to the ethnographic literature, however, it may be supposed that the most popular type was the two-room cottage, with the two rooms on either side of a hall in the middle.

The furnishing of the interiors of the Olęder cottages consisted of beds, standing most often against the walls, chests for keeping clothes, a table under the window, and benches for sitting and for mangling linen. Not every room had a stove. Shelves hung on the walls, and there was also (probably above all in the houses of Catholics) the so-called "holy corner", where a crucifix and other devotional objects were placed.

In the interiors of the Olęders' houses there were also a fair number of the utensils needed in the household, most probably like those used in other, non-Olęder settlements and known from the ethnographic literature. They included wooden stave vessels: for water, used for drawing it (węborki) and carrying it

Of other equipment, the querns for grinding grain and the looms for making linen deserve notice.

In the farm buildings were kept all kinds of tools: carts, scythes, radła (ards), ploughs, harrows, rakes, pitchforks and others. Among them the wooden radło rylcowe (sole ard) used in western Greater Poland, Bohemia and Silesia is noteworthy: it consisted of a straight beam, forked and running into handles, and of a share-beam set slantwise in the beam, with an iron share with an eye fitted on it. Such a share was found in 1958 in the Jarantowkie [sic] Ol. (Jarantów Kolonia), and its occurrence here (and not only here) is explained in the literature by the inhabitants of this village descending from Olęder villages inhabited by Czech people from the area of Zbąszyń.

People dressed according to the customs brought from their places of origin, differently – as is obvious – on weekdays and on feast days, in clothes probably mostly of their own making, of linen and sheep's wool, but partly also sewn from cloth bought in the towns and little towns.

The food of the people of the Olęder settlements that arose in the Pyzdry Forest probably did not differ fundamentally from that of others, in proportion to their prosperity. They ate rye bread and other grain or flour dishes, groats, vegetables, butter, cheese, from time to time meat, in Lent probably herrings and other fish, and honey from their own apiaries, and fruit, and they drank beer, then general, and also milk.

At family celebrations (christenings, weddings) and on other occasions they were obliged (under the manor's monopoly and the compulsion of propination) to drink vodka and beer in the lord's inn or from the lord's distilleries and malthouse. This is stated expressly in the foundation charters for the Cekowskie Nw. Ol., the Przespolewskie Ol., the Zbierskie Ol., the Grądy St. and Nw. Ol. and the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol.. A ban on bringing in "beer and spirits and any drink" from elsewhere was in force in the Cekowskie Nw. Ol., the Dzierzbińskie-Zamęty and Zdanowiec Ol., the Plewińskie St. and Nw. Ol., and also in the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol..

dress and customs even more than a hundred years after they had settled. According to his observations: "the Olęder men were in general shorter than the Polish peasants, but more "thickset, sturdy and strong". Their faces were typical, German, shaven; they very rarely wore beards. The Polish peasants wore long sukmany (coats), reaching almost to the ground, of grey, coarse cloth, more rarely of coarse linen dyed dark blue, made at home, and under the sukmany long cloth waistcoats with shining glass buttons. Their trousers and shirts were of linen; the former were sometimes sewn of the same cloth as the sukmana. Their boots were ordinary ones, bought at the fair. On their heads they put in summer a black felt hat with a small brim; in winter the taller ones wore caps of grey lambskin, extraordinarily high, with a blue cloth top and narrow blue ribbons drawing it in, tied in a bow, and the shorter ones a so-called kaptur, that is a low four-cornered cap, also trimmed with grey lambskin. The Olęders, like the local peasants, often wore grey or blue sukmany, but these were shorter and of a different cut. As headgear they almost never wore hats, but cloth caps, and in winter black lambskin ones. The Polish women dressed in skirts and jackets or bodices in which red always predominated, and only among the older ones was one to be seen the navy-blue cloth kabat formerly in general use, fairly short, reaching perhaps half an ell, with a small, roundly cut cape, and gathered at the back. Married women, with their hair cut short, wore on their heads (though not all of them) muslin or tulle caps, bound round the head with a twisted patterned kerchief. Girls plaited their hair into braids, pinning part up at the back and winding part round the ears. Both married women and girls liked to attach bright coloured ribbons to the beads (corals) they wore round their necks. On their feet all the women wore shoes, sometimes adorned with ribbon bows. The Olęder women, on the other hand (married women and girls alike), went about in striped woollen skirts of their own making and aprons of the same, and put on a fustian or other jacket. In summer, instead of the woollen skirts, they wore calico dresses. On their heads they put woollen kerchiefs, but dark ones, of the town type, which they tied in the same way as women of all estates. On their feet they wore shoes.

The customs and manners of the people of these settlements in the second half of the eighteenth century are not known.

As for customs, the Olęders blessed at Epiphany (the Three Kings): amber, myrrh, bryony, marjoram and garlic, which was to protect against an evil person. They also blessed then, for the same purpose, the so-called "devil's dung" (asafoetida), with which they fumigated themselves", giving it also to the cows to eat against bewitchment, especially at the new moon and before Whitsun. They also introduced a way of treating cattle, later known to the Polish peasants, by giving them animal oil. Both they and the Polish peasants, in treating people as well as cattle, set great store by various "ninefold" herbs, grasses, roots, drops and ointments. They also believed that someone could fall ill, for instance, from bewitchment by "cioty" [witches]. Besides herbs, a favourite medicine were various fats, such as those of the dog, the bear, the lion [sic!] and the badger, which were to help used internally as well as externally. A remedy against worms in children, to be effective, had to be prepared not in the house but behind it. They also used other, magical ways of healing. A remedy that radically helped a child who "screams from morning to evening", [supposedly]
chodyla2015/136:
because of pain in the small of the back, was to cut crosses with an axe in the three beams supporting the powała [ceiling] at sunrise. According to S. Ciszewski, because the Polish peasants lacked an innate capacity to assimilate, there were clear differences between the two groups of the rural population, caused also by Protestantism, which was the main confession of the Olęders, and by the foreign language. Marriages of an Olęder with a Polish peasant woman, or the other way round, did not occur in the eighteenth century, or at least he had not heard of them, and on the Polish side the lack of relations and the separateness of the two groups were stressed. The Polish peasants were pious and fond of the outward rites of religion, but on the other hand enormously superstitious, mistrustful of the manor and of people from the town, of officials, but also humble towards them, not valuing education, but loving their land and judging a man by his work, but only manual work. Among their faults were a lack of respect for other people's property, especially forest property, and perhaps a somewhat loose life of the women. The Protestant Olęders were not inferior to the Poles in piety, and in superstition they far surpassed them, using, especially in raising cattle, a host of sorcerer's practices, which their Polish neighbours borrowed from them. At the same time, however, they showed a greater knowledge of farming. In their dealings with more educated people the Olęders were less humble than the peasants, showing more worldly manners. They did not attach much importance to learning either; many of them could not write, though probably most could read. Although they lived in Poland, not all of them could speak Polish. There were among them individuals who, having been in the army, had learnt to speak Russian fairly well. The Polish peasants, on the other hand, tried to say at least a few words in their dialect, which was rather hard to understand, even for persons who knew German reasonably well. The Olęders were also distinguished by their industry, but did not show such attachment to the land as the Polish peasants. Among the Olęders one did not meet very poor people, frequent among the Polish villagers, which also followed from their having farms of larger area and from their ingenuity and good husbandry. A fair income came to them, for instance, from home weaving, practised by the Olęder women and neglected by the Polish peasant women. From the sheep the Olęders raised, almost all the Olęder women made very fine and durable woollen skirts, thicker and thinner, and aprons, giving the yarn to the town only for dyeing. The Polish peasants, on the other hand, made only coarse linen, which they sometimes had dyed blue in the little town and from which they sewed trousers and sukmany for the men, or else they bought factory goods. The prosperity and higher culture of daily life of the Olęders compared with the Polish peasant showed itself also in their love of a tidy dwelling. The [Polish] peasants' huts looked worse beside the neat Olęder ones, but as a worker, a so-called "manual" one, the Polish peasant was more sought after.

As for the spiritual culture of the people of the Olęder settlements that arose in the eighteenth century in the Pyzdry Forest, the sources allow us to grasp, directly or indirectly, their confessional relations, schooling and religious worship, and the culture of daily life (chiefly material).

The teacher in the school was a person employed specially for the purpose or (as often happened) one of the inhabitants of the village who could read and write. His duties were to teach the children the catechism, to prepare them for confirmation at the age of 14, and to teach them the basics of reading, writing and arithmetic. The children of the Protestant settlers went to the schools, and until the First World War teaching was in German. The children of the Polish Catholic settlers were brought into schooling only at the beginning of the twentieth century.

Schooling lasted at first only two years and, as was general at the time, only in winter and early spring, because the children were used for herding cattle and for field work. Besides, because he could write and read, the teacher was at the service of the settlement's self-government. At the same time the teacher performed religious services to a basic extent (he led the Sunday services and funerals). Sunday services were held not only in the Protestant churches but also in the schools or in chapels built beside the schools, as for example in the chapels still standing today

For baptisms and weddings, on the other hand, the Olęders living in the Pyzdry Forest went to the pastors of the Protestant churches at Grodziec, Nowa Kaźmierka, Konin, Stare Prażuchy, Stawiszyn, Zagórów and Żychlin.

The schools, confirmed in the foundation charters for 16 settlements, which stood in wooden cottages on half-peasant or smallholder holdings with land and garden, mostly also housed the houses of prayer; in the nineteenth century these were replaced in some settlements by newer wooden buildings, exceptionally still standing today, in Piskory and Stary Borowiec, and above all by brick ones, which survive today in, among other places, Białobłoty, Łazińsk Pierwszy, Nowe Grądy, Michalinów Trąbczyński, Stare Prażuchy, Stawiszyn, Wrąbczynkowskie Hol., Zamęty and Zagórów.

An important element of the spatial organisation and the cultural landscape of the Olęder villages were the village burial grounds. For some of the settlements they are mentioned in the foundation charters cited above. Their existence is also shown by their positions on old maps (especially on the Map of the Quartermaster General's staff of the Polish Army of 1839), and above all by their remains (chiefly with gravestones of the second half of the nineteenth and the first half of the twentieth century) surviving to this day in more than 50 settlements, among them: the Ciemierowskie Stare Ol. (today Ciemierów Kolonia), the Wrąbczynkowskie Ol., the Cekowskie Nw. Ol. (Prażuchy Nw.), Plewnia Kolonia, Kuźnica, Poroże (Stare), Szadykierz, the Piskory Ol., and the Orlińskie Duże Ol.. They varied in area according to the size of the village's population. In their centre a tall wooden cross was put up. They were surrounded by a low fence, exceptionally by a wall, also of bog iron ore, as can be seen in Orlina Duża. The existence of burial grounds is confirmed, for instance, by the foundation charters for 10 of the 26 settlements in the district of Kalisz: the Dębniałki and Piskory Ol. (they were to receive land for a common "burial ground"), the Dzierzbińskie – Zdanowiec and Zamęty Ol. (they were to receive for a common cemetery for the dissenters a plot of 14 by 14 rods), the Kuszyńskie or Jaszczurowo Ol., together with the Kosmowskie Ol. ("...for the smallness of the place on the said Holendry called Jaszczurowo..., so these Jaszczurowo Holendry are to be buried on the Kosmowskie Holendry..."), the Przespolewskie Ol. (they received a plot for a cemetery, which they were to enclose with a fence), the Stropieszyńskie St. and Nw. Ol. (they received 3 morgen for a school and a cemetery, and timber from the manor), and the Zbierskie Ol. (for the "kirchow", that is the cemetery, they received a plot of 15x15 rods).

and the parish priests, binding the Olęders to pay the Catholic clergyman the so-called pokładne (burial fee). The charter for the Stropieszyńskie-Radzany and Gostynie Ol. of 1791 stated: "Since by a recent law [that is the constitutions of the Diet of 1768 – added Z.Ch.] freedom of worship has been reserved for all people of the Protestant [sic!] religion, therefore, as regards confession and burial, they shall be free to go to their own church, and the manor will give them protection in this, on the foundation of the said law, against all impeachments [attacks] of the clergy (should there be any)".

 Cf. n. 114.
chodyla2015/140:
Conclusion

This outline of the earliest history of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest in the years 1746-1793 has many gaps, which follow from how far the sources survive and how much they contain. It does, however, allow a few final conclusions to be drawn concerning: 1) the chronology, organisation, character of the land, conditions and causes of the founding, and the naming of the settlements, 2) their area, layout and buildings, 3) their population in the years 1789-1790, with the numbers and structure of the inhabitants by sex, age, social and property standing and occupation, 4) the legal, administrative and judicial situation of the Olęder population, 4) the economic and social life of the settlements, and 5) the material and spiritual culture and the daily life of their inhabitants.

1) The Pyzdry Forest, from the early Middle Ages to the present day one of the still fairly large forest complexes in Greater Poland proper, is an area in which, in the eighteenth century, Olęder settlement developed fairly vigorously; it was one of the main forms of rural rent-paying settlement in Poland in the period from the sixteenth to the beginning of the second half of the nineteenth century. In all, 58 Olęder settlements were founded in it in the years 1746-1792 (1793), within three Old Polish districts: the most in the district of Konin (28), then in that of Kalisz (25) and of Pyzdry (5). They belonged to three types of feudal property: royal, or more exactly at that time Crown (7, 1 of them on the estates of the royal town of Pyzdry), church (3, of them 1 on the estates of the bishopric of Poznań and 2 on monastic estates) and as many as 48 on noble estates, mostly on such as Grodziec-Królików, Gadów and Trąbczyn in the district of Konin and Dzierzbin, Chocz, Kosmów and Lipe in the district of Kalisz. Of these, two villages (the Kazimierskie Stare and Nowe Olędry) in the parish and on the estate of Chocz, which formed the endowment of a noble foundation of the mitred provostship of the collegiate church of Chocz, are sometimes regarded in the sources as church villages. Today 67 villages or parts of villages correspond to these 58 Olęder settlements, mostly under changed names, in 15 communes and six districts. The time of origin of 31 of the 58 Olęder settlements that arose in the Pyzdry Forest in the eighteenth century is fixed exactly by their foundation charters; for the rest it can be fixed exactly or approximately from the first mentions in other kinds of sources. Within the periodisation adopted
chodyla2015/141: for the history of Olęder settlement in Poland and Greater Poland, they arose in the second phase (1660-1793/1795) and the third period (1721-1793/95), most of them (44) in the third and last sub-period (1773-1793) of that period. The Olęder settlements were founded by the founders, owners or holders of landed estates, in agreement with locators acting individually or as a group on behalf of the whole future commune, or, mostly, with whole communes; they often issued to them first individual or collective but preliminary charters, and only later (for instance once the necessary number of settlers had gathered) collective and final ones, which settled the Olęder character of the village. On the royal estates they were founded by their tenants of the time (starosts, lessees), on the church estates by the bishop and by the superior and other members of the governing body of the convent of the Franciscan nuns in Kalisz, on the town estates by the magistrate of Pyzdry, and on the noble estates by the rich and middling nobility. The co-founder or founder of the largest number of Olęder villages was, on the property of Grodziec-Królików, Count Fraciszek Stadnicki, who in the district of Konin alone owned as many as 21 rural settlements. The founders of several dozen others, 12 persons, owned at least several such rural settlements, and sometimes little towns. The oldest settlements, at least 12 of them, were founded in the years 1746-1771; the rest, the great majority, were founded in the years 1772-1792. The founding of the Olęder villages was decided by the founders' wish to raise their income by settling and bringing into use land that had formerly been deserted and depopulated, or wooded, and often not taken up by settlement until then. The settling of Olęders, who answered jointly, in accordance with one of the basic principles of Olęder law, for paying money rents to the lords, assured their founders of a steady and regular income. For the Olęders the motive for settling were favourable legal and economic conditions of life, far better than in the country and the place of their origin or their earlier residence in Poland, and the assurance of religious freedom and freedom of public worship, guaranteed to the settlers in the foundation charters in accordance with the principles of Olęder law. As to the character of the land, of the 58 Olęder villages at least 37 were founded on woodland, and of these at least 27 on raw root, that is in places not settled before, in forests or woods (which is also shown by the long free years, 7-8, meant for clearing, setting up and building the settlements), 5 were founded on the site of settlements or parts of settlements that had existed earlier under the same names, even since the Middle Ages, and had been deserted and overgrown with forest at the end of the sixteenth and the beginning of the seventeenth century, and 5 on land partly tilled and ready. Of the 58 settlements founded in the Pyzdry Forest, 27 were founded on podzolic soils, 4 on black earths, 6 on marsh soils, 13 on muck soils, 4 on river alluvia, and 4 on mixed soils, 1 of them on podzolic soils, muck soils, river alluvia and dune sands, and 3 on podzolic-muck soils. So half of them arose on fertile and moderately fertile soils, half on infertile ones, and 4 on mixed soils, though with infertile soils predominating. Most
chodyla2015/142:
of the Olęder settlements received new names: possessive ones, derived from the names of a former village, or topographical names not tied to such names but referring to the local names of the woods, thickets, forests and wilds in which they were founded. Some villages received characteristic names, formed independently of the naming of old settlements, that is, among others, personal names, derived from the first names and surnames of the founders and members of their families. Some settlements bore names inherited from settlements long deserted, overgrown with forest and bushes, or cleared of their old inhabitants, on whose site or lands they were founded with new colonists settled under Olęder law, or from settlements still inhabited wholly or partly by their existing inhabitants, moved to this law – topographical and possessive names. In both cases the names of these settlements most often appeared with the addition (H)olendry or (H)olędry. It has survived to this day only in the names of 6 settlements.

2) The area of the Olęder villages that arose in the Pyzdry Forest depended on the reserves of land (forest or other) at the founders' disposal, and also on the number of settlers obtained or coming forward. The holdings of land granted to the settlers ranged from 1 to ½ huba, that is włóka (łan), though often of various kinds and sizes according to the length of the basic measures – rods and ells – by which they were measured. Besides, the Olęder villages received smaller holdings of land for the innkeeper, the school (house of prayer), the teacher and the burial ground. In these 58 Olęder settlements there were in the years 1789–1790 about 651 hearths (farms) in all. In the number of farms there was a wide range between settlements – very small ones of 2-5 hearths were 9, small ones of 6-10 hearths 11, middling ones of 11-15 hearths 5, larger than middling, of 16-20 hearths, 8, large ones of 21-25 hearths only 2, and very large ones, of 26 hearths or more, only 1. For 15 settlements the functional and social-economic structure of their hearths is known. Among them, if we leave aside 2 breweries, 6 inns and 2 craftsmen's hearths, hearths with one farmer decidedly predominated, found in all 15 Olęder villages, 636 in all. Hearths with 2 farmers, 37 in all, were found in only 5 settlements, garden hearths with land and garden, 16 in number, in 3 settlements, and those without land and garden, 2 in number, in 1 settlement. Most of the hearths were "self-tilling hearths", that is farms, of which there were 662 in 1791. The layout of the Olęder settlements in the area of this forest complex varied. 9 settlements were row villages on marshy, uniform land, with rows of buildings in various arrangements, sometimes partly scattered; regular and irregular street villages founded on mixed land were 2; as many as 40 settlements were loose, scattered settlements, and 7 were mixed. The buildings of the farmsteads (farms) – dwellings and farm buildings – were scattered; the buildings were usually put up separately on a quadrangular plan; the cottages were most probably, as in all the villages of the time, mostly arcaded; and the farm buildings consisted of barns, stables, cowsheds and pigsties, put up by various
chodyla2015/143:
techniques, of wooden logs, clay and bog iron ore. In the buildings and layout of the Olęder villages in the Pyzdry Forest, most of which were wholly or partly inhabited by people of the Protestant confession, important elements were the houses of prayer – schools – and the burial grounds, which lay on the whole on the edges of the villages.

3) In the 58 Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest there lived in the years 1789–1790 about 3,815 persons in all, of whom 499 in 5 settlements in the district of Pyzdry, 1,457 in 25 settlements in the district of Kalisz, and 1,859 in 28 settlements in the district of Konin. The statistical average number of inhabitants per settlement was 65.77 persons. In the 45 settlements for which the demographic structure of their inhabitants is known there lived 3,154 persons, 1,707 (50.32%) of them male and 1,685 (49.68%) female. Of these 3,154 persons, 449 (234 male and 215 female) lived in 3 settlements of the district of Pyzdry, 1,368 persons (691 male and 6776 female) lived in 22 settlements of the district of Kalisz, and 1,337 persons (654 male and 683 female) lived in 20 settlements of the district of Konin. The social, property and occupational structure can be grasped for only 25 Olęder settlements (3 in the district of Pyzdry and 22 in the district of Kalisz). There were in all in them 1,518 farmers and rent-paying cottagers (that is Olęders proper with the members of their families), who can in principle be regarded as one and the same social and occupational category, 50 lodgers, 7 craftsmen, 13 innkeepers and tapsters, 102 farm servants and servants, 68 luźni (landless persons) and 59 other persons. The confessional structure of the inhabitants of the 58 Olęder settlements founded in the years 1746-1792 in the Pyzdry Forest varied. A population Protestant by confession predominated in them, and, judging not only from religion but also from names and other indications, ethnically German, but it made up no more than about 52% of the whole population. The composition in this respect of the 1,337 inhabitants of 20 of the 28 Olęder settlements in the district of Konin, which is known more exactly, was as follows: there were 6 settlements inhabited exclusively by dissenters, 385 in all (Lutherans, and perhaps to a small degree Reformed Protestants), 4 with a Catholic population, 210 in all, and 10 settlements with a mixed population, Catholic and Protestant (almost exclusively Lutheran), with 365 Catholics and 377 dissenters in all. So in all these settlements there lived 575 Catholics and 762 dissenters in all, that is Protestants – Lutherans, and perhaps in two or three of these settlements also Reformed. The places the settlers came from are not exactly known, but on the strength of certain indications given above (the measures of land, the similarity of names, the dialects used) it seems that they came to the settlements from the borderland of Greater Poland and Silesia and from Silesia, and from older Protestant Olęder, and perhaps sołtys, settlements, chiefly in western Greater Poland, not known by name, but mostly from the same places (as their kinship, legible in identical surnames, seems to show). Ethnically about 52% of them were Germans. Assuming that confession and ethnicity coincided in about 90%, it may be accepted
chodyla2015/144:
that about 38% of the inhabitants of the Olęder villages in the Pyzdry Forest were Poles. Exact findings cannot be given here, since the sense of identity and ethnic identification among the population, especially the peasants, was not then as clear-cut as it is today, and was only beginning to take shape.

4) The inhabitants of the Olęder settlements that arose in the Pyzdry Forest lived according to the principles of Olęder law, that is the solidarity of the whole commune towards the manor and internal equality among themselves. The Olęders, unlike the peasants owing labour service, were always personally free. The Olęders' subjection as to the land showed itself in their rights in rem to the land, through the definition of the forms of holding it and the conditions of the freedom to alienate and sell farms, in their rights of use on the lord's land (the so-called servitudes of pasture, fishing and others), and in their dependence on the manor's monopolies (chiefly that of propination). The most important of them, the right to the land, took in Greater Poland in the eighteenth century, apart from a few exceptions of emphyteusis in the sense of a short-term lease of land, for several decades, in principle the form of emphyteusis in the sense of a lease unlimited in time, perpetual, tied to the requirement that the holding of land first be bought by entry money, which once the entry money was paid turned in practice into a perpetual rent tenure (German Erbzinsrecht). The ownership of the land assigned to the Olęders was not full but usufructuary and divided, since its legal owner was still the lord, who, however, had no right to remove an Olęder from it as long as he used it in accordance with the provisions of the charter. The self-government of the Olęder communes consisted of a sołtys and, mostly, two assessors, elected by the commune assemblies, with in principle a one-year term. As the commune court, the sołtys and the assessors were to keep internal peace and order in the settlements and to settle quarrels and disputes. They judged by Olęder law, whose terms were set by the foundation charters of the individual settlements and, for some of them, also by the wilkierze. From the judgments of the commune court the Olęders had the right of appeal to the manor, that is to the dominium (lord's) court, for which the right to judge in criminal cases of robbery, arson, homicide and serious bodily harm), and of course all offences against the lord, was also reserved. The Olęders' judicial subjection consisted precisely in their being subject to the dominium (lord's) court to this extent. The villages they inhabited were for the most part independent spatial-economic, legal-constitutional and administrative-judicial units (communes). Some of them, however, namely 14, formed two-village communes, and in one case even a three-village commune, with common sołtyses. 5) The inhabitants of the 58 Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest in the eighteenth century were nearly 98% directly occupied in farming. This is confirmed, indirectly, by the fact mentioned above that of the total of 681 hearths in 1789, as many as 662 hearths were counted as farming hearths in 1791. For the innkeepers, smallholders, teachers and others with smaller holdings of land, too, work in farming was an important additional occupation. The basic branch of the Olęders' farming was crop-growing, and especially grain. Garden crops were of secondary, supplementary
chodyla2015/145:
importance. The second important branch of the economy of the inhabitants of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest was the raising of animals – cattle, sheep and pigs, and also horses and poultry. The Olęders took an active part in trade, selling the surplus of their crops (grain) and their stock (cattle, horses, pigs, poultry and dairy produce), sometimes also trading in goods made or obtained in non-farming occupations (for instance crafts and bee-keeping), and buying in return grain and other foodstuffs, timber, or tools at the markets and fairs in the towns. On account of the perpetual, hereditary use of the land, the inhabitants of the Olęder villages founded in the Pyzdry Forest were bound to render to the lords – the founders of the settlements and their heirs – money rents for the land, dues in kind and labour (tłoki, seasonal labour service at harvest and haymaking, and other services, and carting journeys), paid on a yearly basis after the free years had run out, and to buy the manor's drink under the compulsion of propination. They also bore some administrative fees, for instance on the sale of land. The most important burden was the money rent, paid on the whole once a year, on a set date, and in an amount according to the size of the holding (farm). It was collected from the individual farmers and handed over jointly by the sołtys of the village against a receipt from the feudal lord or his representative. The inhabitants of all the Olęder settlements founded in the eighteenth century in the Pyzdry Forest were also bound, like the inhabitants of other villages, to render to the state taxes in money, paid every year in two instalments (March and September) – the poll tax, attested in separate tariffs for the years 1775 and 1789-1790, the hiberna in the settlements on royal estates in the tariff of 1775, the offering of 10 gr (on noble estates) and 20 gr on church estates of 1789 – and a tax in kind, the so-called levy (zsypka) from the "self-tilling" [farming] hearths, in the form of a set number of korzec of rye and oats from such a hearth. Besides, all the inhabitants of many Olęder settlements, Catholics but also, to a large extent, Protestants, were bound to render to the Roman Catholic Church dues in the form of fees jura stolae (that is for baptisms, weddings and funerals), meszne and kolęda. The Protestants were bound to pay jura stolae both until 1768 and often after the toleration law of that year, especially when they settled on land formerly settled and later deserted, in Olęder villages that arose on the site of medieval settlements assigned in this respect to a parish, sometimes also in the foundation deeds of these parish districts.

6) The material and spiritual culture and the daily life of the people of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest in the eighteenth century are not easy to describe, because the information in the written sources is very scanty. Supplementing it with data from museum documentation, the ethnographic literature and modern research, it can be said that, in the case of dwelling and farm buildings, the architecture of the buildings has common features characteristic of the area of the Pyzdry Forest.
chodyla2015/146:
As for spiritual culture, it can be said that the inhabitants of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest were guaranteed religious freedom and freedom of public worship in the form proper to their religion. The place where it was practised in this period, in every village inhabited by Protestants, was the school-house of prayer, and the services were led, to a basic extent, by the teachers (readers) who taught the children in them, especially the basics of religion, and prepared them for confirmation. The Olęder dissenters (Protestants) also had their own burial grounds, whose remains have survived to this day in practically all the villages in which they lived. The culture of daily life of the people of the Olęder settlements was made up of their housing (the dwelling houses and their furnishings), work, clothing, food, and the customs and manners connected with their production, division and use. People dressed according to the customs brought from their places of origin, differently – as is obvious – on weekdays and on feast days, in clothes chiefly of their own making, of linen and sheep's wool, but partly also sewn from cloth bought in the towns and little towns. The food of the people of the Olęder settlements that arose in the Pyzdry Forest did not differ fundamentally from that of other settlements and was in proportion to their prosperity. They ate rye bread and other grain or flour dishes, groats, vegetables, butter, cheese, from time to time meat, in Lent probably herrings and other fish, which the Olęders had the right to catch in the waters adjoining their land, and honey from their own apiaries, and fruit; they drank beer, then general, and also milk. Various manifestations of the Olęders' material and spiritual culture showed differences, even after a century, compared with those known for the Polish rural population. This followed from the separateness of language, the religious separation and the unwillingness to assimilate on the Olęders' side, and also from differences in the mentality of the two sides. Nevertheless there were some contacts between them, and some practices were taken over or imitated, especially in farming and stock-raising, in which the Olęders led.

Summing up this outline of the earliest history of the Olęder settlements in the Pyzdry Forest, it must be said that, because of the number of these settlements and the detail of some of the source information on some questions, together with its absence on other matters, and the limited size of this study, it was impossible to create an even, full and exhaustive picture of it.

In appreciating the contribution of Olęder settlement to the development of the network of settlements and to the social and economic development of the area, it should be seen in the context of rural settlement as a whole, not only that of its own time but also earlier and later. For in the years 1794/1796-1863 further changes took place in the settlement structure of the area of the Pyzdry Forest. In this period at least 28 settlements were founded. Of these, at least 17 Olęder settlements arose by the 1840s, and by the beginning of the 1860s 11 other rent-paying settlements, among them such as Święcia, Olchowo, Emilienheim, that is Oleśnica, Michalinów, Tarszewo, Grądzeń Las, Mały Las, Chruściki, Grądzeń, Drzewce, Kopojno, Oleśnica Kolonia, Oleśnica Wielka and Zarzew, in the then communes of Dąbroszyn, Oleśnica and Dłusk. Some of them were founded in the period of South Prussia on the site of old villages, deserted or
chodyla2015/147:
cleared of their existing inhabitants. At the same time and later, the individual parts of the Pyzdrskie Olędry turned, as the area of the larger farms was divided and new settlers were brought in, into villages of many farmsteads spatially and separate administratively. As a result, what was originally one settlement in administrative and judicial terms, with colony-type, scattered (dispersed) buildings in the form of so-called pustkowia, turned into 9, or even, counting in turn round the edge of the forest, 12 separate settlements: Kruszyny, Zamość, Grądy Dolne and Górne, Baraniec, Zimochowiec, Tłoczyzna, Glinianki, Trzcianki, Zapowiednia, Żdżary and Królewiny. At this time, too, 2 or even 3 separate settlements in time split off from some other Old Polish Olęder settlements; for instance the Białobłockie Ol. divided into Białobłoty, Garncarski Kąt and Krzyżówka.

After the enfranchisement of the peasants in the Kingdom of Poland (1864), a new wave of settlement appeared in the years 1870-1880 on private landed estates, among them those bordering on the town woods of Pyzdry from the south and east, on the parcelled lands of demesne farms. Then and later, up to 1914, 55 rural settlements, on the whole smaller ones, and at least 9 industrial settlements were founded on them. Among the settlers of the Old Polish and later Olęder settlements and other rent-paying settlements in the Pyzdry Forest, at least 82 in all, the German element predominated. The population of the new colonies, partly forming fairly compact groups, partly scattered, differed from the native population in language, religion, its own social institutions, such as the school and the house of prayer, dress, customs and manners. It came chiefly from Silesia and to a lesser extent from the Neumark (Ciążeńskie Holendry, Wrąbczyn, Wrąbczynkowskie Holendry, Olchowo, Mały Las, Tarszewo, Babia, Józefów, Zarzew, Augustynów, Święcia). In the nineteenth century there were significant changes in the buildings, the population and the confessional, and probably also the ethnic, composition, and in the literacy of the inhabitants of the Olęder settlements that arose in the Pyzdry Forest in the eighteenth century.

In the nineteenth century there were also changes in the church organisation of the Olęder settlements. The settlements with an exclusively or mostly Protestant population, almost exclusively Lutheran, were joined to the Lutheran parishes of the Evangelical-Augsburg diocese of Kalisz. It used the Protestant parish churches at Stawiszyn (1780), Grodziec (from 1796), Prażuchy (from 1808), Konin (from 1826) and Zagórów (from 1858) and the filial churches at Józefów near Kaźmierka Stara (from 1843) and Lisewo (1858) and at Żychlin.

In the inter-war period about 12 new settlements arose, often in the character of hamlets or outlying hamlets with their own names (though etymologically mostly tied to the names of old villages). They were founded on the lands of estates parcelled out in carrying out the provisions of the agrarian

chodyla2015/148:
reform of 1925. At that time too, in carrying out those provisions that concerned the abolition of servitudes, the town of Pyzdry lost 785 ha of woodland to the owners of plots that had been burdened with the duty of protecting the town forests. The newly created plots were laid out as enclaves within forest areas with valuable stands of trees, mostly oak. This operation, carried out chaotically, contributed to the disorganisation of what had once been a rational forest economy, and to the appearance of a considerable number of new farms, also within older villages, without any planning principles. At the same time the process of the fragmentation of farms, begun already in the nineteenth century, went on, lasting here, with some breaks, until the law on the protection of farm and forest land was passed in 1971.

In the years 1945-2015, and also later, as a result of this process up to that time, and also of the creation of recreational plots, 10 new small settlements appeared. Today in the area of the Pyzdry Forest, which lies within the one voivodeship of Greater Poland and the 6 districts and 15 communes mentioned above, there are 328 settlement names, among them 6 little towns, 323 villages and other settlements.

Today the Old Polish, and also the later, Olęder settlements are inhabited only in a smaller part by the descendants of the first settlers – Catholics – and in a minimal part also by the descendants of the Protestants – Germans. This is because almost all the German Protestant inhabitants of these settlements were expelled from the Pyzdry Forest and forced to leave for Germany after 1945. The Olęder settlements they had inhabited until 1945 were settled to a greater or lesser degree by Polish newcomers, and some were afforested.

There have survived to this day in the Olęder settlements of the Pyzdry Forest – from the enfranchisement of their inhabitants on, really post-Olęder ones – such elements of their cultural landscape as the layouts of the villages and their fields, ditches and dikes, the course of some roads, plantings of trees, the former Lutheran churches, traditional farmsteads, schools and cemeteries. Unfortunately, the original names of these villages have survived only to a very small degree, since most of them were changed in the inter-war and post-war periods, among other things with the intention of Polonising them and shortening their linguistic form. Only six settlements contain the characteristic distinguishing element (H)olędry or (H)olendry: Ciążeńskie Holendry, Wrąbczynkowskie Holendry, Złotkowskie Holendry, Gadowskie Holendry, Holendry Jaroszewickie and Olendry Smaszewskie.

These monuments and this toponymy, being a common historical – human, European – cultural value, raise the tourist attraction of the micro-region of the Pyzdry Forest. They should be protected and cared for permanently by the local communities, local government institutions, religious bodies, schools, and social, cultural, sightseeing and tourist organisations. The Cultural Society "Echo Pyzdr" has done much to protect these monuments, document them and spread knowledge of them in society. Its work helps to deepen the historical awareness of the inhabitants of the individual places and of the whole region, and to spread knowledge of the important elements of the historical space and the cultural heritage not only at the local but also at the wider regional and national level.
chodyla2015/149:
Glossary of Old Polish terms

asekuracja – here: a security, a written guarantee.

bicie rowów – digging ditches and lining them with fascines.

cekowska dzierżawa (the lease of Ceków) – an organisational unit of the royal/Crown estates in the district of Kalisz, with the village of Ceków as its centre; in the 1770s made up, besides that village, also of the newly founded Cekowskie Stare and Nowe Olędry.

czeladź – village servants, hired people, recruited from peasant youth (male and female) (of full peasants, more often of smallholders, cottagers and lodgers), mostly before marriage, employed on peasant farms (chiefly full peasant farms) and on demesne farms, under agreements usually made for a year, and paid with lodging, food, clothing and small sums of money (the so-called myto).

czerwony złoty (red złoty) – a ducat, a gold coin weighing about 3.5 g of almost pure metal, from 1787 equal to 18 Polish silver złoty.

czynszujący (rent-payers) – here peasants, Olęder farmers, who under their agreements paid, as their most important due, a money rent and possibly an additional rent in kind (grain, poultry) in return for the use of the land, most often perpetual.

dezerta (from Latin deserta), see pustka.

dobra stołowe (mensal estates) – estates forming the endowment, the source of income and the basis of maintenance of a particular office or official connected with the court (household), in this case the mensal estates of the bishop of Poznań.

efemeryda (ephemeral settlement) – here: a settlement undoubtedly Olęder in its legal constitution and economy, but existing as such only for a time, turned into a labour-service settlement, not through evolution but for other reasons.

emfiteuza (emphyteusis, from Latin emphiteusis) – in the feudal period it was most often understood as the long-term (renewable) and perpetual lease of land by peasants, tied to the obligation to pay an annual rent and to inform the owner of an intention to sell, since the owner had the right of pre-emption or 10% of the sale price of the land.

fundator (founder, from Latin fundo, fundator) – here: the feudal founder of a settlement, in this case a rural, Olęder one.

garniec – a measure of capacity, from 1764 equal to 3.77 litres, divided into 2 half-garniec, 4 kwarty and 16 kwaterki.

kasztelan (castellan) – an Old Polish official, in the Middle Ages the governor of a castle (gród, kasztel, from Latin castellum, castle) and of the castle district (castellany), military commander and judge in the monarch's name in its area, a member of the royal council, in early modern times a senator; castellans were divided into greater (provincial) and lesser (district ones, also called drążkowi).

kmiecie (full peasants) – the basic stratum of the rural population in the thirteenth to nineteenth centuries, holders of farms regarded as full ones. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, when German law was introduced, they were usually settled on farms of one łan (one włóka), but then and later they often received larger holdings, of two łany (and as such were also called farmers, gospodarze rolnicy), or smaller, of half a łan (half-peasants, półrolnicy). In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries the main burdens of the k. were money rents and dues in kind (chiefly in grain) to the lord and tithe to the Church; in the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries they were burdened more and more with labour service, reaching in the seventeenth century 5-6 days, and in the eighteenth century sometimes a dozen or so days a week per łan, which forced the k. to employ servants. To till their own and the lord's land the k. kept a considerable team (in the seventeenth century usually 2 horses and 4 oxen). In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the size of full peasant farms shrank considerably, to ½ and even ¼ łan, and the percentage of k. in the structure of the rural population fell. Beside the k. owing labour service there was a far less numerous group of rent-paying k. (for instance the Olęders), as a rule richer and more independent economically.

komornicy (lodgers) – a category of the landless rural population found in the fourteenth to nineteenth centuries, owning neither cottages nor land, living most often with farmers (Olęders too) and living by hired work for them or at the manor, often as servants; sometimes owning a few animals and tilling, in return for work, scraps of land; the poorest stratum of the settled rural population.
chodyla2015/150:
kontraktowy (contract man) – a peasant (Olęder too), more often a craftsman, settled in a village under an individual contract, that is an agreement made with the feudal lord, the owner or the holder of the landed estate.

kontrakt (contract, from Latin contractus) – here the agreement of the founder of a settlement with the settlers or their representatives and the whole village commune, most often in the form of a unilateral charter issued by the founder; it could be individual and preliminary, or collective and final, and according to its legal character emphyteutic – short-term (for several decades) or perpetual.

korzec warszawski (Warsaw korzec) – a measure of capacity, from 1764 equal to 120.6 litres; it was divided into 2 Gdańsk korczyki and 32 garniec.

lokacja (from Latin locatio) – here the founding of a settlement, based on an agreement setting its legal and economic conditions, formulated by the founder in agreement with the settlers.

lokator (from Latin locator) – the osadźca, the representative of the settlers who made the agreement with the founder of the settlement on their behalf, a settlement entrepreneur who brought in the settlers and organised the new settlement; most often he settled in the village founded and (at least at the beginning) held the office of its sołtys, and also drew material benefits from his function (for instance in the form of additional land).

łanowy układ przestrzenny (łan layout) – a layout of arable land in the form of a łan, the area of a full peasant farm, whose size, according to how it was understood as a unit of measurement, ranged from 16.7 to 25.8 ha, and which was laid out with various kinds of rods and ells.

łokieć (ell) – a unit of measure; from 1764 the Warsaw ell equalled 59.6 cm (a measure of length) and was divided into 24 inches; the square Warsaw ell equalled 0.354666 m² (a measure of area).

niwowy układ (niwa layout) – a layout of arable land in the form of a niwa, that is a new area of land won for tillage chiefly by clearing forests, belonging to one or several farmers, its shape and size depending on the conditions of the ground and the property relations; it was characterised by the marking out of three basic fields (winter, spring and fallow), in which the peasants, sometimes with the lord's manor, held separate strips (płosy) forming a łan (włóka), which divided the niwa into long strips.

oblata (from Latin oblatus, and that from offerre, oblatum, to bring before; to leave) – here: the entering (copying) or taking of a legal act into the books of a court and office (for instance a municipal court).

okupne (entry money; in German most often called Grungeld) – the payment for land used in perpetuity, for the perpetual right to hold it and draw its profits.

plenipotent – the attorney of another person, acting on his written authority, most often declared before an office.

podkomorzy (chamberlain) – an Old Polish land official, presiding over the chamberlain's court, the boundary court, legal representative of poor widows and orphans of the noble estate and (only in Greater Poland and only until the turn of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries) a member of the land court.

podwoda – a transport service, otherwise called a journey (droga), rendered by peasants, in this case Olęders, to the manor (mostly once a year) as part of their labour services, one of the forms of manorial obligations, sometimes commuted into a payment; podwody were used to carry the demesne farm's grain and other goods to local markets (the so-called small journeys, up to about 35 km) and more distant ones (great journeys, up to about 84 km), made with the peasants' carts and two-horse teams.

pręt (rod) – a measure of length, from 1764 equal to 4 m 46 cm 6.54 mm; it was equal to 7½ ells.

przestęp – (white or red bryony) – a perennial, a common plant of the gourd family with black or red berries.

przymus propinacyjny (compulsion of propination) – the absolute obligation of the peasants (Olęders too) to buy the drink produced on their feudal lords' estates, under threat of heavy money fines and even removal from their farms.

pustka – the land of a village deserted for various reasons, overgrown again with forest and unused, needing clearing.

rudunek (from German Rodung) – clearing, also called rumunek.

rumunek – clearing, or cleared places, or a settlement founded on the site of felled woods; the name comes from the German räumen (to empty, to clear away, to remove).

rychwalska miara (the Rychwał measure) – here: a local variety of the wiertel, referring to the standard of this measure probably kept in the town hall of the little town of Rychwał; not exactly known.

siąg kwadratowy (square siąg), otherwise sążeń – a non-metric measure; the Old Polish one – 1.786 m (according to the constitution
chodyla2015/151:
of 1764); derived from the sążeń is the sąg, a cubic measure of wood: 1 sąg (forest, for wood) = ½ cubic sążeń = 2.58 m³.

skarbnik latyczewski (treasurer of Latyczów) – an Old Polish land official, in medieval Poland caring for the royal treasure – valuables, jewels and documents; in early modern times an honorary, titular office tied to a voivodeship or district or land, the last in the hierarchy of land offices; in this case tied to the district of Latyczów/Latyczew in Podolia.

starosta (starost) – "with judicial power" (castle starost, general starost) a judicial and administrative official appointed by the king, over a land, a district or a larger area, who also held on lease royal (state) estates forming the endowment of his office; "without judicial power" only a tenutariusz, that is the lessee and manager of larger or smaller organisational and economic units of the royal or state landed estates, called starosties, tenuty or leases (dzierżawy), and sometimes only of single villages, farms (sołtys or wójt holdings) and objects (such as mills).

stolnik – an Old Polish land official, in the Middle Ages in charge of the ruler's table, in early modern times an honorary, titular office of a voivodeship or a land.

sucha beczka ("dry barrel") – an empty barrel, not filled with beer, the symbol of a set money fine paid to the manor for evading or breaking the compulsion of propination.

szambelan (chamberlain), otherwise court chamberlain (podkomorzy nadworny) – a court official responsible for the monarch's residence, with authority over the chamber servants and courtiers assigned to serve the king, attending the king at the sessions of the Diet and of the court, on journeys and on campaigns; in the eighteenth century a purely titular, honorary office.

szarwark – the compulsory service of the peasant population, Olęders too, in labour or with teams, in repairing and building roads, bridges, dikes and flood embankments.

talar (thaler) – a large silver coin weighing about 28 g, of good metal, struck in many countries of Europe from the end of the fifteenth and the first half of the sixteenth century; after 1764 in Poland it equalled 8 złp.; from the sixteenth century in the countries of the Holy Roman Empire (the Reich) called the reichsthaler, the Imperial thaler, struck also to its proper standard in Polish mints.

tatarka – a grain, a species of buckwheat.

tenutariusz – see starosta.

tynf, tymf – the colloquial name of the silver Polish złoty pieces struck in the years 1663-1667 at Bydgoszcz and Lwów by Andrzej Tymf, lessee of the Crown mints, which had a set rate of 30 gr. but were really worth 12-18 gr.; their enormous production (about 6 million pieces) helped to intensify inflation.

wiertel – before the partitions of Poland a measure of farmland equal to 3,591 m² [sic]; later, as the Berlin wiertel (Viertel, the Prussian quarter), a measure of capacity of liquids and of the volume of dry goods (grain too), equal to 7.9 l.; here it occurs in the latter sense.

wizja (inspection) – a detailed official description of the real and movable property and of the rent drawn from peasant or burgher farms, drawn up most often in connection with a change of the holder of the estate, at the request of the parties concerned, carried out on the spot by a sworn court usher representing the office, the municipal court or the land court, in the presence of witnesses, and differing in this from a private-law description such as other inventories.

wojski – an Old Polish land official, in the Middle Ages the castellan's deputy for military affairs, responsible for order in the district during a military expedition, guardian of the wives and children of the nobles at war; in early modern times an honorary, titular office, the last but one in the hierarchy of land offices.

wolnizna (free years) – the time of several years, set in the foundation charter, meant for taking up and bringing into use the land received as a holding (the area for a farm), free of obligations to the manor, the state and the Church; its length depended above all on the character of that land.

wywód (churching) – here: the blessing of a mother after the birth of a child, when she is led into the Catholic church.

zagrodnicy (smallholders) – otherwise ogrodnicy, a category of the peasant population with little land, mostly subject, existing in the thirteenth to nineteenth centuries, holding small farms, on the whole of 5-6 morgen; in the Olęder settlements there were also, besides such smallholders, "smallholders without land and garden", who had cottages but were probably in fact people living by hired work.

złoty polski, or złoty (złotówka) – a Polish silver coin, from 1764 equal to 4 silver groszy, 2 half-złoty, or 30 copper groszy.
