guradze1898/c07:
Chapter V.

Some Insights into the Service Obligations of the Farmers of South Prussia.

During the time of South Prussia, noble landowners still had considerable leeway in their treatment of their subject farmers. For example, until 1803, these farmers had to tolerate arbitrary relocation. When filling the vacancies left by deceased non-hereditary farms—most socage farmers' farms were not hereditary—the discretion of the landowner was unrestricted. With respect to support during calamities, there were no specific rules, and although it was generally the custom for the landowner to take care of major repairs and new buildings while the farmer handled minor repairs, the only standard was the needs of the subjects on the one hand and the goodwill of the estate owner on the other. Non-privileged farmers were supported either through the remission of services, through cash advances, or not at all in maintaining buildings and during calamities.

Grazing and forest rights were generally considered appurtenances of the estates, and heath pasturing was usually permitted for a moderate fee or even for free.

The dues on noble estates were usually higher than on the domains and often so high that it seems astonishing how the farmers could manage. This can be partially explained by the fact that there was often an excess of services available, and therefore some were not demanded by the landowners. For instance, in the Polajewo estate, there were 11,039 more labour services available than were needed; that is, of the 21,069⅓ labour services that could have been demanded, more than half were superfluous. Also, where farmers had high dues to pay, they were often in continuous arrears. This was particularly common in bad years, as frequently mentioned in the official monthly reports of the governments of Bromberg and Posen to the King, called "newspaper reports."

Whether the services and dues were burdensome in individual cases is hard to say. One would have to at least determine the size of the field and other appurtenances of the estate from the land settlement records to get an accurate picture. Because the size specifications of that time are usually so vague that it is impossible to draw any definite conclusions. The conditions of dues and the situation of the noble farmers were extraordinarily diverse in South Prussia, not only in different regions of the province but even on estates located very close to each other, often even within the same manor. All of the reports in the files talk about the complexity of the conditions, which arose because the services of almost every farmer were determined in a different way and were usually entirely independent of the size of the field belonging to the estate. A uniform presentation of the farmers' conditions concerning dues would therefore be entirely impossible; I refer to what was said in the chapter that deals with the conditions of the Netze District, which generally also applies to the conditions in South Prussia.

Thoma indicates that one would hardly find a socage farmer in South Prussia who cultivates a Magdeburg Hufe (a unit of land) and is burdened with fewer services than 104 hand days, 100 team days, 30 domestic chores, 20 garden tasks, and 20 forced labour days (tłuki, mostly during sowing and harvest time). This would be an average of 2 team days and 3⅓ hand days per week throughout the year. However, this information seems to be based only on a completely arbitrary estimate of the average.

Overall, the services were only measured up until 1793 insofar as they were measured at all, in that the numbers expressed what the landowner intended to demand from the serfs; there was a very one-sided legal obligation on the part of the farmer, which could be unilaterally increased or reduced by the landlord at any time, and to which no corresponding legal obligation of the landlord was opposed. Even if the numbers quoted may often have sounded extremely high, it would still always have to be determined whether as much was actually demanded as they indicated, and that may often enough not have been the case, corresponding to the above-mentioned conditions of the Polajewo estate.

"The treatment in terms of services," says von Holsche, "was bearable. For most farmers, they were determined for a series of years, according to the needs of the estate, for certain weekly services, forced labour days during the harvest and sowing season, and for long hauls; rarely was more demanded of them. This had a good reason; because the farm and the entire inventory belonged to the lord. If he thus burdened the farmer beyond his capacity with services, the farmer could not cultivate his own field and could not live from it with his family, his cattle would collapse, and the lord would have to give him back sowing and bread grain along with inventory livestock if he wanted services from him, or he would risk the farmer running away altogether. The strictest lords were therefore, because their own advantage depended on it, induced not to impose more burdens on their farmers than they could bear, and whoever went further was considered by others to be a poor farmer."

"That these farmers could achieve nothing was due to the nature of the matter itself because they had nothing of their own, and if they came into better condition than their neighbours, they had to maintain their buildings and supplement the inventory from their own means. All that the good farmer could have ahead of the negligent one was that the good farmer lived somewhat better than the negligent one."

"The demands of the serfs are certainly not determined by the yield of their farms, but by the needs of the estate or noble property; hence some farmers serve two, others three and four, and still others six days a week, and must also drive to the market for the lord on Sundays. However, this is again due to the fact that the farmer has nothing of his own, and even if personal serfdom is abolished, the lords cannot be forced to reduce the demands." Holsche seems to have had the right feeling that the farmers would have been far better served by improving their material situation than by abolishing the personal restrictions that arose from serfdom. The government probably also intended something similar when it set up the Urbarial Commissions in 1793\. The aim was probably not only to determine but also to reduce the farmers' contributions. Even if this, as it seems to me, has not been directly stated, both the extremely low assessments of the farmers in the tax assessments and the fact that the subjects were directly pointed to the impossibility claim indicate that even then a relief of the service and tax relationship was being sought where this was absolutely necessary. It is quite natural that the farmers, either by themselves or through the commissioners, had to become properly aware of what they were actually accustomed to doing when taking up the urbaria, and thus the incentive to bring the impossibility claim may have arisen in many cases. However, it seems that the judiciary of the province was by no means in a position where such claims could have been quickly settled in large numbers.

In fact, even considering the above, one cannot assume that the contributions were generally extremely exaggerated; it would have only gone up to the point where, in the sense of the proverb, the other hand would have had to start helping to wash the one. So if the contributions of the peasants seem to have been generally very high, one cannot say, like Rummler does, 'And what were the counter-contributions of the landowner? A small piece of arable land with 18—20 bushels of sowing.' The arable land may have been the only counter-contribution from the landowner to which the corvée peasants had a real right during Polish times. But the actual counter-contributions of the landowners of South Prussia are the same as those previously said of the Netze District, and these actual counter-contributions had become legal obligations of the landowners through Prussian legislation. Then one can see nothing from the specification '18—20 bushels of sowing.' Because if this should serve us as a useful example, it would still have to be added whether these 18—20 bushels mean 'sowing in winter fields,' as was usual, or the sum of all sowing, and how large the bushels specifically meant were. Beheim-Schwarzbach has already pointed out the variation of the measure. The South Prussian bushel 'large measure' has, according to Stenger, amounted to four Berlin bushels. So if this should be about 80 Berlin bushels of winter field sowing, considering the landowner's obligations related to pasturage and forest rights, building and maintenance of inventory etc., it would perhaps be a very appropriate counter-contribution for the services and levies mentioned for the peasants of Althöfchen. Namely, they had to provide 14 geese, 2 capons, 2 chickens, 4 quarters of heather oats, 2 pieces of spun yarn, 28 groschen of guard money, 18 quarters of grain, and 3—4 cart services per week. But one cannot even judge that if one does not know the quality of the soil, the sowing quantity per acre, the sales opportunities, and everything else that needs to be considered.

Another conclusion from Rummler is also incomprehensible to me. He says, “traces can be found that the free farmer's rights were curtailed and he was pushed down by the landlords into the position of a leaseholder,” and substantiates this claim by stating that the information table of the ecclesiastical property of Barcinek identifies three local residents as emphyteutic free farmers and explains this term as follows: “The emphyteutic lease would last until the fourth male generation.”

Firstly, there is as little contradiction in 'free farmer' (Freibauer) and 'leaseholder' (Zeitpacher) as there is in the term 'free farmer' and 'emphyteutic tenant.' The term 'free farmer' describes a personal legal relationship, while 'leaseholder' or 'emphyteutic tenant' describes the farmer's legal relationship to his landholding. All emphyteutic tenants in Poland were free farmers. Long-term emphyteusis for multiple generations, instead of for a specific series of years, has been a common occurrence. I only refer to the cited document in which Abbot Szołdrski grants free farmer Thomas Kaminski a place with emphyteutic rights 'pro se et successoribus usque ad tertiam progeniem inclusive' (for himself and his successors up to the third generation inclusive). There is therefore absolutely no impairment of hereditary lease rights in the case mentioned, as Rummler may have been suggesting.

During the South Prussian period, as well as previously during the last period of the Polish realm, a trend emerged among the owners of manor estates aimed at improving the conditions of the peasants. This was in the correct understanding that by doing so, they were simultaneously promoting their own prosperity and that of the entire country. Owners of significant estates granted freedom to their subordinate peasants and turned them into rent-paying farmers, such as the Lords of Brzostowski, Chreptowicz, Zamoiski, Felix Potocki, St. Poniatowski, as well as the Provincial Director von Schlichting at Roehrsdorff and the Chamberlain von Bojanowski at Nitsche, in the Fraustadt district.

Such occurrences can also be noted in other parts of Poland, e.g., the reforms of the Kock estate reported by Bochenski.

So it is evident that among the estate owners in the Polish territories, there were those who wisely progressed with the times by implementing reforms with their peasants, as well as those who remained at the opposite extreme, exploiting their subjects as much as possible. Although the latter are almost exclusively discussed, the majority of the estate owners are likely to be found neither among the former nor the latter, but somewhere in between.

What has been said so far in this chapter about the peasants naturally only applies to the subordinate, noble corvée peasants. I have refrained from further describing their conditions, as these essentially corresponded to those of the Netze District; the same applies to the rent-paying farmers.

To illustrate the variety of service relationships within the same estate, some information about the Polajewo estates is provided here. This originally noble property was owned by the Royal Prussian Maritime Trading Mill and gained domain status at the same time as the confiscation of the ecclesiastical and so on estates. The corvée peasants of this estate, during the South Prussian period, received either the beneficial ownership or the hereditary possession of their holdings in exchange for rent and services. The procedure was such that an agreement was made with an interested party if the previous owner was deemed unsuitable; the latter was then provided with a settlement and expelled without further ado, in accordance with the procedure approved by the King through a royal rescript dated December 12, 1800\.

During the South Prussian era, these services were reduced to "an appropriate measure" upon hereditary and granting, which unfortunately is not specified.

As a general rule, the services of the domain peasants in South Prussia, after their renewed determination for full farmers, amounted to two days of team service (Spanntage) and one day of manual labour (Handtage) or one day of team service and two days of manual labour weekly. Furthermore, 1—2 bushels of oats, 1 pair of chickens, 1—2 dozens of eggs, and 1—2 pieces of spun yarn per year. Additionally, a number of 'Struzen' (domestic work), 'Darmachen' or 'Dramachen' (unspecified, usually gardening tasks) and tłuki (urgent or forced labour during sowing and harvest time).

This was indeed perhaps three times as much as was demanded of the estate farmers in the Netze District. However, it is easily understandable that the reforms in East and West Prussia were not taken as a model in South Prussia, since the entire administration, due to the personality of Graten Hoym, was conducted more along the lines of the Silesian model.

This is probably the source of the entire difference in legislation between South Prussia and the Netze District, mentioned at the end of the previous chapter, to the extent that it cannot be attributed to the fact that after the suppression of the uprising of 1794, a large part of the planned reforms were abandoned, rather than implementing them with redoubled energy, as far as they were justified.

Chapter VI.

The Time of the Grand Duchy of Warsaw 1807–1815.

When Napoleon created the Duchy of Warsaw through the constitution of July 22, 1807, with the King of Saxony as Grand Duke at the helm, to which the entire present-day province of Poznań belonged, except for 52 localities of the Netze District that remained part of West Prussia in 1807, he declared in Article 4, Part I of the constitutional document: 'All slavery (esclavage) is abolished, all citizens are equal before the law, the status of individuals is under the protection of the tribunals.

The term “esclavage” here did not only mean serfdom, which had already been abolished in Prussian times, but also hereditary subjugation. One may hold the view that the abolition of Prussian laws during the war formally reversed the changes to the subjugation system that had been made in favour of the peasants. However, from now on (1807), not only was serfdom abolished, but also hereditary subjugation was completely done away with. This is evident from the decree of King Friedrich August of Saxony on December 24, 1807, “Regarding the Implementation of Article 4, Part One of the Constitution,” which will be discussed shortly. The Constitution not only further assured the peasants of the legal hearing, jurisdiction, and protection of their rights already granted to them during Prussian times, but the personal status of the hitherto subjugated peasants was extraordinarily improved by the abolition of the subjugation ties.

Since it was necessary to more precisely define the relationship that existed between the landowners and the peasants after the abolition of subjugation, and particularly to establish the new relationship of those peasants who held their positions for an indefinite period without contracts, the aforementioned decree appeared on December 21, 1807, which due to its importance should be reproduced here in its wording:

Article 1\. Every farmer and day labourer, who does not possess property rights in perpetuity or for a certain number of years due to a previous, voluntarily made agreement, can freely leave his current place of residence and settle wherever he wants within the Duchy of Warsaw.

Article 2\. However, he is obliged to first report to the landowner, who does not have the right to hold him back, and to the authorities appointed for this purpose by the district administrative bodies, which must report to the higher authorities about anyone arriving or departing in their district.

Article 3\. Those countrymen and day labourers who wish to remain in their current place of residence are granted the freedom to live there for another year, on the condition that they fulfil the same obligations to which they have been subjected so far. The landowner cannot force them to move out during this period, nor can he increase the services previously provided, regardless of what they may be called.

Article 4\. Upon any request, authorised judicial persons will take on all voluntarily made contracts, whether they concern hereditary or temporarily secured possession, according to the mutual conditions entered into between the landowner and the countrymen, either with their previous or with another landowner. The judicial person is to act as a witness on behalf of the government and is personally responsible for ensuring 1\. whether the contracting parties are capable of entering into such voluntary contracts; 2\. whether the contract is truly being concluded freely and not under fear, coercion, or deceit. Every point of the negotiation must be precisely defined or described in the recorded protocol.

Article 5\. Finally, any countryman who wishes to leave his current place of residence is obliged to hand over the property belonging to him to the landowner, which consists of the farming equipment and the sown crops. He cannot be exempted from this obligation unless he proves that he has lost this property after October 1, 1807, whether through livestock disease or other misfortunes.

All other demands that the landowner could make against the farmer, and which the latter disputes, can be asserted through a lawsuit in court. However, under no circumstances can the landowner retain the farmer against his will, but is only entitled to seek his disputed property through legal means.

As a supplement to this ordinance, the royal decree of January 18, 1810, established that the departing peasant persons should seek certificates from the authorities of the place, district, or department they were leaving, confirming that they had complied with the provisions of the decree of July 22, 1807, and that they would not be accepted at the place to which they were going without such certificates.

The legislation of the Grand Duchy of Warsaw even granted, and this is to my knowledge the first case of its kind in Eastern Europe, some members of the peasant class, namely the property owners, political rights. The constitution was known to be a monarchical-constitutional one, and laws were to be decided in the Diet by the country's representatives. For this purpose, not only was the nobility elected, but also in community meetings. According to Article 58 of the Constitutional Document, all non-noble, property-owning citizens could participate in these elections, thus also farmers if they were property owners.

On July 23, 1809, the formation of municipalities and municipal self-administrations was ordered. However, the actual changes brought about by these measures were small, as everywhere the landowner remained the judicial lord and chairman of the municipality. Plichta does report that in the Płock Department, where the matter was pursued with the necessary seriousness, an excellent influence was exerted on the farmers appointed as 'village councillors.' “They felt elevated by their new dignity, began to pay attention to their behaviour, and also to work on the order in the village.” But the turmoil of war also put an end to any flourishing development here again.

The change in applicable laws, which occurred with the introduction of the Code Civil as statutory law, could have no positive influence on peasant conditions. The French laws, assuming the equality of all inhabitants of the state, contained only general provisions, none that specifically related to the manorial-peasant relationships. Therefore, the conditions of the peasants during that epoch must solely be judged from the standpoint of Polish law and the new Warsaw laws.

The ducal government had by no means considered the legislation in this regard as complete. Surveys were continually being carried out, and inquiries were being made to find a good basis for changes for the benefit of the peasants. However, as they had set themselves the insoluble task of improving the situation of the peasants without diminishing the landowners' rights, who were already financially weakened significantly by Napoleon's war and other financial demands, naturally no result was achieved. The only positive proposal that had almost come to fruition was to levy an annual tax of several thousand thalers on the landowners and to give it as a premium to the best peasant farmers in the Duchy to encourage them to purchase their farms as property. But before this certainly good plan could be executed, the Warsaw regime had come to an end again.

From this brief epoch, the ordinance of December 21, 1807, seems to be of immense importance for shaping peasant conditions. It grants the corvée farmers, who hold their positions for an indefinite period (what was legally referred to in Prussia as “for cultivation and use against services and levies”), the right to leave them and to establish an existence elsewhere at their discretion. A simple deregistration with the landowner and the authorities sufficed; then the peasant, who had previously been tied to the land for his entire life, could go wherever he pleased, where he found lighter work or a fairer master. There was no longer any talk of ransom money, forced labour service, leaving behind adult children, etc., upon departure; only the inventory, which belonged to the landowner, had to be left behind. On the other hand, the landowner had to keep the peasant on his property for a year after the announcement of the ordinance, that is, until December 21, 1808, if he fulfilled the previous services; after that, he too could make arbitrary changes in the occupation of the positions.

It is inexplicable how one could infer a mutual one-year termination right from the wording of Article 3\. Nonetheless, later Prussian legislation did just that. The Cabinet Order of May 3, 1815, stated that the mutual one-year termination right introduced during the Warsaw period should remain in place. However, the Warsaw laws do not reveal any such thing; they merely stipulated that the peasants in question had to be left in their positions with their previous rights for one more year after the publication of the above ordinance. However, it does seem that specific moving dates were indeed observed. For example, the records indicate usual moving dates such as St. John's Day (Johanni), St. George's Day (Georgi), Feast of the Immaculate Conception (Mariä Empfängnis), the feast day of St. Adalbert, and others. If a one-year notice was really common after 1808, it was in no way legally justified by the provisions of the ordinance of December 21, 1807\.

This law has now given the peasants the opportunity to escape any oppression from their masters by simply leaving them, thereby exerting pressure on the landowners who could not do without their peasants, to reduce the burdens and make the treatment more lenient. On the other hand, the landowner could rid himself of peasants who seemed superfluous or useless to him without being forced to reoccupy the positions.

Even though these two factors could have had a profound impact on the peasant situation, at least in the Poznań Government Department, everything remained the same. In the Netze District, the law seems to have had some effect, which will be discussed later. On the other hand, the consequences in inner Poland are said to have been extraordinary. A then Duchy of Warsaw official, the later Prussian Government Councilor Plichta, describes his personal observations as follows: “As soon as freedom was granted to the rural population, it began forcefully to tear itself away from the soil to which it had been inhumanly and unnaturally chained for centuries, particularly in the Płock Department. It gave notice en masse to their landlords regarding the land they possessed, thereby causing the landlords, given their inability to manage their farms other than through corvée labour, considerable alarm and making them inclined almost throughout to reduce the peasants' services and thus alleviate their lot. And, in order not to find themselves in the same predicament again, caused by such terminations, as long as the current state of culture and population continues in deeper Poland, most of them have endeavoured to enter into contracts with the peasants for as long a time as possible.”

However, these contracts still bore the stamp of one-sided superiority, even though they were voluntarily entered into, as the government, despite the relevant regulations, did not support the peasants—who were still mostly intellectually quite backward and dependent—in concluding the contracts to the extent that they would have been fully equal to the landlords.

In fact, freedom of movement has resulted in a reduction of the peasants' burdens in those areas. Naturally, negative consequences could not be avoided for those peasants who gave up their property without having a new place to stay in sight, and who then unexpectedly did not find one. However, it is unlikely that this happened too frequently, because on many estates there were vacant farmsteads whose landlords were glad to find new tenants. One only has to read the descriptions provided by Beheim-Schwarzbach to readily admit that it was indeed in the interest of most landlords to attract as many new peasants as possible. Why should the effect of freedom of movement not be favourable back then when no landlord even considered the possibility that the peasants' land would ever actually be owned by the current tenants, when only a few considered the possibility of abolishing forced labour, and therefore almost everyone had an interest in having a large number of peasants? Despite this, the prevailing opinion in the literature is that the ordinance of December 21, 1808, did nothing but harm the peasant class, as freedom of movement was introduced without the landlords being obligated to reoccupy the positions. This view is a result of the widespread misconception that landlords generally had an interest in taking over vacant farmsteads, which may occasionally have been the case, but was by no means the rule, as already elaborated above. Thus, the statement of Minister Baden was partly correct when he said, “the Warsaw law may have freed the peasants from their chains but also took away their boots,” but these words must at least be supplemented as follows: “however, the peasant could easily and without money buy new boots everywhere.”

"In the Poznań Department," says Plichta, "it is true that peasants here and there have changed their landlords, but the obligations have apparently remained unchanged. The reason for this is to be found in the fact that there were very extensive estates here, whose few owners could assert all the advantages against the peasants that are available to monopolists. The fact that many of the local landlords were already familiar with the advantages of the large-scale farming common in other countries, without corvée labour, and therefore no longer considered the retention of the peasants as the only tools of agriculture to be absolutely necessary. Hence, they were not unsettled by the migrations of the peasants that also took place here, and that the peasants did not yet dare to migrate to distant regions, but usually restricted such migrations, either due to a lack of means or due to the shyness still attached to them from the time of serfdom, to the neighbourhood."

However, these reasons do not seem to be entirely exhaustive, and the first one is incorrect, because a size difference between the estates of that time in Poznań compared to those in inner Poland is unlikely to be demonstrable. Moreover, it seems strange that the peasants in Poznań should have been too timid to make use of a freedom available to them to the same extent as the peasants in the eastern departments, who were certainly not at a higher level of culture. The number of landlords who would have liked to have dispensed with managing their estates through corvée labour is also unlikely to have been as large as Plichta assumes.

Much more plausible is what Zerboni di Sposetti, the later Chief President of the Province of Poznań, states in an opinion. He says, “The peasants in Poznań partly had no knowledge of the freedom they had gained,” which already sounds credible for the reason that the authorities who should have informed them of this law were precisely the landlords in their capacity as village chiefs, who had an interest in keeping their peasants without reducing their obligations; “also, the peasant, who wanted to leave his previous conditions and enter into more favourable ones on another estate, was taught that no changes of ownership were permissible during the war.” It is understandable that these statements usually sufficed to persuade the peasant, accustomed to blind obedience to his master, to stay.

“One would have found the peasants in the Grand Duchy of Poznań,” Zerboni continues, “more enlightened about their situation, in a more favourable position, had the Royal Saxon decree fully taken effect. Human labour is an extremely sought-after commodity in Poland, for which every estate owner competes against the other. This decree could only bring about beneficial consequences for the peasants.”

In the hope that landlords and peasants would conclude contracts for the properties, which had previously been made available for an indefinite period, officials had been sent to the various districts of the Grand Duchy according to Article IV, Section 2 of the ordinance, to record such contracts; however, this task made no progress in Poznań, and neither landlords nor peasants seemed inclined to put their mutual obligations into writing. It was in the interest of the landlords to keep as much leeway for their arbitrariness as possible; the Polish peasants, on the other hand, who generally could neither write nor read, had great respect for the written word and were very reluctant to sign contracts, behind which they always suspected deceit.

In the Netze District, as already mentioned, the law seems to have actually led to a reduction in the burdens on the peasants. In the deliberations of the Bromberg Law Commission (1818), the member from the class of estate owners, Mr. von Loga, states that it is the general wish of the estate owners that in the event of upcoming redemptions, the services and burdens of the peasant holdings should be assessed according to the status quo of 1806, as after this time 'due to the burdens of war,' the peasant obligations have been almost universally reduced. One is probably not mistaken to see this reduction in obligations as a result of the ordinance of December 21, 1807, and not as a consequence of the war burdens, a view also expressed by the Poznań Law Commission, since the war burdens would have only caused extraordinary, momentary, not permanent remissions. But even if the war burdens would have caused this reduction in peasant obligations, which is hardly to be assumed, one would still see the beneficial effect of the Grand Ducal Warsaw ordinance in that the estate owners had not been able to raise the obligations again later, as this would have risked the departure of the peasants and thus of their necessary labour force.

The reinstatement of the peasant protection, exercised during part of the time of the first Prussian rule, took place automatically through the repeal of the Prussian laws. The official reports of later times contain no information that would suggest that this repeal had a particularly detrimental effect on the existence of the peasant holdings, as Klebs claims.

Incidentally, there were also efforts at that time to make it obligatory for the estate owners to maintain the peasant holdings. Thus, the Bromberg government says in a report of May 3, 1816: “We have found in the files of the dissolved prefectural authorities general decrees by the same, which prohibit the withdrawal of rustic holdings for manor land, but there is no legal provision presented to justify these decrees,” etc.

The content of the Warsaw legislation can thus be briefly summarised as follows: all peasants were made personally free, the subject associations and all obligations arising from them were abolished, village communities were created but without a good community constitution, and full freedom of movement for service peasants was introduced for an indefinite period.

The effect of these changes in the Poznań Department was virtually nil or at least very low, whereas in the Netze District, as a result, there has been an almost universal reduction in peasant obligations.

It is permissible to point out here the inaccuracies contained in Klebs' depiction of this legislative era.

Klebs says that the Warsaw legislation led to all the formerly subject peasants, who under Prussian rule could only be dispossessed of their holdings by judgement and law, now being able to be dispossessed at the landlord's discretion after one year's notice, and that the abolition of peasant protection greatly disadvantaged them.

The peasant-friendly provisions of the land law had indeed, as already mentioned, fallen out of effect due to the repeal of all Prussian laws. The loss of peasant protection was therefore a mere coincidence, not an intentional abandonment of peasant lands. This abolition hardly had any adverse influence during the Warsaw era, as Klebs claims; rather, the trend towards dispossession of peasants only gained momentum after 1815\. “Withdrawals of peasant holdings have occurred here and there under the protection of laws under the previous (Warsaw) government,” says a well-informed contemporary, so certainly not on a large scale.

The provisions on permissible termination do not concern, as Klebs suggests (he also incorrectly speaks of a one-year termination right created by the law), "all former subjects," but only those who held their positions for an indefinite period. This does not include the inheritable tenants and also not the contract farmers (time lessees). Klebs seems to have come to his understanding because the article of the law speaks of "property rights forever or for a certain time," when it should have more accurately said "rights to the position forever or for a definite time;" because it refers to all farmers except those who are sitting "at the mere favour of the lord" for an indefinite period. The law is characterised by such faulty expressions. For example, it always uses the term "hereditary lord" and "new hereditary lord," although the law specifically abolishes hereditary subjugation; it mentions "land ownership, which consists of the courtyard, the buildings, and the sowing," from which one could conclude that the fields and meadows, etc., were not included, and so on. However, it emerges from the entire content of the law that its provisions only apply to the one class of rural inhabitants set for an indefinite period, and that disadvantages for the other classes, which had no property, cannot be derived from it, as Klebs portrays this to us in the most horrifying images.

All officials who lived through that time either assume this as self-evident or explicitly point it out. For example, Appellate Court Counselor Fischer says: "The ordinance refers, as far as it speaks of farmers and their possessions, only to the peasant owners who had manorial farms for cultivation and use for services to be performed for an indefinite period."

Klebs concludes as a result of his, as shown above, incorrect understanding: "Even those residents who held their positions with a hereditary right of use and often had their own buildings and inventory, could be removed after the expiry of one year. In several cases, the landlords exercised their rights, but even more often, the same was used to increase the peasants' burdens, which was previously forbidden."

I have previously explained that hereditary corvée farmers, at least in South Prussia, were almost only present in the crown lands. If there were any in noble estates, they usually bought the inventory and the courtyard, and the land was then given to them hereditarily. None of the contemporaries of that time say anything about their rights or those of the time lessees being curtailed during the Grand Duchy of Warsaw, even though numerous essays by officials and private individuals are included in the files I used. Nor is there anywhere talk of an increase in burdens during the Warsaw era, but rather often of a reduction of the same.

Klebs provides this flawed depiction of the impact of the Warsaw legislation, whose good side and intentions, which I have highlighted above, he does not recognize.

Knapp has given a judgement on the Warsaw legislation, which he knows from Dönniges' brief description; wherein he characteristically "points out" and gives the following sentences: "From December 21, 1808, the former subjects, now completely free people, were no longer protected if they did not hold their possessions hereditarily, but only for an indefinite period; the former hereditary lord could terminate their tenure, and it might have been poor consolation that they could also terminate his. They were free and at the same time uprooted."

"Through this, the Polish landlords had achieved exactly what those in the province of Prussia were also expecting at that time, but could not obtain so unconditionally: 'Freedom for the peasants, but the land for us.'"

"Not as if they had immediately taken possession of all peasant land; they did it only as needed."

I have previously explained that there was by no means the level of interest among the landlords in taking over peasant lands, as Knapp assumes. The peasants were no more or less "uprooted" after December 21, 1808, than they had always been until the introduction of peasant protection in South Prussian times (1797). It was also not such a poor consolation for them to have the right to terminate the landlords, because from my previous explanations it follows that in certain regions it was precisely the peasants who made the most extensive use of this right, while the landlords, precisely because they usually had an interest in keeping their peasants, often found themselves compelled to reduce their services. On the other hand, there is nowhere to be seen that the landlords had already frequently exercised their right to terminate and had taken over the properties.

"The majority of the residents have been in undisturbed possession of their farms for a long period of time, despite the termination rights granted to the landlords by law; most of them do not even know how very insecure their ownership rights are," it says at one point in the files.

The claim that the landlords in the province of Prussia had the tendency at that time to give “freedom to the peasants, the land for us,” also seems to me to be an erroneous exaggeration; for from Knapp's source excerpts it only becomes apparent that the nobility's aspiration was to gain freer control over the peasant lands.

The wishes aimed in that direction appear, when considering the conditions after the devastating war, to be partly justified for that time and have also been appropriately considered in the edict of October 9, 1807, and the accompanying regulations. However, to the extent that they go beyond the bounds of what is justified, they still do not, in my opinion, allow for the exaggerated conclusion that Knapp draws, namely that the landlords generally aspired to take the peasants' land for themselves in return for the freedom of the peasants—i.e., to completely eliminate the peasant class from the world. A sharp, albeit not total, conflict of interest between peasants and landlords emerged, in my view, only when the project of the proprietary allocation of lands to the corvée farmers was raised by the state. At that time, the landlords feared that their previously undisputed property rights to the “for cultivation and use” leased-out peasant farms would be taken away from them. Not only the fact of the impending state intervention in the property rights of the landlords but also the circumstance that they feared they would not be sufficiently compensated, and also considered most of the service peasants incapable of managing independently and properly fulfilling their new rental payments; moreover, that they faced a shortage of labour and a complete, costly, forced overhaul of their farms, make the existential struggle at that time seem as understandable as it is incomprehensible why the landlords should have previously sought to acquire all the peasants' lands as compensation for their personal freedom.

In 1813, the Grand Duchy of Warsaw was occupied and organised by Russia. Russian authorities also dealt with the peasant conditions, although no significant reforms occurred in the short period until the Treaty of Paris.

The Heart of the Matter.

1801.

Everywhere and nowhere.

> There is no gain so legitimate but that it is surpassed by what one can make illegitimately, and the wrong done to one's neighbour is always more lucrative than services rendered. It is therefore only a question of finding the means to secure impunity, and it is to this that the powerful devote all their strength and the weak all their cunning. 
>

> Discours sur l'inégalité, Note 9.

To the Exalted and Supreme Judicial Majesty of the Now-Reigning King of Prussia, Frederick William III.

(blank)

Most Serene, Most Exalted Monarch, Most Revered and most upright Sovereign Lord in the State!

Before you permit the sale of this book to be forbidden within the country, devote to it but a single solitary half-hour to read it through Yourself. For its content is truly important. Then judge for Yourself as well. Your judgment alone do all those hold to be competent who see in You not only the first but also the most upright man in the State, and who revere Your exalted office and Your person far too sincerely to be capable of attempting, against both, the criminal and wretched game of an anxious and cunning cabal. You stand too high, You stand wholly independent in the sanctuary of justice, for partisan considerations

toward persons within the State, who after all are always only Your servants and subjects, to be able to determine Your judgment. If need be, You may indeed inquire of a few other honest men — an Arnim, Struensee, Menke, Hoff, etc. — as to their opinions.

But properly speaking — that Your own free and just judgment should decide the fate of these pages, this is the most respectful and most humble prayer of

Year 1801

the most upright of Your servants and most faithful of Your subjects.

To the Readers.

On my last journey in the summer of this year 1800, from Breslau — Whither? may be a matter of indifference to the readers — my road led me through the little South Prussian town of Krotoszyn, situated hard on the Silesian border, 12 German miles east of Breslau. I had my horses fed at the inn there, sat down on a beam before the house door, and was just musing on what sort of book might come into being if the
held1801/2: biography were written of a certain Minister who still figures and manoeuvres most imposingly in the Prussian State, when yet another stranger arrived in a kibitka. The man looked very morose, pale, and mistrustful; nor did he descend from his conveyance, but remained lying within it, reading in a book. My efforts to draw him into conversation were fruitless. Meanwhile it so happened that we set off almost at the same time, he ahead and I behind, upon the same road. His horses were somewhat quicker than mine, and so after a while I lost sight of him in the still, dense woods of Krotoszyn. By chance I leaned out of my carriage to blow out my pipe and saw, beside the wheel-track, precisely where the man had driven, a black leather portfolio lying, which I had handed up to me. Naturally I supposed that it had fallen from the stranger's carriage, and I hastened to overtake him. But
held1801/3:
all effort was in vain; I never saw him again.

Curiosity — I gladly confess this impulse in myself — at last made me open the portfolio, which was in any case not locked but only buttoned shut, and behold — I found within it the wholly finished, very neatly written manuscript which, since to judge by the introduction and the notes it was plainly intended for print, I herewith impart to the reading-eager world, for its edification. Long did I struggle with myself whether I ought to do so or not; in the end, however, the conviction gained the upper hand that, for the gain and victory of truth and virtue, it is always good to bring such characterizing infamies — especially when documented from the records — before the judgment seat of contemporaries and of public opinion. I therefore give my find exactly as it came into my hands; the morose stranger will not, I hope, on that account
held1801/4:
be angry with me. The circumstance that this manuscript so unexpectedly corresponded to the reflections which I had brought with me from Breslau and had continued to pursue while sitting before the inn at Krotoszyn seemed to me a hint from fate, to convey further what it had cast to me.

If I am not mistaken, all the most essential documents concerning the case in question are here supplied, so that nothing is wanting that belongs to its history and development. Whatever was secretly corresponded between v. Hoym and v. Goldbeck on the matter, the gentlemen have probably burned. Yet it might be that with the justice commissioner Früson in Posen many a written original voucher of these knaveries still lies hidden, which the possessor perhaps withholds only because his experiences have robbed him of courage and love of country. For the presentation of the heart of the matter these pages meanwhile fully suffice. The readers may
held1801/5:
for the rest judge for themselves. To anticipate them in this would, with regard to the honest, be an insult; with regard to the knaves, labour lost in any case. To both the compiler has at least spared the tedium, in that he has omitted all useless papers which concerned merely the shells and not the kernel.

I must not forget to mention a slip of paper which lay in the bottom of the portfolio and appeared to be written in a different hand than the one from which the notes proceed. It ran thus:

> "Should these pieces be falsified, and should this be capable of proof, or a refutation of them be possible, this could only be done by comparison with those two files lying in the archive of the Regierung at Posen which bear the following titles:
held1801/6:
Acta primae Instantiae

"Of the Regierung at Posen, in the matter of the Ober-Amtmann Früson of Slawitz in Silesia, against the Seehandlung at Berlin, concerning reinstatement in the lease of the lordship of Krotoszyn. Begun 4 January 1794. And

Acta primae Instantiae

Of the Regierung at Posen in the matter of the Amtmann Früson against the Maritime and Salt Trading Society at Berlin and the War and Domains Chamber at Breslau, concerning the ejection from the lease of Krotoszyn. Begun 22 December 1797."

Now whether such records really exist, and whether from them a refutation of the proceedings here delivered might be drawn, or a proof of falsification carried out, the gentlemen v. Hoym
held1801/7: and v. Goldbeck will surely know best. The public expects the former, in case the said gentlemen should still feel some desire to save their honour; or else, if no refutation whatever appears, it will believe in the authenticity of these proceedings, and will so long hold them up before the throne of a King who makes a false conclusion only when his first servants of state lie to him — a King whose only fault is that he is not yet stern enough for these vice-ridden times — before the throne of Frederick William III, who in the present case was deceived with incredible insolence and shamefulness, until at last He shall become
held1801/8: attentive and conclude: Those who were capable of carrying out so base a trick are capable of several like it. Berlin, in November 1800, at the beginning of the 4th year of the reign of Frederick William III.
held1801/9:
Introduction.

The Maritime and Salt Trading Society (the Seehandlung) in Berlin has from of old had much commerce with those regions which were formerly called: Poland. At the head of this institution Frederick the Great — who in the choice of persons was not always quite so fortunate as in the judgement of affairs — once placed the well-known Minister von Görne. This man of honour accordingly came, through the nature of the business entrusted to him, into
held1801/10:
all manner of connection with Poland, and soon also upon the idea of buying great landed properties there for himself; indeed, it was said he had entertained the project of becoming King of Poland himself, and that those great purchases were to have been merely the means of attaining this end. If there was anything in the matter — and it is almost credible, since this dunderhead was surrounded by the silliest flatterers that ever stood about a minister — then the project becomes at the least highly ridiculous, when one pictures to oneself the utterly repulsive caricature of a figure that was Görne, together with the sceptre, crown, robe, and sabre of the Polacks. And yet — such a people would have deserved such a king. Stanislaus Poniatowski was not a hair better than Görne.

However that may be, enough! Görne bought the considerable and extensive lordship of Krotoszyn in Great Poland on the Silesian border, opposite Breslau. He employed for the purpose substantial ready sums from the royal
held1801/11:
treasuries entrusted to him. This was noticed, and therefore Görne, at the beginning of the year 1782, pursuant to a cabinet order of Frederick the Great, was arrested by the then Governor in Berlin, General Ramin, in a manner attended by many comical incidental circumstances, in his palace Unter den Linden, and some weeks later was brought to Spandau. There he sat for several years, until the late King Frederick William II gave him back his freedom. He now lives in the country between Brandenburg and Potsdam.

After his above-mentioned arrest Frederick the Great had his property placed under seizure, in order to make good the treasury deficits therefrom. In this manner the lordship of Krotoszyn, lying in what was then Great Poland, became a property of the Seehandlung in Berlin, which drew the revenues through the Chamber at Breslau. The Breslau Chamber for its part had the lordship administered, during the first nine years after Görne's fall,
held1801/12:
by a certain Triebenfeld, whom it had found there as a huntsman, timber-clerk, or forester who had stood in the private service of Görne, and it credited the Seehandlung with some 17 to 18,000 reichsthalers yearly, until in the year 1791 the then Privy Finance Councillor v. Struensee held the leasing of the lordship to the Amtmann Früson, who engaged to give 30,100 reichsthalers yearly, to be more profitable, brought it forward, and carried it through.

Until the year 1782 Görne frequently employed a War Councillor Bernhardi in Berlin for the oversight of his husbandry at Krotoszyn, and often sent the simple old man thither. Bernhardi at last, about the time when Görne was arrested, was living at Krotoszyn with his numerous family, and remained there a while afterwards as well. The forester Triebenfeld thereupon soon married — under circumstances that revolt every moral feeling — a daughter of Bernhardi (his
held1801/13:
present, still ever unhappy wife) against her will, and then his first business was to drive out his father-in-law and, as has already been mentioned, to attain to the sole administration.

From this vantage point the genius, or rather the demon, of Triebenfeld met that of the Minister Hoym in Breslau, and forthwith both hell-spirits founded between their respective protégés that friendship which not only subsists to this day but is knit all the closer by their common disgrace. Triebenfeld began to prosper; he carried on, well-nigh openly, a contraband trade in English stoneware, Hungarian wine, and so forth, out of Krotoszyn into neighbouring Silesia and its capital. He became rich, important, and acquired friends. His boldness and prompt readiness for any piece of business which would still cost other rogues of the common stamp some scruple, won him in short order the interest and the whole affection of the Silesian satrap.
held1801/14:
Hoym needed, especially after the decease of the great Frederick, a henchman eminently disposed and resolved to every evil, and therefore the formerly unknown Triebenfeld was heartily welcome to him; whom, in reward of his services and for encouragement to acquire yet more of them, he thereupon decorated in quick succession with a patent of nobility, a title, a forester's uniform, and a collegiate cross. Krotoszyn became the depot of all the ministerial vices that were to be hidden away from Breslau, and at coarse nocturnal bacchanals in the castle at Krotoszyn one could hear bandit throats bellowing the toast: Long live little brother Hoym!!!

What was there not to be done in the hybrid little land of Krotoszyn? In this corner, about which no authority properly troubled itself, in this island between two realms, where Triebenfeld was king, as it were — so that one might have compared him with Sancho on his island of bread-rolls and sausages,
held1801/15:
did Sancho not possess infinite moral advantages over Triebenfeld? True, Krotoszyn stood, in name, under Polish sovereignty — that is to say, under the most wretched and confused sovereignty in all Europe — but it was nevertheless in Prussian possession, which meant something more than mere seigneurial possession. As one pleased, one could regard it as a little piece of Poland or else as a little piece of Silesia. Triebenfeld made excellent use of this double character. According as it was advantageous or harmful to the precious Herr Administrator, he sheltered himself now behind Prussian, now behind Polish laws, or pushed both away from him. Now he drew the boundary line dividing Poland from Silesia with great sharpness; now he declared it once more a chimera. Now he threatened with Prussian arrangements; now again he spoke with great unction of the prerogatives of the Republic of Poland. To the Prussians he was a Pole, to the Poles a Prussian.

It was accordingly no wonder that he
held1801/16: looked upon it with mighty ill favour when this splendour was to come to an end and Krotoszyn was to be leased to the Amtmann Früson in the year 1791. To the Minister v. Hoym this change was, for a thousand reasons, inconvenient in itself in any case, and he suffered it to happen only because, at its inception, he was unable at once to thwart it with becoming pretexts. Consequently, both Hoym and Triebenfeld agreed without much ado that the best means of turning the lease once more into the former administration consisted in making life in Krotoszyn so bitter for Früson in every possible way that he would find himself moved to withdraw from there again before long. Hoym gave his consent, and promised to cover his back; Triebenfeld undertook the execution. The latter was all the easier since Triebenfeld, as Chief Overseer of the extensive forests, which were not included in Früson's lease, remained resident in the castle at Krotoszyn,
held1801/17:
and Früson had to pay him his salary and give him a large deputat in kind — relations which, however fairly Früson might always conduct himself, nevertheless afforded a multitude of occasions for quarrel and vexation, which Triebenfeld could use and did use.

The collection of documents here laid before the public contains, then, properly the history of the chicaneries and acts of violence which, introduced and instigated by Triebenfeld, did indeed very soon drive the Amtmann Früson out of Krotoszyn again. From it one sees, with horror and disgust, how easily an unscrupulous minister decrees the injury of a private man when it comes to obliging another minister, or extricating him from an embarrassment; how little self-conquest
held1801/18: and cunning a sun-clear fraud costs men of this stamp and rank, and how sans façon they not only play fast and loose with state revenues and private welfare, but even lie to the face of their sovereign when fear and breaking shame drive them to cover their old base acts with new ones. That during the reign of the late King much was possible which properly never and nowhere ought to be possible — to that one has by and by become resigned; but — who can ever moderate his astonishment that under the reign of Frederick William III a cabinet order such as that of 24 December 1798, at the end of these records, could issue? Whoever runs through these pages entire with even a little attention must feel, with oppressive clarity, to what manifold criticism
held1801/19: of truth, of logic, indeed of plain sober common sense, that cabinet order is exposed from the first line to the last. What conjecture is one to give room to? What in any way tolerable explanation is one to make? Reason stands still. It is painful, most painful, in this connection to think of the Privy Cabinet Councillor Beyme, who passes for upright and noble and is at the same time known as a good jurist, and to picture him in the distressing necessity of having to draw up and dispatch such cabinet resolutions. Is not the cabinet the very last instance for eight million men who, in cases of wounded justice, are to direct their hopeful glances thither, are to take their refuge there? May the sovereign leave the demand to be just unfulfilled? And — such a cabinet resolution!!! —
held1801/20: That Triebenfeld stands throughout behind the scenes in the transactions that follow need hardly first be pointed out to the readers. They are therefore only reminded further to keep it always present to themselves, as an important turning point of this history, that Great Poland, and consequently Krotoszyn too, came under Prussian sovereignty in the spring of 1793.
held1801/21:
Frederick the Great to the Minister of State von Hoym in Breslau.

My dear Minister of State von Hoym. Since the hitherto Chief of the Maritime and Salt Trading Company, von Görne, is indebted to the treasury of the said Company, as I have already told you, in considerable sums, and I must therefore recover payment for myself and the treasury as far as possible out of his estate, I have accordingly resolved to have his estates purchased in Poland taken into possession forthwith,
held1801/22: and their revenues sequestrated and collected toward the reduction of the von Görne deficit, until perhaps an opportunity may arise for the sale of the estates themselves. But since these estates lie very far distant from Berlin, and the administration could not be overseen from there, whereas their distance from Breslau is by no means considerable, I hereby charge you, without any loss of time, to send off to Poland a councillor of the War and Domains Chamber there, one who has sufficient knowledge and experience of estate management, together with some capable subordinate servants, and through him to have all the estates of von Görne situated there taken into possession and sequestrated, namely the lordship of Krotoszyn and Rosdarczewo, and also the lordship of
held1801/23: Polajewo. And in order that this taking of possession may proceed without any difficulty or prolixity, von Görne himself shall instruct the servants he keeps upon the estates not to resist it, which instruction my Grand Chancellor von Carmer will procure and forward to you. As soon, then, as the commissioner arrives on the spot, he must arrange the estate administration — which has hitherto been conducted in so wasteful a manner that scarcely anything could be left over from the revenues — according to sound economic principles in the most thrifty way; in general he is to draw as much money as ever possible from the estates, and in particular to attend to the sale of timber, and to correspond thereon with my Principal Utility-Timber Administration as soon as he has to some degree informed himself of the state of affairs; whereby I make known to you that, although the said Administration has already purchased a large part of the timber
held1801/24: from the lordship of Krotoszyn, yet a very great deal of timber still remains, which, in order to raise money, must be cut down foot by foot and gradually, as it is possible and feasible, converted into cash. Next, the commissioner must also be intent upon leasing out the estates advantageously by Trinity, since no buyer is likely to be found so soon. All the money he takes in he must, together with the administration account, remit to the Breslau War and Domains Chamber, which shall have oversight of the administration and shall direct it; and this Chamber may deliver the money to my Bank at Breslau against a receipt,
held1801/25:
but the receipt, instead of ready money, is to be transmitted to the treasury of the Seehandlung at Berlin, on account of the von Görne deficit; wherefore, only as regards that which may in this matter require closer consideration, you have to correspond with my Minister of State Baron von Schulenburg, to whom I have entrusted the supreme oversight of the Maritime and Salt Trading Company, and thereafter to see to all that is needful with the utmost dispatch. I am your well-affectioned King.

Potsdam, 26 January 1782.

Schulenburg.
held1801/26:
The Breslau Privy Councillor v. Hoym, cousin of the Minister v. Hoym, to the Ober-Amtmann Früson.

Well-born Sir,

most honoured Herr Ober-Amtmann!

Since, in view of the recommendation and the good testimonials which the Royal Chamber has given Your Honour, I presume not without reason that on the part of the Seehandlung Your Honour may be considered for the Krotoszyn lease,
held1801/27:
I request you to let me know by the bearer of this whether you will offer the oblatum of Matthiae at 30,100 thalers, or perhaps even add something more, since I then intend at once to set the matter in motion here with the Privy Finance Councillor v. Struensee .

It would be most agreeable to me if Your Honour would take the trouble to come here yourself, since we could then arrange many things verbally on that account. I shall remain here until the seventh.
held1801/28:
In expectation of seeing Your Honour here, I have the honour to be, with especial respect,

Your Honour's

Rothland 
3 July 1791.

obedient servant 
v. Hoym.
held1801/30:
The Minister von Struensee in Berlin to the War Councillor von Triebenfeld in Krotoszyn.

The Ober-Amtmann Früson, during his presence here in Berlin, has complained that in the conduct of his lease you have placed many
held1801/31: obstacles in his way. I have communicated this complaint to the Breslau War and Domains Chamber, so that it may investigate the same, settle the misunderstandings that have arisen,
held1801/32: and forestall all future collisions; I herewith at the same time make you aware that you are on no account to meddle in the economy of the lordship of Krotoszyn, but are to leave the same entirely to the Breslau War and Domains Chamber, and
held1801/33:
are in general to take care that you give the said Früson no occasion for complaints, but rather live with him in peace and concord.

Struensee.
held1801/34:
The Composition Wrung from Früson by von Triebenfeld and Neumann, Whereby He Was to Relinquish the Lease of Krotoszyn Once More.

The undersigned Ober-Amtmann (senior domain lessee) Johann George Früson hereby attests and acknowledges, that he once again submits to the eviction from the lease of the Krotoszyn estates dictated against him by the Kalisch
held1801/35: War and Police Commission, that he has wholly relinquished the lease, and that with respect to all claims which might arise out of this lease and the surrender thereof, he submits himself entirely to the decision of the Minister Count von Hoym qua super Arbiter!, without forming against it the least further claim by way of law, in whatever forum it might be; but in particular, in order that all legal proceedings in the Polish courts may from now on wholly cease, he declares that he entirely desists from all further lawsuits, and especially from the complaint lodged on the 11th of this month with the Civil Commission, and that he declares invalid the
held1801/36: citation issued upon the memorial, upon which the said Herr von Husarzewski, the War and Forest Councillor von Triebenfeld, he himself, and the town of Krotoszyn are to appear before the same on the 25th of this month. — Likewise he annuls the power of attorney granted to Herr v. The War and Forest Councillor v. Triebenfeld promises moreover that he will procure receipts concerning the annulment of the lawsuits pending between the Herr Border-Judge,
held1801/37: Herr v. Zablocki, v. Kordaszowski, and Herr Ober-Amtmann Früson and his son, and of all lawsuits yet to be raised, and will see to the quashing of the same.
