 The town and lordship of Krotoszyn lie in the former Great Poland, now South Prussia, hard on the Silesian border, about 12 German miles east of Breslau. — Ed.

 Frederick the Great, of course, when he issued this uneconomical command, did not know with certainty in advance that already eleven years later the lordship of Krotoszyn would come under Prussian sovereignty and state administration. — Ed.

 The present Minister, and unquestionably the one among all the Prussian statesmen of that time who as a man of affairs and as a thinker deserves the greatest respect of his contemporaries and of posterity. He already stood as Privy Finance Councillor at the head of the Seehandlung. — Ed.

 The Privy Councillor von Hoym, who handled this affair and clearly foresaw that the Seehandlung would carry through its intention of wresting the lordship of Krotoszyn from the hitherto unrestricted Triebenfeld administration and handing it over to a more lucrative lease, and that the solid Ober-Amtmann Früson would obtain the latter from the Seehandlung, in this letter is merely currying favour. Already beforehand he had made an arrangement with the still-living preacher Matthiae at Zduny, in the then Great Poland, now South Prussia, that if the latter obtained the lease of Krotoszyn, on which he too had bid, he was to give him a thousand thalers cash annually and to supply his kitchen in Breslau with all manner of victuals. Rothland is a Silesian village where the said Privy Councillor v. Hoym was staying at the time — who knows now, moreover, why. His post he held at the Breslau Chamber. Now he is President of the Chamber at Warsaw. — Ed.

 The War and Forest Councillor von Triebenfeld, who, God knows how, comes under the jurisdiction of the Breslau Chamber, but is always absent and travelling, partly on his own and partly on other people's dirty business, is the chief favourite of the Minister von Hoym, and through the latter's advancement was by the late King Frederick William II not only ennobled but also later presented with such a quantity of South Prussian estates that their value by judicial assessment amounts to over seven hundred thousand thalers. By origin he is a huntsman's lad, and without any real culture — coarse, crude, and brash. When the Ober-Amtmann Früson leased the lordship of Krotoszyn, the very considerable forests were not leased along with it to him; these rather remained under the special administration of Triebenfeld as Chief Forest Overseer, and for that reason Triebenfeld retained a free residence in the castle at Krotoszyn, in which Früson as general lessee naturally also resided. The two therefore soon fell into conflict with one another, if only on account of this domestic proximity, and all the more so because Triebenfeld, at the very beginning of the Früson lease, was brooding over the plan not only of dislodging Früson again, but rather of driving him out of the lease entirely, so that he himself might, as in the end also happened, obtain the administration back. Was it, on the other side, to be held against the said Früson if he wished to be rid of his not merely most burdensome but truly devilish adversary, and to have sole disposition over the castle, as belonged to him as general lessee? — Ed.

 This clean piece of work is at the same time a proof of what a stylist Triebenfeld is, for he is the author. — Ed.

 This Neumann was formerly Assessor at the Breslau Chamber, then in the year 1793, when South Prussia became Prussian, became War and Domains Councillor at the Chamber in Posen, and now stands again in that same capacity at the Chamber in Breslau, in the sphere of his high patron and friend the Minister von Hoym. — Ed.

 Now Government Councillor at Kalisch. In the present affair he conducted himself, if not indeed badly, then at least very weakly and timidly. — Ed.

 Früson, father and son, thereupon kept silent, until in the following year, when Great Poland and consequently Krotoszyn too fell under Prussian sovereignty, an apparently greater possibility of reproving the wrong they had suffered arose for them. This possibility they used through the ensuing judicial suit. The correspondence that meanwhile occurred between Früson and the Ministers von Hoym and von Struensee is here omitted, partly because it is too prolix, partly because it is wholly unessential and also had no success whatever, so as not to weary the reader. Struensee would gladly have helped, but he neither dared nor could, and, as a judge of men, remained by the simple view of the matter, the correctness of which the outcome has proven. — Ed.

 The lease contract, which is signed by Früson dated Krotoszyn 4 September 1791 and by the Minister Struensee dated Berlin 2 December of the same year, has here, on account of its great length and diffuseness, been omitted. The essential part of it, insofar as it bears on the present case, is everywhere correctly and clearly alleged in these documents, and the allegations have nowhere and never been contradicted by the opposing party. — Ed.

 These impudent and stupid machinations of Triebenfeld are described still more circumstantially further on. Among such silly, drunken, and self-serving people as the Poles on average are, they were of course very easy to bring about with a little wine, brandy, and money. — Ed.

 Freyhahn is a small little town in Silesia. It belongs to a Count von Zedlitz, and lies hard on the formerly Polish, now South Prussian border, opposite Krotoszyn. — Ed.

 Früson junior had given up his referendaryship in Breslau, had gone with the Minister of Justice Dankelmann to Posen in the spring of 1793, had remained there and become justice commissioner. He now finds himself in person in quite good circumstances, and regards this struggle as a game that the world has played with him and he reciprocally with it. — Ed.

 About this time the hitherto — and to this very hour perfectly well — Silesian Minister of Justice von Dankelmann at Breslau, under whose supervision the organization of the judicial system in South Prussia had stood since the acquisition, and thus for two years, and who discharged this laborious business with the most praiseworthy zeal, was suddenly dismissed from his offices by a courier from Berlin that reached him just at Posen; and since the hitherto Grand Chancellor von Carmer, on account of genuine infirmity of age, likewise quit his post about this time, the Berlin Kammergericht President von Goldbeck — although in more than one respect he had assuredly the least claim to it — attained the dignity of the Grand Chancellorship, which he still holds even now, to the great astonishment of both the foreign and the domestic public. Truly, a peculiar and very suspicious concurrence of striking circumstances! It seems almost as though, in order to draw the Minister von Hoym out of the embarrassment in question, one had wished to remove a man burdensome through his uprightness, and as though Dankelmann had drawn enemies upon himself and made himself disagreeable because, to keep up the course of this Früson lawsuit, he had several times exerted his authority; for in the natural course of things he must, both by his rank and still more by his merits, have succeeded Carmer. Since the day that courier arrived, which brought him at the same time the news of Goldbeck's elevation, the ex-Minister von Dankelmann has lived in philosophical seclusion on his estate Peterwiz, four miles from Breslau, and studies the ancient classics. The English give their Grand Chancellor the fine name: Keeper of the King's Conscience. What the Prussian state had to expect of the new Keeper of the Conscience of its Kings is taught by the following rescript, which Goldbeck let go off to the Regierung at Posen as speedily as possible and in the very first days of his exalted Grand Chancellorship. — Ed.

 How could Goldbeck quash this lawsuit without at least first calling for the opinion of the Regierung at Posen upon the memorial of the Breslau Chamber, and even without informing himself from the records of what Früson had actually brought forward on his side, which had hitherto remained unknown to him, Goldbeck? For surely the maxim holds: Audiatur et altera pars. And was Früson's suit really so frivolous as it is here called — did it then require a violent quashing, since in that case, if it had been left to the ordinary course of law, it must indisputably already have been lost for Früson before the Regierung at Posen? Or was the whole Regierung at Posen perhaps so incompetent or so bad that it could not, or would not, distinguish frivolities from very serious matters, so that the Grand Chancellor was needed as a Deus ex machina to instruct it on the point? Of fatigue there could reasonably be no question, for a Regierung before which five and a half thousand lawsuits are pending is not fatigued by one more or less. — Ed.

 Namely to the War and Police Commission at Kalisch. One sees from this what confusion, if nothing worse, prevailed among the Polish judicial authorities, and how easily in the same matter a sentence pro et contra was to be obtained from them. — Ed.

 This administration of the lordship of Krotoszyn was continued by the said Triebenfeld, after the expulsion of Früson from the lease in August 1792 — not for long, however. Tossed about by many diversions, journeys, and affairs (which, be it well noted, were not official business) amid the occupation of South Prussia that soon set in at that time in the year 1793, he came to see that his constant absence from Krotoszyn must damage his purse. He therefore gave the lordship of Krotoszyn to a certain starosta Gajewsky (owner of the South Prussian little town of Storchnest, and — until his ill star brought him together with Triebenfeld — a rich but simple man) for 10 years in a kind of sub-lease, on the condition that Gajewsky should hand over to him yearly 5,000 thalers of the profit to be made. Gajewsky entered into the bargain. Soon afterward Triebenfeld persuaded Gajewsky, under all manner of dangled advantages, to pay him the five thousand thalers ten times over, and thus fifty thousand thalers in advance; but Gajewsky did not have so much ready money, and now Hoym advanced it to Gajewsky out of one of the great Silesian treasuries, so that the latter could pay Triebenfeld, whereupon Gajewsky pledged his entire fortune, the lordship of Storchnest and the starosty of Powidz, to the treasury that furnished the loan at Breslau. Meanwhile the case arose that Hoym, through the first Früson lawsuit conducted under Dankelmann's supervision, before Goldbeck could quash it in July 1795, was already so alarmed at the beginning of the year 1795 that, as the best means of forever bolting the door against all Früson's pretensions, he obtained from Frederick William II a cabinet order dated 4 March 1795, pursuant to which the Seehandlung had, from Trinity 1795, to sell the lordship of Krotoszyn for one million thalers to the South Prussian domains treasury. Krotoszyn thus became a South Prussian domain, and now Gajewsky saw himself compelled, at Trinity 1795, to migrate out of Krotoszyn much as Früson had done 3 years before. Notwithstanding this, Triebenfeld did not pay back the advance he had received to Gajewsky, while Hoym covered the treasury with Gajewsky's fortune, and in this way Gajewsky was made a poor man, who goes about in South Prussia as a living monument to Hoym's weakness and wickedness and tells his lamentable story to everyone who will but hear him. Whoever can dispute the truth of this piece of knavery, committed as it were merely in passing, and can refute the many witnesses who know of it at the Chambers in Posen and Breslau — why, let him step forward! — Ed.

I. The Kalisch Diocese.

A comprehensive survey of its historical course.

The Reformation movement in Germany found a strong echo also in Poland, favored by particular preconditions. Within a few decades the land stood in religious ferment: in the struggle of the leading circles for or against the new doctrine of faith. The conditions of that time, with their abundance of creative ideas and manifold influences, brought it about that Protestantism in Poland first found its characteristic form in three separate evangelical churches. In Greater Poland, where the center of gravity of the Lutheran church lay, divine service according to the Augsburg Confession was held in German at 110 places and in Polish at 32. Reformed services were held here, according to more recent research, at 80 places. "The figure cited for Greater Poland includes within itself also the Brethren's congregations, which had entered into a union with the Calvinists at the synod of Koźminek in 1555" In the Kalisch land, in the Warthe lowland and in Kujawien — on the territory of the present Kalisch Evangelical-Augsburg diocese — there existed in the 16th century about 25 Reformed and Brethren's congregations, whose number, however, diminished more and more in the course of time. From the beginning of the 17th century the Reformed in Kujawien lost one church after another to the Catholics, last of all in 1615 the church at Radziejów with its school and seminary. In consequence the Reformed senior Mikołajewski resolved to join the Brethren in order to strengthen the seven Reformed congregations still preserved. In December 1627 the final union was accomplished at the synod of Ostroróg, whereby the Reformed confession in Greater Poland once more lost influence

Built on a narrow congregational base, worn down by internal struggles, harassed by the Roman Catholic church, Protestantism in Poland moved toward its decline. In the Catholic Counter-Reformation there grew up against it an opponent whose attacks it proved unable to withstand in the long run Until the granting of freedom of religion in our land (1768) there remained in Greater Poland only seven Reformed congregations, very much weakened in their existence, one of them in the Warthe lowland and another in the Kalisch land — at Żychlin (near Konin) and Wola Tłumakowska

A vigorous strengthening and promotion of Protestantism in Poland came only in modern times through the German colonization. In the Kalisch land it began as early as about 1750. Numerous larger and smaller settlements arose here, as also in the Warthe lowland and in Kujawien As an urban place of immigration Władysławów (Rosterschütz) is to be named for 1727. In the Prussian period seven large Swabian villages were founded: Neu-Renneberg (Wygorzele, formerly the parish of Dąbie, now Łęczyca), Schwedelbach, Rosental, Wilhelmstal, Friedrichstal, Lilienfeld, Czarnocice. In South Prussia, in the towns of Kalisch, Dąbie, Kowal, Przedecz, Chodecz and others, German officials, craftsmen, and clothmakers settled. In the period from 1815 to 1863 rural and urban settlement activity made further progress. In the Kalisch land the founding of Wojciechowo took place in 1845, after that those of Michalinów, Łagiewniki, Sołomina. In Kujawien the colonies were laid out: 1840 Morzyczyn, 1842 Władysławów, 1850 Marcinkowo, 1855 Szarłatowo, 1859 Mieczysławowo, 1866 Besiekiery. Of far greater economic and church significance was the settlement of the towns

This had as its consequence, in the territories named, the rise of numerous German-evangelical villages, which in turn, in the course of development, led to the founding of congregations. After 1890 hundreds of colonists emigrated from the Kalisch land, but especially from Kujawien, to America.

The ecclesiastical gathering of the evangelical population settled in the villages and towns often met with considerable difficulties. At first it was chiefly economic reasons that stood in its way. The processes of settlement and of the putting down of roots by the colonists extended for the most part over one or two decades. How difficult these beginnings were the archives bear witness again and again. Thus Pastor Grimm-Stawiszyn writes, for example, of his congregation members that they "dwell in huts of turf." These huts of earth were precisely emergency forms of settler life, which played itself out in merciless narrowness and hardness Only after the German peasants, in laborious years-long work of clearing, had wrested from the often meager soil bread for themselves and their families could they set about building up a cultural and religious life of their own. Already at the laying out of a colony it was the custom to set aside a plot of land for school and house of prayer. After the distressful time of putting down roots had been overcome, simple school and prayer houses, mostly thatched with straw, were erected, and a teacher and cantor was called (often a landless farmer or a craftsman). "In most places, especially in the voivodeship of Kalisch, the evangelical schools came into being in this way: when one, two, or three evangelical families settled in a place remote from all evangelical churches, they chose out from among themselves someone who would instruct their children and hold edification hours for them on Sundays . . ." Through the union of the school with the house of prayer there arose everywhere in central Poland, and later also in Volhynia and other territories, that cantorate system so characteristic of the Evangelical-Augsburg church in Poland, which in all probability represents an intermediate form between the Swabian "Stunde" and the "pre-state" type of school and is an original creation of our colonist people.

As for the schooling of the evangelical town children, matters were in part better, insofar as in several South Prussian towns garrisoned by troops — like Peisern, Kalisch, Petrikau and others — military and burgher schools were founded. With time the number of schools grew constantly, so that about 1865 in the Kalisch land it had risen to 42, in the Warthe lowland to 22 and in Kujawien even to 77 evangelical village schools and cantorates. Through the "provisional school ordinance" of February 7, 1797 for the evangelical schools of South Prussia, then through the school constitution of February 24, 1834, further through the decree of the Warsaw school curator of August 16/18, 1847 and the Supreme Edict of August 30/September 11, 1864, all these schools were given legal security. About 1850 (with individual schools already earlier!) there made itself felt on the part of the school authorities the endeavor to transform the cantorate schools in towns and larger villages into elementary schools. Thus in 1857 the Kalisch land (including the Warthe lowland and Kujawien) had approximately 34 evangelical elementary schools with 37 evangelical teachers out of a total of 39 evangelical elementary schools in the Kalisch school district.

The German settlements were at first typical islands of language and religion in the midst of an environment of another kind. As such they sought, in order to maintain their faith and hand it on to coming generations, to draw close to one another, and thereby marked themselves off religiously from their surroundings. This endeavor, supported by Roman Catholic lords of the manor out of economic considerations, found clear expression in the founding of congregations. In the period 1776–1799 the parishes came into being: Władysławów, Stawiszyn, Kalisch, Grodziec and Babiak; in the 19th century: the parish congregations Kowal-Chodecz, Dąbie, Prażuchy, Łask, Sobiesęki, Wieluń, Przedecz, Konin, Zduńska Wola, Turek, Sompolno, Zagórów, as well as the filials Maślaki, Józefów and Lissewo-Pyzdry; in the 20th century: the congregations Koło, Izbica, the filial Ludwikowo, Kozy and Sieradz.

All evangelical-Augsburg congregations that took shape after 1775 on the territory of the present Kalisch diocese were administratively attached to the church district of Bojanowo. This latter, however, with its 16 churches and 18 preachers, together with the 7 other church districts (the Fraustadt, Lissa, Birnbaum, Karger, Meseritz, Posen and Gnesen districts), was subject to the consistory at Fraustadt, which counted in all 69 churches and 82 preachers Since the church district of Bojanowo was too wide-ranging, it was, by supreme appro-

The latter comprised the parishes Zduny, Adelnau, Ostrowo, Krotoszyn, Koźmin, Rosterschütz (Władysławów) and Kempen. As senior of the Kalisch church district Pastor Christoph Dienegott von Geißler of Zduny was called, while Pastor Hellwig of Rawitsch was assigned the oversight of the church district of Bojanowo as co-senior. After Pastor Geißler's death — "old and weak he died in the first days of October 1795 in the 73rd year of his life" — on February 25, 1796 Pastor Paul Immanuel Matthiä became senior of the Kalisch church district. The year 1797 brought a "new departmental organization in church and school matters." Thereby the congregations of Adelnau, Ostrowo, Kempen, Pleschen, Kalisch, Stawiszyn, Grodziec and Rosterschütz were incorporated into the Kalisch church district. In 1798 the South Prussian consistory at Petrikau was transferred to Kalisch. "The consistory at Kalisch consists of the provincial governor, a governmental director, five governmental councilors and one consistorial councilor . . . With the Lutheran consistorial affairs the Lutheran school system also is joined . . . Moreover in every county an inspector is appointed, who is called the county senior" Consistorial councilor of the Kalisch departmental consistory, which was subordinate to the Posen higher consistory, and inspector (superintendent) of the evangelical-Lutheran churches and schools, as well as first pastor of the Kalisch congregation, became Pastor Karl Friedrich Herzberg (†1812) After him, in the archival records, Pastor Karl Michael Christian Sienell of Kalisch is repeatedly mentioned as Kalisch superintendent, "senior of the evangelical clergy" (†1820).

As early as 1807/8 Pastor Karl Diehl, the Reformed consistorial president in Warsaw, was striving for the union of the Evangelicals of both confessions in a common consistory. From him comes the "Project of a constitution for the evangelical general consistory of the Duchy of Warsaw." His endeavors met at first with success. "With fullest conviction Karl Herzberg, superintendent of the Lutheran church in the Kalisch department, declared himself, after consultation held, for the project, and did so at the same time also in the name of the preachers placed under his supervision." But as the "project" met with great diffi-

The ordinance of the Ruling Commission of April 22, 1807 had as its consequence the formation of an evangelical consistory at Bromberg, into which the congregation of Babiak too was incorporated for a time. Through the decree of February 22, 1817, in place of the departmental consistories existing before, a "provisional evangelical consistory U. A. C. for the Kingdom of Poland" was created at Warsaw. Members of the consistory later included, among others: Pastor Karl Gottlieb Bartsch of Władysławów and Pastor Ernst Johann August von Modi of Kalisch.

In the year 1828 the Reformed Pastor Diehl was permitted to carry out his old favorite plan: by imperial ukase of February 14/26 of that year the Warsaw general consistory for both confessions was founded. It comprised 3 dioceses: the Warsaw, the Płock and the Kalisch. To the last were assigned from the Kalisch voivodeship the congregations: Kalisch, Konin, Żychlin (Reformed), Władysławów, Grodziec, Stawiszyn, Prażuchy, Sobiesęki, Pabianice, Petrikau, Zelów (Reformed), Wieluń and the projected parishes in Zduńska Wola and Kleszczów; from the Masovian voivodeship: Konstantynów, Alexandrow, Lodz, Zgierz, Dąbie, Ozorkow and the planned congregation at Tomaschow. In all there were thus 21 parishes. As superintendent of the Kalisch diocese Pastor Ernst Johann August von Modi of Kalisch was appointed, who held this office until his death (†1860).

The church law of February 8/20, 1849 dissolved the union between the Lutherans and the Reformed, in that it subordinated the Lutheran congregations in the Kingdom of Poland to the Warsaw evangelical-Augsburg consistory. To the three earlier dioceses there was added as the fourth that of Augustowo, whose parishes until then had been incorporated in the Płock diocese. Territorially the Kalisch diocese embraced the government of Kalisch, with the exception of the county of Łęczyca, and the government of Petrikau, without the counties of Lodz, Brzeziny, Rawa and Będzin. About 1865 it counted 19 parish and 13 filial congregations with 18 preachers, namely the parishes: Kalisch, Prażuchy, Sobiesęki, Stawiszyn, Grodziec, Zagórów, Konin, Władysławów, Dąbie, Turek, Wieluń, Zduńska Wola, Alexandrow, Konstantynów, Pabianice, Bełchatów, Petrikau, Tomaschow and

Superintendent von Modl was, although not entirely free of rationalistic influences, an active and energetic administrator of the diocese entrusted to him The visitations of the congregations lay very near his heart. Thus he visited, for example, in the year 1829 nine parishes, in which he always took care to promote the religious-ecclesiastical life in them and to convey appropriate impulses. As he himself attested, at the visitations he wished to ascertain how the pastors "sought to make themselves worthy" as preachers, liturgists, catechists, shepherds of souls "in the vineyard of the Lord," whether the "cura animarum" was their chief task. Of the church councils he wrote: "Our church colleges have lost the significance of the presbyteries . . . and have become merely ordinary stewards of the church's property." He therefore called the attention of the church elders all the more to the fact that "their sphere is a greater one than that of mere stewards of the church's property . . ., that the promotion of the salvation of souls" must also lie near to them. Unfortunately, he said, he had "heard only a few voices in the church colleges which expressed a pious wish directed to the salvation of the congregation's souls . . ." On the school question Sup. von Modl expressed himself in a report to the general consistory to the effect that "our congregations have almost no properly organized schools of their own at all . . . Can we, few excepted, call the institutions that exist under cantors etc. schools? May we designate the prayer-readers and teachers in our colonies and Hauländereien with the name 'schoolmaster'? . . . If our Zion is not to collapse, it is high time to hasten to the aid of the congregation of the Lord by taking more Christian care of its youth." Illuminating also are his earnest proposals concerning the preachers, the "bearers of the philosophy of heaven." Already on December 28, 1827 he petitioned the then consistory U. A. After Sup. von Modl's death, on May 24/June 6, 1861 Pastor Franz Johann Wladislaus Stockmann in Kalisch was elected superintendent of the Kalisch diocese and in 1865 appointed consistorial councilor. When he died on January 15, 1869, the pastorate chose from its midst, under the chairmanship of Gen.-Sup. Ludwig, on May 16, 1870, Pastor Karl Ludwig Teichmann of Turek as his successor. On the model of the other dioceses Superintendent Teichmann held pastoral synods, of which the diocesan synod that took place on July 16 and 17, 1879 at Bełchatów, in which 16 pastors took part, was at the same time joined with the 25-year jubilee of office of the pastors Haberkant-Kalisch and Fiedler-Bełchatow. The subject of the deliberations was: lectures by P. Biedermann-Tomaschow on occasional addresses and by P. Zander-Alexandrow on visits to the sick, further on the melody collection to be introduced, cemetery boards, the reordering of congregational boundaries, among other things Sup. Teichmann (†1890) was likewise concerned to influence congregational life in a positively ecclesiastical sense. After him Pastor Ludwig Julius Daniel Müller-Petrikau became superintendent of the Kalisch diocese. "His administrative experience permitted him to express the right and clear opinion in many a dark and difficult matter. The late Gen.-Sup. Everth therefore distinguished him with great appreciation and often asked his counsel in confidence" Sup. From 1910 to 1914 the diocese was administered by Superintendent Rudolf Buse of Grodziec, who directed his attention especially to the raising up of the cantorates. To this end he held cantors' conferences in his congregation and thereby spurred other pastors on to give more attention to the cantorate system, until then treated rather stepmotherly, and to hold like gatherings, from which manifold impulses and influences went out to the cantorates. Since Sup. Buse was banished to Russia at the outbreak of the war in 1914, where he died in 1917, Pastor Eduard Wende of Kalisch first represented him, then was entrusted wholly with the direction of the diocese.

In the years 1906–1914, as also after the recovery of Polish statehood, Gen.-Sup. Bursche visited the congregations of the Kalisch diocese repeatedly. In the detailed, clear visitation protocols composed by himself, which are to be reckoned an important contribution to the history of the diocese, the whole life of the parishes mirrors itself in a definite present situation.

The Kalisch diocese embraces a large part of the Lodz voivodeship — the counties of Koło, Konin, Turek, Kalisch, Sieradz, Łask, Wieluń — and a smaller part of the Warsaw voivodeship — the counties of Kutno, Łęczyca, Włocławek and Nieszawa. The number of evangelical affiliated parishioners in the diocese amounts to 65,200 souls; that of the German-evangelical schools — avowedly evangelical-confessional schools are not permitted by law — is subject to constant fluctuations

According to the new church law, which will presumably come into force in the course of this year by decree of the president of the state, 16 parish and 5 filial congregations are to be included in the Kalisch diocese (instead of the hitherto existing 19 parishes and 4 filials).

3. Kalisch.

Kalisch is the oldest town in Poland concerning which we possess historical records from the earliest time. Thus already in the 1st century A.D. the Roman historian Caius Plinius the Younger mentions in his "Historia Mundi" the settlement "Calisia". Likewise the Greek Claudius Ptolomaios of Alexandria names it in the 2nd century A.D. The old trade route, the so-called Bernsteinstrasse, led from the south to the Baltic Sea by way of Kalisch.

Among the Polish chroniclers the first report concerning Kalisch comes in the year 1108. Since then it looks back on a richly eventful past. It was the scene of armed conflicts, capital of the Kalisch territorial principality, an important trading place, a focal point of religious and cultural endeavors.

The environs of Kalisch show German settlers already in early times. Around 1280–1300 localities are founded here "under German law" (Breitenfeld, Rajsko); in 1597 the village of Olędrowo. Before 1260 Kalisch was furnished with German law. In 1264 Rithwinus was Schulze and locator here. From the 13th to the 16th century the burghers of Kalisch were of German nationality "One could put together long lists of German councilors alone, not to speak of burghers . . . Over 4 centuries the names Hering, Linke, Loy, Opitz, Pilars, Schwarzbach, Thomas have endured. Mayor and vogt families were the Hannasmutter, Kunisch, Margraf, Tischler and Kupferschmidt" In the 16th and still in part in the 17th century evangelical congregations existed in the Kalisch land at Kalisch, Kamień, Marszewo, Broni-

szewice, Gołuchów, Koźminek, Żychlin and others), which exercised a considerable influence on their surroundings. This is attested also by the papal nuncio Giovanni Francesco Commendone, staying in Kalisch in 1565, in his letter of November 4 of that year to Carlo Borromeo. In Kalisch itself Reformed, Lutherans, Bohemian Brethren and Socinians were represented, of whom apparently only the first had a congregational organization and a preacher here (Paul Paliura). At that time there distinguished himself in Kalisch as an excellent educator (from 1588 at Lubartów) and speaker, as a man of rich knowledge and author of numerous writings (among others "Schola Levartoriana Restituta", printed 1593), the Socinian Albertus Calisius, a decided opponent of the Jesuits. These set themselves the goal of the complete extermination of Protestantism in the Kalisch land.

Introduced at Kalisch in 1581 by the Gnesen archbishop Stanislaus Karnkowski, they went eagerly to work. Toward the end of the 16th century the Jesuits took over the direction of the so-called "Academy Colony" and transformed it into a five-class school; about 1591 they founded an ecclesiastical seminary, in 1595 a "Collegium Nobilium" for the noble youth of the Kalisch land; about 1603 they acquired the printing establishment of Johann Wolrab and soon afterward issued the "Roman Catechism" in the Polish language The religious center of their counter-reformatory activity was the college built for them by Karnkowski together with the Jesuit church (with three naves and a beautiful baroque altar). This house of God, consecrated on September 8, 1596, was erected according to the plan of the Milanese Jesuit architect Gian Maria Bernardone (†1605) "In the year of the completion of the church building Sigismund III came in person to Kalisch and inspected in every detail the new foundation of the shepherd, thereby giving expression to his favor toward the archbishop, whom he loved for his sense of justice and honored for his merits"

The Protestants in Kalisch were in the long run unable to withstand the onslaught of the Jesuits. After Sigismund Grudziński (1572–1653), the mighty voivode of Kalisch, had become Catholic shortly before his death, the evangelical-Reformed congregation in Kalisch came to an end.

kneifel1937/57:
The evangelical cemetery in Kalisch, dating from the 17th (or indeed already the 16th) century, lies on an eminence which the common people formerly called the "Lutheran hill." On September 26, 1790 this cemetery was handed back to the Kalisch Evangelicals and fenced in by them in the following year. This proves that Evangelicals were likewise settled here at that time They had their religious acts performed for the most part by the pastors of the Stawiszyn congregation.

Through the second partition of Poland (1793) Kalisch fell to Prussia. Into the newly acquired town came German-evangelical military men, officials, craftsmen and merchants. In the environs of Kalisch, in the "Dember Holland," evangelical farmers settled, whose "Schulhalter" (school-holders) were in 1796 Christian David Paetzolt, in 1805 Johann Gottlieb Schultz. In the year 1795 the number of those who had immigrated into Kalisch, together with the Evangelicals already settled here before, was so considerable that they petitioned the town administration to call a preacher for them. They also submitted to the government and to the consistory in Posen the request to establish in Kalisch "a church system of its own and to appoint a preacher, who was at the same time to fill the office of school-rector." Their efforts had complete success. On September 3, 1795 the "concession for the establishment of an evangelical church system of its own at Kalisch for the evangelical congregation there" was granted. Still in the course of that year Pastor Karl Michael Christian Sienell assumed the pastorate of the newly organized congregation. In a rented hall on the Old Ring, in the so-called cobblers' stalls ("jatki szewskie"), he held divine service for two years. Thanks to the intervention of the Prussian government Pope Pius VI, on the basis of the brief of August 27, 1797, made over to the Kalisch Evangelicals the Jesuit church standing empty since 1773 "cum pleno jure patronatus". The house of God, become evangelical by historical dispensation, which by Archbishop Karnkowski's will was to be a bulwark of work hostile to Protestants in the Kalisch land for all time, Pastor Sienell consecrated according to evangelical rite on the first Whitsun holiday 1798 The relief monument, which shows the primate Karnkowski before the cross of Christ in an attitude of prayer,

The new congregation embraced, besides Kalisch, Opatówek and Dęby as well, then Koźminek and for a time also Sieradz. In Opatówek Gottlieb Lucae filled the office of teacher in 1805.

After the creation of the province of "South Prussia" Kalisch became in 1798 the seat of the "South Prussian evangelical consistory," of which Consistorial Councilor Karl Friedrich Herzberg became a member and at the same time preacher at the Kalisch evangelical church. He died on November 10, 1812 "of consumption and lung disease at the age of 43 years . . ." Pastor Sienell served the parish until his death, which took place on October 12, 1820 He reached an age of 45 years (died "of lung disease").

In the course of time there made itself felt within the congregation the desire for a fixed church order. At the wish of the Kalisch church council Deybel von Hammerau sent the "Warschauer Kirchliche Ökonomie-Ordnung" (Warsaw ecclesiastical economy ordinance) and announced on June 12, 1820 that the "ordinance," as experience had taught, was not without defects, wherefore in its use "only the best and most suitable was to be chosen." The congregational meeting that took place on September 20 of that year called, for the purpose of working out a church order, the following 12 committee members: Nieszkowski, Prof. Borodicz, Assessor Welke, merchant Elbel, treasury controller Rebsch, manufacturer Meyer, Weygert, Wölfel, Eiselin, Hoffmann, Rothert and Scheppe. From 1820 to 1824 the preliminary work lasted, which the church elder Assessor Gerhardt furthered with his "Proposals for the organization and direction of the accounting and treasury system," in which the principal labor was performed by Pastor Ernst Johann August Modl, appointed in 1821 as Sienell's successor. In 1824 the "Economy Ordinance" was drafted. In the year 1824 the bishop of Kalisch-Kujawien, Koźmian, came before the public with the proposal of handing over to the evangelical congregation at Kalisch the Franciscan church, but taking back into possession the former Jesuit church and opening in it an ecclesiastical seminary. This plan, which had already begun to take effect, met with so decided a resistance on the part of the Catholic population of Kalisch and its environs that Bishop Koźmian had to let it fall. To the petition of the town dwellers Emperor Alexander I replied, among other things: ". . . I praise the zeal of the inhabitants of Kalisch that they wished to protect the church with their prayers . . . I praise the unconcern of the Protestants that they were not hasty about the taking away (of the church) . . . We therefore determine that the church shall remain with the same monastic connection."

The founding of an evangelical school at Kalisch received the greatest attention from the church council. In the years 1798 to 1810 there existed here an evangelical school whose rector was Pastor Karl Gottlieb Bartsch; then it came to an end. For years the church council strove in vain for the reopening of the school. It turned, among others, also to State Councilor Radoszewski, the president of the Kalisch voivodeship commission. The latter showed himself well disposed, but was of the opinion that the evangelical school to be opened must have suitable premises. Therefore Radoszewski commissioned the voivodeship master builder F. Reinstein to work out a building plan together with a cost estimate for the schoolhouse to be erected. This was done. Yet the church council drew back from this undertaking and acquired instead, in the year 1826, a spacious house on the Piekarska-Str. with rooms for the school as well as apartments for the pastor, the vicar, the teacher, the sexton and the bell-ringer. This house was remodeled and enlarged in 1844. On February 24, 1834 the Kalisch superintendency reported to the consistory that an evangelical elementary school had been founded at Kalisch. If in 1846 two teachers (Kaselitz and Schroeter) were already at work in it, after a decade there were already four teachers (Schroeter, Rasch, Ecke and Foerster) active here. In the year 1857 the teacher and cantor Schroeter suggested the formation of an evangelical singing choir at Kalisch. Soon a number of song-loving town burghers joined the choir (among others Robert Franken, Johann Blüml, Einhorn, R. Wüstehube, Bertelmann sen., Thiele, Bothner).

On November 20, 1858 the Kalisch Evangelicals Dr. Adolf Sturm, Stanislaus Kossecki, Johann Niedomański, the notary Emiljan Ordon and K. Dabenbuth turned to the consistory with the request
kneifel1937/60:
to hold divine service in Polish on every second or third Sunday. According to the petition, services were held in the Polish language on Sunday mornings after the first [Sunday] of each month and on the afternoon of the first Christmas and Easter holiday, as also the celebration of confession and the Lord's Supper on Maundy Thursday. On the Sundays after the First there took place, alongside the Polish morning service, a German mission service in the afternoon as well.

For four decades Pastor Modi (†April 22, 1860) was shepherd of souls of the Kalisch parish, for which, as also for the development of the Kalisch diocese, of which he had been superintendent, he rendered great service.

After Pastor Modl's death the neighboring pastors Orive-Grodziec, Jarnecki-Prażuchy, Teichmann-Turek and Fiedler-Sobiesęki administered the vacant congregation, whose administration was later entrusted to the local vicar Ernst Wilhelm Bursche. From 11 candidates who applied for the pastorate the church council chose only 3, namely the pastors Stockmann-Radom, Tydelski-Włocławek and Benni-Tomaschow. On October 8, 1860 the congregation elected Franz Johann Wladilaus Stockmann as its pastor. Until 1869 he exercised his office here; from 1861 he was superintendent of the Kalisch diocese, from 1865 member of the Warsaw evangelical-Augsburg consistory. On January 15, 1869 Pastor Stockmann died a tragic death in Warsaw and was buried in the Lutheran cemetery there

After a short vacancy the parish elected on March 14, 1870 as its shepherd of souls Pastor Hermann Immanuel Friedrich Benni of Tomaschow, who however already in the next year was called to the University of Warsaw as lecturer in the English language. Thereupon Pastor Johann Adam Haberkant of Dąbie entered the service of the congregation in 1872. In the years 1877 and 1882 he renovated the church, for which in 1887 the Kalisch artist Bertelmann painted the beautiful altar piece "The Ascension of Christ." Since there were several secondary schools in the town, Pastor Haberkant diligently concerned himself with the evangelical instruction in religion in these schools, until then treated rather stepmotherly.

On July 16, 1904 Pastor Haberkant celebrated his 50-year jubilee of office, in which the pastors Krempin-Prażuchy, Serini-Stawiszyn, Wojak-Brzeziny, Buse-Grodziec, Winkler-Wieluń and Semadeni-Żychlin (Reformed) took part. After almost 33 years of activity in the Kalisch congregation Pastor Haberkant departed this life on September 12, 1905 and was buried in the Warsaw evangelical-Lutheran cemetery.

kneifel1937/61:
From December 28, 1902 Eduard Wende labored at Kalisch as vicar; after Pastor Haberkant's death, in the month of April 1906, he was called by the congregation to be its shepherd of souls and was installed by Gen.-Sup. Bursche on the first Whitsun holiday of that year, with the assistance of Pastor Manitius-Lodz.

The new local pastor introduced Passion services, increased the number of Polish services, and in the year 1903 held for the first time the confirmation in the Polish language for children who had no command of German. In 1906 the singing choir received its first officially confirmed society statute and was registered as the "Kalischer Gesangverein". On January 1, 1907 there took place the detachment of the cantorate congregation of Koźminek from Kalisch and its attachment to Prażuchy. The proximity of the cantorate of Prażuchy determined this measure. In the session of the church council on October 30, 1907 the thought arose of erecting an evangelical home for the aged at Kalisch. At the basis of the thought, "res sacra miser" (a sacred thing is the wretched man), lay the wish: "No Evangelical may beg." In spite of all hindrances (especially also concerning the building permit) the home for the aged could be erected, consecrated and handed over to its purpose "after two years and three days." "On that day (November 16, 1909) namely, in quiet seclusion from our town, on the so-called 'Piskorzewie,' it was consecrated, and there was opened the new place of the love of God and of one's neighbor . . ." The consecration was performed by Pastor Wende with the participation of Pastor Sachs of Stawiszyn The building site for the home for the aged was presented by Mrs. Johanna Kunig. The costs of the building amounted to 26,550 rubles 68 kopecks and were met almost entirely by voluntary gifts. The congregation pledged itself to provide for the maintenance of the home. Thus, for example, in the year 1910 the costs of maintenance amounted to 1529 rubles 76 kopecks. In the year 1907 there arose at Kalisch the "Christliche Gemeinschaft" (Christian Community), whose founders are to be regarded as the manufacturer Hugo Müller-Kalisch and Ludwig Hausmann-Rokicie. In the period 1912–1914 the Community preacher Blümke labored here.

The congregational meeting that took place on December 1, 1912 resolved to sell the old parsonage for 20,000 rubles and to erect a new parsonage at the Niecałastr. No. 8, in the immediate vicinity of the beautiful park of Kalisch. This resolution soon became deed, for already on September 8, 1913 the new parsonage could be consecrated. Besides the local pastor there appeared for the celebration the pastors: Edmund Bursche-Łowicz, Buse-Grodziec, Sachs-Turek and Mergel-Sobiesęki. The total costs of the building (including the site) amounted to 81,750 rubles. For this purpose notable gifts came in, among others from the former manufacturer of Kalisch

The parsonage, one of the most beautiful in our territorial church, is a modern, spacious building, in which on the ground floor the church chancellery is housed, further on the first floor the pastor's apartment, and on the second the apartments for the cantor and the sexton.

Through the building of the home for the aged and of the parsonage Pastor Wende acquired enduring merit in the development of the Kalisch congregation. In the building of the parsonage there stood at his side in especial helpfulness the members of the church council: A. Fibiger, E. Fulde, R. Fibiger, A. Stenzel, E. Rathe and A. Knoch.

In the World War 1914/18 Kalisch, as then a border town, suffered severely. Already in the first days of August 1914 the German troops (the 155th regiment, Major Preusker) bombarded the town, which was in part sorely devastated. As the reason there was given the shooting of German soldiers by civilians. The partial destruction of the town also involved many evangelical congregation members in suffering. After the close of the war Kalisch slowly recovered, rising like a phoenix from the ruins to new bloom. Through the shifting of the border, however, it lost its former interstate economic significance.

In the year 1922 the church was renovated; in 1930 three bells were procured in place of those confiscated in the war). On April 12, 1922 the singing choir received a new statute, confirmed by the Lodz voivodeship office, on the basis of which it now bears the name "Kalischer Evangelischer Gesangverein". In 1928 Pastor Wende celebrated the 25-year jubilee of his activity in the Kalisch congregation, at which a number of pastors, among others Gen.-Sup. Bursche, numerous congregation members and representatives of the authorities took part. In the year 1921 Pastor Wende, as then deputy chairman of the town council,

Emil Repphan endowed the city of Berlin by deed of gift of December 27/29, 1913 with 5 million marks for the establishment and maintenance of a forest school, the "Repphan'sche Waldschulstiftung der Stadt Berlin" [Repphan forest-school foundation of the city of Berlin]. The donation, burdened with a life annuity, was accepted by resolution of the municipal corporations of January 15, 1914. By supreme decree of April 27, 1914 the acceptance of the donation was approved. The founder Emil Repphan died on March 30, 1931, his widow Marie Repphan née Jouin on March 12, 1932. We know that you built Poland already at a time when it did not yet stand on the map of Europe, that you built it in our hearts, believing unshakably in what was not yet there, and kindled this holy fire of faith with word and deed in the hearts of thousands and of millions. No. 4, for the factory premises placed at its disposal by the firm of Müller proved much too small. Since the work of the Community required constant care, in 1929 the preacher Alfred Hoffert was appointed here. In the Community there exists a youth league of the E. C., a Sunday school and a singing choir16).

On Sunday, December 4, 1932, the Kalisch singing society celebrated its 75-year jubilee, which was joined with the consecration of the first banner. At that time the society counted 35 active and 90 passive members as well as 3 honorary members, namely Pastor Eduard Wende, Johann Gustav Hammermeister and Alexander Schaub. Chairmen of the singing society from its founding to the present were: Ernst Schröter, Wilhelm Feiler, Julius Betting, Julius Kunig, Adolf Stenzel, Alexander Schaub, Gustav Hempel. As conductors there were active in the course of the years: Ernst Schröter, Loy, Müller, Hammermeister, Padyga, Horky, Madlo, Ziebart, Hill, Cepelli, Bielecki, Emil Ismer. To the former chairman of the society Schaub belongs the merit of having acquired a plot of ground for the building of a society home. This plot is to be sold and a smaller, more suitable one acquired in its place. At present the premises of the singing society are at the Dobrzecka-Str. 21, in the Hempel hall. 4. Grodziec.

In the year 1772 the German-evangelical villages of Borowiec, Konary, Grunde and Wielołęka were founded on the estates of Grodziec. The owner of Biskupice settled colonists in Orlina (Adlerholland) in 1784; in the same year Peter von Sokoła-Gałczyński, the lord of the manor of Gadow, settled German peasants in Gadow Holland. In 1787 F. Stadnicki, the starost of Adelnau, laid out the Holländerei Białobłoty. In the records the villages are designated "gminy holendrów" [gminas of the Holländer]. The pastors of Władysławów visited all these localities1). On July 12, 13 and 14, 1796 the representatives of the villages named concluded with Count Stadnicki, in the presence of the judicial commission of the county of Pyzdry (Peisern) assembled on the manor farm of Grodziec, a contract concerning the establishment of the evangelical parish congregation of Grodziec2). According to the agreement reached the count pledged himself to present all building sites on which the church, the parsonage, the cantor's house, the farm buildings and the like were to be erected; he declared himself likewise ready to assign to the Evangelicals a place for a cemetery ("by the road to the glassworks"). Further, he held out the prospect of his energetic help in the erection of ecclesiastical buildings, in that he promised to furnish all requisite building material — timber, brick, lime, glass — "so that the congregation, promoted by this benefaction, might the sooner complete the building of the house of God and of all churchly edifices." Stadnicki gave expression to his good will also in this, that he presented for the pastor 2 Morgen of meadow and 1 Morgen of garden land, likewise for the cantor 1 Morgen of garden land, as well as an annual allowance

 2) The contract is divided into 15 sections and treats in detailed fashion all the duties arising from it, both of Count von Stadnicki as founder and patron of the congregation of Grodziec and of the colonists settled around Grodziec as co-founders of the parish.

For himself and his descendants he reserved the right of patronage, especially in the filling of the pastorate, yet permitted the holding of trial sermons before the congregation, which "might represent to him its opinion of the qualifications of the candidate." As first pastor of the congregation of Grodziec the church patron and the representatives of the localities elected unanimously the candidate of theology David Bergemann of Fraustadt. At the same time they requested the Royal Consistory at Posen to perform his ordination in the shortest time and to entrust him with the administration of Grodziec3). In conclusion Count von Stadnicki and the representatives of the villages declared "they were minded to keep this contract forever and under no circumstances to depart from it." This act of foundation was confirmed on January 9, 1797 by the South Prussian government at Posen.

Hard were the beginnings. The building of the church, begun in 1797, was completed only in 1803. The house of God was not large, only 14 ells high, built in the manner of a "preußische Mauer" (Prussian wall), that is, of timber with bricks laid in between. The parsonage, a simple wooden building (erected 1800), consisted of three small living rooms and was thatched with straw. The cantor's house and all the farm buildings (of timber with straw roofs) Pastor Bergemann erected likewise in the year 1800. His activity in the congregation lasted 10 years. On August 11, 1807 he died unexpectedly "of bodily pains" at the age of 41 years. His earthly remains were buried on August 13 of that year before the altar in the old church by Pastor Friedrich Heinrich Wilhelm Ernst Jonathan Grimm of Stawiszyn4).

The congregation, now shepherdless, called as its shepherd of souls Pastor Johann Christian Gottlieb Rissmann, a native of Glogau, who exercised his office here until 1815. He then went to Ostrowo5). Into the period of his activity fall the grave events of the year 1812, which did not remain without influence upon the religious life of the little congregations.

After Pastor Rissmann the pastorate was assumed in 1815 by Pastor Johann Stegmann of Krojanke5a). Under his direction the affiliated parishioners

The religious life of the parish suffered for a time under sectarian agitation. In the year 1823 enthusiasts appeared who called themselves "Erweckte" (the awakened), held assemblies in private houses and interpreted the Bible according to their own judgment. A particular veneration was accorded a girl of 16 years, who in a state of ecstasy presumed to know about life after death. The sect, however, did not spread. After a few years the "Erweckten" rejected their false doctrines and returned to the bosom of the evangelical church.

The Polish-Russian war of 1830/31 involved the congregation in suffering. It was not granted to Pastor Stegmann to serve his parishioners in this hard time, for already on January 29, 1831 he departed this life at the age of 69 years. He was buried in the evangelical forest cemetery at Grodziec.

The parish, vacant from 1831 to 1832, then received in the person of Pastor Joseph Spleszyński a new shepherd of souls. In his work he directed his attention chiefly to the building of a new church, whose necessity he recognized, the more so as the old house of God was quite dilapidated and almost unusable. On September 1, 1834 a meeting took place in the matter of the church building, at which, besides the local pastor, Sup. Modl of Kalisch also took part, as well as the church elders: Gottfried Kurtz of Grodziec, August Matheke of Alt-Grądy, Georg Heintz of Borowiec, Gottlieb Janott of Konary, Gottfried Reich of Wielołęka, Gottlieb Drewitsch of Neu-Grądy, Johann Rentz of Białobłoty and Christoph Polsfuth of Klein-Orlin. There appeared further, at this exceedingly important deliberation, the village headmen of the congregation: Michael Lempke of Borowiec, Andreas Fengler of Konary, Gottfried Gützel of Wielołęka and Gottfried Splistösser of Neu-Grądy. Those assembled resolved to build a new church with seating room for 800 persons. Plan and cost estimate were prepared by the voivodeship building councilor Reinstein at Kalisch. For the examination of the cost estimate Pastor Spleczyński held on October 5 of that year a second consultation with the church elders, the cantorate elders and the village headmen, at which the covering of the church with roof tiles (not with sheet zinc, as had at first been intended) and the procurement of the building material were negotiated. At the instigation of the Kalisch voivodeship there was drawn up on November 18, 1834, in the presence of Sup. Modl, building councilor Reinstein and the church council of Grodziec, a protocol concerning the complete unusability of the old house of God and the pressing necessity of the church building. Shortly thereafter the cost estimate of 47,209 zt.

Namely, the first installment was to be payable after the laying of the foundation stone, the second after the erection of the shell of the building, and the third after the completion of the church. The remaining sum of 22,994 zt. 7 groschen was to be borne by the lordship of Grodziec according to the act of foundation. Yet it could not fulfill its obligation, in that the government took it into receivership and at the same time notified the evangelical congregation on December 28, 1836 that the affiliated parishioners themselves must bear all the costs of building, although it too was ready to grant an aid. This letter greatly discouraged the local pastor and the congregation. The new building of the church seemed, in consequence of this position taken by the authorities, not capable of execution. For still greater sacrifices could not be imposed upon the poor parish. Therefore the building matter rested. In the year 1839 Pastor Spleszyński left Grodziec and assumed the administration of the evangelical-Reformed congregation of Warsaw6).

During the vacancy the parish was administered by Pastor Karl Friedrich Orive of Stawiszyn, who, after the election had taken place, was confirmed by the government on July 24, 1841 as local pastor. The new shepherd of souls was deeply concerned for the welfare of his parish, in which above all the church building lay at his heart. The documents of the parish archive bear witness to this. On April 13, 1841 he induced the congregation to vote a higher building contribution and to apportion the cost estimate in such a way that farmers with one hide each should pay 87 zlotys, farm hands and inhabitants (tenants) 6 zt., maidservants and female inhabitants 4 zlotys. On the other hand the members of the cantorate of Obory, which lies far from the parish town, had to pay of the hide only 58 zlotys, farm hands and inhabitants only 4 zlotys, maidservants and female inhabitants 3 zlotys. This favor was granted them also for the reason that they had built a house of prayer at their own cost. By this apportionment of the cost estimate it was hoped to raise a building sum of 37,410 zlotys 22 groschen, namely after deduction of all the amounts which for various reasons could not be collected (niedobory). The deficit of 9798 zlotys 20 groschen was to be granted as assistance by the government, which was petitioned to that end.

Count von Bieliński, the later lord of Grodziec, showed at first understanding for the church building. After an evangelical

 6) On June 19, 1849 appointed superintendent of the evangelical-Reformed church in Poland. He is known also as the author of Polish-evangelical hymns, of a Reformed catechism and as editor of a Polish hymnal for the Reformed church. Pastor Spleszyński died a sudden death in 1879 in the church during the performance of a wedding (Zwiastun Ewangeliczny, Jahrg. 1879, pp. 114 ff. Ks. Władysław Semadeni, Z dziejów zboru ewangelicko-reformowanego w Warszawie, 1927, pp. 18 and 19).
kneifel1937/71:
divine service at which he was present, he declared verbally and afterward also in writing: "as church patron I am minded to further the building of the house of God to the utmost of my powers . . . Within a period of 8 years I shall furnish all the roof tiles (computed according to the cost estimate at 10,426 zt.) and all the building timber (estimated at 4938 zlotys)." Yet this under the condition that the congregation must work up the material he was to furnish at its own cost and haul it to the building site, which he himself would assign to it.

The hope set upon the help of the authorities was fulfilled only in part. In the letter of March 2, 1842 the governmental commission announced that it confirmed the plan and the cost estimate for the new building of the church, and declared its readiness to contribute the missing sum from the evangelical fund.

The church building took on ever more tangible shape. On August 14, 1843 the county building office at Konin resolved to carry out the building by administrative procedure, the more so as no building contractor showed himself inclined to undertake it. Alexander Pawłowski, the estate steward of Grodziec, began in 1846, as plenipotentiary of the count, the building of the house of God. It was erected, against the wish of many congregation members, on a hill of sand. The solemn laying of the foundation stone of the church took place in the presence of Sup. Modl on August 9, 1846. Soon the shell of the building (up to the roof) was finished. Then there came unexpectedly an interruption of the work, partly because the lordship would not fulfill its obligations, partly also because the energetic estate steward Pawłowski had left Grodziec. Pastor Orive, notwithstanding all difficulties, did not remain idle. He negotiated with the county building office, with Count Bieliński, took steps with Sup. Modl-Kalisch and with the consistory, in order only to push the building forward.

Meanwhile the old dilapidated church threatened to collapse. Therefore the authorities saw themselves compelled to order the sealing of the church. This took place on October 24, 1850. By this measure the holding of divine services met with difficulties, for the uncompleted new house of God could not yet be used. In consequence the church council of Grodziec petitioned the county office at Konin to have the old church repaired so far until the new one should be built. The county office, however, did not consent to this. It is to be assumed that the divine services took place in the open air for lack of a suitable room. At Whitsuntide 1852 the congregation celebrated its first divine service in the church, not yet fitted out within. It did so reluctantly, in the fear that the further building might thereby be hindered. Sup. Modl sought to dispel these misgivings. In the letter of May 26, 1852 he encouraged "his dear parish children at Grodziec" not to despair but to trust in the success of the work begun
kneifel1937/72:
with faith. "Be firmly convinced — he wrote — that the holding of services of worship in the new church will in no wise hinder the building of the same. Your old superintendent, under whose eyes a part of you has grown up and who himself has reached the age of gray hairs, will do everything that your church may be completed and adorned with a tower." These comforting, fatherly words instilled into many new courage and new cheerfulness. In spite of all — the building stagnated. The roof of the church was covered only by half in makeshift fashion, the tower not built, the interior of the house of God not finished. Nevertheless the zeal of the church council did not flag. On May 22, 1852 it concluded a contract with the organ builder and cabinetmaker Karl Köhler of Kalisch, according to which the latter pledged himself to rebuild the organ and set it up in the new church; besides, he was to deliver pulpit, altar, baptismal font and altar rail. At the same time the church board ordered of him also benches, hymn boards and the like. All the work was executed in 1853.

Years passed, but the completion of the house of God was delayed ever more. The ministry of the interior decreed indeed on May 12, 1859 that Count Bieliński was obligated to complete the church building according to the original plan and cost estimate. Soon afterward Count Bieliński died († 1860), which was quite unfavorable for the further building. The widowed Countess Virginia von Bielińska, to whom the church council of Grodziec now turned again and again in the building matter, held out in 1865 the prospect of an assistance of 5000 zlotys, without, however, redeeming her promise. The Kalisch superintendency therefore saw no other way out than to call upon the help of the government. The latter, by its measures, moved the countess to make good the obligations assumed by the lordship. On September 22, 1866 the building of the church, which had lasted 20 years, was finished7).

On August 2, 1860, together with the old house of God (St. Peter's and Paul's church), the dilapidated cantor's building also was torn down. The plan and cost estimate for the erection of a parsonage and cantor's house the government confirmed on March 9, 1863. In the spring of the following year the building of the parsonage was begun by the architect Reich of Pleschen and completed in 1868. It cost 2971 rubles 33 kopecks, the consistory granting 750 rubles.

On March 9, 1868 fire broke out on the parsonage premises, which burned to ashes the farm buildings of the parsonage and the old parsonage. Through the fire the congregation saw itself confronted with new

The duties of the sexton were performed in the congregation at first by two so-called "Kirchenväter" (church fathers) chosen for the purpose. As they had, indeed, too much to do, they transferred this office about 1850 to a man named Gottfried Blesing, who thus was the first sexton of Grodziec.

On May 16, 1872 the lordship changed owners: Count Mieczysław v. Kwilecki acquired Grodziec. Through the village bailiff he gave the cantor notice of his dwelling and gave expression through his further conduct to his aversion to the evangelical parish. The allowance accruing to the congregation on the basis of the erection charter of January 9, 1797 was lost to it, because it was not secured by mortgage (lawsuit 1884). The close relation, though not always free of friction, which for decades had existed between the dominium of Grodziec and the evangelical parish, dissolved.

In exemplary fidelity and devotion Pastor Orive administered Grodziec. The welfare of the congregation determined his course of action always, even when he personally had to suffer under it. His outward situation was shadowed by the care for an existence worthy of a human being. Especially heavy the years 1865–1876 must have been for him, for he complains that the parish owes him for some time past his salary, and that the dominium does not give him the allowance. The material need sharpened for him to such a degree that beside his pastoral work he still filled the office of a clerk in the civil commune of Grodziec. On August 3, 1876 he died at the age of 72 years.

After his death the parish was administered by Pastor Erdmann of Zagórów, who then from 1878 to 1892 was pastor of Grodziec. In 1883 he obtained from the firm Schlag u. Söhne in Schweidnitz an organ for 2357 rubles. — It is related that Pastor Erdmann was suddenly taken ill in the pulpit during the sermon, so that he had to be carried out of the church. In the parsonage garden he is said to have died († October 17, 1892).

The administration of Grodziec was entrusted by the consistory to Pastor Joseph Rosenberg of Stawiszyn, who visited it until 1894. From 1894 to 1898 (April) Pastor August Loth labored here, at present first pastor of the Warsaw evangelical-Lutheran congregation. According to the annual report of 1895 there dwelt at that time within the bounds of the parish 20 Reformed persons, whom the pastor of Żychlin cared for spiritually. On April 13, 1898 Pastor Loth petitioned the consistory to relieve him of the direction of the Grodziec pastorate and to appoint him admini-
kneifel1937/74:
strator of Rawa and of the filial Błędów. The consistory complied with this request and at the same time declared Grodziec vacant. Since, however, no candidates presented themselves, it again entrusted the administration of Grodziec (until September 1899) to Pastor Rosenberg of Stawiszyn. For the vacant pastorate Pastor Arnold Hoffmann of Rożyszcze applied, whose candidacy the consistory, however, declined to confirm, because he did not belong to the body of pastors of the Warsaw consistorial district. Meanwhile Pastor Rosenberg removed to Konstantynow, and administrator of Grodziec became, from September 10, 1899, Pastor Karl Henkel of Konin. On October 29, 1900 the congregation again received a shepherd of souls of its own, Pastor Rudolf Buse.

Proceeding from the recognition that the work of the cantors is exceedingly important for the congregation, Pastor Buse instituted cantors' conferences, which enjoyed great popularity. From July 8, 1910 he labored also as superintendent of the Kalisch diocese. In the World War, arrested by the Cossacks in 1914, he was banished to Russia8). After severe suffering he departed this life on January 3, 1917 at Saratov, where on January 5 of that year he was buried by his predecessor in the Grodziec pastorate, Pastor August Loth.

The care of Grodziec was assumed by Pastor Sachs of Turek. In June 1915 Pastor Otto Krenz came here, who officiated until 1919. After Pastor Sachs had once more administered the congregation, the pastorate was assumed on May 1, 1922 by Pastor Adolf Gustav Ulbrich.

As the farm buildings had burned down, he built new ones in 1923. In the years 1924/25 he surrounded the church square with a beautiful brick fence, for which among other things 481.50 dollars flowed in from America from former congregation members. On the front side of the parsonage Pastor Ulbrich erected likewise, from voluntary gifts, a fence. In the year 1924 the house of prayer at Orlina-Wielka burned down. It was then rebuilt, enlarged and provided with a gallery. Scarcely was it erected when the school inspectorate of the gmina Rzgów sought to appropriate it. The congregation set itself against this. There came a protracted lawsuit, which was decided first in the supreme administrative court in favor of the evangelical parish.

 8) The author remembers still vividly that autumn day of the year 1914 on which Pastor Buse, with 3 or 4 other evangelical fellow-sufferers, sitting on a wagon, surrounded by about 15 Cossacks, drove through the author's home town of Władysławów. The wagon halted before the commune office at Russosice (in the immediate vicinity of Władysławów). Many of the curious hastened thither. "We have taken spies — said the Cossacks — and among them is also the pastor of Grodziec". The author, who was present there, approached the wagon to see the pastor and the fellow prisoners. Sad and downcast they sat there. —
kneifel1937/75:
On June 27, 1926 the congregation celebrated, after many years, again a mission festival, in which the pastors: Consistorial Councilor Loth, Friedenberg, Erich Buse, Gross and Doberstein took part.

On the basis of the bequest of January 9, 1797 the congregation possesses: 1 Morgen of land and 2 Morgen of meadow (at Stare-Grądy) for the pastor and 1 Morgen of land for the cantor. In the year 1927 the parish acquired, at Pastor Ulbrich's suggestion, a further 9.5 Morgen of land for 10,000 zlotys. This land was bought in order that the local pastor might have his own team of horses for the visiting of the congregation. In 1929 the organ was repaired and a congregational library established. On September 9, 1934 the parish received back from the gmina Szymanowice the property of the cantorate of Obory (prayer hall, schoolhouse, farm buildings and 15 Morgen of land), which in the year 1919 the "dozór szkolny" (school board) had taken over. The lawsuit instituted against this was won by the evangelical congregation. It is the third cantorate (Orlina Wielka, Obory and Gadow) that has become finally the property of the congregation of Grodziec. Concerning Białobłoty (12 Morgen) and Wojciechów (5 Morgen) like lawsuits have been instituted. For the recovery of these cantorates, as also for the development of the whole congregational system, Pastor Ulbrich acquired enduring merit.

The religious-moral state of the parish is satisfactory. Church attendance is good, Bibles and devotional books are everywhere present, family prayers are held in many households.

In the congregation there still prevail particular customs and usages. Thus, for example, the local pastor performs all burials, even those of children. The confirmation takes place here always on Maundy Thursday. On Christmas eve the children recite the Christmas gospel.

12. Konin.

The county town of Konin on the Warthe is a foundation under German law (13th century). As vogt Wilhelm is named here in 1365. In 1331 Konin was destroyed by the Knights of the Cross. During the war against the German Order of Knights King Wladislaus Jagiełło sojourned several months at Konin in 1433. In the wide environs of the town, back of Gosławice, there stretch two lakes: the Gostawicer and the Pontnower lake. Above the two bodies of water lies the village of Pontnow1). The road, which formerly separated the two lakes and formed, as it were, a bridge between them, is the so-called Bernsteinstrasse, which led from old Rome by way of Kalisch to the Baltic Sea. The movement of the Reformation in Poland sent its waves also into the Konin region. In the year 1590 (exact records only from 1630) there came about, in Żychlin 3 km from Konin, the formation of an evangelical-Reformed congregation called into being by the noble family Żychliński, which has preserved itself to the present day. The beginnings of the evangelical-Lutheran church system in the Konin district go back into the first decade of the 19th century. About this time efforts were afoot to gather all the Lutherans here into one congregation, the little town of Slesin, 20 km from Konin, having been designated as parish town. Already since 1790 Slesin, with the preaching places Butter Hol. (Maślaki), Szyszyner Hol. and Grabina, was a filial of Witkowo and was cared for by Pastor Johann Gottlieb Bothe2). In the year 1810 there was active at Slesin, without being authorized thereto, the rector and candidate of theology Radke, who held divine services in the evangelical localities and performed acts of office. In consequence Pastor Bothe petitioned the prefect of the Posen department on July 24, 1810 that he might forbid Radke all further officiating and settle the question of his own accord,

 1) This place name is often derived from the Latin word pons = bridge.

 2) Werner-Steffani, Geschichte der evangelischen Parochien in der Provinz Posen, p. 414.
kneifel1937/164:
whether "the evangelical congregation of Slesin with its environs would be in a position to maintain a church system of its own or not"3). To ascertain this was all the more necessary, since through this uncertainty the congregation was bewildered. Superintendent Ernst Wilhelm Drechsler of Rogasen warned the Evangelicals in and about Slesin, in the letter of March 31, 1810, "not to let themselves be led astray by the candidate Radke to Slesin nor to be held back from their lawful parish (Witkowo). The candidate has no authority to attach parishes and equally little authority to baptize and to marry or even to administer the sacra; since he has done this hitherto without all permission of the secular and spiritual superiors, he will be called to account therefor . . ." On August 30, 1810 there sojourned at Slesin Superintendent Ephraim Gottfried Stechebahr of Posen, who recorded in protocol that without the evangelical colonies about Slesin the maintenance of the evangelical-Lutheran preacher at Witkowo could not be met. Since Pastor Bothe of Witkowo had likewise raised objection to the establishment of the Slesin congregation, the prefect of the Posen department called upon him on March 13, 1811 to present documents or copies of them, in order to prove that the evangelical villages in the Slesin region were legally attached to the parish of Witkowo. He was unable to furnish this proof. In the same year Pastor August Bernhard Christian Drechsler came to Slesin, son of Sup. Drechsler of Rogasen4). From his period of office date the "Tauf-Buch der Sleszyner Evangelischen Parochie, angefangen den 1. April 1811" (Baptismal book of the Sleszin evangelical parish, begun April 1, 1811), and the "Todten-Kirchenbuch der Evangelischen Gemeine zu Slesin" (Death register of the evangelical congregation of Slesin), which are preserved in the Konin parish archive. As the "Tauf-Buch" reports, many Evangelicals had their churchly acts performed also in the neighboring Roman Catholic congregations of Lubstów, Kazimierz, Skulsk and Wilczyn. "The disorder — so it further reports — was very great, because the Slesin parish was not yet regulated". This never took place either.

Since Pastor Bothe, notwithstanding the calling of P. Drechsler to Slesin, continued to visit individual outlying localities, the provisional consistory U. A. C. of the Posen department instructed him to desist from this in the future. In the year 1815 Pastor Drechsler left Slesin and went to Obornik, probably moved thereto by the changed conditions of the frontier. After his departure Pastor Karl Gottfried Röhl — Pastor Bothe's successor at Witkowo — received from Walichnowski, the owner of Slesin, the permission to visit this place, as also Szyszyner-Hol. and other colonies.
