Therefore on October 20, 1815 Pastor Röhl petitioned the Grand-ducal Posen governmental commission for a frontier passport to travel, in order that "I may visit my spiritual children in the present Poland safely and unhindered as before." His request was granted. In spite of the frontier the Evangelicals in and about Slesin were regarded as belonging to Witkowo. On March 26, 1816 the church elder Gottfried Kunkel reported to Pastor Röhl that at Slesin the evangelical congregational life had died out, because Walichnowski had taken from the Evangelicals the house in which they had held worship. This circumstance, he said, compelled them to transfer the place of assembly for the evangelical population of Slesin to Szyszyner Hol.5) In 1817, however, the school and prayer house at Szyszyner Hol. burned down, so that Walichnowski saw himself constrained to the declaration that he would assist the Evangelicals in the building of a house of God at Slesin. But this never came to pass. Until 1817 Pastor Röhl visited regularly every 6 weeks the colonies Butter-Hol., Szyszyner-Hol., Grabina and Józefowo, "until at last the frontier separated them from the parish"5). The "Slesin parish," which embraced a part of the present congregation of Konin and of the filial Maślaki, was accordingly only an attempt at a permanent founding of a congregation. The attempt miscarried.

In the course of the years, especially in the Prussian period, German-evangelical officials and craftsmen immigrated into Konin6). In 1820 there were settled here: Friedrich Öhlers, Samuel Fibich, Michael Lempke, Karl Liebe, Nikolaus Wunderlich, Johann Schönweiß, Christoph Höft, August Reder, Michael Friedrich, Christian Thimm, Gottlieb Engel, Johann Gesse, Martin Petschke, F. Orive, Friedrich Schicke. In the open country about Konin German settlement activity had begun already after 1750. In 1767 there arose on the lands of the estate of Sławsk, whose owner had been Leszczyc-Zielonawski, the settlement Węglewskie Holendry (Wenglewer Hol.). At the same time the Holländereien Sławsk, Kolno and Rumin were founded. About 1775 the colony Brzezińskie Holendry (Briesener Hol.) was laid out. Many others followed these village foundations7).

The deed of purchase of this plot was entered on October 15, 1825 (No. 928) before the notary Kroszczyński at Konin, but confirmed by the authorities only in 1827.8) In the year 1824 the Evangelicals acquired the former Roman Catholic church of the Holy Ghost (17 ells long, 14 ells broad and 8 high; built of timber 1801), which at that time lay on the place before the present evangelical church. The Evangelicals of Konin were cared for religiously by Pastor Bartsch of Władysławów and by the Reformed pastor Johann Scholtz of Żychlin.

In 1826 the congregation of Konin came into being, into which the former Slesin parish passed for the most part. Its first shepherd of souls was Pastor Johann August Kegler, a native of Görlitz (according to his passport No. 83 of July 22, 1826), who was installed on July 29, 1827 by the consistorial councilor Pastor Modl of Kalisch. To him goes back the "Kirchenbuch des im Jahre des Herrn 1826 neu errichteten evangelisch-lutherischen Kirchspiels der Kreisstadt Konin, enthaltend Taufen, geführt von August Kegler, erstem Pastor" [Church book of the evangelical-Lutheran parish of the county town of Konin newly founded in the year of our Lord 1826, containing baptisms, kept by August Kegler, first pastor]. Scarcely had he undertaken the preliminary work for a better development of the congregation when death overtook him on December 27, 1830.9) He was buried in that part of the Catholic cemetery that was appointed for the deceased of evangelical confession.10)

A serious time broke in upon the congregation of Konin after the death of its first pastor. The Russian-Polish war of 1830/31, the cholera, the waning of the religious-ecclesiastical sense and other unwelcome phenomena threatened the existence of the newly founded parish. For a time the sect of the "Zaftianer," which had many adherents in the country, was of special disadvantage to the congregational life. These sectaries held for a sign of "true conversion" when "the Spirit compelled the sinner to lamentation and crying out." The sect gained ground so long as it was combated with outward means. But when, in place of these, biblical instruction and teaching entered, it dissolved.11) How grave the economic situation of the congregation was we see from the letter of July 21, 1832, which Pastor Johann Scholtz-Żychlin, who administered Konin after Pastor Kegler's death, addressed to the consistorial councilor Karl Gottlieb Bartsch-Władysławów: ". . . It would be necessary that you come again to Konin and breathe new life through your pre-

To be sure, many have now to struggle with want of sustenance. But how is the poor Keglern (the wife of Pastor Kegler is meant) in this way to come to her own?"

In the year 1837 Pastor Justus Hermann Otto Hinz, who came from Wilhelmsberg in East Prussia, became shepherd of souls at Konin. In the villages houses of prayer and cantorate schools arose, whose number constantly increased. Thus there were in 1839 — 16 and in 1866 already 21 village schools united with houses of prayer. In Konin itself the evangelical school could be opened only in 1849. The obstacles that had to be removed here seemed at first insurmountable. After Pastor Kegler's death the office of cantor and teacher at Konin lapsed. The evangelical town dwellers had to pay their school contributions to the Catholic teachers. The Kalisch voivodeship commission decreed indeed that in the school at Konin visited by evangelical and Catholic children one of the two teachers must be of evangelical confession. The carrying out of this ordinance, however, the Catholics knew how to hinder for a longer time. Then Pastor Hinz addressed a petition to the viceroy Paskiewicz, who sent a commission of investigation to Konin and thereupon brought about the opening of the evangelical school in the school building erected jointly by Catholics and Evangelicals.

In the year 1840 Pastor Hinz built the present brick parsonage. In 1843 he founded the filial Maślaki, which he visited 12 times a year. Thanks to the energetic help of the evangelical town burgher A. Schuppe, who presented to the congregation a site on the highroad Konin–Koło as a place of burial, the evangelical cemetery at Konin could be laid out in the year 1846. In 1849 the three Lutheran cantorates of Święcia, Borowo and Brzezińskie Holendry, which before had been included in the Reformed congregation of Żychlin, were attached to Konin. In the years 1853/54 the building of a new church on the site bought in 1820 was begun and completed. In the year 1859 an organ was procured for 1287 rubles and in 1872 a bell tower built. Further, steel bells (of the weight of 60 puds) were procured for 452 thalers.

On June 10, 1876 and June 4, 1880 Gen.-Sup. Bishop Everth visited the Konin parish. He was very well satisfied with the state and the direction of the church system and thanked the "worthy pastor, whom he commended to the divine assistance of grace for the further faithful conduct of his office." After 45 years of blessed service, on August 28, 1882, Pastor Justus Hermann Otto Hinz departed this life. The congregation of Konin preserved a faithful remembrance of its shepherd of souls.
kneifel1937/168:
For the vacant pastorate, administered by the pastors Edmund Schultz-Prażuchy and Kasimir Lembke-Dąbie, there applied the Reformed pastor Karl Henkel of Żychlin. The evangelical-Augsburg consistory at Warsaw refused, on grounds of confession, to confirm his candidacy. Notwithstanding this position of the consistory, the Konin church council championed Pastor Henkel all the more, as it knew that herein it represented the opinion of the congregation. And in truth, the whole congregation of Konin desired Pastor Henkel as its shepherd of souls. As local pastor of Żychlin (from 1869 to 1884) he enjoyed so good a reputation that the name "Pastor Henkel" everywhere in the Konin region stood for that of a faithful, considerate and kindly shepherd of souls. The consistory, perforce, laid aside all its misgivings, after Pastor Henkel had pledged himself to hold and to represent the confession of the church in which he wished to labor. Elected shepherd of souls of Konin on April 30, 1884, he entered upon his new pastorate already on July 27 of that year. 11 days later (on August 7) Gen.-Sup. Bishop Everth visited the parish.

Quietly, without much ado, Pastor Henkel went at the outer and inner development of the congregation. In order to serve it better, he induced the affiliated parishioners to buy land, in order that with his own team he might visit the sick and perform other journeys of office. On July 7, 1894 the congregation acquired from Karl Fibich 15 Morgen of land (10 Morgen of arable land and 5 Morgen of meadow) for 1982 rubles 50 kopecks. Further, at the instance of the local pastor, on the plot which the evangelical town burghers Paul Michel and Daniel Stark presented to the church, there was erected a house with rooms for the evangelical school, for the teacher and cantor, the sexton and the gravedigger. Soon thereafter there was built on to this house a "home for the aged for poor Evangelicals of the town of Konin," whose consecration took place on July 8, 1905. In the next year the evangelical school was then transferred into the congregational house and consecrated likewise by Pastor Henkel.

On the high holidays the house of God built in the year 1854 was much too small and in need of enlargement. With the consent of the congregation members a tower was built on to the church (laying of the foundation stone on June 26, 1901). Soon thereafter, however, it appeared that the house of God must be remodeled and also surrounded with a solid fence. The two congregational meetings (on February 9, 1902 and March 11, 1906) determined the funds for this. The costs of the remodeling of the church amounted to 8306 rubles 42 kopecks. The tower building itself cost 11,302 rubles 78 kopecks.

After the completion of these works there arose the necessity of providing for the interior fitting out and a worthy furnishing of the house of God. Therefore the local pastor held a congregational meeting on February 14, 1909, at which he reported upon the works still to be executed
kneifel1937/169:
and presented the cost estimate, which was also approved. In all the costs of the interior fitting out, the renovation and the furnishing of the church (altar, pulpit, benches and the like) amounted to 10,022 rubles 30 kopecks.12) The total costs of the tower building, the remodeling and interior fitting out, the renovation and adornment of the house of God amounted to 29,631 rubles 50 kopecks.

On May 3, 1915 Pastor Karl Henkel died of the consequences of a long throat ailment. His death was sincerely mourned both by his congregation members and by those of other faith. In the evangelical cemetery at Konin he found his last rest.

The temporary administration was assumed by Pastor Sachs of Turek and after him by the pastor Schnorr from the Reich, who laid down the pastorate in 1917 in order again to care for his home congregation of Feuchtwangen in Bavaria. He was followed by Pastor Adolf Löffler from 1917 to 1927.

To Pastor Löffler there fell the hard task of protecting the evangelical population of the country from the excesses of the local authorities. It was especially the cantorates that he had to defend. While the German-evangelical country population gave him its full confidence, the Polish-speaking Evangelicals of Konin, together with the local authorities, stood opposed to him.13) This cleavage led to unpleasantness and conditioned also Pastor Löffler's transfer to Chodecz.

After Pastor Krempin-Koło had temporarily cared for the congregation of Konin and Pastor Kreutz-Sompolno for the filial Maślaki, the consistory appointed on April 1, 1928 Pastor Robert Gustav Badke administrator (Verweser) of the parish and filial congregation. He unfolded his activity: "1. in the direction of the completion of the restoration of the church begun in Pastor Henkel's time and 2. in the direction of the work of building up the congregation by the deepening of pastoral care"14). In the year 1929 the church and the parsonage were renovated, the organ put in repair, for which about 12,000 zlotys were expended. The electric lighting plant in the church was presented by August Walter of Konin (it cost 4000 zlotys). In the parish as also in the filial Maślaki Pastor Badke instituted in the year 1928 mission festivals, gathered the confirmed youth, founded singing and brass choirs, held cantors' conferences in 1929 and 1930. kneifel1937/175:
a) Maślaki.

The lord of the manor Bogucki of Dębowiec concluded on December 9, 1779 with German-evangelical colonists a contract concerning the purchase of the colony of Maślaki (Butterholland)1). For the school he set aside 15 Morgen of land, which, however, since the founding of a school did not immediately follow, the settlers distributed among themselves. The later protracted efforts of the consistory to recover this land for the purpose named were without success. In 1799 the Evangelicals built here a schoolhouse. The school garden comprised 216 square rods, the churchyard 49 square rods. In place of the old house of prayer, which in the year 1800 fell a victim to a conflagration, the evangelical farmers erected in the following year a new wooden house of prayer — 17 ells long, 14 broad and 8 ells high2).

Maślaki was also "among the 70 villages" which held to Slesin as their religious center. The pastors of Witkowo, then of Slesin, Babiak and afterward of Konin cared for this region. But after Pastor Drechsler had left Slesin in 1815, this place lost its former local-ecclesiastical significance, and the evangelical house of prayer there was taken from the evangelical population again3). From the year 1838 efforts made themselves felt to gather the evangelical settlements about Maślaki into a filial congregation, in order thereby to give them again an ecclesiastical support. kneifel1937/176:
evangelical parish towns lying near was great. As gathering point of the filial there was now designated the little town of Kleczew. On August 21, 1840 the general consistory at Warsaw accordingly announced to the gubernial government at Kalisch that "the boundaries of the Kleczew filial must extend over all those localities which in their situation lie nearer to Kleczew than to Sompolno, Babiak, Konin, Koło, Grodziec, Pyzdry and Zagórów".

Against the choice of Kleczew as filial town Walichnowski, the owner of Slesin, turned. In a letter of the year 1840 to Pastor Hinz at Konin he reported that certain "eldest ones from the evangelical villages" had petitioned him, with reference to the resolutions of the former Prussian government, to build a church at Slesin, offering him at the same time "their help or voluntary contributions". On October 27, 1840 Walichnowski wrote to the general consistory that the establishment of the filial, "in consideration of the convenience of the colonists," would be more suitable at Slesin than at Kleczew. He declared also that he wished to present the whole building material for the building of the house of prayer. In consequence the consistory requested Sup. Modl on December 30 of that year for an opinion in the matter. Already on January 16, 1841 Sup. Modl announced to the consistory that neither Kleczew nor Slesin, but Maślaki alone, was suitable as filial town, because it possessed a numerous evangelical population and lay in the center of the evangelical colonies. In this sense the consistory also decided. On January 13, 1842 the first church council of the filial was elected, namely Peter Kitzmann, Martin Kintop, Gottlieb Kuk, Daniel Zorn and Johann Lehmann. In the same year the filial congregation of Maślaki was formed, whose number of souls at that time (according to the register of the evangelical population of January 13, 1842) amounted to 1584, divided into 305 families; of these 4 families, or 14 souls, were of the Reformed confession. The civil register office has existed here since 1843.

The school building at Maślaki, which had only one room with a chamber, "which served at the same time as dwelling room for the cantor and as room for the school youth," was in the year 1843 in a forlorn state. In 1851 it was rebuilt and enlarged. On July 2, 1850 Pastor Hinz installed as first elementary teacher of Maślaki Ludwig Fiedler, whom he "admonished in a fitting address to the zealous fulfillment of his duties and handed to him, in the presence of the congregation assembled in the little church there, the document of appointment". In 1868 the elementary school here was again transformed into a cantorate school. In the month of March 1870 the county master builder of Słupca and the lord of the manor of Kopydłowo, Julian Kitzmann, inspected the evangelical school, in order to reach a decision concerning its further use. The county master builder declared that the schoolhouse was "no longer usable on account of its age, so that a new building must be erected". In 1881
kneifel1937/177:
the new school — 28 ells long, 9.5 broad and 5 ells high — was erected "of unburned brick" at the cost of the members of the filial.

As early as 1888 the filial considered erecting a new solid church at an expenditure of 6568 rubles 17.5 kopecks. The building plan, together with the cost estimate, was submitted to the Russian authorities for confirmation. But since this project was not approved by the authorities, the filial congregation was compelled to repair and enclose the old defective house of prayer, to lay a cement floor within, and even to put a wooden tower on the "church," as the plain house of prayer is here designated. Nevertheless the house of prayer remained much too small and cramped, so that the building of a new church was here felt to be the most pressing task. Pastor Henkel of Konin indeed supported the plan of the church building, but wished at first that the house of God should be built "not at Maślaki on the border of the filial, but in the market town of Kleczew, which forms the center of the filial congregation"4). In the meantime years went by. When Gen.-Sup. Bursche visited Maślaki in 1908, he emphasized the indispensable necessity of the church building. The members of the filial were in principle agreed with this. What divided them into two parties was the opposed conception concerning the place of building of the new house of God. While some advocated Maślaki, the others desired that the new church be erected at Kleczew. The filial assembly of June 29, 1910 indeed voted 15,000 rubles for the building, which were to be paid in three annual installments, yet the differences of opinion continued with unabated sharpness. The consistory definitively appointed Maślaki as the place of building, whereupon on April 10, 1913 the ministry of the interior granted the permission for the church building at Maślaki for the sum of 17,392 rubles 41 kopecks. The disunity in the filial, as also the outbreak of the World War in 1914, hindered the execution of this work. To the present day the question of the church building has unhappily not been settled here.

On April 29, 1912 the cantor Christoph Möller died, who had served the cantorate of Bolesławowo uninterruptedly for 58 years. "For 58 years he has proclaimed to us and to our forefathers the precious Word of God, taught the youth and called back to God many a hardened heart. His sermon readings and his singing penetrated into all hearts, and Möller was often envied by his colleagues because of his voice and his gift"5). On September 22, 1904 he was privileged to celebrate his 50-year jubilee as cantor.

 4) Church chronicle of the evangelical-Augsburg congregation of Konin.

 5) Johann Schmaltz, Nachruf — Kantor Christoph Möller †. Unsere Kirche, Jahrg. 1912, pp. 173/4.
kneifel1937/178:
In the year 1918 the farmer Emil Kaschube of Neu-Kopydłowo was appointed to the Polish council of state as representative of the German colonists.

In the time of the administration of Pastor Löffler-Konin there was built at Maślaki in 1921 the congregational house (chancellery, confirmands' hall, 3 rooms and kitchen for the cantor). The building site was bought from Wilhelm Hein. In the same year the house of prayer at Brzozogaj (Birkenholland) was set on fire by the hand of villainy. Since the members of the cantorate were left without religious care, the churchly life suffered greatly thereby. In the year 1926 the cantorate built, thanks to the direction of Pastor Adolf Löffler and the help of the church elder Ludwig Martin, a new house of prayer (prayer hall, school room and cantor's dwelling). In November 1926 Pastor Löffler consecrated it. In 1930 the brass choir at Brzozogaj was founded, in 1934 the youth league. The religious-ecclesiastical life here received a gratifying impulse through the appointment of the cantor Erwin Benoist, who has come out of the work of helper and youth leader at the Lodz congregation of St. Trinity. "In devotions, Bible hours, house assemblies, youth and children's hours the Word of God is proclaimed for the awakening and deepening of the religious life"6). From November 10 to 13, 1929 there took place at Brzozogaj, under the direction of Pastor Badke-Konin, the first cantors' conference in the filial.

On Ascension Day of the next year Gen.-Sup. Dr. Bursche visited Maślaki and on this occasion inducted into their office the newly elected filial elders. In place of the organ, become unusable, the filial congregation procured a new organ harmonium, which was consecrated on July 31, 1932; in 1935 the premises of the congregational house were fenced in; further, the cemetery here is to be enlarged.

In the course of the year 1934 the lawsuit between the cantorate of Genowefa and the gmina Sławoszewek came to its conclusion. In 1921 the gmina named expropriated from the cantorate congregation of Genowefa the schoolhouse with three Morgen of land. In spite of all the efforts of the evangelical population, which even produced the deed of purchase found in the evangelical chancellery at Konin, nothing could at first be attained. In 1932 the cantorate again entered upon the path of litigation. The Kalisch district court decided in favor of the congregation of Genowefa, awarding to it the expropriated property as well as 1500 zlotys compensation. The gmina thereupon turned to the Posen court of appeal, yet without success. House and land Genowefa took again into possession; on the other hand the gmina long refused to pay the compensation. The school class is housed further in the canto-

kneifel1937/248:
17. Zagórów.

In the year 1145 the German Cistercian monks founded the monastery Ląd on the Warthe (Lond, Lande). The first 25 abbots were of German origin1). Only with the year 1553 did the German monastery pass into Polish direction. The first Polish abbot was Jan Wysocki. After his entry upon office the German monks fled with the records of the monastery of Ląd to the monastery Heinrichau in Silesia.

To the colonizing activity of the monastery there go back, among others, the foundations of the towns: Lądek (Landeck) 1269, Pyzdry (Peisern) 1257, Zagórów 1445. In order to connect the last-named town with the nearby monastery, a dam 4 km long was thrown up.

The immigration of German-evangelical colonists into the Zagórów region can be documented from the year 1746. At that time Paul von Kolno-Prusiński, owner of the estate of Trąbczyn, concluded with German peasants a hereditary lease contract, by virtue of which he left to them for clearing woodland on which they founded the village of Łazińsk. It is the oldest settlement in the commune and at present also the largest cantorate, with over 150 evangelical farmers. In Łazińsk itself there are 115 of them, besides 15 farmers of the Huta Trąbczyńska, 10 from Trąbczyn B, 5 from Trąbczyn C and about 12 farmers from Trąbczyn D. The present school at Łazińsk was built in 1838/39, the bricks being replaced by the so-called "Sumpferz" or "Wiesenerz" (bog ore or meadow ore), a building material of importance in this region.

 1) Albert Breyer. Das Kloster Lond (Unterhaltungsblatt zur "Freien Presse", Jahrg. 1931 Nr. 16). The names of the abbots were: 1. Henricus Butgen 1145, 2. Henricus Buscraff, 3. Theodoricus, 4. Tyllmann, 5. Conradus, 6. Bertholdus 1213, 7. Christianus, 8. Joannes, 9. Philippus, 10. Giselbertus, 11. Jacobus, 12. Gierardus 1313, 13. Engelbertus, 14. Mathias 1325, 15. Gierardus 1399, 16. Bernardus 1417, 17. Henricus Roilen 1418, 18. Hermanus, 19. Sigfridus 1429, 20. Joannes 1433, 21. Joannes Fulich 1437, 22. Mathias 1445, 23. Ludovicus 1463, 24. Cornelius 1483, 25. Henricus 1553.
kneifel1937/249:
The school and prayer house were endowed with 18 Morgen of arable land and 2 Morgen of meadow, the cemetery with 2 Morgen 180 square rods of woodland.

Further foundations here are: Friedrichsfelde (Tarszewo), Adelshof (Chruściki), Emilienheim (Michalinów gmina Oleśnica), Sophiental (Olchowo), Ludwigslust (Mały Las), Ingelfingen (Anielewo), Augustinenhof (Augustynów). In the South Prussian period evangelical clothmakers also settled at Zagórów. The immigrants came from Silesia and the Posen land.

Until 1817 the pastors of Wreschen visited the Evangelicals in and about Zagórów, then those of the neighboring congregations of Grodziec, Konin and Żychlin (Reformed). In the year 1829 efforts made themselves felt to found an evangelical-Lutheran parish in the Zagórów region and to call a preacher. Karl Gottlieb Weigel, the lord of the manor of Kopojno, intended at that time to build on his possessions an evangelical church as well as the other needed buildings and to grant "for the clergyman to be appointed there an yearly quantum of 40 quarters of rye, 10 quarters of barley and 25 quarters of oats, as well as later additionally 6 barrels of beer . . ." The protocol taken on the manor farm at Kopojno on December 7, 1829, as also Weigel's two declarations of November 15, 1833 and July 8, 1834, made the expectation of the impending founding of a congregation appear justified, for which the Evangelicals from the Zagórów environs pleaded as warmly. On March 22, 1836 Weigel wrote, among other things, to Sup. Modl at Kalisch: ". . . Long since, and truly from purely Christian intentions, for the furtherance of religion and morality among the numerous evangelical colonists of my estates and their neighborhood . ., it was my most earnest wish, . . . to see the building of an evangelical church upon my territory really brought to fulfillment. The unhappy events in Poland have also held up this undertaking . . .

Weigel's death († 1836 at Breslau) worked out unfavorably in this, that his son and heir (Alexander Weigel) was finally unwilling to make any endowments whatever for the congregation to be founded. Nevertheless the matter did not rest. Still in 1836 men were elected into the "congregational board" (provisional church council): Matthäus Luther, Ludwig Sperling, Johann Kelsch, Johann Gottlieb Kittel, Karl Heit. These petitioned Sup. Modl to assist them in the church building at Zagórów and in the establishment of the parish. Sup. Modl let them know that he would energetically support their endeavors with the competent ecclesiastical and secular authorities. From the petition of the congregational board it appears that now the town of Zagórów was chosen as parish seat.

According to the "Project of the establishment of the evangelical congregation at Zagórów" transmitted in 1836 to the Konin district commissioner
kneifel1937/250:
the Protestant population here numbered 2937 souls. The fund for the church building and the parish buildings amounted to 1727 zlotys. For the maintenance of the pastor there were appointed: 253 zlotys 28 groschen, 40 quarters of rye, 25 quarters of oats, 10 quarters of barley and 6 barrels of beer.

Meanwhile the choice of Zagórów as parish seat did not meet with the undivided approval of the evangelical country population. Thus on February 9, 1837 "in the name of the Evangelicals of Lissewo" Christian Wolf, Gottlieb Weber and Christian Kannwischer declared that they did not intend to take part in the building of the church at Zagórów, since they had a school (that is, also a house of prayer), "which the king has built for us," and were content with the administration of Grodziec. The same they repeated on July 28, 1840. There joined themselves to them the Evangelicals of Adelshof (Chruściki), who wrote on February 10, 1837 that they did not wish to take part in the church building, the more so as they "still have their dear evangelical preacher at Grójec (Grodziec)". Further, on February 9, 1837, in the name of the "Alt-Tomnitzer Hauländer," Martin Kannwischer, Gottfried Schnitzer and Gottfried Schultz announced that they had resolved not to attach themselves to the church at Zagórów. Likewise the Evangelicals of Peisern (Pyzdry) and the environs declared, at the meeting in the town hall there on June 21, 1838, that for the reason following they did not wish to be attached to Zagórów, because they wished to found a separate evangelical-Lutheran congregation at Peisern. Likewise the "Ciemierower Hauländer" refused to be attached to Zagórów (declaration of July 28, 1840). It was chiefly localities of the present filial of Lissewo-Pyzdry that stood opposed, for local and economic reasons, to the congregational organization to be created at Zagórów.

In the letter to Sup. Modl of August 30, 1839 the Warsaw general consistory gave expression to its opinion that "in consequence of insufficient means an evangelical congregation in the Zagórów region cannot at present be founded". Although the circumstances compelled abstention from an independent parochial foundation at Zagórów, yet the Evangelicals resolved, at the meeting of July 29, 1840, to establish first a filial at Zagórów and to elect the first church council. Into the church board there were elected: Matthäus Luther, Johann Abramowski, Johann Friedrich Rasch, Johann Eichhorst, Ludwig Neumann and Gottlieb Schnitzer. On January 24, 1841 Pastor Scholtz-Żychlin offered, in his letter to Sup. Modl, to care for the Zagórów Evangelicals, whom he had already visited for 5 years before. Therefore Sup. Modl proposed to the general consistory that Pastor Scholtz be entrusted with the visiting and further development of the filial. The general consistory, however, entrusted on June 28 of this year Pastor Orive of Grodziec with the administration of Zagórów.
kneifel1937/251:
The register of the villages to be included in the filial, prepared on July 31, 1841 by the burgomaster of the town of Zagórów, which showed a number of 3924 souls, was confirmed on October 29, 1842 by the governmental commission for internal, spiritual affairs and public instruction. The high number of souls of the settlers dwelling round about induced the general consistory to call Sup. Modl's attention to the fact that at Zagórów in reality not a filial but a parish congregation ought to be organized. Yet the filial should exist only so long, "until the congregation can show sufficient means for the erection of a parish".

The filial had at first no house of prayer, so that the divine services were held in a rented hall. This displeased a number of villages which already had houses of prayer of their own and therefore stood in a better position than Zagórów. On November 23, 1845 Łazińsk, Michalinów (gm. Trąbczyn), Stara Huta, Emilienheim (Michalinów gm. Oleśnica) petitioned to remove the filial seat from Zagórów to Łazińsk. They grounded this on the fact that at Łazińsk there was a brick house of prayer which "could accommodate over 300 persons". In the month of January 1846 the Evangelicals of Anielewo expressed their readiness to attach themselves to Łazińsk, in case the filial should be transferred thither. Of importance also was the declaration of the owner of Trąbczyn, Michalina Miączyńska, who informed Sup. Modl on February 10, 1846 that she would be inclined to give grain and firewood "in proportion to the size of the congregation," if Łazińsk had a church and a pastor. In consequence Sup. Modl came to Łazińsk on July 6, 1846 and established, after careful examination of the situation, that the evangelical colonists there desired to have the center of the filial and in that case would be ready to rebuild the house of prayer at Łazińsk. Sup. Modl indeed supported their efforts, yet the general consistory did not concur in his opinion, because the Evangelicals of Koszuty, Młodojewo and Kossewo had raised objection to the transfer of the filial from Zagórów to Łazińsk.

In the year 1850 the filial bought a half-timbered house in Zagórów at the Koninerstr. No. 54, one half of which was used as prayer hall, the other as school room and cantor's dwelling. Only until Christmas 1856 was Zagórów a filial of Grodziec, whose shepherd of souls Karl Friedrich Orive administered the new congregation uninterruptedly. From Christmas 1856 Pastor Wilhelm Winkler officiated as first local pastor of the parish, now become independent.

In 1857 the congregation acquired in Zagórów at the Koninerstr. No. 51 and 52 two little houses, of which the one served as parsonage, the other as kitchen of the parsonage. In 1859 the parsonage was correspondingly fitted up.
kneifel1937/252:
The raising of Zagórów to a parish congregation did not, however, please the lord of the manor Weigel of Kopojno. Therefore he caused, through his plenipotentiary Wilhelm Jaenike, on January 10, 1858, the protocolary declaration to be given that he was ready to present 12 Morgen of parsonage land and bricks for the church building, if the center of the congregation were removed from Zagórów to Emilienheim (Michalinów Kopoiński). On February 28, 1862 the Warsaw consistory decided that, in consideration of the local situation and the conditions of traffic, only Zagórów could come into question as parish seat, and that here also the church must be built. Although the Evangelicals of Trąbczyn directed to the consistory on September 26, 1862 the petition to determine Emilienheim as the parish center, yet this had no practical consequences.

In 1860 Pastor Winkler left the congregation, after heavy dissensions with the church council, which rested upon unsachlichen accusations; into his service there now entered Pastor Eugen Biedermann. "The parish was small, the salary of the pastor very small, and the little house appointed for him as dwelling was so low that the threshold had to be taken up in order to carry into it (at the entry of the pastor) a wardrobe. Besides, the dwelling was cold and damp, which drew after it a grave illness of his wife, and this moved the young pastor in the year 1865 to removal to Pułtusk"2). Pastor Biedermann was indeed concerned to erect a church at Zagórów, toward which he also took the first steps, but soon there broke out in the congregation disputes concerning the place of building, which he was unable to compose. This also influenced his resolve to leave the parish. After his departure Zagórów was administered for a decade by Pastor Haeßner of Stawiszyn. In the year 1876 Pastor Karl Eduard Erdmann came here, who however after only two years assumed the neighboring pastorate of Grodziec, from which he continued to administer his former congregation.

Since the Zagórów prayer hall had room for only about 80 persons and was so low "that the pastor, standing before the altar, reached with his head to the beams," the building of a church was felt as the most pressing concern of the parish. Already in 1863 the consistory turned to Count Taczanowski, the owner of the estates and of the town of Zagórów, with the request to grant an assistance for the church building and for the maintenance of the pastor. Of significance, however, was first the congregational meeting of July 27, 1872, which passed the resolution for the church building. From that time this question took a slow but steady development. On April 8, 1877 the ministry of the interior approved the building and granted for this purpose 3000 rubles.

 2) "Zwiastun Ewangeliczny", Jahrg. 1912, p. 49. Cf. also Unsere Kirche, Jahrg. 1907, p. 213.
kneifel1937/253:
On August 22, 1877 Pastor Teichmann, superintendent of the Kalisch diocese, visited Zagórów. In the visitation protocol he noted that the parish possessed only 1 elementary school with 60 children at Michalinów and 7 cantorate schools with approximately 230 pupils. He mentioned also that in the congregation the Neu-Strelitz catechism was to be introduced. Of the parish buildings, which Sup. Teichmann inspected, he let himself say only that they were in an unwelcome state.

The foundation stone of the building of the evangelical church at Zagórów was laid on May 8, 1878 by the local pastor Karl Eduard Erdmann. For the building the congregation members were to raise within 4 years a sum of 8000 rubles, while 3000 rubles, as already mentioned, were granted by the government. Members of the building committee were: Alexander Arndt, Wilhelm Schmechel, Wilhelm Münch, Wilhelm Kuck, Martin Ziegeldorf and Emanuel Munk; of the church council (elected on July 5, 1882): Christian Schultz, Karl Pfeifer, Heinrich Zelmer, Alexander Arndt and Johann Schütz. The technical supervision of the building was in the hands of the county building inspector Przanowski of Słupca. All the work at the building was undertaken by the master mason Gustav Jursch of Orlina Wielka for the fee of 3000 rubles. The town of Zagórów presented for the church building 110 trunks of building timber from the town forest. The building of the house of God cost 13,131 rubles 78 kopecks. In the late autumn of 1882 the church was already erected. On July 1, 1883 the church council ordered of the firm Schlag und Söhne in Schweidnitz an organ. The congregational meeting of June 29, 1884 resolved also to tax itself 25 kopecks per Morgen for the purchase of two bells. The consecration of the new church took place, according to oral tradition (the records report nothing more definite concerning it), on the first Advent Sunday 1882. In the beginning of October 1883 there took place the protocolary handing over of the church to the congregation.

Until his death († 1892) Pastor Karl Eduard Erdmann-Grodziec cared for the Zagórów congregation, which, mindful of his merits for the parish (the building of the church), honored his memory by the placing of a corresponding marble tablet in the house of God.

The administration of Zagórów the consistory then entrusted to Pastor Henkel of Konin, whereupon from the middle of July 1898 until the beginning of November 1903 Pastor Bernhard Erdmann, formerly vicar at Zgierz, labored here as settled shepherd of souls.

In the year 1890 the sheet-metal roof of the church and of the tower was torn off by the storm wind. The church council expended 760 rubles for the new roofing. Since the parsonage was too small and also otherwise did not answer the needs, the congregational meeting of October 3, 1893 resolved to buy from the married couple Ulatowski, for 2600 rubles, a house which lay opposite the church, as
kneifel1937/254:
parsonage. On January 18, 1896 the supreme permission for this was granted. In 1898 the house of prayer at Michalinów burned down. In the same year it was resolved to build a new house of prayer at Chruściki (repaired 1918).

For a long time the church council had carried the thought of erecting a new cantor's house, the more so as the old one no longer answered its purpose. In consequence it petitioned the consistory on October 15, 1902 to permit it to sell the old cantor's house. The parochial assembly of December 13, 1907 therefore resolved to erect at Zagórów a new cantor's house and at the same time also a new parsonage beside the church. Pastor Buse of Grodziec, the then administrator of Zagórów, succeeded in convincing the congregation that through the building of the parsonage it would again have the possibility of obtaining a shepherd of souls of its own. According to the estimate of the year 1908 the building of the parsonage was to cost 7972 rubles 75 kopecks, that of the cantor's house (school room, dwellings for cantor and sexton) 6596 rubles 5 kopecks. The ministry of the interior confirmed on September 26, 1912 the plans and cost estimates. On March 7, 1913 the congregational meeting resolved, for the purpose of enlarging the building site for the parsonage, to buy from Johann Milner a small plot of land for 311 rubles. The parsonage (opposite the church), unsuitable because of its dampness, was sold in 1913 to the congregation member August Driesner for 3000 rubles. On October 16, 1913 the foundation stone of the parsonage building was laid. For this building the affiliated parishioners pledged themselves to pay a contribution of 1 ruble per Morgen, in all about 6000 rubles, besides 1000 rubles from the building fund; the remainder was to be covered by voluntary sacrifices. In the same year the erection of the cantor's and school house was begun. The building committee comprised: August Driesner, Wilhelm Neumann, Paul Rentz, Ferdinand Schulz, Friedrich Schütz, Christian Münch, August Kintzel, Julius Schneider, August Giebel, Daniel Gliege, Eduard Kuhn and Heinrich Kinast. In 1914 the World War broke out, which abruptly interrupted the works already begun. Only in 1916 could the cantor's house be continued and in 1917 completed. On June 4, 1917 the congregation bought yet from Milner two plots lying between the evangelical church and the cantor's house.

In the year 1923 Pastor Alexander Groß entered upon the pastorate of Zagórów. In place of the bell requisitioned in 1918 by the German occupation authorities a new bell was procured in 1923. In the years 1926/27 the remodeling of the organ was accomplished at an expenditure of 6000 zlotys (in 1910 the organ was repaired). In 1927 there was erected on the parsonage premises a farm building. In 1927 the married couple Ferdinand and Luise Krüger of Olchowo presented, in memory of their son Rudolf Krüger, missing in the Polish-Bolshevist war (1920), the present tower clock, which cost 5000 zlotys
kneifel1937/255:
with its works. From September 1 to 11, 1927 Pastor Groß, to whom the religious work lies very near his heart, held in the Zagórów congregation as also in the filial of Lissewo-Pyzdry an evangelization week, in which, besides Pastor Groß, the pastors Löffler-Gąbin, Paul Otto — Christian Community Lodz, and the preacher Mark of Leonberg (Lwówek) near Gąbin labored.

In the year 1931 the building of the parsonage was taken up again. At the end of 1934 the shell of the building, including the roofing, was finished. It is presumed that it will be completed in 1937. The whole building costs of the parsonage will probably amount to 35–40,000 zlotys. In October 1933 the congregation celebrated the 50-year jubilee of the consecration of the church.

In 1934 the congregation (together with the filial of Lissewo-Pyzdry) entered upon the path of litigation concerning the legal award of the cantorate land and of the buildings standing upon it at Łazińsk (20 Morgen), Ciemierów (13 Morgen) and Wrąbczynkowska Kolonia (10 Morgen). The two last-named villages lie in the filial of Lissewo-Pyzdry. The lawsuit concerning Ciemierów the congregation won, while the judicial decision in the two other lawsuits is still awaited.

The parish of Zagórów, which counts 3500 souls, is an avowed colonist congregation. The affiliated parishioners live for the most part close together; those dwelling farthest have 10 km to the parish church.

The parish was visited: on August 10, 1884 by Bishop Everth, on May 10, 1903 by Gen.-Sup. G. Manitius, on May 23, 1909 and on July 6 and 7, 1925 by Gen.-Sup. Bursche.

kneifel1937/259:
a) The filial of Lissewo-Pyzdry.

The town of Pyzdry (Peisern), which arose in 1257, is a foundation of the Cistercian monastery of Ląd on the Warthe. In the 14th century (about 1370) it belonged to the six towns whose elected councils "formed the highest municipal court for the province of Great Poland, without appeal to Halle and Magdeburg"1). According to the "inspection" of the year 1564 there were here alone 182 tax-paying craftsmen and "33 butchers". In the years 1790/94 Peisern counted over 3000 inhabitants.

Evangelical life in Peisern and its environs is demonstrable only from the Prussian period. For the German population numerously represented here it was intended to organize a congregation, for which on June 6, 1806, 100 Reichsthaler were appointed. Since 1798 there existed at Peisern an evangelical burgher and garrison school in a rented house. The teacher received 60 thalers salary for the instruction of the garrison children from the Royal war treasury and 10 thalers school money from the burgher children. The school was visited by 34 pupils2). The Prussian authorities also concerned themselves with the erection of schools in the country. Thus on September 3, 1799 the intendant Kolbe "of the intendancy of Peysern at Ciążyń" made proposals concerning the erection of new rural schools at Ostrowite (Ostrowska Kolonia), Wola Łaszczowa, Młodojewo, Lissewo, Kąty, Ciążyń, Gozdowo and Rataj. "The timber for it — he wrote — can be granted free. The inhabitants would . . . find themselves very ready, not only to accomplish the hauling of the timber," but also "to procure from their own means the materials, such as stones, lime and straw, for the roofing." At Lissewo a school and prayer house was in fact built, to which the colonists appealed again and again in the following decades. In 1797 there existed already also at Wierzchy a

 1) Michał Baliński i Tymoteusz Lipiński, Starożytna Polska pod względem historycznym, geograficznym i statystycznym, vol. 1, pp. 149/150

 2) State Archive Posen. SPZ, Generalia III B (Acta von Einrichtung der Stadtschulen behufs Erziehung des Bürgers) [Records concerning the establishment of town schools for the education of the burgher].
kneifel1937/260:
school. After the abolition of the Prussian rule the garrison and burgher school at Peisern came to an end. Equally there could no more be talk of a "church system to be established at Peysern".

In the year 1809 the evangelical population of Peisern exerted itself for the taking into possession of the Roman Catholic hospital church (church of the Holy Ghost) there, in part burned down in 1807. For decades it held to this plan without, however, attaining its goal. On February 16, 1844 even the Roman Catholic town dwellers Josef Laskowski, Wincenty Basiński, Kazper Borysiewicz, Martin Powalski, Anton Jumrich, Karl Jumrich, Josef Jankowski, Jakob Nowiński, Anton Kruszyński, Wojciech Gieryn, Josef Maytler, Johann Lesinski (and some twenty others) turned to the governmental commission with the request to hand over to the Evangelicals of Peisern the church named for their use. The commission refused this, with the hint that the Evangelicals could acquire the church standing empty only by purchase. To this, however, the evangelical population here was not in a position. Therefore it also let fall the thought of taking possession of the Catholic church without payment, the more so as the Kalisch voivodeship commission required that "the evangelical congregation must first show the presence of sufficient funds for the maintenance of the pastor and of the church servants". For many years no evangelical services took place at Peisern, because there was no suitable room. The Evangelicals here went to Wreschen for divine services or "to a Hauländer prayer house 1.5 miles away" (Lissewo). At the request of the "elders of Peysern," Andrae and Farner, Pastor Samuel Gottlieb Schröck of Wreschen came again and again to Peisern, where he held divine services in a rented hall. A school also was established here. In 1814 the school room burned down, and the school thereupon came to an end. Only "the service we continue in the suburb and meet the costs from our own midst"3).

After the Congress of Vienna the region of Peisern fell to Russia, whereby the parish of Wreschen lost a number of evangelical colonies4). Nevertheless Pastor Schröck cared for the Evangelicals in and about Peisern until his death († November 15, 1818). After him Pastor Stegmann of Grodziec cared for the fellow believers here.

The very difficult ecclesiastical conditions required here a stricter gathering of the scattered evangelical local-

 3) From the letter of the elders Andrae and Farner of October 16, 1819 to the Warsaw consistory.

 4) Werner-Steffani, Geschichte der evangelischen Parochien in der Provinz Posen, pp. 422 and 423.
kneifel1937/261:
ities. It was necessary on the one hand to form a center for the surrounding villages, on the other to soften, if not to remove, the opposition between Peisern and the diverging cantorates. On March 4, 1841 Sup. Modl reported to the gubernial administration that Pastor Orive of Grodziec had received the commission to call into being a filial congregation at Peisern. Pastor Orive communicated this in his turn also to the general consistory on June 12 of this year. In 1842 the filial also was founded. But with this the cantorates were not in agreement. When on April 15, 1841 the first church council was elected for the filial congregation in process of formation (Daniel Bräunig, Wilhelm Knoll, Friedrich Blum and Jakob Ephraim), then "the rural congregations did not wish to take part in the election, because they possessed houses of prayer of their own and therefore wished to belong to no church system". On June 26 of this year Wierzchy and Śnietnia petitioned to be incorporated in the parish of Grodziec. They grounded this on the fact that their distance from Grodziec was the same; besides, "the way to Peisern led through forests, . . . the Warthe too, at Peisern, overflows in very wide compass, which hinders all traffic".

In 1843 Pastor Orive wrote to Sup. Modl concerning the decided refusal of the cantorates to take part even in the divine services at the filial seat, the colonists of Lissewo being especially opposed. Thus they even forbade their cantorate teacher Christian Wilhelm Friedrich, on pain of removal from the colony, to attend the divine services held by Pastor Orive at Peisern. The owner of the estates of Ciemierów, Nepomucen Gliszczyński, had the teacher Friedrich come to him repeatedly and declared to him in the presence of the colonists that "if he (Friedrich) should presume to go to Peisern, then he would be removed from his post by the wojt". Gliszczyński intervened in this dispute because he was economically interested also in the closing of the filial at Peisern and its removal to Ciemierów or Lissewo. Enraged by the conduct of Gliszczyński and of the colonists, Pastor Orive proposed to Sup. Modl that the house of prayer at Lissewo be sealed and the cantor there transferred. Sup. Modl did not accede to this rigorous demand. But since the disputes between Peisern and the cantorates did not cease, Sup. Modl visited Peisern on June 18, 1845, in order to learn the conditions on the spot. Sup. Modl established (according to the visitation protocol) the difficult situation of the filial. Thus the Evangelicals at Peisern had a rented hall, in which every 4th Sunday divine services took place, but no teacher and cantor. Of this the filial elders complained to the superintendent, to whom they made known that through the insufficient religious care "many Evangelicals have already gone over to the Catholic church
kneifel1937/262:
and others there have their children baptized"5). Therefore they petitioned him for a teacher and cantor, for "otherwise in the end most of the Evangelicals (at Peisern) would go over to the Catholic church". Still in the same year (1845) the Evangelicals of Lissewo and Ciemierów came forward with the request to make Lissewo, where a house of prayer for approximately 100 persons was present, the center of the filial. Likewise in 1845 the colonists of Wierzchy desired the transfer of the seat of the filial to their village. Taking account of all these wishes and endeavors, Sup. Modl reported to the consistory on February 6, 1850 that, in case of the transfer of the filial from Peisern to Lissewo, the localities Piotrowo, Koszuty and Młodojewo could under no circumstances belong thither, because the distance was far too great. Besides, through this change the evangelical population of Peisern would be exposed to the danger of a stronger Catholization. Accordingly the consistory left the filial further at Peisern, which in turn called forth a counteraction on the part of the discontented cantorates. On February 7, 1851 the cemetery boards of Lissewo, Wierzchy, Ciemierów and Koszelewska Łąka petitioned the consistory to abolish the filial of Peisern and to establish the congregation of Zagórów. The consistory refused the dissolution of the filial, which since then bears the designation "Lissewo-Pyzdry"6).

In the year 1850 it was intended to erect a wooden church at Peisern, for which the former burgomaster Strużewski (later city president of Kalisch) promised to give a site and timber from the town forest. His successor, however (burgomaster Szydłowski), did not show himself well disposed toward the Evangelicals, so that the church building did not come about. In consequence the Peisern Evangelicals had also further to hold their divine services in rented halls (1847 in the "first side street at the market"; the room here was "12 ells long and 15 broad," and "in it there were 10 benches, each seating 10 persons"; in 1860 rented from Karl Balk; in 1864 from Jastrzębski). Only in 1909 did the Evangelicals of Peisern receive the supreme permission to buy a house destined for purposes of worship (from the married couple Kuske for 1500 rubles) at the Neuer Markt No. 101. In this house are the prayer hall and the cantor's dwelling.

The religious-ecclesiastical care of the filial took place from Zagórów, and when that congregation was vacant, the pastors

kneifel1937/263:
of Grodziec, Konin or also Stawiszyn cared for Peisern. Pastor Eugen Biedermann of Zagórów visited in the year 1864 Peisern 4 times a year, Lissewo 3 times, Ciemierów 3 times, Wierzchy 2 times and Wrąbczynkowska Kolonia 1 time. During the administration of the filial congregation by Pastor Haeßner of Stawiszyn, the filial members desired that Pastor Julius Binner of Miłosław (province of Posen) should represent the administrator in case of sudden illness. The Warsaw consistory, to which Pastor Haeßner turned in this matter, declared itself on July 20, 1873 in agreement with this representation.

The house of prayer at Wierzchy, which lies on the evangelical cemetery there, dates from the year 1803. In spite of the many renovations it is very dilapidated. Already in 1906 there was the intention here to build a new house of prayer. The building site was to be bought from the married couple Martin and Auguste Schwartz. Even the supreme permission for the building of the house of prayer was granted. Nevertheless no hand was laid to the work.

Before the World War of 1914/18 the religious life in the filial was very weakly developed. Much contributed to this the circumstance that the Evangelicals here dwelt for the most part near the former German-Russian frontier, whereby many fell into temptation to occupy themselves with frontier smuggling. Money easily earned in dishonest ways led many to drunkenness and other vices. After the shifting of the frontier a certain improvement in religious-moral respect has set in.

The cantor's dwelling at Peisern was for many years officially under seizure. The filial members thereupon, with the help of the consistory, instituted a lawsuit, which they also won. They thereupon renovated prayer hall and dwelling and called to be their cantor Gustav Adam, who is also teacher in the general elementary school with 7 classes at Peisern.

The Evangelicals of Ostrowska Kolonia, belonging to the cantorate of Wierzchy, are attached to the congregation of Grodziec, where they also pay their church contribution and enter all acts of the civil register.

The cantorate members of Wrąbczynek, a part of the cantorate congregation of Wrąbczynkowska Kolonia, have been included in the parish of Zagórów.

The filial of Lissewo-Pyzdry has no civil register office and therefore also no filial cantors. Concerning the place where the civil registers are to be kept, the filial members can still come to no agreement. If the Evangelicals of Peisern wish that the civil register office should be there, then in turn the fellow believers of the country demand that Ciemierów be determined as the place of the civil register office, because here
kneifel1937/264:
allegedly lies the center of the filial. In consequence of these differences of opinion, which since the founding of the filial congregation have shown themselves in various ways and last to the present day, the records of Lissewo-Pyzdry and those of the congregation of Zagórów are kept jointly. Every cantorate has, as also Peisern itself, its own cantor, whom it also pays.

The pastor of Zagórów visits the filial 12 times a year. The church contribution the filial members pay to the pastor of Zagórów, because no special filial budget is in existence.

III. The flowering of new evangelical life

in the 17th and 18th centuries

1. The rural colonization

To the German colonization movements in the East, beginning with the medieval period of early and high settlement, there followed, as the next, that of the modern age (1550—-1800). Under Sigismund August it set in and reached its high point under King Wladyslaw IV. The causes that triggered this eastward settlement were of a religious, economic and social kind. Difficult, for example, was the situation of the Evangelicals in Schlesien, where they could get no joy of their faith. Not less did the 30 Years War (1618—1648) lay waste wide areas of the German Reich, while Poland remained almost untouched by it. Under the protection of Polish nobles, who were often themselves Protestants, one hoped to be able to found a new existence and to live in the evangelical faith unchallenged. And so there poured from Schlesien, Pommern, Brandenburg, from the Neumark and from other areas a stream of immigrants into Westpreußen and into the adjoining Posener Land, where new cities and villages were founded and the old places were enlarged and peopled by influx. With this colony there stood on a small island of the Weichsel the ruins of the old knights' castle Beberen (Bobrowniki). In the year 1630 there arose, through the initiative of the Starost of Bobrowniki A. Tulibowski, the lowland village Neu-Bögpomöz. In 1625 the colony Lentzen was founded, then around 1650 Woluszewo. Up the Weichsel as far as Warschau the German peasants pressed forward. Thus in the year 1629 several families settled on the so-called Sächsische Kämpe on 136 Morgen. The everyday language of the Weichsel peasants was Low German. Beside agriculture they pursued fruit-growing (plums) and in part fishing. For centuries they had to struggle with high water and inundations. As to their origin, the German colonists who immigrated into Mittelpolen in the first half of the 17th century came from the colonies already „established" in the previous century around Thorn, Graudenz, Schwetz, Kulm, Bromberg, Dirschau and from the Danziger Great and Small Werder. If the German rural settlement movement in the 17th century was restricted exclusively to the Weichsel lowland, it extended in the following century over all areas of Mittelpolen

After 1725 the German colonization set in again in increased measure. The old villages in the Weichsel lowland created new daughter colonies right and left of the river. In 1731 there arose on the lands of the lord of the manor I. Milewski Osieker Lengden. The founder of Rajszewo in the year 1775 was Archbishop Prince Poniatowski. To him the villages Wiesendorf and Skierdy near the town of Neuhof (Nowydwör) also owe their origin in 1782. The Mennonite settlement Kazun the brothers Husen laid out in 1776. A decade later there followed near Kazun the colony Dembina-Holland. Adjoining the Weichsel lowland, one began with the colonization of the Dobriner Land. Around 1700 Michael Hieronymus Podoski, Castellan of the Dobriner Land, founded Michalki (Michalke) near Rypin. According to the church chronicle of Rypin there existed already in the year 1719 the villages Oborki and Tomaszewo, likewise in 1720 Kierz and Gaj. Around 1750 were founded: Bialowiezyn, Ryszewek, Kotowo and Witkowo. The inhabitants of the Dobriner Land came presumably predominantly from West- and Ostpreußen. This is confirmed partly by the places of origin in the marriage and death registers of the evangelical church congregations, partly also by the dialect of the colonists. The colonists in the 17th and until the end of the 18th century were exclusively Lutherans. During my earlier years-long researches I have found no traces whatsoever of a possible immigration of German-Catholic settlers into Mittelpolen in that period. In the appraisal of the German rural colonization in the named period let it be stated:1.

Leading secular and spiritual personalities of the Polish people called German peasants to the clearing and settlement of their lands and allotted to them the soil that became for them the new homeland. 2. By the offer of settlement they gave them not only trust but also the legal possibility of striking root in the new homeland and of becoming citizens of the Polish state. 3. The colonists repaid the trust placed in them with achievement, by transforming great areas of Poland into fruitful cultivated land and thereby promoting as best they could the general prosperity and the wholesome development of their new chosen homeland. 4. In none of the numerous founding charters of our settlements was the demand raised that the new inhabitants of the land give up the Lutheran faith and the German mother tongue. The Polish lords of the manor took account of these two facts. They took them up into the reality of Polish-Catholic life, by which the land was after all stamped. 5. The German-Lutheran peasants brought material benefit not only to the Polish-Catholic lords of the manor but also to the state itself. In bearing and achievement they were not a negative and destructive but rather a state-affirming and constructive element. Their German virtues — industry, thrift and endurance —, paired with religious earnestness, inwardness and liveliness, and carried moreover by a cultural will and striving, meant for Poland a notable increase in inner values and gifts that the land needed for its building up and expansion.

In Kujawien there were about 25 German schools until the taking over of the land by Prussia, while in the Warthebruch their number was ten. In the Kalischer Land German schools formed: 1740 in Wladyslawow-Rosterschütz, then in Prazuchy, Zbiersk, Danowiec, Zamenty, Zakrzyn, Przespolew, Czachulec, Grodziec, Mycielin, Obory, Bialobloty, Gadowskie Hol., Orlina, Wierzby, Lazinsk. In all one counted in the Kalischer Land 16 and in the Gostyniner district about ten schools. Further there constituted themselves in the Lodz area schools among others: in Dombrowa Hol., Mileszki, Groß- Bruzyca, Klein-Bruzyca, Radogoszcz, Kaly, Slowik, Swendow, Glogowiec, Domaradzyn, Paprotnia Hol. With the schools in the cities there existed here until 1793/95, i.e. until the incorporation of Mittelpolen into the Prussian state, approximately 125 German-Lutheran schools.

With this basic stock was laid, in a manner of speaking, the foundation for our school system. While the Polish-Catholic peasant at that time stood in a relation of serfdom to his lord of the manor and culturally on a low level, the German-Lutheran colonist was a free man and, thanks to his schooling and his more progressive manner of farming, far his superior. Only in the cities, though by no means sufficiently, did the Polish population have schools.

In the German village schools, generally called cantorate schools (religion schools), the teachers taught — almost down into the first decades of the 19th century — only in the winter half of the year, i.e. from late autumn to spring. But even then instruction as well as school attendance left much to be desired. The subjects of instruction — religion, German (writing and reading) and arithmetic — exhausted themselves in imparting the most necessary things and for the most part did not go beyond the rudiments of very modest knowledge. Naturally there were among the teachers also such as filled the gaps of their knowledge despite their low degree of education and honestly strove to raise their schools in every respect and to give the children not only knowledge but also to form and strengthen them in character. In instruction the greatest stress was laid precisely on religion (Bible, catechism, hymnal). Naturally every school session began and closed with song and prayer.

Besides their service as teachers the „school-holders" were also cantors, i.e. readers in the service of worship and rural representatives of the pastors. On Sundays and feast days they held a reading service, performed churchly acts (baptisms and burials) and represented the pastor also otherwise, for example in confirmation instruction. To the cantor was subject the religious care often of several localities, which were joined together into the so-called cantorate. According to their size a rural church congregation was made up of a number of cantorates. They lay from the parish place on the average five to twenty kilometers and even more distant away. In consequence of the great distances, especially with the bad conditions of the roads, the pastors visited them only two to three times a year. VI. The Church in Prussian Times

(1793 — 1806)

1. The Prussian Colonization in Central Poland

From the Polish territories acquired through the partitions of 1793 and 1795 and administered until the Peace of Tilsit of 1807, Prussia formed the provinces of South Prussia and New East Prussia and New Silesia. In 1793 the South Prussian territories were divided into two administrative districts: into the Posen and Lentschütz ones, respectively in place of the latter the Petrikau or Kalisch one. In 1796 three chamber departments took their place: the Posen, Kalisch and Warschau ones. New East Prussia was divided in 1795 into two chamber departments: the Plozk and Bialystok ones1)

With the Prussian administration, which set the state Prussian colonization in motion, an epoch of development important for Protestantism began.

In New East Prussia, in the Plozk chamber district, the number of evangelical-Lutheran families, including those that had immigrated, amounted around 1798 already to 5879 and continued to rise. In the Bialystok chamber department likewise a few thousand Lutherans had moved in. In South Prussia, in the Kalisch and Warschau chamber department, there were, according to the „Generaltableau über den Fortgang des preußischen Kolonistenwesens vom 13. Februar 1806", 7885 souls. At the same time there settled in the towns of the province of New East Prussia 778 craftsman families with 2654 souls. In the Central Polish towns of South Prussia the number of immigrants was probably, if not higher, then certainly not lower. For the founding of colonies in South Prussia in the period from 1798 to 1806 there were expended from the extraordinary budget of the Prussian state 1 841 083 Reichstaler. The mere establishment of a settler holding cost here 1000 thaler.

3. Schools and Cantorates

The school system in the country was directed and supervised in place of the Chamber of Education (Edukations-Kammer) by the Commission for Popular Enlightenment (Kommission für Volksaufklärung) in the Kingdom of Poland. The school ordinance of the year 1808 and the new school law issued in 1834 obligated Roman Catholic and also evangelical pastors and estate owners to supervision and reporting on the schools in the congregations. The school law of 1840, which the Russian minister Uwarow had drafted and Emperor Nikolaus L had confirmed, was unfavorable for the Lutherans insofar as it opened door and gate through its unclear provisions to the interference (Ingerenz) of Polish-Catholic authorities in the German-evangelical school system. Thus, among others, the curator of the Warschau school district took in the rescript of 23 February 1843 to the General Consistory a position against the sending of Roman Catholic books and writings to evangelical schools. Likewise the school curator declared in the decree of 28. August 1847 that the viceroy had, for the cultivation of a religious spirit and the preservation of the German language, ordered not only the separation of the German-evangelical schools from the Polish-Catholic but also the founding of new schools in the German-Lutheran congregations. Through this ordinance the confessionally and nationally mixed schools were for the most part separated according to the language and confession principle. The Polish-Catholic authorities attempted to thwart the realization of the ordinance by making difficulties in the conversion of the Simultanschulen (interconfessional schools) or in the founding of new evangelical schools. After 1830 the striving of the government went toward converting the cantorate schools into elementary schools so far as possible. It thereby wished to raise their level. For in many places they were in a lamentable state. After 1840 there existed in the Weichsel lowland, besides numerous cantorate schools, the following elementary schools: in Bögpomöz, Osieker Lengden, Witoszyn, Rybitwy, Wolfswinkel, Lentzen, Modzerowo, Groß-Domb, Troszyn, Borki, Sady, Wymysle, Wionczemin, Kladow. VARIA

Robert Kucharski

Judiciary of the nobility from the 15th to the 18th century

Abstract

The judiciary of the age of the feudal monarchy changed its character in a natural way into an estate one, which was bound up with the emergence of the social estates, above all the nobility, which as a result of the political processes and the social changes under way won ever greater privileges, among them judicial immunities. This study has sketched in general the judicial organs of the administration of justice in the Polish Commonwealth from the 15th century to the decline of the Polish state. These organs were naturally not uniform in structure or organisation, and their competences overlapped. They evolved with time, though it is a fact that these changes did not keep pace with the changes taking place in the international environment around the First Commonwealth, and were not able to answer the needs both of the reform of the state and of the social changes. At a certain stage they even became a burden on the political reforms, adding their share, as it were, to the ossification of the structures of the then Polish state and its fall at the end of the 18th century. 1. The land law

As has already been said, in the age of the Kingdom of Poland, in the times when the noble judiciary was separating out, it rested on customary law. There was no uniform codification of the laws and procedures used by the judicial organs in the process of the administration of justice. This caused an enormous legal chaos and an uncertainty of legal dealings, and the erosion of the courts' authority and, indirectly, of the State's as well. The lack of consistent procedures was not, however, the chief cause of the courts' weakness but the dead execution of their rulings. That weakness was bound up with the nobility's fear that its privileges and liberties would be infringed by a strong central power. Through the whole existence of the First Commonwealth that state of things held, and every attempt to change it was torpedoed, which in the end led to the fall of the State. The same troubles touched the administration and the organs of the state in general, whose practice and activity, minimalist in their form and substance, was tolerated just so long as it did not enter on a collision course with the particular interests of the nobility.

Customary law never saw a true codification, though as is known Casimir the Great in the Statutes of Wiślica of 1347 introduced the principle of setting aside the force of a custom that worked to the harm. This led neither then nor in the later ages to a codifying of the laws in a uniform manner, one that would have strengthened the central power and the unitary function of the state, though it should be noted that such attempts were made.

The best known of the sources of customary law was the so-called Book of Elbląg of the 13th century, which owed its name to the place of its discovery, that is the town library of Elbląg in the 19th century. It held a register of the legal customs in force in the Polish lands, used by the Teutonic Knights to judge the Polish population under their rule.

Another source of the laws and procedures in the field of the law of the early age of the nobility was the Book of Henryków, called the Book of the Foundation of the Monastery of Saint Mary the Virgin at Henryków, which describes the history of the foundation and the endowment of the Cistercian abbey at Henryków, written in Latin after the year 1268. That work is a document of great historical value also because of the minute description by its author of the social relations of Poland in the age of the fragmentation of the realm, and it stands as one of the most precious monuments of letters and of the law in force in the Polish lands.

Customary law was gradually extended and supplemented by the privileges and the statutes of the Polish rulers and in later times by the constitutions of the Sejm as well. It made up a tangled and not fully consistent system of land law, the basis of judicial adjudication, both in the criminal field and in the civil one. Though the west of Europe began already in the 16th century to reach for the Roman jurisprudence containing practices and institutions most useful for the judicial and legal practice of the time, that practice did not take root in Polish legislation, though certain patterns passed into judicial activity through the efforts of the reformers (e.g. the bishops Jan Konarski and Piotr Tomicki). Most useful and serviceable for judicial practice proved the Statutes of Łaski of 1507, which were a successful attempt at the codification of the law at the beginning of the 16th century undertaken by the chancellor Jan Łaski, and the Lithuanian Statutes (1529, 1566, 1588), a source

2. The noble courts

Once the nobility had taken shape as a separate social estate, it followed as a natural course of things that the noble judiciary won a form specific and separate from the remaining courts of the Commonwealth of the time.

At the very bottom of the structure of the judiciary stood the land courts, the municipal courts and the podkomorski courts as the courts of first instance.

The first kind of courts: the land courts descended from the structures of the starosts' courts, adjudicating in the king's name. The starost judged in the name of the king, who could not be present at the court sittings in person. Hence there took root the practice of delegating the judicial powers to the office of the starost. He heard the matters over a larger territory, which resulted in the delegating of the judicial acts to judges, who had earlier attended the starosts at the court sittings. Thus gradually the function of the judging of matters passed to the judges, who began to specialise in the acts entrusted to them. The composition of the court was filled out by the representatives of the local nobility (as assessors), which was to underline not only the solemnity of the rulings and the authority of the court, but lent the legitimacy of any possible execution as well, for the organs of execution and of police did not exist yet. The execution of the rulings went through the intervention of the nobility of the given land, and so their presence on the bench had significance beyond measure. A deputy judge and a scribe were chosen for the composition. The land courts so formed covered the individual voivodeships, which already at that time were large units of the territorial division. It was necessary, then, for the composition of the land court to move between the districts and to hear there the local matters brought to its cognisance. These sittings were called the district sessions (roczki), which as a rule took place four times a year, but it happened also, that in case of need. At the end of a district session the judge proclaimed the term of the next sitting, guided by the principle that they were held again in the same place. With the development of the infrastructure the custom of the courts sitting under the open sky, in tents, dies away. The courts begin to gather in the castles, the manors, the land offices, in the monastic rooms and in the churches. The subject-matter competence of the land courts covered at first chiefly the civil matters between noblemen, and at times the criminal ones too. Curiously, they performed the functions that we today assign to the notarial offices, namely it was before them that the contracts of the purchase and sale of landed estates and buildings were concluded, the pledge agreements drawn up, the acts of settlements with the clergy over the tithes, the divisions of the estates in the process of inheritance, the marking out of the boundaries between immovables, the writing of the donations for the monasteries, the loan agreements, as well as the suits for the payment of debts and other dues, and the entries into the land books (the perpetual ones) of the titles of ownership. The land courts adjudicated the questions of the disputes over the ownership of land and of other immovables, both between two parties of the noble estate and between a nobleman and a townsman or a churchman. A distinctive feature of that kind of courts was the hearing of the matters of the settled nobility only, the landholders. These courts gradually began to lose on their importance in the 17th century, which is bound up with the fall of the land sejmiks, which did not gather and did not elect judges nor fill the offices. The abuse of the liberum veto brought the paralysis of those sejmiks, and in consequence the nobility had no judges for the disposing of the cases pending before the land courts.

Meanwhile the unsettled nobility was subject to the jurisdiction of the second type of court — namely the municipal court. That type of judiciary had different competences, composition and manner of functioning, and its first beginnings are to be sought in the 14th century in Lesser Poland, where it supplemented the land courts functionally. They were held in the castles (in Lesser Poland at Kraków, Biecz and Sącz) and their territorial competence was close to that of the land courts, yet in its subject-matter that type of courts was proper to the civil and criminal matters of the unsettled nobility. With time the criminal jurisdiction of the municipal courts was also extended to the settled nobility, along with the moving away from the armed raid and the nobility's self-help as the chief way of the meting out of justice in the so-called four municipal articles: of arson, of the attack on a noble
