The municipal court was led by the castle starost, and the adjudicating composition was filled out by the deputy starost, the municipal judge, the municipal scribe and an assessor. The technical and the order matters were secured by the usher. In the 17th century the land courts entered the period of stagnation and of fall, for the land sejms did not gather for long periods, which caused their role to be taken over gradually by the municipal courts, which judged continually, and through that they gradually took over the competences of the making of the entries in the perpetual books, which before had belonged only to the land courts. The sitting of the court was opened by the castle starost, the usher called the case and the parties were called upon to present their case and the proofs in its support. Here a field for display opened for the various substitutes in procedure, who with time grew ever more active as the law grew complicated. The judgment fallen after the bench's deliberation was written into the special books, of which more will be said below, at the discussion of the working of the court chancelleries and of their role in the practice of the administration of justice.

The third kind of the courts of first instance were the podkomorski courts, arisen in the 14th century in Lesser Poland and gradually formed in the remaining voivodeships, though one must grant that their subject-matter competence was limited only to the contentious and the non-contentious matters bearing on the fixing of the boundaries between the landed immovables of the nobility and between the nobility and the royal domains, whose significance and territorial range gradually diminish, along with the grants of the royal domains made by the rulers of Poland. The bench was presided over by the podkomorzy, who was the first in the hierarchy of the land offices after the senators, in accord with the sejm constitution of the year 1611, which formally ordered the sequence of the offices in the Crown. The court of the podkomorzy had the task of the hearing of the boundary disputes, which required the personal presence of the court in the field, for the marking out of the boundary and the settling of the dispute, and thereby excluded the recourse to the commissioners, the specialists, or a relying only on the documents on which the judgment was to rest. The criminal judiciary in the period after the unification of the Kingdom rested in the hands of the court of the oprawca, that is an official of the municipal court appointed by the starost, that is an organ coming from the royal nomination. In the period before the institution of the royal instygator had taken shape, he had the task of the pursuit of the crimes threatening the safety and the public order. An office with competences so shaped gathered in its hands the investigative and the jurisdictional acts: it established, pursued and confined the perpetrator of a crime. One cannot refuse that office an exceptional effectiveness and efficiency of action for the practice of the time in the field of the execution of the laws, as the numerous complaints of the nobility against the abuses of the oprawca point to — one who, in their belief, infringed their rights and liberties. It is a fact that the court of the oprawca had an efficient and a harsh investigative apparatus, and the cases pending were judged quickly. This did not however stop the noble brethren from the criticism of the oprawca and from the fierce combating of that judicial office, which led at the end of the 15th century to the liquidation of that institution. Reminiscences of its existence function to the present day through the pejorative meaning given to the word "oprawca" (the bailiff).

In the 15th century the wiec courts keep on further, one in each voivodeship, which were in a straight line the functional heirs of the district courts of the princes. The close of the 15th century, however, is already the decline of that kind of institution, and the competences pass to the sejm court, which adjudicates in the presence of the nobility under the presidency of the voivode. The judgments fall in the sejm courts in the king's name, who is the highest judge. The most important deeds of the high officials go precisely to the king's court, though to relieve the king, a practice takes shape that in his stead a dignitary indicated by him presided over the court. In the practice of the time of the functioning of the organs of the administration of justice it was accepted that the multiplicity of the types of court had the task of the relieving of the ruler of the personal judging of the matters, which the monarch had the right to take over always to his own cognisance. That competence engaged itself always at the moment when the ruler appeared in a given land; then all the courts stopped their activity and the judge, the sub-judge and the scribe took their place at the ruler's side, to serve him with their help in the giving of the rulings. Such a ruling enjoys a high prestige and a solemnity in its substance and form. There is no ap-

3. The judicial offices

A discussion of the institutions of the administration of justice of the Noble Commonwealth will not be full without a discussion of the judicial offices. As is known, the efficient functioning of the administration of justice rests on two pillars: the rules and the personnel. The institutions discussed appear in all the courts of the Noble Commonwealth.

3.1. The professional judges

In the functional sense at the head of the judicial offices always stood the representative of the king in a given land, so that it might be the starost, the voivode or a commissioner. In the period of the monarchy the administration of justice was exercised in the name of the sovereign, who is the king. In the exercise of that function, which demanded a specialisation and with time also an ever greater knowledge, the Polish monarchs made use of the judges and the sub-judges they appointed. The judge thus became the president of the adjudicating composition in the name of the king and came from the royal nomination, filling his function for life. After the taking of the opinion of his advisers the king named a nobleman to the post of judge, from among the candidates chosen by the land sejmiks. It was required that the candidate be a landholder, settled in the given land, meeting the requirement of worthiness, so that he enjoyed the respect, the good opinion and the trust of the local noble brethren. Requirements so laid with respect to the judge were to give a warranty of the honest exercise of the duties and to help raise the prestige of the rulings made through him, which had no small significance given the weakness of the institutions of execution and the relying in that field on the general levy. The knowledge of the specific character of the given land and of the personal [relations] of the noblemen settled there had a great significance for the effectiveness of the judging. The judges of the noble courts performed their duties without a pay, which was bound up with the fairly common conviction that as an honorary function it was to bring prestige and respect. Where the judge nominated by the monarch could not fill his function, he had recourse to his substitute — the komornik, towards whom likewise the require-

 J. Bardach, B. Leśnodorski, M. Pietrzak, Historia ustroju i prawa polskiego, Warszawa 1998, p. 277.
kucharski2023/237:
ment of the settledness in the given land was laid. Similar requirements, as towards the judge and the komornik, were laid on the sub-judge. A characteristic feature of all those functions was the absence of the requirement of the possession of a legal knowledge. To gain it was extraordinarily hard, and so it was accepted that the judges would gain the knowledge, the experience and would form the skills, according to the principle that practice makes the master, considering the individual cases. The process of that period gradually takes on the formulae and the legal institutions shaped in the European practice, yet it will never take on the uniform and consolidated form that was known, say, from the canon law. That was bound up with the resistance against the changes, which the nobility held for the danger of an "absolutum dominium" and combated by all the means. In the municipal courts the judges are appointed by the starost (with time the nobility will take over that competence too), while in the land courts the land sejmik appoints and the king confirms.

3.2. The lay judges – the assessors

Beside the professional judges, in the compositions of the courts there sat the lay judges, who represented the interests of the nobility as the whole of a given land, called the assessors. They were noblemen of the given land, whom the professional judge chose for himself, so that they adjudicated together with him in the judicial composition. As a rule there were six of them in the composition; they had no legal education and rather advised the judge in the giving of the judgments. As we read in the literature, "a court assessor is a person who, either by virtue of an entitlement belonging to her, or of a calling by an empowered judicial authority, or of an office she holds, assists the judge or the tribunal in the acts of the adjudication, contentious and non-contentious, being at the same time a witness of the course of the trial". Curiously, the assessors were standing and non-standing, and the former were recruited from among the noblemen holding the offices in the given land and appointed by the king. It is thus a second function in the judicial composition of the land court nominated by the ruler, while in the municipal courts there was no requirement of their appointment, though that practice began to fix itself. "The szlachta sat not only on their own land and municipal courts, but also on the town courts; on the other hand, on the noble courts there often sat as assessors townsmen, and not only the local officials, the burgrave, the wójt, the jurymen, but also ordinary townsmen, holding no office, and also Latin clergy and even Ruthenian. (…) This admission of the various strata and estates to a share in the court sittings was a proof of a high tolerance, and at the same time it strengthened the authority of the court and the trust in its justice, regardless of the differences of estate".

3.4. The court chancellery

The court chancelleries were kept by the scribe, who was responsible for their efficient functioning. A curiosity is that the fairly uniform practice of the keeping of the court books fixed itself on the Polish lands in the 15th century.

The court books were destined for the entries of every kind of judicial ruling of a criminal as well as of a civil nature. With the beginning of each year new books were opened, to ease the chancellery work and the use of the data contained in them. The entries in the books were made in the Latin language, in a general manner describing the subject of the proceedings and the content of the ruling. The judicial practice of the time cared for the highest securing of the rooms of the chancellery, which were located in buildings of brick bought and kept specially for that purpose, with the aim of ensuring the perpetual durability of the documents. With the fixing of the new structures of the courts and of the practice of the administration of justice of the noble age, separate buildings appear, where the land courts have their seats and at them the court chancelleries are located, where the court documents are kept. The authorities cared in particular for the proper securing of the archives, through the providing of solid gratings in the windows and of doors covered with a thick sheet iron with locks, for that was indispensable for the assurance of the certainty of the legal dealings through the securing of the court documentation. The court books at the beginning were not surrounded by any particular care, for it was accepted at the time that they were the property of the starost, and as such were treated, after his death, as parts of the inheritance. Only the winning of the right of perpetuity by the courts changed that situation, in particular after the taking of the sejmik constitution of the year 1496, where it was resolved that "in case a starosty falls empty, the books are to be laid in the town halls, in separate chests, under the keys of the voivode, of the land judge and of the starost in office".

3.5. The usher

The technical and the order outfitting of the courts of the time was provided by the usher, who did not have to be a nobleman, which caused that in that role there appeared many people of peasant origin. The name of the office came from the function of the carrying of the documents of the princely chancelleries as a carter. They were nominated by the voivode, and in the later period by the sejmiks; they took the oath, after which their symbolic hair-cutting was done, which symbolised the submission to the power of the voivode, who performed that rite in person. To the basic tasks of the usher belonged the delivering of the summonses, of the various official letters,

the calling of the parties before the court, the care for the order in the court room during the hearing, the organising and the securing of some of the acts of the court bound with the views in the field and the local visitation, lastly the carrying out of the executions of the rulings fallen before the court. The procedural statutes of Volumina Legum surrounded the usher with a particular protection, for whoever should beat him or kill him was subject to the same punishments as for that deed done to the harm of a nobleman, and so the punishment on the throat. The same regulation ordered the nobility to treat the usher's acts seriously and forbade the refusal of the taking of the summonses and the court calls. For his work the ushers were remunerated, receiving a penny for a mile of road covered to the addressee of the letter, and also for the various other acts performed for the court.

3.6. The instygator

The noble judiciary formed the institution of the public prosecutor — the instygator, called also the delator. His role was the representing of the general interest both in the criminal and in the civil processes, e.g. defending the interests of the nobility in the processes for damages of a given land, if the neighbourhood suffered through the march-through of troops. With the shaping of the practice, that the victim of the misdeeds should be represented and in some way recompensed, and the legal order infringed by that deed restored through a just punishment, the land instygators appear gradually in the judicial practice, though not at once do they gain the functions that in the modern times are assigned to the prosecutors. They appeared before all the kinds of courts, and were chosen from among the noble landholders, of an acknowledged social position at the land sejmik. In the 16th century the instygator appears as a central royal office — the Instigator Regni. The name of that office comes from the Latin word instigare — to accuse. By the title of the exercising of his tasks the land instygators took no pay, and their function, as the judicial one, was bound with the duty towards the community and tied itself with the prestige of the holding of the post.

3.7. The advocates

The defenders in the processes before the land courts were called the advocates, the jurists, the palestrants, the patrons. An opinion prevailed of them as of purchasable pettifoggers, able to tangle a case in such a way that the guilty escaped the punishment if he paid well, and the ruling in the court often depended on the oratorical talent of the palestrant. The function binds itself with the receiving of a remuneration from the parties represented, and it did not come from a nomination on the side of the public offices.

4. The judicial process

Let us look then at how the process before a land court of the age of the Noble Commonwealth looked, on the example of a criminal process. In that time a clear division into a criminal and a civil process had not yet taken shape, and so the procedural elements interweave for both types of the proceedings. A criminal case began with the bringing of a complaint by the wronged party himself, whom with time the instygator supported before the court. Then the court chancellery draws up the document called the summons, which was to be served on the settled nobility by the usher in writing, 14 days before the term of the hearing, while to the landless nobility it was announced orally. That important document is issued by the land scribe at the court, furnished with the royal and the land seal, in the Latin language and from the mid-16th century in the Polish language. The serving of the summons was attested by the deposition of the usher in the court book, which was held as the fact of an effective service. A frequent practice, however, was the ignoring of the summonses. The noble Arnold of Kościerzyna sued Mikołaj, the castellan of Bydgoszcz, before the land court at Nakło in a process "over the fled subjects", which was a rather frequent subject of the disputes between the nobility. "The court summoned lord Mikołaj, who did not stand at all, holding in contempt the summonses brought by the usher: 'the same usher, giving his account in the face of the court, attested publicly that he called the first, the second, the third and a fourth time over that lord Libijski of Złotów to stand and explain, which lord Mikołaj neither himself, nor through a substitute, stood forth and made no effort to explain'". The court scribe entered the case in a separate book called the wokanda or the register, from which the successive cases were called. It was technically the role of the ushers, yet

The courts gathered in the rooms called the audience chambers, where at the chief place stood the table called the "tribunal", with a cross set on it. In the middle of the table sat the judge in the surroundings of the assessors. The parties entered the hall after the calling of the case. The standing forth of both the parties was obligatory, and the absence without an important cause was punished with a fine, called also the non-standing. The procedure of that time, from the statute of the year 1578, allowed the possibility of the putting off of the case, which was called the dylacje or the puttings-off, at most four times, with the taking of the next term as a fatal one. The judge opened the hearing, which went orally and openly and was made up of three stages. At the first term every question of organisation was considered, the puttings-off, the further terms were planned. In the second stage, the plaintiff proclaimed his summons, described his claims and cited the rules on which he based his pretensions. The defendant answered the claims of the plaintiff, raised his own arguments and declared whether he accepts the judicial summons or contradicts it. The outline of the most important claims of the parties was written into the court book by the scribe. The plaintiff could no longer withdraw his complaint from that moment, unless with the agreement of the opposite party. Then followed the third part of the process: namely the evidentiary proceedings, during which the parties presented their findings, called the witnesses or delivered before the adjudicating bench the material proofs. The processes were not divided into civil and criminal, and so both the elements of those processes in the present meaning interwove. In the evidentiary proceedings before the courts of the time the rule found its application that it was the parties who had to gather and themselves present every proof before the adjudicating bench. "The court did not seek the objective truth, but contented itself with the proofs, which made the formal basis for the giving of the ruling". The so-called propinquity of the proof was applied, which consisted in the determination that the right of the priority in the carrying out of the proof belonged to the party higher in estate. of the Middle Ages knew the ordalias, that is the judgments of God, the backward reference (the invoking of a ruling that had fallen in the same matter in another court), the attestation of the judge, consisting in the confirmation through the judge that a given ruling was given. These means die away gradually with the spread of the court books, in which the rulings are written. The oath of the parties was applied too, the depositions of the usher, the depositions of the witnesses and the proofs from the documents, growing in weight. With time, however, ever greater significance is gained by the official investigation called the skrutynium, conducted by the instygator as an organ neutral and objective with respect to the parties, who in turn did not know the law and were not able to prove their arguments duly, in particular in the criminal matters, where the official authority to make certain findings mattered. In the situation when the defendant did not stand forth at the fatal term (at the first one unexcused, or after four puttings-off), a default hearing was held (called also the non-standing one), in the absence of the defendant the perpetrator. If still in the 16th century the calls of the usher to stand forth before the court were respected, with time there appeared ever more default hearings. The Commonwealth of the time possessed no organs that could bring the defendant before the court by force, the various offenders avoided the justice effectively, holding the legal order in contempt. To be sure, the default ruling was given to the advantage of the plaintiff, yet given the lack of the execution it was ineffective, and the perpetrators of the crimes often fled beyond the borders of the country, e.g. to the Dzikie Pola or under the protection of the neighbouring rulers. An example of such a behaviour is the case of the kniaz Michał Gliński, who after the death of Aleksander Jagiellończyk sought the power over the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. The lawful heir of the throne offered the usurper an armed resistance and defeated Gliński. That one, however, making as if to amend, laid down his arms and humbled himself before the king Zygmunt Jagiellończyk. Quickly he began again to conspire against the sovereign. The case of the treason of the estate stood before the royal court, and the treacherous traitor was prosecuted as instygator by the Marshal of Lithuania Jan Zabrzeziński. In the face of the unavoidably approaching punishment, he fled to the Moscow prince, to whom he declared his help in the war with Poland and where he finished his vile life in the Moscow prison in the year 1534.

The rulings given by the land courts were called the final rulings, from which, after the introduction of the institution of the appeal, one could appeal. The bringing of the means of appeal held back the execution of the punishment. The giving of the ruling itself, however, bound itself with a ceremonial, underlining the weight of the ruling. A curious description of the giving of a ruling adjudging the punishment of death is brought by the Lublin palestrant Jan Duklan Ochocki: "When the decree condemning to death was to be read, the judges covered their heads, the presiding one called louder — 'Open the doors! The decree of death!' The usher too, with his head covered, three times opened and shut the doors and shut them with a crash, calling: — 'Be silent, gentlemen, for the listening to the decree of death!' During the reading of the decree the delinquent stood before the court. After him three days were given him to prepare himself for the death, and the priest no longer left him. (…) The headsman too was constantly at the delinquent, slept with him and accustomed him to himself".

The punishments meted in the period of the Noble Commonwealth answered the conviction of the time of the necessity of the laying of the stress on the general prevention, which cannot wonder, for given the weakness of the execution of the laws, the individual prevention often proved illusory. The conviction of the exceptionality and the inviolability of the nobility caused that towards the representatives of that estate no tortures were applied during the skrutynium, and even from the heaviest misdeeds one could buy oneself out.

So Wacław Matuszewicz, after a quarrel, beat and shot with a pistol his adversary, the nobleman Parowiński, who soon died of the wounds taken. The companions of the dead man caught the perpetrator, to set him down to the castle, which guaranteed a quick administration of the punishment. The body of the dead man was delivered to the municipal court at Brześć as the chief proof in the case. Into the chancellery came the manifest of the instygator and the process moved. The perpetrator had, however, an experienced palestrant, who so tangled him in the case and taught him "how to stand in the court", that it was adjudged that Wacław Matuszewicz shall take the oath and cleanse himself of the accusation of a murder wilful. He was then set free, after the paying to the wife of the killed man 3000 zlotys and to the court 1000 zlotys. It was not an everyday ruling, for in the judicial practice the kinds of homicide were distinguished: such

A nobleman who would kill another nobleman paid the punishment of 240 marks; making use of an edged weapon he was threatened with the punishment of one year and six weeks of the lower tower, while if he made use of a firearm the punishment was twice as long. The sejm constitution of the year 1588 determined the depth of the lower tower at 12 ells from the floor to the ceiling. The orderedness of the dimensions of the prison rooms the starosts were to watch over, and severely to combat every attempt at making an ease for the convicts. One may assume that the coming out alive of such a room, without windows, dark, unheated and damp-foul, where the convict slept on the ground or on hay, was practically impossible, the more so that the food had to be delivered by the family of the wronged party, which won the process. "If pity or the goodwill of the warders did not ease them this punishment, most often the death of the punished interrupted its sitting out" — as Kajetan Koźmin justly observed. The convict, after his being led to the undergoing of such a punishment, went down the ladder to the bottom, it was drawn out and the entrance was bolted. Far lighter was the punishment of the so-called upper tower, where the cells had little windows, the furnishings stood there, and the prisoner could be visited. The rule held, however, that if the prisoner put his head out of the window or crossed the threshold of the cell, he underwent the punishment from the beginning.

kucharski2023/248:
The only institution appointed and entitled to the execution of the rulings was the starost, who, as we know, acted in the name of the royal power. The starost took into the prison the perpetrators, whom the wronged had caught and delivered at once to his office. The prisoner sat in the arrest only as long as the interested wronged party or his family delivered the means for his keep. Curiously looked the practice of the execution of the rulings against immovables. The starost's service met enormous obstacles in the carrying out of such rulings, but the situation was easier all the same than in the case of the pursuing of the criminals condemned to death. The mighty noblemen disposed of a numerous service and let no representatives of the judicial powers into their estates. In such a situation the starost organised an armed raid on the estates of the disobedient convict. The whole nobility of the district had the duty of the delivering of the victuals and the support for such an expedition. The sejm statutes of the beginning of the 17th century already clearly laid such a duty on the nobility, foreseeing the punishment of 100 marks for its not being carried out. The person against whom such a raid was organised had the status of a banite, that is of one taken out from under the law, and so his murder went unpunished. The estates of such a person could be plundered, and after their taking the feasts lasted at the banite's cost. The life of such a nobleman was not at all easy, for one condemned by a judicial ruling to banition could be killed unpunished by anyone whom he offended, caught and given to the starost for the carrying out of the punishment. He was moreover deprived of honour, which at that time bound itself with a civil death. No self-respecting nobleman would give him his hand, nor wish to enter any relations. A person held for unhonourable, and such was an infamis, counted for nothing socially and had no right to stand at the sejmiks.

The court acts of the age deliver numerous examples of the people of noble birth troubling themselves with the common criminal misdeeds. A rather frequent practice was the meting out of the justice on one's own hand, not believing in the effective execution of the rulings fallen, which the condemned held in contempt and ignored. A known Kraków rich merchant, Walerian Montelupi, a descendant of the Italian immigrants, held a landed estate in the village of Piersice near Sandomierz. One day in the year 1609, staying at his manor, he was fallen upon by an armed band under the command of Zygmunt Łaziński. The merchant was taken, beaten, bound and stolen away in a stolen coach to Łaziński's village of Siniawy in the district of Sanok. There the Italian was shut in a dungeon, and to the family there were sent letters written by Montelupi with the demand of a ransom for the freeing of the kidnapped, under the threat of his being tortured
kucharski2023/249:
and of his death. To frighten the wretch, Łaziński ordered him to dig a grave in the cellar if he did not persuade the family and the other Kraków merchants to pay a ransom at the height of 12600 zlotys. The merchant was unbending and refused, at which Łaziński, fearing to keep him in his own house, carried him over to the popa at Moszczeniec. There the dashing merchant, left alone, entered into a good understanding with the churchman and, having described to him his lot, moved him to send the messages to the castle at Sanok. In reaction to the above the deputy starost arrived at once and, together with the starost's guard, took the prisoner from the hands of the kidnappers. Łaziński hid himself, reckoning that the matter would die down and he would escape the responsibility. The merchant Montelupi did not however give up, hired an armed band and a year after the event came to Siniawy, to Łaziński's manor, in the company of his son-in-law Damian Baliński. The manor was surrounded and Łaziński was caught. Montelupi did not plan at all to hand his tormentor into the hands of justice, but meted the punishment to him himself. After the binding of the robber to a post he was shot, and then the whole band, undisturbed, drove off quietly.

The bad example from the elders passed to the youth, which despite the harsh upbringing and the moral and the religious rules inculcated at times demoralised itself too and entered the road of the criminal misdeed. In the historical sources there is found the description of the case of a noblewoman of Zakroczym, Katarzyna of the Kwasieborscy Fałęcka, who lodged at the municipal court of Zakroczym a protest against her unnatural son, for that he did not want to go to school, and given to a clerical seminary for the learning, soon fled. After the return home he prepared his mother a hell. He carried out the furnishings and the clothes of his siblings, which he sold. To the household trying to oppose that behaviour the youthful offender threatened with a beating, swinging at the same time a knife and an axe. The noblewoman wrote in her complaint: "my own sister, standing personally before these present acts, he beat without any cause, made the marks of bruises, and drove all the people from the manor, and tried to set the manor on fire, the windows in the manor and in the village he knocked out, and he promises certainly to beat, to kill and to burn the manor and the village. Wherefore, forestalling the evil, lest he accomplish his senseless intention, this complaint is brought into the present acts – Katarzyna Fałęcka".

The land judiciary in the 17th and the 18th century lived through a crisis because of the estate specificity of the participants appearing in the proceedings carried on before them. In that period the municipal courts play a greater role. Only in the year 1765 does the revival of the activity of the land courts begin, which compete effectively with the municipal courts. Stanisław Staszic criticised the doubleness of the courts with reason: "The municipal and the land courts are needless, so long as these have an equal power of the judging of the same matters and their rulings an equal force. If the Commonwealth does not distinguish the matters of the kind proper to each of these courts, it will act wisely and destroy the disinclinations — the quarrels between the land and the castle — when instead of these two courts it establishes one court permanent". The reforms of the state carried out at the end of the 18th century abolished the division of the judicial organs. The Four-Year Sejm liquidated the land, the municipal, the podkomorski courts, introducing in their place the uniform noble courts, made up of 10 judges appointed for 4-year terms and adjudicating through the whole year. In this way the chapter in the history of the Polish judiciary closed — the period of the noble administration of justice.

Judiciary of the nobility from the 15th to the 18th century

Abstract

The judiciary of the feudal monarchy naturally changed its character to the state one, which was associated with the emergence of social classes, especially the nobility, which, as a result of the ongoing political processes and social changes, obtained more and more privileges, including
kucharski2023/253:
judicial immunities. This study will outline in general the judicial organs of the judiciary in the Republic of Poland from the 15th century until the end of Polish statehood. Naturally, these bodies were not uniform in terms of structure and organization, and their competences coincided. They evolved over time, although the fact is that these changes did not keep up with the changes taking place in the international environment around the First Polish Republic, and were not able to meet the needs of both state reforms and social changes. At a certain stage, they even became a burden in political reforms, contributing in some way to the ossification of the structures of the then Polish state and its collapse at the end of the 18th century. This period was characterized by a multitude of types of judgments, their cognition and territorial properties, which overlapped and yet did not constitute the uniform and coherent structure to which we are used these days. The subject of this study will be a discussion of these organs with an outline of their practice and a short description of the specificity of land law.

DARIUSZ ŁUKASIEWICZ (Poznań)

A NEW ANALYSIS OF THE "BLACK REGISTER".
A SOURCE STUDY

The "Black Register" is a commented list of the estates in Great Poland that the Prussian occupier gave away in the years 1796-1797 to Prussian officers, officials and junkers. The aim of the present analysis is to assess its value and significance. Sources that throw new light on the "Black Register" justify its use. The list of the estates given away also has a wider significance for assessing Prussian policy in South Prussia and Polish-German relations in this period. We shall therefore present the aims, the course and the effects of the giveaway of estates, taking into account a wider context than has been done so far.

The state of research

After 1945 Jan Wąsicki was the only student of the "Black Register", devoting to it his article Rozdawnictwo dóbr ziemskich w Prusach Południowych w latach 1796-1797 (The giveaway of landed estates in South Prussia in the years 1796-1797). He set as the limit of his analysis the presentation of the giveaway of Polish estates by the Prussian authorities, which had earlier not been a separate subject of study in Polish historiography. Jan Wąsicki's article was a pioneering work — like a series of his other studies probing the history of South Prussia. It was also thanks to this historian that the subject was introduced into the history of Great Poland and into the synthesis of the history of Poland.

On the German side several works appeared on the giveaway of domainal estates in South Prussia. The most new material was brought by

From the beginning of the twentieth century no new work on our subject has appeared. The "Black Register" nevertheless found its place, often with an effect worth recording, in German monographs of broader themes.

While in the works of Polish historians the stressing of the rapacious and Germanising aspect of the giveaway of estates dominated, German historiography showed interest chiefly in the economic significance of the operation, interpreting the giveaway of estates as the drawing of Prussian capital into economically neglected Polish lands. The justification for selling off the domainal estates to private owners was the miserable state of the Prussian state's finances. It was therefore more profitable to hand the neglected estates to good husbanders, who would not only pay for them but also invest in them, and then pay taxes to the state treasury. Yet there were also many historians (Mayer, Philippson, Stadelmann, Bissing, Simsch, Beheim-Schwarzbach) who noticed that in practice the giveaway was very far from the ideal presented above. They pointed to corruption, the depriving of the state treasury of its due revenues, speculation in landed estates.

C. Grünhagen, on the other hand, not only came out in defence of the giveaway — as lying in the interest of the Prussian state — but, drawing on sources unknown until then, attacked the whole critical current against Hoym and his "cabal" and against the rule of Frederick William II. Grünhagen began by forcing the thesis that the donations were a real reward for officers and officials who had deserved well of the Prussian state, and ended by writing of them as an acquisition for the donataries so burdensome and unprofitable that it might have been the king's spite towards his Prussian subjects and a wish to fleece them under the perverse pretext of a gift. The donataries (Donatarien), as Frederick William II had them called — first had to pay for the estate often the ordinary — in Grünhagen's opinion — price. Then, from these doubtful gifts — as Grünhagen would have it — the unhappy Prussian generals were to pay 74 or 100% tax, and then still invest in the estates thus paid for as tribute, spending money on Polish peasants unfit, in the author's opinion, for proper husbandry. Meanwhile, as if in defiance of these circumstances, the Prussian donataries not only did not receive these estates with disgust, but sold them on afterwards at great profit. This aspect of the unfortunate end of the giveaway the author passed over entirely. Grünhagen's error also lay in adopting the superficial assessment that the owners of the former starosties paid 24% contribution and 50% Kompetenzgeld, that is 74% tax of the net revenue; and the owners of church estates 50% contribution and 50% Kompetenzgeld, that is 100% of the net revenue. This was supposed to have been possible because everyone knew anyway of the under-declaration of tax returns. In fact the donataries in the department of Poznań paid in every case only 24% contribution and 50% Kompetenzgeld. This by no means amounts to 74% of revenue. The contribution was reckoned on the net revenue (reine Ertrag), in Poland of the time — the intrata, that is the net income, after the deduction of the costs of husbandry (sowing). Then the 50% Kompetenzgeld likewise was not reckoned on the income, but on the net revenue, after deducting 5% for the costs of administration and 10% for the upkeep of buildings and farming stock. Only now can one say that by the Prussian standards of the time this was an extraordinarily burdensome taxation, and one must ask why in spite of it the donataries made enormous sums out of the undertaking.

 Kompetenzgeld — this pension or compensation for the former Polish owners of church estates and leaseholders, paid out of the confiscated estates, was reckoned by deducting from the net revenue the contribution (24 or 50%), the costs of administration (5%), the upkeep of stock and buildings (10%). This "Kompetenz" is not to be confused with Competenzgeld, a tax relief for towns afflicted by fires and epidemics etc., where part of the taxes due was kept back by the town authorities to cover losses or pay off debts. It should be marked that the smaller estates were left to the clergy, and in those cases no Kompetenzgeld could be in question. A misunderstanding also arose over who paid the Kompetenzgeld — the state (the Chambers), or the new users of the estates. J. Wąsicki judged it was the Chambers (as followed from the account of A. The "Black Register" and new completions

We have reached the manuscript of the "Black Register", probably one of the copies. It is a small quire of 12 leaves, written in a legible hand, after the scheme repeated in the printed versions of the list. Likewise — as C. Grünhagen supposed — in 1849 J. Löwenberg used a copy in the possession of Tytus Działyński, and the anonymous publisher of the work Materialien zur Geschichte polnischer Landestheile unter preußischer Verwaltung (Leipzig 1861, H. 1, s. 140-171) used Löwenberg's edition. There should also be recorded the Polish edition of 1878 — anonymous and without commentary. In 1886, on the basis of the "Neue Feuerbrände", Władysław Smoleński published the "Black Register" as an appendix to his work Rządy pruskie na ziemiach polskich 1793-1807 (Warsaw 1886), Gdzie się podziały nasze królewszczyzny (Poznań 1878). Besides, Janusz Iwaszkiewicz published a list of 5 private estates confiscated by the Prussian authorities, Wykaz dóbr ziemskich skonfiskowanych przez rządy zaborcze w latach 1773-1867 (Warsaw 1929).

The register was first published by Joseph Zerboni di Sposetti in the periodical "Annalen der leidenden Menschheit" in 1801. The manuscript he extorted from Hans von Held; it was Friedrich von Cölln, a councillor of the Poznań Chamber, who completed Zerboni's compilation. He then published it in the periodical he edited in Amsterdam, the "Neue Feuerbände". Zerboni's compilation bore the name General-Tableau von sämmtlichen in Südpreußen von des Königs Majestät Friderich Wilhelm II verschenkten königlichen und geistlichen Gütern. H. von Held gave it the title aimed against Hoym and preserved by history: Das schwarze Register oder General Tableau der von Friedrich Wilhelm II in Südpreußen verschenkten Güter während der Minister von Hoym diese Provinz verwaltet hat in den Jahren 1794-1798. It was of this version of the manuscript that we made use. The numerous interesting completions in the appendices to the monograph mentioned above were presented by C. Grünhagen. Jan Wąsicki published only incomplete data for 40 donataries. Omitted by him were councillor Unruh (Ritterschaftsrath), the president of Berlin Eisenberg, chamberlain St. Patern, Prince Antoni Czetwertyński, Count Łuba, Dzierzbicki, director Goldbeck, minister Hoym. Before the Second World War — in 1936 — sample data for 22 donataries was published by Kazimiera Jeżowa.

The basic problem has arisen so far from the discrepancy between the information declared on the first page, of both the manuscript and the printed editions of the source, that the real value of the 241 estates sold to 52 donataries was 20 million thalers, the nominal one however 3.5 million thalers, and the content of the register itself, where much lower figures figured. A doubt therefore arose whether von Held had not left yet other indications about the remaining estates, not listed in the register. Meanwhile as it turns out, the material printed by Zerboni-Held, then by Friedrich von Cölln in 1807 and further in the years 1849, 1861 and 1878 does not differ from the manuscript in the Berlin archive. Besides, we managed to find three other lists of estates, not connected with Held's register. The first two are official lists of the contribution of the donations for the department of Poznań, the third is a Polish list from the period of the Duchy of Warsaw for the whole of South Prussia, differing slightly from Held's list. These compilations are marked by small though interesting differences against the "Black Register" — thus Massów figures there (probably not Julius Anton the minister, partisan of Karl August Struensee, but the court marshal, who was to have received Kopanica in 1796 and resell it to the Bloch brothers). Likewise absent from the "Black Register" are Colonel Massenbach and Tschammer, which shows on the one hand the incompleteness of Held's list, on the other — and this is more important — that these gaps are not considerable. Martin Philippson as early as 1882 mentioned another list, coming from Bucholtz-Alvensleben, which was to have been far more compromising for Prussia than the "Black Register". The same compilation Grünhagen then recognised as the basis for Zerboni and Held. We used the compilations of Grünhagen and Philippson supplementarily, to verify the data.

The archival tax returns that we confronted with the "Black Register" come from 1797/8 and give a contribution the same as or very close to the sample data printed by Grünhagen. We set these returns together in the table that crowns our work. Lists I-II have a tax character, and hence it was necessary to compute the value of the estate from the height of the tax. of Hans von Held in the "Black Register" itself. For it was assumed that a landed estate ordinarily yields 5% net revenue (reine Ertrag). That means that the net revenue of an estate, after the deduction of the costs of husbandry, makes 5% of the value of that estate. Thus Held assessed the value of councillor Beyer's estate at 160 000 thalers on the basis of an income of 8 000 thalers; General Blücher's estates yielded 6 000 thalers a year and were therefore to be worth 120 000 thalers. In a similar way the donations were assessed of Major Hünerbein, Prince Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, Marshal Keyserlingk and the Master of the Horse Krackwitz. This assumption was received both in the Commonwealth and in Prussia, and then also in the Duchy of Warsaw and still in the Congress Kingdom. It made an essential premise for tax settlements, and then for assessments of the mortgaged value of estates. The tax sources have however this undeniable advantage, that they are the result of the fiscal endeavours of the state, so there can be no question here of a deliberate (on the part of the state itself) deflation of the value of the estate, as was the case with the nominal price of the donation. We possess the most diversified material for the department of Poznań, where the nominal value of the estates was 1 025 250 thalers, while from the tax returns there follows a value of 1 638 000 thalers, that is a sum almost twice as high. Nevertheless it is at the same time a magnitude twice as low as the one given by Held on the title page of the "Black Register" — the "true" value of these estates, that is 3 million thalers. That true value of the estates was either the price of their sale, the sum of the lease, or the income from which Held in the way we have described computed the value of the estate. In this way, after counting the estates of all the departments, we obtain the sum of 7 036 160 thalers. It is an approximate magnitude, because in the case of some estates the author of the list entered the description "insignificant" or "value unknown". Such items are however barely four and cannot have a significant influence on the magnitude of the sum of the values of the estates given away. Somewhat greater is the sum of the values of the estates that follows from the Polish list, for it comes to 7 243 675 thalers. It should further be added that the "Black Register" has not 52 donataries, as its title page declares and as is usually said, but only 48; there are, however, 52 donations, because Treskow, Hohenlohe, Lüttichau and Wendessen appear twice — in different departments. The number of estates given away amounts, if every separate item is counted, to 245, not 241.

Held gives us yet one more indication, perhaps a decisive one, writing that the tax losses of the state from the estates given away come to 50 000 thalers. In the report of 25 November 1797, at the close therefore of the giveaway action, Karl Georg Hoym reported to the king that the estates given away yield 111 199 thalers of income, from which likewise (after conversion) the 20 million of value is infinitely far off.

On the one hand, then, the mortgage value of the noble estates gives us a convenient measure for assessing the donations; on the other it confirms the Prussian opinions of the considerable deflation of the Polish tax declarations. In the end everything points to it that only the sum computed from Held's compilation, and not the one named on the cover of the list, may perhaps be taken as the basis for further analysis. Why then does even this sum — let us recall — for the department of Poznań 3 million thalers, almost twice exceed the value of the estate that follows from the tax burden. The explanation of this question is of decisive significance for establishing whether those 3 million answered the "real" value of the estates, as Held wanted.

The "conjuncture" of agriculture and speculation in estates

To answer this question it is necessary to take into account several phenomena occurring then not only in South Prussia. The period of the close of the eighteenth and the beginning of the nineteenth century, up to 1806, was marked by violent speculation in estates, being on the one hand a cause and on the other an effect of the rise in the prices of landed estates. That rise in prices however also followed from other premises. For South Prussia there had beyond doubt significance the renewed connection with the port of Gdańsk and the relatively favourable customs policy of the Prussian state, whose promoter was in particular Minister of Finance Karl August Struensee (especially after 1797). Accompanying it was the generally favourable conjuncture in the sale of farm produce and a considerable rise in grain prices — which contemporaries already perceived as a tendency and precisely as a conjuncture, Frederick William III among them. Of essential significance was also the creation of the Prussian mortgage. It strengthened the value of estates, whose registers were put in order, and the buyer of an estate had sight of its encumbrance and real value. Finally, the violent revival in the trade in estates was brought about by the enormous credit granted by the Prussian public banks to the Polish nobility in South Prussia on the mortgage of landed estates. This credit, assessed at 27 million thalers, answered the annual budgetary receipts of the Prussian state, and could come into being only thanks to the fact that it came from the private deposits of Prussian citizens. The Prussian state was after all in a state of deep financial crisis.

 Which does not remove the justification of the reproaches of A. Simsch.

lukasiewicz1997/41:
The failure of the giveaway of estates

Such a state of things was as far as possible from the assumptions of the whole operation. It had several aims: on the one hand the procuring of money for the stripped bare Prussian treasury, on the other the economic elevation of the domains, which were in a bad state, by means of the private money of the Prussian nobility.

No less essential was the introduction into Great Poland of the German national element. It made — as was often stressed — an outpost and support for the Prussian state among a Polish population hostile to Prussia. If the Prussian authorities complained of the low economic level of the seized lands, it must be remembered that they themselves laid hands to it in the mass trials of the insurgents after 1794. Confiscations of estates were admittedly a rarity, but the basic form of punishment — the money fine — was onerous. As many as 2000 persons were brought before the court. Janina Muszyńska gathered information on 567. As follows from the list she presents, the punishments were extraordinarily high — on average 200-1000 thalers. Already on 16 May 1794, in the edict on the ius incolatus, a loophole was left which gave the king, in accord with the law, the possibility of granting landed estates to nobles from outside the province. As it says in the edict — "the concession of particular estates honoured by Us (that is, by the king — p. m.)". In fact however Frederick William II waged to an equal degree a struggle against the unlawful buying-up of estates by Prussian speculators, encouraged by the favourable prices of estates in Poland — for in Prussia complaints were already being made in the eighties of speculation and the rise in the prices of estates. In connection with this there appeared on 12 VIII 1795 a "Publicandum" threatening confiscations against speculators who come to South Prussia and, contrary to the law on the ius incolatus, buy up landed estates, thereby winding up a speculative conjuncture, artificially driving up prices on the local market and so diminishing the purchasing power of the towns. The central Prussian authorities assessed the phenomenon in such a way that on the one side stand the producers inclined to speculation, on the other the consumers, afflicted by the prices rising artificially through speculation. This was however to be a self-driving mechanism, brought about by other factors too. Thus the producers, from the wish for gain, hold back the grain, waiting for a rise in prices — for the same reasons the buyers try to buy it up as quickly as possible. The royal order speaks of the necessity of increasing the interventionist purchases of grain into the magazines, there where its greatest shortages occur. The Councillor of the Regency Juliusz Schwartz (b. 1759) — the organiser of the South Prussian mortgage, at the same time a satirist and editor of the „Südpreußische Zeitung" — rightly predicted already in 1802 that harmful speculation in estates and the winding up of the conjuncture of prices could lead to catastrophe, when the price of grain falls or when the government is forced to block its export.

This came about after 1806. In 1809, however, the deputy of Konin Bielski explained the motives of speculation. Already at the threshold of Prussian rule many of the nobility foretold that the founding of the mortgage and the opening of cheap credit would automatically cause a rise in the price of land — it must therefore be bought and credits taken, since the rise in prices, with a premium, will even out the payment of interest.

The corrupt aspect of the giveaway of estates

Likewise the giveaway of estates itself could in no way answer the intended aims. It quickly became obvious that events had gone in quite the opposite direction, and the new owners — chosen not according to economic reason but according to Hoym's comradely preferences — treated the estates acquired at half price as a source of easy enrichment. This fact also aroused particular indignation among the remaining part of the Prussian officials — Hans von Held and Joseph Zerboni di Sposetti were connected with the minister Karl August von Struensee and the people gathered around him (Schulenburg-Kehnert, Stein, Schrötter), with whom the young heir to the throne sympathised, the future Frederick William III.

Hence too the whole affair — admittedly with enormous difficulties, but still — made its way into public knowledge. There appeared here charges of corruption, ineptitude and nepotism reigning in the South Prussian administration, whose aftermath was a series of contemporary writings, headed by the publications of Friedrich von Cölln. He asserted that the originator of the whole action of the giveaway of estates was the wife of General Bischofswerder, the king's adjutant. She was to be gnawing at her husband's head all day long — as Cölln presented it bluntly — that he would "die as a beggar" if he did not exploit the last days of the king to do "something" for his family. True or not, such information could seem so far probable that in fact Bischofswerder — the king's adjutant, owed everything he possessed to Frederick William II, whose companion he had been from childhood. It is also true that the action covered above all the circle of Hoym's camarilla, and nothing of the spoils fell to the people connected with the minister Otto Karl von Voss, pushed aside in the years 1794-1798, Struensee, Schulenburg, Schrötter, Klewitz, also Stein and Schön, who were only beginning their careers. It must also be said that after the sidelining of Voss Hoym filled the chief posts in South Prussia with his people; then too Buchholtz was appointed to the office of over-president in Poznań. Likewise Wilhelm Anton von Klewitz arrived in South Prussia together with Voss's taking of office, and was dismissed in 1795 by Hoym. Then his return came about after Hoym's fall, in 1798.

The disclosure of the abuses connected with the giveaway of estates came at the highest levels of power. Buchholtz, at odds with Hoym from 1795, on the very day of the death of Frederick William II, 16 November 1797, handed to the heir to the throne a memorial containing in the appendix a list of the South Prussian donations, which then became the basis for the "Black Register". The memorial pointed to it that with million-fold losses to the state treasury Hoym conducted on his own hand "for a song", more precisely for 1/3 of the true value, the giveaway of state estates, taking no account at all of the interest of Prussia. The officials opposed corruption with full self-sacrifice and did not count the consequences. Joseph Zerboni di Sposetti paid for it with imprisonment in a fortress, Hans von Held with removal from his post in Poznań and then a year and a half in the fortress at Kołobrzeg, Friedrich von Cölln with removal from his post in Poznań, the president of the Poznań Chamber von Garpe with removal to retirement in April 1797. The war and domains councillor Otto von Reinebeck, second director of the Kalisz Chamber, saved himself thanks to the intercession of his brother-in-law, the secret superior finance councillor Burghoff, wherefore in spite of the efforts of the Silesian minister, Frederick William II recommended only that "the young man be kept briefly". A ricochet struck Johann Kausch, who was imprisoned only on account of keeping up a correspondence with Zerboni, "appointed" by Hoym head of an anti-state conspiracy. It was to be a callow association of several officials from Głogów, of whom Hoym wrote „Se. Majestät werden sogleich finden, daß eine schon seit mehreren Jahren existirende geheime Ordensverbindung in einen förmlich Revolutions-Club hat verwandelt werden soll..." In reality it was a fashionable pastime of the youth of the period in masonry, and it is obvious that for Hoym it was merely a pretext for tripping up the critics of the way the giveaway action was conducted. In consequence its stopping came only with the death of Frederick William II.

Speculation in estates

The technical side of the giveaway of estates was in the hands of councillor Peter August Triebenfeld, Hoym's confidant and right hand, who prepared the deeds of donation. Of course, the first on the list of buyers was himself. In 1797 for 50 000 thalers he bought an estate, which he then sold in 1801 for 450 000 thalers to the Prince of Hessen-Darmstadt, as it turned out at a low price. The next owner sold the acquired estates still in the same year for 750 000 thalers to the Saxon master of the hunt Schürding. Triebenfeld himself described in a memorial published later by Wilhelm Dorow what course such operations took. Thus the buyer, after the purchase of the estates, sought an official judicial valuation of the estate. In the case given by Triebenfeld the buyer bought the estate for 230 000 thalers, then the buying of the head of the valuation commission cost him 35 000

Attempts to limit the speculation in estates found reflection in the legislative activity of the Prussian state. In the "Publicandum" first issued in 1797 in Silesia, and in 1802 in South Prussia, it is announced that there is a fictitious sale of landed estates, aiming at the obtaining of a higher entry in the mortgage registers, thanks to which it was possible to cheat the true buyer, the leaseholder, and above all to obtain a higher mortgage credit. To prevent this the authorities ordered that in all operations the mortgage extract should give not only the last but also the earlier entries of the value of the estate, as well as the basic valuation. The selection of the donataries, contrary to economic reason, additionally deepened the speculative way of treating the donations. Of the lack of any proper control over the conducting of the action testifies the fact that the post director Goldbeck received outright an estate worth 11 000 thalers by mistake, instead of the son of the minister of the same name. It did not behove the director indeed to take the estates any more, but the interests of the young councillor Goldbeck also did not suffer. The mistake was put right and he too got his share. The assessment of the value of the estates given away

Ultimately, with reference to the estates given away the most cautious assessment would say that their value was from 4 to 7 million thalers, which lies between the value that would follow from the tax estimates and the maximum value — given by Held. Nearer the truth however is the sum of 4 million. For while we are aware of the deflation of the value of income for tax purposes, this value is nevertheless comparable with the assessments of the noble estates and with other data. That the noble estates however did not in their mass fall so far to speculation was pointed out for South Prussia already by Holsche, which Danuta Rzepniewska confirmed. If Holsche warned against the new valuations of estates, which give 2-, 3-fold their real value, this did not relate to that degree to the mortgage valuations of a few years before. The above assessments are also confirmed by the "Black Register" and the structure of indebtedness from Prussian credits. Admittedly the indebtedness of the noble estates reached over 33% of their value, but at the same time credit covered only 14% of the owners. Then of 600 estates covered by credit the owner changed in about 70, and that often twice. Finally, if 10% of the debtors were Germans, the height of the loans granted them was 20% of the average indebtedness of an estate by way of Prussian credits. In sum one may say that, because of the better access to credit, the speculative character of the purchase itself, the lack of putting down roots in Poland, the estates of the "Black Register" had

The data of Held and Zerboni were cited in their day by serious Prussian statisticians, although incidentally and without comment. Leopold Krug wrote that Frederick William II gave away in South Prussia a considerable number of state estates, „denen Wert von manchen Schriftstellern zu 20 Millionen Thaler angegeben worden ist". Quite similarly caution was kept by Karl Holsche: „Einige wollen den Werth dieser Schenkungen auf 20 Millionen Thaler angeben, welches ich jedoch nicht verbürgen mag".

Both the work of Krug and that of Holsche met with letters of praise from Frederick William III, and this was not the only reaction of the young king to Hoym's machinations, who in 1798 himself asked to be relieved of the post of minister of South Prussia. He was replaced by von Voss, removed after the insurrection of 1794. Holsche however doubted whether the dimensions of the donations could be so great, citing the fact that the „Canon", that is the height of the taxation of these estates, was for the department of Poznań only 15 816 thalers. Admittedly the archival list of the „Canon" exceeds 20 000 thalers, but even that does not change the state of things. The revenues from the domainal estates put together by Wilhelm Klewitz show that their whole value could not exceed 15 million thalers. All these coordinates strengthen us in the conviction that the value of the estates given away was nearer 4 than 7 million thalers.

There took place however a quite spontaneous process of the estates given away passing either into Polish hands — without regard to political reasons — or into Prussian hands, often unconnected with the circle of the donataries. As the lists of borrowers from the years 1795-1806 show, there appeared also a group of officials who acquired estates in Poland for the economic reasons indicated earlier. Joseph Zerboni di Sposetti in the period of the rule of Frederick William III became, without a donation, a considerable landowner in the department of Kalisz, first taking a credit of 30 000 thalers on the estate of Pługawice in the Berlin Widows' Fund, and then in 1805 acquiring, for the enormous sum of 460 000 thalers, likewise coming from credit, Opatów and Wieruszów, where he really did farm and invest.

Among the later ministers of South Prussia the sympathies of the Polish nobility were enjoyed rather by Karl Georg Hoym than by Voss. The latter held that for the economic elevation of the province it was necessary to carry out quick reforms, which the nobility feared. Hoym on the other hand kept up good contacts with Feliks Łubieński, Bishop Ignacy Krasicki, Józef Wybicki. To Łubieński he proposed in the framework of the giveaway the estate at Koski, which the latter, as he boasted in his memoirs, did not accept, but arranged its purchase for 40 000 by the hitherto leaseholder Szymanowski. This was to serve the keeping of the estate in Polish hands. Szymanowski however straightway sold it for 90 000. Łubieński mentions only in his memoirs that his son Piotr was married to the daughter of Michał Szymanowski.

Łubieński mentions further that the donatary — General Favrat — was a figurehead, in whose name the estate was received by one Count Lubiński appearing in the German sources, director in Kalisz of the College of Landrats and landrat of the district of Kalisz. That enigmatic Count Lubiński is the Count Feliks Łubieński distorted in German spelling, civil-military commissioner with the Kościuszko army in 1794, brought before the court by the Prussians and sentenced to a fine of 400 thalers, after 1806 minister of justice of the Duchy of Warsaw and one of the most eminent of its organisers, the educator of the sons of those merited in the work of building the Congress Kingdom. As Tadeusz Mencel gives in his biography, thanks to the intercession of Giorolamo Lucchesini he also received the starosty of Nakło. Baron von Schilden received the estates from the starosty of Kościan, which before the insurrection had belonged to Józef Chłapowski. He resold them to that same starosta (see the Appendix, Tabela 4, s. 61), a known speculator, who drove the family estate to the edge of bankruptcy, whose spectre only his son Dezydery was to push away. Of course the legal norms intended to hinder the taking over of donative estates by Poles had an anti-Polish dimension — as Jan Wąsicki writes. It must however be noticed that the very fact of the issuing of such ordinances meant that the donataries were not very anxious about the keeping of the Prussian possessions in Great Poland. This is confirmed by the royal rescript of 19 XII 1796, which limited the donations to persons born in the old Prussian provinces or to foreigners possessing agricultural qualifications. It also obliged the owners to inform the authorities of the intention of undertaking any transactions with these goods. Since however the estates were being resold to Poles, another rescript was necessary in 1800, calling attention to the fact that not only the first but also the later owners cannot be Poles. Another loophole was being found, so in 1801 there appeared an order announcing that donations may also not be given to Poles in perpetual lease. There now remained only the selling-off by persons put up to it. With the ordinances characterised above one must also connect the letter of Frederick William III to Minister von der Recke. The king writes of the violent endeavours of the townsmen for the possibility of buying noble estates and of the need of expressing agreement to such contracts, but in a limited number of cases („um den Adel in den Besitz der Landgüter zu sichern"). These limitations were soon to come to the foreground; what interests us however is the undoubted symptom of the growth of demand for land appearing here. Frederick William III regarded the trade in landed estates as an unfavourable phenomenon, but he regarded secret cessions of the leases of domainal estates as particularly harmful. The affair of the "Black Register" influenced negatively the attitude of the Polish nobility to the Prussian administration and notably undermined the authority of the Prussian state, the more so as it was not an isolated case of irregularity in the functioning of the Prussian administration in South Prussia.

It is however impossible to deny that Wilhelm Klewitz was right when in 1812 he wrote that on the one hand nowhere as in South Prussia could such a number of "base" and "self-interested" persons squeeze into the administration, and yet even now, in the time of the Duchy of Warsaw, "the Prussian book-keepers are to this day still pleasant to you". Prussian officials were gladly made use of by Feliks Łubieński, with a demonstrative dislike of them. After 1806 they were indispensable for the continuation of the work of the administration of the Duchy of Warsaw.

If then the state of the Prussian administration in South Prussia was regarded at the time as lamentable, we cannot ignore the fact that in relation to the arrangements before the partitions the very manner of the organisation of the state institutions brought enormous progress and was appreciated by the Poles, which revealed itself bluntly precisely in the Duchy of Warsaw. On the one hand, then, moderation in criticism is necessary; on the other it is hard not to notice that neither in the times of Frederick II nor of Frederick William III did any other Prussian province enjoy such a bad name, as far as the condition of the administrative apparatus goes. In 1800, after the complaint of 77 citizens of Kalisz against the local tax councillor Joachim Denso, who committed financial robberies, Minister Voss judged it necessary, "in a province which possesses so many bad officials", to treat this offence exemplarily and punished Denso with three years of fortress, annulled however in the second instance. The German inhabitants of Rawicz, after the removal of councillor Below, sent in 1797 a deputation to the minister, which asked for an official "honest, not acting for his own advantage and against his subjects".

Soon after taking power, on 23 XI 1797, Frederick William III ordered the carrying out in the state administration of thorough purges. To be dismissed immediately were to be all the dishonest, those deprived of qualifications, the idle.

There is no doubt that in the first rank these words related to South Prussia. After the journey through Southern Great Poland in 1798 the king wrote of the legacy of Hoym's rule that the Poles have nothing to thank it for. Again and in far sharper words, referring to the letter of 1798, Frederick William returned to the question of the fatal state of the administration in 1800, where he wrote of the almost wholly extinct spirit of fidelity, selflessness, diligence and order, for which the Prussian "civil service" had once been famed. From 1798 only small steps had been taken — he asserted — or indeed nothing had been done to change this state of things.

After 1797 the estates given away remained however in the hands of the donataries. Frederick William III assured that he would act according to the law and would not trample on the documents signed by the Prussian king.

lukasiewicz1997/53:
Summary

As we have shown, the value of the estates given away can be assessed at 4 million reichstalers, whereas in consequence of the artificial raising of the prices of estates they were assessed at the time (1801) at 7 million reichstalers. The sum of 20 million reichstalers given on the title page of the "Black Register" must be recognised as wholly false. We then established that in the light of the "Black Register" itself the number of donataries was not 52, as had been given so far, but 48 persons; there were however 52 donations. From the tax returns there follows however a somewhat greater — though not by much — number of donations.

For the carrying out of the analysis of the list of estates given away and of the action of their giveaway it was necessary to take into account the wider context of the phenomena occurring: the so-called agricultural conjuncture, the rise in the prices of landed estates, speculation in estates, the consequences of the founding of the Prussian mortgage, land credit, the state of the Prussian state's finances, the state of the Prussian corps of officials in South Prussia at the turn of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and the clique struggles at the Prussian court.

In the light of our findings the aims of the giveaway action must be considered in a broad context. There appear here above all two aspects. Different were the official aims of the Prussian authorities, different those of the team of Hoym conducting the giveaway action directly. The official assumption of the giveaway action was the modernisation of the domainal estates with the private money of the Prussian junkers. The state gave up the domains, not possessing the means for their putting into husbandry. Thanks to such a decision it obtained, moreover, additional revenues from their sale, which, with the debt of the Prussian treasury at about 50 million thalers, was not without significance. Sincere too were the declarations that the Prussian nobility is to serve the Polish neighbours as a model of modern husbandry. Besides, the action was also to serve the rewarding of the officers and officials who had deserved well of the Prussian monarchy in a situation when the state possessed no other means.

Onto these premises there overlaid themselves clear political advantages, consisting in the creation in Great Poland of a group of German landowners, making up a support for Prussian rule in the seized Polish lands. The giveaway of estates was an undoubted manifestation of the policy of "subordination". It must however also be clearly marked that Prussian policy towards the Poles had also a clear aspect of "winning over" (at the time one spoke of "adoption"), of which the land credit for the Polish nobility was one manifestation at least. Both these ways of proceeding served, on the one hand, the assuring of the obedience of the nobility and control over it, on the other the formation among it of a group of partisans of Prussia, who were to consolidate Prussian rule in Great Poland. The successive partitions of the Polish lands named West Prussia, South Prussia and New East Prussia set the Prussian state before the necessity of absorbing new considerable areas. The taking of the decision on the staffing of the administration with German officials brought in from the Prussian provinces weighed fatally on the course of this process. In comparison with Poland before the partitions the Prussian corps was expanded, modern and educated. Yet for the realisation of the task set before it too few in number and subjected to negative selection. In consequence in the Prussian administration in South Prussia there came about various degenerations, unfavourable for the Prussian state itself.
lukasiewicz1997/54: Prussian. One of the essential manifestations of this was the complete distortion of the intended aims in the course of the giveaway action. It changed into a corrupt affair, joined with a speculation in estates serving no one beyond the donataries themselves, in consequence of which the estates often returned into Polish hands. It is worth marking that — as the researches of Danuta Rzepniewska showed — the Prussian credit action in South Prussia ended in an analogous fiasco, its consequences being far more unfavourable for the Polish lands than the effects of the giveaway action. On the other hand the history of the Duchy of Warsaw shows that from the positive, that is effective, patterns of the Prussian organisation of the state the Poles were able to profit without prejudice towards the occupier.
