The school authority in the territory of South Prussia was not uniform. Catholic schools were subject to the Chambers, Protestant ones to the consistory, which depended on the Regierung. Supreme supervision over the whole of the school system belonged to the Higher School Board (Oberschulkollegium) in Berlin.
muszynska1947/18:
In the work of introducing the new institutions in Greater Poland there were occasional interruptions on account of exceptional celebrations.

First of all, to seal the new state of affairs, in accordance with the provisions of the partition convention of 23 January 1793, the inhabitants had to pay homage to the King of Prussia. It was rendered in all the larger centres on 7 May 1793. On that occasion 1,500 representatives of the noble estate and 700 of the urban estate came to the capital of Greater Poland and, into the hands of the commissioners Möllendorff and Danckelmann, swore the oath of subjection to their new ruler. To lend splendour to the moment, a solemn service was held in the former Jesuit church, and in the evening a magnificent ball was given for the deputies in the Gurowski Palace, later called the Działyński Palace. On the occasion of so great a celebration, festivities were held throughout Greater Poland. Frederick William was pleased. Möllendorff — a man "shrewd and cunning, a master of political intrigue, able to cover everything with a semblance of good nature and to charm with his grey hair, sweet glance and courteous manner", soon popular in Poznań and among the nobility of Greater Poland — received, in recognition of his services, his nomination as field marshal.

More than three months later, on 18 August, it was ordered that the surrender of Mainz by the French be celebrated, and on 25 September — at the very time when the Sejm assembled at Grodno, terrorised by Sievers and Buchholtz, was signing the partition treaty with Prussia — the king's birthday.

Not long afterwards the king himself visited Greater Poland and the rest of the seized lands. He set out from Frankfurt an der Oder at the beginning of October and on the 10th of that month, in the company of Lucchesini, a man well remembered from the time of the
muszynska1947/19:
Polish-Prussian alliance of 1790, and of several officers, arrived in Poznań. From there he went to Kościan [Kosten], then to Wschowa, Rawicz [Rawitsch], Kalisz, Płock, Łowicz and Piotrków. Everywhere he was warmly welcomed by Jews and some Poles, although few in number. The Primate, Michał Poniatowski, came from Warsaw to Łowicz to greet the king, and the Radziwiłł princely couple gave a magnificent ball in honour of the Prussian monarch at Nieborów. Having stayed on Polish lands until the end of October, Frederick William returned to Berlin on 10 November. The fruit of this journey was the conviction that the Greater Poles were not glad to have passed under Prussian rule, whatever Lucchesini vainly tried to make the king believe. For the generality of the inhabitants did not even come out to meet their new master.

Nor is it surprising that this was so. In those few months of rule the Prussians had already made themselves felt by the Greater Poles. Slowly but systematically they uprooted everything that breathed of the Polish past and stamped the Prussian imprint on every sphere of life. Efforts were made to give the offices a Prussian character. Poles were removed from them. Only out of necessity, in order to communicate with a population that did not understand German, was the office of Landrat entrusted to Poles, together with the dignity of one of the chamber councillors. These officials, however, were forbidden to wear Polish dress, lest they recall the bygone order of things. The Prussian government extended its supervision over the Catholic clergy, the confraternities and the guilds, it checked the activities of the town councils, it sent in colonists, and it took the youth of Greater Poland as recruits. Deepening the distinctions of estate among the inhabitants, it permitted by the edict of 24 July 1793 only the nobility to own estates. It threatened the clergy with the loss of their landed property, and the holders of starostwa (crown estates held by a starosta) with the loss of these, intending to turn these estates into
muszynska1947/20:
state domains; in the end, however, so as not to alienate its new subjects, it left them until the year 1796 in the hands of their existing holders, against a levy of 50 per cent on income.

Embitterment among the local population was caused by certain Prussian ordinances touching everyday life, such as, for example, the raising of the price of salt by nearly 50 per cent, and the order to pay a tax on the so-called "Musikzettli" (music permits), which authorised the holding of entertainments accompanied by music, and so on.

Although the Greater Poles received the Prussian innovations with reluctance, they nevertheless did not rise to any more serious resistance against the invader. At the beginning of the Prussian invasion, when Prussian troops were entering Poznań and a Polish infantry regiment was withdrawing to Kórnik [Kurnik], the Poznań burghers were not moved by this to any great extent. This passivity must puzzle us all the more since it was precisely they who had played a great role in the movement that led to the Constitution of 3 May, and at one time maintained lively relations with the plenipotentiary of the towns of the Poznań district at the Four-Year Sejm, Józef Wybicki. A few months later, in the year 1792, when danger began to threaten the new constitution, the Poznań burghers were ready to stand in defence of the endangered order. This is stated plainly in the letter of the then syndic and town councillor Sobolewski of 25 May, in which he wrote to Wybicki that among the burghers "zeal is growing for putting up lanterns for the opponents of the constitution"; Sobolewski himself gave his assurance "that if he heard anyone speaking against the constitution", he would be "the first to put the noose" on him. And so the calm behaviour of the inhabitants of Poznań at the moment when Prussian troops entered the city exceeded even the expectation of Möllendorff himself. Möllendorff
muszynska1947/21:
had expected disturbances in the city instead, and had assigned a strong garrison to it. For he knew that the nobility of the surrounding area was gathering in Poznań in great numbers and that the wealthy burghers favoured the slogans of the French Revolution. His fears nevertheless proved groundless. The capital of Greater Poland then managed nothing more than the tearing down of Prussian proclamations. Nor did the population of other localities react any more keenly to the Prussian incursion.

It was only the insurrection that was to rouse the Greater Poles from their slumber.

Chapter II

THE OUTBREAK OF THE KOŚCIUSZKO INSURRECTION — THE REASONS WHY IT DID NOT SPREAD TO GREATER POLAND FOR A LONG TIME
muszynska1947/22: The intention of saving the fatherland, threatened in its very existence, by means of armed struggle against the partitioning powers began to mature among the Poles in the spring of 1793. Numerous secret societies arose with the aim of preparing an insurrection. There were three principal centres of conspiracy: one in the army, which felt the humiliation of the country with particular keenness and which, moreover, as a result of the curtailment of the state's frontiers, was threatened in its own existence; a second among the "Jacobins" in Warsaw; a third among the émigrés in Saxony, extending in part to Paris. The moderates, such as Ignacy Działyński, colonel-proprietor (szef) of the 10th infantry regiment and the "soul of the conspiracy", such as Kapostas, a Warsaw banker, such as Jelski, starosta of Starodub and a deputy from the time of the Great Sejm, together with the emigration headed by Ignacy Potocki and Kołłątaj, intended to take up arms after suitable preparation and mutual understanding between the emigration and the country, and with support from abroad. The radicals, who were young and inexperienced men such as Józef Pawlikowski, a burgher's son and a writer of the era of the Four-Year Sejm, Eliasz Aloe, of a family of French descent
muszynska1947/23:
, Jan Czyż, a cavalry major, and others, wished to proceed to action at once.

How the conspiratorial activity developed we do not know precisely. In any case, the conspirators in the country were not idle. They intended to extend the plot to other provinces, as is proved by the sending out of emissaries, who soon reported the readiness of Greater Poland, Lesser Poland and Lithuania. They then dispatched a delegation to Leipzig, made up of Aloe and Walichnowski, to come to an understanding with Kołłątaj and Potocki, and with Kościuszko, generally marked out as the future Commander (Naczelnik) of the insurrection. According to a plan adopted, it seems, under the influence of the radical faction, it was intended to begin the uprising in the autumn, when the enemy troops would go into winter quarters. The outbreak was to take place simultaneously in many places, and Warsaw was to give the signal for battle. It was supposed that the five-thousand-strong garrison of Polish soldiery in the capital, aided by almost as many burghers, would easily overcome the eight-thousand-strong Russian garrison. Beyond this it was intended to rely on the regular soldiery stationed between the Pilica and the Vistula; of its total strength of thirteen thousand, six thousand would strike at the Prussian troops, and the remainder, together with part of the Warsaw garrison, at the Russians in Volhynia and in the Lublin region.

Kościuszko, like Kołłątaj and Potocki, took a sceptical view of the conspirators' plan. He judged that an outbreak of the uprising in the autumn would be premature, but, in keeping with the promise given to the delegation, he appeared on the Galician border in order to become better acquainted with the preparations. Meanwhile Zajączek, who accompanied him, went to Warsaw and from there reported to Kościuszko that the uprising could count for the moment only on the army, and in particular on the readiness of only two generals,
muszynska1947/24:
Madaliński and Działyński, and besides these on the common people of Warsaw and the petty nobility in some voivodeships, but nowhere on the help of the peasant masses. Under the influence of this news the future Commander was confirmed in his opinion that the time for action had not yet come, and in order to await a more suitable moment, and at the same time to lull the vigilance of the partitioning powers, he went to Italy. He left with the Warsaw conspirators instructions ordering them to form patriotic clubs in all the voivodeships and to awaken the people's awareness. He himself intended to seek a loan from the Committee of Public Safety, and to persuade the Porte and the Swedes to render assistance to Poland.

In the first days of November a delegation set out again, in the persons of Jelski and Gorzkowski, to Kościuszko, who was staying in Italy. It did not, however, receive a positive answer. Kościuszko ordered them to wait. The reason for the delay was, besides the failure of the conspirators to carry out his instructions, his conviction that foreign political relations were developing unfavourably for the insurrectionary cause.

Empty-handed, too, more than three months later, the last emissaries from the country returned from Kościuszko at Dresden: Prozor, Dmochowski, and Gliszczyński, who had arrived with a report from Greater Poland. This time, too, the same considerations as before, and chiefly the wish to await help from France, led Kościuszko to hold back the outbreak of the uprising. Unfortunately Kościuszko did not know that the revolutionary government had no thought of giving the Poles any real help. Its empty promises had as their sole aim the exploitation of the situation in Poland for its own plans in the struggle against the coalition.

The constant postponement of the outbreak of the uprising did the national cause no good. In the spring of 1794 the prospects of
muszynska1947/25:
success of the armed movement were no longer as favourable as in the autumn. The political situation had by no means improved. The conspiracy had not embraced the peasant masses, who, like the greater part of the landed gentry, were to remain indifferent in the year 1794. To make matters worse, the country's strategic conditions had deteriorated in the course of the winter. The Russians had regrouped the Polish corps in such a way that none of them could resist the Russian troops surrounding them; Madaliński's brigade was moved as far as Ostrołęka [Ostrolenka], and the greater part of the Polish forces was pushed into Volhynia, between two cordons.

The conspirators, however, could no longer delay. Ferment reigned in the army when the reduction of the Polish army from 30,000 to 12,000 soldiers was ordered. It was intended to begin military action even without Kościuszko. On 7 March the conspirators held their final deliberations in Warsaw, fixing the outbreak of the uprising for 9 March. General Igelström, however, learned of the meeting and ordered the arrest of several Poles, among others Kapostas and Działyński. The former happily hid himself in Kraków, but Działyński was seized on the Galician border.

The capture of the chief leader of the conspirators no longer halted the course of events, which tended towards armed action. On 12 March the bold deed of Antoni Madaliński put an end to all uncertainty. This general, initiated into the conspiratorial plans, did not obey the order to disband his soldiers. On that day he set out from Ostrołęka with 700 horse of his brigade, composed chiefly of Greater Poles, first north to Mława, and then southwards, moving along the new Prussian border.

The impression made by this step throughout the country was extraordinary. The carrying out of the reduction suddenly stalled. General
muszynska1947/26:
Igelström lost his head and for a long time could not reach a decision on action. At last he sent two small columns in pursuit of Madaliński, but they did not manage to overtake him. Madaliński soon crossed the border of South Prussia, and in the night of 14 to 15 March attacked at Szreńsk [Schrensk] a post of Prussian hussars, scattering it and seizing the cash box. He then turned towards the Vistula, and having attacked the Prussians again at Wyszogród on the night of 16 to 17 March, crossed the river the following night below that town, went on along the Bzura, and then towards the Pilica.

Command over the Prussian army in South Prussia was then held by the governor of Toruń up to that time, Lieutenant-General Count Schwerin. His headquarters was at Piotrków. At first, in consequence of information received from Buchholtz, he thought that Madaliński intended to enter Prussian service; only the entry of the Greater Poland brigade onto Prussian territory and the events at Szreńsk changed the whole aspect of matters. Schwerin therefore sent several detachments to stop Madaliński; they fought feeble skirmishes with him near Skierniewice [Skiernewitz] and on the Pilica, but did not manage to stop him. When, after crossing the Pilica, Madaliński halted at Opoczno, Schwerin supposed that he intended to reinforce his detachment there in order afterwards to break into South Prussia once more. For rumours had appeared that on 25 March an uprising, allegedly long prepared, would break out in South Prussia, and Schwerin regarded Madaliński as its commander. Madaliński, however, after a rest at Opoczno, went on further south, into the Kraków region.

The news of Madaliński's entry onto Prussian territory caused lively agitation in the Berlin Cabinet. Fear arose for the security of South Prussia, in which until then there had been stationed in the more important towns
muszynska1947/27:
and at certain militarily important points, apart from a few infantry detachments drawn from West Prussia, only 8 battalions and 30 squadrons, as well as 1 horse battery. To reinforce this inadequate garrisoning, Lieutenant-General Schwerin was to draw in, according to the instruction of 20 March, as many troops from East Prussia, West Prussia and Silesia as he should consider necessary to secure that province, and moreover, in order to achieve this security the better, he was to move troops into the Commonwealth and occupy its territory from the Vistula as far as the Narew. In this last case the Prussian king would be committing a new act of lawlessness towards the Poles, though this lawlessness had long been foreseen. Already at the time of the Second Partition, Russia, Austria and Prussia had jointly resolved to occupy the country in the event of disturbances in Poland; to Prussia fell the observation of the entire course of the Vistula and the greater part of Samogitia. At this opportune moment, the violation of the territory of the Commonwealth by Prussian troops was now announced by Buchholtz's diplomatic note of 24 March, sent to the Permanent Council. In it Buchholtz complained of the violation of Prussian territory by Madaliński and reported that the Prussian king, to secure his borders, would draw a cordon from Zakroczym to Ostrołęka. In reply the Permanent Council expressed the hope that the entry of Prussian troops into Poland did not signify a lasting occupation, and that the Prussians would make good the damage caused in connection with this entry.

As a result of the instruction received, Lieutenant-General Schwerin carried out the following changes in the disposition of the Prussian troops along the eastern Prussian border. From the area south of the Vistula, from Silesia, he sent Eisenhart's Jäger battalion from Namysłów [Namslau] to Mysłowice [Myslowitz], and Hanenfeldt's grenadier battalion from Nysa [Neisse] to
muszynska1947/28:
Tarnowice [Tarnowitz] and the vicinity of Bytom [Beuthen]; from Brzeg [Brieg] to Woischnik (?) [Translator's note: so printed, in the German form and with the author's query; probably Woźniki in Upper Silesia, German Woischnik.] and Częstochowa Rüts's infantry regiment; on the line Bytom, Siewierz, Koniecpol he deployed 1,000 cavalry from the regiments of Dallwig, Mengden, Manstein and Görtz; 5 squadrons of cuirassiers from the regiment of Prince Eugeniusz Wirtemberski he transferred from Oleśnica [Oels] to Częstochowa; Anhalt's infantry regiment he advanced from Głogów [Glogau] to Poznań; Schwerin's infantry regiment likewise from Toruń to Sochaczew and Łowicz; Lieberoth's Jäger battalion from Bydgoszcz [Bromberg] to Toruń.

There were likewise regroupings of troops north of the Vistula. Lieutenant-General Wolki concentrated on 27 March at Dobrzyń Thiele's fusilier battalion, 5 squadrons of Brückner's dragoon regiment and 3 squadrons of the regiment bearing his own name, and having crossed the South Prussian border on 1 April, reached Pułtusk and its environs 5 days later and remained there. Lieutenant-General Wildau united at Nidbork [Neidenburg] 4 squadrons of dragoons from Werther's regiment, Frankenberg's dragoon regiment, and the infantry regiment bearing his own name, and occupied the border at Mława. Major-General Günther, with his Bosnian regiment, which stood as garrison on the East Prussian border, and Rembow's Jäger battalion, set out from Königsberg towards the Narew to secure the sector between the mouths of the Omulew and the Bóbr. Favrat's infantry regiment, stationed at Brunsberg [Braunsberg], together with 1 regiment of grenadiers and 1 battalion, occupied the Vistula at Płock, Wyszogród and Zakroczym, and also took possession of the small town of Szreńsk. Bonin's infantry regiment, quartered at Grudziądz [Graudenz], was moved together with half a regiment of grenadiers and 1 battalion to Toruń, while with half a battalion it occupied the Drwęca [Drewenz] between Lubicz [Leibitsch] and Brodnica [Strasburg]. The rest of Wolki's hussar regiment took up position at Dobrzyń. General Brüneck, who held the supreme command in East Prussia, moved, to cover the treasuries
muszynska1947/29:
at Gąbin [Gumbinnen] (East Prussia), Bardeleben's dragoon regiment from Wystruć [Insterburg] to Stołupiany [Stallupönen] and Piłkały (Pillkallen).

Meanwhile, in Kraków, under the influence of Madaliński's movement, decisive events took place. To the city, which had been freed of its Russian garrison as a result of the concentration of all Russian forces ordered by Igelström, Kościuszko, who had been hiding in the vicinity, came on 23 March, and on the following day proclaimed the official Insurrection Act. The aim of the armed struggle became "the liberation of Poland from the foreign soldier, the restoration and securing of the integrity of her borders, the extirpation of all violence and usurpation, foreign as well as domestic, the consolidation of national liberty and of the independence of the Commonwealth". The Act was directed against Russia and Prussia alike. In its second, dispositive part it contained the organisation of the insurgent government. This government was represented by Tadeusz Kościuszko as "Supreme and sole Commander" and "administrator" of the entire armed movement, and by the Supreme National Council, appointed and organised by him. In the voivodeships the citizens were to form local Commissions of Order. A criminal court, composed of members appointed by the Supreme Council, was to punish with death crimes against the nation, and acts contrary to the aims of the insurrection.

For some days after the Act of Kraków Kościuszko did not leave Kraków; he was occupied with military matters. He set out only on 1 April and near the village of Luborzyca joined some of the Polish detachments, among others the brigade of Madaliński. The armed force numbered at first some 4,000 men, but it soon grew, owing to the peasants from the surrounding villages brought in by a member of the Kraków Commission of Order. At Racławice on 4 April a clash with the Russian army took place; Kościuszko, with the help of the peasant
muszynska1947/30:
masses, scattered the corps of General Tormassow. For the national cause this victory was of great significance, for it brought enthusiasm into the insurgent ranks, deepened confidence in the commander-in-chief, and above all cleared the way for a swifter spread of the insurrection.

For at the beginning of the armed movement insurrectionary enthusiasm had not shown itself decisively. Let the conduct of the inhabitants of Mazovia in the areas along the Narew serve as an example.

At the news of Madaliński's march, his ranks were reinforced only by a few representatives of the petty nobility, while the great landowners, in contrast to their wives, who sincerely favoured the uprising, preferred to sit quietly on their lands. Among the common people national awareness still lay deeply dormant beneath the cover of their own misery. When Prussian troops occupied this territory, the hitherto downtrodden peasant rather expected relief in his lot from the invader. Among the burghers there, the only opponents of the Prussians were those whose commercial interests had suffered as a result of the war. The Jews, having their own advantage in view, took the side of the occupiers, whom they considered the stronger. Only the clergy proved a determined enemy of Prussia.

Things began to go differently after the victory at Racławice.

The organisation of the uprising in Chełm Land and in the Lublin voivodeship followed. Most momentous, however, was the outbreak of the insurrection in the capital. The Warsaw conspirators, having learned of Igelström's planned stroke against the arsenal, hastened the outbreak of the uprising to the night of 17 to 18 April. In the struggle with the Russian troops and the Prussians reinforcing them
muszynska1947/31:
from the corps of General Wolki, the enemy was driven out of Warsaw. The new authority became the Provisional Deputy Council, headed by the newly elected president of the capital, Ignacy Zakrzewski. General Mokronowski became commandant of the city. On 19 April the inhabitants of the Duchy of Mazovia, together with the king, declared their accession to the uprising. The example of Warsaw was soon followed by Vilnius, which, on the night of 22 to 23 April, under the leadership of Jasiński, removed the Russian garrison from the city and created its own insurgent authorities.

Only Greater Poland did not stir. In 1793, when the secret societies arose, this region too was embraced by the conspiracy. Among the agitators active there were Gliszczyński, and also Wybicki, who found fertile ground for his work among the citizenry of Poznań, Gniezno and Kalisz. After all, both the chief leader of the conspirators, Ignacy Działyński, and President Zakrzewski were natives of Greater Poland. Nevertheless the insurrection was to break out there later than elsewhere, although the inhabitants of that land declared their solidarity with the Act of Kraków and felt themselves bound to fight in defence of the fatherland. What held them back from active action was the scattering of Prussian troops about the country, and above all Kościuszko's policy towards his western neighbour.

At first Kościuszko, as the future Commander, was undoubtedly resolved to act against the Prussians, when in mid-September 1793 he is said to have spoken these words to the conspirators: "I myself shall strike at Piotrków, at Möllendorff, with the troops that are between Warsaw and Kraków, and having cleared Greater Poland I shall turn towards Warsaw...". Fear, however, of inadequate preparation of the uprising did not then permit Kościuszko to carry out this intention, although the chances of success were considerable in view of
muszynska1947/32:
the small number of Prussian troops in the newly annexed territory. The Act of Kraków of 24 March, as we know, proclaimed a settling of accounts by force of arms with Frederick William II, when it expressed indignation at the falsehood, hypocrisy and deceit of Prussia and Russia and announced the restoration to the fatherland of its integrity and independence. To carry out that announcement, however, a struggle on two fronts was necessary. Yet Kościuszko, although he was devoted with his whole heart to the cause of liberty, would gladly have avoided that struggle. For that reason, no doubt, he passed over the best opportunity of striking at the Prussians right at the beginning of the uprising, when their mobilisation was only in its initial stage and when Lieutenant-General Schwerin felt himself so weak that he did not dare to heed the repeated summonses of Igelström and of the War College in Berlin to attack Kościuszko, in conjunction with the Russian forces stationed west of the Vistula, and crush the uprising in the bud. Soon the situation became so unfavourable for the Commander (his being pushed into a corner by the Vistula) that he could act in no other way than by proclamations. He then abandoned the idea of fighting for the western borders of the Commonwealth, and the work of the emissaries, supposedly already dispatched to the Sieradz and Łęczyca, Kalisz and Poznań regions in order to extend the movement in those parts and to carry it over into Silesia, could for the time being produce no result.

The policy of the Supreme Commander towards Prussia is characterised most eloquently by the instructions he gave to the president of Warsaw, Zakrzewski. He ordered him, namely, to come to an understanding with Buchholtz in secret and to declare that it was "only a war declared on him for policy's sake", and that therefore "let his Court give peace to our borders, and we shall not touch him". And indeed negotiations on this matter with the Prussian envoy went on throughout May. Hence, out of regard for Kościuszko's intentions,
muszynska1947/33:
efforts were made in Warsaw to prevent Buchholtz from leaving, when he received from Berlin an order to quit the borders of the Commonwealth. Unfortunately it was not suspected that detaining him suited the Prussian king down to the ground. For the order was only a formality, and Frederick William secretly instructed Buchholtz to remain in Poland for some time yet and to conduct negotiations, so that in the meantime Prussia might arm itself properly. For this reason, therefore, Buchholtz remained in Warsaw until 23 June, although he did not cease to complain, falsely, of being detained. Throughout this time he beguiled the Polish diplomats, with Dzieduszycki at their head, with the favourable attitude of his court.

President Zakrzewski himself took a different view of the relation of the insurrection to Prussia. A thoroughgoing patriot, he wished to extend the uprising to that region as well. For that reason he advised Kościuszko to send Colonel Sokolnicki there, who was ready to undertake the task, and as proof of the favourable prospects of the cause he cited the small number of Prussian troops in Greater Poland. In a letter of 12 May he wrote thus to Kościuszko: "There have come to me from the Greater Poland voivodeships delegates with an assured and settled plan of our uprising; these I shall send to You in person, Commander of the nation's rising, for they are worthy both of Your trust and of Your orders, and I assure You that they will not fail". Kościuszko, guided, as is known, by a different policy towards Prussia, did not avail himself of the services of his brethren from Greater Poland. On 22 May the delegation, with the chamberlain Moskorzewski at its head, returned to their family seats, bringing with them no signal for the immediate beginning of the uprising.

Meanwhile the Prussians' preparations for war pointed unmistakably to their hostile intentions towards the insurrection. Lieutenant-General Favrat, deputising for Schwerin, who had been on leave since the middle of
muszynska1947/34:
April, was accelerating the mobilisation, which until then, because of difficulties with equipment, had proceeded at a very slow pace. He contributed to the establishment in Poznań of a field war commissariat, and, anticipating a possible offensive against Kościuszko, he ordered the magazines to be filled and pushed forward. For the same reasons he drew from Nysa into the vicinity of Bytom the remainder of Hanenfeldt's infantry regiment, and from Reichenbach Schulz's Jäger battalion. He then concentrated near Łowicz and Częstochowa the corps that until then had been scattered along the left bank of the Vistula over a distance of 40 miles, so as, in the event of an attack by the insurgents on South Prussia, to hold them back until the mobilisation was completed and reinforcements had arrived.

Soon the Prussians' preparations for war were nearing completion. During May and at the beginning of June reinforcements arrived. From Silesia came Pellet's Jäger battalion and Dolfs's cuirassier regiment; from the Mark the infantry regiments of Lichnowski, Jung-Schwerin and Frankenberg; from Pomerania the infantry regiment of Klinkowström and the dragoons of Bieberstein; from West Prussia the infantry regiments of Amandrüz and Bonin; Anhalt's infantry regiment left Poznań and Gniezno and joined Favrat's field army, and to garrison the two Greater Poland cities Kunheim's regiment came up from Frankfurt an der Oder.

At the beginning of June the disposition of the Prussian army assigned to cover the borders and to take the offensive against the Poles was as follows: South of the Vistula, on the Pilica, stood Lieutenant-General Favrat with 17 battalions, 27 squadrons and 2½ batteries. Major-General Rüts, with 7 battalions and a cavalry detachment totalling 1,300 horse, guarded the Upper Silesian border. To cover the magazines there stood at Piotrków 3 battalions, and at Częstochowa 1 battalion and 2 squadrons
muszynska1947/35:
. With the exception of 4 battalions from Rüts's corps, this entire force was already mobilised. In addition, the following still unmobilised units stood at the main centres: Lichnowski's regiment with a grenadier battalion at Poznań, with its 1st battalion at Wieluń, with its second at Częstochowa; Jung-Schwerin's regiment with a grenadier battalion at Piotrków, with its 1st battalion at Łowicz, its 2nd at Sędzin [Translator's note: probably the village in Kuyavia; author to confirm.] and Koło; Frankenberg's depot battalion (Depot-Bataillon) at Kalisz and Krotoszyn [Krotoschin]. General Bonin, with 8 battalions, watched the Prussian border against the Poles. He also exercised command over the Russian troops who had fled from Warsaw.

The Prussian forces north of the Vistula, on the Narew, were at first commanded by Generals Wildau, Günther and Wolki, who skirmished from time to time with the insurgents. In the second half of May the place of all these commanders was taken by Lieutenant-General v. Schönfeldt. His corps numbered 12 battalions, 32 squadrons and 1½ batteries.

In East Prussia, near Stołupiany, stood General Brüneck at the head of 7 battalions and 20 squadrons.

In the theatre of operations there were magazines: principal ones at Częstochowa, Piotrków and Płock, and staging magazines, for a period of 4 weeks, at Sieradz and Łęczyca. At the end of May the magazines and field bakeries intended to supply Rüts's corps were moved forward to the vicinity of Katowice [Kattowitz] and to Bytom; those intended for Favrat's corps, to Siewierz, Żarki and Koniecpol. Bonin's corps and the Russian troops subordinate to him had a magazine at Łowicz at their disposal. For Schönfeldt's corps a staging magazine was established at Zakroczym.

Soon the movements of the Prussian army were to be directed more closely by King Frederick William II himself.

On 12 May he decided to set out for Poland. Hitherto an ardent champion of the struggle against revolutionary France, he yielded to the
muszynska1947/36:
persuasions of Lucchesini and of his adjutant, Colonel Manstein, to reach for the easier booty in Poland. Having left Berlin on 14 May, the Prussian king arrived two days later in Poznań and took up residence in the suburb of Kundorf, in the small house of a citizen of Poznań, Klug. On the same day there appeared, issued in Poznań, a proclamation summoning Prussian subjects in Polish service to enter the Prussian ranks. After a stay of nearly two weeks the king left Poznań and, accompanied by the crown prince and Prince Ludwik Wirtemberski, proceeded via Wrocław [Breslau] and Lubliniec [Lublinitz] to Favrat's army.

That same Favrat, in May, when Kościuszko was occupied at the camp near Połaniec with organising an armed force, was planning an offensive on Kraków. He had been entertaining the intention for a long time, as the measures he carried out immediately after taking over the command would suggest. He even made the first moves, but owing to the slow movements of his troops and the impossibility of coming to an understanding with the Russian general Denisov, who was to support him in the whole undertaking, he soon abandoned the march on Kraków. He fought only a skirmish with the insurgent forces, on 18 May at Skała, the farthest point to which he advanced on this march, but two days later he began a retreat towards his former positions on the Pilica. From the strategic point of view the undertaking of this action must meet with criticism. For although the possession of Kraków was important to Kościuszko, since he drew his manpower from there, yet the loss of that city could not have been decisive for his further conduct of the struggle.

Although in May no cooperation between the Prussians and the Russians came about, it was now only a matter of a few days. Denisov, after unsuccessful attacks on
muszynska1947/37:
Kościuszko's camp at Połaniec, was marching towards the Prussian border in order, on Igelström's orders, to join the Prussians. Having taken up a position at Szczekociny, he called on Favrat to strike jointly at Kościuszko, who was following in the Russians' footsteps. He met, however, with a refusal. Favrat, although at bottom he acknowledged the justice of Denisov's intentions, remained passive, contenting himself with moving from the Pilica to Żarnowiec. For he knew that the king was coming to his camp, and wished to leave to him the laurels of victory.

Yet even the king, after arriving on 3 June at Favrat's camp at Wola near Żarnowiec, did not at once resolve to attack Kościuszko. He wished first to await the arrival of the horse battery and at the same time to induce his opponent to send part of his troops back towards Warsaw, so as to defeat him the more easily once weakened.

To this end, General Frankenberg with the crown prince's corps was to march towards Warsaw on 8 June, while General Schönfeldt was to begin preparations for crossing the Vistula, in order to create in Kościuszko the impression that the enemy intended to strike at the capital. The manoeuvre failed, since Kościuszko had already decided earlier on the movements of his army. On 5 June news suddenly reached the royal quarters at Wola that the insurgent troops had begun a march on Denisov's position and had forced his advance guard to retreat. The Prussian king could therefore no longer delay. Fearing that the Poles might defeat Denisov, he immediately issued orders for a march towards Szczekociny. The battle was fought the next day. Kościuszko took the field with his 14,000-strong corps, of which roughly ⅓ were peasants, facing an opponent superior to him by 12½ thousand. In such conditions the encounter ended in a disastrous defeat. The insurgents' loss amounted, by Kościuszko's own estimate
muszynska1947/38:
, to 1,000 men killed and wounded, and 8 guns. To this must be added the prisoners, mostly wounded, whom the Prussians counted at 500 and of whom Kościuszko makes no mention.

The defeat at Szczekociny finally revealed the true intentions of the Prussian king. The mere fact of a hostile move by the Prussians could not have surprised Kościuszko. He had, after all, received from time to time diplomatic and military warnings to this effect, from within the country and from abroad; he had not supposed, however, that the two enemy armies would join so early. The Commander rather believed, taking into account the skirmishes with the Prussians, weak thus far and not sufficiently determined, that Frederick William would continue to hang back, and that he himself would meanwhile defeat the nearest Russian corps, that of General Denisov. Having accomplished that, he hoped to come to terms with the Prussians alone, and as a last resort to beat them. These intentions of Kościuszko's, justified though they were, were nevertheless obstructed by the slowness of the insurrectionary troops' movements. It was necessary to act quickly, which was possible only with the use of efficient regular forces. Meanwhile Kościuszko, leading with him a mass of peasantry, was forced to move so slowly that Denisov, withdrawing from Połaniec, drew near to the Prussians.

After the defeat Kościuszko fell back in the direction of Warsaw, in this case the best base of operations.

On 10 June he issued from the camp at Kielce an order by virtue of which he directed the commanders of the corps of line troops to advance into Prussian and Muscovite territory and to call the oppressed people to rise. At the same time, by the same order, he commanded the leaders of the levy en masse "to lead at once either volunteers or the border country people... into the lands torn from
muszynska1947/39:
the Polish Commonwealth, and afterwards also into the lands of the former Prussian and Muscovite possession, and to extend a hand everywhere to the inhabitants who wish to return to the sweet liberties of their own fatherland or who wish to win a free fatherland".

Two days after Kościuszko's by now official move against the Prussians, on 12 June, there appeared an appeal of the Supreme National Council "to the citizens of the Greater Poland province" calling for a rising. Depicting emphatically the falsehood, the hypocrisy and the unparalleled greed of the Prussian king, it declared the Prussian annexations "unlawful" and the voivodeships and lands of the Greater Poland province "indivisible parts of the Commonwealth"; it called traitors to the fatherland, and resolved to punish, those "who would insinuate any subjection to the unlawful power of appropriators and invaders".

Yet it was not then that the "revolt" flared up in Greater Poland; garrisons of Prussian troops that were still fairly strong stood in its way. Only later, after this region had been stripped of Prussian troops, which were used partly for the siege of Warsaw and partly on the Rhine, did the appeals of the Supreme National Council turn into deed.

Chapter III

THE SPREAD OF THE INSURRECTION INTO GREATER POLAND — THE INSURGENTS' ARMED MOVEMENTS AND DĄBROWSKI'S EXPEDITION TO GREATER POLAND
muszynska1947/40:
The events after the defeat at Szczekociny were not favourable to the insurgents. General Zajączek suffered defeat on 8 June at Chełm [Cholm], inflicted on him by the Russian general Derfelden. A week later came the capitulation of Kraków [Krakau]. The commandant of the city, Colonel Wieniawski, without having exhausted the means of defence, surrendered the city to the Prussians, and thereby Kościuszko's design collapsed, which was to hand Kraków over in deposit to the Austrians, whom he regarded as the best of the three partitioning powers. The unfortunate capitulation soon had its epilogue in the events in Warsaw. The people, stirred up on this account, carried out a lynching of the Targowica confederates. A further series of reverses was the unsuccessful expedition of Major Liberadzki to Volhynia.

Attempts to enter the Prussian annexation and the Prussians' possessions likewise went badly. Numerous efforts in this direction were directed northward. It was intended to break through the cordon of Prussian troops on the Narew, where from 25 June skirmishes with the Prussians occurred continually. The prospects of success were offered by the circumstance that the commander of the Prussian troops, Gen. Schönfeldt, did not have enough forces to secure well

Jan Henryk Dąbrowski. From the Winna Góra collections
muszynska1947/41:
a line of nearly 250 km in length. For this reason General Karwowski, a land general, managed in July to enter the East Prussian country, but was in the end driven out. At this time only the rising in Lithuania, Courland and Samogitia was achieving successes. Soon the most important event became the siege of the capital.

The victorious Prusso-Russian troops from Szczekociny were making their way there. Their march, however, by the road through Kielce, Końskie and Opoczno, with numerous rests, proceeded with such slowness that the Prussian king's original intentions, to forestall Kościuszko in the march toward Warsaw, came to nothing. For when Kościuszko had already on 28 June taken up positions at that city, the allies were to cross the Pilica only between 30 June and 2 July. Earlier still the Prussians had occupied the Bzura, so that armed insurrectionary detachments should not break through it into Greater Poland. The Prussian crown prince took up guard over this river until such time as the main army should advance closer to Warsaw, and on 27 June he established an entrenched camp at Potoki near Łowicz.

In the first half of July the Prussians and Russians drew up before the earthworks of Warsaw. The siege began, lasting over two months, from 13 July to 6 September.

After the Prussians' capture of Wola on 27 July, a period of little activity followed among the besiegers, while the opposing side for its part tried to act offensively. The Poles undertook a number of sorties against the enemy positions, and even tried to break through the cordon of troops surrounding the capital. In this last case, however, the attempts missed their mark. On the one hand there was a lack of capable leaders, and on the other the undertaking itself proved extraordinarily difficult. The attempts to cross the Narew and to spread the rising in those parts were renewed
muszynska1947/42:
as well, but only at Rzewnie and Słońsk were any gains achieved. Less often now was it intended to get through the division of Gen. Wolka, which guarded the ground between Zakroczym and Zegrze and formed part of the right wing of Schönfeldt's corps. One of these plans was Madaliński's expedition. On 24 August Madaliński wanted to cross the Narew between Dęby and Zegrze, in order afterwards to cross the Vistula and cut his way through to Greater Poland. The Prussians, however, put up such strong resistance to him that he had to fall back.

Completely successful, however, was Bielamowski's reconnaissance, which this lieutenant, from Rymkiewicz's detachment, undertook around the middle of August. He set out from Warsaw with 40 horse from Dąbrowski's Mazur regiment by way of Buraków and the Kampinos Forest, and, keeping constantly westward by byways, reached as far as the Bzura and beyond, to Gąbin [Gombin] and Włocławek [Leslau]. This bold deed alarmed the Prussian officials, since Bielamowski in several instances took the cash boxes of post offices, excise offices and salt depots, and even intercepted a transport of money intended for the pay of the Prussian troops before Warsaw. To render Bielamowski harmless, a Prussian detachment was sent out from before Warsaw. Bielamowski, aware of the impossibility of holding out with his weak little detachment against the Prussians pursuing him, and seeing no possibility either of effectively supporting the armed force that was to be formed in Greater Poland, returned safely to the capital by the same road. To Kościuszko he brought the news of the insufficient number of Prussian troops in those parts. In the entourage of the Prussian king Bielamowski's expedition aroused
muszynska1947/43:
apprehension for the rear of the besieging army. It turned out, namely, that the weak Prussian garrisons in Greater Poland might not be able to cope in the event of possible insurgent movements there.

These apprehensions were not groundless. In Greater Poland a rising soon broke out, which was later to cause the Prussian king to withdraw from before Warsaw, and to inspire the besieged with new zeal.

Already in July the starosta of Śrem [Schrimm], Niemojewski, and the chamberlain Moskorzewski, sent as a delegation to Warsaw, began after their return, in accordance with the instructions, letters and proclamations of the Commander which they had brought with them, lively agitation, calling everywhere for taking up arms. They were assisted in this action by the women citizens of that region. Some of them carried about patents for voivodeship generals, colonels and majors, others, like Droszewska from the vicinity of Leszno, niece of General Madaliński, went from house to house and informed people in secret of the outbreak of the rising that was about to take place.

The moment was opportune. In South Prussia the Prussians had only 8,000 soldiers, distributed in the more important centres, whose purpose was to maintain communication between the army operating in Poland and the rest of the Prussian lands; the main forces had already been directed either to the Rhine or to Warsaw. This slender quantity of Prussian troops in the second annexation was strengthened by reinforcements that arrived in the middle of August. These were the infantry regiment Götze, sent from Silesia under Gen. Manstein, and further detachments of the cuirassier regiments Dolfs and Manstein, and another cuirassier regiment, that of Prince Ludwik Wirtemberski, dispatched from Pomerania. This entire force amounted to 1,500 men.

In the second half of August the torch of "rebellion" was raised. The armed movement was admittedly very weak
muszynska1947/44:
and often flagged, yet it must be remembered that the Greater Poles were for the time being dependent only on their own forces. For the help of regular troops promised by Kościuszko they were to wait for quite a long time yet, since as long as the enemy besieged Warsaw it was impossible to send it.

Nevertheless, small detachments of partisans were more than once able to harass the Prussians.

The first in Greater Poland to raise the standard of the rising was the castellan of Kuyavia, Dionizy Mniewski. On 20 August, with a detachment of Kuyavian partisans, he attacked the Prussian posts at Brześć Kujawski [Brest-Kujawski], destroyed them and took possession of the town treasuries. There fell then "the valiant citizen Skarbek", and "Trzebuchowski, deputy for Kuyavia, made a colonel of the rising, and Wichrowski and Kosiński, citizens, contributed much to this rising". From Brześć Mniewski hastened to Włocławek and halted there on 22 August. In driving out the town's garrison, Lieutenant Marwitz of Alt-Pfuhl's regiment and several soldiers fell. An hour later 11 boats with ammunition, intended for the Prussian besieging army, came up the Vistula from Grudziądz. Taking advantage of the opportunity, Mniewski with his detachment struck at the Prussians escorting the boats. The attack succeeded. Thirteen Prussians fell, and the whole transport fell into the insurgents' hands. Being unable to use all the ammunition, the Poles sank the greater part of it. For themselves they kept 100 barrels of powder, of which, however, 3 blew up. After accomplishing so bold a deed, Mniewski's insurgents made camp near Włocławek on the road leading to Brześć. According to further reports carried by the newspaper then appearing in Poznań, the "Südpreussische Zeitung", an entrenched camp of the Kuyavian insurgents was also supposed to be at Radziejów, from where through the surrounding country as far as Toruń there spread
muszynska1947/45:
circulars signed by Mniewski and dated at Nieszawa. In the same newspaper there appeared at the same time a report of the appearance in the forest near Rypin in Dobrzyń Land of 100 armed peasants under the leadership of Zieliński, a native of the village of Skąpe. Lieutenant Branky, who had set out against them, was captured, whereupon the treasuries in Rypin fell into the hands of the insurgents.

While these things were happening in Kuyavia, the inhabitants of the other voivodeships likewise set about action.

In the Poznań voivodeship, citizens such as Hipolit Rogaliński, Józef Niemojewski, Antoni Gliszczyński, Józef Miaskowski, Antoni Wyganowski, Hieronim Jaraczewski, Wojciech Sadowski, Sebastian Bieńkowski, Ireneusz and Bonawentura Koczorowski, Piotr Zaremba and Jan Zembrzuski gathered on 21 August at a general assembly in Kościan, resolving to act at once. First they seized the Prussian magazine in Śrem and set up an insurgent camp near that town. From there, 600 horse strong, they moved towards Rąbiń, where they drew up and swore the insurrection act. At the same time they issued a proclamation calling on the peasants to join their ranks, promising each, as a reward, a reduction by half of the dues to the lord. At Rąbiń, too, members were appointed to the insurgent authorities for the Poznań voivodeship, that is, to the Commission of Order and the criminal court. The first of these consisted of: Celestyn Sokolnicki, Józef Jaraczewski, Hipolit Rogaliński, Antoni Wyganowski, Antoni Gliszczyński, Jan Zembrzuski, Józef Sczaniecki, Piotr Zaremba, Rev. Śmigielski, Ignacy Kurowski, Hieronim Jaraczewski and Stanisław Mycielski. The criminal court was made up of: Wojciech Węgorzewski, Józef Miaskowski, Ireneusz Koczorowski, Faustyn Zakrzewski, Eustachy Kowalski, Ignacy
muszynska1947/46:
Wilczyński, Wit Pomorski, Antoni Żółtowski. From Rąbiń the insurgents moved under Niemojewski, chosen general for the Poznań voivodeship, to Śmigiel [Schmiegel], where the inhabitants declared for the uprising and handed over whatever arms each had. From there they proceeded in turn to Racot, whence their detachment then set out for Kościan and there, on 31 August, fell by surprise upon the already mentioned General Manstein, who had arrived with 150 horse and, having garrisoned Leszno and Wschowa, was marching on Poznań. During the attack the insurgents captured the general's adjutant and took 6 horses. But Manstein soon recovered the adjutant, and the insurgents had to fall back before him with a loss of 16 men and made for the village of Mchy. Manstein, who had lost 5 men in the skirmish and had 20 wounded, did not continue his march but set out on the return road to Leszno and Wschowa. In the palace of the Sułkowski princes at Rydzyna [Reisen], near Leszno, all the arms were confiscated on his orders on 1 September, namely 6 large cannon, 1 small cannon and 31 old rifles, 9 sabres, 4 rapiers, pistols, etc..

Independently of the insurgents who had gathered under Niemojewski's leadership, other armed detachments were also active in the Poznań voivodeship. Thus, according to the memoir of Adam Turno, there assembled on 22 August in the village of Morków in the Leszno district "some 2,000 of the people, infantry for the most part armed with scythes, and cavalry of nearly 200 horse". Unfortunately, however, the commander of the insurgents, Bolesz, proved a most imprudent man. "Having taken up quarters in the manor house with all the citizens, and having set no picket or guard even on the chimney, he ate and drank in peace. Following the commandant's example the peasantry too "drank on the highway, having stood their scythes in the stable in the yard". Such carelessness soon brought disastrous
muszynska1947/47:
consequences in its train. Unexpectedly there arrived at Morków the detachment of Czettritz's hussars, subordinate to Manstein, who took away the scythes, wounded 8 insurgents and took 30 prisoner. "The commandant with the other gentlemen" saved himself by flight through the windows. Only the village head from Koronowo, who stood with his men on a hill beyond the village, suffered no loss and withdrew safely; the rest of the insurgents were dispersed.

Another insurgent episode took place in the district of Rawicz, at Jutrosin. The armed movement in that small town began through the doing of the mayor Walenty Zatorski, the parish priest Gogolewski, Skoroszewski, the leaseholder of the parish estate at Dubin, and a Mr Budziszewski. On 21 August, for 1 o'clock in the afternoon, Mayor Zatorski summoned the burghers to the town hall, whereupon he ordered them to assemble in the market square and there await the arrival of Skoroszewski's detachment of insurgents, with which they were to unite and march on without delay. Whoever had no rifle was to stand at the place of assembly armed with a scythe, a pike or a pitchfork, and each was obliged to provide himself with food for three days. On 24 August a certain Umiński arrived in the town at the head of a detachment of 24 men and 4 wagons, took down the Prussian eagles and took, against receipts, a small amount of money left in the town treasury. He forbade the Prussian officials, on pain of death, to communicate with the authorities. The insurgents, however, were not masters of the little town for long. From Rawicz there came up Colonel Dossow, who, having just come from Silesia at the head of the 2nd battalion of the Götze regiment and 2½ squadrons of Dolfs cuirassiers, was marching by way of Rawicz and Zduny to Kalisz to cover the magazines there, and he began a search for the accused. The mayor was betrayed by his own farmhand, who, when seized, confessed that on his orders he had carried scythes
muszynska1947/48:
to the blacksmith. Nor did Father Gogolewski, hidden from them in a cupboard, escape the Prussians.

In the Gniezno voivodeship, in the part that came under Prussian rule in 1793, the most zealous propagators of the idea of insurrection were Józef Lipski, lord of Czerniejewo, and the Rogoziński brothers. The nobility from the neighbourhood of Gniezno declared for the fight against the Prussians, and succeeded in winning over even the peasants of that area and part of the burghers of Gniezno. On 22 August the insurgents arrived at the assembly point at Gniezno and the next day attacked the Prussian garrison, numbering about 210 men, and disarmed it. At the same time the Prussian emblems were removed from the official buildings, after which the citizens assembled in the town hall swore the insurrection act. Seated on the commission chosen for civil and criminal matters were: the castellan Walenty Godzimirski, elected chairman against his will and in the end removed as suspect; Korytowski, who succeeded him in that office; Józef Jaraczewski; the chamberlain Piotr Kaliszowski; the canons Loga, Skiwski and Murzynowski (the last soon expelled); Colonel Twardowski; the Protestant clergymen Bothe, Schocken, Koch and Hanke; the burghers Gostomski and Kłosowski; and several peasants. The town hall became the seat of the commission, from which appeals went out over the whole district calling the population to arms. At this call peasants armed with scythes and pikes began to stream in from all sides. The monastery of Wągrowiec [Wongrowitz] alone supplied 100 peasants. Near the village of Winiary they set up a camp, where the sense of discipline was instilled in the masses with great diligence. Unfortunately, however, right at the very start, the camp did not escape quarrels. Lipski, the commander of the armed force, having fallen out with the Rogozińskis, all but cut down one of the brothers. The peasantry, again, rose against the nobility, regarding some of them, such as, for example,
muszynska1947/49:
Count Wołłowicz of Witkowo, as traitors. The dissensions were all the more deserving of condemnation because the arrival of Prussian troops from Poznań was expected at any moment. To prevent the German officials from reporting everything that had happened to their superiors in Poznań, all the Prussian officials were imprisoned on 24 August in the Franciscan monastery. On 3 September the commandant of Poznań, Colonel Diether, came up with one battalion, three squadrons and as many guns. The insurgents, with whom the Kalisz and Poznań voivodeships under Niemojewski had by that time already joined, withdrew before the Prussians in the direction of Słupca. For there the union of all the voivodeship risings was to take place. In the haste with which the departure was made, 2 cannon and part of the magazine were left behind in Gniezno, but, most important of all, the order to withdraw the post at the Franciscan monastery was forgotten. Made up of 30 peasants, it at first would not give way, but in the end fled. Only two peasants from Żerniki held out to the last with scythes in their hands, until they fell to enemy bullets. In recognition of their sacrifice the Poles later laid their bodies in the cemetery of the Franciscan monastery near the tomb of the Blessed Yolanda. Col. Diether, having carried out a search for arms in the monastery and set the Prussian emblems up again in the town, marched back to Poznań. The released officials went with him.

We must now sketch in turn the early history of the insurrection in the south-eastern part of Greater Poland, in the neighbourhood of the upper Warta and Prosna.

In the Sieradz voivodeship, after consultations among the more eminent citizens at the house of the starosta of Brodnica, Ignacy Błeszyński, in Złoczów, they assembled in arms on 23 August in the forest near Sieradz. Those who
muszynska1947/50:
had no firearms came supplied with iron rails, beaten flat in the shape of broadswords. On the following day, at one o'clock at night, after prior agreement with the inhabitants of Sieradz, they fell unexpectedly upon the Prussian garrison in the town, which consisted of 46 soldiers.

The surprised Prussians shut themselves up in the town hall, but after an hour's resistance they surrendered, losing to the victors a rich magazine and a cash box containing 700 thalers. The prisoners taken, after swearing that they would never take up arms against the Poles, were sent by the insurgents, together with the Prussian officials, to the Silesian border. On the same day Lipski and Zbijewski were elected land generals, the Rev. Prelate Ostrowski, who had arrived at the insurgent camp with a detachment of 20 men, was made a rotmistrz (cavalry captain), and a civil-military commission and a criminal court were called into being. An expedition to Łęczyca undertaken on 6 September to attack the garrison there did not succeed, and the reserve of 50 men left behind in Sieradz for that time had to retreat before the troops of Major Bonin, who was leading from Silesia a grenadier battalion from Pfuhl's regiment to cover the magazines at Sieradz and Kalisz . Bonin took cruel revenge on the people of Sieradz for their joining the rising.

For he plundered the town and the surrounding country, then set out toward Piotrków, and, having received a relief force of 150 infantry and 800 cavalry, turned through Sieradz toward Kalisz. On the way he seized the castellan of Wieluń, Karśnicki, the master of the horse Bartochowski, and the citizen Bąkowski, whom he put in chains and sent off to the Silesian fortress at Nysa. At that time even several women fell at the hands of the Prussians. Thus there were murdered the rotmistrz's wife Kożmińska, Miss Gątkiewiczówna, and the citizen Krąkowska, who was cut down with broadswords.
muszynska1947/51: Kościuszko's proclamations were brought to the neighbourhood of Wieluń by the citizen Konopnicki. Psarski, podkomorzy of Wieluń and owner of numerous estates, contributed greatly to the outbreak of the rising in those parts. He arrived in Wieluń on 26 August with his sons, his son-in-law Ciemniewski and his servants, took up quarters at an inn, and ordered the court official he had summoned to enter an insurrection act in the castle-court registers. Despite his threats he was unable to induce the authority to carry out this legal formality, but in return the town council and the officials swore to him an oath of fidelity to the national cause. On that same day Psarski set out for the village of Naramice to persuade Józef Stokowski to take command of the rising in the district. His son Mikołaj he sent to Opajowice, the estate of the citizen Topolski, where on that day the local nobility gathered in large numbers, so that he might call them to arms. On the next day many of the nobility, armed and mounted, arrived in Wieluń. Among those assembled confidence in success grew. Still on that same day, 27 August, the rising was proclaimed in the Wieluń and Ostrzeszów [Schildberg] districts, Stokowski was entrusted with the dignity of general, and a commission for civil and criminal matters was appointed. To the membership of this authority were called Psarski, Ciemniewski and Wierzylecki, who summoned the inhabitants of the surrounding towns and villages to declare themselves for the rising. Soon further ordinances of the commission appeared, directing the population to arm, to prepare pikes and scythes, to hand over to the commissariat, against receipts, the taxes and goods that the commander of the armed detachments, Stokowski, might demand, to detain all Prussian transports and mail, and finally to send spies and suspect persons before the criminal court. For the success of the insurrection services were held in the churches, and the priests read proclamations from the pulpits, endeavouring to convince the people of the impor-
muszynska1947/52:
tance of the moment. Since the commission's chief concern was to have a suitable armed force, at the end of August Michał Jerlicz, formerly a colonel in the Polish army, was ordered, under threat of punishment, to see to its formation from various fugitives, riflemen and cantonists. The craftsmen were ordered to work on the making of the things needed for the army, and the Jews of Działoszyn were to supply arms and ammunition. In the summonses that were sent out in the neighbourhood of Wieluń and Ostrzeszów, dated 15 August and signed by Stokowski, the nobility were called upon to present themselves under arms. Whoever could not come in person was obliged to send substitutes. From the noble estates one recruit was to be supplied for every 5 houses, and from the royal and ecclesiastical estates two in the same proportion. In the small town of Grabów in the Ostrzeszów district the armed movement had begun earlier, on 23 or 24 August. At that time a detachment of insurgents under the command of Kazimierz Madaliński and Jabłkowski came to the town; they received from the town council and the burghers an oath of fidelity to the fatherland and took the cash box. To complete the account of the events that took place in these parts, it must be added that Psarski summoned 12 citizens from Kępno [Kempen] to Ostrzeszów, swore them in, and chose 4 of them for the Commission of Order and as many for the criminal court. At Bobrów he urged the burghers to rise against the Prussians, set up insurgent authorities, and ordered the collection of a double hearth tax and of the "ofiary".

In the Kalisz voivodeship the insurrection was proclaimed on 22 August; Paweł Skórzewski became commander of the armed force. Jan Sieroszewski, a former colonel of the Bar Confederation, took a lively part in the rising in this land. In the middle of August Sieroszewski, having received
muszynska1947/53:
the summons and patent from Kościuszko, "in consequence of the proclamation sent to him was the very first to mount his horse and ordered the proclamation to be published at once from the pulpits." Later he gathered 25 horsemen and, on news that the town of Kalisz was fighting the Prussians, hastened there with them. The alarm proved false, but it aroused the vigilance of the Prussians, who placed two cannon on every road and reinforced the guards. The insurgents therefore withdrew, attacking on the way a detachment of Prussian hussars convoying wagons loaded with grain; 13 hussars and 700 korcy of oats fell into their hands. Sieroszewski then went with his detachment to Stawiszyn, and from there to the village of Kosmów, to rescue the citizen Kawiecki, whom the Prussians had seized for supplying arms to the insurgents. The detachment of Prussian soldiers conveying the prisoner, at the sight of the insurgents, retreated into the fields, abandoning Kawiecki. Sieroszewski dashed after the retreating men and took their whole detachment, consisting of 30-odd soldiers, prisoner. In this action the deserving citizens Maciej Konopnicki and Józef Cybulski fell. Sieroszewski then set out back to Stawiszyn, where General Skórzewski marched in with scythemen, whereby the insurgent detachment grew to 300 men. From there they pressed on to Koło, near which town a junction was made with the detachment of Andrzej Jachowski. The Prussian hussars were driven out of Koło and pursued as far as Kłodawa. 19 Prussians were killed on that occasion and 40 were taken prisoner. The Poles had 4 killed and 6 wounded. After this event there was again a return to Stawiszyn, whence, after a few days' rest, the insurgents went to Słupca, the assembly point of all the voivodeship forces.

Of the events that took place in the course of August in the Kalisz region we also have an account from the opposite side, the Prussians,
muszynska1947/54: It is the report of Lieutenant v. Milkau sent to General Manstein at Leszno . Lt. Milkau set out, by order of the commandant of Poznań, Diether, on 10 August into the Kalisz region with half a depot battalion from Frankenberg's regiment and 1 cannon, to cover the magazines at Koło and Konin. On 23 August it was reported to him at Koło that the insurgents, whose gathering had long been rumoured, were planning a simultaneous attack on Koło and Konin with a force of 800 men. From Konin, on the following day, Lt. v. Prittwitz, who was stationed there as garrison, informed him that the insurgents had likewise gathered in large numbers in the neighbourhood of Miłosław and intended on the next day to go to Słupca with a detachment of 400 armed men, as a result of which communication with Poznań would be cut. Shortly before that he had also received news from Kalisz of the appearance of insurgents at the gates of that town and of their firing on the guard. On 25 August Lt. Milkau arrived at Konin to cover the considerable magazine in that town. He learned then that a detachment of 300-400 insurgents had entered Stawiszyn. He remained at readiness through the nights, and his pickets were constantly alarmed. On 27 August the outposts of the insurgents appeared before Konin at a distance of half a mile. Milkau sent a patrol against them, but the insurgents attacked it. They killed 1 Prussian and took two prisoner. On the same day a Prussian detachment of 23 men escorting 25 prisoners arrived at Konin from Łęczyca. Insurgents attacked it on the way, between Koło and Konin, but achieved no success. On 29 August 200 armed men burst into the suburb of Konin and took the cash box from the salt depot there. Communication was cut in all directions and no one was willing to offer the Prussians his services as a messenger. On the following day, 30 August
muszynska1947/55:
news reached Milkau that the insurgents were uniting in order to strike at Kalisz or Konin. Having received an order to maintain communication with Kalisz and to join the garrison there, he set out on the road the next morning, although he was surrounded on all sides by insurgents. He nevertheless reached Stawiszyn without hindrance. There he learned that some 1,500 insurgents, foot and mounted, were stationed in the town. He at once formed his detachment into a square and moved on, and in passing Stawiszyn he fired the cannon several times, as a result of which the enemy withdrew somewhat deeper into the town. Soon, however, 300 peasants, armed with scythes and pikes, sallied out of the town to block the Prussians' passage. Under a hail of bullets they nevertheless fell back, and Milkau passed the town. During the further march he still had for some time to skirmish continually with the insurgents, who had set out after him from Stawiszyn but afterwards turned back. At night he finally reached Kalisz; he had 1 soldier killed and 1 wounded. The insurgents' loss was said to have amounted to 54 killed and many wounded. Two hours after the events that had taken place at Stawiszyn, another 500 insurgents arrived there, whereupon the whole host set out for Pyzdry with the intention of entrenching themselves near that town.

Having thus become acquainted with the beginning of the insurrection throughout the entire second Prussian annexation, let us move farther north, to that part of Greater Poland which the Prussians had already seized in 1772. This is the so-called Netze District [Netzedistrikt], forming part of West Prussia.

The commander of the armed force in those parts was Grudziński. His troop never numbered more than 1,300 men, yet it proved sufficient to alarm the local Germans and Jews. Hence requests for help were sent from Bydgoszcz and Inowrocław to the King
muszynska1947/56: of Prussia, but in vain. The Prussian headquarters reported that it could detach no troops, although in the whole Netze District there was only one company of invalids, at Bydgoszcz. On 26 August a detachment of insurgents entered Żnin [Znin], removed the Prussian eagles, seized the treasury, induced the citizens to swear an oath of loyalty to the Commonwealth, and issued a proclamation summoning the owners of estates to appear at Gniezno together with their subjects, bringing arms and provisions. These proclamations, as elsewhere, were announced from the pulpits by the parish priests. From Żnin the flame of revolt began to spread farther and embraced Szubin [Schubin], Barcin, Gąsawa, and even Sępolno [Zempelburg] in Pomerania. The Prussian authorities, seeing no other way of checking the spreading insurrection because of the small number of troops, issued proclamations calling on the population to remain faithful in their subjection and to seize the insurgents, and also recalling the benefits that flowed to it from Prussian rule. A circular was also issued at Kwidzyn [Marienwerder], warning the clergy against supporting the rising and forbidding clerics from South Prussia to enter West Prussia. For the Prussians considered priests very dangerous. They were, after all, above all the ardent propagators of the insurrection, and through their frequent journeys they could easily spread the watchwords of revolt. These measures were, however, ineffective. The rising spread, and even in Piła [Schneidemühl], so thoroughly Germanised later, it had its supporters. Everywhere the clergy and the poor nobility sincerely favoured it. Thus in the small town of Kcynia [Exin] Krupecki was a zealous champion of the insurrectionary idea. Seeing the sluggishness of the magnates toward the national cause, he compelled several of them to take part in the insurgent movement. There was, however, little benefit from the Poles won over in this way. Two
muszynska1947/57:
of them, Fryderyk Skórzewski and Baranowski, fled at the first opportunity to Piła, under the protection of the Prussian government. Nor did the starostas Dąmbski of Kaczków and Mieczkowski of Żelechlin prove any better; they lodged a complaint against the insurgents with the King of Prussia.

Meanwhile the Germans in the towns, unable to wait for the Prussian army for which they had petitioned, began to arm themselves. At Barcin and Łabiszyn [Labischin] they tried to repulse the insurgents, and in the latter place they captured 15 and sent them to Bydgoszcz. The insurgents, however, quickly dealt with such slight resistance, and still at the end of August the whole southern part of the Netze District was in their hands. Krupecki, having obtained from the Gniezno confederation the dignity of commandant, continued to bustle about the Kcynia area. The receipts he issued in return for the requisitions made in the name of the insurrection of the Gniezno voivodeship bore the inscription: integrity, liberty, independence.

The spread of the insurrection throughout Greater Poland was particularly favoured by local conditions there. For the whole country was covered with forests, the largest belts of which stretched along the Noteć [Netze] and south of the sources of that river, and farther along the Warta [Warthe] and the Prosna. So great a wealth of forests was of first-rate importance for guerrilla warfare. The individual detachments of Greater Poland partisans, who in the open field would not have been able to match the Prussian army, nevertheless found a safe hiding place for themselves once they had taken refuge in the forests. There the Prussian soldier, not yet familiar with the terrain, could not track them down, whereas they could undertake unexpected forays into the countryside, cut communications, paralyse the Prussian authorities, take money from the Prussian treasuries, and escape pursuit safely.
muszynska1947/58:
To crush the rising was therefore not easy. To secure the royal magazines at Sieradz and Kalisz, troop detachments arrived at the end of August under Colonel Dossow and Major Bonin, of whom the first dispersed the insurgents at Jutrosin, and the second did the same in the Sieradz region. At about the same time reinforcements were even detached from before Warsaw under Colonel Székely and Major-General Schwerin. The first went in the direction of Gniezno, the second to Kalisz. The rising in Greater Poland thus absorbed Prussian forces and constituted a successful diversion on behalf of the besieged capital, and in the end was chiefly to induce the Prussian king to withdraw from the entrenchments before Warsaw.

How, then, did the situation in Warsaw develop at this time?

At the end of August the enemy began to attack the city with increased strength. On 26 August the Prussians launched a violent assault and took Wawrzyszew and the Swedish Hills, but two days later, when they renewed the attack, they were completely repulsed. Rymkiewicz distinguished himself on that occasion by his defence of Bielany, being at once promoted from lieutenant colonel to general, and so did General Dąbrowski by his stubborn defence of Powązki. Facing the opponent on 28 August inspired the Poles with new zeal. Attacks were undertaken on the Prussian positions: on 29 August on Wola, though without success, and on 31 August on Wawrzyszew, and part of this outpost, lost five days earlier, was taken back from the Prussians.

The hearts of the besieged were also fortified by news of the favourable development of the rising in Greater Poland. On 3 September envoys from that land, the citizens Hoffman and Buchowski, appeared before Kościuszko; they gave an account of the armed movement up to that time in their
muszynska1947/59: region and asked for help to be hastened. On the following day Kościuszko shared the joyful news "with the citizens, inhabitants of Warsaw", and, pointing at the same time to the effects that the Greater Poland rising might have on the further course of the siege of the capital, included in the proclamation the following words: "This happy event will upset certain designs of our enemies, but may also drive them to desperate steps and to hastening against Warsaw all the exertions of their fierce and vindictive pride". Kościuszko also held up the Greater Poles as a model to the citizens of the Volhynia voivodeship and others "torn from the body of the Commonwealth by the last violent Muscovite seizure", reproaching them in a proclamation sent out on 5 September that, while everything that bears the Polish name seizes upon every means of throwing off the "insulting yoke", they alone "remain in sluggish tranquillity", and with these words he encouraged them to rise: "You have no army in your country, but you have people, and these people will soon become an army. The Greater Poles had no army, yet having made a holy pact in one day in seven voivodeships, they crushed the invaders and raised an armed force of more than ten thousand. They gave all their brethren an example, one very necessary for them, that a rising can be carried out without the help of an army, provided only that the interest of the Fatherland unites the minds of all, and the love of liberty kindles them with a holy fire. The difference of faith and creed did not hold them back from this work. Both of these are no obstacle to loving the Fatherland and liberty. Let everyone honour God according to his own faith, and there is no faith that forbids a man to be free. This truth united the Greater Poles; despite the multitude of people of various creeds in those parts they felt that they cannot be
muszynska1947/60:
happy without freedom and dared to be free. Do likewise yourselves".

The news of the Greater Poland uprising also found a lively echo in the chambers of the last of the Polish kings. On 4 September Stanisław August wrote to Naruszewicz: "Today God has given an event that revives our hopes: from the Wieluń Land as far as Kuyavia all the Greater Poland voivodeships have risen, joining themselves to the rising of the Commander," and at the end, as if by way of warning, he added: "whether we shall know how to make good use of it"?

Meanwhile the reverses of the last few days had shaken the Prussian army's faith in certain victory, and in the staff quarters they made a depressing impression. For 2 September the Prussian king was preparing a new assault, but on the evening of 1 September he withdrew the orders already issued and resolved to break off the siege.

The reasons for this decision were also weighty.
