Lieutenant-General Schwerin, ever cautious, who had returned to the army in mid-July, drew the king's attention to the shortage of provisions and ammunition, to the great number of sick soldiers, and to the possibility that even after the capture of Warsaw the weakened Prussian army would meet in the Polish capital the same fate that had once befallen Igelström's garrison; finally he put forward the strongest argument, namely he pointed to the ever more violent spread of the insurrection in Greater Poland and advised that peace be restored there first. In addition, relations with the commander of the Russian forces, General Fersen, which had long been strained, had worsened, and from Vienna came word that Austria, which at the beginning of July had itself brought its troops into the territory of the Commonwealth, would not support the besiegers with troops. This sufficed to convince the king of the pointlessness of continuing the siege. Not wishing to expose his army to greater danger, and above all not wishing to
muszynska1947/61:
have behind his back a country engulfed in the fire of revolt, Frederick William began the retreat from the entrenchments of the capital.

In the night of 5 to 6 September the Prussians began to draw in their troops. During this operation, so as not to draw the attention of the besieged, guns thundered incessantly and watch fires burned. After the guns withdrawn from the trenches and the baggage had been transported away, the individual corps marched off. On 5 September General Amandrüz set out for Zakroczym in order to join the corps on the Narew. On the same day General Frankenberg began his march toward the Bzura by the road through Sochaczew, and General Elsner turned southwest by way of Mszczonów to suppress the insurrection between the Vistula and the Silesian border. At the same time General Pollitz was detached to the Pilica to take over the command of the troops there. On the morning of 6 September the main army under General Bonin and the heir to the throne set out toward Raszyn. Following the Prussians' example, General Fersen also left his position before Warsaw and made for Piaseczno, in order afterwards to cross the Vistula and cooperate with the Russian corps operating in Lithuania.

The unexpected withdrawal of the enemy troops from the entrenchments of Warsaw filled the hearts of its inhabitants with joy. The capital breathed again, but it soon became apparent that the situation was by no means easy. It was found that the Prussian troops on the left bank of the Vistula, though they had withdrawn a few miles, nevertheless continued to blockade the city. Their posts stretched without a break along the left bank of the Bzura and the right bank of the Pilica, and between these rivers, on the stretch from Łowicz to Rawa, the main army was quartered with a fortified camp at Chrzonowice. North of the Vistula the column on the Narew stood opposed to the corps of General Favrat,
muszynska1947/62:
but in Lithuania the insurgents were faring ever worse. After the capitulation of Vilnius [Wilna] on 11 August, the Lithuanian army resisted the Russian troops with difficulty and began to fall back toward Grodno and Warsaw. Only the events in Greater Poland were a brighter page of the uprising, although even there the situation was now becoming less easy.

The Prussian detachments under Col. Székely and Major-General Schwerin, which had been withdrawn from before Warsaw to Greater Poland while the siege was still in progress, were stamping out the insurgents there; and as soon as the siege was raised General Elsner was dispatched against the rebellious provinces and went to the left bank of the Warta, General Frankenberg toward the Bzura. The greater part of the Prussian forces, which until 9 September remained at Raszyn, then began a further retreat, drawing close to the borders of Greater Poland.

There, of the Prussian commanders, the most dangerous was Székely.

He set out from the camp before Warsaw on 29 August at the head of Hinrichs's rifle battalion and the squadrons of Trenck, Czettritz and Wirtemberg, by the road through Sochaczew, in order to rout the insurgents gathering near Gniezno. He did not, however, go in the intended direction, but on hearing of the notorious events in Kuyavia changed his route and made for Włocławek. Having reached it, he met with considerable resistance from the insurgents, from whom he captured 4 guns, but he could accomplish no more. For 600 armed peasants and 200 horsemen were moving west to join the other Greater Poland risings. On 8 September Székely sent detachments of cavalry after them, while he himself remained with the rest of the corps in Włocławek. Only when he was informed of an alleged assembly of all the voivodeship forces near Inowrocław did he leave a company of infantry in
muszynska1947/63:
Włocławek and set out in the direction of Toruń and Bydgoszcz to cover the rich magazines in those towns; he reached Bydgoszcz on 12 September. On the same day the Kuyavian and Sieradz insurgents took Inowrocław, seized the treasuries and the Bydgoszcz post, but on the very next day, on the march against Bydgoszcz, they suffered defeat at Rynarzewo at Székely's hands and fell back to the neighbourhood of Szubin and Kcynia. As a result of the victory Bydgoszcz was saved from capture by the insurgents.

In this short time Székely became a veritable terror to the insurgents and to the districts through which he passed. According to Rymkiewicz's words, his entry into Greater Poland was "like a violent storm that overturns and lays waste everything it finds on its way". Already on the day after his departure from Warsaw, on 30 August, he issued at Sochaczew a proclamation, which he ordered published as quickly as possible by all ecclesiastical and secular authorities. The four articles of this proclamation contained the broad plenipotentiary powers he had received from the king. Thus he threatened all those captured with arms in their hands with hanging. The same fate, or the penalty of life imprisonment in fortresses and in addition confiscation of property, was to befall those of the more prominent nobility who should be leaders or participants in the rising, and even their wives if they proved to be accomplices. Corporal punishment or death threatened also all those who hid insurgents on their estates and failed to report them to the nearest authority. Székely was likewise to seize suspected persons and send them to fortresses. All sentences were to be passed without prior investigation and without any legal formalities. Although in the proclamation Székely, on the express order of the king, threatened the penalty of death in many cases, in practice he did not dare to carry out this ruthless
muszynska1947/64:
threat. Fear for the fate of the Prussians in Polish hands, as we shall see later, obliged him to proceed more mildly. In return he strictly enforced the other penalties mentioned in the proclamation. In the neighbourhood of Gąbin, Gostynin and Włocławek he seized the leaders of the rising and priests and sent them to the fortress of Toruń. The property confiscated from the insurgents he used for his own enrichment. He simply stole whatever could be taken from manors, churches and monasteries, for which he earned severe condemnation even from the Germans of the day.

Yet Székely was not to rage with impunity much longer on the lands of Greater Poland. From Warsaw General Jan Henryk Dąbrowski was marching there with regular troops, a capable and valiant leader who was to win a complete triumph over the brigand commander. This was the help promised to the Greater Poles by Kościuszko.

Its dispatch was preceded by writs of the Supreme National Council of 6 September appointing several Greater Poland citizens as plenipotentiaries for the voivodeship there. According to extensive instructions the plenipotentiaries were to publish the declaration of the Supreme National Council of 12 June, which annulled the duty of obedience to the Prussian king; to swear the citizens to fidelity, obedience and defence of the fatherland; to call upon them to take up arms and join the army of the Commonwealth; to order that a foot recruit from every fifth hearth, and a mounted one from every fiftieth, "armed and clothed in the shortest possible time", be delivered "where the commanding general shall make disposition"; to collect taxes; to requisition against receipts the things needed by the soldier; to establish, together with citizens of unblemished character, a Commission of Order, which would see to forage and produce for the army and the whole armed force
muszynska1947/65:
composed of citizens, and to take into administration the national estates, namely those of the primacy and of the archbishoprics of Gniezno and Poznań; to seek out a citizen fit to be a major-general, ordering him to "gather military strength in his voivodeship and unite with the army"; and finally to inflame the civic spirit and to punish severely those "who should show ill will toward the fatherland". The dignity of plenipotentiary was conferred on: for the Poznań voivodeship, Hipolit Rogaliński; for the Kalisz voivodeship, Hiacynt Zakrzewski; for the Gniezno voivodeship, Nicefor Gorzeński; they were to send the Commander a report of their activities every week. On that same day, 6 September, there also appeared an appeal of the Supreme National Council to the Greater Poles, whose purpose was to strengthen the civic spirit among the citizens. It emphasised the service the Greater Poles had rendered to the national cause by their action in these words: "You have risen, fellow citizens, and God has not failed to bless your rising. Numerous hosts of hired champions trembled at the first sound of your endeavour, and those who had come with insolence to the capital of the country to threaten a free people and finally to put it in the chains prepared for it, fled shamefully by night, giving by their example a loud lesson to such invaders that the assailing of a free land cannot go unpunished".

Three days after the issuing of the appeal, on 9 September, a corps stood ready to march to Greater Poland at Młociny. In view of the anticipated clashes with Russia, which was drawing troops from Livonia, White Ruthenia and Ukraine, Kościuszko did not send many soldiers, wishing as he did "to make up for the deficiency in the person of the commanding general". He therefore entrusted the command of the corps to Dąbrowski, the more so as the Greater Poles had earnestly asked for it. On that same day, 9 September, Dąbrowski also received
muszynska1947/66:
an order from the Commander "to proceed with the army entrusted to him to Greater Poland by the road and by the means that his prudence and talents shall show him to be best and most convenient". The further words of this order ran: "He shall endeavour to unite as speedily as possible with the corps assembled in that province, shall assume the supreme command over them, and shall have the power to command and to issue his orders to all voivodeship generals and to all officers of the Greater Poland armed force, of whatever rank, to turn their detachments wherever he shall judge necessary; he shall confer with the civil government concerning the provisioning and supplying of the national army with all necessities. He shall use all his strength to harass the enemy and drive him from the invaded lands, to seize treasuries and magazines, in a word, to do the enemy the greatest possible harm and destruction; he shall endeavour to maintain the greatest possible communication with the main corps and its divisions, and shall give reports of his movements as often and as cautiously as possible".

Aware of the importance of the mission entrusted to him, Dąbrowski set out at once. He took with him the brigades bearing his own name and Rzewuski's, amounting to 900 cavalry and 1,000 infantry from the 4th and 13th regiments, together with 100 riflemen of Sokolnicki, recruited from Warsaw youth alone, and in addition 12 three- and six-pounder guns. The strength of the corps was soon increased by the joining of Madaliński's detachment, consisting of 600 horse and 400 recruits from the first regiment, together with 4 cannon. In quality the soldiery was mixed. The cavalry was the best, and among it Madaliński's brigade had already more than once given proof of its mettle; Dąbrowski's brigade, formed only during
muszynska1947/67:
the siege of Warsaw, was less practised. It was different with the infantry. It consisted for the most part of scythemen, and only the 13th regiment was wholly skilled in the handling of firearms.

Dąbrowski was accompanied on the march by Józef Wybicki, appointed on 9 September plenipotentiary for the Łęczyca, Kuyavian and Sieradz voivodeships. He was to remain constantly with the division of "citizen General Dąbrowski", and received from Kościuszko instructions identical with those that Rogaliński, Zakrzewski and Gorzeński had received three days before; with them he was also obliged to confer and cooperate.

Wybicki writes of himself in connection with this appointment in his memoir "Whether from his own conviction, or from the inspiration of President Zakrzewski, or finally at the request of General Dąbrowski himself, I do not enter into it, the Commander named me plenipotentiary with the corps destined for Greater Poland. For some days I resisted my nomination, for I confess frankly that it was easy to reckon that, despite the Spartan zeal of my Greater Poles, that small handful of regular troops which was coming to their aid could not in the end overcome the enormous Prussian force... Yet I yielded at last, as befitted a good Pole, to the Commander, and accepted with ample powers the instrument of plenipotentiary, which was very flattering to me".

Meanwhile, in order to cover Dąbrowski's march toward the Bzura, Kościuszko dispatched several detachments. There set out from Warsaw: Madaliński, with a force of 1,000 men, toward Witkowice; Kołysko, with a detachment half as large again, by way of Nadarzyn toward Bolimów; Prince Józef Poniatowski, at the head of 2,000 soldiers, to Mszczonów.

Dąbrowski decided to cross the Bzura at Kamionna, on the left wing of Frankenberg's position, and made the crossing on 13 September, attacking the weak Prussian posts
muszynska1947/68:
at Kamionna and Witkowice. Driven out of both places, the Prussians lost 100 men; several officers and 80 soldiers were taken prisoner, and in addition rich provision magazines fell into Polish hands. Kościuszko, informed of this event in a report, congratulated Dąbrowski on his success, promising to send "tokens of the nation's gratitude" for the officers who "distinguished themselves". A few hours later a detachment sent out by Dąbrowski attacked the Prussian detachment at Pieczyska, where the magazines "were taken despite the enemy's strong defence, and burned through carelessness". On the following day, 14 September, Madaliński joined Dąbrowski at Witkowice. Wybicki was present at the meeting of the two generals, and it is also his merit that Madaliński, although "the general senior in rank", submitted to Dąbrowski's authority. He was, after all, "only a soldier of fortune and did not have those talents which Dąbrowski could have acquired in the Saxon army", yet he continued to lead his own brigade.

To continue the further march in safety, Dąbrowski asked Kościuszko to order Gen. Bronikowski, who was standing idle with a considerable detachment, to join him. Bronikowski did indeed receive such an order, but sent out his infantry too late. For this reason Dąbrowski was unable, as he himself recalls, to strike at the rear of the enemy army marching on Koło and Radziejów, nor to arrive in time at Gąbin and halt that army's pursuit of the Kuyavian insurgents.

The enemy army of which Dąbrowski speaks was commanded by Major-General Schwerin, formerly an adjutant and favourite of Prince Henry of Prussia. He set out from Łowicz at the head of two battalions of the Kunheim regiment and 2 squadrons for the Warta region by the road through
muszynska1947/69:
Gąbin, Gostynin, Izbica and Sompolno. On 14 September he halted at Konin, sending from there 2 squadrons against the insurgents toward Koło. This small detachment forced the insurgents to retreat and inflicted on them a loss of 80 men and 2 small cannon. Two days later Schwerin attacked, near Konin, the Kuyavian rising under Mniewski, who had hastened there after the defeat at Rynarzewo. Having occupied Konin, he wished to move after the retreating insurgents to Koło, but learned that Dąbrowski had sent there a detachment of regular troops, 300 men strong, under the command of Gen. Rymkiewicz. He therefore did not go in the intended direction, but by way of Tuliszków and Stawiszyn to Kalisz, where a considerable magazine was guarded by only a garrison of 1½ battalions.

At that time Dąbrowski with the main forces, having before him the corps of Major-General Schwerin, on his left flank the greater part of the Prussian army withdrawn from before Warsaw, and on his right Colonel Székely, was heading into the heart of Greater Poland. He himself marched on Gąbin and Kłodawa; his right wing under Bielamowski went along the Vistula through Tokary toward Włocławek, his left under Madaliński toward Sochaczew, Łowicz and Łęczyca. On the way Wybicki issued a proclamation "to the citizens and inhabitants of the Evangelical confession, as well as to the so-called Hollanders in Polish towns", calling them to arms, and Madaliński intercepted the Prussian post coming from Łowicz. It contained very valuable correspondence. Thus there was found a letter of Frederick William II to Col. Székely with an order that he should enter into as few negotiations and promises with the insurgents as possible, and, when nothing was gained in that way, should at once carry out the instructions concerning the suppression of the insurrection; there was also a letter from the commandant of Gdańsk informing him that "because of the spirit of revolution making itself manifest" he had had to take arms from the citizens
muszynska1947/70:
finally a letter from Székely to the king, in which Székely reported from near Inowrocław that he had seized insurgents. They were: Stanisław Dąmbski, the cavalry captain (rotmistrz) Kownacki, Lt. Potocki, the castellan Bogatko with his wife, then the castellan's wives Lasocka and Mikorska with her sister, together with the citizens Sopliński and Korczelski, and the canons Osiński, Wochelski, Ostrowski, Złotnicki and Żynda, and the parish priest Piotr Osiński. Székely would gladly have hanged "some half a dozen" of those seized, had he not feared for the fate of the Prussian officials held in Polish hands. He therefore confined himself to setting the captives beneath the gallows in order to frighten them, after which he sent them all off to the fortress at Toruń .

In a report of 18 September Dąbrowski informed Kościuszko of the interception of the mail, but, being unable to entrust the "letters of much interest" which he would have liked to see printed, he confined himself to giving the most important news contained in them. He wrote at the same time that the detachment advancing along the Vistula had taken possession of the Prussian salt magazines at Tokary. The next day he reported that Madaliński had beaten the Prussians at Kutno, where there had been eleven of them, six had been taken prisoner, and the rest had saved themselves by flight. Although he had earlier received a warning from the Commander that the Prussians had moved from the Narew toward Wyszogród, he did not abandon the plan once conceived, but hastened with the corps to Koło "to save the union of Greater Poland." He merely asked Kościuszko that, in support of his expedition and to maintain communications, he extend one observation corps along the Bzura and another from Błonie to Łowicz.

At the same time serious changes took place in the Prussian camp. On 18 September Frederick William II left the army and, ill
muszynska1947/71:
and in very bad humour, made his way to Berlin by the road through Wrocław . Supreme command on the left bank of the Vistula was given to Lieutenant-General Schwerin. Before his departure the king gave him the following instructions: 1) to deploy the army along the Bzura, the Rawka and the Pilica, so as to keep Warsaw shut off at a distance and to prevent new corps from breaking through out of Warsaw; 2) not to strip the garrisons from the Kraków and Sandomierz voivodeships; 3) to suppress the rising in Greater Poland. It was a difficult task, and the means of achieving it were meagre, but the Prussian king counted in this case on the help of Fersen's Russian troops on the Pilica. He also hoped that Schwerin, better than other commanders, would manage to maintain good relations with the Russian headquarters and, by joint forces, to starve out Warsaw, hold the line of the Bzura and the Pilica, and above all defend the territories newly acquired by Prussia against the insurgents and against Austria, which was likewise striving for new acquisitions.

At the moment when Lieutenant-General Schwerin assumed supreme command, of the army that had taken part in the siege of Warsaw there remained in the fortified camp at Chrzonowice only 12 musketeer battalions, 10 squadrons of dragoons and the same number of hussars, one six-pounder battery and one field battery, and in addition two 12-pounders. The remainder of the corps entrusted to him was scattered over a wide area. Thus the corps of Major-General Frankenberg, with 6 musketeer battalions, 5 squadrons of dragoons, a detachment of 120 horsemen picked from among hussars and dragoons, and 1 six-pounder battery, stood guard over the Bzura from Łowicz to Kamionna. Major-General Pollitz, stationed in the Sandomierz voivodeship, guarded with 6 musketeer battalions, 1 rifle battalion, 4 squadrons of hussars and 1 heavy six-pounder battery the line of the Pilica from Nowe Miasto all the way to its confluence
muszynska1947/72:
with the Vistula. Further, in the southern part of that voivodeship, in the vicinity of Opatów, stood Major-General Lattorff with 1 rifle battalion and two musketeer battalions (all three unmobilised), and in addition a strong cavalry detachment, composed of 1,891 horse. The corps which Major-General Schwerin commanded, operating near Kalisz, consisted of 2 musketeer battalions (on a peacetime footing), 4 squadrons of hussars and 2 field guns. The detachment of Major-General Elsner, no longer so strong, composed of only 1 rifle battalion and 3 squadrons of hussars, operated in the vicinity of Leszno. Finally Colonel de Székely, with the same strength and in addition 2 field guns, manoeuvred near Inowrocław.

On news of Dąbrowski's march, Schwerin, on the king's advice, reinforced the Prussian posts on the Bzura, sending there the infantry regiment of Jung-Schwerin, 3 squadrons of Wirtemberg's hussars and 2 of Prittwitz's dragoons together with two field guns. With the help of these forces the Prussian commander on the Bzura, General Frankenberg, with a corps consisting of 9 battalions, 12 squadrons and 2 cannon, was to recover Kamionna or at least to prevent the Polish army from fresh attempts to break through toward Greater Poland, to garrison Łowicz and Sochaczew with strong forces, and at the same time, jointly with Major-General Schwerin and Colonel de Székely, to destroy Dąbrowski. Soon, however, General Frankenberg was relieved of his command, and his place was taken by Major-General Klinkowström, who was now left to carry out the orders given to his predecessor, and above all to restore Kamionna to the Prussians at all costs. According to a further royal order, Lieutenant-General Schwerin was to storm Kamionna with the help of 3 battalions of Rüts's from Pollitz's corps and a detachment of soldiers taken from the Chrzonowice camp, and afterwards to strike
muszynska1947/73:
from the rear at the column of Polish troops supporting the Greater Poles.

In carrying out the commissions of his monarch, the old Schwerin proved extraordinarily cautious and timorous. He was kept in this state by rumours reaching his headquarters which bore only too eloquent witness to the grave situation of the Prussians. It was said that the 4,000-strong corps of Prince Józef Poniatowski and Zajączek had halted near Kamionna, that an army of 5,000 had encamped at a distance of 2 miles from Błonie which might threaten Łowicz or Sochaczew, and that another detachment of Polish troops, numbering 3,000-4,000 soldiers, had pitched camp, as Jews reported, near Nadarzyn. All these rumours so affected Schwerin that he still held Frankenberg back from attacking Kamionna, ordering him to await further events, while he himself, in order to preserve for the king the whole of his acquisitions, saw no other way out than to withdraw his troops from the Sandomierz and Kraków lands or to obtain reinforcement of the army by fresh relief forces. On the strength of new royal instructions he tried to operate as circumstances required, but this too was not easy. Communications, increasingly obstructed, made proper liaison with the separate corps impossible. With Berlin there was a connection only by the road into Silesia through Częstochowa, and with the centre of Greater Poland it was at times completely broken. The commanders of the individual corps in this sector, receiving orders late because of the interruptions in communications, and unable themselves to send reports in good time, acted on their own and therefore rather chaotically.

This circumstance, as we shall see, was to have a very favourable effect on the course of the expedition to Greater Poland. Its commander meanwhile, having rested a day
muszynska1947/74:
at Koło, then crossed the Warta at Konin on 20 September and the next day encamped at Słupca. Here, on 24 September, took place the planned union with the risings of the Kalisz, Łęczyca and Kuyavian voivodeships and of the Poznań and Gniezno voivodeships. The latter two, two days earlier, in conjunction with the insurgent detachment of Krupecki, had clashed with the detachment of Székely's corps at Kcynia . The armed strength of the Greater Poland insurgents who had arrived at the assembly point did not exceed 4,000 and had first to be "regulated". It turned out that the cavalry, though on good horses, was badly armed and for the most part ignorant of the simplest rules of military service. Yet young men and decrepit old men alike had presented themselves, and all were seized by the ardour of love of country. The main voivodeship forces retained a separate organisation and entered Dąbrowski's corps as regiments of light cavalry. Employed together with the regular army on various patrols and pickets, they gradually, under the skilled hand of their leader, acquired a sense of discipline. The infantry, which in Dąbrowski's division was in general inferior to the cavalry, swelled the ranks of the regular soldiers. The whole strength of the corps now amounted to over 6,000 men, besides the 600 horse of Madaliński's brigade.

With such an army Dąbrowski set out in 3 columns for Gniezno and arrived there on 25 September. On the following day he sent to Kościuszko the citizen Miaskowski, "known to the public," with a request for the dispatch of a few 12-pounder guns and howitzers, paper money and more infantry. Miaskowski was also to renew the request that the corps stand at Gąbin, "not allowing the enemy to extend himself over the Warta and the Bzura".
muszynska1947/75:
In this case, however, a bitter disappointment awaited Dąbrowski.

The position on whose retention the fate of his entire corps depended had already been lost. Prince Józef Poniatowski, who had entered Kamionna after Dąbrowski left the line of the Bzura on 17 September, withdrew from there after a few days. In the night of 23 to 24 September word of this reached the Prussian camp at Potoki, but at first they were unwilling to believe that the Poles had vacated so important a position. When, however, a cavalry detachment that had been sent out confirmed the news, Colonel Keppern hastened with one battalion of the Frankenberg regiment, one squadron and four guns and occupied Kamionna. On the initiative of Captain v. Brodowski two redoubts were raised there, and the garrison was increased by yet another battalion of the Frankenberg regiment. In this way the division that had been dispatched to Greater Poland, surrounded on all sides by enemy forces, suffered a grievous blow, losing the possibility of joining up with Warsaw.

Not yet aware of his grave situation, Dąbrowski spent three days of rest at Gniezno with his whole corps, full of the best hopes for the future. "The 27th was devoted to thanking God for supporting, with His almighty hand, the prosperity and glory of Polish arms in this province". The suffragan bishop Szajowski celebrated a solemn Mass in the cathedral, concluded with the hymn "Te Deum", at which General Dąbrowski was present "with his staff and officers of the first ranks, with the heads of the risings and their foremost citizens". After the Mass "an excellent address, suited to the occasion, was delivered by citizen... Lipski, as head of the rising of this voivodeship. Once again they swore to live free or to die. This oath, repeated with enthusiasm even by feeble youth,
muszynska1947/76:
decrepit old men and the delicate sex, could not but be moving and draw tears... General Dąbrowski then invited everyone to a soldiers' dinner, where, with a modesty becoming to republicans, they made merry until evening". On the same day Dąbrowski and Madaliński issued a proclamation in which they acquainted the population at large with the plunder and cruelties committed by Col. Székely. They declared that all this had happened on the express order of Frederick William II, as was irrefutably proved by a royal letter, intercepted between Łowicz and Gąbin and now in their possession. They announced that in this letter the king expressly recommended to Székely that he set up gallows for the nobility and imprison them, and burn the letter "C" into the hands of the peasants, and that only the fear that a similar fate might befall the Prussian officials taken prisoner had kept Székely from carrying out the ruthless order. Yet this fear, as they demonstrated in the proclamation, was in vain. For Székely, as a "barbarian", did not know the magnanimity of the Poles, who abhor such deeds. Finally, the proclamation appealed to the Poles of the First Partition to return to the bosom of the fatherland, joining those who had come to rescue them, and to the inhabitants of both banks of the Oder, the former Slavs, the Brandenburgers and the Prussians, "subjugated for centuries by the house of Brandenburg".

On the following day, early in the morning, the Polish army left Gniezno. Dąbrowski sent a detachment of 200 horse under the command of the intrepid partisan Bielamowski toward Poznań, "to put it into the enemy's mind" that the Poles intended to attack that city. He himself, as he writes in his Memoir, could not march on Poznań, since he had "no more than 2,400 regular men, among them only 1,400 infantry and 16 pieces of
muszynska1947/77:
small-calibre guns", and with such a force alone to take Poznań "with fitting success" was an impossibility. Bielamowski's expedition achieved its intended aim. For three days the Prussians reckoned with the possibility of an assault on the city by Polish troops. They took Bielamowski, who had reached the very gates of Poznań, for the advance guard of Dąbrowski's corps and hid themselves in the city and in the entrenchments. The alarm of the commandant Diether was all the greater at that moment because he did not know how large the enemy was, while the newspapers reported that Dąbrowski was leading a corps of 18,000. Diether himself, it is true, had done what was in his power to secure Poznań and had already thought of strengthening the city's fortifications almost from the outbreak of the Greater Poland insurrection, that is, from 24 August. He therefore reinforced, and raised new, entrenchments before the Wrocław Gate and on the hill of St Martin, which was designated as the main point of defence; he then threw up a redoubt before the "Brumska" gate, at the spot where the Muscovites had entrenched themselves 23 years earlier. He regarded these measures as insufficient, however, and so, in response to his alarm about the danger threatening the capital of Greater Poland, the generals Elsner with a thousand men from Leszno and Manstein with a detachment half again as large from Kościan, by way of Mosina, were hastening there at a rapid march to help.

While Bielamowski was marching toward Poznań, General Madaliński at the head of 100 riflemen with two guns marched on Trzemeszno [Tremessen], into the region of Inowrocław, in order to draw the enemy's whole attention to himself, so that the enemy could not guess Dąbrowski's real intentions and hinder the corps itself in its crossing of the Noteć. The third column, dispatched from Gniezno and made up of Greater Poles, went under its general Lipski to Barcin and destroyed the Prussian post there. Dąbrowski
muszynska1947/78:
advanced with the corps in the direction of Łabiszyn "in order to meet Colonel de Székely at Bydgoszcz or Inowrocław. On the way the armed force grew, and "through voluntary ofiara the soldier abounded in plenty and almost in luxuries".

General Madaliński was the first to reach Łabiszyn, on 29 September, and he destroyed the Prussian post there, which defended itself fiercely in the monastery under the command of Lieutenant Beyer. In the course of the fighting 3 riflemen were wounded, and in addition the towarzysz (cavalry trooper of noble rank) Stan. Grabowski and the citizen Leszczyński from the Kalisz Land, who succumbed to his sufferings after 3 days. Dąbrowski estimates the Prussians taken prisoner at Barcin and Łabiszyn at 6 officers, 63 soldiers and 10 officials. Having spent the night at Łabiszyn, Dąbrowski intended to "fall upon" Bydgoszcz, while Madaliński was to keep watch on Székely. Events, however, took a wholly unexpected turn. Székely, having learned that Dąbrowski was standing at Łabiszyn, wished to forestall him in the march on Bydgoszcz. He therefore set out from Inowrocław at one o'clock in the afternoon and at twelve o'clock at night on 29 to 30 September attacked Dąbrowski's camp outside the town. He thought that in this way he would take by surprise the Poles quartered in the town and already felt himself certain of victory, since he estimated Dąbrowski's armed force at only a few hundred regular riflemen, regarding the remainder as a "rowdy rabble of rebel Greater Poles". He began the attack with guns, "so that the balls reached into the town", while he himself with his troops turned to the hill beyond the town and struck at Dąbrowski's left wing. He "advanced" with such insistence that it came to small arms, and "some wounded one another with bayonets". The fighting grew fiercer when Dąbrowski's brigade fell upon the enemy infantry with such courage "that it left its pennants among the corpses and only then to retreat
muszynska1947/79:
began." In the skirmish the infantry of Bielamowski's regiment held "most valiantly," sustaining, under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Mchowski, who "together with Captain Grzegorzewski distinguished himself," platoon fire that lasted nearly an hour. There was a moment when Dąbrowski very nearly fell into captivity, and only thanks to the help of the citizen Dziewanowski, from the Kuyavian uprising, and of Lieutenant Dąbrowski did he escape the hands of the enemy cavalry. The battle ended in defeat for the Prussians. Székely, leaving on the field 1 officer and 23 privates, together with many severely wounded soldiers and dead horses, withdrew under cover of night in the direction of Bydgoszcz, dragging behind him 12 wagons of the gravely wounded. The Poles had 7 killed and 9 wounded, and in addition 30 horses run through with bayonets. The most grievous loss was the death of Major Jarząbkowski of the 13th regiment, who "performing his duty with distinction," died the next day of the wounds he had received.

In pursuit of the retreating Székely General Rymkiewicz dashed off, on Dąbrowski's orders, with 800 horse toward Bydgoszcz and reached it without hindrance. Half a mile from the town he scattered the hussars who raised the alarm against him, then took the heights above the town, posting vedettes on them, while he himself halted with the cavalry by the forest in such a way "that everyone had to suppose that infantry was with him." The town itself, surrounded by an old and not very high wall, lay before him as on the palm of a hand. Székely stood beyond the town in the forest, on the other side of the water. From Germans who had run out of the town Rymkiewicz learned that there were no more troops in the town than three battalions of garrison infantry. He therefore sent a report to General Dąbrowski on the night of 1 October with the assurance that, having placed guns on the heights, he "held the town in his hand." He wrote that half of the corps would have sufficed to take the town, for he had found it "unprepared."
muszynska1947/80:
At the same time as the report Rymkiewicz dispatched a letter to Wybicki, entreating him, for the love of the fatherland, that in case Dąbrowski should delay in striking at Bydgoszcz, he should forget on this occasion that he was his friend, and make use of the power of the law entrusted to him by the nation as its plenipotentiary, and prevail upon him to take this much needed step."

Dąbrowski was at that time still at Łabiszyn, from where he had sent out numerous detachments to patrol as far as Walkowice [Wałkowice], Żnin, Rynarzewo, Strzelno [Strelno], Barcin, Pakość [Pakosch], Gniewkowo [Argenau], Nakło [Nakel], Podgórz near Toruń, and Inowrocław. Major Bielamowski he ordered to set out from the vicinity of Poznań toward Pyzdry, in order to observe Major-General Schwerin, who was supposed to be in the neighbourhood of Kalisz and Śrem. He did not move to Bydgoszcz with his whole corps, as he himself says, because he did not wish "to expose the soldiers and ammunition at such a distance, in driving the enemy from his entrenchments and storming the town."

Meanwhile Rymkiewicz's report settled the whole matter. When Wybicki, "full of satisfaction that Bydgoszcz would be ours," went to Dąbrowski "with the determination not to leave him until the order to march was given to the corps," he found him already "disposed" to this step. Dąbrowski only enjoined Rymkiewicz, before setting out, that, "since the whole fate of this expedition depended on the seizing of the heights," he should seek "by various means to hold on to them, and, having reconnoitred all the positions as exactly as possible," should man them with artillery, which would hasten the surrender of the town.

On the evening of 1 October, at 9 o'clock, the corps set off, and despite the wearisome night march it stood the next morning before Bydgoszcz. At once General Niemojewski was sent
muszynska1947/81:
out with the advance guard, in order that he should "move secretly along the forest to the right and occupy Bartodzieje [Bartelsee]." The rest of Dąbrowski's brigade, with 2 three-pounder guns, turned toward Wielki and Mały Wilczak, to observe the enemy and prevent him from crossing the Brda and the Bydgoszcz Canal. Dąbrowski himself, at the head of the Greater Poland insurgents and 4 battalions, moved out in 2 lines; on both wings of the infantry he placed the remainder of the cavalry; in reserve he left Colonel Sokolnicki with 1 battalion and several detachments of riflemen, while the guns he set up in front of the first line so that they could fire on the town and the Prussian artillery.

In this battle order the Polish army advanced right up to Bydgoszcz and took up positions near the Jewish cemetery. Székely, with three companies of Hinrichs's rifle battalion, with artillery and cavalry, stood on the left bank of the Brda; in Bydgoszcz there remained only 4 garrison companies under the command of Colonel de Witten. Before long firing began on both sides, but it had little effect. Dąbrowski, not wishing to waste ammunition, therefore sent his adjutant, Major Zabłocki, to Colonel Székely with a proposal to surrender the town. Székely, acting "against all the customs of war," replied that "either Dąbrowski had himself lost his reason, or he supposes that he has lost his," in demanding such a thing of him; that Dąbrowski "ought to know that he is dealing with the famous de Székely, who has beaten the French everywhere." Finally he threatened Major Zabłocki that, if he did not leave the town at once, he would "have him shot in the head".

Having received such an answer, Dąbrowski gave the order to storm Bydgoszcz. Four battalions
muszynska1947/82: of regular infantry began to attack the town from four sides. The first battalion of the 13th regiment, with 1 gun, struck under Colonel Burzyński at the gate on the Łabiszyn side; the second battalion of the same regiment, commanded by Major Szwykowski, advanced straight toward the sugar refinery; the first battalion of the 4th regiment, with 1 gun, attacked under General Rymkiewicz's command the Nakło Gate; finally the first battalion of the 1st regiment "marched forward, as if intending to enter the town between Łabiszyn and the Nakło Gate." Székely, wishing to induce Dąbrowski to send away a part of his forces and thereby to weaken the strength of the Polish attack on Bydgoszcz, began a manoeuvre in the direction of Czersk. There, however, the reserve under Sokolnicki was at once dispatched by the shortest road, and "with this relief force the detachment of Niemojewski, to whom the guarding of the Brda had been entrusted, was reinforced." The attack continued. When Székely learned that those 4 garrison companies would not be able to defend the town, he hastened in person with his corps to their aid, but arrived too late. Major Szwykowski at the head of his battalion had already burst inside the walls from the side of the refinery and, in street fighting, won the victory over the Prussian garrison, which defended itself for 2 hours with great stubbornness. At the moment when Székely came running up with his troops and was crossing the bridge over the Brda, a cannon ball shattered his left leg. Lying "on the paving of a street near the bridge," he called on the Polish soldiers for help, and then one of the scythemen recognised him and cried: "This is Székely, who burned and plundered us." At these words the soldiers threw themselves upon him, but he was rescued from the perilous situation by that same Major Zabłocki whom Székely had treated so badly an hour and a half before. The unfortunate enemy begged for forgiveness and for his life. "You would have received both without asking for them,"
muszynska1947/83:
Zabłocki answered, whereupon he ordered the wounded man to be carried to a nearby house and "decently provided for".

Meanwhile Colonel Hinrichs, who had taken over the command in Székely's place, seeing the Prussian defeat, withdrew with the remainder of the corps and with two guns in the direction of Świecie [Schwetz], losing "many captives" on the way. Madaliński dashed after the retreating force at the head of 2 brigades of cavalry and pursued it as far as Fordon. The Polish riflemen also went there, leaving their former position between Bartodzieje and Czersk. On that same day Dąbrowski extended his outposts toward Wtelno as far as Osielsko and Pałcz on the Vistula. In the battle, which was the bloodiest that fell to be fought in the course of the whole expedition, 100 Prussians fell, 50 were wounded, and 313 were taken prisoner. The Poles had 25 killed and 30 wounded. During the fighting, as Dąbrowski states in his reports, the Greater Poland scythemen distinguished themselves most particularly. Madaliński also stood bravely, setting a good example to his soldiers.

When the victorious Polish troops entered the town, they found the houses shut up, and the inhabitants of both sexes "made an immense outcry and lamentation, begging for life and mercy." From some of the houses shots were even fired; Dąbrowski, however, ordered these to be opened at once, warning that "if any house is found closed, it will be subject to plunder." Assured of their safety, the people of Bydgoszcz came out of their houses and treated the soldiers, but lest "on account of the treating any offences should occur," the latter, at the first signal for departure given on the commander's order, "fell in in their usual order." Dąbrowski pitched his camp on the right bank of the Brda. 300 soldiers from the reserve formed the garrison of Bydgoszcz.
muszynska1947/84:
In his report to Kościuszko Dąbrowski stressed with full satisfaction the orderly conduct of his own soldiers, who in the first moment after the victory, being masters of the city, "did little to violate this natural power". They neither plundered nor wronged the inhabitants, and there was no need to restrain them from excesses. There were even cases in which the old soldiers forbade the scythemen entry into houses, lest it be thought that they wished to rob.

This great discipline was Dąbrowski's merit. For it was he who, brought up on the military principles of Frederick the Great, sought to instil in the soldiers a sense of discipline, punishing even the slightest offence against the service. The second man who saw to it that the army did not commit abuses in captured Bydgoszcz was Wybicki. He did not allow the private property of the inhabitants to be touched, and of what was found in the public stores he ordered, as he himself writes in his memoir, an inventory to be drawn up and the goods to be turned to the needs of the soldiers. In a proclamation to the people that he issued he declared that the Poles had come "to free their brothers from foreign rule and to return them to the bosom of the common mother". Using the authority entrusted to him by the Commander, he abolished the Prussian court of justice and the Prussian Administrative Chamber, and in their place he restored "to the city, which had been Polish from time immemorial, the national offices". As the highest administrative authority he set up a Commission of Order under his own direction, which occupied itself chiefly with intelligence work and with the use of the richly stocked Prussian magazines. Its members were: Zakrzewski as president, and as members Twardowski, Nadratowski, Karski, Bulewski, Rudowski, Modliński, the Protestant preacher Stellmann, and the merchants Oppermann and Ziegler. At the same time the newly appointed town council, headed by Mayor Puhan, also took up its
muszynska1947/85:
office.

On the day after the capture of the city, 3 October, according to the account of a German eyewitness, all the officials and some of the citizens were summoned to the building of the Chamber. Dąbrowski, Wybicki and a number of Polish generals and officers also arrived there. In the presence of all, the cash boxes were counted and carried off, and the portraits of the Prussian kings Frederick II and Frederick William II were removed from the conference hall. After this had been done, General Dąbrowski, who spoke correct German and was "a very modest man, wise and of great polish", stepped forward and ordered the local merchants to pay a contribution of 300,000 thalers, which in the end, owing to the intervention of 2 citizens, was reduced to 10,000 thalers. Next the officials were required to swear that they would hand over all the money and valuables in their keeping that Colonel de Székely had plundered, to which the Germans questioned, however, answered unanimously that they knew nothing. After a while General Dąbrowski spoke again, declaring that the Poles had come not as enemies but as friends. He referred to the cruelties perpetrated by Col. Székely, described his inhuman treatment of the clergy at Włocławek and of persons of both sexes whom he had robbed and wished to hang, and finally had brought beneath the gallows at Inowrocław. As proof that the Prussian king approved of Székely's "tyrannical" conduct and had recommended that he be even more savage, Dąbrowski showed those present a royal letter intercepted near Gąbin. Finally he announced that he was arresting all the Prussian officials, so as to hold hostages in exchange for the imprisoned Poles. Wishing, however, to show that the Poles are magnanimous and do not take revenge even on
muszynska1947/86:
an enemy, he ordered the arrested men to send a delegation to their king with a request for the release of the Poles, whereupon they too would regain their freedom. After this speech all proceeded to the parish church, and only in one of the rooms did the arrested men remain, under the guard of 8 soldiers. In the church the citizens swore loyalty to the Commonwealth, after which Wybicki went once more to the board of the Chamber, where in the presence of the officials he called the Prussian king a "tyrant". At that moment the arrested councillor Broskovius approached him, asking him to release his countrymen. Wybicki, in his excitement, interrupted him and called him an "unreasonable man, a slave who does not perceive the yoke of his bondage". Broskovius, however, did not give up and presented his request for the release of the arrested men a second time. This time Wybicki heard him out, but soon flared up again and called Székely a brigand, threatening that, should the Prussian king wish to hang any of the imprisoned Poles, ten Prussian officials would immediately meet the same fate.

When everything had calmed down, Dąbrowski visited the wounded Colonel Székely. Székely feared that the Poles would take revenge on him, but Dąbrowski assured him that he could be at ease and that he would endeavour "to sweeten his lot as much as possible". At the wounded man's request doctors and a priest were sent to him, and Dąbrowski gave him money. Other Poles came to visit him as well, among them Mniewski, "a general worthy in every respect of admiration", in whose house Székely had formerly been a guest, and whom during the insurrection he had robbed "first of all". On seeing Mniewski, Székely fainted, and when he came to, the latter addressed him in these words: "as far as my own person is concerned, I forgive you everything, and if you wish to be at peace, return the plundered property to those from whom
muszynska1947/87:
you took every means of living". Thereupon Székely declared that he wished to speak with Dąbrowski and Mniewski himself, and when all had left he told them that his baggage was at Grudziądz and advised that the Poles should not advance further, because a corps was marching from Pomerania and Brandenburg that was to have joined him. As a token of friendship he gave Dąbrowski 6 riding horses, which the latter never claimed. The doctor who was called did not predict a long life for the wounded man, and indeed four days after the assault Székely died and was buried with military honours.

The capture of Bydgoszcz made a great impression throughout Prussia. Berlin was ashamed of the defeat and at the same time anxious for the fate of the seized provinces. In Poznań people simply would not believe Schwarz, the eyewitness of the Bydgoszcz events. He himself relates that when, on 6 October at noon, the day after his arrival in Poznań, he stood before General Elsner, who was then in command in the city, the latter at first took the news of Székely's disaster and the capture of Bydgoszcz by the Poles for a fable, until towards evening a rider who had come from Dąbrowski's corps confirmed it. At the court of the Prussian monarch there now arose a fear for the security of West Prussia. It was thought, namely, that in that whole region there were too few troops to be able to oppose the Poles effectively. The garrison of Toruń under Colonel Hundt could be reinforced by only seven more companies, and the state of the city's entrenchments left much to be desired. Frederick William was therefore ready, in the last resort, to heed the advice of General Favrat and, to save Toruń, to fold up the front on the Narew and thus reinforce the threatened fortress with troops. Grudziądz too, where Colonel Pirch was commandant,
muszynska1947/88:
had a weak garrison, and besides, in the whole of West Prussia, apart from the garrison of Gdańsk (6 battalions of the Raumer and Manstein regiments, 2 depot battalions, an artillery battalion and a squadron of dragoons, whose composition, moreover, was made up of soldiers recruited in the former Polish provinces), there were no more Prussian troops. The remnants of Székely's corps, which Col. Hinrichs had gathered at Świecie, were too weak to undertake any action. In the Prussian camp, therefore, there was a lurking fear that Dąbrowski, whose forces were greatly overestimated, would strike at Gdańsk.

The commandant of Gdańsk, General Raumer, also reckoned with this possibility, especially when he learned that Polish patrols were already reaching Chojnice [Konitz], and he applied appropriate measures. He placed guns on the ramparts, strengthened the guards, erected palisades, sent out patrols, and finally set up a camp on Bishop's Hill (Bischoffsberg). The matter could not be taken lightly all the more because the people of Gdańsk favoured the Poles, and even the inhabitants of Starogard [Preußisch Stargard], Kościerzyna [Berent], Skarszewy [Schöneck] and Nowe Miasto were ready to supply them with help and with men for the ranks. In order, therefore, to halt Dąbrowski's possible march on Gdańsk, General Raumer used a ruse. He sent small detachments of troops into the vicinity of Kościerzyna and Starogard and ordered them to collect provisions and forage, to create the illusion that a larger corps was approaching in those parts. General Dąbrowski, who had previously learned of the concentration of General Beyern's corps, and, not being informed of it in any detail, formed the supposition that it was this corps that was marching to West Prussia, abandoned the march on Gdańsk.

The success that had attended the column of Polish troops sent to Greater Poland must have terrified
muszynska1947/89:
also Lieutenant-General Schwerin. He saw no other way out of the difficult situation than to draw General Pollitz's corps away from the Pilica and turn it against the South Prussian insurgents. He therefore divided the corps in question into two detachments. The first, made up of 4 battalions, 3 squadrons, two field guns and one howitzer, set out on 2 October under Colonel Ledivary for Toruń to reinforce the garrison there; the second, under General Pollitz himself, consisting of 3 battalions, 3 squadrons of hussars and 2 howitzers, marched out on 8 October from Wolbórz by the road through Lutomierz and Szadek, and then along the Warta through Koło and Konin to Gniezno.

General Pollitz was to destroy any enemy he encountered, in accordance with the plan of cooperation previously drawn up with Major-General Schwerin, Elsner and Székely. Lieutenant-General Schwerin also made other arrangements. On 4 October he ordered General Lattorff to withdraw behind the Nida, and four days later to quit the Sandomierz region altogether. He took this step chiefly on account of reports received from Lieutenant-General Lichnowski at Radomsko and from the Prussian treasury office at Piotrków, reporting unrest among the nobility there. He also intended to send some troops into the neighbourhood of Sieradz and Wieluń, and for that purpose dispatched General Lichnowski there with 1 battalion and a regiment of cuirassiers, whose mobilisation he had carried out. 3 battalions of infantry and 3 regiments of cuirassiers, whose mobilisation was nearly complete, he stationed from Zitena(?), Koniecpol, a place on the Pilica near the source of that river, and from Skała, as far as Kraków. To cover Gdańsk, he asked the king to send new corps to West Prussia from Berlin or Szczecin [Stettin]. He himself remained in the camp at Chrzonowice.
muszynska1947/90:
Dąbrowski meanwhile was thinking of spreading the insurrection in the Netze District and in West Prussia. To that end, and in order to obtain fresh reinforcements as well as provisions and forage, he sent numerous cavalry detachments out from Bydgoszcz .

Colonel Sieroszewski set out for Nakło and on the Noteć seized 13 vessels coming from Berlin with salt, iron, linen, cloth, etc.. The detachment of Lipski, major-general of the Gniezno voivodeship, sent in the direction of Chełmno [Kulm] and Grudziądz, dispersed an enemy patrol at Chełmża [Culmsee], taking 18 prisoners. Colonel Wyganowski, with 300 horse from the Poznań rising, went to the Wałcz district in order to raise an uprising there and choose recruits. Colonel Sokolnicki hastened to Fordon, to occupy that town and gain control of the banks of the Vistula, and moreover to round up vessels, wagons and men fit for transport, and to procure provisions of every kind. General Mniewski, with the whole detachment of his cavalry, and Colonel Mchowski, with 50 horse, together with infantry and artillery, were also directed to the Vistula, toward Solec Kujawski [Schulitz]. The former was to keep in touch with General Lipski, patrol toward Toruń, leave one detachment at Panadzewa and another at Podgórz to observe the Toruń bridge, which he was to burn in case of need; the latter was to station himself at Solec, send patrols toward Toruń and Gniewkowo and spies into the neighbourhood of Toruń, round up as many vessels and men useful for that purpose as possible, and maintain communication with General Mniewski. Dąbrowski ordered Lieutenant Moszczeński to remain with the cavalry at Łabiszyn, to send patrols from there toward Żnin, Wałkowice and Inowrocław, and to report as often as possible on the enemy's movements. Finally, Vice-Brigadier Łaszczyński, "a weak officer", was dispatched
muszynska1947/91:
with the remainder of Dąbrowski's brigade to Świecie, to halt vessels and carts, round up provisions, and always keep in touch with Wybicki, the plenipotentiary attached to that expedition.

According to a contemporary account by Lainé, the town secretary of Świecie, the Polish troops arrived there at noon on 6 October. Wybicki took possession of the treasuries, abolished the Prussian offices, and established a commission for civil matters, composed of 5 representatives each from the nobility, the burghers and the clergy. The town secretary Synakiewicz was elected president of the town, but as he refused to take up the new office, the mayor in office hitherto, Gannowski, was left in that post. Citizen Kruszyński became general of the rising, and Moszczeński, the owner of the village of Niewieszczyn, colonel. On the following day a fair was held at Świecie, and taking advantage of this the insurgents seized cloth and leather goods against receipts. The inhabitants were disarmed and ordered to furnish a recruit. 60 young men from the town itself and 200 from the commune were incorporated into the insurgent ranks. Craftsmen had to work day and night preparing the necessary equipment. On the night of 11 to 12 October the Poles marched out of the town, but returned the next day, 13 October, and left for good on the same day, taking with them, besides horses, all the local tailors and musicians. To supplement this account it should be added that when the Yellow Hussar regiment, stationed on the other bank of the Vistula, saw the Polish troops entering Świecie, it did not dare to attack them. Wybicki, who writes of this in his memoir, then experienced "what power belongs to opinion spreading alarm in a revolution". For the enemy took all "objects, trees, herds" for "an enormous force", with which he supposed that
muszynska1947/92:
detachments of insurgents and regular troops were "marching into Prussia".

Eight days after the capture of Bydgoszcz, on 10 October, Dąbrowski set out in 2 columns for Toruń. The first, which he led himself, crossed the Vistula at Solec; the second, under Rymkiewicz, crossed at Fordon. At Zła Wieś (Bösendorf), on the Fordon-Toruń route, the two columns joined. The strength of this force was 1,000 infantry, 1,500 cavalry and 10 guns. Only 1 battalion of the Greater Poland rising remained in Bydgoszcz. On the following day, 11 October, Dąbrowski halted in the vicinity of Przysieka, where preparations were being made for the assault planned for the next day. According to the plan drawn up, the cavalry were to blockade the town on all sides and set it on fire in several places, in order in this way to create confusion in the town and enable the infantry to attack from a single point. Nor was Hundt, the commandant of the fortress of Toruń, idle. Fearing that the strength of the garrison might prove insufficient, and knowing how important Toruń was to the Prussians on account of its richly stocked magazines of munitions and provisions, he applied, immediately after the capture of Bydgoszcz, to General Favrat, who commanded the corps on the Narew, with a request for reinforcements. Soon 2 companies of Pfuhl's regiment did arrive in Toruń; a further 5 companies of the same regiment took up position at Płock and Bobrowniki, in order to come to the aid of the threatened post if need arose. On 7 October detachments of Polish cavalry appeared on both sides of the Vistula near Toruń, intending to quarter at Podgórz. Hundt's adjutant, Second Lieutenant Voss, then crossed the Vistula with 30 hussars and dispersed the cavalrymen already in Podgórz. Those dispersed
muszynska1947/93:
retreated into the forests south of Podgórz and joined a detachment of infantry there. To gain his bearings, Hundt sent Lieutenant Voss toward Fordon, still on 7 October, with 40 foot soldiers, as many hussars and 1 three-pounder gun. Marching all night, Voss reached the vicinity of Czarnowo early on 8 October, and having learned that 100 insurgents were encamped in that village, resolved to attack them. The attack succeeded for the Prussians. 2 officers, 15 soldiers and 50 wagons of forage fell into Prussian hands. On news of stronger Polish patrols approaching in the direction of Chełmno and Chełmża, and of an intended crossing at Solec by 2 companies from Dąbrowski's corps with two guns, Voss set out on the return journey.

Meanwhile Dąbrowski did not storm Toruń. When he already had everything in readiness, he received certain news "that relief had reached Toruń". At first he supposed that "a corps had arrived at Toruń from Płock", but soon he was informed by reports that this relief was the corps of Colonel Ledivary. On hearing of the danger threatening Toruń, Ledivary had set out at once from Brześć Kujawski. On 11 October he stood already on the left bank of the Vistula, at Podgórz, and after leaving one battalion and cavalry outposts there, he crossed the Vistula in the night of 11 to 12 October, sent detachments out along that river, and marched to the village of Mokre in order to strike the enemy's left wing with his main forces. In such conditions Dąbrowski, who "at almost the same moment received a report from Włocławek that a corps was marching from Poznań and that the posts around Łabiszyn were retreating", was forced to abandon the attack on Toruń and "return again across the Vistula to Bydgoszcz". On 14 October he crossed at Fordon. The detachment
muszynska1947/94:
consisting of 200 infantry, 400 cavalry and 4 guns, was meanwhile stationed at Solec Kujawski, to prevent the Prussians from attacking Dąbrowski on the flank. During the crossing Madaliński's brigade and 200 riflemen raised an alarm at Toruń, and as a result of this manoeuvre "the enemy corps stationed at Podgórz [Podgorz] went in large part across the bridge into Toruń". Colonel Ledivary, whose soldiers were exhausted by the ceaseless march, confined himself to a trifling harassment of the rear of the retreating Polish troops. Dąbrowski himself admits that he did not lose a single man, because the enemy "followed him sluggishly.

The unsuccessful march on Toruń was not what Dąbrowski had intended. His aim was "to remain with the combined forces at Bydgoszcz and hold out through the winter between the Vistula, the Brda and the Noteć, to detach his numerous cavalry in all directions, as far as possible, to watch every step of the enemy; to this end to send from each rising, as far as circumstances allowed, considerable detachments to their own voivodeships, lands and districts to increase their strength, collect taxes and alarm the enemy everywhere; to help the rising in those places where it could not yet be carried out; to set up magazines at Bydgoszcz and Inowrocław, to bring the old regiments and brigades up to strength and form new ones, all of which could be done without oppressing the citizens, simply from the domains (Ämter) of the Prussian king, which are very numerous in these parts; to uniform and drill the army, so that in the coming campaign it might act with greater energy and benefit to the country". To storm a fortress with a fairly strong garrison, with the help of only a small number of regular troops, who would first have to be ferried over to the other bank of the Vistula, was in his view a bad move. The situation was made worse by the circumstance
muszynska1947/95:
that Prussian troops stood behind him, and he was not certain whether communication with Warsaw had not been cut, leaving the corps entrusted to him at the mercy of fate. The march on Toruń, undertaken in spite of everything, might be explained by a wish to calm the agitated minds of Dąbrowski's subordinates, who were dissatisfied with his tactics.

For after the capture of Bydgoszcz, even before the departure for Toruń, reproaches had arisen against Dąbrowski "that he is not active enough and has no determination at all, with the result that not only do all the operations of the war proceed at a tortoise pace, but many are even omitted..., that from day to day the march on Toruń is put off, giving the garrison time to strengthen itself" Rymkiewicz reproached him for not having stood before Toruń on the day after the capture of Bydgoszcz, for then "this town would have surrendered or been taken easily by force of arms. Even Madaliński, "always honest, forgot in this moment what he owes to the Fatherland". Envy arose in him "that the name of Dąbrowski is famous, while his own is barely mentioned, and he already imagined for himself a right to the supreme command, which was due to him as a general of higher rank, as the first to the national rising". Realising, however, that he could not himself command so large a corps "in the sight of a more numerous enemy", he proposed to Rymkiewicz that the latter should "command under his name". He met with a refusal, however. Rymkiewicz, when he "could no longer bear the spirit of faction, armed with pure patriotism, rose up with republican energy, reminding Gen. Madaliński of his praiseworthy deeds;...he opened his eyes to the consequences that must inevitably be expected from division; he recalled to him the confidence which the Most Serene Commander and the whole nation placed
muszynska1947/96:
in the virtue and talents of Gen. Dąbrowski, which he knew how to earn and still earns". But the "factionists" did not give way. "They advised forming a military commission, composed of brigadier generals, which would henceforth govern". Dąbrowski, aggrieved that they wished in this way to deprive him of the command, appealed to Kościuszko's order, by virtue of which he had received command of the army. He declared "that he had so far done nothing without common deliberation", but "to a formal commission he cannot consent from his post", and in that case he resigned the command. "The obstinacy had already reached such a degree that Madaliński with his brigade and some of the risings wanted to separate from Gen. Dąbrowski", and only Generals Rymkiewicz, Mniewski and Skórzewski and the plenipotentiary Wybicki "used all their eloquence and reason to soothe minds so bitterly at war with one another". In time "though only on the surface, harmony, friendship, unity and love returned again".

Bielamowski learned of Ledivary's march to the relief of Toruń during his stay at Strzelno, from a letter of Col. Ledivary of 7 October to Major-General Schwerin, intercepted by an insurgent from Mniewski's detachment. Ledivary wrote that he had been ordered by the chief commander to scatter and defeat Dąbrowski's corps together with Major-General Schwerin, and that he was now marching to Toruń, to save that town, which Dąbrowski was threatening. Bielamowski sent the intercepted letter on to Dąbrowski, but the latter received it too late to avoid the pointless march on Toruń. For the letter reached Dąbrowski only in the night of 11 to 12 October, whereas on the 10th Dąbrowski had already crossed the Vistula on the march to Toruń.
muszynska1947/97:
After returning to Bydgoszcz on 14 October, the commander of the expedition to Greater Poland soon received exceedingly sad news. He learned that the Commander had been beaten and taken prisoner, that communication with Warsaw had been broken because Prince Józef Poniatowski had abandoned Kamionna, that Generals Schwerin and Elsner were to march out of Poznań to destroy him, that a corps was approaching from Pomerania and Brandenburg, and that Lieutenant-General Schwerin had marched from the neighbourhood of Rawa to cut him off from the Bzura. Nothing was left to him, therefore, but to fall back toward Warsaw.

In Greater Poland, from the first days of September and simultaneously with Dąbrowski's operations, independent guerrilla warfare continued to be active. We must return here to its description, although an exact picture of this movement, that is, all its manifestations, is difficult to reconstruct. For the sources dealing with the matter were exceedingly meagre and confined for the most part to a contemporary newspaper published in Poznań under the title "Südpreussische Zeitung". Given the state of the means of communication at the time, this periodical could not record all the events connected with the guerrilla movement of the Greater Poles, and moreover the insurgents, by their frequent attacks on the posts, prevented news from getting through to Poznań. We know, however, that the partisans, moving from one manor to another in more or less numerous bands, induced the owners of estates, partly by persuasion and partly by force, to join their ranks and supply recruits; they appropriated the chests of the Prussian king, took salt from the Prussian magazines and then sold it more cheaply to the population, imprisoned officials, and above all greatly obstructed communication.
muszynska1947/98:
Events such as the above, although typical of guerrilla warfare in Greater Poland and frequent, nevertheless cannot be generalised to the whole area of this region. For the patriotic ardour that had shown itself there at the beginning of the insurrection was now no longer so great, and in places it died away altogether. This can be explained both by the increased counteraction of the Prussian troops, which followed once several corps had been detached to Greater Poland during the last days of the siege of Warsaw and after its lifting, and by the proverbial straw fire of the Poles.

A few fragments given below, which the sources have preserved, may serve to illustrate the development of the independent insurgent movement.

Thus on 4 September at daybreak the leaseholder of Porażyn, Borzęcki, accompanied by 6 armed peasants and 2 representatives of the nobility, burst into the post office at Pniewy [Pinne]; he took 9 horses and a small mail cart, issuing the official in exchange a suitable certificate. The incident had the consequence that the Berlin mail reached Poznań with a delay of two days. The same had happened earlier at Słupca, Września [Wreschen], Kostrzyn [Kostschin], Czempiń, Kościan and Śmigiel. In these places the insurgents took horses and destroyed the postal emblems. At Słupca they deprived the postmaster Sadowski of his office, whose place was taken by the former retired postmaster Michalicki. In the Śmigiel district they again levied a recruit, but had to use force, because the peasants did not join them voluntarily.

In the Netze District, in the neighbourhood of Kcynia and Gołańcz [Gollantsch], the insurgents under Krupecki's leadership continued to be active. In both places they seized the salt depots, confiscated the money collected from the hearth tax, removed the Prussian eagles, and tried to induce the mayors to swear the oath
muszynska1947/99:
to loyalty to the fatherland. Their whole band then set off in the direction of Wągrowiec, from where on 20 September an emissary of Krupecki appeared before the mayor in Rogoźno [Rogasen] with a demand that men be supplied to bear arms. Two days later this same detachment, together with the Poznań insurgents under Niemojewski and the Gniezno insurgents under Lipski, clashed, as we know, with a detachment of Székely's corps at Kcynia . Colonel Hinrichs, who had come to the aid of the fighting Prussians, had to fall back to Szubin in the face of the steadily growing number of insurgents. The Poles had 22 wounded in this skirmish and as many taken prisoner; the Prussians only 5 wounded and 2 horses killed.

According to the "Südpreussische Zeitung" of 24 September, insurgents were also gathering in the vicinity of Zduny and near Śrem, from where a considerable detachment of theirs, though estimated on too high a scale, being reckoned at 2,000 peasants, was said to have set out in the night of 19 to 20 September in the direction of Kłecko. Only in Leszno and its surroundings, ever since General Manstein had been stationed there as garrison, did quiet prevail.

From the time of the capture of Bydgoszcz, before Dąbrowski sent detachments out into the Netze District, dates an attack by insurgents on Chodzież [Kolmar]. On 4 October 40 armed men halted outside the town, whereupon 24 of them rode into it, took cloth from the local Jews against receipts and seized the whole stock of salt, at once selling it off at a low price to the citizens. With the 400 thalers received from the sale the insurgents set out on their way back. Even before they had left the town a small episode took place. A patrol of Trenck's hussars arrived from Piła, but, informed in good time of the presence of the insurgents, halted outside the town. One of the hussars, a bolder man, nevertheless dashed into the town and ran straight into 2 soldiers and 2 armed peasants standing in front of the mayor's resi
muszynska1947/100:
dence. Having wrested a lance with a pennon from one of the peasants, the Prussian fired his pistol and began to flee. The insurgents, alarmed by the shot, at once rushed in pursuit of the fugitive, but at the sight of the remaining hussars turned back. Three days later this same band of insurgents seized the Prussian mail sent out from Piła.

In the districts of Wieluń and Ostrzeszów the armed movement, begun successfully in the third decade of August, weakened considerably in the course of September, although there were no Prussian troops nearby. Michał Jerlicz, who was to form an armed force, returned home to the region of Działoszyn. Nor did the head of the rising, Colonel Stokowski, hold out, and he soon disbanded his detachment for want of any means of feeding it. It was he, writes Kierzkowski in his memoir, who, "standing with 500 insurgent horse", at the moment when the Prussian king was travelling by post from Warsaw through Wieluń towards Silesia, "played at cards, and the insurgents slept well". When he later learned of the passage of so important a person, "it grieved him greatly that, when he could have seized the king, he had neglected the opportunity. He threw his cap on the ground, but that was of no further use". Of the other organisers of the rising in this district, Psarski, so zealous at the outset, returned to his estate of Bobrownik. After some time the rising gathered strength again. At Bobrownik deliberations were held on how to restore discipline in the loosening insurgent ranks, and the dignity of deputy commander was entrusted to an old officer of the Polish army, Korycki. Psarski went to Ostrzeszów and there kindled anew among the citizens zeal for the national cause, and ordered Stokowski to justify himself for his conduct. On 9 October, with an armed force by now organised, they set out for Kępno and took away
muszynska1947/101:
a stock of salt there, in order to sell it off afterwards among the inhabitants of the neighbourhood. Lenartowicz, head of the rising in the Sieradz region, soon joined Korycki, and under Stokowski's supreme command expeditions were mounted to the neighbouring small towns of Wieruszów and Bolesławice and to the Opatów estates. Psarski, marching with the troops, set up commissions for civil matters in the several localities, took the oath of fidelity, and on the estates of Count Maltzahn ordered the labour dues to be reduced by half; he ordered the supply of recruits and provisions. It was also intended to extend the rising to the Silesian border towns, such as Byczyna [Pitschen], Rychtal [Reichthal], Międzybórz [Neumittelwalde], Wołczyn [Konstadt], Oleśnica, Bralin, Namysłów and Syców [Groß Wartenberg], and to send appropriate summonses there from the camp at Węglowice. The owner of Ligota, a village lying on the border, Wiewiórski, received these appeals, but forwarded them, still unopened, to the Landrat (district commissioner) Teichmann in Wartenberg. The armed movement in the neighbourhood of Wieluń and Ostrzeszów could not, however, assume any greater proportions, since many inhabitants of that land did not believe from the outset in its success, and the Jews were slow in supplying arms and ammunition. It even happened that the mayor of Wieluń, Olszanowski, taking advantage of the insurgents' having left the town, ordered the scythemen keeping guard in their absence to go home, and instructed the town servants to destroy their weapons.

In another part of old Greater Poland, in Dobrzyń Land, the fortunes of the rising likewise took an unfavourable turn, because the citizens there lacked perseverance in the undertaking once begun. Around 10 September the rifles and uniforms once taken were returned to the Prussian post at Rypin and the captured hussars were released, together with Lieutenant Branky. Many insurgents even presented themselves
muszynska1947/102:
voluntarily to the Prussian detachment at Sierpc with the notification that they wished to "return to their duties"; the rest, who had not yet fallen so low, hid in the surrounding forests. These events, favourable to the Prussians, were promptly noted by the newspaper "Südpreussische Zeitung", with the remark that the insurgents seemed already to regret their deed; let us remember, however, that at just that time the formidable Colonel de Székely was raging in Kuyavia, spreading terror among the population by his inhuman conduct.

To subdue the Greater Poles there were, besides Colonel Székely, also Generals Schwerin and Elsner, of whom the first, as we know, had moved against the rebellious provinces a few days before the suspension of the siege of Warsaw, and the second at the moment of the Prussians' withdrawal from the entrenchments before the capital.
