General Manstein, who had arrived in Greater Poland shortly before the outbreak of the insurrection, and Colonel Dossow, sent there at the end of August, also went on clashing with the insurgents.

General Elsner with his corps arrived on 15 September at Rogoźno near Widawa in the Sieradz region and from there, for the purpose of cooperation, established contact with Colonel Dossow, stationed at Widawa; on 17 September he moved to Sieradz, cleared the forests there of insurgents, and then, having crossed the Warta, proceeded by the road through Kalisz to Leszno. His companion Dossow remained for the time being in the Sieradz region, in order, with the help of the Łęczyca garrison, to destroy a detachment composed of several hundred insurgents who were crossing the Warta at Uniejów in the direction of Łęczyca. General Manstein, until the middle of September, chased fruitlessly after the insurgents in the forests between Dolsk and Śrem, after which on the 21st of that month he set out for Mosina, wishing to manoeuvre in the neighbourhood of the Warta together with the commandant of Poznań, Colonel Diether. The plan of joint action was not
muszynska1947/103:
carried out, however, since Diether was afraid of weakening the garrison of Poznań in view of the favourable manifestations towards the insurrection in that city, and preferred first to await from Międzyrzecz [Meseritz] the reinforcing battalion of Cronsatz together with detachments of riflemen and cavalry. Manstein now moved towards Gostyń [Gostyn] with the intention of cooperating with General Elsner. On the road to Leszno, at Poniec, Elsner received on 27 September word from Manstein of his march on Gostyń, together with a summons to go with him towards Jarocin [Jarotschin], in order to support Major-General Schwerin in a planned attack on the insurgents at Konin and to prevent the Polish troops from withdrawing towards Silesia. But this plan too came to nothing. For on that very same day, 27 September, alarming news reached Elsner and Manstein that Dąbrowski was marching on Poznań; they therefore turned back from their road and by forced march went to the aid of the threatened city. Elsner arrived on the spot on 1 October, Manstein the next day. This was during Bielamowski's approach to Poznań, already described by us, which gave rise among the Prussians to the belief that it was Dąbrowski's advance guard, he intending to take the city. All suppositions of this kind, moreover, had their source in the lack of precise information. The capital of Greater Poland, as a result of the loss of communications, as the "Südpreussische Zeitung" of the day writes, had become like an "island in the sea" cut off from the rest of the world.

The arrival of new troops in Poznań by no means put an end to further fears for the safety of the city. How very great these fears were is shown by a grotesque description, preserved for us by the Prussian official Schwarz, already mentioned, in his recollections, which, in view of the closeness of the dates concerned, can be connected with that consternation which
muszynska1947/104:
was caused by the appearance of Bielamowski near Poznań. Schwarz recalls that when he arrived in Poznań on 5 October he found the Prussian officials in the church of St Martin, where they had hidden in order to resist, at least for a time, the "superiority" of the insurgents from this highest point of the city and under cover of the Prussian troops. The sight that met Schwarz's eyes was as follows: the floor of the church was covered with straw used for sleeping, and those gathered there ate and drank, laughed and wept by turns, believing that the coming day would be the last of their lives. As time passed in this way and the insurgents somehow did not come, the Germans gradually recovered from their fright and on the following day left their hiding place.

At that time the third of the Prussian generals operating in the territory of Greater Poland, Major-General Schwerin, was approaching Poznań. Until then he had been stationed at Kalisz, to which he had withdrawn before the advancing corps of Dąbrowski. On 23 September he set out by the road to Raszków against a band of insurgents near Dobrzyca, but after 2 days he returned to Kalisz, fearing for the magazine there. On 27 September he moved to Konin, where together with Generals Manstein and Elsner he planned an attack on the insurgents there; but on news that Dąbrowski was said to be at Słupca and a detachment of scythemen at Pyzdry, he went back again to Kalisz and for the moment contented himself with gathering information about the enemy. Schwerin set out toward Poznań only on 2 October, by the road through Pleszew [Pleschen], Jarocin, Śrem and Kórnik . At Pleszew he robbed the castellan Gorzeński, but he was reportedly not to get away with the loot any farther than Radlin. In that place, as Adam Turno describes in his memoir, Captain of Cavalry (rotmistrz) Łojewski, sent by Kościuszko with an order to the Greater Poland insurrections, was at that time staying as a guest of the parish priest. Having learned that Schwerin
muszynska1947/105:
was in the village, Łojewski resolved to drive him out of there and used the following stratagem. When it had grown quite dark, he mounted his horse and rode toward the right wing of the Prussian camp, while he ordered his orderly to ride to the left. Both began to fire pistols and to give the command "squadrons forward". Schwerin, not suspecting the ruse, took such fright that he left behind everything he had robbed from Gorzeński and "fled through Witaszyce all night, so that he did not halt until Gostyń". How much truth there is in this story is not known, but it must be stated that similar alarms occurred often at that time. Of other places, Schwerin plundered the small town of Żerków [Zerkow] and the villages of Miniszew and Panienka, and in the course of his further march, on 6 October, he stripped Eleonora Zabłocka, née Bogacka, at Śrem completely; her husband Jan was in the insurrection. He took her food, all her wardrobe, and all her livestock, and so laden with spoil he finally reached Poznań 3 days later. The number of Prussian soldiers in the city was now considerable, for it amounted to 6 battalions and 20 squadrons.

Bielamowski followed Schwerin's movements. On 5 October Dąbrowski sent him from Bydgoszcz an order to march with his detachment at once to where the column of Major-General Schwerin was, with the instruction that he should start no engagement and should spread the word "that our army is leaving this region and is to attack General Schwerin". Bielamowski carried out the task entrusted to him conscientiously and with great skill. In a report of 12 October he gave Dąbrowski precise information on Schwerin's movements from the moment of his leaving Kalisz up to his entry into Poznań. He wrote that a detachment had set out from Poznań toward the small town of Kłecko, whither he too had been obliged to go, but that it afterwards
muszynska1947/106:
withdrew to Murowana Goślina, and he to Rogowo, for "both" were afraid of each other. The report ended with the words: "among the Prussians I have the reputation of marching in the vanguard before His Excellency's column, and therefore they fear me, for they think that the column is always following behind me..."

The rising in Greater Poland, which could not be so easily crushed by force of arms, which checked the plans of the Prussian king and hampered the movements of his troops, caused the Prussian king to try to master the situation not only by arms but also by means of proclamations, now threatening the Greater Poles, now, for a change, containing gentler turns of phrase.

Accordingly a patent appeared, dated 24 September at Wrocław, issued during the stay there of Frederick William II on his way to Berlin, in which this monarch stated "with just displeasure" (mit gerechtem Unwillen) that in carrying out the intention of bringing happiness to Greater Poland, from the moment of the occupation of this province, "various restless heads " had stood in the way. For the breaking of the "sacred bonds of fidelity and obedience" the patent threatened the participants in the insurrection with imprisonment and even death, and the nobility moreover with the loss of noble status and of estates that were to fall to the share of "faithful and deserving vassals". Finally the king expressed regret for those of his South Prussian subjects who, in fear for their lives and property, had taken their places in the ranks of the "troublemakers", causing, together with them, alarm among the peaceful inhabitants of the province; he refuted the rumours of persecution of Catholics and of an increase in taxes, and, wishing to win over the peasant estate, he abolished the tax on the so-called "Musikzettli".

Despite the threats with which the patent menaced the insurgents, the armed movement of the Greater Poles did not abate. Soon there
muszynska1947/107:
came the days of the greatest triumph of the insurgent arms in this region, crowned by the capture of Bydgoszcz. It then seemed to the Prussian king that the troops of Generals Elsner, Manstein and Schwerin, shut up in the capital of Greater Poland, were unable to withstand the power of Dąbrowski's corps, which threatened at once Poznań, Toruń and even Gdańsk. True, from his Potsdam residence the king surveyed the situation in Poland with a critical eye and could rightly suppose that, in view of the rapid marches of Suvorov's Russian army, the Polish troops before Warsaw were passing through very hard moments; but on the other hand he could not make light of events in Greater Poland, all the more because the fate of the Prussian officials seized at Bydgoszcz lay in Dąbrowski's hands. For that reason, in the edict of 11 October issued at Berlin he spoke to the "rebels" in an already more gracious tone. He promised not to punish the insurgents without first examining their guilt, but only to place them in a safe place and afterwards to try them according to law before the civil authorities; he promised all citizens freedom of conscience, equality before the law and in tax obligations, and above all the paternal care of the Prussian government.

The edict appeared just in time, for ominous clouds were already gathering over the insurrection. The guarantee of cardinal civil rights contained in it was in future to shield the inhabitants of Greater Poland, at least in part, from the arbitrariness of the victors.

Chapter IV

THE FALL OF THE INSURRECTION — DĄBROWSKI'S RETREAT AND THE LAST ARMED EFFORTS OF THE GREATER POLES
muszynska1947/108: While the armed movement in Greater Poland was developing favourably, to the glory of Polish arms, the situation in the other theatres of insurrectionary fighting was growing ever more grave. True, on the Narew the Poles were still holding their ground against the enemy, even gaining certain successes over the Prussians, but the Lithuanian troops, whose morale had deteriorated considerably after the fall of Vilnius, were no longer capable of resisting the pressure of the Russians. One after another the corps withdrew towards Grodno, abandoning even Samogitia, the holding of which Kościuszko had recommended. Meanwhile Suvorov was approaching Brest-Litovsk with a corps of 18,000 and 60 guns. To check this column Kościuszko sent Józef Sierakowski with a division numbering some 8,000 soldiers, but fortune did not favour Sierakowski. On 19 September he suffered a great defeat near Brest; Suvorov took all 28 of his guns and scattered his division, all but annihilating it. The Russian General Fersen, who had until then been stationed in the vicinity of Kozienice, deceived the vigilance of General Poniński, whose task it was to watch him and not to let him pass to the right bank of the Vistula, and on 4 October, with the whole corps that
muszynska1947/109:
had taken part in the siege of Warsaw, he crossed the Vistula. This step had unpleasant consequences. First, Fersen was cutting one of the main routes by which Warsaw was supplied with food, and besides, there was the fear that he would join Suvorov, who was holding the line of the Bug.

In these circumstances Kościuszko considered it necessary to destroy Fersen's corps, and on 7 October he set out from the Mokotów camp. When, on that same day, a halt was made at Korytnica, Major Molski arrived in the evening, sent by Dąbrowski with a report on the capture of Bydgoszcz. The favourable news, proclaimed at once to the soldiers, raised their spirits. It was, however, the last ray of joy. Three days later, on 10 October, a catastrophe occurred unexpectedly. At Maciejowice, where an engagement with Fersen took place, Kościuszko's corps of 7,000 was almost completely destroyed and 22 guns were lost. Kościuszko himself, gravely wounded, together with his adjutant Fiszer and his secretary Julian Ursyn Niemcewicz, and Generals Kamieński, Kniaziewicz and Sierakowski, fell into captivity.

On 12 October the news of this rout reached Warsaw, causing great agitation and dejection. The new Commander chosen that same day at a session of the Supreme National Council was Tomasz Wawrzecki. He was a man personally worthy and a great patriot, a former deputy to the Great Sejm, lately distinguished by his part in the rising in Lithuania, but otherwise "in knowledge not exceeding the intellectual sphere of a Lithuanian landowner". Wawrzecki himself was also aware that he lacked the qualifications of a leader, and for four days he declined to accept the honourable office, but in the end he yielded to the entreaties and urgings of all.
muszynska1947/110:
In order not to allow despair to take hold, the Supreme National Council issued appeals, encouraging the citizens to further strenuous action. On 16 October it addressed a separate proclamation to the Greater Poles, calling upon them not to bury "the hopes of the Fatherland through the loss of a man, albeit a most estimable one, whose fate cannot and ought not to determine the fate of the Fatherland". On the same day a letter also appeared, directed to the citizens of the Sieradz voivodeship and Wieluń Land, urging them to apply themselves to the rising and to support the work begun "most valiantly and most eagerly". The Supreme National Council appointed for them a new plenipotentiary in the person of citizen Okołów, because the plenipotentiary Józef Wybicki "is not in a position to fulfil the duties entrusted to him with regard to the Sieradz voivodeship and Wieluń Land".

These efforts to sustain the spirit of the nation were, however, in vain. Most Poles already regarded the defeat of 10 October as the end of the insurrection and all further exertion as pointless. For the catastrophe of Maciejowice had checked "the impetus of the revolution".

Dąbrowski, having learned on 14 October, on his return from the march on Toruń, of the defeat at Maciejowice, as well as of the severing of communication with Warsaw and of the planned destruction of his division by the Prussian forces, considered it necessary, without waiting for an order, to leave Bydgoszcz and return to Warsaw. He began the preparations for the march back at once, and on the following day set out from Bydgoszcz with the main corps in the direction of Gniewkowo. He took with him more than 400 prisoners, among them also the arrested Prussian officials: the councillor Grabowski, Broskovius, the director of posts Tschepius and the mayor Radzibor.
muszynska1947/111:
Behind the army trailed an enormous baggage train consisting of nearly 200 provision and field wagons, loaded with cloth for 4,000 men and with many other military supplies. The Greater Poland cavalry detachments sent to Nakło, Łabiszyn, Barcin [Bartschin] and Żnin received orders likewise to begin their retreat on 15 October and, advancing slowly towards Konin, to destroy all the bridges on the Noteć; their task was to cover Dąbrowski's right flank. Bielamowski was instructed first to observe the enemy in Poznań, and then to go by way of Pyzdry and Konin and join the main corps. Colonel Sokolnicki with his riflemen and Dąbrowski's cavalry brigade closed off the left bank of the Vistula opposite Toruń from Zielona Woda to Czerniewice, in order to make it difficult for Colonel Ledivary, encamped at Podgórz, to observe the movements of the corps.

The march proceeded at first at a slow pace, since the roads were sandy and the soldiers tired quickly. For this reason Dąbrowski encamped near Gniewkowo on 15 October itself and rested there the whole of the following day. On 16 and 17 October Colonel Sokolnicki, under cover of a thick autumn fog, attacked Ledivary's outposts, after which on 18 October, not even pursued, he set off towards Nieszawa. Dąbrowski with the corps marched out of Gniewkowo on 17 October and the next day reached Włocławek, while the baggage train together with the prisoners reached Brześć Kujawski. At Włocławek Dąbrowski learned from Major Molski, and from citizen Miaskowski, whom he had sent out from near Gniezno, further details of the battle of Maciejowice. The former brought him, moreover, a commission as lieutenant-general and "a very fine broadsword for his successful action"; the latter brought exact news "of the enemy's strong vigilance".
muszynska1947/112:
And indeed the enemy was vigilant. On 13 October old Schwerin learned of the defeat at Maciejowice from the lips of an eyewitness of those events, Lieutenant von Heiligenstadt, and from then on his attention was occupied by one thought only. He was certain that Dąbrowski would have to fall back, and he began to ponder how to set up a barrier against this enemy, who could be dangerous even in retreat. He knew that Dąbrowski had three roads to choose from. He could withdraw by the old road across the Bzura, by which he had set out from Warsaw, or by new ones, of which one led across the Warta in the direction of Wieluń and Sieradz, and further between Radomsko and Częstochowa and through the Sandomierz voivodeship, while the other ran along the right bank of the Vistula, in which case he would have to cross above Toruń and cut through Favrat's corps on the Narew. Schwerin tried to prepare for all these possibilities, and even took into account a march by Dąbrowski on Gdańsk. At first, as late as 16 October, he thought that Dąbrowski would go by the right bank of the Vistula, and therefore intended to reinforce Favrat's corps, wishing to leave to it the merit of destroying so elusive an enemy. This rather strange supposition Schwerin formed before he had received news of Dąbrowski's return from Toruń to Bydgoszcz. Only when on the following day he learned that Dąbrowski had returned to Bydgoszcz did he himself intend to deal with him.

To this end he made the following dispositions. From Rawa he moved a magazine to Piotrków, and from there in turn he ordered the siege artillery to be transported to Silesia, so as to be able to act freely and not to scatter his forces among numerous garrisons. Beyond the little river Rawka he dispatched 3 battalions and 5 squadrons with guns, from where, in case of need, they were to be directed to Łowicz or Piotrków. Now, having

Antoni Madaliński. From a miniature in the Princes Czartoryski Museum
muszynska1947/113:
with him still 7 battalions and 12 squadrons, he was waiting only for news from Toruń and from the commanders of the remaining corps sent to Greater Poland, so as to know in which direction to march for the destruction of Dąbrowski's division. In this action he was to be assisted, should the encounter with the enemy take place near the Bzura, by General Klinkowström, as well as by Colonel Ledivary, who was following in the enemy's tracks from Toruń, and by Generals Pollitz and Schwerin the Younger, once they had united their corps. The forces thus combined, drawn up on the line from Kamionna to Sochaczew together with a powerful artillery, would then have amounted to 15,000 men.

Dąbrowski meanwhile left Włocławek on 19 October and directed his march towards the lower course of the Bzura, to Gąbin, while Madaliński, to cover his right flank, went with his brigade and Sokolnicki's riflemen in the direction of Kiernozia by way of Gostynin and Slesin. Only now did Colonel Ledivary rouse himself and set out from Podgórz to pursue the enemy in retreat. He still caught up with the Poles' rear guard at Służewo, dispersed it and took some baggage, but just two days later, on 21 October, he lost all contact with his opponent.

Dąbrowski was by then already at Gąbin, and there he formed what was almost a new plan of action. He wished to wait "for relief or for the making of a communication across the Bzura, and then to strike at Ledivary and force his way into Greater Poland again". There was, however, no time for waiting. Patrols reported that the enemy stood close by, and "willy-nilly it was necessary to cross the Bzura" and abandon Greater Poland.

Meanwhile the insurgent supreme command in Warsaw spared no effort to make it possible for Dąbrowski to cross the Bzura. The corps of General Kołysko, stationed at Błonie,
muszynska1947/114:
was reinforced to 3,000 men and sent to attack the Prussian post at Sochaczew. Prince Józef Poniatowski set out from Warsaw towards Kamionna with the same strength. On 18 October both corps drew near the Bzura, crossing the exceedingly dense forests of those parts, which made their march wholly unobserved. The next day Sochaczew and Kamionna were attacked, but the Prussians repulsed the attack. General Klinkowström, alarmed by the roar of the guns, marched out of the camp at Potoki, reached both bombarded places, restored communication between them, but on the second day returned to Potoki, fearing for the magazines at Łowicz. On 20 October Kołysko, reinforced with troops from Warsaw, renewed the attack on Sochaczew, received two days later the help of a detachment of Prince Józef's corps, and on the 23rd of that month attacked the town again "unluckily but with stubborn courage". At the same time the Poles also shelled Kamionna, though from a respectable distance.

The events that began to unfold on the Bzura moved Lieutenant-General Schwerin to take new steps. He understood that the decisive moment was approaching. He therefore sent off as quickly as possible 2 battalions to reinforce General Klinkowström's corps, and himself resolved, with the rest of his army, to leave at last the camp at Chrzonowice and take up position in the proper theatre of war. Before the march he issued final orders: he sent 3 battalions of Bonin, 5 squadrons of Bieberstein and 1 of Trenck in the direction of Rawa, and the battalion of Pfau and 2 squadrons of Bieberstein's regiment to reinforce the garrison of Piotrków, and, delaying no longer, set out on 20 October with 5 battalions and 11 squadrons for Skierniewice, and then for Łowicz and Kiernozia. He halted at Kiernozia on 22 October, and there learned,
muszynska1947/115:
that Dąbrowski had marched out of Gąbin on the previous day in the direction of Mistrzewice on the Bzura. It was Schwerin's duty to occupy at once this point, which, as could be foreseen, was to serve the Greater Poland corps as its crossing place; there a mortal blow was to be dealt the opponent. Schwerin was now 25 km away from Mistrzewice and could have arrived in time, but he did not hurry. On 23 October, in view of the wooded country and of soldiers weakened by incessant marching, he advanced only a little and pitched camp at Kocierzów, south-east of Kiernozia, at a distance of 2 miles from Mistrzewice.

The consequences of this slowness soon became apparent. At the moment when the Prussian commander was only setting out from Kiernozia, Dąbrowski had already reached the Bzura and at 7 o'clock in the morning, under cover of a thick fog, began to cross to the other bank of the river. Amid the roar of the guns at Sochaczew, which was being attacked at that time by Kołysko, one detachment of troops after another entered the river bed and took up position on the heights of Brochów; at last the wagons with the booty came down, and at about 4 o'clock in the afternoon the crossing was completed, without the slightest hindrance from "even one Prussian": In the evening Madaliński arrived with the rear guard, still later the Łęczyca rising, and the night from 23 to 24 passed quietly, although word of the enemy came from all sides.

This enemy had, however, his reasons for not venturing to engage his opponent at so decisive a moment. The troops remained unconcentrated, and thereby the hopes vanished that it would be possible to surround Dąbrowski's division and force it to lay down its arms almost without bloodshed. After all, the junction of the corps of Generals Pollitz and Schwerin at Słupca, planned for
muszynska1947/116:
19 October, did not come about. On that day General Pollitz did reach Słupca by way of Łęczyca, Koło and Kazimierz, but waited there in vain for the arrival of Major-General Schwerin, who seemed to be acting contrary to orders. The latter was still in Poznań, where on 17 October news of the defeat at Maciejowice was brought to him also by Lt. von Heiligenstadt, and only on 21 October, on the express order of his monarch, did he leave the city, to join General Pollitz at last, four days later, at Słupca. The reason for his long stay in the capital of Greater Poland was fear of the might of an enemy standing nearby, which in reality was only Bielamowski's elusive raiding party.

Since it was impossible to surround Dąbrowski's corps, there remained now only the possibility of fighting an open battle with the enemy, but to this way of extricating himself from an awkward situation, which only incompetent commanders resorted to, Lieutenant-General Schwerin would not consent. After all, he knew neither the enemy's manner of fighting nor his strength, supposing it to amount to about 10,000 regular soldiers. In such conditions he feared a defeat, which would draw after it a strengthening of the insurgent movement, and perhaps even the loss of Greater Poland. For that reason, when on 23 October, at 5 o'clock in the afternoon, General Klinkowström appeared at Kocierzów with the news of the attack on Sochaczew and of Dąbrowski's possible simultaneous crossing, Schwerin pretended not to believe it, or perhaps really did not believe it, "as one long refuses to believe in misfortune". He did set out at last from Kocierzów towards Mistrzewice, and, having joined Klinkowström's corps at Sochaczew, arrived on the spot at 8 o'clock in the morning of the 24th. He at once ordered the firing of
muszynska1947/117:
cannon, to which the Polish guns replied from the opposite bank, but it soon became clear that "on both sides it was a vain waste of powder and shot". When the pointless cannonade died down, Schwerin ordered a rest, but did not go in pursuit of the Polish army, even when towards evening Colonel Ledivary arrived at Witkowice.

Meanwhile on the other side of the Bzura Dąbrowski, having first sent the prisoners and the booty off to Warsaw, began to entrench himself at Brochów, in order "to operate further from there both offensive and deffensive". On 24 October he received from Warsaw the order to storm Kamionna and Sochaczew anew together with Prince Józef and to clear the Bzura of Prussian troops, but he did not obey the summons, just as earlier he had not obeyed the instruction to support Poniatowski in his uncertain attack on Kamionna. Surveying the situation with a keen eye, he realised clearly that it was impossible to withstand the mighty army of Lieutenant-General Schwerin, once the latter should unite all his corps. He therefore handed over the command to General Rymkiewicz on 27 October and set out for Warsaw, summoned there to a council of war.

By leading the Greater Poland division to a place of safety, Dąbrowski fulfilled his duty. Of all the commanders of the Polish forces, he alone rose to the height of the task entrusted to him. During the 40 days that the expedition lasted he always operated successfully, though he had arrayed against him a Prussian army seasoned in battle. He himself led an army that was far inferior to its opponent in numbers and in quality, yet he was able to work a miracle with it. He crossed the Bzura, the Warta, the Noteć and the Vistula "always in the face of a superior enemy". He took Bydgoszcz and aroused in the Prussians anxiety for such towns as Poznań, Toruń and Gdańsk.
muszynska1947/118:
There was a period when, in view of the defeats on the other theatres of the insurrectionary struggle, favourable news of the movements of his corps was the one thing that cheered the hearts of the inhabitants of the capital and sustained faith in the future of Poland among the army and at those foreign courts that were well disposed towards the Polish nation. It was clear that he could not venture upon the destruction of an enemy who surpassed him in every respect, and that he was often compelled to avoid battle and confine himself rather to guerrilla warfare; yet he absorbed all the enemy's forces and, together with the Greater Poland insurgents, managed to bear almost the entire burden of the war west of the Vistula. When he could no longer expect further successes owing to the fatal turn of events on the main theatre of war, he set out on the return march and withdrew successfully with his whole corps to Warsaw, although the entire effort of the Prussian commander was directed against him, and the king repeatedly sent him orders to destroy the Greater Poland division by every means at his disposal. Dąbrowski's expedition also had considerable significance abroad. It undermined the position of the Prussian king in the partition negotiations, deprived him of part of the land in the Sandomierz and Kraków regions, discouraged him altogether from waging a simultaneous war in the west, showed the world that the famous army of Frederick the Great had incompetent commanders, and proved that "above the most seasoned routine there always prevails a spirit of civic self-sacrifice and zeal for a good cause".

In the annexed territories, meanwhile, after the departure of Dąbrowski's troops, Colonel Hinrichs, the worthy successor of Székely, set about restoring the old order. And all the gains recently achieved by the arms of the Polish army went for nothing. At Świecie
muszynska1947/119:
Hinrichs removed the insurgent commission and put up the Prussian emblems again. On 25 October he arrived at Bydgoszcz and restored Prussian authority there. On the following day the people of Bydgoszcz were already swearing a renewed oath of fidelity and obedience to the Prussian king, and soon, at the summons of the town's president Korkwitz, the Prussian officials returned to their official duties. Cavalry detachments sent out by Hinrichs removed the traces of the insurrection at Nakło, Żnin, Barcin, Kcynia and Gołańcz, while Hinrichs himself soon moved from Bydgoszcz to Inowrocław. There, on 2 November, he issued an order to seize insurgents and to notify the nearest posts of them, and for every insurgent captured by the population he set a monetary reward. From Inowrocław Hinrichs proceeded by way of Gniewkowo towards Nieszawa, in order to suppress the armed movement completely in that quarter as well.

General Beyern pursued the same aim. On 23 October he was at Czarnków [Czarnikau], on the 25th at Rogoźno, and finally on the 27th he reached Gniezno by way of Kiszkowo and remained there for several days.

Major-General Schwerin alone continued to show little enterprise in hunting down the enemy. Having no clear grasp of the situation because communications were hindered, he set out only on 26 October from Słupca by way of Kazimierz and Kliszewo to attack Dąbrowski's returning column near Włocławek. On the way he learned that 1,200 insurgents had occupied Pyzdry, but he advanced slowly, until at last a patrol sent towards Brześć Kujawski reported to him that Dąbrowski had left that district a week before. He therefore had no reason to go to Włocławek, turned back from the road, and directed his march to Koło, where he arrived on 30 October.
muszynska1947/120:
At the same time as the actions of the Prussian generals, the insurgents won a number of successes, which show that the armed movement in Greater Poland, although it did not grow in scale, nevertheless did not die out after all. Bands of partisans continued to roam there, paralysing the offices, attacking Prussian posts, seizing treasuries and magazines, destroying state emblems and cutting communications. In numbers these detachments were still quite considerable. In the neighbourhood of Gąbin as many as 3,000 confederates from the Poznań and Kuyavian voivodeships had halted, having separated from Dąbrowski's division in order to continue the fight against the enemy on their own. On the afternoon of 25 October 500 horsemen from this corps attacked Włocławek and soon sold off the entire stock of salt, collected 6,820 thalers of war contribution, and on the night of 25 to 26 October fired upon the weak Prussian post at Bobrownik, until finally the whole band made off in the direction of Brześć Kujawski. On 27 October Mniewski seized Nieszawa with an armed detachment. The insurgents, moreover, were busy in the Sieradz and Łęczyca regions. In the vicinity of the Warta, south of Uniejów, the intrepid Bielamowski was manoeuvring with part of Dąbrowski's brigade; General Pollitz's troops prevented him from joining the main corps at Gąbin on 18 October.

The armed movement in Greater Poland continued to disturb Lieutenant-General Schwerin and to restrict the freedom of his movements on the main theatre. When he received Suvorov's summons to bring the capital of Poland to its fall by joint forces, he replied that for the moment he could not heed it. He feared an attack by the Greater Poland insurgents on the rear of his army, and it was with them above all that he now wished to deal. His anxiety grew when Ledivary's reconnaissance, sent in the direction of Błonie, reported to him
muszynska1947/121:
that new corps were allegedly intending to break through into Greater Poland. In order to be able to cooperate with Suvorov "most effectively in forcing Warsaw to surrender and in bringing the war to an end", he devised a new plan, according to which a suitable disposition of the troops was to protect South Prussia from a fresh invasion on the one hand, and on the other to blockade Warsaw and force it by hunger to surrender. The plan was to come into force on 11 or 12 November. But when, in accordance with the new plan, the troops had already occupied the positions assigned to them, when General Pollitz had occupied the passage between Gąbin and Iłów, where a breakthrough of the enemy was to be expected; Major-General Schwerin had taken up positions inside Greater Poland on the Warta, resting his right wing on Szadek and keeping in communication with General Pollitz; General Beyern, after occupying Włocławek, had reached the Vistula with his left wing and extended his right towards the Warta, in order to cover Poznań, Gniezno and Toruń; and Schwerin himself had at last gone from Łowicz to Skierniewice in order to secure the area from Łowicz to Rawa, it was then, on 12 November, that Favrat arrived to take over the command in place of Schwerin, whom the king was removing, dissatisfied with his lack of activity.

Meanwhile the heart of the Commonwealth, its capital, had already ceased to beat.

Amid the general confusion, as the front on the Narew was breaking up (it had, among other merits, that of holding back part of the Prussian forces from striking at Dąbrowski's division), as the Lithuanian army was disintegrating, and as enormous desertion took hold of the whole army and entire corps surrendered, Suvorov was approaching Warsaw by forced marches at the end of October.

At such a moment Wybicki's report on the successful expedition to Greater Poland was received "as
muszynska1947/122:
in a violent conflagration where everyone bustles about out of his senses". The Supreme National Council, in this almost last hour of the Commonwealth's existence, sought ways of rescue in new military combinations, though of little realism; it offered a large reward to the corps that should be able to "clear the river Bzura of the enemy and open up Greater Poland". At the council of war in Warsaw on 27 October, Dąbrowski put forward, as yet another way of rescue, the abandonment of Praga and Warsaw, which in his opinion were not capable of defending themselves. He advised "marching into Greater Poland with the whole strength of the Commonwealth and with numerous artillery", with the king and the Supreme Council, and there, despite the fall of the capital, to see the winter through with the surviving army and government, awaiting French intervention or a falling-out on the part of one of the neighbouring states.

The premises of the plan were sound and rested on rational foundations. For winter was approaching, desertion was beginning to creep into the Prussian ranks, diseases were rampant, and there was considerable "discontent" there on account of the unsuccessful campaign. The corps left behind in Greater Poland by Dąbrowski were "growing immensely". Major Bielamowski's detachment numbered 600 horse, and the Łęczyca, Sieradz and Kuyavian risings were already 3,000 strong. If, therefore, the main army, advancing westwards, had taken the line of the Bzura, the Prussians would have been caught between two fires, and it would then have been easy to cut all their communications together with the supply of provisions. Pressed from two sides, with an army partly disorganised, they would have retreated behind the Oder, or at least behind the Warta. The Russians' pursuit of the Polish army would have been very difficult and slow owing to the lack of means of subsistence.

Dąbrowski, however, did not find a majority among those deliberating on the fate of the fatherland who were willing to support his
muszynska1947/123:
project. Two days thus passed, and the Commander and the Council took no decisive step. Only on 29 October, when Suvorov had already begun to bombard Praga, did an order come that the corps of Dąbrowski and Giedroyć should move towards Rawa in order to observe the Prussians. There they stood idle for several days.

Meanwhile, on 4 November, Suvorov took the entrenchments of Praga after a brief attack; they had been thrown up without any plan and served only for a reflexive defence, and he inflicted a bloody slaughter on the inhabitants of Praga. The capital, fearing a similar fate, surrendered on 6 November, with the proviso that troops who did not lay down their arms might leave it. The Supreme National Council dissolved itself. On 9 November the victorious Suvorov already rode ceremonially into Warsaw.

After the fall of the capital, complete disorder reigned in the army. The soldiers, abandoned by their commanders, threw down their arms in crowds, heedless of the fate of the country or of their comrades; they wished only to save themselves. Dąbrowski alone in this general confusion did not lose his head. With his corps, not yet touched by the ferment, he began a march to the south. His intention was "to hold out in the Sandomierz and Kraków regions, and from there to extend operations into the Sieradz region and farther into Greater Poland". He also spun plans that, given favourable circumstances, he might perhaps realise his cherished idea of breaking through to France by way of Silesia, Moravia, Bohemia, Bavaria and Swabia, "straight to Landau, or else to Switzerland towards the Rhine". During the march, however, "the misfortune of Praga and Warsaw" made itself felt in his ranks as well. When he encamped at Gostomia, "generals, officers and soldiers from both places" began to arrive, bringing fear and dread with them. Dąbrowski sought a way of sustaining the spirit of his soldiers
muszynska1947/124:
and found none other than to assure them that within three days he would lead them to Greater Poland, where he would begin a new campaign. In order not to deprive the soldiers of this hope, and also in order not to be cut off from the banks of the Pilica, he disobeyed Wawrzecki's order to withdraw from Gostomia towards Tarczyn or else to Grójec.

Meanwhile the situation worsened with every moment. Denisov and Fersen, having crossed to the left bank of the Vistula, began to pursue the Polish corps withdrawing from Warsaw. The Austrians had already taken Radom and cut off the supply of provisions and forage. There was moreover the fear that the Prussians too would move from Rawa, Łowicz and Piotrków to destroy the remnants of the Polish army, which dwindled with each day. The division of Prince Józef Poniatowski had already ceased to exist, capitulating on 7 November before the troops of General Klinkowström, and Generals Zajączek, Mokronowski, Wyszkowski, Kołysko and Ożarowski had left their corps, which themselves dispersed. Even Madaliński, "that ever well-meaning Pole, deluded by base men", left his detachment at Białobrzegi; his gallant brigade arrived at Gostomia on its own. There too took refuge the Commander Wawrzecki, President Zakrzewski, and Generals Giełgud and Niesiołowski; soon Major Bielamowski also arrived with his cavalry, returning from Greater Poland.

On 12 November, on the strength of Wawrzecki's order to march in haste into the Kraków region, Dąbrowski left Gostomia. On the same day a Russian officer sent by Suvorov, who was carrying the terms of capitulation for the army, was stopped on the road. Wawrzecki sent a letter to the king through General Gorzeński, urging him, in accordance with the earlier resolution of the Supreme Council, to negotiate with the Russian general. In the evening a Prussian trumpeter arrived with a letter to Dąbrowski from the Prussian
muszynska1947/125:
General Kleist. General Kleist asked "most humbly" on what terms Dąbrowski would be willing to "enter and join the army of His Prussian Majesty the King" together with his regular troops. Dąbrowski read the letter and translated it for the Commander in the presence of all the generals. There was much dispute over the reply, until at last it was decided to give an evasive answer, although Dąbrowski himself was of the opinion that matters should have been handled otherwise. He considered that in so grave a position, when there was no hope left, when Russian and Austrian troops surrounded the insurgents on all sides, and when the soldiers, "the infantry above all, for a thousand reasons neither wished nor was able to fight", Kleist ought to be answered with points: 1) a general amnesty in Greater Poland; 2) the placing of all officers in the Prussian army according to their commissions; 3) payment of 4 years' salary to officers unwilling to serve. The Greater Poles, Dąbrowski writes in his memoir on the end of the insurrection, liked the proposal, but Wawrzecki and Zakrzewski opposed it. Dąbrowski did not press the matter, yet "the greater part of the Greater Poles" begged him not to abandon the proposal. He therefore put it forward again, and, so that it should not be supposed that he was seeking "a decent place of maintenance" for himself, he assured them "on his honour" that he would take his dismissal. He hoped that the Greater Poles would not refuse him 6,000 Polish zlotys a year until such time as he might again serve the country. This time the declaration was received fairly well; nevertheless the Commander had weighty reasons for "not approving Dąbrowski's opinion"

The question of negotiating with the Prussians arose a second time in the course of the further march, at Opoczno, where some citizen came from Major Kloch to confer with Dąbrowski concerning the proposal of General
muszynska1947/126:
Kleist. Dąbrowski, however, no longer had any "inclination" to surrender his corps of regular troops to the Prussians; he wished only to treat on behalf of the "unfortunate citizens of Greater Poland". Colonel Gorzeński of the Greater Poland rising, who knew German, was therefore appointed to him, to be a witness at the talks with the Prussians; but the meeting did not take place. Meanwhile a courier arrived with word from King Stanisław August that General Suvorov was "bloodily" crushing those who would not comply with his demands, and had ordered a warning that the rest should not suffer a like misfortune. The last attempt at an understanding with Dąbrowski, which the Prussians made during the march of the Polish troops towards Radoszyce, likewise came to nothing, because "it had already been decided not to engage with the Prussians". Thus the securing of the fate of the Greater Poles, who above all could be called "rebels" and who for that reason were threatened with repression by the Prussian government, was not accomplished.

Faithful to the national cause to the last, the Greater Poland insurgents accompanying Dąbrowski did not desert their ranks. Towards the end, another 1,000 horsemen from the Sieradz and Wieluń risings joined, and these, together with the other Greater Poland risings, under the command of General Skórzewski, and with the brigades of Dąbrowski and Madaliński, represented, after the dispersal of all the regiments that had joined Dąbrowski on the way, the Polish army by themselves. They saw how Dąbrowski, after the unfavourable reply of Suvorov brought by the dispatched Gorzeński, in utmost despair, not knowing what to do next, wished to reach the vicinity of the Galician border, burn the weapons there, and disband Madaliński and his own brigade. They were witnesses when on 18 November General Denisov arrived at Radoszyce
muszynska1947/127:
with several officers and took with him to Warsaw the Commander Wawrzecki, General Dąbrowski, Giedroyć, Niesiołowski and Giełgud; while President Zakrzewski and General Rymkiewicz, not wishing to share a like fate, had already escaped earlier to Galicia. And before they themselves, after this de facto capitulation, went with General Skórzewski across the Prussian cordon, they were bidden farewell in tears by Wybicki and Mniewski, who addressed them in these words: "May God keep you in His care; we shall go to seek protection, and when we find it we shall return to you and shall not forget you".

In Greater Poland the flame of rebellion smouldered throughout November and even into December. The ranks of the insurgents had, it is true, shrunk, since many of them had returned home, but the rest, mostly people of no means who had nothing to lose, went on roaming the forests in more or less numerous bands and carefully avoided contact with the Prussian army.

The last armed efforts of the Greater Poles deserve all the more attention because they had help from nowhere, since already at the beginning of November the enemy had won the victory in the main theatre, and afterwards the new commander, Lieutenant-General Favrat, moved against them with redoubled energy in order to establish peace as quickly as possible in South Prussia. Colonel Hinrichs, who on 6 November had taken up position at Włocławek and was crushing insurgents in the forests between Płock and Włocławek, he ordered to remain in the Vistula region and to watch over the security of communications on the Vistula. He then divided the corps of General Beyern in such a way that 3 battalions and 4 squadrons, operating in the area Gostynin, Gąbin, Kutno, passed under the command of General Elsner, who also commanded the corps of Major-General Schwerin, who for his passivity was sentenced to 2 years in a fortress; the parts
muszynska1947/128:
of Beyern's corps that had been left in the vicinity of Gniezno (2 battalions and 3 squadrons) he directed to the Warta, to guard the crossings of that river from Pyzdry to Sieradz and, by sending out "flying columns" (fliegende Kolonne), to attack the insurgents at their assembly points.

Writing of the unceasing disturbances in Greater Poland, the newspaper of the day called the insurgents "deaf to the voice of reason," since instead of trying to earn the favour of the victor, lest in time it should be too late, they continued to roam the country with arms in hand.

Numerous mentions of the armed movement of the Greater Poles in November and December have been preserved in the sources.

In Kuyavia at that time Ksawery Dąbrowski held out at the head of 500 insurgents. On 6 November he was selling off in Włocławek a large stock of salt taken from the Prussian magazines, but Colonel Hinrichs, arriving unexpectedly, soon took the salt back, thinned out his detachment and drove it from the town. Of the other insurgent commanders, Colonel Sokołowski stood for some time near Brześć Kujawski with a force of about 1,200 men. Near Dobiegniew, opposite Dobrzyń, was Colonel Wolski with 300 armed men.

Driven by Hinrichs from the Vistula districts, the Kuyavian insurgents withdrew to the west, towards Radziejów and Piotrków Kujawski, in order to undertake guerrilla expeditions from there even in the second half of December. Hidden in the dense forests and marshes of that region and making use of byways, they became elusive, and establishing their numbers was not easy. The Kruszwica [Kruschwitz] domain (Amt) estimated these Kuyavian insurgents at several thousand. Their smaller detachments reached as far as Kruszwica, collecting food and forage from the neighbouring villages. News also arrived of a so-called "Kuyavian

Fryderyk Adam Székely. Wierzbiczany
muszynska1947/129:
regiment," which was active south of Radziejów under the orders of Colonel Trzebuchowski, or else Dąbrowski. Its strength was estimated at 600 men and more. The soldiers of this regiment took horses, forage and rents from the district, imposed contributions, collected recruits, and forced some of the nobility by violence to join the rising. On the night of 21 to 22 November three insurgents of the Kuyavian regiment rode into Strzelno, two of them fully armed and the third with only a scythe; they announced that a larger detachment of insurgents would arrive in the town within the next few days, took 300 thalers from the cash box, and then departed.

In view of such events the Prussian officials in Kuyavia did not feel secure. The most various and contradictory reports heightened their anxiety. They expected a new invasion. Indeed, leaflets distributed in the villages as far as Podgórz near Toruń announced plainly the early arrival of a corps already on the march under General Mokronowski, for which forage and provisions were to be collected. In Inowrocław the Germans addressed a request to the commandant of Toruń to reinforce the town's garrison as quickly as possible. Hundt then sent 106 infantry and 7 hussars, so that the garrison grew to 133 men. In Gniewkowo the tax collector sent money to Toruń every day so that it should not fall as booty to the insurgents.

Nor was there yet peace in the neighbourhood of Szubin. In the forests there the indefatigable Krupecki roamed throughout November together with the leaseholder Śminowski. Their detachment numbered 60 armed men, and grain for its maintenance was supplied by a certain clerk from the surrounding estates. On 12 November 2 insurgents from Krupecki's band came to Szubin, where a fair was then being held, and gathered information about the stationing of the Prussian troops.
muszynska1947/130:
Insurgents also still held out in the neighbourhood of Gniezno. According to the Südpreussische Zeitung small detachments of them were still roaming there at the end of November. On the 10th of that month a single insurgent, armed with 4 pistols and a broadsword, fell between Trzemeszno and Wilatowo upon two couriers dispatched from Gniezno and destroyed them completely.

Throughout November the insurgents were active around Wieluń and Sieradz, despite the defeat that Colonel Dossow had inflicted on them there at the beginning of that month, and also in the Kalisz region, reaching as far as Częstochowa and Rawa. Their bands numbered for the most part 50 or 100 men. By day they hid in the forests, and by night they left their hiding places and carried out raids to the detriment of the Prussian government.

In the Sieradz region especially their "escapades" caused much trouble. On the night of 8 to 9 November the insurgents burst into the customs office at Panke(?) in the Krzepice district and took the cash box from it. They were commanded by Major Pągowski and Captain of Cavalry Karski. The Prussian lieutenant von Lüttwitz, hastening to help from Kłobuck with 20 cuirassiers of Görtz's regiment and as many infantrymen of Lichnowski's regiment, was attacked by an insurgent detachment consisting of 300 foot and 300 horse. Lüttwitz could not withstand such superiority and was taken prisoner together with 21 soldiers. On 9 November Generals Lipski and Stokowski took up position at Krzepice with the intention of gathering more insurgents and attacking the weakly garrisoned Częstochowa. It went no further than a plan, however. At about this time the insurgents came to Kłobuck, removed the Prussian emblems and soon departed. According to news of 23 November, given in the Südpreussische Zeitung, there stood near Wieluń and in the Ostrzeszów district 2,000 insurgents, supplied with two guns. They spread unpunished from there in a westerly direction as far as
muszynska1947/131:
Jutrosin [Jutroschin] and Sarnowa [Sarne], taking money from the cash boxes. The Germans consoled themselves that perhaps Major-General Elsner, who at this time with his corps ought to be in the neighbourhood of Sieradz, would be able to curb their "wilfulness."

In November insurgents were still wandering in the western part of the Poznań voivodeship, in the neighbourhood of Grodzisk. On the 9th of that month 20 armed men came to the manor at Karczewo and the following night halted in some other village near Grodzisk. A somewhat larger detachment of 30 men came at this time to Grodzisk, where with drawn broadswords they rode through the town, announcing that "the insurrection is rising anew from the ruins" and would soon be drawing peasants into the insurgent ranks. The owners of the village of Turkowo at once informed their peasants of this, adding that 2,000 insurgents were assembling near Kościan, ready to join those who would once more seize arms and try a better fortune in the struggle with the Prussians. The peasants near Grodzisk were said to have been urged to insurrection by Faustyn Zakrzewski of Rakoniewice [Rakwitz], a member of the criminal court for the Poznań voivodeship, who at the beginning of the rising had attacked the Prussian post office.

The surrounding peasants were also called to arms at the beginning of November by the mayor of the town of Krzywiń [Kriewen], who was at the same time steward of the Konarzewo estates, with the intention of marching with them to seize Poznań. The Prussian detachment at Leszno, however, learned of the whole affair and sent out Captain of Cavalry Kottuliński with 30 horse. Finding the peasants assembled on the occasion of his arrival, Kottuliński sought to win them over to the Prussian government. He therefore set before them into what misery they would fall by following the voice of the nobility, which under Polish rule had alone enjoyed freedom while oppressing the peasants; he
muszynska1947/132:
assured them that freedom could be given to the villagers only by the Prussian government. Having finished his speech, he distributed a certain sum of money among those assembled, so that they might drink the king's health with it. The effect was extraordinary. The peasants promised to follow his advice, and out of gratitude revealed to him the hiding place of that steward and mayor. Kottuliński seized him and sent him to the justice commission at Wschowa.

For a long time, until as late as 7 December, the partisan Ksawery Łukomski harassed the Prussians. With a detachment that by some accounts numbered 5 or 8 men, by others 30, he ranged over the neighbourhood of Książ [Xions], Środa [Schroda] and Zaniemyśl. He was marked, moreover, by great recklessness. The Prussians also set a reward of 50 ducats on his head. On 7 December Łukomski was captured and handed over to the investigative commission in Poznań.

The events described here, fragmentary as they are, give a picture of the last insurgent struggles in Greater Poland. After the fall of the uprising in the main theatre of the fighting, further efforts by the Greater Poles could not avail much; they were not able to save the national cause. It is true that when the Polish army was making its last march towards the Pilica, the Greater Poland insurgents still sustained themselves with the hope that the armed movement might revive once more, if the soldiers leaving Warsaw were to set foot on their soil. This hope was not groundless. Dąbrowski, as we know, long insisted on his plan of transferring the war to Greater Poland. But from the moment the Polish troops fell into disarray and the Greater Poles could expect rescue from nowhere, they finally had to regard the continuation of the struggle as pointless. So they returned slowly from all sides, nobles and peasants, to their homes, to resume their former occupations. The scythes, so recently turned into weapons,
muszynska1947/133:
changed back again into tools useful at harvest time. After the Radoszyce capitulation Stokowski, Lipski and Lenartowicz disbanded their detachments. Deprived now of guiding aims, the insurgents, insofar as they had not laid down their arms, acted on their own account. The Prussian offices in small towns without garrisons continued to be exposed to danger from them, and communications were uncertain. Yet even these most persistent men were unable to resist the victorious Prussians for long. The year had not yet run out, and the insurrection in Greater Poland already belonged to the past. The advancing Prussian troops met with no resistance from the inhabitants, and "only neighbourly jealousies, mutual accusations and anxious politeness towards the officers" recalled the times so lately past.

The activity of the Greater Poles during those few months of the insurrection in this region may be characterised as follows those to whose credit the kindling of the revolt belongs were the nobility and the clergy; the Prussian government, too, regarded them as its greatest enemies. It was above all the petty nobility, who had little to lose, that took up arms willingly. Owners of larger fortunes, fearing damage to their property, often kept away from the uprising and frequently had to be forced into it. There were even some who, stripped of patriotic feeling, fled from the insurgent ranks to the protection of the Prussian government. The burghers, too, made common cause with the national movement, but only in small towns where the garrisons were weak or absent altogether; and always at the instigation of the nobility and clergy. The principal towns, such as Poznań, Łęczyca and Piotrków, where Germans formed a large percentage of the population, remained quiet, although cases of anti-Prussian agitation occurred there as well. Thus in Poznań the investigative
muszynska1947/134:
commission had to issue a proclamation refuting rumours of an alleged slaughter of Catholics by Protestants. The peasant, although not opposed to the insurrection, if only because he regarded the colonists sent by the Prussian government as heretics and despoilers of the land, nevertheless did not march in a mass into the insurgent ranks; only a few went there of their own free will. The Prussian government, for its part, from the very beginning of the insurrection let slip no opportunity to win over this very class of the population, the least nationally conscious. In its proclamations it warned the peasants not to let themselves be seduced by the nobility's "lying" promises of a reduction of labour dues; it compared their former position to bondage and assured them that only the Prussian king could confer benefits on them.

The strength at the insurrection's disposal was small. The creators of the voivodeship militias, despite a period of five months, did not know how to organise it properly, and later it proved impossible even to concentrate these risings of the individual lands, so that they could effectively resist the detachments of Prussian troops which, however small their numbers, advanced against them from Pomerania, from Silesia and from the vicinity of Warsaw. It happened that discord among the leaders of the risings, or a lack in them of the abilities needed to direct the movement, made unanimity of action impossible. For just this reason, at the agreed signal to unite all forces at Gniezno, only the insurgents from the Kalisz and Poznań regions appeared, under Niemojewski, that is about 1,300 men. When Dąbrowski halted at Słupca, 4,000 Greater Poles joined him. At first the commander had little satisfaction from them, for they lacked military training and a knowledge of the elementary rules of the art of war, but in time even this could be remedied. At Łabiszyn and Bydgoszcz the Greater Poles won for themselves
muszynska1947/135:
a glorious page of remembrance. Nor were the small detachments of the Greater Poland rising, which acted on their own account, idle. They cut direct communication with the centre of the Prussian lands, hindered transports and paralysed the civil authorities. It is chiefly to the credit of the Greater Poles that the Prussian king suspended the siege of the capital, for their armed movement was a successful diversion in the rear of the Prussian forces besieging Warsaw. By their participation in the insurrection the Greater Poles proved that they did not reconcile themselves to the new state of affairs, and that in defence of the fatherland they too were ready for sacrifices and self-denial. This circumstance, together with the incompetence of the Prussian generals, rendered a great service to Dąbrowski's military operations.

Chapter V

AFTER THE FALL OF THE INSURRECTION
muszynska1947/136:
With the fall of the insurrection the fate of the Polish nation came to depend entirely on the will of the triumphant partitioning powers. Nothing was any longer able to hold back the final partition. The insurrection, that armed reflex of a nation being quartered, which was meant to tear it from the hands of its butchers, in the end brought it political death.

The superior force ranged against it, however, was great. Hopes of help from other states proved vain. France did not grant the 12-million loan on the mortgage of the starostwa, which Potocki and Kołłątaj had expected from that quarter. All the efforts made in this matter by the Polish diplomatic agent to the revolutionary government, Franciszek Barss, were futile. The Committee of Public Safety objected that he had no official standing and that the rising in Poland "had been made by the nobility", and in the end it announced that "France will not let go the smallest particle of gold, nor expose the life of a single man for the sake of consolidating the revolution in Poland, if it is aiming at an aristocratic or royal government, or at a change of the reigning dynasty, or at a change of the form of government to another no less bad". This unfavourable stance of the French government of the time is significant,
muszynska1947/137:
since the insurrection in Poland was a diversion in France's favour, holding back part of the enemy forces from striking at the revolutionary armies. When in November the new Committee of Public Safety took an interest in foreign policy, the Polish cause again became topical. The old project of a Swedish-Danish-Polish-Turkish coalition was then brought forward; Parandier, appointed provisional agent to the provisional Polish government, was instructed to establish relations with the insurrectionary government based on trust and friendship and to declare that the French Republic would not refuse Poland help, so far as its own situation permitted, provided only that it had a guarantee that this help would serve the cause of liberty. Yet this help would have been belated and unnecessary. For it was not known that Kościuszko had already been a month in Russian captivity, and that the cause of the liberty of the Polish nation had been decided a few days earlier.

The insurgents also counted on the service that Turkey was to render their cause. They hoped that, under French influence, it would declare war on Russia or Austria in order to make good the losses suffered two years before. These calculations too, however, were to fail completely. In Constantinople the former French envoy in Poland, Descorches, did indeed work in this direction, but his influence carried little weight. Forgotten by the terrorist government, he waited in vain for those 4 million francs so indispensable for setting the project of a Swedish-Danish-Polish-Turkish coalition on a real footing.

Sweden, which was to join the coalition, although it regarded the insurgents with sympathy and had established diplomatic relations with the insurrectionary government, gave no help whatever.
muszynska1947/138:
Efforts to secure the neutrality of Austria, which Kościuszko, as we know, considered the best of the three neighbouring states, likewise failed.

The machinations concerning the final partition of Poland had begun as early as the middle of 1794. On 4 June the Austrian minister Thugut received a dispatch from Austria's representative in St Petersburg, Count Cobenzl, that Catherine regarded a new partition of Poland as unavoidable and promised to support Austria's aspirations in this respect. Thugut, who had dreamed of a third partition of Poland even earlier, succeeded in winning the emperor over completely to his plans of partition. Francis II therefore laid the duty of wrestling with the revolution on the shoulders of his generals and on 19 June returned to Vienna to watch, first and foremost, over his interest in Poland.

In August the final partition negotiations began, to the immense joy of the Prussian king, who had for months been awaiting that moment with impatience. The new Prussian envoy in St Petersburg, Count Tauentzien, then demanded, in accordance with the instructions he had received, so extensive a share for Prussia that he provoked the decisive protest of his Austrian colleague Cobenzl, likewise supported by Russia. For he demanded not only the areas on the Narew and the Niemen and the lands west of the Pilica and the Vistula with Warsaw, but also the Kraków and Sandomierz voivodeships. In order to avoid bordering on Russia, he proposed carving out of Mazovia and Samogitia two separate duchies for Platon Zubov and Prince Nassau-Siegen. The Empress had no thought of agreeing to such far-reaching claims by Prussia. She assigned the Kraków and Sandomierz regions to Austria and Samogitia to herself. Prussia, however, did not give way, with the result that relations between it and Austria became so strained that they even threatened a breakdown of the
muszynska1947/139:
negotiations. Both states were by then ready rather to see in Poland the state of affairs of 1793 than to yield.

Russia took a decided stand on the side of Austria. Between her and Austria a partition convention was concluded on 3 January 1795. It assigned to Russia an area of 120,000 sq. km with 1,200,000 inhabitants, namely: the remainder of the Vilnius, Nowogródek and Brest-Litovsk voivodeships, part of Volhynia and of Chełm Land, and almost the whole of Samogitia; to Austria, a territory amounting to 47,100 sq. km with a population of about 1½ million, that is, the remainder of the Kraków voivodeship (with the exception of a small strip which fell to Prussia), the Sandomierz, Lublin and Bełz voivodeships, part of Chełm Land, a considerable part of the Podlasie voivodeship, Liw Land from the Mazovia voivodeship, half of Warsaw Land and of Czersk Land, and a piece of the Volhynia voivodeship. The remaining lands of the Commonwealth were to fall to Prussia, that is, the remainder of the Rawa and Mazovia voivodeships with Warsaw (with the exception of those lands which fell to Austria), a fair part of the Troki voivodeship and a small piece of Samogitian land, and a small part of the Kraków voivodeship with the Duchy of Siewierz, together 48,000 sq. km with a population of almost 1 million.

For some time Prussia did not consent to the area assigned to it. Above all it began negotiations with the Committee of Public Safety in order to conclude peace with France. Prince Henry of Prussia, the brother of Frederick the Great, pushed it onto this road. He saw in the war with France "the suicide of Prussia for the benefit of Austria", and he regarded peace as the more necessary the more he feared that the victorious French might later make the conclusion of peace with Prussia conditional on its renouncing the Polish provinces. And indeed peace was concluded at Basel on 5 April
muszynska1947/140:
1795, and Prussia gained a free hand to settle the matter of its acquisitions in Poland. Its resistance was, however, soon broken by the Empress. Ostermann declared to Count Tauentzien that the Polish question must be brought to an end, and that if Prussia intended to attack Austria, the Empress was determined to support the latter with all her strength, while the emperor would make peace with France and himself take the field against Prussia. The threat had its effect. On 3 September 1795 Tauentzien held the first joint conference with the representatives of Russia and Austria, Markov and Cobenzl, and on 24 October the partition treaty between Prussia and Russia, with the participation of Austria, was concluded, in which Prussia agreed to the provisions of the convention of 3 January 1795.

The Prusso-Russian partition convention was supplemented by an additional one of 26 January 1797, accepted by Austria. A separate and secret article of this convention erased from memory for all time the name of the Polish Commonwealth (Rzeczpospolita Polska).

Of the lands which Prussia received in the last partition, the area on the left bank of the Vistula with Warsaw was incorporated into South Prussia. The area on the right bank of the Vistula and north of the Bug formed, together with the Płock voivodeship and the small piece of the Warsaw voivodeship which Prussia had gained in 1793, New East Prussia [Neuostpreußen]; and part of the new lands in the south, namely the Duchy of Siewierz and a piece of the Kraków voivodeship, formed New Silesia [Neuschlesien]. South Prussia was in time divided into the departments of Poznań, Kalisz and Warsaw; New East Prussia into those of Płock and Białystok.

The loss of its own state was the consequence of the fall of the insurrection for the whole nation. What, apart from this, were the consequences of the collapse of the uprising, in particular for the Greater Poles, and what was the situation in their country?
muszynska1947/141:
In Greater Poland, alongside the restoration of the old order, trials of the insurgents now began. Their tracking down and punishment was undertaken by special commissions, which had been appointed while the insurrection was still in progress. For East Prussia [Translator's note: so printed; South Prussia is evidently meant: the commissions at Wrocław, Brzeg and Głogów, in Silesia, dealt with the insurgents of South Prussia (see p. 143).] they were installed in Wrocław, Brzeg and Głogów; for West Prussia, in Grudziądz and Toruń. The former were presided over by Minister Danckelmann, the latter by Minister v. Carmer. With the establishment of the West Prussian commissions, the commission set up in Toruń by Székely, under the chairmanship of the judicial councillor (Justizrat) Kühze, ceased to function. On 26 January 1795 an order was issued that there was to be no appeal from the verdicts of all five commissions, but that for a verdict to become valid royal confirmation was required.

From 1 February 1795 Count Hoym, who after the recall of Voss in September 1794 had become chief minister of South Prussia, was appointed to supervise the commissions in Silesia. His intention was to bring the trial of the insurgents to an end as quickly as possible, and in accordance with the royal instruction fines and confiscation of property were to replace prison sentences. Hoym meant to devote the fund thus collected to the reforms in South Prussia that had been announced in part in the Wrocław patent of 24 September 1794, probably drafted by himself. For while on the one hand he had resolved to teach the Greater Poles obedience by punishing the rebels, so as to deter them in future from stirring up any disturbances, on the other hand he intended to introduce certain reforms, to remedy the lack of credit and cash, to put the mortgage registers in order and to lower the rate of interest, in order to inspire confidence in the new ruler among the inhabitants. Observing social relations in his province, he had come to the conviction that since its seizure by the Prussians
muszynska1947/142:
the magnate had lost his influential position and had become a mere landholder, that as a consequence the petty nobility, whose voice had formerly been needed by the lords at the sejmiks, had lost its means of livelihood, that the burgher was oppressed by the obligation to quarter Prussian troops, and that the material position of the peasants had deteriorated considerably because of the requisitions by the insurgents and by the Prussian army, which out of hatred for the insurgents had utterly ruined some estates. He held that the Prussian soldier in Greater Poland should change his hostile attitude towards the population, cease abuses and strive to win its affection.

According to a plan adopted in advance, the whole enormous trial of the insurgents, embracing more than 2,000 accused, was to be completed by 1 June 1795. After that date the cases of the accused not yet judged were to be taken up by a special commission. All the others were to be dissolved. Minister Hoym made the establishment of this commission known in an announcement of 24 April 1795. Poznań was designated as its seat, and it was subordinated to the former Prussian envoy in Warsaw, Buchholtz, who since September 1794 had held the dignity of Oberpräsident of South Prussia. The members of the commission were: the president of the Płock Chamber, Privy Councillor v. Harlem; the president of the Piotrków Regierung, Count Reuss; and the director of the Piotrków Chamber, Privy Councillor v. Zitzewitz; the assistant was Lt. v. Klebowsky.

Patents issued from time to time called upon the insurgents to appear voluntarily before the commissions, promising those who proved obedient to the summons a remission or reduction of punishment. The patent for the inhabitants of West Prussia, issued while the insurrection was still in progress, on 23 October
muszynska1947/143: 1794, went furthest in this respect. It promised all participants in the uprising release "from every and any penalty, whether of life or of body, or of confiscation of estates and other penalties on estates", as well as complete amnesty, "every pardon and remission", if within a period of two weeks from the date of publication of the patent they laid down their arms and returned to their homes; those who would not comply with the appeal were threatened by the government with severe penalties. The Landrat of the Bydgoszcz district, Twardowski, who had been an active insurgent at the time of Dąbrowski's expedition, placed his trust in this appeal, but was nevertheless arrested on 25 November 1794. For in the meantime the king had issued to the West Prussian commissions an order to mete out punishments to the "rebels" with complete ruthlessness. On 10 December 1794 a proclamation appeared concerning the treatment of the insurgents of South Prussia. It ordered the release of Polish prisoners. Former officers were to give a written undertaking that they would not enter service in any army that might take the field against Prussia. The common soldiers were to be incorporated in part into the Prussian army, or else sent out into the province as settlers. The nobility and clergy who had taken part in the uprising were threatened by the appeal with the loss of their estates and dignities if they did not present themselves before the appropriate authorities by 1 January 1795; the principal "rebels" and leaders of the insurrection it ordered to be arrested and delivered for interrogation before the commissions in Wrocław, Głogów or Brzeg. A publicandum (public notice) of 10 February 1795 extended the term for the appearance of the insurgents from South Prussia to 1 June 1795, threatening otherwise punishments as before. Finally, the patent issued in Wrocław on 24 April 1795, concerning the treatment of the South Prussian
muszynska1947/144:
insurgents, announced the execution of severe penalties only on a small number of the principal culprits; it sentenced those starostas who had taken part in the uprising to the loss of their starostwa, and the remainder of the accused to fines, with the intention of turning these to the benefit of the country.

Few former insurgents, however, presented themselves voluntarily to the authorities. The most guilty, those accused of crimen perduellionis (treason against the state), did not return.

In vain did the edictal citation (summons) of the Royal Regierung of South Prussia of 12 September 1795 call for the return of Józef Wybicki, of Generals Lipski and Niemojewski, and of the Rev. Canon Prolewicz of Nietrzanowo near Środa. Of all these, however, Niemojewski was arrested and confined in Magdeburg. His companions in misfortune there were Madaliński, Jerzy Grabowski, Giełgud and others.

The commissions conducted the investigation of the former insurgents with great thoroughness. Officials in West Prussia and South Prussia submitted lists of persons compromised in the events just past, specifying who had gone into the insurgent ranks of his own will and who under compulsion. Participants in the insurrection were punished with penalties on their liberty, such as detention in a fortress or imprisonment; estates were sequestrated; noble as well as church and monastic estates were confiscated; non-castle starostwa were taken away; finally, the "rebels" were removed from the offices they sometimes held, and sentenced to pay sums of money that were at times very high. No insurgent was sentenced to death, although the royal instruction to the West Prussian commissions recommended its execution in the case of very aggravating circumstances.
muszynska1947/145:
How many Greater Poles underwent fortress imprisonment is hard to establish. It is known, however, that at the beginning of 1795 the Prussians were holding in Toruń 42 citizens from West Prussia and 60 from South Prussia; in Grudziądz, 48 from West Prussia and 25 from South Prussia. As to the names of these prisoners, we can give barely a few. Thus in the fortress of Grudziądz were confined, for a period of 2 years, Piotr Trzebuchowski, captain of cavalry in the Kuyavian uprising, and the monks of the Benedictine monastery at Mogilno, Kajetan Smoliński and Izydor Domagalski, for 3 and 4 years, because they could not pay the fine imposed on them, in the amount of 6,000–8,000 thalers. In Toruń, Jan Żmichowski of Rawicz, private secretary of the starosta Mycielski, spent nearly half a year in detention. There are no closer data which would allow us to establish how many, and which, of the Greater Poles were held in the Silesian fortresses.
