We know only that in Głogów a citizen of Gniezno, Kłosowski, was kept in detention for 6 weeks. Those released had to swear the oath of allegiance anew.

In South Prussia the Prussian government placed under sequestration the estates of the following Greater Poles: Wojciech Węgorzewski of Objezierze, Antoni Chłapowski of Dąbrówka, Celestyn Sokolnicki of Jarogniewice, Mateusz Rosen of Kruchów, Biskupski of Kuchary, Jan Zembrzuski, owner of Great and Little Siekierki, Antoni Grudziński, lord of Popowo, Kukulin, Rybkowo, Łagiewniki, Jagniewice, Sarbia and Podlesie, Ksawery Łukomski, lord of Drzazgowo, Wysławice and Sokolniczki, Florian Borzęcki, leaseholder of Porażyn, the starosta Leszczyński of Grabów, who died of wounds received in the uprising, the Landrat Józef
muszynska1947/146:
Koszutski, Józef Lipski, Władysław Gurowski, Józef Niemojewski, starosta of Śrem, whose estate was finally confiscated as that of one of the principal leaders of the insurrection, Emanuel Polster, Józef Roseroni, Piotr Dapfontaine and Neopold, former bookkeeper of the Poznań banker Klug. We do not know which of the Greater Poles resident in West Prussia had their estates sequestrated.

Nor can we say which of the numerous estates that the Prussian government generously distributed to Germans over the next few years came from confiscation, or had been taken from starostas as punishment for their part in the uprising, or who their previous owners had been. We know only that of the estates lying in the most fertile area of the former Poznań voivodeship, namely in the districts of Śrem, Kościan, Krobia [Kröben] and Wschowa, which were received by the former royal adjutant, Major-General Zastrow, a part had been confiscated and had previously belonged to Józef Wybicki.

The former Greater Poland insurgents whom the Prussians removed from office included Twardowski, Landrat of the Bydgoszcz district, and Józef Koszutski, Landrat of the Gniezno district. In place of those removed, veteran Prussian officers were appointed.

Most often the "rebels" were assessed fines, which also frequently took the place of imprisonment. A sum of 2–6 thousand thalers was equivalent to a penalty of one year in a fortress, depending on the insurgent's financial standing. From the former insurgents of South Prussia the Prussians expected to collect 300,000 thalers. King Frederick William II assigned one third of this sum to his discretionary fund (Dispositionskasse), one third to the building of a fortress at Łęczyca,
muszynska1947/147:
winter uniforms for the soldiers, compensation and the costs of the insurgents' trials, and the remainder to the purposes of reform in South Prussia. Despite the strenuous efforts of Minister Hoym, the collection of the fines proceeded very sluggishly; in addition, some had to be partly remitted and a few even entirely. By 1 June 1798 a total of 1,707,168 Polish zloty, that is 284,528 thalers, had been collected from the whole of South Prussia. In all, 1,195,506 Polish zloty, that is 199,251 thalers, flowed into the Prussian treasuries in the Poznań department. As appears from numerous receipts found in the files of the State Archive in Poznań, those sentenced paid the fine imposed on them in instalments. The largest sums, that is, those amounting to 2,000 thalers and more, were paid by: Bieńkowski Sebastian — 5,000 thalers, the heirs of Bolesza — 8,000 thalers, Gliszczyński Antoni — 7,000 t (remitted — 1,000 t); Gurowski Władysław — 6,000 t; Gorzeński Nicefor — 4,000 t (remitted — 6,000 t); Jaraczewski Hieronim — 3,000 t; Koszutski Józef — 4,500 t (remitted — 1,500 t), Gen. Korytowski — 3,000 t (remitted — 9,000 t); Lipski Józef — 7,000 t (remitted — 1,000 t): Radoliński Piotr — 5,000 t; Rogaliński Hipolit — 6,000 t; Rosen Mateusz — 2,000 t; Sczaniecki Józef — 6,000 t; Sczaniecki Łukasz — 3,000 t; Sokolnicki Nepomucen — 2,000 t; Sokolnicki Piotr — 4,000 t; Swinarski Wincenty — 5,000 t; Taroni Jan — 2,500 t; Węgorzewski — 2,000 t; Wyganowski Antoni — 4,000 t (remitted — 14,000 t); Zakrzewski Hiac. — 4,000 t (remitted — 2,000 t).

When in 1807 the lands of the Second and Third Partitions (with the exception of the Białystok district, which Russia received) formed the Duchy of Warsaw, the citizens of South Prussia who had been wronged by the Prussians were ordered to submit their claims to the new government. In the Poznań department this matter was handled by
muszynska1947/148:
Rożnowski, councillor of the Administrative Chamber of that department.

We do not know how large a sum the insurgents of West Prussia had to pay by way of penalty. In any case it must have been small, since it did not suffice even for repairing the damage caused in that area by the insurrection. For that reason the authorities there made representations to the king that he should assign to West Prussia at least a part of the sum collected in South Prussia. The representations, however, foundered on the resistance of Minister Hoym. By virtue of a royal rescript of 17 October 1796 the injured parties of West Prussia could only claim compensation for damages from those who had caused them. In this way the matter was referred to private proceedings. Since, however, the guilt of the defendants often could not be proved, and many of them were abroad or were altogether poor, even by this route some compensation could be obtained only in a few cases. The small sum that came in from the insurgents in West Prussia is explained, in general, by the fact that the area affected by the revolt was small and was confined chiefly to certain parts of the Netze District. Of 138 accused, only 63 inhabitants were found guilty. Of these, 26 came from West Prussia proper, the rest from the Netze District. What fine was imposed on these 63 is not known, since no closer data are available.

The punishment of the insurgents, which was intended to deter the Greater Poles from starting revolts in the future and to teach them obedience, evidently did not produce that effect, since the Prussian king in the patent of 9 August 1796 warned against a new uprising. He threatened the owners of estates with responsibility for subjects
muszynska1947/149:
who rebelled, and ordered the peasants to report to the nearest authority the revolutionary intentions of their lords. The numerous landless nobility, residing with the more powerful landowners or loitering about the towns, was regarded as an element especially susceptible to revolution; the Prussian government accordingly extended watchful control over it. Within six weeks of the date of publication of the said patent, every individual of this kind was obliged to report to the district authority, present a certificate of origin, name his settled acquaintances, friends and relatives, and declare whether he intended to remain in the country or to go abroad. The emigration of this nobility was highly desirable to the government, which therefore announced that "permission for it will be neither refused nor made difficult"; on return, however, a passport and various credentials were demanded, and every effort was made to make it as difficult as possible.

The Prussian government likewise paid close attention to the clergy, for the clergy had "in the last unfortunate insurrection justly drawn upon itself the suspicion" of being guilty of "genuine revolts, of personal partiality and active support for harmful conspiracies, and even of secret associations and agreements aimed at the overthrow of the government of the country, and of other culpable undertakings from which every feeling of respect for law and moral order recoils." The patent of 9 August 1796 contained four points concerning the clergy: 1) bishops, officials (diocesan judges), deans and heads of monasteries are liable, for the conspiracies of those subordinate to them, to loss of office and sequestration of revenues; 2) for concealing rebellious intentions, priests will incur expulsion from the country, and for active participation in a conspiracy, the penalty for lèse-majesté and treason; 3) in the event of the complicity of several members of a chapter, monastery or other ecclesiastical community, besides the punishment of the guilty,
muszynska1947/150:
the cathedral or convent will be abolished, their estates confiscated, and their buildings converted to public purposes; 4) the same penalty threatens the concealment, within ecclesiastical buildings or outside them but with the knowledge of the clergy, of gunpowder, lead or firearms. Appeal to the duty of not revealing confidences entrusted to them did not release priests from responsibility. A conspirator who informed could expect a mitigation of his penalty, and one who took no part in it, a reward for denunciation. The patent assured informers of discretion and threatened with punishment those who knowingly made false accusations.

Simultaneously with the punishment of the former insurgents the Prussian government set about improving anew the whole administrative and judicial apparatus introduced in Greater Poland before the uprising, introduced further innovations, and spared no effort to turn the seized lands into a Prussian province.

On 5 January 1795 the South Prussian courts resumed their interrupted activity. In the judiciary the German language came to reign supreme, and Prussian procedure was introduced. This caused great discontent among Polish citizens, and the bolder among them even addressed the king on the matter. As a result of their efforts a publicandum appeared, dated 16 November 1795, intended to adapt judicial proceedings "as far as possible to the character and way of thinking of the nation". German was not, however, removed from the judiciary; it was merely promised that extracts from the general Prussian law (das allgemeine Landrecht, the General Land Law for the Prussian States) and the procedure would be published in Polish. The Regierungen were instructed to translate judgments and summonses into Polish, in whole or in abridged form. In 1797 Polish laws lost their binding force.
muszynska1947/151:
For Prussian legislation, the so-called Landrecht, was introduced.

The Greater Poles were removed from participation in public affairs; the Prussian government extended over them the tutelage of the German bureaucracy. Special regulations concerning the clergy, the nobility, the peasants, the burghers and the Jews governed the manner of ruling the population by means of the administrative organs. The clergy was placed wholly under the authority of the state. Through its commissioners the Chamber directed the elections of bishops, prelates and the superiors of religious congregations; from priests it received the oath of allegiance as subjects. In civil and criminal matters the clergy were subject to the jurisdiction of the Regierung. Only matters of a purely ecclesiastical nature belonged to the competence of the ecclesiastical courts. In 1796 the ecclesiastical estates were seized for the benefit of the treasury. For the maintenance of the clergy the treasury set aside a part of the revenues from the church properties it had taken and the interest on the capital belonging to ecclesiastical corporations and lent out privately; it allowed the clergy to collect fees for religious services according to an official tariff.

The nobility retained the privilege of owning landed estates, but with certain restrictions. Those among the nobility who had held no landed property at the time of the fall of the Commonwealth could now acquire it only after obtaining the incolat (indigenat, the right of a native noble to hold land). If anyone who had neither any right to landed property nor the incolat wished to acquire an estate, he had first to secure a special permission from the Prussian king. Inheritance, bequest by will and gift did not confer the right to hold landed estates without the incolat or royal permission. A contract of purchase or sale of noble estates was not legally valid without the approval of
muszynska1947/152:
the Regierung, which had first to obtain information about the new purchaser from the police organs. The owner of an estate had supreme authority over the peasant, but did not exercise it directly. For the administration of justice he had to maintain a justiciary (Justitiar), and he exercised police authority by means of the village head (sołtys; German Schulze); he appointed these officials after consultation with the Landrat. The justiciary and the village head sowed discord between the lord and his subjects.

The royal towns lost the right to elect their officials. In the private towns in the territory of South Prussia the government did, it is true, assure the hereditary owners and the commoners, by a patent of 18 April 1795, the right to nominate or elect the town councils, but it reserved to itself the appointment of the mayor. It controlled the municipal revenues, devised ways of repaying debts, and so on.

The Prussian government paid close attention to the Jews. In the annexed lands only those Jews could live who had settled there in the time of the Commonwealth; those who arrived later had to leave the country. A Jew entitled to reside in the country possessed a so-called letter of protection (Schutzbrief), which meant the same as a passport. The district offices imposed German surnames on the Jews, often ridiculous ones. Without the authorisation of the Chamber, Jews were forbidden to change their place of residence and their occupation.

In organising social relations the Prussian government was guided not by the good of the inhabitants but by the aims of the state. It made officials of the priests. The nobility it now favoured, now extended police control over. In order to curry favour with the nobility, it undertook no improvement of peasant conditions and did not abolish labour dues, despite announcements to that effect. The restriction of the self-government
muszynska1947/153:
of the towns and the manner of treating the Jews likewise served the aims of the state.

In order to safeguard the Greater Poles against undesirable influences, a severe censorship was introduced. The author was answerable for the content of a book even after it had been censored. Publication of a work without censorship entailed a fine.

Simultaneously with issuing new regulations, the Prussian government sought to extract from Greater Poland the greatest possible material benefits. It paid particular attention to agriculture and forestry, since the main part of its revenues flowed from them. It forbade the division of the so-called knightly estates (Rittergüter) of no more than 10 włóki (the włóka being c. 17 ha), which, as a result of the incessant partitioning among the members of expanding families, were falling more and more into decay. In addition to the ecclesiastical estates, in 1796 it also seized for the treasury the non-castle starostwa. Both kinds formed the so-called domains, whose administration was directed by the Chambers. The government raised taxes, increasing the ofiara to 24 groszy, and the hearth tax by one half. To improve communications it cleared the Warta and made it navigable.

The Prussian government likewise spared neither effort nor expense in order to entrench the German element in Greater Poland. For this purpose it brought in a multitude of officials, sent in colonists and peasants for public works, and leased the domains only to Germans. In South Prussia alone, within 4 years under the administration of Minister Hoym, 241 estates were distributed among 52 grantees. The starostwo of Międzyrzecz, with a number of picturesquely situated manor farms, was received, as a token of the royal "satisfaction" for services rendered to Prussia over many years, by Lucchesini. The Prussian government also took up a plan to dispossess the Greater Poland nobility
muszynska1947/154:
in favour of the German element. It was assisted in this by the thoughtlessness of the landowners, such as living beyond their means, readily availing themselves of easy credit, and squandering.

Schooling also served the aims of Germanisation. In the elementary schools a German primer was introduced. The German language was the main subject of instruction in the newly founded cadet school in Kalisz. In order to force the youth of Greater Poland to enter German universities, the government founded no institutions of higher learning on Polish lands. Only in 1804 did it establish the Warsaw Lyceum.

The efforts at Germanisation, undertaken already at the beginning of Prussian rule and continued later with ever greater ruthlessness, nevertheless did not succeed in killing the Polish spirit in the nation. The idea of independence was always alive. The Greater Poles longed for freedom, like the whole Polish nation. Polish blood was shed in cruelly suppressed uprisings. The Greater Poles watered the fields of their land abundantly with it in 1848, until at last, after more than a century of bondage, the sun of freedom shone for the oppressed nation. In vain, 20 years later, did the rampaging Hitlerite beast strive, during more than 5 years of occupation of the Polish lands, amid murders and the bloodiest persecutions known to history, to erase the name of Poland for ever; in vain was Greater Poland, Germanised at lightning speed, to be turned into a province German from time immemorial. From the martyr blood of the best sons of the Fatherland Poland rose up free, to prove to the world the truth of Staszic's words that "even a great nation may fall; only a worthless one can perish."

Jan Fryderyk Székely, Hungarian by birth and "a true spawn of the Huns", as Wybicki calls him in his memoir, had a reputation as an outstanding commander of light cavalry and at the same time as a brute, a cruel extortioner and a persecutor of the weak. He entered the Prussian army in 1758 during the Seven Years' War, later took part in the War of the Bavarian Succession, like Dąbrowski (1779), and in 1792, already with the rank of colonel, which he had earned 2 years before, fought on the Rhine. When the insurrection broke out in Poland, Székely was already over 50 years old. Sent by the king to crush the Greater Poland insurgents, he proceeded with the utmost severity. He was even a terror to the German population in the Netze District. After the defeat at Bydgoszcz attempts were made to blame Székely for the loss, whereas the commandant of Poznań, v. Diether, was also at fault, who should have attacked the rear of Dąbrowski's forces at the moment when he became convinced that Dąbrowski would not strike at Poznań but was heading for the Noteć. It is Székely's fault, on the other hand, that before the start of the battle that was to decide his fate he did not, despite the advice of the old Colonel Witte, occupy the hill dominating the town. In Toruń Székely set up a special commission under the chairmanship of the judicial councillor Kühze, which was to carry out systematically the confiscation of the insurgents' estates.

 Skałkowski, Mon. IV, 150, 151, 372; cf. Treskow, 323—325. Wilhelm, Fryderyk, Karol, Count Schwerin, was born on 11 December 1739 in Berlin. In 1753 he entered the Prussian army, serving in the regiment of his paternal uncle. At the outbreak of the Seven Years' War in 1756 he was adjutant to General Winterfeld, and after the latter's death (1757), adjutant to the king. In 1758 he was wounded at Zorndorf and taken prisoner by the Russians. There he managed to win over the Grand Duke Peter, and in 1760, exchanged for a Russian prisoner, he was sent back to Prussia. After the conclusion of peace at Hubertusburg in 1763 he returned to the army, later became a lieutenant-general, commander of an infantry regiment for the district of West Prussia, and governor of Toruń (Allgemeine deutsche Biographie (Leipzig 1891, vol. 33, p. 427)). Of the supreme command of the Prussian forces on the left bank of the Vistula, entrusted to him in mid-September 1794, he acquitted himself as badly as possible. According to the opinion of Prussian military men (Treskow, 282 ff.; Boyen, 79 ff.; Knoll, 156 ff.), Schwerin ought, immediately after taking over the command, to have concentrated his forces and attacked the opponent standing between him and Warsaw. The Polish troops equalled the Prussian neither in numbers nor in quality. During the attack mentioned above it was necessary for Generals Lattorff and Lichnowski to occupy Kraków and Sandomierz and to guard the regions of Piotrków and Łowicz against intrusion by the Greater Poland insurgents, while the corps of Elsner, of Schwerin the Younger and of Székely, joined together, were to strike at Dąbrowski's division. Later still, after the defeat at Maciejowice, when Suvorov was approaching Warsaw, Schwerin could have attacked the Polish troops stationed before his front and beaten them separately. Even if he had merely succeeded in pushing the opponent back towards Warsaw, he would already have gained freedom of action, and then he could have turned with the greater part of his army against Dąbrowski. But Schwerin remained indecisive even then, frittering away his forces from day to day, detaching more and more units against the insurgents; in the end he set out with 5 battalions to destroy the returning Greater Poland column, but as a result of false combinations he chose the wrong road. He allowed Dąbrowski's troops, together with a considerable baggage train, to cross the Bzura in peace, and afterwards took no step to support the Russians at Warsaw. He lacked, as indeed throughout the whole campaign, a clear judgment of events and decisiveness. He had set against him a very able opponent in the person of Dąbrowski, and by that measure he assessed the rest of the Polish army and its commanders (Skałkowski, Mon. IV, 151). For all the oversights and errors committed in his responsible post he answered with the loss of his command. The king took it from him under the pretext of weakened health and sent him back to his former governorship at Toruń. Schwerin, being certain that an injustice had befallen him, asked for an inquiry to be opened. His demand was granted. The inquiry was conducted by Lieutenant-General Brüneck at Königsberg. On 9 May 1795 a court martial assembled in Berlin under the presidency of General Rohdich and pronounced a sentence by virtue of which Schwerin was condemned to lose his regiment, to resign the governorship of Toruń, to one year's detention in a fortress, and to repay the costs of the investigations. He served the sentence at Grudziądz. After the death of Frederick William II he made efforts to return to the Prussian army, but the new king, Frederick William III, opposed this; he was permitted only to enter foreign service. On 17 August 1802, during a journey to Hamburg, Schwerin died. In his own justification he wrote "Wahre u. mit Aktenstücke belegte Darstellung der Veranlassung auf welche ich nach 43 Dienstjahren aus dem Königlichen Preuss. Militärdienste entlassen worden bin" (Leipzig 1798). The title of the second edition (Leipzig 1799) read: "Muster für Stabsoffiziere Rapporte zu machen". In the above treatise Schwerin accused Lieutenant-General Klinkowström as the one who in October 1794 had allowed Dąbrowski's division to slip away across the Bzura (Allgemeine Biographie. vol. 33, 428). Klinkowström rejected the charges made against him by Schwerin in the work: "Berichtigungen einiger Angaben, welche in dem vom General-Lieutenant Grafen v. Schwerin herausgegebenen Buche... enthalten sind" (Berlin 1799). The blame that he attributed to Schwerin during the campaign of 1794 he set out in points: 1) the unnecessary drawing in of General Lattorff's corps from the Sandomierz region and the consequent loss of that province; 2) the pointless formation of the corps of Pollitz and Ledivary and their unsuitable use for holding back the opponent in West Prussia; 3) remaining idle in the camp at Chrzonowice, on the strength of false assumptions, until 20 October 1794; 4) the undertaking on 22 October of a march from Łowicz to Kiernozia and Osmalin that was pointless in the highest degree, as a result of which the enemy was able to cross the Bzura with impunity; 5) the failure to undertake, jointly with the Russian troops, an offensive against Warsaw, contrary to the royal orders and to the very nature of things, and instead remaining idle at Łowicz from 26 October until 10 November (according to Klinkowström, Berichtigungen.... 11, 12).

ostensacken2001/33:
III. Marianne Countess of Hoym and Friedrich Ludwig Prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen

Amalie Louise Marianne Charlotte Countess of Hoym was counted one of the wittiest and most charming young ladies of her time. She knew how to move in society with an elegance that was yet natural, and not only this: as the future sole heiress of the extensive possessions in Saxony and Silesia she was one of the richest women in the duchy of Sachsen-Weimar-Eisenach and in Prussian Silesia. Her circumstances nonetheless did not permit her the free choice of her future husband. In noble circles as among the peasantry the contracting of a marriage had for a long time, quite independently of the literary impulses of Sturm und Drang, the character of a contract of sale, "in which the bride was nothing but the object being sold - without an opinion of her own". In contrast to her future husband, whom the young woman had even been commended to by Frederick the Great, she, as a well-brought-up daughter of a good house, can hardly have had the chance at nineteen to make enquiries about the hereditary prince Friedrich Ludwig zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, eighteen years her senior. What course the marriage contracted on 8 April 1782 at Gleina in Saxony would take, the young countess could not have foreseen with the best will.

The hereditary prince Friedrich Ludwig zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, born on 31 January 1746 at Ingelfingen, seemed destined for a military career. At ten the young hereditary prince was already yearning for his first military deployment, for Prussia had just begun the Third Silesian War, which it waged against Austria, Russia, France, Sweden and the majority of the princes of the Empire. At barely thirteen he received a captaincy in a Franconian circle regiment, but by the time he might have taken up the post at sixteen the war, now seven years old, was almost over. Frederick the Great, however, was and remained his great model, which he strove to emulate. He therefore did not seek military renown among the Imperial troops either. He soon stood in the particular favour of the Prussian king Frederick II. As a major he entered Prussian service in 1766. In 1775 Friedrich Ludwig received the patent of lieutenant colonel. In 1778 he became colonel of infantry in an Upper Silesian corps. In the War of the Bavarian Succession he could not however prove his military talent, for the Prussian

ostensacken2001/34:
leadership prudently kept out of every battle. Still in 1786 he rose to major general and was named commander of the infantry regiment Alt-Rotkirch, which received the name "Hohenlohe". The esteem Frederick II had shown him was also paid him by the successor and nephew of the king who died in 1786, Frederick William II, who on 27 March 1788 transferred to him the general inspection of the Silesian fusilier battalions with a permanent seat at Breslau and on 24 March 1791 named him governor of Breslau.

The Prussian roi philosophe Frederick II with his strong affinity for an Enlightenment of French provenance, and Karl August von Hardenberg - a friend of Prince Friedrich zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, who in Ansbach-Bayreuth had already set an example in the enforcement of necessary reforms - may also have served him as models in his efforts at reform in the Hohenlohe heartland. Until the French Revolution the reigning princes of Hohenlohe had lived on in an absolute political dead calm, in the conviction that their hallowed by tradition sense of right would outlast the coming centuries as well.

The research of the historians Hansmartin Decker-Hauff and Gerd Wunder establishes the origins of the house of Hohenlohe in the year 1095 at Weikersheim in the Tauber district. There Konrad von Wikartesheim from 1207 first used the name "de Hohenloch" in his seal. His sons, Heinrich and Albert, bore this name from then on and added to the seal a coat of arms - two leopardised lions arranged one above the other. Emperor Frederick II, in whose campaigns they served faithfully, rewarded them with the lordship of Langenburg, when the Staufer was at odds with his son Henry VI about 1231.

Two of the five sons of Heinrich von Hohenlohe, Gottfried and Konrad, were able to extend the lordship around Waldenburg and the richly endowed collegiate foundation of Oehringen. Beyond this they were charged with the exercise of the protection-

 4 In October 1790 Karl August von Hardenberg, at first responsible for financial and accounting matters, entered the service of Margrave Alexander of Ansbach-Bayreuth. There he rose to the summit of leadership within two years. After the abdication of Margrave Alexander he was named Prussian minister of state and war. He began the incorporation of the margraviates into the Prussian state and ruled there as independently as the Silesian provincial minister Carl Georg Heinrich Graf von Hoym. Despite massive resistance he quickly unfolded his ideas of reform and developed new political concepts, creating, joined with the introduction of a liberal economic policy, a unified modern structure of state that had model character for Prussia. The collegiate foundation at Oehringen later became the starting point for a lordship reaching beyond the Hohenlohe territory, joined with the comital rights in the northern Kochergau and the right of high jurisdiction. In 1418 the sole-reigning Albrecht von Hohenlohe received the sovereign territorial supremacy, after King Sigismund had granted him unrestricted jurisdiction at the Council of Constance. The lords of Hohenlohe were raised to the rank of count by Emperor Frederick III in connection with claims of inheritance to the counties of Nidda and Ziegenhain. In these regions, remote for the house of Hohenlohe at the time, it could not indeed hold its ground against the landgraves of Hesse, yet the comital title remained to it, which for the consolidation of the territory immediately surrounding it mattered in so far as it helped to stabilise and extend the territorial supremacy in the Hohenlohe heartland.

Toward the Reformation, which elsewhere had not only split the faithful into two camps but had also become a matter of politics, the house of Hohenlohe behaved rather hesitantly and wait-and-see. An impulse to take "sides" came first from a petition of the town of Oehringen directed against the frivolous goings-on of the canons. With the church order of 1553 the Reformation was sealed. Two years later the counts Ludwig Casimir and Eberhard resolved the partition of the land into the two main lines Hohenlohe-Neuenstein and Hohenlohe-Waldenburg. In the course of the seventeenth century further splittings of the land followed from rules of inheritance, and with them the arising of numerous side lines. From the main line of Neuenstein the lines of Langenburg, later Oehringen and Weikersheim, branched off in 1610. From the line of Langenburg there formed in 1701 the lines of Ingelfingen and Kirchberg. The main line Hohenlohe-Waldenburg divided once more in 1688 into the lines of Schillingsfürst, Bartenstein and Jagstberg. Already in October 1667 the sons of Count Georg Friedrich II of the line Waldenburg-Schillingsfürst, Count Christian (1627–1675), progenitor of the house of Bartenstein, and Count Ludwig Gustav (1634–1697), founder of the house of Schillingsfürst, had returned to the Catholic faith. Confessional differences and notorious disputes of inheritance weighed on the relations of the various lines the more also because the Catholic counts had already been raised to the rank of prince in 1744, while the counts of the Neuenstein line were raised only in 1764.

The tiresome quarrels among the various side lines had hardly left time to take up ideas for the reform of the administration and of the economy-

ostensacken2001/36:
to set the princely household on a solid footing again. As the only one of the princely house Friedrich Ludwig von Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen dared the leap forward.

Though branded by many of his peers as a betrayal of emperor and empire, he had seen to it that Hohenlohe was included in the Peace of Basel. The neutrality of Hohenlohe prevented not only the danger of becoming a theatre of war; the prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen moreover achieved that it was freed from the payment of 300,000 livres of contributions, which would have been laid upon the principality of the Franconian circle of the Empire. Nonetheless the quarterings of Austrian and French troops beginning in 1798 weighed heavily on the budget of Hohenlohe.

Even before his marriage with the rich heiress Marianne Countess of Hoym the prince's finances had been in disorder. Friedrich Ludwig zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen cherished the pious belief that with the revenues of the estates lying in Upper Silesia he could set new projects on the way in his heartland. After the peace congress of Rastatt he tried to attach to the Hohenlohe territory the lands of the monastery of Schöntal, the Teutonic Order's district around Mergentheim and parts of the Palatinate as well as of the archbishopric of Mainz. After a then following new ordering of the German Empire he would have wished for himself the dignity of a duke of Franconia. But of this nothing came, on account of the political development. Still, Friedrich Ludwig von Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen had in his heartland been able to streamline the house authorities by the creation of a central instance and to renew the police administration. To the economy he sought to help with the building up and extension of commercial undertakings. Thus in 1794 he had conceived the plan of founding a joint-stock company for Hohenlohe coal mining. As the diggings brought no hard coal to light, this undertaking had to be dropped, as had the reactivation of the princely salt works at Weißbach, existing still from before the Thirty Years War. Encroaching Kocher floodwater and the influence of carbonic acid gas had prevented a profitable operation. Profit from these undertakings had been drawn above all by Hofrat Glenk as his adviser, who had counselled him to invest ever larger sums and to demand a high salary for himself, which was also granted him. The deficit that arose, which still in 1809 amounted to the enormous sum of 400,000 gulden, had later to be made good by his son and heir, August. Realised

ostensacken2001/37:
could only be the building begun in 1782 of the Mariannenvorstadt named after his wife, a settlement whose purpose was to foster trade in his small residence. To raise the attractiveness of the settlement he put ground and land for the building of houses at the disposal of the tradespeople partly free of charge, so that craftsman families, such as clothmakers and stocking-knitters or hatters, could soon make their home there. A gold wares factory founded afterwards, partly with princely money, partly on shares, had however to cease its operation in the long run as well, since it yielded no profit.

The good will of Friedrich Ludwig von Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen to advance his heartland economically cannot be denied him, all the more as he could look with pride on a numerous posterity which it befitted his rank to provide for. Even before the beginning of the French Revolution four of six children had been born to him by his wife. The youngest child, Prince Ludwig Wilhelm Eduard, however died a few years later on 9 February 1790. There followed the trio named so by the princess of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen: Friedrich August Carl, born on 27 November 1784 at Breslau, the future heir, then Adelaide (Adelheid), (1787–1858), who later married Ludwig of the line Hohenlohe-Kirchberg, and on 20 November 1788 Emilie, who was later wedded to the count of Erbach-Fürstenau († 1859). On 16 November 1793 Auguste saw the light of the world, and on 29 January 1797 Prince Adolph. The latter became Prussian minister president and married Princess Luise von Langenburg. On 3 July 1798 Prince Alexander was born last († 1829). From the trio a sextet had become, which Marianne zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen sought to educate with the greatest care. Because of the outbreak of the French Revolutionary War on 20 April 1792, through which her husband was ordered to his post, she was at times separated from her children, whom she loved above everything. Her personal displeasure she by no means concealed:

The fatal king of France, (…) the revolution in my heart, for which he is guilty, is truly greater still than the one in his realm, and many a struggle in it is as serious as the one before the National Assembly.

In her principles of education she was an enthusiastic adherent of the views represented by Jean-Jacques Rousseau in his work "Emile ou de l'education". Of the Hofrat Kahlert, later teaching as professor at Breslau, who during her absence oversaw the children's upbringing, she required

that no stays be put on the little daughters. My hatred of these shells goes so far that I must repeat it - no stiff politeness, no artificial bouton. - If on my stepping down from the carriage all Three do not spring to my neck with the ordinary entrechats that mother nature taught them, embracing and kissing me as awkwardly as possible, and if for that my Adele makes me a stiff, grand curtsy with elbows stretched out backwards by way of welcome, truly, I believe, I could bring an action against you.

 21 Ebd., S. 292. The welcome that was finally prepared for her by her children, who had been brought to their grandmother in Berlin, must have been quite to her taste. To her husband she wrote: "Mon cher ami! Enfin me voici arrivée après bien des peines en bonne Santé ici – le Mercredi après minuit j'ai été rendue ici, – et j'aurai peine à Vous exprimer la sensation de mon Coeur en me rapprochant de nos chers Enfants – ces chers petites Creatures ayant été éveillée par le Postillon sont sortie tous hors de Leurs Nits pour me recevoir et me temoigner Leur joie – Ils ont très bien grandies – Auguste s'est beaucoup formés par ses Etudes – Il parle coulament le francais, le prononce bien – et s'est appliques en general – Adele est come Elle a toujours été – vive, drôle, mais excellente – elle était si touchée en me revoyant qu'Elle a pleurée et rie en même temps et n'a pue s'arracher de mon Coeur – aussi a-t-Elle voulue recevoir tous ses Droits, Elle loger chez moi, ne me quitte pas – et s'attacher plus que jamais à moi. (…) Emilie a grandie – et bien plus regulièrement bien que sa Soeur – mais sa Physionomie est moins Spirituelle – et Elle est beaucoup plus indolente qu'Adele – mais c'est un bon Enfant, et Nous ne saurions rendre assez grée au Ciel des ces bonheur de les posseder tous trois tel qu'ils sont." [My dear friend! At last here I am, arrived after much trouble in good health here - on Wednesday after midnight I was returned here, - and I shall have trouble expressing to You the sensation of my heart as I come near to our dear Children - these dear little creatures, having been woken by the postilion, all came out of their beds to receive me and show me their joy - They have grown very much - Auguste has much formed himself by his studies - He speaks coulament [fluently] the French, pronounces it well - and has applied himself in general - Adele is come as She has always been - lively, funny, but excellent - she was so moved at seeing me again that She cried and laughed at the same time and could not tear herself from my heart - She also wanted to receive all her rights, She lodges with me, does not leave me - and attaches herself more than ever to me. (…) Emilie has grown - and much more regularly well than her Sister - but her physiognomy is less spiritual - and She is much more indolent than Adele - but she is a good child, and We cannot thank heaven enough for the happiness of possessing all three as they are.] Letter of Marianne Fürstin von Hohenlohe Ingelfingen to her husband of 4 February 1792, HZAN 47, K 1, F2
ostensacken2001/38:
It is natural that Prince Friedrich Ludwig zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen as a loving and solicitous father worried about the future of his children. The debts heaped up additionally in the course of the years therefore weighed on him urgently. A possibility of securing his family's livelihood in the long term he believed he could accomplish with the purchase of the Rittergut Bytkow in the Upper Silesian district of Beuthen, which he acquired on 24 April 1801 for a consideration of 43,000 Reichsthaler. To this Rittergut belonged a zinc smeltery in the wood of Bytkow and two hard-coal pits at Ignazhütte. After the purchase the complex was renamed "Hohenlohe-Hütte".

With the engagement of the engineer John Baildon, who came from Carron near Edinburgh, the prince had drawn to himself a first-class adviser. The director of the Silesian mining office, Friedrich Wilhelm Graf von Reden, had been made aware of Baildon on an instruction journey in 1793 and had first taken him into the Prussian state service. With his technical knowledge Graf Reden succeeded in laying the foundations for an enormous industrial upswing in Upper Silesia. Still in 1790 the annual cut of wood had amounted to 200,000 Festmeter. The region embraced, by estimation, nearly 28 million cubic metres, but by the usual charring the wood was badly used, and experts complained of the increasing ravaging of the woods. In the nearer surroundings of Beuthen mighty seams of hard coal had been discovered, and the task had fallen to Baildon to erect at Gleiwitz the first coke blast furnace on the mainland.

The first experiments with coke in the winning of iron had been undertaken on the instruction of the superior mining office in 1789 at Malapane. In the early nineteenth century coke blast furnaces were also put to use now and then in the private iron-

With John Baildon's support a blast furnace provided with coke firing could then be lit at Hohenlohe-Hütte in 1804, which in its technical equipment did not need to shun the comparison with the state works. Besides, a coal pit lying in "Fristen" was set up again. The outbreak of war between Prussia and France in 1806 led the undertaking, only just begun, into a severe crisis.

"It is hard to judge from afar", the privy councillor Johann Wolfgang von Goethe had once observed. The duties of service which Prince Friedrich Ludwig zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen had to perform as Prussian general and governor of Breslau prevented both a regular presence in his residence at Ingelfingen and in the immediate neighbourhood of the Upper Silesian industrial works. In his nature the prince was already rather like the people of the post-industrial age. Having to be present, by his profession, at constantly changing places of deployment brought with it a flightiness of presence that had especially fatal consequences for his economic interests. In the summer of 1806 the loss of the independence of the Empire struck him, joined with the annexation of his lordship by king Friedrich I of Württemberg.

Of his military capacities, despite strong short-sightedness and violent fits of gout that plagued him at times, still entirely convinced, he had once on the occasion of a banquet in the Hohenlohe heartland announced to the representative of the French military of his "greatest" political antagonist, Napoleon: "J'estimerai le jour pour le plus heureux de ma vie, ou je pourrai me trouver vis-à-vis de lui, pour le combattre." [I shall esteem the day the happiest of my life on which I may find myself face to face with him, to fight him.] In the following autumn of 1806 the exact opposite came to pass. By Napoleon and his troops the Prussian field commander was taught the most painful defeat in the double battle of Jena and Auerstedt, which finally put an end to his military career.

From the battle, which had been fought by the Prussian main army with 58000 soldiers and 46500 soldiers of the Saxon division as well as by Rüchel's reinforcement corps with 15260 men, the prince could send home only a remnant troop of 12000 survivors. Napoleon's victory meant not only the prince's greatest personal military defeat, it was the complete collapse of Prussia. Not least because of the extremely hard terms of peace which the French emperor, out of his own grace, dictated to the Prussian king Friedrich Wilhelm III already on 25 October 1806: beside the recognition of the Confederation of the Rhine he demanded a war indemnity of 100 million francs and Prussia's renunciation of the land west of the Elbe, but also the greater part of the Polish territories occupied by Prussia with the town of Danzig. This was altogether 190,000 square kilometres with 3.8 million inhabitants.

When Prince Friedrich von Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen after the end of the battle wanted to withdraw to his Upper Silesian possessions, to look after the smelting works that had run into trouble, this was at first denied him. He was brought to Oehringen as a prisoner. The engineer John Baildon, with whom he stood in correspondence to keep him informed of the state of the works, he could no longer help out of his own strength.

The only person who was in a position to halt the collapse of the works was the princess Sacken. At first she was not ready to do so, because Prince zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen had carried out the purchase of the Rittergut Bytkow without consulting her, and she was of the opinion that the estate could have been brought to the house on more favourable conditions than it had been. Of the acute misery in which the prince found himself she had in the end nonetheless received knowledge. She now wanted to await the bankruptcy, in order then to acquire the Rittergut Bytkow. Only the earnest plea of Prince Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen to preserve the estate "durch ihre Fürsorge auf ehrenvolle Art der Familie zu erhalten" [through her care, in an honourable way, for the family] changed her attitude. On 13 October 1808 she therefore wrote to him:

We would both now have a large portion less of sorrow if you had earlier granted me the trust that I deserve so completely. Through want of trust you have harmed the good cause, and it can now no longer be carried out so well as it could have been done before.

After the prince had thus appealed to her sense of family duty, she had the possession transferred to herself, paid the debts resting on it, and united Bytkow with Schlawentzitz into a Fideikommiß. Although she was no longer willing to make money available for the completion of the blast furnace building begun by John Baildon, because she herself had no reserve of money left, John Baildon succeeded under the most difficult conditions in building at Blechhammer a first plate-rolling works after English plans, which could begin operation in November 1807.

This changed nothing however in the disastrous financial situation of the prince, who, although he no longer had the means for it, kept up great house as before. Adolf Fischer, the historiographer of the house of Hohenlohe, described him thus:

In matters of money he was like a child that does not know the worth of money. As often as he received any, existing debts were paid, wherefore he did not long want for credit. Even after the catastrophe of 1806 he could not for a long time accustom himself to the necessary restriction. (…) When money arrived, a pressing creditor was satisfied, even if nothing remained over.

In a letter to the grandson and heir August of 9 August 1810 the princess Sacken expressed her displeasure very plainly: Prince Hohenlohe husbanded

dreadfully at Schlawentzitz, meanwhile resorting to very humiliating means. He would be capable of selling the moss from the roofs to raise money. If she could not render him harmless out of her own strength, she would have to have recourse to the help of the courts and withdraw from him the right of co-administration of the Silesian and Saxon possessions. The princess did indeed succeed in inducing the prince to renounce his rights of administration, but perhaps too late, for over the amount of the total mortgages the prince had taken up on his possessions she had for a long time no exact knowledge. The debts now weighed altogether on the son and heir alone, Friedrich August Carl zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen-Oehringen, to whom his father, shortly before the mediatisation, had ceded the Hohenlohe heartland and with it the likewise considerable liabilities.

The daughter of the princess Sacken, Marianne, had after eighteen years of marriage with the prince drawn her personal conclusions. She separated from her husband in 1799 - and this was especially hard for her - also from her children, filed for divorce, which then took place judicially in 1801 at her wish. Over the reasons that had moved her to this step she remained silent however at first toward her mother, so that a severe rupture came about between the two women. The princess Sacken reacted to her daughter's wish for divorce with complete lack of understanding and thereupon compelled her, in a house regulation drawn up on 9 November 1799 in Berlin, the so-called "Zransact", to renounce the sole right of inheritance due to her under the testamentary disposition of count Hoym in favour of the grandson August. Only later did Marianne zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen give her sons, prince August and prince Adolph von Hohenlohe, full knowledge of the primary motives that had induced her to part from her husband. As compensation for the complete renunciation of the inheritance Marianne zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen received yearly 4,000 thalers from the Silesian possessions and 3,000 thalers from her mother, the princess Sacken. After the marriage of Marianne with the prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen was divorced on 1 September 1801, she married yet in the same year the count Friedrich Ludwig von der Osten-Sacken, with whom she moved to his estate of Bellin in Mecklenburg. From this marriage two more daughters came forth: Angelika Friederike Natalie Louise, born on 4 May 1802, and another girl who received the names Auguste Friederike Wilhelmine Charlotte and came into the world on 5 September 1804. Her last years of life Marianne countess of Osten-Sacken spent on the Marienhof near Rostock, where she died on 20 April 1840.

With the consent of the daughter Marianne, provision had already been made in the marriage contracts concluded at Leipzig on 9 October 1781 and 8 August 1787 that aimed at clearly restricting any claims of possession and the enjoyment of the Hoym estates on the part of the future husband Friedrich Ludwig zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen. As guardian of her daughter the princess Sacken reserved to herself the right of the administration of the estates of her first husband, count Hoym, for as long as she wished. According to the marriage contract which she had concluded with count Hoym while still Freiin von Dieskau, half of the whole revenues from the Silesian and Saxon estates was due to her, that is, about 8250 thalers. She would however have renounced 2250 thalers of the revenues if that money had been applied to the extinguishing of the debts still resting on the estates. The sum was then to be invested, with the prince's share, in a money-Fideikommiß:

As has been observed as law until now, to lay up yearly four thousand Reichsthaler of the revenues for the increase of capital, so it shall also remain in the future with this useful institution, and the capitals arising from it shall be regarded and treated as a money-Fideicommiß entirely in the same spirit and according to the same rules as the estates themselves.

As a further precaution it was expressly declared,

that His Serene Highness has no authority to alter the natural or legal substance of the estates and capitals and ever to burden them with a debt or other charge,

in order to preserve them "zum Flor beiderseitiger künftiger Descendenz" [for the flourishing of the future descendants of both sides]. Rather, for the lifetime of the princess it was to remain unalterably with the "Commun-Administration introduced as expedient vermöge Abkommens Breslau, den 8. August 1787" [by agreement of Breslau of 8 August 1787]. Because of the prince's incapacity to manage economically, all the more as his creditors constantly pressed for the settlement of the debts accumulated with them, he, to come by "ready means", sold on again far below their worth considerable family possessions he had acquired, such as the lordships of Betsche, Zogorowo, Trobczyn, Botkowo and Winiec. With the transfer of the Rittergut Bytkow into the existing family Fideikommiß of Schlawentzitz the princess Sacken had at least in this case put a bar before the complete selling-off of the estates.

ostensacken2001/325:
Appendix 8

"Ein Wort des Vertrauens" [A Word of Trust]

In a very personal writing of countess Marianne von der Osten-Sacken, who had been married in a first marriage to the prince of Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, this countess set out her motives for the separation from her first husband:

A word of trust to my two sons, the prince August von Hohenlohe Oehringen and the prince Adolph von Hohenlohe, and for the present in his stead to His Excellency the justice minister von Kircheisen, the privy councillor of justice von Sack and the chief medical councillor Cosmar.

With my son, the prince August von Hohenlohe, and with the aforementioned gentlemen guardians of my remaining children, I permit myself, with the enclosed declaration over the testament of my departed good mother, to speak yet a word of trust. Until these named persons, and my children still under age, have reached the years of their Vollblütigkeit [full maturity], these confidential lines are for no one. I beg therefore that they not be laid among the papers that can fall into the hands of any third party outside this small circle.

It is now twelve years since I left prince Hohenlohe, - in my view I had to take this step, to save my children's fortune. More than once I had had to sign sums of enormous amounts for the rescue of the prince, against my mother's wish, and yet his mass of debt grew again like the crop of the rooster. Had I remained in relation with him these 12 years, then, especially in the last time, when every household, even economically conducted, was falling into money troubles anyway - the splintering of my fortune would have been certain.

I therefore renounced the splendour of my station, I renounced the advantage of my rank - but I renounced at the same time also the renown and the greatest happiness of my life, in that I tore myself out of the midst of my children and fled into a foreign land, given over to the vengeance of the world, to the momentary displeasure of my mother, beloved by me above all, so inwardly honoured and worthy - who at the time was less informed of some of the occasions of my step than she later became. In the first upsurge of her displeasure she demanded of me, perhaps excited by other impulses, a multitude of sacrifices, which I brought to her all willingly for her sake. I marvel now myself, when I read through the Transact of 19 November 1799 and the revers and declarations that followed it, which I had to sign within a short space of time, over the demands that were made of me. As mistress, lawful heiress of the most beautiful estates in Saxony and in Silesia, I was not left even a little place of my paternal ancestors on which I might have lived quiet and withdrawn from the world that misjudged me, but I was thrust out with a cold hand beyond the borders of the possessions of my fathers.

I know, and I knew it then just as well as now, that no power in the world could have compelled me to sign all these documents which were to be the legal necessity of my temporal welfare; I know that it would have been easy for me to obtain far more favourable conditions

 4 HZAN K 172, F1, F2, Brief von John Baildon an Fürst Friedrich Ludwig zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen vom 8. März 1808
 5 APK Hohenlohe Koscz. 480, Brief der Gräfin Osten-Sacken vom 12. Oktober 1811
ostensacken2001/326:
- but I signed with mute obedience all these papers. Good transfigured mother! they did not flow from your heart, these cold demands of those documents - therefore they shall not rest on your coffin; I alone will bear all their consequences for myself! I signed all those papers partly to reconcile my kind mother with my unconditional submission, partly because I recognised with gratitude that the welfare of my dear children was secured by them. In this great pledge my own welfare was given away.

What should have been sacrificed of the princess Hohenlohe, of the heiress of the Hoym stock, for me, the mother gave up with loving intent, for she gave it to the dearest thing in the world, her children.

The feast of reconciliation that I celebrated with my kind mother in a quiet corner soon led me back to the warm mother-heart, and I went, now reconciled with myself, into a foreign land, there - so indeed Convenience willed it - separated from my dear ones, to spend my life if possible in quiet.

The mother travelled into the land that unlocked not etiquette and calculation but love and regard - heaven gave me two children - the care of their upbringing - the untiring diligence for their education, was the only compensation - the greatest joy of the burnt mother-heart separated from my other children - and I doubled this diligence for their education, since it is the only treasure I could gather for these poor creatures. Yet my motherly duty commands me to stand up for the peace of these my younger children with the same warmth with which I sacrificed myself for the welfare of the children of my first marriage. You all! have lain on my heart, you all! are to my heart alike dear, alike precious!

The welfare of my youngest children suffers from the dispositions of the maternal testament, if I die earlier, so is my husband hardly able to bring them up according to their station.

My son August knows his sisters - He received them with love and that brotherly goodwill which His good, noble and feeling heart only marks the more; and I am convinced also of my son Adolph - they are both too good, too noble, for a stepbrotherly streak against their sisters, in every respect harshly set back, to be feared from them, and certainly, you cannot wish the misfortune of your poor innocent sisters. I demand no generosity - and beg I will not for my children - least of all from their siblings - I therefore only commend to my beloved sons my two youngest daughters and repeat, for the satisfaction of all parties concerned, those fair proposals of settlement regarding the purchase of Bellin which I set out, dated the 22nd of September, in my letter to Herr O.M.R. Cosmar and detailed there more closely, and to which I refer in all points.

If this proposal is approved, then I declare, this time not after prescribed formulas but - with a completely free and happy heart, that I then regard myself and my children as fully satisfied, and preserve the love of my sons for your sisters and for me in tender motherly care - and acknowledge the co-representation of the gentlemen curators with warm gratitude.

Berlin 12. October 1811

Marianne countess of Osten-Sacken

née countess Hoym

Appendix 10

Clarification of the debt relations of the daughter Marianne countess of Osten-Sacken

Beside the debt obligations that Marianne countess of Osten-Sacken had signed for her first husband, the prince Friedrich Ludwig zu Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen, she had also, in her second marriage with the count Friedrich Ludwig von der Osten-Sacken, got into a debt situation which she could hardly still manage without her mother's help. Her mother therefore attempted to reach a settlement with the creditors. For this purpose she had charged her confidant, the medical councillor Cosmar, to travel to Güstrow, to examine the situation there. The agreements reached there were taken up into her codicil of 6 November 1807:

Since my lady daughter, the countess von Sacken, is so deeply entangled in debts that the opening of bankruptcy over her fortune is to be feared, I hereby charge the chief medical councillor Cosmar to betake himself to Güstrow and to regulate the debt relation of my lady daughter and her husband, the count von Sacken, as well as is possible, to come to an agreement with their creditors over their satisfaction resp. treatment according to his best judgement and conscientiousness, to examine and fix the amount of their claims, to determine whether they are satisfied entirely and completely or whether only a part is paid and in what terms the creditors are to be discharged. I give to Herr Cosmar full power and authority herein, that he, with all the creditors, both those [creditors] secured on the Gülzow estates as on the estates of Hülseburg and Bellin, or on one of these estates, as also with the ordinary credi-

tors, examine and conclude as well as he will and can, and regulate everything completely, so that the peace and contentment of my lady daughter is restored. I authorise Herr von Cosmar further, over the estates of Bellin and Hülseburg, to conclude every contract and settlement that may be necessary and expedient. (…) All sums which Herr von Cosmar will promise to the creditors of the two Sacken estates I will pay out of my means and from my fortune. Jan Pachoński

THE POLES IN THE REPUBLIC OF VENICE

(1794-1797)

The beginnings of the Risorgimento coincide with a period of Polish struggles for independence and social progress. One little-known stage of Polish-Venetian relations, which preceded the formation of General J. H. Dąbrowski's Polish Legions in Italy, deserves in particular a careful examination.

The year that followed the failure of the Kościuszko Insurrection, in the autumn of 1794, saw the final partition of Poland between Russia, Prussia and Austria, military powers with

 The sources of this article are drawn from:

a) The Archivio di Stato di Venezia (cited as AS Venezia). In the section Inquisitori di Stato are the lists of Forestieri [foreigners], 1794-1797, comprising the registers of entry and the police reports for the Inquisitors (772-780); in the section Democrazia (160 et seq.), material on the growth of the progressive currents on the lagoons, to which Poles also contributed.

b) The Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Paris: A. Mémoires et documents, ms 650-655, France et divers États de l'Europe, 1794-1796; B. Correspondance politique: Autriche – ms 365, Pologne – ms 323, Prusse – ms 222-223, Toscane – ms 150, Venise – ms 251-253; and the Archives of the Ministry of War in Paris, Subdivision Sud-Est, B³ – correspondence of the Army of Italy, 34 et seq.

c) From the Polish archives destroyed during the Second World War: the Archives of the Legions and of General J. H. Dąbrowski (AD), the collections of the entailed estates of the Krasiński, Przeździecki and Zamoyski, of Rapperswil, etc.

A few scattered details on the Poles of Venice (1794-1797) have been given by Władysław Smoleński, Alexandre Kraushar, Simon Askenazy, Marian Kukiel and Adam Skałkowski. The reader will find a somewhat fuller account of these events in the monograph of Jan Pachoński, Légions Polonaises, vérité et légende, 1794-1807, vol. 1, Warsaw, 1969 (in Polish).

 This insurrection was launched to free Poland from Tsarist occupation, but it was directed against Prussia as well; it hoped, however, for the benevolent neutrality of Austria. The insurgents looked to social changes in an independent Poland.
pachonski1973/238:
despotic government. They divided among them a booty of twelve million people and an area of 730,000 km².

But the Poles did not think of surrendering: on the territory dismembered into three parts a clandestine network began to work, directed by the Lwów Centre. Some of the leaders of the Insurrection managed to get abroad, from where they meant to direct the struggle to come.

Venice – centre of action

At first it was rather difficult to find a seat from which the struggle would be directed. Saxony, close at hand, refused asylum under pressure from Prussia. The fighting on German territory made contact between Paris or Frankfurt on Main and occupied Poland difficult. In Hamburg the influence of the Russians and of the Targowica prevailed. The French agent for Polish affairs, Pierre Parandier, proposed Altona, in the duchy of Holstein, as the centre.

The main current of the emigration went south, however, towards Vienna and Prague, but the many vexations the emigrés suffered opened their eyes to Austria's want of goodwill. Their eyes then turned to the Republic of Venice, which lay between Paris, Vienna and Constantinople, and whose trade gave it the freshest news and easy communications. Its neutrality made it, besides, a meeting ground between the camp of the coalition and that of the revolution, and gave the Polish emigrés a certain freedom of movement.

The Republic of Venice comprised, besides territories in the north of Italy, possessions on the Adriatic coast, the whole inhabited by three million people, 130,000 of them in the capital. The Republic was going through an economic and commercial crisis, together with the decay of its army and fleet.

 The Confederation of Targowica – a plot of the magnates against the reforms of the Four Years' Diet and against the Constitution of 3 May, in fact made at Petersburg on 27 April 1792 under the patronage of Catherine II, and proclaimed at Targowica, in Ukraine, on 14 May 1792.

 Venice had an army of nearly 25,000 men, 50 ships and 700 merchant vessels, but their armament, training, drill and discipline left much to be desired.
pachonski1973/239:
Salvation could come only from radical reforms, to which the ruling oligarchy, selfish and idle, would not consent. To keep Venice from invasion this oligarchy relied on the Republic's former glory and on its neutrality, which had just been proclaimed. The tragic fate of Poland taught it nothing. It feared only a revolutionary upheaval, and above all kept a vigilant watch on foreigners.

The make-up of the Venetian "Polonia"

As early as the summer of 1794 the Prince and Princess Charles and Charlotte of Nassau-Siegen (born Godzka) came from Poland to the lagoons. Deprived of his inheritance by the Prince of Orange, Prince Charles had sought protectors among the monarchs for military and diplomatic services (he was, among other things, a Russian admiral), and had travelled in Africa and Australia. A rich marriage made in Poland (1780) had brought him connections and the privileges attached to the titles of Polish citizen and deputy.

After the proclamation of the Kościuszko Insurrection he declared his solidarity with Poland in arms by giving up his Russian dignities; but as a monarchist he would not join the insurgents, who were growing more and more radical, and he emigrated with his wife to Venice. In the palace they rented on the Rio Foscari (near the Grand Canal) they set up a royalist centre: the prince and princess were partisans of Stanisław August and gave money to the Bourbons. Soon they were helped in this by the King's nephew, Lieutenant-General Stanislas Mokronowski, an active fighter of the Insurrection.

From October 1794 the first emigrés arrived from the territories where the fighting of the insurrection had taken place. According to the reports of the Venetian police, "the Polish adherents of French maxims" met at D. Petrillo's inn, beside the Rialto Bridge and the Malibran theatre.

 Divorced from the Marshal of Lithuania, Janusz Sanguszko – fuller information in J. Pachoński, Les Polonais à Venise, 1794-1797, in "Kwartalnik Historyczny", LXXV, 4, 1968, p. 372.

pachonski1973/240:
Towards the end of 1794 there were some fifty Polish emigrés in Venice, among them six members of the insurrectionary government, a senator, seven deputies to the Diet, three diplomats, three starosts, a few landowners and, among the military, eight generals, several staff officers and others of lower rank.

In the emigration it was not only former offices and merits that counted: one also needed a certain fortune, connections, foreign languages and enterprise. Pierre Potocki, Michel Ogiński, Charles Prozor, Denise Mniewski and Stanislas Sołtyk excelled in this.

Three main parties formed quite quickly: the partisans of a strong monarchy, the adherents of constitutional monarchy, and the republicans. The first were represented by the Prince and Princess of Nassau-Siegen and General Mokronowski. At the head of the second party were diplomats, S. Sołtyk, P. Potocki and M. Ogiński, commonly called the moderates. In their view the Constitution of 3 May had the nation's favour and, abroad, would reduce the number of the opponents of Poland's restoration. This party was the strongest in Venice, without being united, for its progressive wing, with Charles Prozor and Joseph Kociełł at its head, looked to deep changes in the Constitution once independence had been recovered, and fought Stanisław August.

Resolutely republican opinions, and even the wish to model Poland's future régime on revolutionary France, were represented by the former left of the Insurrection, led by Hugo Kołłontay and General Joseph Zajączek (Zaïonchek). In the second half of December 1794 the closer watch of the Venetian police alarmed the Poles. Fearing complications, they sent a delegation to the French Embassy made up of S. Sołtyk, M. Ogiński and F. Dmochowski. The French ambassador at Venice at the time was Lallement, a man of about sixty. He knew the situation in Italy very well, having spent some thirty years in diplomatic posts at Ragusa, Messina and Naples.

Luca; a wing of the palace had been made into a hotel for travellers of progressive views. In May 1795 the ambassador moved to the Palazzo Rosso, a larger palace on the Mestre side, on the Cannaregio Canal.

The minister Lallement and his son, secretary of the Legation, received the Polish delegation very kindly, promised their help, and put the rooms of the Embassy at the Poles' disposal for their meetings. The minister assured them that France held to the restoration of Poland, whatever its future régime, and that the emigrés could count on its full support. This stand was bound to be disavowed rather quickly by the French government. But for the moment, encouraged by this declaration, the Polish emigrés addressed a memorandum to the French government (31 December), in which they stressed the ideological kinship of the French and the Polish Revolutions, and the unequal effort of a struggle waged for eight months against some two hundred thousand invaders, which had drawn off substantial Austrian and Prussian forces fighting revolutionary France on the Rhine. The Poles now asked for a return for this service. They explained that it was in France's interest to defend the cause of Poland, Turkey, Sweden and Denmark, or else the riches of those countries might serve to crush the French Revolution; a liberated Poland, on the other hand, would be its devoted ally in the east of Europe.

The memorandum put forward the idea of a great coalition of progressive states and of forming a "restricted" Diet abroad, and declared that if the French army attacked from the Rhine towards the Vistula, Galicia would take up arms and go to meet it. It also proposed raising a Legion of four thousand Poles who had been forced to serve in the Austrian army, and it was hoped that this Legion

pachonski1973/243:
would quickly grow into a powerful army of liberation.

The Polish Committee at Venice

In January 1795 the Poles, trusting in the minister Lallement's promise and encouraged by the news of French successes in Holland, decided to form a provisional government under the name of the Polish Committee at Venice. M. Ogiński, S. Sołtyk, K. Prozor and, of the republicans, F. Dmochowski entered it; the right was reserved to co-opt representatives of the Altona centre, should that be wanted.

The appeal to patriotic generosity secured considerable funds. Straight afterwards Ogiński and Dmochowski were sent to the French agent Cacault at Florence, Major Thomas Maruszewski to Basel, to the minister Barthélemy, who had great influence there, and Michel Skrzetuski to Constantinople, to watch over the Polish-Turkish alliance and the forming of Polish armed forces.

For the Paris mission, the most important, Charles Prozor was chosen; he left for Paris by way of Florence on 7 February 1795. He was to take over the duties of François Barss, the representative of the Insurrection, tolerated by the French government but blamed for his want of energy. Prozor thus became the Polish spokesman to the French government.

In Paris Prozor met many Poles ready to recognise the authority of the Venice Committee, but he soon came himself to the conclusion that the Polish government in emigration should have its seat not in distant Venice but near the revolutionary government, in Paris itself.

And so he acquired, with part of the funds he had brought,

La Roche – Paris, October 1795; AE Pologne, vol. 323, f. 22, 200; J. Pachoński, Les Polonais à Venise, p. 876.

Barss, Paris, 27 February (f. 44).

the abandoned Diesbach palace, at no. 54 Faubourg Saint-Honoré, which he turned into a lively centre of Polish propaganda. He could not, however, push Barss aside: the French government would not agree to it. Already on 5 February 1795, moreover, the minister Lallement had been reprimanded for having made promises to the Poles. The government declared that France could not concern itself with the Polish question at that time, that help should rather be sought from Turkey, and that time alone and the energy of the Polish emigrés themselves could change the situation. In consequence the Venice Committee was not recognised, and the plan to form the Legion was given up.

The importance of the Peace of Basel

The treaty of Basel concluded between France and Prussia (5 April 1795) was an unpleasant surprise for the Poles and a proof of France's ingratitude. The French assured them that the treaty was precarious, and urged the Poles to turn to Prussia in their efforts for independence. This view brought together Barss, Prozor and Joseph Wybicki, who were inclined to support it. The last two, on 15 April, addressed a manifesto to their compatriots in Venice, recommending patience and the steps to be taken to make the Diet work abroad, and advocating a Franco-Prusso-Turco-Swedo-Danish coalition.

At that moment French diplomacy, through the minister Lallement, asked M. Ogiński and S. Sołtyk to act as intermediaries in the negotiations with the Spanish ambassador,

 Ciphered dispatch of 5 February 1795, AE Pologne, vol. 323, f. 18. Unaware of the difficulties Prozor was struggling with, the Venice Committee sent General F. Wyszkowski to join him on 6 March 1795, as the candidate for chief of the projected legion (whose organisation had been worked out in detail). Wyszkowski reached Paris (10 April) by way of Nice, AE Pologne, ms 323, f. 67; cf. the report of General Ernouf to the minister of war, undated, Arch. de la guerre, B³ 50.

 Joseph Wybicki (1747-1822), Polish politician and writer, took part in drafting the Constitution of 3 May 1791 as a deputy to the Great Diet; in the insurrection he was a deputy councillor of the Supreme National Council, in the department of military supplies, and then the government's plenipotentiary in General J. H. Dąbrowski's expedition into Greater Poland.

Don Domingo d'Yriarte, whom they had known for a long time. P. Potocki even went with him to Basel, supporting the minister François Barthélemy, his friend, during the negotiations that ended with the conclusion of the Franco-Spanish treaty (22 July 1795). The Poles of Venice also negotiated with the French ambassador A. Verninac, who was about to leave for Turkey and promised the Poles substantial support.

The treaty of Basel allowed the Polish emigrés to go to Berlin, Leipzig and Dresden and to move their main seat to Paris; they could thus make contact, through the German states, with occupied Poland, and this led many Poles of Venice to leave for the banks of the Seine.

Changes in the balance of forces within the Venetian "Polonia"

Meanwhile the situation in Venice had changed appreciably. The royalist centre suspended its activity, because the Prince of Nassau-Siegen had to leave for Spain and Austria in search of funds, which he found unexpectedly through settlements and inheritances. At the same time General Mokronowski went to settle in Florence.

From May 1795 the palace of S. Luca ceased to be the main centre of activity of the Poles of Venice, after the disappointments that the minister Lallement had caused the "hotheads"; he had moved into the Palazzo Rosso, larger still than the one before.

The Poles now met at Joachim Durante's inn in the Calle del Forno, near St Mark's Square and the La Fenice theatre. They also took over the neighbouring inn "3 Stelle" (owned by Antonio Urbani), and besides the Albergo Reale, the Locanda del Leon Bianco (sestiere of San Polo) and the Albergo Regina – probably the present Hotel Regina – (contrada
