CHAPTER II Demographic conditions in the Olęder settlements

A. The numbers of the Olęders

The considerable number of Olęder settlements suggests the supposition that the Olęders constituted a substantial proportion of the population of the former voivodeship of Poznań. For that reason the detailed examination of the demographic structure of these settlements must be regarded as a matter of importance. Owing to the lack of sources it is not possible to present the changes in the size of the Olęder population over the whole period of the colonisation's existence; the source data do, however, make it possible to carry out a fairly exact calculation of this population in the period of the partitions 1. In view of the greatest abundance of the source tradition we shall adopt the year 1789 as the moment of the calculation. For Kościan county we possess from this period the following statistical materials: I. the “General table of the population” (Tol.), compiled by the Tax Commission of Kościan county on the basis of an ordinance of the Crown Fiscal Commission of 1789; 2. the “General table of hearths” (Tod. 89), compiled by the same commission; 3. the Tariff of hearths and of the hearth tax for the years 1789 and 90 (Tp. 89, 90). The first table does not include the szlachta and the clergy, and moreover contains a considerable number of numerical errors and omissions. It is likewise, just like the second table, incomplete territorially. The third table, however, is compiled more exactly, and for that reason, despite certain gaps ?, it inspires considerably more confidence. The hearths are shown in it in two columns: in the first for 1789 on the basis of the declarations sworn by the owners, in the second for 1790 on the basis of the official lustration. The numerical differences between the two columns are small; the more important point is that in the tariff of 1789

B. The religious composition of the Olęder population

We possess no source statistics from which the religious composition of the population of the Olęder settlements could be reconstructed; certain general conclusions can be drawn only on the basis of the loose, chance mentions and data found in the sources. The question of the religious affiliation of the Olęders had already been discussed by German authors; a few, contrary to the obvious, tried to maintain that the whole Olęder population was Evangelical,1 but the majority admitted, that a certain percentage of the Olęders belonged to the Roman Catholic confession. The question therefore reduces to establishing what part of the population of the Olęder settlements was made up of Catholic settlers. The sources show that the population of the settlements founded in clerical estates on the territory of the Poznań voivodeship was always Catholic. In the Kościan county there existed 3 such settlements with a population of 401 souls. In the Poznań county 17 settlements belonged to church property. Their population, on estimation from the number of hearths, will come to 1,252 persons. From chance mentions we learn that in the Kościan county alone, besides the foregoing, wholly Catholic were Ol. Important conclusions concerning the religious relations of the Olęder settlements are suggested by the social stratification of the population of the settlements. As follows from Table IV, about 36% of the population consisted of landless people, who for settling in the settlement needed neither an individually expressed consent of the lord nor material means for redeeming themselves and establishing a household. On the other hand, on the basis of settler registers sometimes inserted in charters, and of inspections of one and the same settlement carried out at different times, it can be established that the settlers did not bring with them the needed contingent of hired labour forces, but hired them as the farm grew and the demand for labour increased. It is most probable that the Olęders sought such labour forces in the nearest neighbourhood. This met with no obstacles of a legal character, owing to the fact that in the villages of Wielkopolska there existed a number of labourers who were not subject (the free, contract workers), whom the Tol. even groups into the categories: "the free, occupied with work" and "beggars". Undoubtedly their ranks were also powerfully swelled by runaway subjects. Hence it must be accepted that, especially in settlements located among Polish villages, the poorer, landless population was Polish and Catholic. This conclusion is confirmed by contemporary sources1 and later Prussian returns of population. C. The nationality of the Olęder population

Determining the ethnic affiliation of the Olęders presents very great difficulties. Direct source information in this respect is almost entirely lacking. For contemporaries this question had no significance whatever in view of the complete equality of rights enjoyed by both nationalities. Indirect indications are supplied to us by the surnames of settlers given from time to time.

The national character of the Olęder settlement on the territory of the former Poznań voivodeship was not uniform throughout the whole duration of the colonization. It cannot admit of any doubt that the first settlers were authentic Hollenders. They were settled in the oldest settlement on the territory that interests us, namely in the Olęders of Ujście (Olędrowie), and in the four oldest settlements of the Wieleń estate: Folsztyn, Herbardowo, Marianowo and Nowe Dwory. We possess in this respect a series of certain, irrefutable source data:

I. All the settlements mentioned are located on the waterlogged Noteć lowland. As in Prussia, the Holendrzy were brought in for the purpose of draining the lands assigned to them.

 On the other hand there did occur an infiltration of Catholic farmers into Evangelical settlements and conversely. Hence in villages which in the pre-partition period had been purely Catholic, the census of 1843 revealed a considerable number of Evangelicals.

D. The origin of the settlers and the causes of the colonization

The origin of the settlers stands in connexion with their nationality. 3, It is understandable that the fatherland of the first settlers, the Holendrzy, was the Netherlands. As for the Polish Olęders, the Catholic part was recruited from the local population, whereas the Evangelicals, who appeared most numerously in the settlements of the southern part of the Poznań voivodeship, in all probability came from neighbouring Silesia. The coming of the German Olęders likewise remained connected with religion. The Catholics came in all probability from the interior of the Empire, from Bavaria or Swabia. CHAPTER III

The legal relations of the Olęder settlements

A. The Olęders and state law

There were no legal norms concerning the Olęders specifically, issued by the public authorities, in Poland before the partitions. Only the tax universały of the times of Stefan Batory and Sigismund III, as it were, take note of the existence of Olęder settlement, assessing taxes also on "pasture włókas, which the Olęders and others lease for pasture".1 This concerned in the first place the Holendrzy in Royal Prussia, who, sitting on lowland lands, carried on livestock farming on a broad scale. Likewise in the scope of other public-law duties the same obligations weighed on the Olęders as on the remaining peasant stratum. There remains to be decided in turn the question to what extent the Olęders had capacity for legal acts, that is, whether they had the right of appearing before the public court against the lord and third persons, and the right of appeal from the lords' judgments. This matter takes a twofold shape, depending on whether we are dealing with settlements founded in the royal estates or in noble or clerical estates. In the royal estates the Olęders, like other peasants, always had the right of seeking justice from the king. Their affairs, whenever damage to the royal estate came into consideration, were attended to by the crown instigator, and complaints against the possessors of the royal estates, or appeals from their judgments, were heard by the referendary court. Charters issued to the Olęders by the starostas were confirmed by the king, thereby guaranteeing their force and effect. Baranowski, who studied the records of the referendary courts, maintains that the Olęders availed themselves of the rights belonging to them quite often and to full effect. The same is proved also by the decrees of the Crown Referendary concerning the okupniks (tenants who had redeemed their land) (among others also Olęders) of the starostwo

 Vol. Leg. II, 982, 996, 1026, 1302; III, 026.

How these relations presented themselves in the noble estates it is difficult to establish. The old Polish judicial process made no provision in its rules for the peasant population that was not subject. Presumably there existed in this respect some judicial practice, but cases of this kind have not yet been sufficiently investigated. B. Manor law in the Olęder settlements. 1. The legal relation to the lord. a. The charter.

While the public authorities issued no legal norms concerning Olęder settlement at all, the system of norms concerning this settlement issued by the lord was broadly developed. They regulated a range of matters falling either within the domain of public law (the lord's judicature, communal and church self-government) or within the domain of private law (personal status, the law of things, succession). They concerned, therefore, the relation of the Olęders to the lord, the mutual relations of the Olęders within the settlement, and finally the relations of the Olęders to institutions and third persons (among others the church). The basis of the legal relation to the lord was the common charter (contract, deed — Latin privilegium, ius, German Gerechtigkeit), issued to the Olęder community by the lord, most often after the surveying of its lands, more rarely at a later period. Exceptionally the proper charter was replaced by its surrogates, for example a provisional preliminary agreement, or else the parties accepted as binding the charter of another community. Although the charter formally was not a contract but a unilateral act, issued and signed by the lord, in fact its content was settled by way of agreement between the lord and the settlers. As a rule the charter was written on parchment, in a more or less ornate form, with the lord's seal pressed in wax directly on the document, or hanging on a ribbon or cord threaded through a cut in the lower part of the parchment. More rarely the charter had the humbler form of a sheet of paper with the lord's signature and seal. The language of the charters was mostly Polish; of the 142 known charters 108 were issued in Polish, 32 in German, and 2 in Polish and German.

The matter presented itself differently in those few cases in which an Olęder sat on unredeemed land. Here the relation of the Olęder to the land was rather like a perpetual lease.

It is characteristic that in the charters, apart from a few exceptions 5, no sanctions were provided for the event of the Olęders failing to pay the services provided in the charter. This is explained by the fact that the Olęders answered for the manorial duties for the most part solidarily, so that the obligation of bearing the services for a dilatory Olęder, or one not in a position to pay, fell upon the remaining members of the community.

The charters enumerated in detail the rights belonging to the Olęders by virtue of their possession of the land: "of which land both they themselves and their possessors may make use at their pleasure; namely it shall be free for them to sell it, to give, to bestow, to barter away and to turn to their own best advantage". The right of disposing of the land was, however, not un-limited. Beside substantive restrictions on the alienation of the land we have a series of formal conditions which the seller, and at times also the purchaser, had to fulfil before the deed of sale was recognized by the lord as valid.

Summing up the considerations so far, it must be stated that although as a rule the lord, and at times also the community, set certain conditions at the sale of Olęder farms, these did not — apart from the rarely occurring obligation to obtain the lord's permission for the sale — seriously restrict the principle of the free disposal of the land.

The sale as a rule comprised both the land itself and everything that was on that land (timber, grass, at times sowings and buildings). At times the lord reserved to himself the right to the oaks standing on the Olęder lands. Similarly the barcie (bee-trees) which the lord's beekeepers, or the inhabitants of the surrounding villages, had on the ground assigned to the Olęders, usually remained their property so long as bees were there. Ores (minerals) that might possibly occur on the ground assigned to the Olęders remained the property of the lord. The Olęders themselves built the buildings on the lands assigned to them; these were their indivisible and unrestricted property. It was the same with the live and dead stock. The community, too, appeared as owner. At times it possessed its own common pasture. Its common property also comprised the public buildings, such as schools and houses of prayer. The community likewise had at its disposal the field forming the endowment of the teacher of the settlement.

On the lands of the Olęders there could exist certain servitudes in favour of the lord or of third persons. To these must be reckoned the sporadic right of the manor to pasture its own cattle on the Olęder lands. The neighbours of an Olęder sometimes had the right of digging ditches through his land for the discharge of water, at times there belonged to them the right of driving their herds across Olęder land. 3. The law of succession. Of the norms of succession in force in the Olęder settlements the sources contain only very scanty information. If an Olęder died without leaving heirs behind him, his property always passed into the ownership of the manor. As can be inferred from the divisions of property registered in the community books, the children inherited from their parents in equal shares, one of them as a rule taking over the farm and paying off the remaining siblings. Wills registered in the community books seem to indicate that the complete disinheritance of one of the children was not practised, perhaps not even permissible. As a rule the interests of orphans were protected by special provisions, or, in the event of the remarriage of one of the parents, the interests of the children of the first marriage. Wills had sometimes to be drawn

 The charter for Ol. Karpicko (AW. A. 1) provides: "but should an Olęder die without an heir, all his goods shall fall to the lord". Similar provisions are found in the charters for the Olęders of the Sieraków estate, for Ol. Kobus, Krosna etc. Somewhat differently does the charter for Czapury treat this matter (AW. B. 1 a): "but should any of them die without issue and without a natural successor, then the goods of that one go ad fiscum Conventi [to the treasury of the Convent], and the Convent shall be able to sell them at their proper valuation to whom it will; the nearest, however, to buy shall be the nearest neighbour, and should he not wish it, any one whatsoever of our Czapury Holendrzy...". Erroneous is the supposition of Schmidt (p. 348) that in the earlier settlements, after the death of an Olęder without issue, his property passed into the ownership of the community. Cases of inheritance by the community of part of the property of an Olęder who died without issue, though beyond the borders of the former Poznań voivodeship, are recorded by Baranowski (Wsie holenderskie, p. 73).
 The principle of inheritance of the land by the eldest son, to which Schmidt refers, did not exist. On the contrary, as can be inferred from the entries in the community books, the inheritance of the land even by daughters, with payment to the sons, was a matter of daily occurrence.

4. Communal self-government. a) Organisation. The broadly developed communal self-government constituted, as we have mentioned, an essential feature of Olęder settlement. In principle every settlement formed a separate unit of self-government. In exceptional cases two or even three settlements could have self-governing organs in common. The constitution of communal self-government in the Olęder settlements presented itself differently from that in the remaining villages. This concerned above all the organs of self-government. These organs consisted of an elected sołtys and ławniks. Their term of office lasted one year. Quite exceptionally in the Radoszkowskie Olęders the sołtys, and in the Uścikowskie Olęders the whole village bench, was elected for life, while the common sołtys of the Czerwonackie, Janikowskie and Kliny Olęders was elected for a three-year period. The choice both of the sołtys and of the ławniks was made by the assembly of all the farmers of the community. Only in the Karpickie Olęders did the choice of the ławniks belong to the sołtys. The ławniks were most often 2 in number, more rarely 3, exceptionally 4. In the same composition the substitutes were appointed. As a rule the choice of the organs of self-government fell at Whitsuntide, at times, however, the term of office ended at St Martin's (11 November) 5, or St John the Baptist (24 June) 8. We meet no provisions restricting passive or active electoral rights. Undoubtedly, however, there existed in this respect certain customary rules. It is certain only that women had neither active nor passive electoral rights. The choice fell as a rule on the older farmers of the settlement. In the few cases

The constitution of the communal organs did not present itself uniformly throughout the whole period of the colonization. On the part of the lords there sporadically revealed itself a tendency to restrict the collegiate prerogatives of the communal authorities in favour of the sołtys and to make the sołtys more dependent on the manor. At the location of several later settlements even a hereditary sołtys was instituted, whereby these settlements became, constitutionally, to a certain degree like settlements located contemporaneously under German law. In Appendix I these settlements have been included in the group of transitional settlements. The same significance attached to the command that the electors of the community be presented to the manor for confirmation. Considerably rarer were attempts to transform the communal constitution of settlements already in existence. Above, on p. 40, there has already been presented the evolution which the settlement of Jędrzejewo underwent. At the close of the eighteenth century an attempt was made to impose a hereditary sołtys by lordly nomination on the Stare Jaromierskie Olęders, and on the Olęders of Stare and Nowe Ujście. Conversely, however, the settlement of Rzecień, located on the principles of German law, became with the passage of time, constitutionally, like the Olęder settlements. In general it must be stated that the Olęder communal constitution once granted to a settlement in the location charter was respected by the manor also later.

b. The functions of self-government may be divided into delegated and own functions. In the first case the organs of self-government performed duties falling within the scope of the manorial administration, entrusted to them by the lord. Thus the sołtys and the ławniks were bound to see to it that the whole community punctually and completely performed the manorial duties. It was also the duty of the sołtys to collect the rents and fees due to the lord and hand them over to the manor. Moreover, as regards the fees from the sale of farms, from contracts, he had to see to it that no embezzlements were committed and that no false sums were declared. After the expiry of the period of freedom the communal authorities were bound to report to the manor the names and surnames of all the settlers. To them also belonged the duty of watching over the boundaries between the lands of the settlement and the neighbouring lands.

rusinski1947/52:
The competences of the communal organs in their own sphere comprised two kinds of matters: communal administration and communal judicature. The administrative provisions binding the members of the community were gathered together in the so-called wilkierze (Wilküre). Although issued at different times and by different lords, in their content they are almost identical, which indicates that they were written according to a common pattern, or rather that the later wilkierze were modelled on the wilkierze written earlier. Comparative research into the origin of the norms contained in the wilkierze would exceed the framework of the present work; in any case it seems a certain thing that these norms are based on foreign models. We quote one of the wilkierze in full in the appendix. From the wilkierze there shines forth a strong sense of communal solidarity. A considerable number of the provisions contained in them are designed to remove the sources of discord between the individual members of the community, or bind them to help one another in need. The latter, moreover, lay in the Olęders' own interest, for the community answered for the manorial duties usually solidarily; the property situation and solvency of a neighbour could therefore be a matter of indifference to none of its members. Control over the farming of the individual members of the community belonged to the important functions of the communal administration. The communal organs were even bound to remove by force an Olęder who farmed badly and to fill the farm with another. That this duty was in fact performed is proved by the note on p. 38. In some settlements the individual farmers were bound to report to the communal authorities the more important legal acts accomplished by themselves (contracts of sale and purchase, wills, bequests etc.). These acts were entered in a special book kept by the self-governing organs for the time being. Several such books have survived;3 they contain much interesting material on the life of the settlements. At times the legal acts entered in the community books had to be presented for additional lordly approval. On that occasion the lord collected certain fees.4

rusinski1947/53:
The communal judicature comprised above all cases of offences against the provisions of the wilkierz and the administrative orders of the communal organs, further all other cases (quarrels, brawls, thefts, boundary disputes) apart from matters of greater importance reserved to the lord. To the competence of the village court belonged also cases of offences against the provisions of the location charter.1 It is possible that the village court also performed the functions of an arbitration court. According to the charter for Borui the village judges "will look most diligently to order, security and tranquillity, indeed to success, order and justice, and will apply all diligence and earnestness of their own to it". The punishment applied by the court was the fine, and in exceptional cases arrest 3. From the judgments of the village court the condemned always had an appeal to the manor. So that the means of appeal should not be abused, the wilkierze provided that "whoever appeals out of spite and needlessly, groundlessly troubling the lord, shall be punished double". While in the sphere of administration the sołtys usually had wider competences than the remaining communal organs, in the panel of judges every member had equal rights. An accused member of the court was judged by the remaining sworn members in the same way as any other inhabitant of the settlement. The wilkierze defined the judicial procedure in detail. In Góździn the sittings of the court were to take place every 2 weeks, in the Jastrzębnickie Olęders every 4 weeks, on a Sunday. The members of the community were bound to appear at every summons of the court, to give testimony and to respect unconditionally all the other judgments and orders issued by the court. Special police provisions were designed to secure the safety and dignity of the court during the hearings. Women as a rule had no procedural capacity, nor could they be present at the place where the court sat. CHAPTER IV

The economic conditions of the Olęder settlements
A. Topography of the settlements. Forms of settlement. Building

I. Topography of the settlements. Olęder colonization was in its entirety agricultural colonization. The configuration of the ground on which the settlements were founded, and the character and productivity of the soil, exercised a direct influence on their economic life, and at the same time exercised a formative influence upon certain manifestations of the material culture of the Olęders, such as the manner of settling (the forms of settlement), building and the standard of agriculture. In view of the foregoing factors, all the Olęder settlements can be divided into two categories: lowland settlements, founded in river valleys and on the banks of standing waters, and settlements situated on dry ground, brought into being by clearing. Intermediate forms, of course, also occurred. The morphology of the lands occupied by the settlements presents, on the whole, a uniform appearance. Almost all the settlements seated themselves upon the outwash plains and dunes of the frontal moraine, frayed by the waters of the ice age. Only around Nowy Tomyśl did the reach of settlement embrace also a part of the flat ground moraine. The soil of settlements of either type was of no great economic value. In the lowland settlements it was, on the side of the water basin, as a rule marshy, more rarely alluvial (the so-called mady), while on the slopes of the valleys it passed into a system of sandy or stony dunes and elevations of the glacial moraine. The soil of the settlements of the second category, sandy and barren over almost its whole extent, only exceptionally rose to medium quality. In the Prussian classification records the soil of the settlements there described is constantly characterized as poor and unfruitful. Even today the districts where

Olęder settlement developed most vigorously (Babimost, Buk, Chodzież, Czarnków, Międzychód, Międzyrzecz, Poznań, Śrem) have the least fertile soils of the whole voivodeship. Only on the outwash plain of Nowy Tomyśl do we meet with soil of average fertility. This fact finds its explanation in the historical development of settlement within the area here discussed. The fertile lands had long since been settled by the local population, which, growing in numbers, occupied later, in part, also the less fertile lands. The colonists of the Middle Ages likewise chose lands as fertile as possible. The stock of land left at the Olęders' disposal therefore constituted the least valuable remnant remaining after the selection of land carried out by the settlement of many centuries.

2. Forms of settlement. In correspondence with the topographical conditions there developed two basic forms of Olęder settlement: the type of lowland settlement presenting itself as a street village, and the type of settlement. In both kinds of settlement the arrangement and disposition of the farm buildings is bound up closely with the character and shape of the piece, or pieces, of land belonging to the individual farms. The lands of the farms comprised in a lowland settlement consisted of a series of elongated strips running at right angles to the edge of the waters or of the morass. Such a strip of land began at the lowest point, by the body of water, and, running up the slope, ended upon dry ground lying higher. Here, at the top, parallel to the edge of the waters or of the bog, ran the road linking together the whole series of strips of land lying next to one another and belonging to the individual farms. Along this road, at the highest-lying end of the land, the Olęders raised their farm buildings. As a rule these stood on the same side of the road on which the land lay, but they could also stand on the opposite side, in which case the road separated them from the lands of the farm. Typical settlements of this kind are the oldest Olęders of the Wieleń estate. In the later period street villages occur also upon dry ground, and the lands are there laid out less regularly.

The settlement of the second type presented itself otherwise. Here the lord allowed the Olęders to clear for themselves lands of a defined size within some larger area of forest or pasture, while every Olęder as a

For economic reasons he endeavoured to prepare for cultivation a piece of land lying in one block, and that in a form approximating a square or else a polygon. For the same reasons he set his buildings at the most convenient point, most often in the middle of the cleared land, without regard to the position of the neighbouring farms. Beyond the two described categories of settlement there occurred Olęder settlements of other types. These arose in a twofold manner. In the first case, when an existing village was transferred to Olęder law, or the Olęders bought up a village left empty together with its buildings, or else, taking over a deserted village already without buildings, restored its original shape, there arose an Olęder settlement in the form existing previously. In the second case, when the Olęders had to conform to the special requirements of the lord, there arose a planned settlement, of shapes traced out in an artificial manner. 3. Building. In the sources we find scanty information on the manner of erecting the farm buildings in the Olęder settlements, on their shape and dimensions, and on the material used in their construction. In principle the complex of buildings belonging to one farm consisted of a dwelling cottage, a barn and a byre. Cart-sheds are met with more rarely. The byre was often built on to the cottage; exceptionally a second byre, or a separate granary, entered into the complex of buildings. The cottage was built either of logs or of sawn boards, or as a clay-walled cottage, and so likewise the byre and the barn. There also occurred buildings simply put together out of brushwood. Part of a building might be of timber, while the remainder was plastered with clay. For the most part the buildings had a covering of straw (sheaves), more rarely of reed, and exceptionally the more considerable buildings were roofed with shingles.

B. Occupational and social composition

The occupational composition of the Olęders. Among the population of the Olęder settlements we must distinguish: 1. the Olęder farmers, who sat on lands received from the lord or bought up, and who stood with the lord in a direct economic and legal relation regulated in the founding charter; 2. the remaining population, economically dependent upon the Olęders, such as, for example, certain craftsmen, the journeymen etc.; 3. it is also possible that in one and the same settlement there dwelt persons who did not belong to the communal society of the Olęders. Such was the case in the instances of mixed settlements already discussed. It could also happen that within an Olęder settlement there lived someone belonging to the manorial household service.

The population of the Olęder settlements was differentiated by occupation only to a small degree. Nearly all the members of the community were employed in agriculture, whether as their principal occupation or at least incidentally. Exceptionally this did not apply to the communal herdsmen, whose basis of subsistence was the rearing of domestic animals; it must nevertheless be emphasized here that stock-raising in the settlements did not pass beyond the bounds of a subsidiary occupation alongside the proper agricultural economy; among the Olęders we nowhere meet with farms devoted specially to stock-raising. Likewise only exceptionally do we encounter craftsmen who at the same time were not engaged in agriculture.

The most important source for the occupational composition of the population of the Olęder settlements of Kościan county is the Tol. It was drawn up according to the scheme laid down by the Crown Treasury Commission, which provided for the division of the rural population into the following groups: 1. farmer peasants (gospodarze rolnicy), 2. cottagers, 3. lodgers, 4. manufacturers, 5. craftsmen, 6. tapsters and innkeepers, 7. journeymen and servants, 8. the unattached “busied with work”, 9. beggars. In practice there was usually indicated as well the economic and legal relation of the inhabitants to the lord, there being added as need arose: “okupnicy” (holders by purchase), “czynszownicy” (rent-payers), “kontraktowi” (contract-holders). In the Olęder villages there was usually given: “Olęder farmers”, “okupni”, “okupnicy”, “czynszowi (czynszownicy)”. This whole scheme leaves much to be desired, for it mixes occupational with social categories, and is thus incomplete. Further, the figures contained in the table inspire far less confidence than, for example, the figures of an inventory or of a lustration, for they are nowhere explained in detail. The categories of persons ad 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8 in the Olęder settlements were without doubt occupied with agriculture. At point 4 we have a term that is rather obscure; the occupational allegiance of the persons classed here must be decided in each individual case. Point 9, as one may easily perceive on glancing into the table, the lustrators interpreted very broadly. Besides undoubted beggars there were assigned to this group all the old persons incapable of work who remained at the charge of the community (widows, orphans), and presumably also other persons who could not be brought under any of the preceding categories. These persons we too have counted among the agricultural population, as occupationally passive. Besides, this column supplements the column “the unattached at work”; the lustrators, as may be gathered from the table, did not in the majority of cases themselves very well know which of the two columns to give precedence.[1] On approximately the same principles the hearth tables were at the same time drawn up. It is harder to determine the social position of the craftsmen. Some of them were endowed with land, which placed them on a level with the independent stratum. The isolation of the craftsmen is, however, a very difficult matter. rusinski1947/65:
C. The individual branches of the Olęder economy

The full sweep of the economic activity of the Olęders will show itself most completely against the background of their share in the social income of a given estate. The division of the Olęders' income according to the different branches of production will lead to a picture of the individual branches of their economy; the division of income between the Olęders and the lord will be connected, on the one hand, with the distinguishing of the income from their own land and of the profits from the lord's land (the servitudes), and, on the other, with a discussion of the manorial dues. The share of the state and of the church in the Olęders' incomes will present itself to us as the public and ecclesiastical dues. Finally, the division of income between the individual settlers will require, among other things, an examination of their endowment with land and of the social structure of the individual occupations. In discussing the economic activity of the Olęders it will be indispensable to distinguish its twofold character: technical and socio-economic.

I. Agriculture. a. The agricultural technique of the Olęders, like the forms of settlement, developed along two paths. In the lowland settlements it consisted, in the first period, in the improvement of the land through drainage, in the second in the keeping, in a state fit for cultivation, of land once drained. In the settlements of the second type it consisted in the clearing of forests and thickets, and subsequently in raising the fertility of the land thus stripped of wood and in defending it against the renewed invasion of weeds and scrub. The considerable number of Olęder settlements justifies the supposition that the Olęders were able to rise to their task. They were enabled to do so by the multi-year exemptions from all dues granted them by the lord (the wolnizny), while the prospect of a free, independent existence upon land bought by themselves doubtless spurred the Olęders on to greater efforts. Not always, however, did the settlers receive as their lot the improvement of the lands allotted to them by the lord. In many instances they took over arable lands already manured before them by the Polish peasant, sometimes even already with buildings and crops. In column 6 of Annex I there is described the economic character of the land in the individual settlements at the moment of the founding of the Olęders. Only certain cases, clearly discussed in the founding charters or in other sources, have been recorded. The terms “village”, “folwark”, “ready-made arable land” signify that the Olęders here took over land already prepared for cultivation, whether after a village or folwark existing there before, or else were settled upon part of the lands of a settlement still continuing in existence. The improvement of the land naturally had no connexion with the rise of the settlement in such cases, likewise when an already existing settlement was transferred to Olęder

In the light of these figures there fade the assertions of German scholarship concerning the pioneering role of the colonists of German nationality in the tillage of the soils of western Wielkopolska. At the same time these figures undermine the assertions of Maas concerning the great afforestation of the Wielkopolskan landscape in the period before modern colonization, and justify the critical position of Hładyłowicz.

The drainage of the land was carried out in such a way that the water was either conducted by ditches to a lower-lying basin (a river, a lake), or else collected in deep ditches and pits. In the charters we occasionally find assurances that these ditches or pits would not be counted in to the Olęders in the measurement of their lands. Exceptionally the Olęders were permitted to dig ditches even through the land of others. The clearing of wooded land was accomplished probably for the most part by the felling and grubbing-up of trees and bushes. Clearing by burning was in-

The lands, doubtless at the settlers' request, were almost always measured out to them in a single block. This property was characteristic, moreover, of the other types of modern settlement in the area here discussed. Exceptionally an Olęder farm possessed lands in two blocks, or even in three, usually when the settlers had bought up deserted peasant farms. For the most part, as the old maps show, the lands were divided into two fields: winter and spring. Probably part of each field lay fallow for a time, so that the system of land cultivation most frequently practised by the Olęders was the three-course system. It is also possible that upon the better lands the improved three-course system was employed at least in part. In many settlements of particularly poor soil the fallow exceeded ⅓ of the total area of the lands; the land had to lie fallow for several years before it could again be taken under cultivation.

b. Endowment with land. The share of the individual settlers in the social income was decided above all by their endowment with land. This was usually reckoned in Chełmno włókas (hubas). The włóka was divided into [—] morgs; the morg contained 300 square rods (30×10). The rod, called also the laska or the różga, was of unequal length; it ranged from 7½ ells (the rod of the new or Warsaw measure)[5] to 9 ells (the margravial rod).[6] In an isolated instance we meet with a mention of lands measured with the Magdeburg rod, but there are no data as to how many ells it contained. Most often the lands were measured with the rod of 8 and of 9 ells, most rarely with that of 7½ ells. The matter was further complicated by the fact that 1 ell itself was of unequal length. The size of the farms in the Olęder settlements underwent considerable changes in the course of the colonization period. In the earlier settlements the norm was the włóka; alongside this, farms of an area of 1½ włókas were also created. More rarely do we meet with farms of other sizes: 2 włókas, ¼, ½ of a włóka. False is the assertion of W. Schulz that at the founding the size of all the farms was equal; one of the charters lays down, for example, that of the land “each of them (i.e. the Olęders) in that forest shall be bound to have one or two włókas”, while in another settlement 2 Olęders are settled upon one ślad, 2 upon 1½ of a ślad, 3 upon 1½ of a ślad. The lustration of the Wieleń estate of 1653 records that at Marianowo an Olęder sits upon 2 włókas, 6 upon 1 włóka and 5 upon ½ of a włóka. The number and size of the farms changed continually as a result of their division by inheritance, and possibly also through partial sale. A change in the area of the farms was brought about likewise by the unlawful ploughing-in of the lord's lands. Attached to the farms there were as a rule gardens. Their size ranged from ¼ to 2 morgs. The ground upon which the buildings stood did not, as a rule, enter into the measurement of the lands, and neither, of course, did the boundaries and balks. Occasionally the lord added to every włóka a piece of meadow.

c. Plant production. More exact data concerning plant production we possess only for the settlements seized by Prussia in the First Partition (of 1773) and for the settlements of the Sieraków estate. The data relating to the settlements in the area of the First Prussian Partition, contained in the Prussian classification records, are schematic and for that reason inspire less confidence; the data relating to the Sieraków estate, contained in the inventory of 1759 already several times mentioned, are on the whole set out conscientiously. As follows from the above sources, the plant production of the Olęders, owing to the poor soil, presented a most modest appearance. Wheat was not cultivated at all. Of the other cereals there were cultivated in the Sieraków estate rye, oats and barley, and among the other produce peas. In the settlements classified in 1773 production embraced sometimes also buckwheat and flax. The sowing per unit of land presented itself variously, according to how long the individual pieces of land had to lie fallow. In the Ol. Króteckie, for example, the land had to remain untilled for 6–8 years, and in the Kwiejce Nowe for 6–9 years. The average sowing in the Ol. Bielawy, Jasionna, Obelżanki and Rzecień, where there is given also a specification of the lands of the individual settlers, amounted, per włóka of 30 morgs, in korcy of the Berlin measure (⅛ of the korzec of Warsaw), to: 10 korcy of rye, 4 korcy of barley, 3 korcy of oats, ⅛ of a korzec of peas, 1¼ of a korzec of buckwheat and 3 garnce of flax. On the whole, however, it would seem, more oats was cultivated than barley. The yield was 3 grains, sometimes still less, exceptionally 3½ grains.

In the gardens hops were occasionally grown, sometimes potatoes and carrots, but as a rule only for household use. Exceptionally, in the Ol. Kwiejce Nowe and Bronice,[8] where the cultivation of cereals was almost impossible owing to the very barren soil, the Olęders lived from the cultivation of potatoes and carrots, which they carted for sale to Drezdenko, distant 2 miles. d. The rearing of domestic animals, in contrast to plant production, developed in the Olęder settlements on the whole successfully. Draft animals, it is true, were kept, in connexion with the small agricultural production, in numbers not very great (on a one-włóka farm on the average 3 or 4 oxen, or else 2 oxen and one or 2 horses), but cows and hornless stock in a quantity approaching the norm prevailing in the corvée villages, and sheep sometimes even in a larger number. As a characteristic feature it should be noted that the Olęders more often possessed horses than the tenantry, who for draft purposes used chiefly oxen. The draft stock was always the property of the Olęders. Since meadows entered only occasionally into the composition of the Olęder lands, and even when the Olęders possessed them, on account of their meagre extent they played no serious part in the stock-raising economy, the breeding of cattle and sheep in the Olęder settlements in the summer season rested almost exclusively upon the pasture servitudes, that is upon the right of pasturing herds, under certain conditions and within a defined range, upon the lord's lands. Since the lord, in his own interest, could not permit the pasturing of his lands by cattle in unlimited numbers, restrictions upon stock-raising came into being. The restrictions concerned as a rule sheep, more rarely goats, whereas hornless stock, cows and draft animals the Olęders were free to keep in any number. We meet with two basic kinds of restriction concerning the keeping of sheep. Relative restrictions, in the form of payments for the pasturing of sheep upon the lord's lands, or in general for the keeping of them, hindered it, but did not by any means make it impossible; absolute restrictions, on the other hand, consisting in the fixing of a certain maximum norm which the number of sheep upon a farm of a given size ought not to exceed,

2. Bee-keeping. Bees in hives the Olęders might keep in any number, without any dues. Sometimes, however, they were forbidden to keep bees in tree-hollow hives (barcie). The products of this keeping (honey, wax) they might dispose of at will. Exceptionally, in the Ol. Złotkowo they were bound to sell the wax exclusively at the manor.[6] The income from bee-keeping did not, however, constitute a serious item in the Olęders' economy. A case such as that of the sołtys in the Ol. Kliny, who possessed 11 bee-hives, the sources quote as a kind of curiosity. Professional bee-keepers there were none among the Olęders.

3. Hunting and fishing. The right of hunting game upon their own land did not belong to the Olęders. They were permitted only to hunt birds. They might indeed also organise hunts of wild boar, bears and wolves, but the animals killed they were bound, on pain of severe penalties, to deliver to the manor. The lord on his part promised them in return a certain reward, not more closely defined. Only in the Ol. Ujskie was the right of hunting unrestricted. The Olęders' income from hunting, within limits thus curtailed, presumably had no great significance. rusinski1947/75:
The Olęders' total income from fishing is made up of two items most closely linked with one another: the incomes from their own fish-farming and the incomes from the fishing servitudes. The separation of these two items is here extremely difficult to carry out. For it is not known whether, and in what cases, the possession of Olęder land carried with it the right of fishing in the bordering waters (rivers, lakes, marshes, ponds). The same doubts are raised by the ponds, which often stood upon Olęder land, and which either did or did not enter into the area of the individual farms. While it seems a certain thing that the adjoining waters, which separated the lord's lands from the Olęders', and likewise ponds lying indeed upon Olęder land but not entering into the composition of those lands, remained the property of the lord, and the right of using them must be regarded as a fishing servitude, it is so much the harder to decide whether, in cases where, for example, the Olęders received lands upon a river or lake bordering upon another estate, they entered into the existing manorial rights to those waters, or whether these belonged to them likewise only in the character of servitudes. The sources rather support the second possibility, for they distinguish fairly clearly the waters lying upon Olęder land and entering into the area of those lands (ponds dug by the Olęders, the seasonal floods upon the riparian lands),[1] and the remaining waters. On this assumption the lion's share of the Olęders' fishing income will fall to the fishing servitudes. The rule was that the lord permitted fishing in all the bordering waters, the manorial ponds upon Olęder land excepted. The Olęders were not, however, permitted to set up wears upon flowing waters. Sometimes the lord forbade the taking of fish in the spawning season. In exceptional cases, when the lord reserved to himself the exclusive right of fishing, he gave the community priority in letting it out on lease.[5] The sources make no mention of professional fishermen among the Olęders.

4. Industry. a. Tavern-keeping. Taverns stood in almost all the Olęder settlements. They were, however, always, as it were, branch establishments of the manorial breweries (mielcuchy), for the propination monopoly was in force in the Olęder settlements and the innkeepers received ready-made manorial liquors, which they were bound to retail in the settlement at a price fixed in advance.

Exceptionally in Ostrówek the settlers, to whom Kerol Maciej Grudziński in the founding document of 1750 made over the brewery with its requisite equipment and a granary for the storing of malt, themselves engaged in the brewing of beer. Production was here organized in the following manner. The individual settlers were bound to deliver to the brewery, from every huba, [—] wierteles of barley and the quantity of hops needed for the brewing of [—] barrels of beer. They were obliged to haul the wood in turn in the amount of 2–3 sążni; for this they received the aforementioned 10 barrels of beer. The rest was presumably retailed by the innkeeper, whom the lord freed from rent, while his remaining dues the sołtys, the ławniks and the community were bound to take upon themselves. The incomes from the tapping of liquors (the production of vodka was similarly organized) the sołtys and the ławniks were bound to divide evenly among all the members of the community. We have here, then, to do with a typical co-operative organization. The organization of the sale of the manorial liquors presented itself in the Olęder settlements as follows. At the founding of the settlement the lord set aside ½ of a włóka (huba), free of rent, for the innkeeper. One of the members of the community paid the okupne, settled on the land, and even before the tavern was built began the tapping of the manorial liquors. His remuneration, besides the aforementioned ½ of a włóka free of all rents,[3] often embraced also the so-called świętojanka, that is the 21st barrel or, respectively, the 21st garniec of the beer or vodka tapped.[4] In rare cases other advantages were granted to the innkeeper. The total number of millers has been given by estimate in Tab. II and III. Almost all the mills existing in the Olęder settlements were windmills. The building of a mill required, in all probability, a special permission from the lord.[5] The Olęder millers paid for the mill only a fixed money rent.[6] The millers' incomes were diminished by the fact that the obligation to grind at the lord's mill did not as a rule bind the Olęders, who might therefore cart their grain to any mill whatever, whereas the neighbouring corvée peasants were bound to grind their grain only in the manorial mills. c. Crafts. As Tab. II and III show, crafts were but weakly developed in the Olęder settlements. This is presumably to be explained by the fact that the Olęders had a closer contact with the neighbouring towns than the rest of the population (cf. above). The lord did not forbid the community to keep craftsmen, requiring only that they be “honest”. In Podgradowice and Rakoniewice the Olęders were permitted “to make linen for their own household needs, but for no one else for money — not permitted, under penalty”..

d. Forest industry, embracing the burning of charcoal, the making of tar and of potash, likewise had no great significance in the Olęder settlements. It is indeed possible that the sources are silent concerning such an industry because it rested only upon the utilizing of the stock of timber standing upon the Olęder hubas and bought together with the land. The working-up of the timber had then, however, only a transitional character and ended with the clearing of the land. A permanent production resting upon the exploitation of the lord's forests was impossible without an agreement with the lord, and of such agreements the sources have preserved very little record. The classification records mention a tar-burner in Herbardowo only once; besides this they also mention the production of tar in the Ol. Króteckie. Concerning this last settlement the records supply a series of very valuable data concerning the production of tar. The Olęders distilled tar in common in the Krótek forests. The burning took place [—] times a year, and from each burning were obtained [—] barrels of tar. The value of each barrel was 10–11 zł. For each burning the Olęders paid the lord [—] zł, or else delivered a barrel of tar. The annual production of the furnace, after deduction of the manorial rent, thus represented a value of 350 zł.

Other occupations. The community might sometimes keep its own watchman. In Popowo the lord assigned to such a watchman, who was at the same time to have an eye upon the manorial buildings, “a piece of land”. A certain percentage of the population of the settlements was formed by teachers or readers, performing the functions of schoolmasters and of religious ministers. Their economic situation will be discussed on later pages. Here we note only that they drew their principal incomes from the land assigned to them by the lord, free of all rents. D. The Olęders' rights of user upon the lord's possessions (servitudes)

Besides the incomes from their own economy the Olęders drew profits from the lord's possessions. These flowed from the servitudes, chiefly the pasture, the forest and the fishing servitudes. I. The pasture servitudes were the foundation of the stock-raising economy of the Olęders. Cases in which the Olęders had no right at all of pasturing their herds upon the lord's lands occurred extremely rarely. By these we shall understand the Olęders' entitlements to the use of the lord's forest within defined limits — apart from the pasture servitudes. The range of the Olęders' forest servitudes presented itself one way in the rent-free years, another in the later years. In the first period the Olęders always had the right of taking timber of every kind from the lord's forest, provided there was not enough of it in sufficient quantity and quality upon the lands allotted to them.[5] After the term of the wolnizna had expired, there belonged to the Olęders as a rule the right of gathering in the lord's forest timber for fuel, while timber for building and rods for fences they might not cut without the consent of the manor.[8] Permission to make use, to any extent, of timber of every kind was a rarity. Often the Olęders received timber free of charge for the repair of buildings, or against the event of a fire, in this last case by a separate agreement with the lord. In general it was a principle that the felling of timber had to be preceded by the obtaining of the appropriate “receipt” from the lord.[19] The sale of timber from the lord's forests was strictly forbidden. In some charters we meet also with permission to gather in the lord's forest pine-needles (igliwie) for manure. E. The lord's non-recurrent economic benefits

To this category belong the lord's non-recurrent material benefits of the nature of gifts, or else immaterial benefits which nevertheless had an influence upon the development and profitability of the Olęder farm. Both the one and the other kind of benefit was promised to the Olęders in the charter, which made it possible to demand them of the lord should certain conditions, defined in the charter, arise. Thus, for example, for building the Olęders received bricks from the manorial brickyard at a reduced price. In another case he promised every settler who completed the building of a dwelling house the gift of a barrel of beer. Such care expressed itself for the Olęders in material advantages, which showed itself above all when the lord guaranteed to the Olęders compensation from the neighbours for damage done (to the crops, to the livestock etc.).

F. Manorial dues

I. Rents. All the Olęders were rent-payers. Labour dues had only a slight significance. Among the rents the principal part was played by the money rent. Independently of the division of rents into money and into kind, there draws itself quite clearly a division of the Olęder rents into dues from the individual branches of the economy (from the land, from the individual servitudes and advantages). As at the colonization under German law, so the Olęders did not pay rent immediately upon settlement, but enjoyed a certain number of so-called free years. The wolnizny had for their aim to make it possible for the Olęders to maintain themselves on the spot so long as the land had not yet been cleared and had not begun to yield incomes. As a rule there was required of the Olęders that in the free years they should erect the needed farm buildings. In settlements founded “from the new root” the wolnizna amounted most often to 6–7 years, whereas at the founding of settlements upon the site of deserted villages there were either no years of freedom at all, or they ranged from 1 to 3 years, according to the state of the lands and of any buildings still existing. In settlements founded upon lands partly overgrown there existed a differentiation of the years of freedom according to the state of the individual pieces of land. Independently of the exemptions in the initial period of the settlement's existence, the lord as a rule promised the Olęders an additional year of freedom in the event that, having abandoned their farms in consequence of the upheavals of war or of other elemental calamities, they should later wish to return to their seats.

Among the money rents the most important, and sometimes the only, item was formed by the rent from the land (the gruntczynsz). In the earliest settlements it was very low: in the Ujskie Olęders (in 1597) it came to 20 zł from a huba of 30 morgs, in the Ol. Nowe Dwory (in 1601) 25 zł from a huba which, as follows from the later surveys, was of 60 morgs. In the Ol. Róża (in 1624) the rent was nominally somewhat higher, amounting to 36 zł from the huba; in reality, however, owing to the fall in the value of the złoty, it was no higher than the rents given previously. The rent remained at this level throughout the seventeenth century. At the end of that century dues began to be reckoned in tymfs. Thus in the Dłuskie Stare Olęders (in 1688) the rent from the ślad was fixed at 64 tymfs. Payment in money was made for the most part also for the pasture servitudes. Separate payments for pasture appear at the end of the seventeenth century. They persist until the partitions in the amount of 2 thalers or 10 tymfs at the fixed rate per huba, or else 6 to 10 gr for every head of cattle. In the Ol. Stodólsko the fixed payment amounted to only 1 thaler, but the use of the pastures was limited in time.[5] In the Ol. Wymyślanka the Olęders were bound to pay both kinds of dues simultaneously. A manifestly punitive character had the sum fixed in the Ol. Głęboczek. There it was permitted to keep 50 sheep free of payment, while for every sheep beyond that a fee of as much as 1 tymf was payable. In a few cases the payment for pasture was already included in the general rent. Sometimes, again, a single payment was made for the pasture and forest servitudes together.

In several settlements the Olęders paid to the lord the so-called stróżowe (watch-money). This was assessed either upon every huba of land (thus, for example, in Krzemieniewo 1 zł was paid from every huba), or the whole settlement was bound to pay a certain fixed lump sum. b. Rents in kind. Rents of this kind we meet with in the second half of the seventeenth century; in the earliest settlements rents in kind do not occur. The most common rent was oats, delivered on the average in the quantity of [—] wierteles or ćwiertnie of local measure. (In the Borujskie Olęders, for example, there was in use the wiertel of Poznań measure, containing [—] garnce.) In exceptional cases the rent reached [—] wierteles of oats from the huba. Far more rarely was the rent reckoned in another kind of grain, for example in rye or in barley. The object of the rent might also be poultry (from the huba on the average 1–4 capons or hens, or 1–4 geese, exceptionally also ducks),[7] or eggs (in the quantity of from 1 mendel to 1 kopa), in rare cases butter (1 garniec) and cut straw (sieczka) (2 korcy). It should be noted that when the rent was reckoned in oats or in other naturalia, no special fees were usually taken for the forest servitudes. The rent defined as a payment for the servitudes amounted likewise on the average to [—] wierteles of oats, more rarely embracing other naturalia. Sometimes, again, naturalia took the place of a separate payment for the pasture servitudes.[11] In an isolated case wood ash likewise appears as a due. And sometimes the lord left the Olęders the choice of paying the rents in kind or their equivalent in money.[1]

rusinski1947/88:
2. Payments. Besides the money rents the Olęders paid various dues. They differed from the rents in this, that they were paid only in certain circumstances (e.g. upon the sale of a farm), whereas the rents were paid always, in a fixed and defined amount. On the border between rents and dues stood the already discussed payment for the pasture servitudes, paid for each individual sheep. The proper dues paid by the Olęders may be divided into 2 groups: dues of an economic character and administrative dues. To the first category of dues belonged the okupne (for land, for buildings), then the eventual market dues. The amount of the okupne fluctuated within very wide limits and it is difficult to give here any average figure. In 2 settlements founded at the close of the seventeenth century the okupne came, for the huba, to 40 thalers, reckoning the thaler at 15 szóstaks (== 120 zł), and 100 thalers at the rate of 5 zł to the thaler (== 500 zł). At the beginning of the eighteenth century there was paid for the huba: 150 zł (in 1701), 30 zł (in 1707), 10 zł (in 1709), 100 tymfs (in 1712). In connexion with the fall in the value of money the sum of the okupne rose nominally, reaching about 1730 exceptionally even 600 zł. On the other hand, in the same period we have to record okupne in the amount of 6 zł, and somewhat later (in 1752) 1 red złoty from the huba. For a longer time the amount of the okupne settles down at approximately 100 zł from the huba. In the last quarter of the eighteenth century the okupne is higher. For the huba there is paid: 900 zł (in 1771 — arable lands with buildings), 24 zł (in 1773), 30 red zł. (in 1775), 900 zł (arable lands with buildings — in 1776 and 1781), 10 red zł. Sometimes the lord exempted the Olęders from the payment of market dues in the towns lying within his estate. One must suppose that when the Olęders were not exempt from the dues, the rates applied generally were binding on them. The sources, however, say nothing about this.

Among the administrative dues the greatest significance belonged to the fee on the sale of farms. Its amount and kinds have already been given above, on p. 66. Apart from this, in a few settlements we encounter the dues already mentioned for the confirmation of more important legal acts (records, wills, divisions of property, marriage contracts). In the Milczewskie and Lubaskie Ol. the lord collected 11 tymfs (14 zł) for each act. In the Stare Borujskie Ol. we encounter a formally administrative fee, though by its character very close to a rent: the Olęders paid it every 50 years at the rate of 36 zł per huba in return for the manor's recognition of their right of ownership to the land they held. Maas's remark that the Olęders paid dues when marrying their daughters off outside the community rests on a misunderstanding 3. Labour dues. In the charters for the two earliest Olęder settlements on the territory of the former voivodeship of Poznań manorial obligations in the form of labour dues do not appear. In the Ol. Róża, located in 1624 in the krobielewskie estate, we already find the obligation to repair the bridge over the river Warta, while the inventory of the Wieleń estate of 1653 enumerates among the Olęders' obligations, among others, one day of labour and the cartage of 3 loads of wood. Labour dues on a wider scale we find only in the charters for settlements located in the eighteenth century. Attention must, however, be drawn to the fact that their character is different from that of the serf labour of the enserfed peasants; the labour dues always burdened the Olęders to a small extent, were for the most part strictly fixed in the charter and arose by way of mutual agreement of the parties, and were not conditioned by a personal dependence on the lord, as were the labour dues of the enserfed population. In accordance with the provisions of the charters we can distinguish labour dues fixed in a definite quantity and labour dues binding in an unspecified quantity. The number of working days, as indeed the quantity of the other labour dues, fluctuated within very wide limits. Beside cases in which there was no labour due at all, we find a case in which it was rendered at the rate of 50 days yearly per huba. On average the number of days of labour due amounted to 6–12 days per huba; lower labour dues or their absence we encounter in cases where other labour dues were also rendered, not specified in days (e.g. cartages). Usually the kind of work and the season of the year in which the work was to be performed were specified (ploughing, carting manure, sowings, the reaping of grain, haymaking etc.). More rarely we meet the obligation to perform certain agricultural works on a defined area of land, that is, the so-called jutrzyny [dawn labours] 3. In exceptional cases an intermediate combination was applied, the so-called apportioned labour due (robocizna wydziałowa), consisting in this, that a certain number of working days was fixed, but at the same time a minimum of work to be performed in the course of the day was specified. Thus, for instance, in one of the settlements the Olęders were obliged to “plough for 3 days, 12 ridges at a time”, in another case it was their duty, from St Adalbert's day to St Martin's day, to plough a morg of land every week. The jutrzyny usually covered ploughing only (30 to 60 ridges), sometimes mowing only, more rarely ploughing and mowing, and exceptionally all the works except sowing. Jutrzyna labour dues could also consist in the mowing and drying of hay on a defined piece of meadow. Closely related to the labour dues were the cartages and the “journeys”. In the first case the Olęders were most often obliged to cart firewood from the lord's forest to the manor, usually twice a year;

at Christmas, Easter and Whitsuntide, in the amount of 1–2 loads of (the so-called festival wood, drzewo świętne). The cartage could be combined with the performance of certain works, as for instance when the Olęders had the obligation to cart wood already felled 4. More rarely we meet the obligation to cart timber in logs to the sawmill, or else the cartage of a certain number of kopas of the lord's grain from the field to the manorial barn 8. In the second case it was the duty of the Olęders to cart to the towns, usually the larger ones, the products of the lord's husbandry (timber, grain, liquors). The Olęders were obliged to carry out the transport with their own teams. The length of the route was either specified in miles 8, or the town to which the future journeys were to be made was named. The towns most often in question were Czersk, Leszno, Poznań and Wschowa, more rarely Komorniki, Toruń and Żydaczów. Sometimes these journeys could be very distant and consequently burdensome. Thus, for instance, the inhabitants of the Karpickie Ol., situated in the neighbourhood of Wolsztyn, were obliged to make the journey to Toruń once a year, or to pay in its stead 5 czerw. zł.

Among the labour dues an important place was occupied by the so-called tłoki [compulsory ploughing-works] (in the sources almost always in the spelling tłuki; German Bit(t)age, Bit(t)dienste. As the very name indicates, these were labour dues performed in case of sudden need. The tłoki differed from the other labour dues in that they were rendered for a remuneration on the part of the lord, usually in beer, so that these labour dues had the character of hired labour. rusinski1947/92:
voluntary labour dues, but bound the settlers just like the other manorial obligations. The obligation to render them was often expressly emphasised in the charter. One may doubt whether the remuneration in beer always constituted a sufficient equivalent for the works performed by the Olęders. Initially, in all probability, the tłoki were rendered in small quantity and only in case of absolutely urgent need. Since the Olęders received remuneration for their work, the tłoki were not regarded as an obligation burdening the Olęders, and sometimes no mention of them was made in the charter. Thus, according to the inventory of the Wieleń estate of 1653, the Olęders who were located in that estate at the beginning of the seventeenth century were obliged to work one day at harvest, and yet in the later charters of 1677 we find no mention of these labour dues. On the whole, however, the obligation of rendering the tłoki is clearly formulated in the charters, and the tłoki are even clearly distinguished from the labour dues “for the breaking-in of new land”. The charter for the Jerackie Ol. provides that: “other labour dues (apart from those for the breaking-in of new land and the customary tłoki) the manor ought not to demand of the aforesaid Olęders”. The fixing of the number of tłoki in the charter must be regarded as advantageous for the Olęders, for it protected them against possible abuses on the part of the lord. Most often hand labour was rendered (hence the tłoki were sometimes called corvée [szarwark]), but we meet also tłoki rendered with draught teams.

Owing to the number of working days being sometimes left undetermined more closely, the tłoki formed a transitional form between labour dues defined in quantity and those undefined. Among the latter, performed “when the need arises”, the most important group was formed by the so-called corvée works. The author's charges concerning the so-called tłoki rest on an obvious misunderstanding. As has already been emphasised, these labour dues never had a voluntary character, and their German name Bit(t)age derives from the word Bede — tax, tribute. The author did not here avail himself of the results of Fr. Guradze's work, which exhaustively explained the matter several years before. In this light the arguments both of Schmidt and of later authors about the oppression of the Olęders through the conversion of the tłoki from a voluntary into a compulsory labour due must be regarded as pointless. Of cases in which the promised payment in beer was refused for the tłoki we have found none in the sources.

A proper view of the development of the manorial obligations of the Olęders is possible only when a broader source basis is taken into account. As regards the rents, their amount, as has already been shown above, rose from 20 zł at the close of the sixteenth century to 100 tymfs in the pre-partition period, that is, 5-fold. Meanwhile the silver content, which in the złoty according to the mint ordinance of 1580 amounted to 20 g., diminished in the tymf to 1.97 g., that is, 10-fold8. In reality the differences were still greater, for in those settlements in which the rents rose at all, the rise was always belated in relation to the fall in the value of money. Thus, for instance, in the Wieleń settlements cited above the rent remained the same from the beginning of the seventeenth century to 1677, although in that period the value of money had fallen by more than half. Moreover the price of land rose as its supply dwindled, and in the same way the value of the pastures 1 forests, and hence of the servitudes, increased. As Kniat has shown, who on the basis of the classification records of 1773 investigated and presented statistically the manorial obligations of the rent-paying settlements of the so-called notecki district, which were mostly Olęder settlements, the dues in kind and the labour dues of these settlements, converted into cash, amounted to 5–30% of the sum of the rent. If we assume that certain fees, e.g. for the servitudes and others, may have been included in the rent, the total value of the dues in kind, labour dues and fees will still not exceed 10% of the rent sum. These results find confirmation in other sources. Of course there are localities in which the dues in kind and the labour dues have a considerably greater value in relation to the rent, but there the rent is lower than the average given by us. In the final conclusion it must be stated that the increase of the manorial obligations of the Olęders was as a rule only nominal, while the real value of the obligations on the whole diminished. This fact will stand out still more sharply if we compare it with the process of the continual increase of the burdens of the enserfed population 5. The legal-moral aspect of the question presents itself somewhat differently. Between the lord and the Olęders disputes sometimes arose, which after the occupation of the country by Prussia expressed themselves in a whole series of lawsuits. The complaining party was most often the Olęders, although it was sometimes the reverse. Three basic causes of the lawsuits may be distinguished: a) the unclear formulation of the obligations 1 rights of the Olęders in the charters, b) the desire for profit or ill will on the part of the lord, c) the same on the part of the Olęders.

rusinski1947/101:
The unclear, often ambiguous content of the charters created in many cases an occasion for disputes and litigiousness. In the charter for the Cisiogórskie Ol. we find, for instance, the following, unclearly drafted provision: “At the harvest they are to help in the work according to need as the other Olęders shall be; in law, however, so many days shall be expressed as is the custom of the Olęders … Wood for the lord's need, as also for the kitchen, they are to cart like the other Olęders 1”. It is an obvious thing that “the custom of the Olęders” can be interpreted very widely. Elsewhere the Olęders are to present themselves for work at call, and at the harvest they are to labour as long as until everything has been cleared away. The scope of the servitudes was likewise unclearly defined; e.g. the provision: “sheep and other cattle they shall keep in moderate number, so that the lord's livestock may have their ease” 3, directly encourages litigiousness.

Disputes arising from the desire to raise the Olęders' hitherto existing obligations and to restrict their rights form a serious percentage of all the conflicts of the lord with the Olęders. The pretensions of the manor, although for the most part, as has been shown above, economically justified, often stood in contradiction to the promises given to the Olęders in the charter; hence, from the legal point of view, they must be qualified negatively. This matter, as appears from the utterances of the contemporary Prussian judge Stenger, caused the courts great trouble, which, although it stood on the ground of the complete respect of the provisions of the charters, could not here fail to notice the discord between law and equity. There occurred also, though rather rarely, demands of the manor bearing already the stamp of exploitation. To such, for instance, belonged the additional fees mentioned by Schmidt (p. 382), imposed by the Szpiech family on the Olęders of the Wieleń estate. Similarly in 1791 Ignacy Bniński tried to impose new charters on the Stare Jaromierskie Ol. and the Stare 1 Nowe Ujskie Ol., in which he clearly raised their hitherto existing obligations and at the same time established hereditary sołtys. It is clear that this had to implant among the Olęders, who were in great part Germans, especially after the catastrophe of the partitions, the conviction that special, far-reaching consideration was due to them from the Prussian authorities. Without entering into whether and to what extent they really profited by these considerations, the lawsuits brought by the Olęders from motives of this kind must be accepted as a natural and practised thing. The litigiousness and ill will of some of the Olęder communities is moreover emphasised by an eye-witness, a perfectly well-informed witness, judge Stenger, who at the same time draws attention to the political back-cloths of the lawsuits, writing that the Olęders were driven into them by “unauthorised advisers of the secular and ecclesiastical estate”. It remains to examine how the economic relation of the Olęders to the manor shaped itself after the partitions. Here we must consider separately the settlements in private estates and in state estates. The number of the latter increased markedly, in consequence of the taking over by the state of church estates and of certain szlachta estates, in which Olęder settlements were particularly numerous (the Połajewo, Sieraków and Międzychód estates). In the szlachta estates the position of the Olęders improved markedly in consequence of the abolition of patrimonial jurisdiction. Undoubtedly advantageous to the Olęders was also the hostile attitude of the Prussian government towards the Polish szlachta. On the other hand, as regards the state domains, the economic situation of the Olęders deteriorated in a perfectly visible way. In all the domains they began to take from the Olęders the lands they had ploughed in, to restrict the servitude rights and to increase the labour dues. We have already adduced examples relating to the Ujście starostwo and the domain of Podstolice. Likewise the inhabitants of the Trzydomy Ol., lying on the ground of the Rogoźno and Budzyń starostwo, write in 1794 a petition to the Prussian king with the request to be kept to the obligations which they had rendered in Polish times. G. Church obligations

Olęder settlements, from the moment of their foundation, entered within the parochial administration of the Catholic church. In connection with this, for the most part, on a par with the other parishioners, the Olęders were obliged to pay certain dues to the parish church. Catholics and evangelicals alike were made liable to these dues. The latter had, in return, just like the Catholic population, a right to the religious ministrations of the parish priests. The church dues paid by the Olęders can be divided into fixed dues and dues for the individual religious services. The fixed dues were the tithe and the meszne. Usually either the tithe or the meszne was paid; exceptionally a certain sum was paid on account of both dues at the same time. Both the tithe and the meszne were paid either in grain or in money.
