As a rule, if a settlement arose on the site of another, previously existing settlement, the obligations paid formerly were binding upon it. The same of course applies to settlements transferred to Olęder law without a change of the previous inhabitants. The manor sometimes took over entirely, or in part, the obligation of paying the church obligations due from the settlement, or else, by way of partial repayment of the dues, bound itself, after grain had been delivered to it, to brew gratuitously for the Olęders a certain quantity of beer. In other cases again the Olęders received the assurance that “they would always have the protection of the lord, so that they should give no more than what equity demands and what the church authority has ordained”. Sometimes also the Olęders had the obligation to pay the church obligations through the intermediacy of the manor. The amount of the dues shaped itself variously. The fixed dues, measured per unit of land, amounted per huba to 2–8 zł, or a korzec of rye and a korzec of oats. The lump-sum due, on the other hand, did not usually exceed 50 zł, or the corresponding quantity of grain; exceptionally it exceeded even 100 zł. One must suppose that in fixing it the decisive role was played by the area of the village and the number of settlers.

The Constitution of 1768 abolished the obligation of paying church dues by the dissenters. The Olęders took advantage of it. According to Kniat's calculations, in 1773 per włóka of land in the rent-paying villages of the notecki district there fell: in the szlachta estates 26–66 gr, in the state estates 19 gr, sometimes indeed nothing at all was paid, in the church estates 7 thalers 42 gr Prussian as tithe. In this last case, however, the payers were almost always Catholics; besides, it is difficult here to distinguish the dues paid iure parochiali [by parochial right] from the manorial obligations. If we take into account that 1 in the rent-paying szlachta and state settlements part of the inhabitants was Catholic, there will fall to the evangelical population a quite minimal sum.

In the northern part of the Poznań county, in places where the parochial administration had been organised by the evangelical church, it also laid claim to services on the part of the Olęders. These services could have a compulsory character, just like the services in favour of the Catholic parish church. It even happened that the Olęders were bound to services in favour of both churches at the same time. The services in favour of the evangelical church sometimes reached a considerable amount.

There occurred, however, cases in which the lord exempted the Olęders for ever from all taxes, thereby taking upon himself the obligation of paying them out of his own purse. Of course the taxes could here be shifted onto the Olęders in the form of an increased rent. We meet the obligation of paying taxes already in the earliest period of the colonisation. Thus, for instance, the Nowe Dwory Ol., founded in 1601, were obliged to pay the “crown levy resolved at the sejm”. The same provision we find in the charters of 1677 for Folsztyn, Herbardowo and Marianowo. In the charters of the first half of the eighteenth century there appear mentions of the hearth tax. The Olęders in the royal estates pay the hyberna. The most important tax, however, from the end of the seventeenth century was the poll tax. The charters either mentioned generally the obligation of paying this tax, or recommended paying it in the amount fixed by the authorities, and then the Olęders were usually obliged to pay into the proper cash-box the amount falling to them, like the other taxes; or else they bound the Olęders to pay on this account a certain fixed lump sum into the lord's hands. The latter pocketed the surplus above the tariff, or else made good the difference between the tariff and the sum paid in. The fixed amount of the tax was determined per unit of land (huba), or else fixed collectively for the whole community, which apportioned it among the individual members. In the first case its average amount lay within 3–6 zł per huba, in the second it amounted to about 50 zł. Only exceptionally, in the Sieraków estate, did the poll tax exceed 100 zł. The general economic situation and the standard of living of the Olęders

Judge Stenger, who wrote his remarks on the Olęders on the basis of personal observation of the settlements in the neighbourhood of Trzciel, Nowy Tomyśl and Zbąszyń, states that in these Olęder settlements a relative prosperity prevailed: “On the whole the Olęder likes to represent himself as quite poor and suffering misery; taking it all in all, he is not rich, but by no means poor”. The same is stated by Holsche: “These people here and there are doing quite well”. The author of the brochure “Uber Ursprung u. Verbreitung” (p. 33) follows the opinion of the writers mentioned above, adding, however, a proviso: “It is true that the unfavourable fact that many of these Olęder settlements were founded on ground too light, sandy, forest soil, and received no meadows, often hindered them in attaining prosperity”. The scanty source materials that have survived with regard to this question speak for the truth of the opinions cited above. On the whole the economic position of the Olęders, despite the poor soil, was satisfactory, but there existed differences in the economic situation of the individual settlements. It seems that the Olęders of the neighbourhood of Trzciel and Nowy Tomyśl were best situated; the soil there reached a medium quality, and the obligations were on the whole low. CHAPTER V

The spiritual culture of the Olęders

A. Psychological type

The Olęders, as has already been said, apart from the first comers from the Netherlands, came from various parts of eastern Germany and western Poland. They were thus, at the moment of the location of the settlements, neither uniform in the racial respect, nor united by ties of character, customs and culture. In the later generations, however, the common conditions of existence largely levelled their cultural and customary distinctiveness, and the self-governing constitution of the communities, above all the institution of the joint liability of all the members of the community in external relations, closely bound together the fortunes of the individual settlers and contributed to the formation among them of a kind of group consciousness. This may be regarded as equivalent to the formation of a distinct psychological type, that of the “Olęder”. Contemporaries did not speak with enthusiasm of the character of the Olęders. A serious observer such as Stenger writes of them as follows: “It is a certain thing that with the ancestors of our present-day Olęders the best part of the German nation did not leave its fatherland; for, although below we tried to find the reasons why the Olęders have become worse, their present corruption could not be explained if one were to assume that they brought with them good customs and character. Diligence and dexterity, as the children of poverty, were probably their only dowry: if only they had at least preserved these qualities intact! The Olęder is not narrow-minded, but by no means intelligent: he is cunning when he fears an attack, and he holds so strictly to old prejudices and habits that, blinded, he does not notice his own obvious advantages; to the most convincing arguments he gives no hearing at all, for the innate fear of everything that is new makes him deaf to it. Further, he is extraordinarily suspicious: the husband does not trust his wife, the father his children, but all unite when it is a matter of distrust towards the lord or the superior. The Olęder is also extraordinarily stubborn, audacious and un-

obliging: he does not willingly do anything that he need not do; finally, he has no religion at all” 1. Elsewhere the author charges the Olęders with litigiousness. This matter has already been discussed above. As a favourable trait of the Olęders the author emphasises their strong feeling of communal solidarity (social sense), and states also that sobriety generally prevailed in the Olęder settlements. These last two remarks must be recognised as correct. It is true that taverns, or the tapping of the lord's liquors, were to be found in almost all the settlements, and for the labour dues called “tłoki” the settlers received their remuneration in beer, possibly in spirits; this proves nothing at all, however, that the use of liquors was practised among the Olęders habitually. In a certain contradiction with the feeling of communal solidarity stood the sometimes strikingly weak attachment of the Olęders to their land 1 and their inclination to move from one settlement to another. It seems to follow from this that the Olęders, often newcomers from abroad, were accompanied even in later generations by a feeling of a certain strangeness. The lord also cared for good morals in the community, threatening sometimes even with the expulsion from the settlement of individuals without moral principles and character.

B. Schooling

According to the Prussian classification records for the part of the Poznań county taken in the first partition, in every third Olęder settlement there existed an evangelical school. Probably the number of schools in the settlements with an evangelical population was still greater in the remaining part of the former voivodeship, where there was a greater number of populous settlements able to maintain a teacher. On the other hand it must be taken into account that in the Catholic Olęder settlements there were no schools at all. In any case, however, the estimated figures given in Table II must be regarded rather as minimal. The Olęder schools were typical denominational institutions (Kantorat-, Lektoratschulen). They were conducted by church singers or other persons who at the same time performed religious ministrations in the community. They stood in for the evangelical clergymen for the Olęders. Hence the inhabitants of a new settlement usually tried to secure for themselves the religious ministrations of a cantor or lector, striving with the lord for permission to found a school and for its endowment. It is obvious that in schools of this kind the first place was held by religious preparation. With regard to some schools the source notices even raise the doubt whether anything other than the teaching of religion 3% was taught there. Similar reflections are suggested also by the circumstance that there were no schools either in the Olęder settlements with a Catholic population, which had easy contact with their clergymen and the possibility of using the parochial schools, or in those evangelical settlements where the pastor was on the spot, or in the nearest neighbourhood (e.g. in the settlements of the Wieleń estate).

The school was usually housed in a separate building, erected with the lord's consent. This building was at the same time the local house of prayer. Only in the Sieraków estate were the Olęders, under the provision of the then owner Henryk Bruhl, not permitted to have separate school buildings, and instruction could take place only in the cottage of one

The school land usually amounted to ½ wł., more rarely 1/4 wł., exceptionally still less. In the Ujskie Ol. one włóka was assigned to the school, from which, however, the Olęders were obliged to pay half the rent. If the lord settled the Olęders on a site where buildings of another village, or of a folwark, still existed, he offered one of the buildings gratuitously for the school. Apart from the income of the school land the teacher drew incomes also from the contributions of the community. In the latter the most common, but at the same time the most precarious item was formed by the dues from each child making use of the school instruction; the rest consisted of certain offerings fixed in agreement with the teacher, in money and in kind. By way of example we state that the income of the teacher in the Siereckie Ol. in 1793 consisted of: 1) the profits from the use of 1½ włóka of school land, 2) a tribute at the rate of 16½ thalers, 3) 4 contributions (Opfer), not further specified, 4) from every farmer one loaf, 5) one pound of butter and 4 cheeses from each huba, 6) from every farmer a cart-load of wood, 7) dues according to a separate tariff for singing at burials, and 8) dues from the pupils at the rate of 6 zł from the older children and 3 zł from the younger children.

The community could not always afford to maintain a professional teacher. The lord also sometimes stipulated in the charter that a craftsman or a farmer should be appointed as teacher. In one of the cases known to us the functions of teacher were performed by a weaver, in another an innkeeper 8, and, as Stenger relates, they were often entrusted to cobblers or tailors. Candidates for teachers came either from the neighbouring little towns, from which lack of work or other considerations had induced them to depart, or else, as regards candidates without a trade, they were recruited from the rural labourers who in one way or another had acquired the ability to read and write. To the teacher's duties belonged the teaching of religion and the performance of certain religious ministrations, and the exercise of the children in reading, writing and counting. At the same time the teacher performed the function of community secretary; he kept the community book, transacted the correspondence of the community, and probably also the private affairs of the Olęders.

The relations of the teacher with the community shaped themselves markedly unfavourably, which in the result greatly weakened the value and level of the school instruction. The cause here was the circumstance that the teacher, as one engaged and largely supported by the community, was entirely dependent on it, and thereby powerless in the face of the caprices and arbitrariness of the settlers. The Prussian officials, who carried out directly after the second partition a revision of the evangelical schools in the occupied territories, reckoned among the most important ailments of the school system, among others: the complete lack of respect and understanding for the persons of the teachers, sometimes indeed through their own fault, and the widespread custom that every settler presumed to be entitled to give commands to the teacher, and, when his child was reprimanded at school, came himself to the teacher and abused him in the most brutal manner. Still more forcefully the attitude of the Olęders to the teachers is characterised by Stenger. The surviving lawsuit records concerning matters between the settlements and the teachers show also that the latter were often charged with utterly unserious accusations and expelled for trivial reasons. Probably a cause of this development of relations was also the insufficient supervision of the school system (partly exercised by the pastors).

It is possible that in practice it was observed for an even shorter space of time.
rusinski1947/118:
lector 1, and in isolated cases also the prohibition of reading the gospel 2%. On the other hand the freedom of the Olęders to exercise their religious practices outside the community (in the town meeting-houses etc.) was not called in question 3. On the whole, if we leave aside the settlements lying in the estates of the dissenting szlachta, disposed with particular favour towards their co-religionists, it must be stated that the lords showed no great interest in the religious affairs of the Olęders. The placement in the charters of the few, above-mentioned restrictions in connection with the obligations towards the church suggests the thought that they were introduced into the charters in consequence of the interventions of the proper parish priests. Sometimes the lords took up no position of their own at all in the religious matters of the Olęders, recommending that in these matters they should proceed as “the Commonwealth permits” 4. The sources contain not a single mention of any control of the religious life of the Olęders undertaken on the lord's initiative with a view to its conformity with the provisions of the charter. Nor is there to be found in the sources a single case of a later restriction of the freedom of confession guaranteed to the Olęders in the location charter. As for the above-mentioned restrictions contained in the location charters, these could not be imposed on the Olęders, as free men able to choose their future lord at will, without their consent.

Where there were particularly numerous clusters of Olęder settlements with an evangelical population, there the Olęders, with the manor's consent, built themselves churches and maintained at their own cost clergymen of their confession 5. On the whole, however, the evangelical churches in the Olęder settlements were few, partly because the laws of the old Commonwealth (before

The sources contain no closer data concerning the pastors; it is to be supposed, however, that they were persons as a rule enlightened and prepared for the exercise of clerical functions. Of course exceptions occurred here too. The relations of the pastors with the community were not always satisfactory. Mention has already been made above of the lawsuits of the Herbardowo community with the local clergyman. A wholly unfavourable testimonial was given to his parishioners by the pastor of the evangelical community of Piotrowo, to which the Króteckie and Miłkowskie Ol. also belonged.

The ordinary religious needs of the Olęders were fully satisfied by the local teacher, often called the “ferlezer” (German Vorleser, Lektor, Kantor). He held the Sunday service in the community (read the gospel, delivered the sermon, sang religious songs), conducted the burial rites (escorted the dead to the cemetery, sang songs and delivered funeral orations), and taught the children the principles of religion. Hence also Stenger speaks of them with irony. rusinski1947/121:
Concluding remarks

In the foregoing considerations the political position of the Olęders has not been dealt with, because the question of a separate attitude of the state and of private individuals towards peasants of Polish 1 and German nationality in the old Commonwealth did not exist. National affiliation was, moreover, at that time, in the period of the continual mingling of nationalities and of two-way processes of assimilation, a notion that could not be established even in rough approximation. The pursuit, therefore, of a national policy, even if tendencies in that direction had existed, was a perfectly impossible thing. All attempts, therefore, at writing about the discrimination of German settlers in relation to Poles must be regarded as an undertaking doomed in advance. On the contrary, the gap between the favourable economic situation of the free Olęders and the incomparably worse position of the subject kmiecie continually deepened. The sources contain likewise no mention whatsoever of any steps on the part of the landowners towards the polonisation of the German Olęders subject to them. Probably processes of polonisation of the settlers did exist, but they took place spontaneously, without any purposeful action on the Polish side.

Since they were not szlachta, the Olęders took no part in the political life of their time. Probably to the constitution of the Olęder settlements, and to the resulting absorption solely in the affairs of the community, together with their estrangement from the neighbouring settlements, must be ascribed the fact that the stratum of Olęders, in contrast to the burgher stratum, produced no personality of any outstanding eminence for those times.

In order to grasp what the Olęder colonisation meant for the old Wielkopolska, we must consider it separately from the economic and separately from the political point of view. As an economic phenomenon the settlement must unquestionably be judged

 Of a different opinion was Schmidt (Geschichte, p. 422): „Der Hass Polen der gegen alles, was deutsch und michtig und wuchs sich leiden- protestantisch war, flammite empor zur schaftlichsten Verfolgungssucht aus” ["The Pole's hatred of everything that was German and Protestant flared up into the most unbounded mania of persecution"]
rusinski1947/122: favourably. On the other hand, as regards the maintenance of the security and integrity of the state, the Olęder colonisation brought no advantage. A considerable number of German settlers on the frontier lands weakened the defensive power of the old Commonwealth in the face of Prussia, created a pretext for the interference of a foreign state in the internal affairs of the country, was even adduced by the Prussian king as one of the causes of the partitions, and finally contributed to a certain degree to the cropping of Poland's borders at the moment of the rebirth of our independence. As for the cultural influence of the Olęders upon the rest of the population, it made no mark because, as has already been emphasised, the culture of the Olęders lacked the fundamental qualities needed for holding a leading position in relation to the native culture.

rusinski1947/145:
ANNEX II — Sig.: AW. Kliny Ol., pow. Poznań-Wschód, CG. 3, Jol. 46 5I. -

Charter for the leaseholders of the Kicin estate complex

Actum feria quarta post Dominicam, ramas Palmarum die scilicet 1l-ma mensis Aprilis Anno 1781. [Done on the fourth day after Palm Sunday, namely on the eleventh day of the month of April.]

The copy of the law of the village of Czerwonak, of the Czerwonak Olęders, of the Olęders on the Kliny and of those dwelling at the Hamer mill, and of the rent-payers at the Mchowo mill, written by the hand of His Worthiness the Reverend Mr Józef de Bończa Miaskowski, Provost of Poznań Cathedral; given in writing to that whole village community and confirmed with his armorial seal in red wax, of which law and of the articles expressed in it the tenor is as follows:

Yielding to the petitions of our faithful subjects paying rent in the Kicin estate complex, and in particular of the leaseholders of the village of Czerwonak, thirteen in number, likewise of the Czerwonak Olęders, eleven in number, as also of the Olęders on the Kliny, ten in number, likewise of the leaseholders at our Hamer mill, three in number, and of those rent-payers settled on our lands at the Miechowo mill, four in number — that to the former, in particular to the village of Czerwonak and to some of the Czerwonak Olęders, laws had been granted by our predecessors, that is: the Reverend Mr Paweł Łodzi Poniński, suffragan and Provost of Poznań Cathedral; likewise His Serene Highness Prince Cardinal Lipski, formerly Provost of Poznań Cathedral and later Bishop of Kraków; the Reverend Mr Wawrzyniec z Wybrarowa Świniarski, Canon of Poznań Cathedral and for that time administrator of the provost's estates; the Reverend Mr Konstanty Moszyński, Bishop of Inflanty [Livonia] and Provost of Poznań Cathedral; the Reverend Mr Józef Tadeusz z Kirska Kierski, Bishop of Boliń and suffragan, Provost of Poznań Cathedral — while to the latter, in particular to the Olęders on the Kliny at the Hamer and at the Miechowo mill, after the expiry of the years of freedom granted by the Reverend Mr Antoni Onufry z Okęcia Okęcki, then Bishop of Poznań and Chancellor of the Crown, formerly Provost of Poznań Cathedral, a share in that same

Polski, 5 10 Prace Komisji Atlasu hist. z.
rusinski1947/146:
law had been bestowed — to all whom it may concern we make known that, having before our eyes the law granted by our predecessors to some of the leaseholders of the Kicin estate complex, we have, in accordance with this, for all the others mentioned above, after measuring out their hubas, granted and written out the law.

First

Establishment of the village office and its duties. Having assembled on the feast of the Three Kings, the communities of the Kicin estate complex, in the village of Czerwonak and at the former sołtys's, are to elect from among the farmers of that village, the most long-standing rent-payers, a sołtys, whose term of office is to last for [printed: from] three years; and if he should prove remiss in anything or wanting in vigilance, and in particular should transgress this present law, and just complaints against him should come from the communities to the manor, then, with the permission received from the manor, they may proceed within the three years to the election of another sołtys. On the same feast the communities are also to elect two ławniks in that village, one from the Czerwonak Olęders, the other from the Kliny Olęders; one of them must at least know Polish and German [printed: 'po niemieckich', recte: 'po niemiecku']; and if within those three years one of these officials dies or sells up, the elder of those remaining is to summon the community at any time to elect another. The duty of these two ławniks will be to come to Czerwonak to the sołtys on every court day and then, together with the sołtys, to hear the complaints that a neighbour may have against another from whichever community, and to punish the guilty party according to the articles of the law written out below. At the same time it will also belong to this office to see to the public roads, the dams and the ditches, to give one another notice in good time of any meadow tax or dues, likewise to collect the taxes from the communities and to pay them over to whom they are due, to take the receipts for what has been paid and to keep them in the chest of the community treasury.

If, however, some new case should call them out beyond those court days — whether by order of the manor or by summons of the sołtys — the ławniks must appear at once and deal with the matter for which they have been summoned. If this village office (into which it should diligently inquire) sees that any of the rent-payers is slothful in the management of his holding or is letting his buildings go to ruin, then, after a triple [warning], it is to assess his huba and his buildings and see to finding a buyer.

Second

Establishment of the community chest.

It is to this end that people join together, so as to be of use to one another; unforeseen events reduce even the mightiest men to nothing and
rusinski1947/147:
to poverty; it is therefore the most just of things that the communities should have their own secure treasury, in which in genuine misfortune they might find help. Accordingly every one of the rent-payers, of all the communities in general, will be bound to pay without fail into the community chest, on every feast of St Wojciech, into the hands of a ławnik or of the sołtys, one grzywna, that is one złoty and fifteen copper groszes; in case of non-payment of that grzywna he will incur the penalty of paying two grzywny. This chest is to remain with the sołtys under two different locks, for which the ławniks are to have the two keys, but no one may open it without the other and without the sołtys. If, however, one of them should fall ill at the time and not be at home when the chest needs to be opened, the key is then to be entrusted to the senior farmer; and on every feast of St Wojciech, when the communities are called together, this chest is to be counted over, and it is never to be lent to anyone without the summons of at least ten farmers and without an evident [cause]; and even then for no longer than half a year, except in case of fire, for which money may be borrowed from the chest for up to three years, and after those years repaid without interest.

Penalties for offenders

If any insubordination against the authority of the manor, or of the sołtys or of the ławniks, should appear in any of the rent-payers, or he transgresses even the smallest point of this ordinance, then, once this is proven to him, he is to pay three grzywny into the community chest, that is four and a half złotys. If a neighbour does damage to a neighbour in the field or in the barn, or causes an uproar, a quarrel or plain abuse of the house, or in an inn — God forbid — a beating (this is to be understood as applying to outsiders as well), and the matter is brought before the village court, then the wrong done to the injured party is to be made good as soon as it can be assessed; as in cases of quarrels and abuse, that is three grzywny for the injured party, and the offender is to give one and a half to the chest. If on a Sunday or on a holy day ordered for public observance in the Kingdom of Poland any of the rent-payers presumes to go to town to sell or to buy, and as a Catholic fails through laziness to be found in his parish church at Kicin, he is to be fined two grzywny to the community chest. If anyone — God preserve him — is careless with fire in his house, as by carrying a burning splinter about the yard or the buildings, or using a candle without a lantern, or not keeping a chimney or ladders, or failing to sweep out the soot on a Saturday or a Friday, or drying splinters at, and yet not properly on, the household oven, he is to be fined two grzywny to the chest; and if from such an occasion a fire of any kind should break out, the injured party is to pursue the wrongdoer for damages on his estate. Should God permit an unlucky fire at any of the farmers', then anyone who is lazy about helping to save the property and does not come with water incurs a fine of three grzywny; 10
rusinski1947/148:
but whoever comes first to the rescue with water, or in any other unhappy accident comes to the aid of life or limb, is to be paid six grzywny by the community chest without delay as recompense, and the village court is to see to this most solemnly. None of the rent-payers remaining under this present law in the Kicin estate complex is to contract a debt upon his huba and buildings from anyone without first declaring it in the village court and receiving written permission from the manor; this permission he must in turn lay before the village court, and only then, if the court judges that there is genuine need of it, is it to accept it; and if the court sees that there is no just reason for contracting the debt, or that the borrower is already heavily indebted, the manorial permission is to be carried back to the manor and the reasons for non-acceptance laid before it, which the manor is to accept as just; otherwise the lender will have no claim against the debtor. Every one of the rent-payers is to take care that all his children, or at least one of them, especially the sons, can read, write and count; whoever neglects this is to pay three grzywny to the chest.

|

Any leaseholder in the Kicin estate complex who intends to sell up must first notify the village court, and it the manor; only after express permission for this has been received, and after the seller has deposited thirty złotys and the buyer the same sum, will he be free to leave his holding — but not before the seller and the buyer alike have each paid three Polish złotys into the community chest.

The dues of the leaseholders of the Kicin estate complex.

Every leaseholder (except those who may hold separate charters) of the Kicin estate complex is to pay into the lord's treasury on every feast of St Martin fifty Polish złotys, 50 zł, counting thirty copper groszes to the złoty, and two wierts of oats; the wiertel is to hold sixteen garnce of the new measure. From the other lordly dues — hens, sheep, spinning quotas, nuts, mushrooms, watch duty — they are freed for ever. Excepted from this common point applying to the other leaseholders are the three leaseholders at the Hamer, who are to pay rent, without the other lordly dues and even without oats, sixty-six Polish złotys. Every one of the leaseholders of the Kicin estate complex, unless he sits under a separate charter, is to go out ploughing three times a year, that is for the root crops, for the fallow and for the winter sowing, and on each occasion he is to plough eight rods, i.e. 8; the rod is to hold seven and a half ells of the new measure. They are also to do nine days' hand labour, that is three in the garden, three with the sickle and three with the scythe. From all the other labour dues, such as the carting of manure from the provost's curia and the carting of wood there, they are freed; in return they are to receive each year six sądki [small casks] of beer of the new measure — three at Czerwonak with their Olęders, two at Kliny, one at the Hamer and the Janikowo Olęders.
rusinski1947/149:
The carting of grain, over a distance of at most six miles, they are to perform once a year; provided, however, that no more than four korcy of the new measure, that is eight wierts, may ever be loaded on to one waggon. If the manor has no need of this, then instead of the cartage over six miles he is to do a day's ploughing and break up and plough eight rods. Each of the leaseholders is to perform one road cartage of at most six miles, and if this is not needed, he is to go out ploughing for one day, eight rods. The Czerwonak Olęders are freed from the grain cartage and from the rod-ploughing of the cartage duty; in return they are to go out ploughing two days a year, eight rods each. For the brewing of beer at the Kicin brewhouse they are to take turns, prepare and cart the wood for it, and carry out the malt and bring it back. All manner of help in building — that is, in bringing timber, stone, brick, lime, clay and sand, in raising buildings and in daubing — they owe in turn. Church dues, as well as taxes and instalments of whatever kind, now or in future, each is to hand over to the sołtys, and he is to deliver them where they are due.

They are to keep the ditches (so that the water has its fall), the dams by the mills and the public roads in the best possible condition and repair them when called upon to do so by the sołtys. As to the laying waste of the Kicin forests, they shall not only not cut there themselves (apart from on their own morgs), but the seizure of what they detect being felled shall be their duty.

So that everyone may know and understand all this, when the community has assembled twice a year at the village court, that is on St Martin's day and on St Wojciech's day, at the sołtys's at Czerwonak, it is to be read out aloud and freely.

Since it is the honour of our leaseholders of the Kicin estate complex that is at stake, the last point concerns theft, namely that if there should appear the least sign not only of actual theft but of complicity with a thief, such a person, as an enemy of the common good, is to be expelled without delay; his estate having been sold, the injured party is to be compensated as the case shows, ten grzywny are to be paid into the community chest, and the remainder given to the culprit.

So that these our present provisions may carry the greater weight, we append them with our own hand together with the impression of the seal. Given at Kicin on the second day of February of the year one thousand seven hundred and eighty-one.

Józef Bończa Miaskowski, Provost of Poznań Cathedral, mpp.

I certify the corrections made above, so that they may not fall under any suspicion that they were made by my own hand. Datum ut supra [as above].

Miaskowski Kat. Poznański mpp.

rusinski1947/151:
ANNEX III

Wilkierz for the Kotusz Olęders. Sig.: Kotusz A. 1 (spelling corrected).

[fol. 5] The laws of Kotusz, from the lords.

Given [1] and confirmed to the Olęders. I give notice and make known to each and every one, and to whomever it is needful to know this: whereas I have sold my hereditary lands named Kotusz to good honest people, and to their children and descendants, for a sum, and have set them the said lands at a fixed yearly rent, yet these inhabitants live without order and without obedience to the laws; therefore, so that in the times to come there may be among them order, justice, peace, concord and obedience, I have judged it well to give and appoint to them the law and articles, fines and penalties described below, which both parties alike are bound to keep and observe as strictly as possible on pain of their own penalty. For the sake of better order the neighbours shall come together and elect for themselves a sołtys and ławniks for the year, and whomsoever they choose I shall always confirm. They are to be such persons from the community as will look after the good of the whole village and of their common property; they are also to judge and settle whatever disputes may arise, according to this law and my direction, strictly to uphold it, to collect and take the fines from anyone who offends against this law, and to render an account of them to the neighbours. I order that the said fines be paid into the official chest, which chest is to be kept at the sołtys's. The ławniks are to have a key to this chest. They are not to spend the fine money on gatherings of any kind, but are to apply the fine money to the good order and benefit of the village, as for instance the dams, the ditches, the causeways and whatever may be useful to the community; this is to be done with the knowledge of the neighbours and of the whole community. The laws and articles set out below are to be read to the whole community twice each year, so that no one can excuse himself out of ignorance when he offends against the law. These are the articles:

1. Whenever the sołtys commands or forbids anything, they are to obey.

If anyone, however, stays at home and does not carry out the obedience owed to his sołtys, he is to be fined five groszes.
rusinski1947/152:
2. If a neighbour addresses the sołtys or his ławniks in discourteous or abusive words, or threatens them with a weapon, and when he comes to court refuses to listen, he is to be fined two good grzywny without any [exception]. If he then behaves worse still, or threatens blows, he is to be sentenced by their judgement to a heavier penalty.

3. But if anyone boldly and violently attacks the sołtys or his ławniks, and having given rein to his anger [fol. 6] refuses to obey, or will not submit, then whoever beats or wounds him in that event, by day or by night, goes free and incurs no penalty, nor is any court needed.

4. Whoever is sent by the sołtys on official business, and anyone presumes to abuse or beat him, shall be fined two good grzywny.

5. When the sołtys holds court with the ławniks, no woman is to be present, unless she herself has some complaint of her own, or her husband is not at home. Otherwise a woman who offends in this is to pay a fine of five groszes.

6. I permit that each year they are to pay the sołtys thirty groszes from every huba for his trouble and toil, and his ławniks fifteen groszes each year. Whoever opposes this is to be punished in duplo [twice over].

7. If the sołtys and the ławniks make any journey on the community's business and for the good of their estate, the costs are to be taken from the hubas according to the account.

8. The sołtys and the ławniks are to watch carefully over the good of the whole village and community, to take care of the fences, dams, ditches and sluices, and wherever harm might come to the community, to block, repair and put it right. If the sołtys and the ławniks are negligent in this, they are to be punished at the discretion of the whole community.

9. When there is any purchase of grain or of cattle, and a sealing drink (litkup) has already been drunk at the purchase, the party who does not keep the bargain is to give a barrel of beer as a penalty.

10. God forbid that a building should catch fire and burn down through a thunderbolt or through the doing of wicked men; the neighbours are then to help him out of Christian charity — each huba contributing, at 100 grzywny, the 15th grosz, according to the assessment of the damage — and they are to help him with timber, reed and carting.

slowinski2023/7:
Introduction

In October 2020 there came into my hands a very well-preserved collection of letters by a Wehrmacht soldier, discovered in the wall during the renovation of the former house of the cantor Gustav Mielke at Łazińsk. The successive letters, as they were translated, proved to be increasingly fascinating reading – a source of precious information, conveyed from the position of a private soldier, about little-known events and fighting on the northern wing of the Eastern Front and about the everyday life of the soldier's family in the Kraj Warty. This brief introduction should help to situate this extraordinary story in place and time.

◼

In the year 1718, fourteen German families arrive from Silesia in eastern Wielkopolska, in the vicinity of the town of Zagórów situated on the southern slope of the Warta river valley; the lord of the manor of nearby Trąbczyn leases them in perpetuity forest lands and fallows, where in time a village comes into being by the name of Łazińsk. Thus begins the history of the German settlers on this small land. Apparently the first experiences proved positive, for in 1746 the owners of the estates in Trąbczyn, Katarzyna and Paweł Prusińscy, designate places for further settlements. The newcomers take possession of the leased land under Olęder law (prawo olęderskie). They are Evangelicals (Lutherans), free people, with their own self-government, a cult of work and strict customs. It may be of interest that in the last of the villages located
slowinski2023/8:
by the heirs of Trąbczyn there was also a group of Polish peasants – Catholics.

In the years 1746–1789 the heirs of neighbouring Łukomie likewise mark out new locations. The population of these villages was in its great majority of German origin. The name Olędrzy, used for a long time in the Zagórów region, was not connected with the nationality of the settlers, but with the law on the basis of which the villages were located and relations with the landowners were regulated. This law was brought into the Rzeczpospolita [the Polish Commonwealth] by Mennonites arriving from the Netherlands, who were fleeing their own homeland from persecution. The Warsaw Confederation, adopted by the Polish Sejm in January 1573, was an important act which secured for the nobility freedom of worship and guaranteed peace between religious dissenters. It was a legal guarantee of religious tolerance. The Mennonites were not a numerous group that had reached the Vistula and the Żuławy, but the law proved very useful in organizing the settlement drive and was applied for a long time – until the mid-nineteenth century. Zbigniew Chodyła, a meritorious researcher and expert on Olęder settlement, assesses that the Dutch and their descendants among the settlers located under Olęder law constituted merely about one per cent of the population. The rest were in their great majority Germans – Evangelicals, and also Poles – Catholics and Protestants. According to the research of the aforementioned Zbigniew Chodyła, in the whole of Wielkopolska, from 1721 to the years 1793/1795, 637 settlements were founded, of which in the Kalisz voivodeship – to which Zagórów belonged – 228.

Peasants arriving from Prussia in the vicinity of Zagórów settle in the surrounding villages, which form a kind of ring around the town. The village of Łazińsk was the oldest and largest settlement inhabited by the German-speaking population. After the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Zagórów and the surrounding lands found

slowinski2023/9:
themselves within the Kingdom of Poland subordinated to the Tsar of Russia. The settling Germans, as well as the Jews, lived for long years in the world of their own language (Yiddish and German) as well as of their religion. These were communities with their own self-government, deep autonomy and distinctness of confession. Such was the case above all in the times of the first Rzeczpospolita. The partitioning powers regulated the social order according to their own injunctions and statutes – yet the cultural distinctness and the special legal status remained.

Contacts between Poles, Jews and Germans until the mid-nineteenth century were almost exclusively of a commercial, economic character. Also in later years it is practically impossible to note (apart from entirely incidental cases) mixed marriages: Polish–Jewish, Polish–German or Jewish–German. Nor are there cases of conversion. Russian rule lasted over a hundred years, but in none of the communities: the Polish, the Jewish or the German, are there testimonies of conversion to the faith of the rulers – Orthodoxy.

What was for the Jews and the Germans – and did it mean anything at all – the idea of a free Poland, nurtured through generations? Both German and Jewish children underwent a short education tied strictly to the religion they professed. For the German Evangelicals it was the Bible, for the Jewish children the Talmud. Mastery of the basic skills of reading and writing, of arithmetic, and knowledge of the holy books formed the foundations of this education. Setting aside the harsh regime of the partitioners' law, from the sources mentioned, even from their own teachers they could not obtain basic knowledge of the history of the country in which they lived.

When independence was regained in 1918, wealthy Jewish and German families, as well as Protestant clergymen coming from the Reich, began to leave Poznań and Wielkopolska en masse for Germany. Throughout the century the Jewish and Evangelical communities had been subordinate to the Tsarist administration. The experiences of ancestors who had crossed the borders of the plundered and disrespected noble Rzeczpospolita no one
slowinski2023/10:
remembered, nor particularly cherished. They functioned within the closed circles of their communities. The German settlers, bound strongly by language and religion, literally hewed out or dug out their place on this land in the forests near Zagórów and on the Warta meadows. When they departed for Prussia, most considered that they were going on a visit. Their homeland was this scrap of earth into which their sweat and tears had soaked.

The German Reich, however, consistently conducts aggressive agitation not only through the state administration. Strong pressure is exerted on the clergy of the Protestant Church. This is the implementation of the idea of Mitteleurope, built for half a century – the subordination, or indeed the subjugation, of Central-Eastern Europe by Germany, the germanization and reduction to the role of slaves of the Slavs and of other nations regarded as lower in cultural and civilizational development. The Konin police report to their superiors that among the national minorities the attitude towards the new state is indifferent or neutral. Only the German Hakata activists and the Jewish Bundists treat the Polish administration with decided hostility. Regardless of nationality or denomination, all 

 Bundowcy – members of the General Jewish Labour Union in Poland, Russia, Lithuania (Bund – the party operated in the years 1897-1948). They regarded the Jews as a separate nation; they strove to create secular schooling and to develop culture in the Yiddish language, which was to strengthen their autonomy. They took part in various formations of the international movement of socialists and social democrats. They criticized the Bolshevik government of the USSR and at the same time urged cooperation with it. In interwar Poland they were a significant and well-organized party. They were opponents of the Zionists and of the religious Agudas Israel movement. Representatives of both these currents were present in Zagórów.

 Hakata – the Association of the Eastern Marches (1894-1934), operating under Bismarck's patronage, regarded as its main goal the Germanization of the Polish lands under the Prussian partition. The Hakatists had the means and a programme for driving Poles out of their land by every method. They strove to eliminate the Polish press and publishing houses, to buy up land from Poles, to bring Germans to Wielkopolska, to develop German schooling. They initiated anti-Polish directives of the authorities. Their organ was the journal "Die Ostmark". After

The problem of national identity, the attempts to define oneself in relation to the new state, were not easy topics. Among the documents discovered in the wall of the cantor's house at Łazińsk there is a letter from Gustav Tonn, a teacher from Płatkownica, to Bruno Mielke, which also reveals the deeper reflection that accompanied some of the German settlers over their fate in the Polish state. These few sentences form a synthetic and vivid illustration of the problems with which they struggled. From the letter it can be inferred that Bruno was rejected by the education authorities, or else was refused the right to teach. Thus Tonn writes to him: "And yet, dear Bruno! Do not be too candid; get to know the man before you undertake anything. Also do not make too much of a show of your Germanness. In order to obtain a piece of bread and keep yourself, one must keep much to oneself. You need not disown anything, but neither should you profess anything. And if Poland is to be our homeland – and it is – then we must also be patriotically disposed towards Poland. In the times of Russian rule I worked for Russia, and now I do it even more willingly for Poland. [Be therefore prudent as serpents, and harmless as doves]. But only do not give up; talk with the inspector and perhaps it will be better. The Lord will assist and help to turn this injustice away from you. […] I, when I came from Russia, was also slandered as a great friend of the Germans, but God sent me a faithful soul who supported me, and everything turned out for the best. Now I hope that my direct school superior is satisfied with me". (Letter of 15 July

HaKaTa – is an abbreviation of the surnames of the founders of the organization (Ferdinand von Hansemann, Hermann Kennemann, Henryk von Tiedemann).

In the letters written in the language of persons well-read not only in the books of the Bible one can find positions of the authors that are well and clearly articulated. Fluent use of the pen was for these inhabitants of Łazińsk an everyday occupation, done with zeal or sometimes even with passion.

Among the numerous threads and information touched upon in the correspondence of the war years, one topic does not exist. In Zagórów, from September to 15 November 1941, the liquidation of the ghetto was carried out. The deported Jews were brutally murdered in the forests near Kazimierz Biskupi. One may get the impression as if the thousand Jews, neighbours for two hundred years, had never been here at all.

Successive generations of Poles, Jews and Germans created that community which, regardless of periodic tensions and collapses, slowly opened up to "strangers" and increasingly often was able to communicate, to build together – the best proof of which was the survival and the wise management of the Zagórów community in the times of the severe crisis of the 1930s. The cataclysm of the Second World War brutally destroyed that world. The war, its fatal consequences and the inexorably flowing time caused this old, yet close-to-us history to be slowly obscured by a "cloud of oblivion".

In the years past there have already appeared many documents, including books, on the history of the inhabitants of the Zagórów land – Poles and Jews. Apart from a few small studies, very little is known about the community of the German settlers, the Evangelicals, and about their history. It is extremely difficult to reach the accounts and documents from the lives of these people. The hard laws

◼

When we browse the pages of the internet records, we in fact have insight only into the times of the Second World War. The scholarly literature is exceptionally modest. I therefore thought that we would never come closer to sketching a fuller picture of the history of the town and of this land if we did not try to learn something more about those who lived here over two hundred years ago and whose traces time is erasing. Despite the whole tragic period of the years 1939–1945, one must remember that this is only a part of the history of this land and of many of its inhabitants, which one should attempt to tell. More persons shared this thinking of mine. In September 2020 an editorial committee came into being and work began on the preparation of a publication about the Evangelicals of the Zagórów land.

In the course of gathering materials for the book there came into my hands an extraordinary collection of letters and books discovered in the wall of the house of the cantor Gustav Mielke at Łazińsk. With the support of a numerous group of translators of German, with a leading share by Jacek Kin, it proved possible to decipher these hand-written documents. This is chiefly the correspondence of Bruno Mielke, a Wehrmacht soldier fighting in the northern sector of the Eastern Front (Eismeerfront), addressed to his brother Gustav, to his father and to his sisters. After the reading of the letters a study came into being which will be placed in the book being prepared for print. I decided nevertheless that the preserved collection of letters and the contents it holds should interest historians and become the subject of a somewhat broader and deeper analysis. Making use of a kind permission, I sent

The German settlers located under Olęder law in the villages and forest settlements surrounding the town of Zagórów constituted a closed community which, despite two hundred years of settlement on these lands, was not susceptible to assimilation. A strong and probably decisive binding agent was the Lutheran religion and the German language. All were free people, whose relations with the landowners, who leased out for use grounds of meagre quality, were regulated by separate laws, customs and self-government. Such was the case in the eighteenth-century Rzeczpospolita, under the partitions and in the reborn Poland. As one of the inhabitants of those days in Zagórów recalls – Professor of the Poznań university Lech Słowiński: "In many villages right up to the year 1939 one heard only the German language. It must nevertheless be admitted that until that time the coexistence between the Polish and the German population was on the whole correct".

The largest settlement in this ring of homesteads was Łazińsk – situated eight kilometres to the south of Zagórów. To this day it is a place that perfectly illustrates the manner of organizing, under Olęder law, the space entrusted to the settlers: the location of the farmsteads, the building of roads and of drainage

 Lech Słowiński – born in Zagórów on 23. 09. 1922 – died on 29.07.2005 in Poznań. Professor of Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań. I publish the memoirs thanks to the kind consent of the closest Family. The typescript is kept in a home archive.

canals. Already in 1839 the first brick building stood here, in which the cantor resided and school lessons were conducted. A hundred years later, by the effort of the whole community of Łazińsk, whose works from 1925 were directed by the cantor Gustav Adolf Mielke, a new building was erected, housing the classrooms, the office, and the dwelling of the headmaster and cantor in one person. Yet Gustav Mielke's engagement did not concern only educational matters and religious duties. He was an exceedingly active propagator of the German nationalists and of Nazi propaganda. This activity must have – even for such a multicultural region – aroused significant reservations on the part of the authorities, for Mielke was forced to leave Łazińsk in 1936 and to settle somewhere in Galicia. He returned together with the Wehrmacht in 1939. Throughout the whole war the school was housed in this building, sizable by village standards, along with a cantorate greatly curtailed in its rights, and the Mielke family lived there.

One must, however, also note further sentences from the reminiscences quoted above. "The aggressiveness of the local Germans towards the Poles and towards the third nation, settled in great numbers since old times in Zagórów – the Jews – will reveal itself only with unprecedented cruelty in the period of the Hitlerite occupation". The entry of the Russians on 18 January 1945 and the rebuilding of the Polish administration put an end to the long history of this cantorate. All the householders in April of that year were expropriated. Eugenia Plitt, an inhabitant of Łazińsk, remembered that at the beginning it was said that this was a temporary measure… Years passed, and the old German school and the cantor's house was adapted into a residential building for teachers. Four flats were carved out. In the year 1993 the allocation of one of the premises was received by the married couple Dorota and Bogdan Karaszewscy. It was also the time in which cars with German

slowinski2023/21:
registration plates began to appear at Łazińsk and on the nearby Kopczyk, and their passengers tried to document the former homesteads. Not all the locals liked these visits. Some even called the police, so that it would identify the newcomers and question them as to what purpose their walks around the surrounding farmsteads served.

Bogdan Karaszewski decided with his wife that the flat allocated to them required a considerable renovation. Possessing numerous skills that come in handy in such work, in 1995 he set about the job. The scope of these works must have been serious, since even the interior doors qualified for replacement. Removing a door together with its door frame – in such a way that the ceiling does not fall on one's head – requires a certain experience. The operation succeeded, and the extracted, rotted-through door frame revealed an unexpected sight. It turned out that this partition between rooms, which everyone had considered a single, monolithic wall, had been built of two walls, between which there is a considerable space. When the dust had settled, there appeared before Bogdan Karaszewski a sizable pile of papers sealed up tightly. Someone had secured them in an extraordinarily careful manner and hidden them cleverly. The first package extracted contained many letters bearing the postmarks of the Wehrmacht field post as well as a Book of Baptisms (Księga chrztów). Further down lay wrapped-up coverings of church altars and carpentry tools. When the find had been taken out, from the narrow crevice, into the empty space, books began to slide down from above… This extraordinary collection of books "descending" downwards was opened by a biography of Joseph Goebbels. In all, thirty-one volumes came into Karaszewski's hands. Apart from three gnawed at and damaged, probably by mice, the majority of the books survived in good condition, with the mark of time visible on the covers or on some of the pages.

In his free moments, the finder tried to interest various people and institutions in the materials he had discovered, but without much success. One must view with great respect the way Bogdan Karaszewski handled what he had extracted from the wall. Everything was packed
slowinski2023/22:
into a cardboard box and placed in a safe location. In this way nearly 25 years passed. In the meantime, the family changed apartments. An announcement posted on the internet seeking materials for writing the history of the Zagórów Lutherans, former settlers from Germany, did not escape Karaszewski's attention. On some October day in 2020 he walked into the Zagórów Community Center and, into the hands of its director Łukasz Parus, handed over the entire collection, untouched by the years.

It is the end of the year 1944. As the east wind blows, one can hear the approaching front, the sounds of artillery salvos. Despite the assurances coming from Berlin radio, it was known that the entry of the Russians was a matter of weeks. We do not know which members of the Mielke family were in the house at that time (from various indirect information one may surmise that it was one of the older sisters, Leokadia). Preparing the hiding place in the crevice between the walls required time, technical skills, and ingenuity. The cache would surely never have been discovered had it not been for the decision to replace the doors. Most likely, the items being hidden were lowered in from above, from the attic, and then the entire crevice was carefully sealed up.

The packed collection contained, in its excellent part, letters from the front from the younger son of Julius Samuel Mielke – Bruno. But there were also letters and cards written by the father, the brother Gustav, the sisters Leokadia (Kadzia), Anni, and Olga to Bruno. Besides this, there were many loose letters, postcards, and documents from the years 1936–1939, such as, for example, a permit from the Konin starosta dated September 26, 1939 (!) for Gustav Adolf Mielke to move freely around the Konin county. He was also permitted to use a bicycle. From later reading one can infer that the siblings exchanged photographs, including those from the front. None of the mentioned photographs was in the hiding place. More interesting is the question of how, among these documents, there came to be letters from the father and siblings sent to the eastern front? Did Bruno leave them in Łazińsk while on leave? The surviving Book of Baptisms (Taufe) in Łazińsk

covers the period from 1912 to 1918. It was kept by the cantor of the time, E. Cellmer.

The collection of books that an effort was made to preserve can be helpful in describing the family that lived in the cantor's house. The very titles say a great deal. Biograpfie Joseph Goebbels by Wilfrid Bade, Lübeck 1938, Die Nationalversammlung von Potsdam. Deutschlands große Tage. 21 bis 23 März 1933 by Hans Wendt, Berlin 1933 [The National Assembly in Potsdam. Germany's Great Days], Deutsche Geschichte im 19. Jahrhundert by Heinrich von Treitschke with an introduction by Alfred Rosenberg, Safari – Berlin 1937 [History of Germany in the 19th Century], Der deutsche Aubruch 9.11.1918 bis 18.3.1938 by Walther Gehl [The German Awakening], Deutsche Haltung vor Fremden by Bruno Behm, Graz 1943 [The German Attitude Toward Foreigners].

A few words about these titles and their authors. Deutschlands große Tage is a little book describing the assembly convened after the elections, which took place on March 21, 1933, in the garrison church in Potsdam, during which Adolf Hitler was entrusted with forming a government. Earlier, on March 15, the victorious leader of the NSDAP announced the founding of the Third Reich and stripped his political opponents of their parliamentary mandates. Walther Gehl (1897–1942), one of the authors of books militant in pen and weapon, simultaneously works "on the spiritual development of the Wehrmacht." He is the author, among others, of Der nazionalsozialistische Staat (1933) and of many history textbooks for secondary school students. He died in June 1942 on the eastern front. Bruno Behm (1892–1974), in turn, is an Austrian writer of very rich biography who came from the far right. He made a name for himself with the statement that "If Jews complain about their fate to the whole world, they must be told that they brought this fate upon themselves." Yet in genre terms, the heaviest volume is the book Deutsche Geschichte im 19. Jahrhundert by Heinrich von Treitschke (1834–1896), the author of the well-known 1879 essay that provoked a broad anti-Semitic response. It is in this text that the sentence appears: "Die Juden sind unser Unglück" [The Jews are our
slowinski2023/24:
misfortune]. The Nazis editing "Der Stürmer" adopted this sentence as the motto of the paper and… of their actions. The deceased author, however, had no influence on whom the publishing house would invite to write the introduction to a new edition. It was Alfred Rosenberg, the creator of a criminal ideology, whose Der Mythus des 20 Jahrhunderts [The Myth of the Twentieth Century], alongside Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf, played a decisive role in formatting German minds in the spirit of the racial superiority of the nation of masters, for whom an appropriate living space is to be conquered. (By 1944, a million copies had been sold).

The little library also contained books about important historical figures, a selection which – I believe – was not accidental. There is the well-known study by the outstanding Belgian classical philologist Joseph Bidez, Julian der Abtrünnige, Munich 1940. Julian the Apostate is the emperor who strove to abolish Christianity and restore the old Roman religious cults. It would be hard to find a clearer analogy to the Nazi idea of Germania. The collection includes a work by Leopold von Ranke, Geschichte Wallensteins. The history of the outstanding commander from the times of the Thirty Years' War. There is also a history of the King of Prussia, Frederick William IV. In the household sewn into the forest, distant from large cities and main routes, there is the popular novel by Wilhelm Raabe, Die Chronik der Sperlingsgasse, 1857 [The Chronicle of Sparrow Lane]. It is the story of a small-town loser who in his eccentricity is able to preserve his own personality, allowing him to cope with an aggressive reality. This "hero of a gray life" brings valuable humanistic ideals into the cold, capitalist society….

Among the books there are, of course, titles such as the Holy Scripture of the Old and New Testament (Die Bibel oder die ganze Heilige Schrift des Alten und Neuen Testaments, Vienna 1886).

The Bible – in keeping with tradition – was a wedding gift for Samuel Julius Mielke and Natalie Tonn in the year 1892. The volume contains, before the title page, pages for keeping a family chronicle with handwritten entries by the recipients, which I write about further on. Among the books there are two collections of sermons, Rozważania na każdy dzień roku [Reflections for Every Day of the Year], a New Testament in a pocket edition, and other mystical, religious works. There are guides to married and sexual life (Liebe und Ehe. Ein Buch Für Eheleute or Das Liebes und Geschlechtsleben des Menschen) as well as songbooks for festive occasions. There is also Schlag nach über England – a guide to England and the British Empire for a mere 50 pfennigs… It is difficult to enumerate all these titles in detail.

It is worth returning once more to the political part of the library collection and devoting a few words to Goebbels's biographer. Wilfrid Alfred Karl Bade (born 1906) belonged to the very active figures in Nazi propaganda. He rose to the position of government counsel in the Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda of the Third Reich. He was one of the leading lecturers and "creative interpreters" of the thought and ideas of the führer and his superior Goebbels. Besides the biography of Goebbels first published in 1933, he also produced such works as: Die SA erobert Berlin [The SA Conquers Berlin], Geschichte des Dritten Reich 4 Bünde [History of the Third Reich in 4 Volumes], Das Hohelied vom Dritten Reich [The Song of Songs of the Third Reich], or Tod Und Leben. Verse des Krieges [Death and Life. Verses of the War]. Bade died in December 1945 in Russian captivity in Kaunas. Yet more important than the author of the biography is its subject – Paul Joseph Goebbels himself. The doctorate in Germanic philology, which he received at the University of Heidelberg in 1922 for a dissertation on the work of the Romantic-era writer Wilhelm von Schütz, was the academic confirmation of the intellectual fitness of the future minister 

 We publish the inventory of the cache in the wall of the cantor's house in the Appendix on p. 99.
slowinski2023/26:
of propaganda. His fanatical service to the führer (whom he "loved for his genius"), his undeniable oratorical talent, and his political path to the heights of power had to make a very strong impression on these "well-read" inhabitants of the cantor's house in Łazińsk.

If someone who is preparing for flight cares about his little library, it must have meant something to this family! Why did this hiding place come into being at all?! Was it out of fear that the collection of front letters of the son and brother would fall into the hands of soldiers, thereby giving a pretext for a harsh reckoning with the family? Was the Goebbels biography put into the hiding place for the same reason, along with other books that the household members considered important, because they constituted their national-socialist ideological identity? Were the remaining volumes hidden out of fear that the Russians or Poles would burn them – just as the works condemned by that same Goebbels were burned? In one of the memoirs we read that the farmers being resettled in April were told that this was a temporary operation. The question is, who was saying this: representatives of the new administration or local Nazi leaders, who believed in the führer's wonder weapon? If documents important to the family are left in a home being forcibly abandoned, then presumably somewhere at the bottom of the soul a little flame of hope burns that perhaps this is only a painful moment, that soon we will return to the family nest and to the land that sustained us for decades. But – and this question also arises – does protecting the writings of Rosenberg, Goebbels, or other authors like them not show that the terrible defeat which the resettlers and all of Germany are experiencing has taught them nothing? Are they unable, or do they not want, to abandon the idea of "their" great Third Reich?

many of his surviving letters – including those from the front – was for Bruno to take up studies at the Evangelical-Theological Faculty of the University of Vienna. Worrying whether he would manage with the demanding studies, he describes his preparation as follows: "I have an education as a teacher (also in music), but unfortunately I do not know any foreign language (apart from Polish, which I have mastered well orally and in writing). But it seems one cannot do without Greek and Latin […] As for ability, I am admittedly not a genius, however – as the former director wrote on my certificate – I am diligent, because I, despite the lack of prior preparation (the director's assessment), with God's help did not have to repeat any subject. I am already 29 years old, I am still a bachelor, but I have a youthful appearance and disposition (this is how I am often assessed)".

But the day of June 22, 1941, came. Hitler opens a new front. He attacks his recent "ally" – the USSR. A letter dated June 26, 1941, to Bruno's sister Flora from the Lehmann family of Dresden has survived. They thank her for the package with sausage and other food items. They report at the same time that the nearest meeting of the Women's League "wants to thank our dear führer for the fact that he attacked at the right time, because it is enough to think about what would have happened if it had been otherwise. Right at the beginning the Russian hordes would have flooded over you, and in the past week we thought of Łazińsk very often". That the Russians might appear in Dresden was ruled out from the start.

No one yet knows what terrible consequences Hitler's decision will bring. Bruno Mielke begins to realize that this war may freeze his plans and dreams for a long time. In a letter dated July 8, 1941, he informs his sisters Kadzia and Flora that he is cramming Latin "for Vienna." He holds to his intention, even if in August or later he goes into the Wehrmacht. The one to blame for his not being able to become a teacher is "the Antichrist". From his sisters he also learned that
slowinski2023/29:
his colleague Rentz had fallen in battle. Again tears and suffering. He will remember him fondly also because he received a keepsake from him – a photograph of the führer.

In a letter to the dean of the Evangelical-Theological Faculty of the University of Vienna he writes: "Dear Mr. Dean! The time of the autumn semester will soon come. I would gladly begin my studies this autumn (for my intention of coming to Vienna has become a certainty). But unfortunately the Wehrmacht and the war will most likely call me away. For the time being I have not yet been called up, but I recently received a summons to be on standby, so that I expect the order to report any day now. As soon as I am released from military service after the end of the war, I will want – if God preserves me in life and health – to lay down my office and come to Vienna. If, according to God's will, I were to fall in the war, then my brother will inform you of it". This letter, dated October 10, 1941, was written by Bruno Mielke in Konary, in the Grodziec commune, where he worked as a teacher. Earlier, from the year 1940, a document has survived signed by him as a teacher and lower school commissioner in Maślaki, in the Wilczyn commune. It is a letter to the Konin starosta documenting the need to build new school buildings in Maślaki and Lipnica. The inhabitants – I quote: "led by the village headman, consider it obvious to build a new school worthy of the New Germany and are ready to help financially".

It may be worth mentioning here that both Maślaki and Konary were, from the end of the 18th century, localities that came into being as a result of agreements made by the local Polish manor owners with German settlers of the Protestant faith. Over more than a hundred years these localities became important regional centers of the Evangelical community – of mainly German origin, but also of Polish followers of Luther (the German element predominated). Earlier, Bruno Mielke for five years helped
slowinski2023/30:
Alexander Gross, the parish priest of the Evangelical-Augsburg parish in Zagórów, and worked as a teacher and cantor in nearby Anielewo. The last months of 1941 were a time of growing expectation of being called up into the army and departing for the front. In one of the cards we find this entry: "I would like to get all my visits done as much as possible right now, because from August I must be on my guard: at that time I may be called up to the Wehrmacht at any moment, for only until 31.7.41 am I recognized as 'indispensable'. In fact I am glad that in this great time I will take part in the fight. I had already wanted to volunteer".

Bruno tries to put some of his affairs in order and writes an application for leave so that he can travel to Konin and visit Łazińsk. In the letter of October 10 he shares with his brother Gustav the information he obtained during some course at an NSDAP school in Będlewo near Stęszew. Namely, an official subordinate to the Reich Governor laid out at length before the course participants visions of allocating land to rural schools, in this way encouraging teachers to settle in the countryside. Bruno Mielke considers that "it is obvious that in the Warthegau proper schools must be built and that the land must not be spared after the war with Russia". And here follows a longer disquisition on the advantages of such a solution in opposition to taking over complete farms, which will be subject to considerably stricter regulations and production obligations (the future school land will, in this respect, have more freedoms). Foreign (read: Polish) farmhands cause the farmers particularly many troubles. Hence he urgently urges his brother to take a prompt interest in the possibility of obtaining such a grant – preferably close to Zagórów or Konin. He writes that Polish owners were there, after all. "I hope that not everything has yet been divided up". In the whole of it – one of the longest letters – there is not a crumb of reflection that he is urging his brother to take part in the plunder of land and houses from those who for years had been their neighbors. Mielke is undoubtedly
slowinski2023/31:
a religious man. Yet one may get the impression that in relations with Poles some of the Ten Commandments had been suspended.

The autumn months of 1941 were a terrible time in this land. From September to November, the liquidation of the Zagórów ghetto lasted. Jews were transported in trucks to the forests near Kazimierz Biskupi (the Wygoda area), in which they were suffocated with exhaust fumes. Those who were brought in alive were shot and thrown into pits with lime. Letters from this period are few, and they are the last before Bruno Mielke's enlistment into the Wehrmacht. Whether there were more of them, and if so, what became of them, we do not know. In any case, of the tragedy taking place in those days in Zagórów we find not the slightest mention.
