> I will praise the Lord as long as I live 
> (Ps 146,2)

The first of the surviving letters from the period of service in the Wehrmacht was written in Vienna on March 30, 1942. Called up to the army, he sets off with other recruits on a long journey. First Chodzież, then Kutno, Poznań, and onward to Wrocław. From there, after eight hours, "we arrived safely in Vienna – the city of my dreams. […] Our final destination, where we will be trained, is Klagenfurt, located about 15 km from the border with Italy, in the south of Austria. It will surely be beautiful there in the Alps; it already was during the journey. Service in the mountains can be exhausting, for we are assigned to the Gebirgsjäger [mountain riflemen] unit. Everything was settled; choice did not come into it at all, besides, every thing and group has its good and bad (hard) sides. It is best to accept what has been given; one does not have to have any reproaches later". In the margin we read an addition: "We finally arrived. Everything is very beautiful and orderly. I feel as if in the boarding house of some seminary. The officers are kind. We get everything". He had taken so many things unnecessarily. And further: "And now my comrades. Most of them are ethnic Germans (without citizenship) and Bessarabians, some are also Germans with citizenship. The majority are weak, some are quite hopeless, and among them there are persons who exploit others. If they can manage, then I certainly can. The fact that among them there are persons who exploit others is not consoling, for as is known the whole group suffers because of it".
slowinski2023/33:
Gustav wrote a long letter to his training brother on May 1. "During all my work one thought now wearies me – it appears since you are far away. Such a will to work as I had when you were still here I no longer have. During lessons you appear every so often in my thoughts. And when the break comes and when I look through the window – then too I see you. You were always nearby, and now you are suddenly so far away – to this is added the worry of where you will be in a few weeks. […] Apart from you I have no one. I have no friends at all; our girls need support themselves, and father… you know after all – he sleeps and eats, and reads all the time. But he is doing well. Without you I am rather lonely and would best like to leave here as well – to where you are and where you expose yourself to dangers". If only he got leave, he would set off to Klagenfurt immediately.

At present he is feverishly occupied with putting affairs in order. A few days earlier they (the cohorts from 1899 to 1895) received a summons to register for the duty of defense. "So we were at the Municipal Office on April 28 and registered. I, Mundt, Grunwald Heinrich, Schmechel, Stolp, and many others. This means that we too may be called up to the army in the coming days". In the closing sentences he writes that he does not understand those people who are "happy" when they try to take away our faith. "I am a Christian and in recent days I have been made to feel it again and again". He could not bear it if some young one tried to arouse disgust or harass them – and misfortune would happen. "I know – you are able to digest something like that. But one cannot tolerate it for too long". (This fragment is precisely the openly signaled contemptuous, even aggressive attitude of adherents of the Nazi ideology toward Evangelicals, Christians faithful to the Church in general).

After the account of the farm work and Stelter's neighbourly help, Gustav announces to his brother that this year he has decided to marry. But there is one problem: "that Stell behaved
slowinski2023/34:
earlier as if she did not want to – but now she is doing everything in that direction. But I cannot decide on her, because I think she is the kind of person through whom discord might arise among my remaining siblings, and I do not want that at any price. Another one will yet be found. I would most like one who comes with a farm. What grieves me most is that you had to become a soldier and are not yet married." He is also very grateful that Bruno wrote a letter to Kadzia. She is at once different after she has read the letter. I tried to tell her this – but with words one cannot always achieve what one would like. Nor was it simple and pleasant. What the brothers tried to talk about and write to their sister about, we do not know. At the end, the good advice of the elder one. He is sending a parcel of food. "And may it arrive safely and taste good to you, and serve your health. Above all you should not go hungry. From the bread and bacon I sent today one can cut two slices and put a piece of bacon in the middle, then hide it in your pocket and nibble at it from time to time. I only fear – for I know your comradeship and your good heart – that you will immediately share everything and keep nothing for yourself. I do that too – but everything has its limits in the world."

Bruno writes from Innsbruck on 30 May that they are finishing their training in the Alps and the next day set off for Lapland. (In Innsbruck was stationed the 2nd Mountain Rifle Division formed on 1 April 1938 – the 2. Gebirgs-Division, and with this formation the war fortunes of the soldier Mielke will be linked). At the Sunday mass many high-ranking officers appeared, and he was also allowed to invite a few of his comrades, Kameraden, to the church. (Perhaps such ostentatious behaviour on the part of the officer corps had something to do with the fact that the 2nd Mountain Rifle Division was formed from the earlier, Austrian
slowinski2023/35:
6th division, where there were not so many adherents of the new "Germanic religion"). From the newspapers he learns that larger combat operations on the Murmansk front can be expected only in the middle of June. He assumes that they will not go directly to the front line, but will certainly take the place of those who go to the first line. He thinks that the time of an important decision "on the matter of Russia" is approaching. The next passage, worth recording in full, is a kind of testament which he sends to his family.

Tactical insignia of the 2. Gebirgs-Division.

"Dear Brother, there is one thing I would like to suggest to you, as man to man: let us not deceive ourselves and let us look the truth in the eye. It is clear (for me and for you) that a stage now lies ahead of me that is more or less threatening to life. (That the English have attacked German ships and will continue to do so is probably certain). Our transports are of course well protected. So if anything should happen to me, according to God's will, I ask you to deal with my property in freedom as follows: 1. That morga of meadow near Zagórów should belong to Kadzia; deal with it in such a way that it is as good as possible for Kadzia. 2. The money gathered in the savings bank in my savings account is to be divided as follows: 30% for Kadzia; 20% for Anni; 25% for the church, the home and foreign missions; 25% for you, at your free disposal. You will have the ways and means. Whatever of the clothes and things you can use, take for yourself; the rest Kadzia may alter for Father. My 'large furniture' should still serve Father. Dearest Brother, I am not writing the above in gloomy forebodings nor out of deep, dark despair and resignation; on the contrary, I feel freer when I know that everything is in order, and therefore I can be at peace."

He writes the letter on the way to the front "on the march" on 10 June 1942. "By God's grace we have arrived happily in Finland. The journey by ship went without problems. The sea was calm and majestic. […] For two days we travelled in Finland by train and found ourselves near a small town close to the Arctic Circle. Now we are to undertake a long
slowinski2023/36:
march, which is to last many weeks. You must understand that for reasons of security we cannot give anything precisely. If – God grant – victory is achieved, then I will describe everything to you exactly and tell you all about it." And then about his worries in service. "Some tasks are very difficult – for example the marching, because I was always a stay-at-home and am not used to it. But since everyone wants to accomplish it, I too will not give up.

I will do everything in my power. Apart from my health and life I can give nothing else. I will keep my oath. […] May God grant victory." He cannot give the field post number, for they have not yet reached their destination.

A letter reporting the company's arrival at its destination has happily survived. "With God's help we survived "the first stage of the great march" to the training ground, where within 6 weeks we are to complete our training. First there were about 300 km, which we covered, doing up to 35 km a day. Usually we marched at night, from 8 in the evening to 3 in the morning, that is, as the night hours are called here. For we are in such a marvellous place where for months there is no night and no dusk. The sun sinks towards the horizon, remains there, to rise majestically again after midnight. All the time during the march you have the impression that you are travelling either in the evening hours or in the early morning. Only my watch told me whether it was evening or morning. Most of the days of the march were, thank God, fair and sunny, and so simply beautiful for walking. Our road led mostly through forest. In Finland forests predominate, but small forests (bare firs, spruces, pines), with bogs and hillocks. One would march gladly, were it not so hard for someone not accustomed to it. In the end I almost collapsed, or rather my legs refused obedience: they ached, pricked and swelled. Therefore for the last 15 km I rode in a vehicle together with the other limping ones to the destination; that saved me, otherwise I would have ruined my legs. At the beginning, that is, during the first days of the march,
slowinski2023/38:
there were no obstacles. Everyone, I too, then went his own way, in the quiet night, and each fought with his own thoughts, was somewhere else in spirit. I was always with you, my Dear Ones. Enlivened, I pictured your house at Łazińsk then." On the margin he adds that it is a good thing to know Russian; interpreters with the rank of officer have a much easier life…

He also reassures the family that they are well supplied. Recently they have received a temporary, borrowed postal code. "You may […] therefore also write to me. Since the code is borrowed, please do not forget to draw a circle (the size of 1 Pfennig) under the sender, without this the letter will not reach me. Address: Soldier Bruno Mielke, postal code: 39 801. Sender: Gustav Mielke. Łazińsk, post office Dromin (Trabczyn) via Konin Wartheland (Germany), and then the circle. Parcels can be sent too, unfortunately only up to 100 g. That is not much. Only what keeps a long time and is light counts". Perhaps it is also worth quoting a rather peculiar request: "bake and dry small biscuits (little cakes) from flour, which you can dry on a pan or on a baking tray, perhaps with fat. They are sometimes also added to clear soup. I would like to dip them in tea or coffee as well, and that will taste wonderful." He writes that they should try to bake exactly such little cakes as he is sending as a pattern. "We received an allocated portion of these biscuits, of which I took 40 g to eat. Since this is forbidden, I afterwards got into unpleasantness, and I would like you to send me some of them."

After the hard experiences of the Winter War of 1939/1940 with the Red Army and the loss of ten per cent of its territory – in October 1940 Finland concludes with the Third Reich an agreement on military and economic cooperation. From that time on the Germans transfer their units to the territories of Lapland. In May 1941 Finland officially becomes an ally of the Third Reich. On 25 June it declares war on the USSR. 

 The postal number denoted Feld-Kommandantur 578 or Ortskommandantur 578, that is, a territorial command not assigned to a specific unit.
slowinski2023/39:
The German-Finnish offensive in the north begins – just as the newspapers had earlier announced! – in June, precisely on 29 June. General Eduard Dietl, commanding the 20th Mountain Army (Armia Leppland), gives the order to attack. The campaign was given the code name Silberfuchs (Silver Fox). As the Finns themselves put it, for them it was a war of continuation – they wanted to win back the territories lost to the Russians.

The Germans wanted something more. The main objective of the operation was the port of Murmansk and, first of all, cutting the route between Murmansk and Petrozavodsk and Leningrad. For the Red Army the railway line, by which military equipment flowing from the USA and England was transported to the port of Murmansk, was of key strategic importance. Finnish Petsamo, lying beyond the Arctic Circle, Russian Pieczenga, where large forces were concentrated, is a settlement lying on the river of the same name, which flows into a fjord whose beginning lies 5 km from the Barents Sea.

From later letters we learn that Mielke was stationed a few kilometres from Petsamo – in Parkkino. In this small locality, situated on the river Petsamojoki, sappers built a bridge through which the entire supply of the attacking troops passed. The task of the company in which Bruno Mielke served may have been, among other things, the protection of this bridge. The attack of the combined Finnish and German formations did not succeed. Already on 17 July the Russians stopped the entire offensive. The terrain, too, proved to be a barrier impossible to overcome. Only 140 km separate Petsamo from Murmansk. The Germans controlled valuable nickel deposits and still tried to resume operations, but on 22 September the führer's order came to break off combat operations. (The bridge at Parkkino was destroyed in a daring action by a Russian flyer on 28 September, thereby cutting off from essential supplies the two fighting divisions that remained in the north-east). The front line on this section remained stable right up to September 1944.

The family followed and deeply felt the events on the distant, northern wing of the Eastern Front. This is attested by
slowinski2023/40:
the profusion of July letters. Father, sister and brother, independently of one another, send mail full of heartening words. Brother Gustav writes (22 July 1942): "Today I was again in Zagórów with Kadzia [sister Leokadia]. Even if in Zagórów one sees and hears more, still nothing could distract my thoughts, and the whole time I thought of you. […] How many hundreds of times the question arises how you are getting on and why it was precisely you who were transferred so far away. […] Sister Anna with her fiancé Hans are at home at Łazińsk. Hans has two weeks of leave. In general many Łazińsk people come on leave often, mainly those who are stationed in Germany or in France." It pains him that his brother is so far away that leave is out of the question. On the southern front it goes from victory to victory, so Bruno, crowned by this victory, may soon return home. He also has a question and at the same time a request. "Have you not yet had the opportunity to have a photograph taken of yourself in your soldier's uniform? In a helmet and with the other things. We – and I most of all – would be very glad."

Two letters of the father – Samuel Julius Mielke – have survived. The one of 20 April was written on the führer's birthday and is dedicated above all to him. "May the Lord God preserve him in good health for a long time, until he defeats all evil and we can sing with him the great Alleluia of peace." He is also worried by the fact that many of the local people avoid the church. In the second letter (28 July 1942) we read: "Dear Bruno, beloved son of my heart! May these lines find you in the best of health and in true soldierly courage. I would most gladly be there with you, to help you carry your burdens! But the distance is too great. Talk there with your commanders. I could be used as a translator of the Russian language and take upon myself the hardships of the journey." Then come news of the much delayed, wet harvest. The letter ends with the words: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with us all. Amen. Jesus works miracles. Heil Hitler!"
slowinski2023/42:
In the letters from sister Olga and brother-in-law Erwin there are great thanks for the monetary gifts and for the fact that with his own body he protects them and their beloved homeland from the evil enemy. One of the letters begins with an exalted supplication for Christ's help, through His wounds, passion and death, in the sudden need in which the brother found himself. The sister believes she has the right to such words, because she and her husband want not only to wear the former hakenkreuz (swastika) but also to cherish it in their religion. "May God Almighty send down upon you grace and mercy. Our single most ardent wish is to see you alive and well when this evil war is over." She briefly describes the christening ceremony of the little son, whom they named Adolf. "The holy baptism was modest, at home." Unfortunately they did not receive permission to slaughter a pig, but at the church the pastor arranged everything nicely and delivered a beautiful speech. The godparents were Gustav and Leokadia. We liked it very much. She ends with the information that she packed a bit of bacon and black bread. Well baked.

Sister Anna also tries hard to support her brother. "When at the cinema I watch the newsreels and the conquerors of the mountains advance, I always think that you too are there. And then I am so proud of you. I know that being at the front is not among the pleasures, but I would set off at once if I were a man. After all, it must be a heartening feeling, to protect the Fatherland so that it does not bend before the wild hordes, and its inhabitants before maltreatment. We shall always be grateful to you for that […] we feel with our heart everything that you physically have to endure." And further: "Actually it is senseless of me to write this to you. You have never complained and you are certainly in this respect an exemplary soldier. You were taught obedience and were never spoilt. You also have a good heart, full of enthusiasm. That is really the only thing that is needed in order to accept everything with joy." At the end she writes that she is going with her fiancé Hans to Dresden – she wants to meet his parents and visit this beautiful
slowinski2023/43:
city. (She takes advantage of an autumn leave from 24 September to 14 October).

A long letter of Bruno's to his brother Gustav, dated 2 August, has survived. It is not a reply to the letters written in July by father, brother and sisters. They evidently crossed in the post. If they reached him at all… For in what way would they have found their way back to Łazińsk? Returned – because there was no longer any unit at the old field post address – or did Bruno himself bring them back in his baggage? But what he writes is to some extent an answer to the family's worries and anxieties connected with the soldierly service of brother and son. He writes, namely, that on the 22nd of that month they are to set out for the front. He asks them to hold off sending parcels until they give the front number of the field post. He does not complain about the supplies. "The food is also good. Every day there is meat or something of the kind of meat. There is also more bread (750 g a day). On Sunday there is even 1/3 of a bar of chocolate and 1/5 l. of schnapps. At the front itself the food will not be worse but even better." The soldier young in service ("until the third year of the war I could have remained in the schoolroom") believes that he joined the Wehrmacht at the end – when the culmination of the fighting is already coming. He fears – of course apart from the fighting itself and its possible consequences – the coming winter. "The old front-line soldiers tell that in the north the harshest was the past winter. Then they had to freeze, because there was no time for preparations. For this winter, however, the preparations are already being made in summer – if those men are still alive, then I hope they will not freeze. So it will probably be with us too, although by that time they may yet be transferred a number of times." Presumably the memories of the front-line soldiers who survived the fighting in the mighty frosts remained firmly fixed in Bruno Mielke's memory. "My hope and my petition is to survive this one winter, and if God grants the grace of victory again, then my hope is not empty. In any case it is beautiful that one of us takes part in this, and for me it is an obvious duty, even if I, with my 31 years, do not quite understand it! Would you believe that I already feel it?"
slowinski2023/44:
It is worth pausing for a moment over this last sentence. How is it to be understood? As the pride of a soldier who is told that he is fighting for a homeland free of Jews and Russian hordes? Or perhaps in this "feeling" there flows from somewhere in the subconscious the question of what, in truth, he is taking part in? He does not write about the war operations – for it is obvious that the censorship would never let such a letter through. But he reveals another enemy – nature, which in his account is more dangerous than the opponent. Or perhaps he indicates that this opponent has an extraordinarily dangerous ally? The question will always arise when reading letters from the front. To what extent should they be understood literally, and to what extent should one read what is not there or what has been "said between the lines"? In any case it is evident that Private Mielke has not yet come to know the true war machine that grinds human flesh, and with growing apprehension he awaits that encounter.

This letter is – to use the language of war – loaded with emotions. Above all he writes about his great dream, of which he thinks unceasingly. "…if I return happily and in good health, I will prepare myself for the most beautiful of professions, in order to exercise it with the greatest blessing […] My heart in any case is full of longing for a life dedicated to God – and as a pastor I know how to do that best." His thoughts also run to his future wife, who must hold views such as his. That is the first condition, about which he will ask her first of all. Does she belong to the Saviour and is she pious? Married life, as he imagines it, must be "the holiness of the Lord and blessed by the nearness of God and the Spirit".

He gives the same advice to his brother, who in a letter asks his opinion about Truthilde. "Observe her and converse with her thoroughly, how far she is sanctified by Christ." Brother Gustav is 43 years old (he had been cantor, teacher and headmaster at Łazińsk since 1925) and, as one can gather from other letters, the search for a candidate for wife has been going on with varying success for quite some time. Yet the advice of the younger Bruno is unchanging – he must know whether
slowinski2023/45:
she is an inwardly seeking, deeply believing soul. It would also be good if she were not bad-looking.

His thoughts return to his school days at Łazińsk, which were the sunniest and happiest of all the periods of his life. With gratitude he thinks of his parents, who despite their weaknesses gave him what is most costly: "a healthy body and blood with the faith of our dear Evangelical Church", and finally of his wonderful siblings, from whose hearts beats only warm love. In the face of what is inevitably coming, we read a letter that is like Bruno Mielke's life credo and an attempt at an examination of conscience. It is also – or perhaps above all – an unspoken, strong reaction to the news reaching them from soldiers returning from the front line.

Letters from loved ones, such as those quoted earlier and the next one from Anna (of 22 September 1942), which I quote below, undoubtedly carried weight and significance in maintaining the psychological stability and resilience of Private Mielke. "I am so proud that you are fighting in this decisive battle. […] I believe that when a man like you stands at the front and looks danger straight in the eye, the petty and insignificant things flee from the soul, and it is then cleansed, and afterwards it becomes strengthened and proud. When you return, you will certainly be a different man. Take hold of everything that is valuable, and rid yourself of everything else. Conquer yourself, and in this way you will return as a man of worth, and nothing will be able to shake you. I would so much like to shield you from all troubles, but such is the lot of man that he must go through everything quite alone." Perhaps this girl, writing her letter shortly before nightfall, intuitively sensed a certain painful paradox that many soldiers experienced. They fought together, in a squad, in a company. On how they supported one another their lives often depended, and yet, on the other hand, an equally dangerous enemy of theirs was the grim and oppressive feeling of loneliness.

Three weeks later Pastor Aleksander Gross writes from Zagórów (13 October 1942) about the mass he celebrated
slowinski2023/46:
on Sunday. "On 27 September we thought in Łazińsk of a prayer of supplication before God, and I recited to the congregation the Lord's verse, as a greeting from the distant front. Everyone was moved by how a man remains brave in the danger of death, because he has entrusted his life to God. Many thought of their own family members, who are also serving their heavy duty somewhere along that long and distant front. We pray every Sunday for our members of the armed forces, even if we do not name each and every one of them. Our dear brothers can be certain that the community of faith and love for the good Lord bind us to one another, even if thousands of kilometres divide us."

The letters dated in December carry the added line: Eastern Front. "Who of us soldiers from the wastelands of Russia would not want to be with his nearest and dearest at Christmas!" "You must surely think – he writes on 6 December – that I will be spending the holidays in sadness and despondency. It is God's will, and my superiors sent me to the front. Resisting this in any form would be resisting the will of God and the authorities." Bruno regards himself as a messenger "for my family in the east, and for her and for my people I want to offer up this small sacrifice and spend Christmas at the front". He honestly admits that he has landed in a good spot – it is a fairly quiet sector. The Russians have so far attacked very rarely – hardly at all. His service consists of standing 6–8 hours of sentry duty (in pairs), bringing food and firewood, and sometimes other things. Apart from that he sleeps, and if there is good light, he writes letters and reads the delayed newspapers. That is why he asks his brother not to submit an application for his release. "First of all, it would do no good; secondly, at the front it is better in winter. In the rear there is training, drills and so on. There is none of that here. It is dangerous, true – but it is calm, and I firmly believe that nothing will happen to me."

Mielke had a great deal of luck… At Stalingrad, a deadly struggle had been raging since the end of August, and by December 1942 it was entering its decisive phase. But of this – silence in Goebbels's
slowinski2023/47:
propaganda. Bruno asks his brother to send him the Führer's address of 1 October, along with pages torn from other newspapers with the speeches of Goebbels, Göring and Ribbentrop. In the five-month battle, one and a half million German soldiers and their allies perished. Of the 91,000 prisoners taken in the Stalingrad cauldron, only about six thousand returned. But what news could this soldier have read in the "delayed newspapers"? Unaware of the westward turn of the wheel of history, he plans to establish numerous pen-pal contacts with potential candidates for a wife, so that after a life at the front full of unrest and renunciation he might look about for a cosy home. "It will be beautiful when I return home after the victory and, with a sense of peace, can lead a quiet life."

In December Bruno Mielke wrote a great deal. The approaching Christmas brought back memories of the family home, of his sisters, his brother, his father, and of his mother who was no longer alive (she died in 1933). "I want to write so that you especially, during the Christmas season, receive more mail from me." His first joy was the three-kilogram parcel received from home, and in it a fir wreath with a little angel's head and tinsel. "I immediately fastened it to my little cupboard, made from an empty grenade crate with two boards fitted in. Several comrades who 'happened' to find themselves nearby and were gazing with longing eyes at the holiday cake being taken out were given a bite to taste. They delivered hymns of praise concerning the delicacy's exquisite flavour."

The letter of 14 December also contains the information that soldiers who have no families should send stamps to the local party leaders, and these will pass them on to the Women's Leagues, which will prepare holiday parcels for the men at the front. The Wehrmacht, too, saw to it that every soldier received a richly stocked parcel, in which, alongside snuff, cigarettes, sweets, chocolate and darning wool, there were also envelopes for letters, a comb, and a bottle of vodka and of wine. Further on there is a paragraph
slowinski2023/48:
of thanks for the fulfilment of his earlier request and ("I hope I am not giving away a secret") for the sending of an ointment against lice, which everyone here has. "On Saturday I washed myself, rubbed the ointment all over, and put on fresh underwear. Now no louse bites me, so the ointment works." The question is, for how long. On the order of the Wehrmacht, a preparation called T-14 was produced – a repellent powder against lice, fleas and mites, etc. Each soldier was issued two such packs.

This letter also contains a description of the prescribed daily order, or rather the day-and-night order. "We now have 6 hours of sentry duty within 24 hours – that is still bearable. Yes, here, dear life functions quite differently, and so do mealtimes. We eat dinner at 6 p.m., supper at 3 a.m., and breakfast at 1 p.m. Why so? Because at night we must be more on the alert and more watchful than during the day. But when day breaks, there is nothing to fear, and then our sleeping time begins." And the most important, joyful news. After barely eight months of service, as of 1 December 1942 he was promoted to Senior Private. Captain Lebech, together with Lieutenant Hensler, made the personal effort to travel to his outpost, and in view of the enemy read out the order of promotion for exemplary service and a deep sense of duty.

 Preparation T-14 Ungeziefermittel gegen Läuse, Haarlinge, Flähe, Rausemilben usw. A powder produced for the army [with DDT?] in Munich, a repellent "against lice, fleas and mites etc.". They were probably attacked mainly by pubic lice. If Bruno Mielke mentions an ointment, he must have received from home an additional product available on the "civilian" market. I thank Mr Tadeusz Karpiński – the organizer of the DDD Museum – for making the illustration available and for his valuable explanations. As an aside, it is worth adding that DDT was also used on a mass scale by the Allied armies as a protection for soldiers against the Salmonella typhi bacteria carried by lice, which cause infection and the deadly dangerous typhus (www.muzeumddd.pl).
slowinski2023/49:
To the soldiers present at the post, the captain said that they should be proud to have such a comrade. "He would be pleased if we had only such soldiers." Curiously, before reading out the order, the commander asked Mielke to which class of nationality he belonged. The answer came that he belonged to the Volksliste. After a moment's hesitation and reflection, the captain read out the promotion order. In that very same letter the Senior Private was already drifting into daydreams about his chances of further promotions… "This I want to include in my prayer: that God may grant victory to our dear fatherland, and thereby peace to Europe and bread; that God may grant my dear siblings a happy, blessed marriage; that God may give me the strength to fulfil my soldier's duty with blessing and with honour."

In the hiding place there were two letters written in December to Bruno. They probably reached him after the New Year – in those days a letter took a minimum of fifteen days to reach the Eastern Front. On 12 December Anna Steinbart, who had replaced Mielke in his work at the school, writes from Konary. "Dear comrade in work in the grey uniform. You cannot imagine how happy the children were that their teacher had written to them. At once they took fire with the desire to reply to you." In the following sentences we read a personal confession that working with small children gives her much pleasure, but that the profession of teacher and educator is difficult and responsible. She feels that what she is doing is not going well, and without inner satisfaction she cannot go on doing it. She also lacks contact with the local people. "So I probably shall not be your successor for very much longer." In reply to the request for a photograph, she writes that she does not like being photographed and can only send one picture, and a somewhat blurred one at that. On the card there is an annotation by Bruno that he replied on 31 January 1943.

His brother Gustav sends copies of documents confirming Bruno's professional standing as a teacher, and reassures him that everything is in order. He is also planning to go to Konin,
slowinski2023/50:
to check at the Sparkasse whether the teacher's salary, together with interest, has arrived in his account. He also talks about two courses he attended: anti-aircraft defence and the conducting of ceremonies. With bitterness he writes about the issued ban on lay preachers and cantors performing baptisms, funerals and other church rites. The previously quoted Pastor Gross wrote about this. "Our neighbouring parishes have been experiencing tensions since the summer, because no cantor or, as it is called in the decree of the Reichsstatthalter, lay assistant may any longer celebrate services; only pastors may celebrate them. Thereby depriving the cantors' councils of the possibility of acting and of experiencing the readings during services every Sunday." The cantors, who were most often also teachers administratively, are, as teachers, being separated from the Church. One may interpret this decision as an effect of Nazi policy, whose aim was to push the Church out of the teaching and upbringing of the young. This ban pained Gustav deeply. He greatly enjoyed active participation in the mass and had always done so gladly. Christmas, New Year's Eve, the New Year – these therefore put him in a sad mood. Apart from that he has nothing special to report. "Yesterday [he writes on 19 December 1942] we had a pig slaughter."

Erich Kunitzer, director of the Teachers' Seminary in Łódź at the time when Bruno Mielke was studying there, is delighted with the letter from his former pupil. He asks at which sector of the front he has found himself, and boasts of his son Friedrich, who as a commander in a special unit is fighting somewhere in the Kalmyk steppe to the south-east of Rostov. Many former seminarians are at the front; of the 120 teachers from Łódź, 50 have been called up to the army. "May God protect you all – Kunitzer writes – so that we may yet see one another. The struggle is hard, but we must carry it through to the end. I, too, would rather die at the front than fall under the rule of the Jews, who have sworn a terrible vengeance upon us."
slowinski2023/51:
> You give me the shield of your salvation 
> (Ps 18:36)

The short letter that Bruno writes on Sunday 20 December 1942 (it reaches Łazińsk on 5 January) announces the sending of a longer description of how he spent Christmas, and contains only one account: "During the hours of the service, from 9 to 11, I stood on duty at my post, which is the more dangerous one (today we had to make a change). The main post consists of an oblong stone bunker. That is where I really ought to be. But 'by mistake' I went to the side bunker. While I was just there, giving myself to prayer, a shell from the Russian artillery struck the main post, broke a hole in the wall, and threw many stones inside. What would have happened to me if I had been there just then?" And he concludes: "Let God be praised and glorified."

Mielke sits down to the account of the first day of the holidays just before midnight, right after coming off the post where, between 9 and 11 p.m., he had stood with his good comrade Schwartz. He honestly admits that he had feared these holidays and an onslaught of longing. But it was not so bad. In the forenoon the captain and the divisional chaplain came on a visit. They even walked up to his post, and the chaplain was so kind that he asked after his family and gave him a bar of chocolate, wishing him a Happy New Year. It was not so bad, either, because "the joyful strength is given me above all by my faith in the living God, who is with me […]". On this evening he could repeat, from his prayer book, which he always carries with him, the magnificent Christmas hymns, and "when I sing them quietly
slowinski2023/52:
to myself, then the holidays are all around me". What was he reading? Might it have been the passage from the Gospel according to St Luke on the birth of Jesus? "And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child." (Luke 2:4–5)

Did he sing the old thirteenth-century carol Adeste fideles (Let all the faithful sing, praising their God), or perhaps "Children, children, hurry all together.//To the manger in the stable at this festive time"? It is an extraordinary image when we try to picture a German soldier, standing on Russian ground stained with blood, at an forward outpost, humming Silent Night. He saw in his mind's eye the family going to church, his father at prayer; he thanks his sisters for the presents sent in the parcels, the tasty cake, the warm leather gloves. Now he will no longer freeze – even if it were 50 degrees below, as happens on the central sector of the front. "The temperature here is such that there was even a thaw the day before, which the warm Gulf Stream ocean current brought from the north." Although the command looks after them, and even the food at Christmas is better, still – they are at the front!

They had to be especially watchful, because the Russians had attacked the previous Christmas. They had expected an attack yesterday as well, but they did not come. "But today, on the first day of the holidays, from 9 to 11 they carried out an attack with artillery and mortars – quite devilishly. Thank God there were no losses or damage. In the afternoon, in reply, our men fired on the Russian bunkers – that is how it is at the front. The day before yesterday, shortly before midnight, blood flowed again – one of the comrades was hit in the face. Among our soldiers behind our walls and bunkers, only head shots occur, and they are fatal." This is the cool account of a soldier under fire, who writes that here danger exists at all times. That is why 

 Quotations from the Gospel according to St Luke added – M.S.
slowinski2023/54: he asks for God's protection and for his family's intercession in prayer. Every one of the December letters written on the Eastern Front by Bruno Mielke ends with words of hope linked to the swiftly approaching New Year. That it will be the year decisive for victory, that "from the hand of God the Father we shall receive everything that He wishes to give us – joy and suffering, happiness and misfortune".
slowinski2023/55:
> Make my steps firm on your paths 
> (Ps 17:5)

The first decade of January 1943 brings letters from sister Anna to her brother at the front (7 January 1943) and a letter from Bruno (10 January 1943) to Anna, which, however, is not a reply. They must have crossed in the post. Anna thanks him for the birthday chocolate sent from the front, which will be the main ornament of the table. Together with her sisters she has prepared a parcel, into which they put socks knitted between Christmas and the New Year; she made a head protector, Kadzia wrist protectors, and Fela knee pads. Anna's fiancé Hans added flash bulbs for the camera. And everyone is delighted that he will be able to take photographs, and cannot wait to see them.

The brother's letter has a completely different character and weight. Everyone is living in anticipation of Anna's planned wedding. Bruno hopes that it will not stop at this one wedding. Perhaps Gustav, perhaps Kadzia too will follow in her footsteps this year. He himself also greatly longs for the moment when he will be able to introduce his sister-in-law to them. He sends a complete set of photographs with the request that Anna paste them into his album. Yet beyond the ritual assurances of remembering her in prayer and the birthday wishes, Bruno believes that in the first days of this year, so very important for his sister, he must share with her the gnawing anxiety he feels about… his sister's spiritual safety. He reports that her fiancé Hans, in his first letter to him, writes clearly and openly that "he rejects the teaching from Scripture and wants to protect you from such things". And so "I am allowed to speak freely and openly to all people, including strangers,
slowinski2023/56:
about the happiness of faith – to everyone, that is, except you, my most beloved sister!" He naturally considers this an exaggeration and laments it deeply. He does not yet condemn Hans, who does not know the splendour of Christ. That is why he quietly wants to give them a Bible as a wedding present. He will not be able to come to the wedding, and in this situation he does not want to, either. He knows that Hans loves her, that he is kind to the family and to him, and this is what is terrible for him. He only hopes that his sister does not share this strict prohibition, and that they will be able to talk about everything. He writes at the end: "this is my request and my wish for you – that you should remain in your faith, which is clear and dear to you, steadfast and faithful. You might yet bring Hans to the faith. But it is not simple".

These deeply zealous concerns about the state of his sister's soul and the attitude of her fiancé must have been repeated, for a letter of Anna's has come to light in which she sets out her position, firmly grounded in reality. "I am sorry that I cause you restless hours, but believe me, there is no need for you to worry on my account. I can neither prove nor explain it to you, but I know that your worries are unnecessary, and they, on the other hand, unsettle me. If I were to leave Hans on your account or on yours, then I would after all gain nothing, since from his side no danger threatens me, if one may call it that. He loves me only too much to want to force me into anything I do not want. Am I to wait for a pastor who perhaps more than once has been insincere? I do not want, like my sisters, to be 40 or more years old and then suffer hysterical fits, because overburdened nerves lose hope. Those I have known were little different from Hans. He is at least loyal and trustworthy. And by no means is he an unbeliever."

She reassures Bruno that there is nothing troubling in this matter. She does, however, consider it unfavourable if he keeps brooding over it, because "at night and in a foreign land everything looks different". "We are all touched by a sentimentality that
slowinski2023/57:
we ourselves do not wish to see and do not wish to admit to. I think we camouflage ourselves rather well." In turn, Anna warns her brother not to fall into a kind of religious mysticism. This Bruno certainly did not expect from his sister…

"I have no opinion of bare realism, but the opposite is equally dangerous. You yourself think that you are not a dreamer, but I think you are not very far from being one, and you must watch yourself so as not to become one. Forgive me if this causes you pain, but I hope that you understand me well and will not take it amiss. I cannot and do not want to believe that you could turn away from me because I do not accept everything intensely. Yet it is true, what I feel. I think it is very unwise to discuss this in letters, because it will only lead to misunderstandings. Remember one thing: that you need not worry on my account."

Two letters to his brother Gustav have survived from January. He writes on the twentieth, heavily burdened by illness, about how he spent New Year's Eve. "At 10 p.m. I was able to disappear behind one of the snow-covered hills and, praying, receive the year 1943 from the hand of God." Bruno is troubled by the state of his brother's soul – he is carrying some great burden, and it stands between him and God. Since that burden could not be sunk along with the old year, let him listen to a brotherly piece of advice and go to a pastor. "He will summon the wondrous, divine power (which Christ passes on to him together with his office) and will name the sin by its name. And then it will turn out that this sin, however great and filthy it may be, will have to give way." An honest conversation is necessary, and the beginning is always the hardest.

As in the earlier letter to his sister, so here too we see the great zeal of a candidate for a future pastor in the religious, spiritual formatting of his siblings. It is hard to say what to call Gustav's sin (if – as Bruno writes – it is a sin at all), but perhaps these torments of the brother may be the aftermath of the ban on administering baptisms, funerals or direct work at the services. "But there is an answer to this, which you will find in the Letter to the Romans 8:35." Yet he does not quote it.
slowinski2023/58:
Let us recall: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution"… and the further verses, which say that no powers "nor height nor depth nor any other creation" will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus, our Lord" (Rom 8:39). The cited letter of St Paul is a confirmation of what we may suspect, and what Bruno Mielke did not write outright for a long time. Amid all the many-times-repeated declarations, the fidelity to the führer and the subordination to the superiors, there is a higher authority over them, to which this soldier gave himself completely. It is God.

The description of frontline everyday life is written on 27 January. The end of the month brings hope for a milder winter. Surely the worst has already passed, and in any case, compared with other sectors of the front it was milder for them – since the temperatures reached at most minus 20-25 degrees. The worst thing of all was the incredibly strong snowstorms, something they do not know in the Kraj Warty. He rejoices at the coming time when their company will be withdrawn a few kilometres to the rear. Probably there will be no "bread and butter" there either, but at least they will be able to sleep more peacefully, wash themselves properly and get rid of the lice. After six weeks, back to the front line. "Perhaps then I will be lucky and my leave will begin, and when I return from leave, that is, after your wedding, it will already be warm and bright; then the great offensives will begin and the war – thus shall God's grace ordain – will end. And what about your wedding? Have you already decided to go to Erika?"

It is hard to establish when the soldier Bruno received the letter written by his brother Gustav on 28 January 1943 (probably around the middle of February). The most important news is the information about the state of Bruno's savings recorded in his passbook (Spaarkassenbuch). The deposits were regular and the interest was added. At the end of the year 1942 he has at his disposal the sum of 4,871 marks. Gustav also reports that he was summoned to the Education Office in Konin. 

 The Letter to the Romans, quotations added – M.S.
slowinski2023/60:
"There I was handed the deed confirming the status of an official. I also had to take an oath right away. So I am an official for life – the Führer's teacher." From Poznań sister Anni brought the developed photographs of Bruno, which he had sent from Lapland to his family. Everyone admires how well he looks in uniform. And in the final lines of the letter, Gustav Adolf, sitting in the forest-surrounded cantor's house, reports coolly and as if in passing: "Every now and again news arrives that some people from Łazińsk or from the vicinity have fallen at the Eastern Front. The fighting is not easy after all. Quite a few of them are dying."

On 30 January 1943, from Berlin radio, at the time of the daily communiqués, the sounds of the sombre adagio from Anton Bruckner's Seventh Symphony suddenly begin to flow. They precede the first official communiqué of this war about the lost battle of Stalingrad, the capitulation of the 6 Armia and the taking into captivity of the thousands of exhausted and starving soldiers encircled in the cauldron. There is no possibility that this communiqué did not reach the front. They surely also had some information channels of their own. Only speaking about this catastrophe threatened with an accusation of sowing defeatism and of repeating the news from the leaflets scattered over the Russian lines. With the obvious consequences.

What a strange letter, then, reaches his brother Gustav. About the planned marriage, about the fact that he will take his wedding vows only when he is released from service. For as a soldier he will get only a few days of leave. The engagement and the wedding are to be the concluding feast of thanksgiving, a joyful beginning of private life. Bruno describes at length the girl from Trzemeszno, Elfride Fiedler: that she is thrifty, lively and talkative despite her low education. But that is good, because he does not want a wife with higher education who would constantly instruct him. There is, however, a certain catch – the girl, her parents, her siblings belong to the community of Sabbath-keepers. But if she decides to marry him, she will have to convert to Lutheranism, and that before the engagement. "I have not the slightest desire to go to church alone." If she does not do this, he will break with her immediately. It is a long letter describing
slowinski2023/61:
the multitude of thoughts that constantly accompany him as he dreams of the longed-for marriage. He asks how his brother is getting on with Erika, whether sisters Anna and Kadzia will be getting married this year. They are not to wait with that until his arrival on leave. That is all. About his frontline service he writes one sentence. "Things go very differently for me." For wartime conditions he receives quite a lot of letters from potential candidates. But the post brings more disappointments than hopes in this matter. The twenty-three-year-old young lady from Trzemeszno thanks him for Bruno's photograph, on which he looks younger than in reality. On matters of religion she states outright: "As for my faith and community, I will tell you, Sir, this very clearly. As I already wrote to you earlier, Sir, I am a Seventh-day Adventist. The greatest privilege is that I sanctify the day which our Saviour also sanctified when he walked the ends of the earth, that is, Sunday. We call ourselves Adventists because we await the second coming of Christ and we keep the seventh day." This declaration cuts short the further acquaintance.

In turn, there reached Bruno from Lipice a letter from Ursula – the leader of a B.D.M. troop (Bund Deutscher Mädel – the League of German Girls). It is the female section of the Nazi youth organisation Hitlerjugend. She is disappointed that the two previous letters she sent came back to her. She encloses them in the envelope again as proof. The girl writes that she has returned to her old path. Earlier her love for Bruno blinded her! What does that mean today, when she reflects on it? That it is the only path for her: "I believe in the almighty God, who will not allow the downfall of Germany. Every faith that is directed against my beloved fatherland I reject from myself. Therefore I do not need any intermediary, those who so often see only their little 'church' and do not perceive the highest goal for the Church, which should be Germany. Our Führer never intended to separate the Church from the state – quite the contrary! In the year 1933 services were established as an obligation for all the organisations of the party.
slowinski2023/62:
But the Church rejected this." Nor was it able to lead the German nation spiritually, and therefore the German youth cannot be entrusted to it. She judges such conduct of the hierarchy as acting together with the enemy states against the Third Reich. Once victory has been achieved, she believes, the affairs with the Church will finally be put in order, for it cannot be that the Church acts against the state. Then, too, she will take decisive steps. It will be either – or. And although she will not try to convince her parents, she at least hopes that they will show understanding for her stance. Of course she believes that "…among the Christians faithful to their Church there are few who stand up in defence of Germany and the Führer, but these are exceptions – among them you are. You have a sincere faith, but you also, after all, have reason, which allows you to discern what the future holds. Earlier you were rooted to that village of yours, cut off from the events of the world. Yet now you cannot close your eyes and ears to all this, which does not correspond to your unyielding views. Do you not see at all what the struggle of nations is about?". She knows that Bruno will want to rebut all this. And she concludes: "Believe me, if I did not like you, your views would be indifferent to me. You are such a dear man, so natural, that I have grown fond of you from the heart." There are no other letters or cards that would attest that this acquaintance was continued.

What happened at Stalingrad was a great shock for the Germans, a source of sharp tensions and discussions in the political and military leadership of the Third Reich. For not everyone agreed with the führer, who called this spectacular defeat (of which the world was already speaking) a "heroic spectacle of German history". Generals Karl Strecker and Helmuth Groscurth did not end their report on the capitulation with the sacramental Heil Hitler, but with the traditional call: "Long live Germany"... The news from the east also brought a spark of hope to the subjugated nations, an echo of which we shall soon see in the letters from the later months. But at the beginning
slowinski2023/64:
of February it was not yet known how great a significance the lost battles on the Wołga and the Don had. The southern front also failed to achieve its intended objectives (the capture of the oil sources) and Grupa Armii A had to withdraw from the Kaukaz. All the signs in heaven and on earth, however, said that something important had happened.

In this sense, Bruno's marriage efforts, his wedding plans, can be regarded as a kind of defensive reaction, an escape from the black everyday reality, a peculiar repression of what was reaching him. For Bruno Mielke was no fool. Two weeks later he sends a letter which is already considerably more open. "For a week now we have been here in the reserve and we lead the barrack life of soldiers. Today is the first Sunday – to my and everyone's joy, without duty. One can truly meditate spiritually and clerically. Spiritually is my thinking and my writing of letters to you. Clerically I am, as before, still lonely and in the desert. When the hours of holding the service come, I always feel the pull. Today, too, I was able to do it. […] I went into the snow-covered mountains and found again an altar for prayer… How good it is then for a poor, lonely soul, if it finds itself near the one who said: 'I am with you through all the days'". But he immediately qualifies: "I cannot tell everyone about this. Most would consider me a dreamer." But for him this is blissful and beatifying dreaming, a real happiness which most pitiable people do not know. "Dreaming" is one of the milder terms he could have heard. Many comrades steeped in the new faith often coarsely mocked the humble adherents of the religion of the weak, the eternal penitents, as Christians were contemptuously called. Hence that search for a solitude. It is a kind of escape, of hiding oneself, in order to devote oneself to prayer in peace.

In Berlin the ministry of propaganda is working! On 18 February, a dozen or so days after the capitulation of the 6 Armia of Field Marshal Paulus, in the capital's Sportpalast Joseph Goebbels delivers the famous speech in which he announces the beginning of the total war
slowinski2023/65:
against Russia and the allies. After the definitively lost battles of Moscow and Stalingrad, when the leading Nazis see the growing threat, first of all a general mobilisation is proclaimed by Hitler. For the first time Goebbels publicly admits that the crisis on the Eastern Front has reached its peak, and that Stalingrad is a great alarm for the fate of the German nation. No German may think of a compromise. The nation is called to a hard war and is to be ready for all sacrifices if the führer gives such an order. In the sports palace, under the slogan "Total war – the shortest war", only selected and vetted guests were gathered. These are 14,000 fanatical Nazis, who sing and applaud after each of the harsher passages of this mainly anti-Jewish philippic. Goebbels calls with the words of the poet: Now, people, arise and let the storm break loose ("Nun, Volk steh auf, und Sturm brich los!"). The whole staging of the rally is meant, among other things, to reject the allied voices saying that the Germans had lost their faith in victory. But at the same time he wants to "feed" his ambitions, counting on Hitler granting him greater power.

On the same day a book publication of the Sportpalastrede appears. The minister of propaganda skilfully reverses the whole agitational machine. The calls about the new space being conquered for the great Third Reich fall silent. In short, it can be put as follows: Now Germany is "defending" old Europe, the whole world, against the Jews and the onslaught of the Bolshevik plague. Bruno Mielke, for his part, writes: "That the decision with Russia and thus the end of the war will come this year, we all feel it, which is why personal matters must now be set aside; when everything is over, there will be a beautiful return home and, as the crowning of the joy, let it be my wedding." On the fourth of March the "enjoying of quiet" in the rear comes to an end. An urgent order arrives, calling up the folksdojczowie (Germans from Poland, that is, the Kraj Warty) to report to the 2 batalion. Right after taking up the positions he sends the family a short message. At first they complained that, laden down, they had to
slowinski2023/66:
move through a blizzard of snow. But the commander sent sledges for them, fed them well and at once distributed them to the forward battle positions. After they had been disposed of, it is visible that they made up for the personnel shortfalls in the companies caused by the losses suffered. Bruno Mielke is assigned as an operator to serve the heavy machine gun and gets as his helper private Atze. This is a weapon of the direct field of combat.

There has been preserved the only description of a battle in the whole collection of letters. "From 12 o'clock at night (from Friday to Saturday) our heavy weapons were made ready (artillery, grenade launchers, anti-aircraft guns). It is unbelievable how everything booms, rolls, seethes and bubbles, and when the shells whistle across to the other side, carrying death and destruction. Again – as always – there were many fallen and wounded on both sides (among the Russians many more). Were all of them ready for death? I think about it in spirit and this is always the most important question for me. One more thing is astonishing, which I heard today: Russian prisoners testified that the Russians in those same days were planning an attack on our positions, only we forestalled them. And yet one can feel such wonderful care and love of God."

One thing is certain – Mielke was in that hell. On Remembrance Day, the first day of spring, 21 March, he writes that the lack of leave is wearing him down, as is the uncertainty whether the information passed on that he would get it will be confirmed. He wants to be with his family for the Holidays and hopes that his brother will hold the wedding which everyone is awaiting. The day is wonderful, sunny and relatively calm. The Russians have not yet answered their last attack of 15 March. But probably they no longer can. Probably it is as Hermann Göring foretold, that the enemy is fighting with his last reserves. And we, "through the totalisation of the war, can field one more army. That is why we are all firmly convinced that the Lord will send us victory this summer and will make the poor people on both sides attain peace." Who, if not the heavy machine gunner, will see better what a harvest
slowinski2023/67:
"Death for the fatherland is worthy of eternal honour." This is a quotation from the writer, poet and officer of the Prussian army Ewald Christian von Kleist, who died of the wounds received in the battle of Kunowice.

This drawing is a motif often exploited in propaganda and war publications. An oak on a hillock, helmets on the grave of the fallen, and cranes returning to their native nests.
slowinski2023/68:
War. He asks how the "total war" has affected their lives. Whether his brother wants to enlist in the army – though he is so needed in Łazińsk, and besides he has a wedding in the plan. (Soon the Wehrmacht itself will decide about this, without asking Gustav's opinion.) At the end Bruno writes: "Two weeks ago we listened to the speech of the Führer. He spoke of how decisive times our nation and fatherland are living through. On this special spring day, when we have happily survived the winter and countless dangers, we should be joyful and grateful that God, through our Führer, is preserving us from the threatening evil, and how this strengthens us, soldiers, that we do not bear our sacrifices in vain, do not suffer in vain and – die in vain."

Still, in many letters from the coming months written by the soldier Bruno we read with a certain astonishment that he believes more in the successive assurances of the leader and the assorted retinue of politicians than in what he sees and must do at the front. How dangerous is the force of propaganda, which falls on well-prepared ideological ground. In what a different tone he writes a letter six days later. He already knows that he will not get leave for Easter; too many with longer service are in the queue ahead of him. "I already long for the quiet, for the blessed hours, and I remember the time I was able to experience in your house, dear brother. Łazińsk, Zagórów, also Anielewo, Białobłoty, Maślaki, Konary, Grodziec – all of these are blessed places!" So he will not be at Anni's wedding, and Gustav's plans, too, may be thwarted. They may call him up into the army. Which would be fatal! Evidently the Lord, who is in the heavens, has so ordained all this. Yet he believes that "He, the faithful Saviour, will never leave me alone, and at Easter again – as every day – he will comfort me with his nearness! This spiritual strengthening is what I especially need now. For soon the decisive attacks must, here in the east, gain in strength, and then various thoughts come. It will be as God wills." He advises his loved ones to listen to and proclaim the holy word in the time of Easter. That of which he now lacks so much.
slowinski2023/69:
In this way they will best arm themselves for the times of drought that may come. Nothing happens without the will and permission of the Lord. These are decisive and grave months; one must be able to sacrifice one's own wishes.

This is the first letter in which Mielke allows himself a certain generalisation of the situation on his sector of the front. Until now these were "narrow plans", showing the individual threats and dangers menacing him directly. Now he says: prepare yourselves for a hard time, for things do not look good. Regardless of what he had in mind and what his knowledge really was, in saying that the fighting was entering its decisive phase he was not mistaken. The next letter preserved in the hiding place is dated Eastern Front, 27 July 1943. At the beginning of the month – on 5 July – the German attack on the Kursk salient begins. The struggle lasted until the end of August. The Russians knew the enemy's plans, codenamed "Cytadela", well and adopted the defensive strategy proposed by Żukow. When the forces of the attacking armies, bogging down in the mud and dying on the mines and under the murderous artillery fire, were exhausted, they launched a counterattack. It was the greatest tank battle in history. The lost battle meant that the German command was no longer able, until the end of the war, to seize the strategic initiative on the Eastern Front. "Things are relatively calm with us" – he writes. "Confirmation of the fact that the Russians are using all their forces in the south in order to win back the central areas again. Here it is often gloomy and misty. Then it is dangerous, because the Russians gladly make raids then, but we are already on the alert and our machines do not fail."

Bruno Mielke's thoughts run to Łazińsk, where people can gather the grain from the fields in peace and run across the stubble fields. Here, on the depopulated and harsh north, one feels nothing of that by which the people in the village are living now. And the harvests are important for the war and for the nation. He thanks his sister Anni for the parcel and, in passing, conveys to her the information that he is no longer writing to Elfride. And it
slowinski2023/70:
is not recklessness or indifference, but rather responsibility. Besides, he is healthy and although they feed one well here, lately he has lost his appetite. "If only dear God, with his grace, would be close to our people, so that everything ends well and so that mankind may again know peace." On Sunday 8 August he sends a letter which he writes in some religious rapture, at 11 o'clock, in the blessed hour of the services. "In spirit I see the churches in all lands, I see in them those who through the blood and salvation of Christ have become my siblings." And he sees himself in the pulpit – in the most splendid of all official vestments, proclaiming the gospel. Instead of greetings he asks them to read out Psalm 23.

psalm 23

The Lord is my shepherd…

Psalm of David. 
The Lord is my shepherd, 
I shall lack nothing. 
In green pastures he pastures me. 
He leads me beside still waters. 
He refreshes my soul.

For the sake of his name.

I will fear no evil, for You are with me,

slowinski2023/71:
> In You, Lord, I place my trust 
> (Ps 71:1)

The September (16 September 1943) dating of the letter carries a new annotation: "in the field". It is above all an extensive text on the occasion of Gustav's 44th birthday. We read a long disquisition on the virtues of 36-year-old Elza – the girl to whom he wants to draw his brother's attention. He knows her only from a friend's account, but what decides her merits (in accordance with Bruno's system of values, which we have already come to know) is the fact that she is pure in faith, character and virtue, that is, she possesses all those most beautiful values which qualify her to be his wife. "Of course you must judge for yourself whether she pleases you […] but you must not set your judgments and demands too high – more important than outward beauty, after all, remains inner worth". As for children, despite her age, she may yet give birth to a few, and surely he does not want a large brood…? The letter also brings thanks to the family for the birthday wishes sent and assurances of prayers to God for intercession on his behalf. He writes all this in the field and explains where such an address comes from. "Being in good health, I am presently helping with road construction. It is not easy to work physically 9–10 hours with pick and shovel, but everything will pass; I am grateful that the food is good (better than last year) and that I can work for Germany, and not like a prisoner of war in Russia – as has happened to many".

Where does this mood come from? Bad news after the heavy defeat at Kursk comes not only from the eastern front. On 10 July the British and Americans land in Sicily. On 25 July the
slowinski2023/72:
Fascist Grand Council carries out a surprising coup, depriving Benito Mussolini of power. A few days later – on 3 September Italy (the government of Marshal Badoglio) capitulates! That same day Allied troops land in southern Italy. The arrested Duce is freed by German commandos on Hitler's orders. And this event awakens the admiration of Bruno Mielke. "I am particularly pleased by our Führer's loyalty. This matter in Italy will at least become clear, and further steps will certainly be taken soon". Under the Germans' umbrella, Mussolini creates in northern Italy the puppet Republic of Salò. This is another letter in which Mielke allows himself commentary on broader events concerning the war and politics.

But that is not all. From the advice he gives his brother, we can infer that Gustav, sitting in Łazińsk, notices a change in the behavior of the Poles, who in various ways give the occupiers signals that they know more than what Goebbels's organs write and proclaim. "One can get angry that the Poles are becoming brazen; nevertheless, I would like to ask you to confine yourself to quiet observing and reporting, provocative intrusions breed hatred, and hatred is capable of many things. So that the saboteurs disappear, let the gendarmerie take care of it; it is called to this. The Poles hope in vain for political freedom. The Germans are in form!". As a birthday present he sends his brother a drinking glass made from the casing of a round fired on the eastern front in Russia. Let it be a small memento from the front and may it always accompany you on your travels.

Perhaps this "raising of heads" of the Poles resulted not only from news from the front, but also from the attitude of the older of the brothers toward their former neighbors. In a considerably later letter of Gustav Adolf to the sister running the household (12 December 1944, postal number 33 977), when he already serves as an artilleryman in the naval infantry in Hamburg, he encloses advice on how to treat the slave woman assigned to the farmstead. "Regarding the Polish girl. To begin with you must take her firmly in hand (ostro w ryzy), so that she knows where her place is. You must lock everything up and
slowinski2023/74:
ration everything out to her. After all, one never knows whether she is not stealing and is not in collusion with the farmhand". Further on he provides an extensive tutorial on how to run the pig breeding. And he adds a warning not to delay the pig slaughter, for they (the girl and the farmhand) might yet steal the pig from the shed.

Preserved in the hiding place at Łazińsk is an interesting example of various forms of a peculiar sapping of the morale of the German home front. It is a planted fake of a document appointing its addressee as a reproducer, who is to "service 9 women and 18 girls" in order to raise the birth statistics. (Probably in the area it was known that Gustav Adolf had for some time been looking around for a candidate for a wife). The authors note that this honorable task cannot be protested against by the wife and will not be recognized as grounds for divorce.

The "official paper" is an example of fictitious, misleading information and directives produced in the underground and distributed among the Germans. A special unit in the information and propaganda directorate of the AK (Home Army) was occupied with this. It must be added that officials of the SS Main Office of Race and Settlement (RuSHA), responsible for the purity and propagation of the Germanic race, carried out a kind of selection among the slaves sent to labor in Germany, qualifying selected men as so-called race men (rasowcy).

Bruno's letters from November already come from Finland. Addressed to Parkkino (the Petsamo region) in the far north. The field post number 31 059 indicates that Bruno served in the 136th Mountain Rifle Regiment. He sends his sister money saved from his pay as a present on the occasion of her approaching birthday. In the package there is also a jar, into which he placed several little bunches of berries found between the snow and the ice. On 8 November, when he writes these words, it is the 10th anniversary of Mama's death. He was at a Catholic field mass. "There, too, one can hear a worthwhile word". Later, as was his custom, he went into the forest to pray and to read the Gospel of St. Matthew appointed for that Sunday: "For many are called, but few are chosen" (Mt 22:14). Great and solemn words, which he passes on to his sister for another, new year of life.

A few days later he writes to his brother. He knows that thanks to his letters to his sisters and father, Gustav is up to date with news from Finland, but he prefers that they write to each other directly. What gladdens him above all is the news of another deferment. He believes that Gustav can accomplish more for the common good on the spot than as a recruit. The fact that he is a teacher would have no significance at the beginning of service. Just as Bruno will be a "Barras" and treated accordingly. He himself remembers that time as very hard, and everyone must go through it. He survived that difficult time; now

Many German writers worked on producing entire series of books intended for Wehrmacht soldiers. These were the so-called Feldpost-Bücher. "Anthologies were published containing a fascist-nationalist mixture intended to provide entertainment, some form of spiritual sustenance, and above all ideological, National Socialist support". On orders from above, no doubt, the "sponsors" of such editions for their compatriots were regions or cities. An example may be the one mentioned by Hubert Orłowski in Literatura w III Rzeszy (Literature in the Third Reich) – Der Posener Türmer. Ein Gruß an die Kameraden im Felde (The Watchman of the Poznań Tower. Greetings to Comrades in the Field), which on the order of the Mayor of Poznań the publisher NS-Gauverlag Wartheland brought out for Christmas and New Year 1943/1944. What could one read in these works? Well, the individual is nothing! "Since the Leader sacrifices himself for all of us and for Germany, it is likewise necessary to sacrifice oneself for Germany and blindly devote oneself to the Leader".
