(In Pieczenga, the former Finnish Petsamo, where Private Bruno Mielke was stationed and fought, there is a cemetery where "Unseren 12 000 Toten Kameraden" lie).

It is not difficult to find in the soldiers' letters quoted here those Nazi canons, stated outright and repeated many times. At times, however, one can get the impression that this is done mechanically, without any reflection, even a hidden one. Mielke volunteers for a medic's course. He does so, as he writes, for two reasons: such skills may prove useful for a lifetime, and secondly, he hopes that in this field promotion will come more easily to him. Latin will come in handy here, which he continually studies in his free moments with a view to studies in Vienna. He is also fully aware that "the medical service is not easy and no less dangerous in time of battle, since it must be at the front and dress the wounds – but it is all the more beautiful for that. […] If the war were to last until next summer, I shall be able to prove myself in action, but I am not afraid. I have a very strong faith". For now – in comparison with last winter – this winter, should nothing extraordinary happen, will be lighter. Of course, if the Russians push too far forward, then all those stationed in the rear will be called up to help.

 Ibid., p. 196.

 Nowadays, in the territory of the Russian Pieczenga [formerly Finnish Petsamo], where the XIX Mountain Corps, which included Bruno Mielke's unit, waged its battles, there are many monuments. Above all, there is a new cemetery (Friedhof, Kładiszcze) built in the years 2000/2001 (in the place of dozens of rows of wooden crosses) for the 12,000 mountain riflemen, infantry soldiers, airmen and sailors who fell in the fighting. UNSEREN 12 000 TOTEN KAMERADEN. On 23 stone slabs are engraved the known names of all who perished there. The bilingual inscription on one of the plaques states that the cemetery-monument came into being thanks to the efforts of the veterans from the Alpine countries, who thank and are grateful to the Russian veterans for their help. A separate plaque commemorates EISMEERFRONT 1941-1944 [the fighting on the Arctic Ocean front]. On a nearby hill the Russians erected a dominant monument dedicated to their soldiers who fought in defence of the Fatherland on the subpolar, Arctic lands.
slowinski2023/80:
So for the time being he is doing well. Sleeping, clothing and food are fine. He is even surprised "how they transport all of it so far, to this wild region". And one more astonishing request. Someone stole 25 safety pins from his medical bag. He asks – if they can – that they be sent to him. He will put them back in, and in this way he will not have to report the theft.

It is worth paying attention to the dense correspondence which Bruno Mielke conducts. And it is not merely his "privilege". The OKW – the High Command of the Wehrmacht – attached great importance to the smooth functioning of the field post. It was believed that frequent contact of the soldiers with home, with their loved ones, raised morale in the army, and also had a positive influence on the mood in the families, that is, on the home front. Regardless of where he was stationed on the distant eastern front, in Finland or Norway, the letters circulated efficiently and as a rule reached their addressee. From reading them one can infer that there were no particular restrictions as to the number of postcards or letters sent. What was rigorously observed, however, were weight and formats. Mail to the front reached the battalion, where it was distributed to the companies, for those units were best informed about the whereabouts of the addressee.

Almost two weeks before Christmas, on 12 December 1943, on another Sunday, Mielke writes from "his cozy little medical room". In this time, when services are being held in all the churches, he can again lead his soul to where it feels best and where it will find untroubled peace. "How this certainty of the deep grace of God fills me with strength and joy". There is no good news for home. He cannot count on leave during the Holidays. The long queue of those senior to him still stands before him. Perhaps they will let him go in January, "which may mean a long cold journey, but others too travel in winter, alive there and back, so I suppose I shall endure it as well". He corresponds constantly with candidates for a wife. At present with two: one – a neighbor from Konary
slowinski2023/81:
– pretty and intelligent, but not a believer; the second a Volksdeutsche (ethnic German). The first began writing to him from Wallensen. Somewhat unintelligently. "But one thing is certain for me: I will not marry before I find a believing girl". He must have the guarantee of a deep communion – especially since in the future he is to become a pastor.

Apart from that, everything is well – also in the military respect. When he compares the lot of his comrades fighting in the south or with his own last winter, things are so far 50 percent better and more beautiful. But the beautiful time can end any day. "Thus our commander said recently – the front from the Arctic Ocean [Eismeer] to Italy can at any moment become open". As a Christmas present he sends to the family the splendid little book Der Weg des Glaubens [The Way of Faith] received from Hamburg. "Write often". Their commander knew what he was talking about. As early as January 1944 the determined offensive of the Red Army set out, whose aim was the lifting of the blockade of Leningrad – which took place on 27 January 1944. The Russian attacks forced Army Group North into retreat. They withdrew to the region of Lake Peipus (now on the border of Estonia and Russia). Bruno Mielke's unit belonged to this formation. In the south, at the same time, an offensive set out which over the following five months would bring the liberation of Ukraine, Volhynia and the Crimea. Still at the end of 1943, in the days from 28 November to 1 December, there takes place in Tehran the meeting of the leaders of the great coalition – Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin.

The next letter that has survived bears the date of 2 March 1944. Bruno reassures his loved ones that they need not be afraid needlessly. "After a heavy week on duty we have, thanks to God's graciousness, quiet days so far. Every day is like a feast, like a present. And if the Lord sends heavy days again, then He will also graciously help to bear their burden. Only to hold out until Easter, and we shall have the winter behind us. Perhaps by the next one we shall already have peace. But since that
slowinski2023/82:
hour has not yet come, we wish to continue faithfully fulfilling our duty, in order to help bring about victory". On the seventh of March the writing was interrupted by an alarm. "We must set out, hard days will come again". (The letter reached Łazińsk on 23 March 1944, from field post 31 059E – the number assigned to the 136th regiment of the 2nd Mountain Rifle Division, 10th company).

The letter written before Easter, 12 March 1944, reaches Łazińsk as early as 17 March! Within five days the mail travels from the distant Finnish north to the village hidden in the forests of Podzagórze. He writes on a Sunday in the penitential season. "How once more God's kindness crowned me, in that He granted me (us) a free and peaceful Sunday, so that in its holy morning hours I might read His holy gospel and then find a quiet place in the sunny, snowy solitude and join the invisible community of prayer in heaven and on earth". Further on he thanks the Lord that He has brought such wonderful, dear people into his life: his parents, his brother, his sisters. "The cross of Golgotha in this exceptional time allows us – sinners – to lay down all our burdens and to become pure and without blemish". This is an important and strong sentence. Soldier Mielke grants himself full absolution.

From everyday life he can report that he is healthy, that he enjoys a good appetite, and he encloses stamps for packages in which he hopes to find "pączken" (pączki – doughnuts). The Russians are not conducting any major operations. For several days they had a combat alert, sleeping in their uniforms and with full equipment, but the comrades at the front managed without their help. Although he knows that in the fifth year of the war there may be hardships and one must husband what one has, if it were possible, he asks that five-fingered gloves be sent to him. He has two-fingered mittens – so his hands do not freeze – but the multi-fingered ones are more useful.

From the next letter that has survived we learn that this correspondence was extraordinarily intensive. If things are relatively quiet, he writes once a week, and if
slowinski2023/83:
the situation is more tense, twice a week! He asks his brother not to burden himself with writing to him every day. A week earlier they were withdrawn to the rear – 70 km from the front. "Here it is nicer and more comfortable than in the previous place. The barracks are spacious and airy. For a whole week now we have been wallpapering and working on beautifying them. The cold and the darkness no longer weary us so much. A little heating suffices, and at 11 o'clock at night it is still light. Soon there will be no night. Outside there is a thaw, and in some places last year's moss is showing". In the next paragraph he shares with his brother joyful news. Namely, on 20 April, on the Führer's birthday, he was promoted to the rank of corporal (Obergefreiter). True, after two years of service it is nothing great, but dear to the heart all the same. He also treats it as a testimony of the grace of God, which blessed his service and above all preserved him from all obstacles. As a corporal he also held his first service in the melting snow. A clump of moss served him as an altar. "This hour in solitude allows one to see one's own weaknesses". He is also saddened by the sight of his chums drinking and carousing all night long. He is almost ashamed that he sits here in the north and listens to the murmur of the pines, while his Kameraden (comrades) must fight heavy battles on the southern front. "Compared with them – we are on furlough here", and he adds at once – "may it not get worse". He is also lucky with his superiors. The commander of his company is Oberleutnant Hengl. He is the son of the lieutenant general Ritter von Hengl, commanding the 2nd Mountain Rifle Division.

 General of Mountain Troops Georg Ritter von Hengl was a distinguished professional officer. During the First World War he fought, among other things, at Verdun and in Russia. Later, as an aviator, he shot down 10 English aircraft. For his war merits as an aviator, in his native kingdom of Bavaria he was granted the title of lifelong nobility, which was connected with adding the appellation Ritter von to his surname. During the Second World War he took part in the campaign on the Arctic front in Russia. In 1943 he commanded the 2nd Mountain Division, and in the year 1944 – during the period from which Bruno Mielke's letters have been preserved – he commanded the XIX Mountain Corps. They were stationed in the area of Petsamo/Pieczenga. These were the last days,

An important question is posed, one that says a great deal about Bruno's spiritual formation. "Is this not a sign of her dubious inner state? Is this not the first sad fruit of 'Germania' with the spirit and 'religion' taken over from Hans?" A few words about what so troubles the writer.

In the 1930s, Nazism became a kind of political religion. Most of German society, unfortunately, believed in the dogmas proclaimed with extraordinary effectiveness in Goebbels's propaganda. It was a sinister mixture of myth and antihumanism. After the First World War, the crisis expressed itself not only in the economic and social sphere, as evidenced by the erupting revolutions and uprisings. The crisis and a marked weakening of influence also affected Christianity. In its place, the idea of nationalism was entering with growing force, taking in Germany the form of völkisch ideology, from the word Volk – nation. The primacy of "race," "society," "nation" over the rights of the individual held sway. The strongest race – the Aryan race – had the right of precedence, even one wrested by force. In this mixture of Nazi, chauvinist moods and various forms of occultism, there also ran a strong criticism of Christianity. It was judged that this religion stood in opposition to the National Socialist ideology,
slowinski2023/86:
for it "was not a religion of the sword". There is no place in it for heroes, for the "Übermensch," the overman. Christians are people guided by the principles of mercy, love of neighbor, penitents... It is the religion of weak people, whose canon of laws cannot apply to a true Germanic man. As one could read outright in the letter of one of the girls to Bruno Mielke quoted above, the Church acts against the Reich and the Führer. The realities of everyday life in the Nazi world forced Christians into conduct that allowed them to survive. But only that? For example, the organization Deutsche Christen [German Christians] was founded – who accepted the suggestions of Nazi ideologues about the chosen character of the German nation. There were also found experts on the Bible proving that Christ was an Aryan...

In Gustav's letter of 1 May 1942 one can find the "fruit" of these fairly widely proclaimed teachings. He writes about the times of Christ: "Should wise people then have lived at all and stopped God, and said: What are You doing, choose the Savior from the Germanic people, not from among the Jews. But it pleased God thus." In May 1942 in Zagórów and the vicinity there was no longer a single Jew. And all those who die faithful to their leader are to be counted as martyrs. This is only a very brief reminder of what the idea of Germania was.

We return to Bruno's letter. He fears whether his sister has taken over from her husband the faith in the new religion. In this "religion" even the concept of the soul was distorted in such a way as to serve as another element of propaganda. The soul in the thinking of national Christianity was to strive to fulfill the divine plan, in which Germany – the nation chosen by God – was to heal and make the world happy. This deep disquiet at the behavior of his sister, who had not been seen in church for a long time, is also a clear, though not directly expressed declaration. His sister faces eternal damnation if she does not turn back in time. Bruno Mielke rejects the new religion with all the might of a faithful Christian. He considers it a road to the perdition of man. A betrayal of God. If in the series of letters available to us he always renews his declaration of fidelity and faith in the Führer, of readiness to serve the nation and of the greatest sacrifices, then in each of these letters there will also be found many, sometimes very emotional, assurances of submission to God. He writes: "We gladly wish to do everything for the Führer and the fatherland, but to become a traitor and a Judas to ourselves and our conscience, and to the Lord of all lords – that is something no one may demand, and which a reasonable man (certainly also the Führer) will not demand. If they (those overzealous improvers of the world) do not want us as we are, do not want to have need of us, then let them 'release' us. It is better to follow this simple, ordinary life than to remain with a broken conscience and without moral support in this bloody – serious period"!

He therefore congratulates his brother that, despite being honored with important offices, he wants to remain faithful to his faith, that he does not do as many did, who for a miserable Judas's payment sold their Lord. "It may not please someone that, in accordance with our

slowinski2023/88:
conscience, we seek in our dear, unsullied Church inner care and strength." We do not have to choose (presumably it was expected of the brother that upon taking office he would sign some ideological declarations?), "we have already fought in the difficult period of Poland, and woe to us if we depart from our so clearly defined path. The decision, therefore, lies on the other side: whether they will allow faithful people to work, or whether they will want to get rid of them." (Presumably the second option was chosen, for from another letter it is known that Gustav was soon called up for service in the navy.) "Now, when the time is dangerous, we must remain with the Lord. Our fate and that of our people is in His hands. Before the war, 'in the difficult period of Poland,' we persevered in the faith, whereas in the young Wartheland everyone became intoxicated with 'the new fame.' They abandoned it and fell far away." This "weakening" in participation in services was also described in his letter by Pastor Gross. Bruno confesses that he too was not free of this sin. However, at this moment, when the Lord has granted them the grace of conversion and forbearance, "we want to fight knightly, unto blood," so that nothing bad befalls them.

Bruno Mielke writes the letter in the first days of May 1944. It is striking that the remarks concerning the course of the war were not challenged by the censorship. Could this "loosening" of control perhaps be evidence of broader moods in the army? Never before in the writings available to us had he noted considerations of this kind. Although he does not write it outright, he nevertheless tries to prepare his loved ones "for the worst" – that is, the occupation of the Wartheland by the troops advancing from the East. "The war situation gives me much to think about. We want to fight and struggle to the last – but must we not look at the dangers – precisely as realistically and soberly looking Germans? I do not want to see the lament, the tears, the suffering that will befall our nation if the threatening dangers come to pass! How will they, the liberated Poles, then treat you, the poorest of you! May God give us the strength to endure and preserve us from misfortune! But perhaps God already wishes to bring
slowinski2023/89:
all matters to an end, then it is indeed not impossible. And therefore we should persevere in the faith, then even the greatest worries will not overtake us." There is also another thought-provoking sentence. "We also wish to forgive those and ask (for grace) for them whom we, by our conduct, have offended and in this way endangered their souls." The letter ends with a candid confession that shivers run through him at the thought that he once urged his brother to move to Konin! "It is the grace of God that in this time heading toward destruction we have this quiet island." He wishes "that they may live through in Łazińsk many sunny and happy days...".

This and other letters show how profoundly the war destroyed, and at the same time laid bare, the complicated sense of national identity, the consciousness of one's own roots, but also of simple human decency, of many German settlers. For we often read about the "wonderfully simple and thereby beautiful childhood," the joyful days spent in Łazińsk, while at the same time Mielke writes that before the war this was for them the "difficult period of Poland." There is in these stories a strange alienation, a peculiar extraterritoriality of the land that nourished them. The system of "values" that Nazi ideologues had been instilling into the Germans for years and that came to reign in the conquered Wartheland shakes or suppresses, in these pious people, the age-old moral order built on the biblical Ten Commandments. There is not a word of protest against what the authority does, whose orders are diligently carried out. They made their neighbors into slaves, they killed patriots, they plundered their homes and land, and still they believe that "in this time heading toward destruction," on this ruin of former ideals, they will preserve their sunny land.

This is a very important and dramatic image of a man embedded, through a cruel and ruthless system, in ultimate situations, a man cornered by great history. For the family members to whom he wrote, such repeated declarations of a man who had fought for many months on the front line and claimed that everything that befell him happened "by the grace
slowinski2023/90:
of God" must have carried a weight and a force of arguments not to be gainsaid. For this is noticeable – even in this relatively modest group of letters – that regardless of whether he is marching to the East to build the promised paradise, or retreating under the growing pressure of the enemy, he never gives a sign that he is undergoing a crisis of faith. Still his chief dream is to become a pastor, to celebrate masses and other rites and to proclaim the word of God. "It is not out of the question that God will have to lead us all through very difficult roads." He did not abandon his God for the new "filthy" faith. But – and this observation is worth raising – the image of the Christian: the tiny, humble "servant of God," mocked by Nazi propaganda, does not quite agree with what we perceive in the stance of this soldier. He fights on the front line, kills enemies and lice, is tough and does not want to be worse or weaker than his comrades. He differs, perhaps, from some of them in that he sees, or only senses, the coming days of defeat. In this sense one may venture the remark that he did not walk those bad roads in darkness. Another matter is whether the light that shone for him was bright to the very end.

Reading Bruno Mielke's letters, one has the impression that they were written in two languages. Personal experiences, concern for the family, confessional declarations – this is vocabulary drawn from the Bible, religious writings and sentimental ballads about love. Here even the descriptions of the side he is fighting against do not "reek" of hatred. These are Russians, opponents, in the sharpest version the enemy. And the pre-war times are an idyllic picture of "blessed hours" and the happy inhabitants of Łazińsk. Quite different phrases flow when he declares fidelity and obedience to the Führer, readiness for every sacrifice for the great Germany that is setting the world to rights. This is a set of ready-made clichés from the language of the Third Reich (LTI – Lingua Tertii Imperii).

The last of the surviving letters is dated 14 May 1944 in Norway. They must therefore have been transferred fairly quickly to an entirely new place. The field post number 48 341
slowinski2023/91:
remained the same. The letter went by airmail, as attested by the Luftfeldpost stamps stuck on the envelope. This is interesting information in the context of what was to happen three months later. For on 4 September the Finns halted their participation in the fighting against the Red Army, and on the 19th of that month an armistice was signed between the USSR and Finland. One of its conditions was the participation of Finnish troops in an offensive against the German troops, which were withdrawing from Lapland to Norway. And so it happened. From 15 September the Finns are already fighting on the side of the Allies, together with their former and quite recent enemy: the Red Army. In October the operation of the Red Army – as it was named, the Petsamo–Kirkenes Operation – will set in motion with full force, as a result of which the German 20th Mountain Army was pushed out of the northern territories of Norway and Finland. Bruno writes: "How it will be for me here and how far my wishes will be fulfilled here remains in God's hands. His will has led me here, to His guidance I wish to continue to entrust myself."

How does he understand his part in this war? As an act of divine will. Is this war, then, also the work of God?

From the company in which he had served until recently, he was suddenly transferred to the medical company. He writes the letter, as usual, on Sunday afternoon. In the holy morning hours they had known no peace. They had to scrub the rooms and clean their weapons. Just before dinner he managed to slip away to a quiet place for "the eternal word." The last sentences of this letter, the last sentences of the 33-year-old Bruno Mielke that have reached us, are the words of a man who seems to perceive the whole tragedy of war. In them there is also a muffled trace that something is beginning to stir in his conscience. "When I returned, two pretty, small fair-haired Norwegian girls shyly approached our soldiers' kitchen with a vessel, to be given something. To my joy I still had with me a roll of sugar sweets (Zuckerchen). I gave them to the smaller of them, who, like her sister, wore on her neck a little box with a Christian cross. The quiet 'thank you very much' and the bright gaze of the blue children's
slowinski2023/92:
eyes was a thanksgiving for me. I would not want to see this child again! (I quietly prayed for this). This and the preceding community of prayer bring peace into the heart, a peace which the world does not know and cannot give".

Appendix

Łazińsk – The Village's History Spans More Than 280 Years

Note in: Der Heimatbote, 8/81–3. Card index Wartheland (Kraj Warty), Poland 
Translated by Jacek Kin

Łazińsk is a village formerly in the Konin county, in which the German population lived for the most part. Heading from the county town Konin along the Warta toward the southwest, after some time one reached the commune of Drommin (Trąbczyn), to which, besides the village of Michalinów, belonged the settlement of Łazińsk, inhabited almost exclusively by Germans. Until the year 1945, some 170 German families still lived there. It was the year 1718 when 14 German families arrived from Silesia with their village headman at their fore, and from the owner of the landed estate of Trąbczyn they received a large forest area in order to develop it. From heavy pioneering work there arose the village of Łazińsk "from a green root" (aus grüner Wurzel). The families living here were called: Kuhn, Merk, Schönfisch, Haupt. These surnames were still encountered in this region until the year 1945, and can be found many times on the ancestors' chart of the Weber/Rhytthammer family.

In the year 1968, the German settlement could have celebrated the 250th anniversary of its existence, had history taken a different course.
slowinski2023/96:
To the left of the cantoral school, on a gently rising hillock, there lay a richly wooded cemetery, on which our forefathers founded the first grave in the year 1727. The most ancient place of rest, whose weathered and rotted gravestones of wood and iron existed still until the year 1945. The colonists built their own school quite early, and at the same time a house of prayer, and before long Łazińsk, numbering 150 inhabitants, became the largest cantorate in the later commune of Zagórów (Hinterberg). The cantor in Łazińsk not only taught, but also held the Sunday services. Until 1933, instruction and services took place in the old building. Under the direction of the then teacher and cantor [Gustav] Mielke, a new building was erected, which served as both school and house of prayer. The Polish authorities allowed him to carry on his activity for four years, until he was transferred to Galicia because of his overzealousness in cultivating Germanness.

As a result of the German attack in September 1939 and the German Wehrmacht's victory over the Polish army, the Polish state ceased to exist for the second time after twenty years of existence. Among the consequences of this were, among other things, displacements, which, however, did not directly affect Łazińsk. The courageous attitude of the Polish and German inhabitants prevented the plundering of German farms by Poles as well as the expulsion of Polish farmers from their holdings. At that time more pupils attended the school at Łazińsk than ever before. Teacher Mielke, too, taught again at this school from 1940. Besides him, his sister taught there, as well as two young teachers from Thuringia. The school was now attended by 153 children. More Germans lived in the area than before; these were Germans who had arrived from the Reich (Reichsdeutsche), as well as resettlers from Volhynia and from other regions. At the end 

 In the letters of Bruno and Gustav Mielke we find information about the search for better, that is to say: richer, farms of Poles to be taken over, as well as instructions on the "short keeping" of Polish slaves.

Łazińsk – A Contemporary Note

At the present time, the former Łazińsk, whose name often underwent various "modifications", exists within the boundaries of the Zagórów commune, Słupca county, in the form of two villages.

Łazińsk Pierwszy

The village was founded in 1746. The initiators of its founding were Andrzej and Paweł Prusińscy. To this day it is a model example of an Olęder village that has preserved its original spatial layout: farm buildings, a mosaic of fields, forests, meadows, canals and field roads. There are numerous wooden, clay and bog-iron-ore buildings. In the years 1975-1998 the locality administratively belonged to the Konin voivodeship.

On the territory of the village there are the remains of an Evangelical cemetery with scant remains of gravestones.

> Wikipedia, accessed 23.10.2023 at 14.10.

The village numbers 159 inhabitants.

> Data of the Office of the Town and Commune of Zagórów dated 23.10.2023.

Łazińsk Drugi (formerly: Holendry Łazińskie, Holendry Stara Huta)

A village in Poland situated in the Greater Poland Voivodeship, in Słupca county, in the Zagórów commune.

The village was founded as an Olęder settlement. At the beginning of the 18th century a glassworks based on the local resources of glass sand operated in the village. In 1943 the Hitlerites opened a bog-iron-ore mine here. The village has a dispersed character.

1. Introduction

The Pyzdry Forest is an area with a superbly preserved Olęder heritage, notable for its large number of old farmsteads, often built of bog iron ore.

What sets this area apart for the better is a local style of architecture with many features in common.

The Pyzdry Forest stretches over several communes: Blizanów, Chocz, Gizałki, Grodziec, Mycielin, Pyzdry, Rychwał, Rzgów, Stawiszyn and Zagórów.

It is an exceptionally interesting area in cultural terms. On a relatively small area a distinctive cultural landscape grew up over the centuries, the result of the changes made by settlers who came not only from Polish lands but above all by Olęder settlers, who began to arrive here from the eighteenth century. The settlers, who came from various German lands and from Silesia, brought with them a cultural baggage which, in contact with the local substance and the conditions of the environment, led to the forming of a distinctive culture. For years the population of Olęder and of Polish descent lived side by side, and only the events that followed the Second World War brought great changes. The Olęders living in these lands were partly resettled, and in their place came settlers from various parts of Poland and people from the neighbouring regions. In time this mixture of population came to identify itself with the area. The new inhabitants of the Pyzdry Forest lived in the old Olęder houses, grew used to the conditions in which they had come to live, and slowly merged with the social fabric they had found.

1.1. The aim of the research and its method

In recent years, since the change of political system and the end of direction from above, we see in many fields the stirring of local communities in search of their own identity.

This project belongs to that current. It aims to help the inhabitants of the region to judge the value of their own historical and cultural heritage, and the value of their architecture together with their native landscape, both natural and built.

Specialists experienced in each field carried out interdisciplinary fieldwork. Ethnographic research (interviews based on a questionnaire) and research on the material heritage (an inventory of the monuments of folk culture: village architecture, churches, small peasant and religious structures, and cemeteries), extended by the reconstruction of local histories, tales and legends, proved exceptionally important in establishing the cultural identity of the inhabitants.

In the planned fieldwork, carried out in the villages of the Pyzdry Forest, the present state of the inhabitants’ sense of cultural identity was in part recorded: who they feel themselves to be, how far
szwiec2009/7:
they identify with the district where they have often lived for more than fifty years; and an attempt was made to find traces of the old Olęder settlers in the Pyzdry Forest.

Regional architecture, in the sense of architecture with definite features, existed in the so-called “Pyzdry Forest” until the end of the 1940s. Later central planning and the promotion of “ready-made designs” of houses and farms imposed from above destroyed for many years the achievement of past generations of the region’s inhabitants. These designs were meant for the whole country, and any regional adaptation touched only their parts, not the whole of the scheme.

Part of the architecture with regional features that still exists today is losing its original function with the economic, social and political changes, and is undergoing an inevitable process of decay, rebuilding or even complete removal.

Details are altered under the influence of fashions and various tendencies. The composition of the settlements is being destroyed by infill building – the filling of gaps with forms often culturally alien, or with buildings of a purely productive and technical character, rooted in no architectural tradition. There is a fear that through this process the groups of settlement preserved until now will within a few decades be made uniform and lose their regional features.

Universal globalisation shows itself in a free flow of disordered information – in other words, in a chaos of information – which touches this field too. Numerous publications and periodicals on architecture, small structures, and landscape architecture, often reduced to garden architecture, give their readers fragmentary knowledge and pass over the complex relations of architecture and landscape. They often present questions without their regional context, and they set patterns that many builders imitate.

In this situation it is necessary both to create a catalogue of architectural forms describing the relations in the existing landscape and to take broader action, such as the administrative protection of the existing regional architecture and spatial planning that is conscious of, and follows, the principles by which that architecture was made. Urban-planning studies that take account of regional distinctness will allow the whole region to develop harmoniously and in proportion.

The knowledge of the features of traditional architecture, of its relation to the landscape and of their mutual influence, must be gathered and preserved. In the long term this may help to create a “style, that is, a so-called school of regional architecture.” A contemporary architecture must arise, suited to the present needs of the inhabitants but growing out of the native building tradition.

The aim of the research was to look for a regional style, and to show the relations of the landscape and their influence on the local architecture and on the rise of a regional style.
szwiec2009/8:
In search of this style, architectural and landscape features representing every phase of the development of architectural forms in the area studied were examined. Both existing buildings and those already rebuilt or wholly destroyed were analysed.

1.2. Gathering the source material, and the fieldwork

The study of rebuilt and vanished buildings was possible thanks to conservation records, archival material and other sources. For these buildings an inspection on the spot was also needed in every case.

The starting material for the report was maps, photographs of architecture, aerial photographs, sketches from nature and surveys (plans and elevations), as well as archival material and local and specialist publications of various kinds (on architecture, urban planning, ethnography and the conservation of monuments). This material was obtained in the course of the research. An analytical method was adopted. The research was carried out directly in the field, in archives and by interviews. Detailed photographic and drawn records and surveys were made. On the basis of the source, cultural and historical data gathered, a catalogue was made of valuable existing buildings with regional features. These buildings were located in the field and analysed, and the conclusions were put into graphic form. Comparative studies were made of the architectural and landscape elements typical of the “Pyzdry Forest”. The catalogue contains general and detailed maps marking where the buildings studied stand, sets of photographs, freehand sketches, drawn analyses and surveys of individual buildings. Maps, archival photographs and written archival sources were analysed and set against reality and against the photographs, drawings and surveys made by the research team.

1.3. The area of the research

The area studied is the communes of Blizanów, Chocz, Gizałki, Grodziec, Mycielin, Pyzdry, Rychwał, Rzgów, Stawiszyn and Zagórów, which lie in the “Pyzdry Forest”.

It is an area with a common cultural landscape, which coincides with the so-called “Pyzdry Forest”.

The research covered the whole area of the so-called “Pyzdry Forest”. The buildings in the following places, with the land around them, were studied in detail in the field and compared with topographical maps (military staff maps at the scales 1:100,000, 1:50,000 and 1:25,000, and topographical maps at 1:100,000, 1:50,000, 1:25,000 and 1:10,000), modern and archival, with the orthophotomap, and with aerial and satellite photographs: Czarny Bród, Dolne Grądy,
szwiec2009/9:
Jarantów, Jarantów Kolonia, Józefów, Kolonia Obory, Królewiny, Lipe, Nowa Kaźmierka, Nowolipsk, Nowy Olesiec, Orlina, Ruda Komorska, Ruda Wieczyńska, Stara Kaźmierka, Trąbczyn, Walga, Wierzchy, Wrąbczynek, Wrąbczynkowskie Holendry, Wronów, Zapowiednia.

Each place was first studied in the field in general terms. At this stage buildings were chosen for detailed study, which was then carried out.

In studying each village the following questions were taken into account: the village’s position in relation to the neighbouring towns, the plan of the settlement, its internal network of tracks and its relation to the road network, the original division of the plots, the layout of the buildings on the homestead, the existing greenery, that is, trees, crops, farmyard planting, orchards and gardens, and woods among the fields, and the natural and altered network of waters.

The research on the architectural fabric of town and village covered the spatial structure of the region, which is made up of its urban and architectural composition and of spatial relations and their mutual influence, in the context of the semantics of space in the broad sense.

1.4. The results expected.

The project aims to gather and preserve knowledge of the regional features of the existing architecture, of its relation to the landscape and of their mutual influence.

The scientific aim of the project is to carry out research on the architectural fabric of town and village, covering urban and architectural composition, spatial relations and their mutual influence, in the context of the semantics of space in the broad sense. The most important result of the research is to be the “discovery” of the regional features of the existing architecture by describing, comparing and evaluating it, and by making
szwiec2009/10:
sample design proposals. The aim is to create guidelines that may become suggestions for those who make regional architecture. It matters that the work should show regional architecture in a broad visual and scientific (physiographic and historical) context.

Publishing the project will let the report reach a suitably wide circle of people, some of whom have, in varying degrees, an influence on the relation between building and landscape. It may change attitudes to their own heritage, lead them to appreciate the qualities of the region’s architecture and its particular character, and to see the physiographic relations in areas transformed by settlement.

In the longer term it may help to save the valuable architectural fabric that exists, understood not only as houses and buildings but also as the relations of the landscape. The research carried out made it possible to document the technique of building “houses of iron”, that is, of bog iron ore, found in this region.

Given the progressive decay and disappearance of regional elements in architecture and landscape, it may be supposed that any further delay in carrying out wide-ranging research in this area may affect the survival of many culturally valuable elements of regional architecture.

Rescue work on existing historic buildings is possible even today. The LEADER+ programme allows to a large extent the co-financing of the repair of roofs and elevations made in traditional technologies that are now dying out, such as roofing with straw or reed, or outer walls – elevations made of bog iron ore. With funds obtained in this way a building can also be modernised by replacing its damaged window and door joinery with new joinery of the traditional proportions and divisions.

The conclusions of the interdisciplinary research are necessary for a full understanding of the relations of the landscape and are needed for the design of new undertakings. The project is addressed both to conservators, planners and architects and to the local community. It is needed because it will also allow the regional features of the man-made landscape of this district to be given their due place in the national heritage.

1.5. How the project was carried out

The project “THE PYZDRY FOREST – The Olęders and their Iron Houses” is addressed to the inhabitants of the communes of Blizanów, Chocz, Gizałki, Grodziec, Mycielin, Pyzdry, Rychwał, Rzgów, Stawiszyn and Zagórów, which lie in the “Pyzdry Forest”.

Once published, the report that results from the research may let many inhabitants see the regional features in the existing architecture, and help to keep its character unchanged.

The project as prepared presents regional architecture. It rests on the research carried out in the area of the “Pyzdry Forest”. Source, cultural and historical data were gathered. The research was done in the field: detailed photographic and drawn records and surveys of many buildings were made. The buildings studied were placed in space, and the existing spatial relations were analysed.

Each of the regions of Greater Poland has its own cultural and historical identity, which arises from the sum of the traditions and experiences of its inhabitants and of their cultural and material achievement. Becoming aware of these differences will let the inhabitants of the region keep their own identity in an age of universal globalisation and uniformity.

These regions are relatively easy to mark off in those parts of Greater Poland whose boundaries are set apart by geography.

The whole area of settlement is bounded and divided by forests and natural barriers of the landscape. These are, for example, regulated watercourses that were once natural (though today they are hard to tell apart in the field from the dense network of drainage canals made when the forest lands were brought into use). The natural barrier formed by compact tracts of forest is for the most part a remnant of the original forest (understood as places where woods grow, for the woods, and above all the peasants’ woods, were and are intensively used).

Settlement in the Pyzdry Forest in the Old Polish period went with the industrial use of its riches and the bringing of the land taken up under the plough, advancing into it in the wake of the clearing of the woods as far as the soils and communications allowed. Land of middling fertility was taken up, mostly sandy loam, well enough watered and easy to till. On its edge arose settlements tied to the use of the forest (Wrąbczyn), service villages (Obory), ore-mining and glassworks settlements – Ruda Komorska, Ruda Wieczyńska, Huta Trąbczyńska, Huta Łukomska – and tar-works (Smoliniec).

In modern times settlement in the Pyzdry Forest grew almost twice as fast as in the Middle Ages. For 188 settlements arose here, at least 117 of them in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, though some older ones were deserted, and 71 in the eighteenth century (more precisely, in the years 1701-1793), among which Olęder settlements clearly prevailed (67.6 per cent).

Zbigniew Chodyła, extract from “Settlement in the Pyzdry Forest, from the Middle Ages to the beginning of the twenty-first century”.

2.1. Dwelling houses in the villages of the “Pyzdry Forest”

The architecture of the dwelling houses of the Olęder villages has features in common. They can be found at every stage of its development, and they occur, more or less strongly, over the whole area of settlement in the “Pyzdry Forest”. The dwelling houses have different proportions according to the period in which they were built. The older cottages, however they are set, are of timber construction, log walls with posts, the corners joined with dovetails, with posts into which the beams of the longer walls and those beside the door openings are fixed. Post-and-plank construction is also found, and in villages near deposits of clay, timber framing filled with clay-wrapped staves, or rammed clay. There are also mixed forms, with a clear preference for the “better” and “worse” constructions: timber was held better than clay, and log walls better than post-and-plank or timber framing.

Another material used in this region for building walls is of interest, namely bog iron ore. Building with ore is indeed found in other regions of the country, but nowhere does it occur in such quantity, and nowhere have so many buildings made of it survived.

The oldest surviving cottages in this region are usually small single-pile, single-storey buildings with a separate entrance hall and a black kitchen on the axis of the broad front. In the less common one-and-a-half-pile and double-pile cottages (usually the larger buildings) there appears a purlin beam, a kind of wooden girder carrying ceiling beams that are too long. Occasionally its end can be seen in the gable (set off-centre along the wall, at distances of 1:2).

The gables (mostly boarded, clad with vertical boards) are mostly set flush with the wall of the ground floor. In that case an eaves board is nailed to the ends of the wall-plate beams that stand out beyond the face of the wall (mostly cut off at an angle of 45⁰). This board is set horizontally, sloping at an angle of 45⁰, at the height of the top edge of the gable wall, and further supported by brackets, sometimes decoratively cut, in varying numbers.

Gables projecting beyond the face of the gable wall by the width of the outermost ceiling beam are also found. This was done by pushing the last truss outwards and resting it on the projecting end of the wall plate or the purlin (the beam carrying the ceiling beams).

The newer houses are all of brick; those of the mid-nineteenth century keep the proportions and look of the earlier timber buildings, also have boarded gables, often with extra doors into the loft, and have no ornament on their elevations.

In some of them it is hard to tell what the construction of their walls really is and what lies under the plaster. The roofs of these buildings have boarded gables

 Unlike the architecture of the Pyzdry Forest, such a construction and a gable set out beyond the gable wall are very often found in the Olęder cottages around Nowy Tomyśl.

2.1.7. The roofs of dwelling houses

The roofs are always pitched, with two symmetrical slopes. Most are constructions at an angle of 40⁰ to 45⁰ set on a broad-fronted building, typical of this region. Buildings with roofs thatched with straw or reed are still found; most buildings now have roofs covered with asbestos-cement sheets (eternit), sometimes with tiles or sheet metal. The rafters mostly rest on ceiling beams projecting beyond the face of the wall, more rarely on a purlin laid on the axis of the wall on the ceiling beams, set off from those ceiling beams.

The construction most often used (bound up with the single-pile plan) is the collar-beam roof. On one-and-a-half-pile and double-pile buildings the construction of the roof trusses is more complicated – mostly a rafter roof on posts (stolcowa).

The roofs are set symmetrically on the building. Their gables are mostly boarded and sometimes have extra doors into the loft.

The roofs of all types of building, both dwelling houses and farm buildings, had no dormer gables.

40. Dwelling house – gable – half-timbered construction – photograph 2009, by Paulina Baranowska.

 The buildings studied that have such a construction are two: one in Dolne Grądy, the other in Wrąbczynkowskie Holędry. Inventory cards 007 and 021.

2.1.8. Windows and doors in dwelling houses

The dwelling houses have rectangular window openings, always set vertically, a “standing” rectangle. The proportions of the windows vary, mostly close to a gentle rectangle (3:4 or 4:5). The windows have composite divisions and are divided by glazing bars into smaller panes. The simplest are single-casement windows (square or a gentle rectangle) divided into four equal panes by bars in the casement. There are also double-casement windows in which each casement is divided into smaller equal panes, two to four of them, or two panes in the proportion 2:3, the smaller pane always at the top. Another, more varied type is the double-casement, side-hung window in four parts, in which the fixed transom is mostly set at a height of 2:3. There are a few exceptions to these rules, for example windows with proportions close to 1:2 upright.

Box windows were used most often. The window joinery was made very simple.

The surviving front doors are of ledged and of frame-and-panel construction, from the simplest, unornamented, in older buildings, to doors more or less ornamented in farms that were once richer, made from the end of the nineteenth century. These last have carved decoration, more elaborate and eclectic, in various forms. The commonest are double doors of many panels with a fanlight, each leaf divided into three or four equal vertical panels, in proportions close to 3:5, and the doors themselves 3:4, or 4 to 4.5 : 6.5 to 7. Newer doors, from the beginning of the twentieth century, are also double and have the proportions 1:2 with a fanlight over the door, the doors themselves 2:3 and ¼, divided into two unequal panels of which the higher is the larger. There are also double doors without a fanlight in the same proportions (2:3 and ¼), and single doors in the same proportions with panes of glass in the upper part of the leaf, the glass divided, for example, into three panes. The division of the whole door is in proportion (glass 1 : 2.5 wooden panels).

2.2. Farm buildings in the villages of the “Pyzdry Forest”

The farm buildings held the rooms for livestock and those that served them, for example fodder rooms or a cart shed. In timber buildings, which prevailed, log construction was used, log construction with posts (in the larger, longer buildings), and post-and-plank. Where clay is plentiful, rammed clay is found, and here and there timber framing filled with clay-wrapped staves. Many farm buildings, like the dwelling houses, were built of bog iron ore.

The last form is the building wholly of brick, and mostly of red brick, unplastered.

The buildings have ground-floor walls built of red fired brick.

2.2.1. The roofs of farm buildings

The single-storey farm buildings have only pitched roofs with two symmetrical slopes, of collar-beam construction, more rarely on posts. The rafters were fixed with tenons and mostly rest on the ceiling beams, which means that there are as many rafters as beams. The outermost trusses are mostly set flush with the gable wall. In buildings of timber with boarded gables, the ends of the wall-plate beams and the wall beneath them were sometimes covered by a horizontal board set at a slant.

Buildings with walls of timber and of clay were roofed with straw or reed, brick ones with tiles of various kinds.

2.2.2. Windows and doors in farm buildings

Because of the building’s use, the window openings in the parts for livestock were made small, and in rooms (where more light was needed) such as workshops or fodder rooms, much larger. At first, in timber buildings, these openings were open or closed only by a wooden shutter. In brick buildings small windows were used, mostly of steel or cast iron, of many panes, with one pane that tilted open, in proportions close to 2:3, straight-headed or with a segmental arch.

Of interest is the use, in buildings of bog iron ore, of window openings with a frame nailed together from boards in the shape of an equilateral triangle.

The doors of farm buildings were made of simple ledged construction, in various proportions according to the kind of room they closed. The larger openings, through which carts passed, were made in proportions close to a square; the smaller, for people only, mostly in the proportions 1:1¾ or 1:2. The door opening was straight or finished at the top with a segmental arch, and the leaves of the door had the same shape. They were made of plain boards set vertically and hung on strap hinges of steel, which sometimes had ornamental ends.

2.3. Architectural detail in the buildings of the “Pyzdry Forest”

The detail of the older dwelling houses and farm buildings, especially those of timber, is very modest and kept to the necessary minimum. Often the only ornament is the patterns on the front doors and the decorative profiles of the ceiling beams in the rooms (mostly in the main room) and of their ends projecting outside the building. Older buildings also had shutters, at first ledged and later panelled.

2.4. Small structures and fences in the villages of the “Pyzdry Forest”

Few original parts survive in the wooden fences that exist today. The reason is that the material does not last. The fences standing now were mostly made after 1945, and so for the most part have nothing to do with the traditional buildings.

Originally the homestead in this region (mostly Olęder) had, besides a paling fence, few small structures, such as wells and a few bread ovens (these stood inside the cottages).

In the older form the wells had wooden sweeps, in the newer often drum windlasses. A few sweeps still survive, especially in the villages deep in the “Pyzdry Forest”.

Bread ovens (only one oven could be recorded in the field) were set at a good distance from the buildings, mostly in the orchard outside the house. It may be supposed that they were found on the farms where new dwelling houses were built, or where the bread ovens inside were done away with when existing buildings were rebuilt. These ovens stood originally in the black kitchen, in the stack of the chimney, and many examples of such ovens, now no longer used, survive.

2.5. Spatial layouts – the plan of the villages.

Because most of the villages arose as marsh row villages passing into scattered settlement, the layout of the farmsteads and their distribution over the land is quite different from that of the older, compact villages on the edges of and outside the Pyzdry Forest (mainly street villages and manor-farm villages).

The whole area of settlement was covered by a dense mesh of farms, and the distances between them follow from the size of the average settler’s plot, 18 to 20 ha, close in shape to a very elongated rectangle.

The arable of such farms was made up of long strips of fields running at right angles to a watercourse or wet ground. The strip ran from the wet field to the dry. All the strips were crossed by a road at right angles to them, which joined the farms. The buildings of each settler were put up near this road; they often lie in rows of several on the same side of it. This way of dividing the land was reasonably fair and in a way evened out the chances of success in farming. As a rule the farms were not, and still are not, joined to one another by roads, for each has roads at right angles to the main road, running the whole length of its land on both sides of the main road.

It is not, however, a typical marsh street village, for some of the farms, because the land was originally wet, were placed on the highest part of the plot, often at some distance from the road, so that they are in a sense scattered.

The character of the region is also shaped by the woods among the fields: deciduous trees and shrubs grow along the drainage ditches, the edges of the roads and the balks.

The villages merge into one great village, in which the farm’s position in relation to the main road decides which village it belongs to.

Each Olęder village had its own cemetery near it, mostly on a hillock or a glacial dune. In some cases these dunes were levelled and shaped. In scattered villages, where there was ground high enough, it was placed near the centre of the village or an important crossroads. In compact villages the cemetery always lies outside the buildings. Mostly there are deciduous trees several hundred years old in it, often oaks, which may remember the time when the cemetery was founded.

5. Summary

The transformation of the native landscape goes on constantly and inevitably, and in recent years we have seen it grow stronger. The rebuilding and modernisation of the village threatens to lose its valuable individual character for the sake of particular universal values, general and often alien, not only in our landscape but even beside other newly built architecture.

The knowledge of the features of traditional architecture, of its relation to the landscape and of their mutual influence, must be gathered and preserved. In the long term this may help to create a “style”, that is, a so-called “school of regional architecture.” A contemporary architecture must arise, suited to the present needs of the inhabitants but growing out of the native building tradition.

In the areas discussed the interdependence of the buildings and the natural environment is plain. The pattern of settlement is closely bound up with the historically formed ways of farming the land: in the classic pattern, manor house – manor farm – farmhands’ cottages – fields, and in the modern one of the Olęder villages and of those founded in the nineteenth century, houses in farmsteads – fields – woods among the fields.

It must be understood that it depends on the inhabitants of the region, who are the builders and the owners of old and new houses, what our surroundings will look like. A very great deal will depend on their decisions about architecture, about the detail of the composition of the landscape, and even about the decoration of buildings.

This should not, however, lead to a kind of artificial open-air-museum treatment of the native architecture: a creative approach to design is needed, one that takes account of regional features, native materials and the proportions of regional buildings.

And what future generations inherit will depend on the inhabitants of the region!

wasicki1953/137:
JAN WĄSICKI

GERMAN COLONISATION IN THE PERIOD OF SOUTH PRUSSIA 1793 – 1806

1. Rural colonisation.

The question of the German colonisation of the Polish lands of the second and third Prussian partitions has not, to this day, been exhaustively studied. The works of bourgeois German historians, and in particular the work of Max Beheim-Schwarzbach, which treats the whole of the Hohenzollerns' colonising activity and is full of praise and adulation for their undertakings in this direction, rest only in small part on archival material and mainly use earlier and fragmentary studies. In this thoroughly tendentious work, moreover, all those studies were rejected that treated critically the colonising action carried out by the Prussian kings. To colonisation in the period of South Prussia Beheim-Schwarzbach devoted only a very short chapter. Its incompleteness and lack of criticism may be shown by the fact that the author relied mainly on the work of Holsche, without presenting the question as a whole. A critical assessment of Schwarzbach's work was already given by Johannes Ziekursch, who showed, on the example of the colonisation of Silesia carried out in the time of Frederick the Great, that even the scanty archival materials the author used uncritically are not only fragmentary but also unreliable.

Of the more recent works of German historians that deal only incidentally with the problem of colonisation in South Prussia, mention should be made of the works of August Müller and Antoni Pytlak. Unlike Schwarzbach's work, both authors used archival materials, coming mainly from the Secret State Archive in Berlin and from the Archive of the Treasury of the Kingdom of Poland in Warsaw. The materials contained in these works make it possible, in broad approximation, to establish the number of colonies founded and the places where they were founded, which is especially valuable when there is no possibility of using the collections of those archives directly. Of the source publications for this period, the publications from the secret state archive edited by Stadelmann and Prümers deserve attention.

wasicki1953/138:
Of Polish studies not relating strictly to the period that concerns us, the work of Stefan Komornicki should be cited, which rests mainly on the results of the work of Beheim-Schwarzbach mentioned above, and that of Kazimierz Zimmermann. Although this last author deals in principle with Frederician colonisation, he also presents very briefly its course in the years 1793—1806 in South Prussia. Finally, the most recent study of the question is the book of Z. Kaczmarczyk. I do not list here other, smaller contributory works scattered through various periodicals, in particular in the Deutsche Wissenschaftliche Zeitschrift f. Polen.

The source basis of the present article is the materials in the Voivodeship State Archive in Poznań, in the section S. P. Z. Although on their basis an exhaustive picture of the principles and course of colonisation in the whole province of South Prussia cannot be given, because of a certain fragmentariness of the material, the action carried on in the years 1793—1806 can nevertheless be reconstructed approximately, especially with regard to the department of the Poznań chamber.

\

After the second and third partitions of the nobles' Commonwealth the former voivodeships of Poznań, Gniezno, Kalisz, Sieradz together with the land of Wieluń, Rawa, Łęczyca, Brześć Kujawski, the remainder of the voivodeship of Inowrocław left after the first partition, and the part of the voivodeship of Masovia lying on the left bank of the Vistula were joined to the state of the Hohenzollerns. From these lands a new province of the Prussian state was formed under the name of South Prussia. From part of the lands of the second and third partitions, that is from the northern parts of Masovia, Podlasie and part of Lithuania, a new province was organised after 1795: New East Prussia. A small strip of the voivodeship of Cracow was joined to Silesia under the name of New Silesia. After the third partition of the nobles' Commonwealth the frontiers of the Hohenzollern state ran in the east along the river Pilica, the middle Vistula, the lower Bug and the middle course of the Niemen.

\

Before proceeding to discuss the colonisation carried on in South Prussia by the absolute Prussian monarchs, it must be stressed that it was nothing new, unknown until then in this former province of the nobles' Commonwealth; on the contrary, it was only a further prolongation of the action carried on for a long time by the Polish feudal lords. The "Olęder" settlements that arose in large numbers in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, founded mostly on uncultivated land that needed clearing and draining, were dictated by considerations of an economic nature. The private initiative of the Polish feudal lords until then was, after the taking of Greater Poland, taken over and carried on, however, by the Prussian authorities.

wasicki1953/139:
Immediately after the taking of the Polish lands in the second partition, Frederick William II thought of colonising his new acquisitions with settlers brought from the Reich. He wrote on this matter to the president of the Poznań chamber, Buggenhagen, that he was very anxious to increase the population of the newly taken province and to raise the standard of agriculture in South Prussia. It would follow from these royal plans that colonisation was to be undertaken mainly for economic and population reasons. Undoubtedly it is from these two aspects that the colonising aims of the Hohenzollerns in the period of South Prussia should be viewed. For the colonisation carried out cannot be identified — as was done until recently — with an action of Germanisation, all the more so since in the times of the nobles' Commonwealth settlers, mostly German, were drawn to these lands. T. Ladenberger also drew attention to this in his work "On Frederician colonisation in Silesia", discussing both the opinions of Polish and German historians on the matter and the course and results of the colonisation of that period. Bourgeois German historians presented the colonising action of the Prussian kings, both in Silesia and in Pomerania, as a "work of culture", and regarded the colonists as "bearers of culture". T. Ladenberger, showing the real aim of colonisation, states at the same time, and rightly, that "colonisation served above all the royal treasury and the great estates", and that its cultural effects were downright lamentable.

The situation in South Prussia took a similar shape, although in this period an attempt was made, at least to some degree, to avoid the mistakes of Frederician colonisation. Colonies continued to be founded mainly on uncultivated land requiring clearing or draining. A considerable part of the settlers who arrived, as I shall show below, were settled on the royal domains, on the manor farms of private feudal lords and in the forests as hired labourers. Often two or three families were settled among the Polish population. The motive justifying colonisation was thus the wish to bring into use land not cultivated until then and to increase the number of hands for work on the domains and the manor farms. In these cases it is therefore very doubtful whether this poorest stratum of the rural population, employed as hired labourers on the manor farms, could fulfil that "cultural mission" so loudly proclaimed by German historians. Nor was there a better opinion of the other categories of colonists and of their knowledge of farming, even among contemporaries. Holsche himself, who had the best knowledge of contemporary conditions, states that the Württembergers, who settled in the greatest numbers in South Prussia, were bad farmers and that the whole action did not pay at all. The settlers who arrived, and especially those who had been given small pieces of land, farming in hard conditions, left South Prussia when the prospect opened before them of obtaining better conditions of settlement in another country. It must be stated, however, that those colonies,

 Stadelman, Anordnungen für die Kultur von Südpreussen, 12 XI 1793, s. 219.

 Ladenberger, op. cit., s. 375.

 Holsche, s. 499.
wasicki1953/140:
where a larger number of settlers were settled, and on land suitable for immediate cultivation, being given moreover considerable areas of land from 1 to 3 łany (Hufen), with hired labourers settled beside them, had assured prospects of development and therefore lasted long. For colonisation in the period of South Prussia was carried on on principles different from those of Frederician colonisation. Large farms, relying on the work of hired labourers, gave a guarantee of survival and development, all the more so since, as we shall see, the legal position of the colonist, who paid only a rent and was not bound by any other ties of feudal dependence, differed from the conditions prevailing at that time both on the nobles' manor farms and on the royal domains.

The Germanising factor was not the most important in colonisation in this period. For not only colonists from the Reich were settled here, but also colonists from Bohemia, inhabitants of South Prussia, and in New East Prussia even Tatars and Lithuanian peasants. This does not mean, however, that the Hohenzollerns did not try at this time to Germanise the Polish nobility. They did so through the administrative and judicial offices, the schools, and by drawing the nobility into military and civil service.

Frederick William II in his first instruction expressly warned that the colonising action should not cause a loss of population from the provinces of the Prussian state. It followed clearly from the royal order, therefore, that above all newcomers from the German Reich were to be recruited and settled as colonists. To encourage colonists to settle in the new lands certain concessions and financial help from the state were usually provided, and in addition exemption from military service. This last point was especially important, since the newcomers were well aware that in the militaristic Prussian state the duty of military service would be their heaviest burden. Had permission been given for colonists from the provinces in the hereditary possession of the Hohenzollerns to settle in South Prussia, there would undoubtedly have been too many willing to improve their conditions of life and to obtain the benefits due in such cases. This outflow of people, however, mainly peasants, on whom rested the whole burden of tax obligations and military service, would for some time have been a great loss for the Prussian state, and so their settling was forbidden from the very start.

From the exchange of letters between minister Voss and the Prussian envoy in Warsaw, Buchholz, it can be established that Buchholz put forward a proposal to appoint a special official to whom colonisation matters would be entrusted. These tasks were in the end entrusted, however, to the war and domains chambers, and minister Voss for his part issued an order that settlers arriving in future in the administrative districts of the chambers be given proper care and suitable help in settling.

 Prümers D. J., s. 441.
wasicki1953/141:
It might seem from the minister's first orders that Voss would at once set about putting the royal commands into effect; this, however, was not so. As we shall see further, Voss and the other ministers took an unwilling attitude to the whole action and set about putting it into effect only on the king's express order.

At the very outset Voss rejected the offer of the notary Hassold of Hamburg, made less than a year after the taking of the province, who wished to undertake the recruiting of colonists for South Prussia. The minister gave as the ground for his position the fact that no preparations had been made in this province to begin a colonising action. Such preparations would necessarily take a long time, to make suitable land ready for settling the arriving settlers. Besides, he considered the method of recruiting unsuitable in this case, because already now, and certainly in future, there would be many willing, chiefly from Mecklenburg, Lüneburg and other provinces of the Reich, who would wish to settle in the new province. In this particular case, then, Voss wished to depart from the method of obtaining colonists by recruiting, as practised by Frederick II.

Minister Voss's unfavourable attitude in this matter must also have been affected by the fact that in none of the royal commands was there the slightest mention of the amount of the fund provided for the colonising action, and without a fairly large sum of money set aside for the purpose the whole action could not have the slightest chance of success. Wishing to begin the colonising action, Frederick William approved a project laid before him in July 1793, under which the nobility receiving the South Prussian indigenat, necessary for acquiring estates in this province, was obliged, in proportion to the value of the estates acquired, to settle a certain number of colonists (one family for every 2000 thalers), but it is not known whether this project was put into effect. The royal edict issued on the indigenat says nothing of this condition. Since, however, the grant of the indigenat depended solely on the king, the project of settling colonists on the occasion of the acquisition of estates in South Prussia by the Prussian nobility might have had a chance of success, and the king would still make attempts to carry it out in 1804. Until then, judging from the king's enquiries addressed to minister Voss, the royal commands were not strictly observed.

From these initial plans it is clear that according to the king's intentions the colonising action was to go two ways: one carried on by the state, the other by the private purchasers of estates in the new province, which in fact happened later.

Frederick William II's colonising plans, however, met with fairly serious difficulties from the very start. Leaving aside minister Voss's unwilling attitude to the action itself, the main obstacle was the necessity
