wasicki1953/142:
of organising the province on the Prussian model. This matter was the chief subject of the work of minister Voss, who administered the province, and then of the Silesian minister Hoym. Interrupted by the outbreak of the Kościuszko Insurrection and its spread to Greater Poland, the efforts were taken up again after its suppression.

Minister Voss's successor, the Silesian minister Hoym, also did not begin the colonising action, although after the suppression of the Kościuszko Rising the starosties and church estates were confiscated and incorporated into the royal domains. Hoym did not comply at all with the earlier royal directions on settling colonists on private estates and leased domains. For under his rule, as K. Marx writes: "... Knights, adventurers, favourites of the royal mistresses, creatures of the ministers, accomplices whose mouths it was desired to shut, were endowed in great numbers with the larger and richer estates in the plundered country... In the course of Hoym's four-year administration ... there were given away in this manner in the Poznań administrative district — 22, in the Kalisz, formerly Piotrków — 19, in the Warsaw district — 11, and altogether 52 large and small possessions, which together comprise no fewer than 240 separate landed estates". It may therefore be said that those endowed with these estates must have taken an unwilling and even downright hostile attitude to the royal orders requiring colonists to be settled on private estates, and this even where the royal order did not concern estates given away for "services".

For those who received these estates treated them only as an object of further trade, naturally at a considerable profit. It must have mattered to them in such a situation that those buying estates from them should not be burdened with additional colonisation obligations towards the state, since these rather onerous and costly conditions might, if not deter buyers, at any rate cause considerable difficulty in selling them.

Besides, the Silesian minister Hoym had already formed an unfavourable judgement of the results of this action as carried on in Silesia in the time of Frederick II. As K. Zimmermann reports, in a memorandum presented to Frederick William II Hoym clearly stressed that bringing settlers from foreign lands does not give the expected results. In his opinion,

> "it is not the first duty of the steward of the state to see that the population increases as far as possible, but to see to its permanent maintenance and to settle it so that it brings the state the greatest benefit. Neither of these aims has been fully attained by settling foreign colonists in compact villages. They usually take advantage of the state's benefits, then move away, and they cannot be blamed for this, since with a disproportionately large number of foreigners they often had to be assigned places where earning a living was very difficult for them. In other places they would have taken from the natives their permanent and secure livelihood and the fruits of their thrift. Encouraging and settling new trades by granting them certain concessions is a salutary thing, and for this there will be plenty ready to settle among the Silesians".

 Marks K. i Engels F., Soczinienija, T. VII, Moskwa 1950, s. 357.

 Beheim-Schwarzbach, s. 4.1.

 Zimmermann K., Tom I, s 40.
wasicki1953/143:
The Silesian minister therefore tried to persuade Frederick William II that the costs of bringing in foreign settlers were too great, both for the state and for the owners of manor farms. Settling the local population could give better results. Many contemporaries, too, shared minister Hoym's view on this matter. Minister Schulenburg-Kehnert, stressing in his remarks on South Prussia the growing number of the population, expressed the view that the colonising action ought to be limited. Efforts should rather be made to improve the condition of the local population and to give it the possibility of acquiring land. This referred mainly to the "Olęders", since the minister had come into contact with this category of the population on his journey through the new Prussian province. They had a little capital, which by their own account they were eating up, because they had no possibility of buying a suitable farm. These people deserve — in the minister's opinion — special support, because they need either no help or very little help from the state. Moreover they understand farming well in local conditions and can serve as a model for the Polish population.

Minister Struensee also spoke out against bringing in colonists from other lands, maintaining moreover that daily experience teaches that colonists brought from abroad disappoint, while the treasury is burdened with great costs. For these reasons, therefore, minister Hoym observed especially carefully the royal prohibition forbidding the settlement in South Prussia of serf peasants from the provinces of the Hohenzollern state. For from the reports of the chambers it appeared that on some nobles' estates in the New Mark there were serf peasants who wished themselves, and persuaded others, to settle in South Prussia as colonists, without obtaining the consent of their lord. The minister drew the chambers' attention to such cases of undesirable and forbidden inflow of settlers from the Prussian provinces. He therefore ordered them to check carefully whether the newcomers were not "in nexu subditela", and whether they had a release from the authorities of the canton.

It seems, however, that such cases must have occurred more often, since a year after the incidents mentioned the order previously issued to the chambers was repeated. It may be supposed, however, from the later measures of the chambers and the General Directory, that the principle that the king's subjects could not settle in the new Prussian province was applied rigorously only to serf peasants.

Thus during the reign of Frederick William II and in the period of minister Hoym's administration in principle no steps were taken to begin a colonising action on a larger scale. This was also affected by the financial situation of the Prussian state, which, exhausted by the expenditure of the war then being waged with revolutionary France, could not set aside for settlement

wasicki1953/144:
the necessary funds. Only in New East Prussia, after its organisation, did minister Schrötter try to attract colonists, recruited mainly from the Tatar population, from Lithuania and from Volhynia. The Tatars, however, were settled in New East Prussia not for economic purposes but rather in order to form from the settlers suitable units of light cavalry, which was in fact done later. The fact that the Tatar population and also Lithuanian peasants were settled in this province may best show that Germanising factors did not come into play here, but, as we have already stressed, population and fiscal factors, and in the settling of the Tatars also military ones.

Besides the Tatars and Lithuanians, colonists coming mainly from the Prussian provinces were settled here at this time, which in principle did not agree with Frederick William's intentions.

A certain revival of the colonising action can be observed only with the accession of Frederick William III and the end of the war with France. At this time, too, there was a change in the post of the administrator of the affairs of the province of South Prussia. In place of minister Hoym, one of its first co-organisers, minister Voss, was appointed again.

At the very outset of his reign Frederick William III ordered the General Directory to draw up a plan of colonisation for the individual provinces and to state what had been done in this regard until then. Unfortunately we have no information on what the plan drawn up by Voss for South Prussia looked like. Presumably the minister, while awaiting the king's remarks on and acceptance of the colonisation plan, issued an instruction to the chambers under him in which he declared expressly that this action had not yet begun. For these reasons he ordered those applying and expressing the wish to settle in South Prussia, both from the Prussian provinces and from other parts of the Reich, to wait until the announcement of the date when the admission of new settlers would begin.

Soon, however, minister Voss together with the provincial authorities was placed in a position of compulsion. In the summer of 1798 the first reports reached Berlin of a larger number of applications from colonists, mainly from Württemberg and Baden. Württemberg had already, during Frederician colonisation, been a region from which a large number of settlers were recruited. The reason for this was the considerable density of population of this part of Germany; besides, strong propaganda was carried on there, as will be discussed below. In Berlin, however, an increased inflow of colonists was expected at this time mainly from the lands lying on the left bank of the Rhine, because of the occupation of this part of Germany by French troops. Everything therefore pointed to the possibility of beginning the colonising action on a broad scale, otherwise, that is, than had been the case under the previous ruler. Newcomers from Berlin, where they at first applied, were to be directed not only to South Prussia but also to New East Prussia. For the unexpected newcomers from Württemberg, in accordance with the royal directions, abandoned peasant farms were to be set aside first of all. For this purpose the provincial authorities were ordered to establish their exact number. At the same time they were asked to inform the General Directory of those parts of the province where there was uncultivated land to which arriving colonists could be sent. Also when royal domains were let on lease, regard should be had, in accordance with the royal directions, to the possibility of settling colonists on them. In the particular cases cited, the General Directory did not lay down as a principle the settling of colonists on abandoned peasant farms; this was rather to be treated as an exception, with a view to finding quickly for the settlers who had arrived land on which they could be settled immediately on arrival. For the fundamental intention of the colonising action was to settle the newcomers on land not cultivated until then, requiring clearing or draining. This may be shown by the king's reply to the complaint of the Württemberg colonists to whom the Poznań chamber had assigned forest land requiring clearing for their settlement. Land of this kind was also set aside for Württemberg colonists in the neighbourhood of Mosina and Puszczykowo, near Poznań. The Poznań chamber's position in this matter met with the full approval of the General Directory. The provincial authorities, however, were not prepared to receive the first settlers. From the conduct of the Poznań chamber it may even be supposed that it wished to rid itself as quickly as possible of the unforeseen settlers who caused it nothing but trouble. Its attitude in this matter is shown by the fact that after the first settlement proposals laid before the General Directory it turned to the Białystok chamber in New East Prussia, asking whether in its district there might not be a possibility of settling the colonists who had arrived.

Colonists who did not possess sufficient means were looked upon unfavourably. The Prussian king, seeing this attitude of the local authorities towards the colonists, drew minister Voss's attention to the fact that in no case should a situation be allowed in which colonists returned to their own country. For this might discourage the rest of the population from moving to the new lands. In such cases even certain sacrifices would have to be made, so long as a steady inflow of settlers from the Reich to the province was assured. At the same time the king promised to grant certain funds to cover the costs of settling the colonists. For at that time, in his opinion, was the most suitable moment to win a larger number of settlers for the colonising action, because of the threat to the southern lands of Germany from the French armies.

A great hindrance in carrying on the whole action was the lack of any guidelines on the principles of admitting colonists and the manner of carrying out settlement. Frederick William III in a letter to minister Voss ordered that in proceedings on colonisation the older models from the time of Frederick II be followed. As we shall see further, however, they were not fully applied during this action in South Prussia. Given the meagreness of the funds set aside for colonisation, Voss recommended the chambers to be economical with the funds intended for this purpose. In a letter of March 1799 minister Voss, informing the chambers of the arrival in their administrative districts of 19 families of colonists, sent at the same time, for the first time, more precise instructions on the manner of settling them. The area of land assigned to colonists, together with meadow, could not exceed 3 łany. The grant of land and its area depended on the settler's degree of wealth. Colonists were to be granted years free of obligations to the state. The instruction did not fix precisely the number of free years, stating rather generally that this would depend on the time needed to set up the farm on the new land. The rent paid by the colonists was to rise in proportion to the size of the area taken under cultivation. The chambers were to try to have suitable pastures granted to the colonists, or the right to graze cattle in the forests for a certain fee. Colonists were released for two years from the obligation of supplying forage. They were to be supplied with timber for building their dwelling houses and farm buildings. The colonists and their sons, and the persons who came with them, were exempted from the duty of military service. The settlers were personally free; they received the land in perpetual lease. The amount of the canon had not yet been fixed. It was decided to postpone this matter until all the colonists had been settled on the land set aside for this purpose. In 1799, carrying out the royal command to conduct the colonising action on a broader scale, by recruiting settlers from the Reich more vigorously than until then, ministers Voss and Schrötter, and especially the latter, set about acting more energetically. Minister Schrötter thought it fitting to send a special commissioner to southern Germany to carry on recruiting among the population there. He intended, after some time, to use the settlers thus won for further recruiting in the Reich. Commissioner Weiss, chosen by minister Schrötter for this task, set out in May of that year for Württemberg, Baden, Hesse-Nassau and the Palatinate, in order to attract "very sturdy and well-to-do colonists". The order of the General Directory on this matter, giving the reasons why this was the right moment for recruiting settlers, read:

> "Advantage must be taken of the present circumstances, which will lead to emigration many an upright and well-to-do inhabitant of those parts who would never have thought of leaving his homeland, and the opportunity must be used to have a shrewd cameralist on the spot choose the most suitable and best material and persuade it to emigrate. All this is most important for attracting foreign colonists and must be used as zealously as possible. Weiss should therefore receive an instruction on the conditions on which and the colonists whom he is to engage for the West and East Prussian department, and especially how far hired labourers and gardeners are to be considered. Perhaps the owners of estates too could use such colonists".

In the principality of Nassau Weiss found a fairly favourable reception from the authorities there, and many willing to settle in the new provinces, who did not, however, possess the means required for this. He did not fare so well in Württemberg, because of the hostile attitude at that time of the authorities there to Frederick William III's colonising undertakings. Besides, the imperial armies withdrawing from Switzerland did not allow the action begun by Weiss to be carried on further. On his second stay in Nassau he could already see that the unfavourable reception of the first settlers from this province in South Prussia, who had returned to Nassau, had discouraged others from leaving. Commissioner Weiss returned from his journey almost empty-handed, because few candidates were found for settlement in the new Prussian provinces. But this was not the only cause of the failure. For, as appears from Weiss's report, the concessions provided in the instruction for colonists were too small in relation to the relatively high property requirements. Minister Schrötter came to an understanding on this matter with the Higher War College (Ober-Kriegs-Collegium), promising at the same time the recruiting officers a reward of 5 thalers for each family of a colonist settling on 3—4 łany, and 3 thalers for each family settling on a smaller area.

Minister Voss, in connection with the expected inflow of settlers from the Reich, reminded the chambers to limit the number of newcomers from the Prussian provinces, but there was no longer an express prohibition on settling them. Subjects of the Prussian king could, however, be settled only on waste land (wüste Ländereien), on condition that they received no help from the state of the kind provided for colonists coming from outside the frontiers of the Prussian kingdom. The Prussian king laid the main stress on developing the colonising action precisely in South Prussia, as a province important to him because of the connection between Silesia and East Prussia. By an order of 15 May 1799 Frederick William ordered Voss to prepare new land for colonists. The minister was also to carry out the earlier royal order issued with regard to the nobility granted the South Prussian indigenat. Besides, the lessees of the royal domains were to be obliged to settle colonists on the domains in proportion to their income (one family for every 1000 thalers).

Voss's efforts to have the royal order issued on this matter withdrawn had no effect, because the king considered that an obligation of this kind laid on the owners of estates holding the indigenat and the lessees of domains would be an effective means of putting an end to trading in estates and, by increasing the population, would contribute to the improvement of the economy. In view of the king's position, aiming at an extension of the colonising action, the General Directory issued an instruction to the chambers explaining what land was to be set aside for colonisation. First among these were reckoned: fallow, waste land, pastures, forest land, small manor farms unsuitable for larger-scale farming, abandoned peasant farms, and finally unused land near the towns, which could be set aside without harm to the manor farms for settling cottagers and gardeners.

As to the first point, the instruction explained that for purposes of colonisation those lands could be taken about which there were no disputed questions. Where there were boundary disputes, colonies could not be founded only in those places that were in dispute, with the proviso that if the chambers lost the case the rent paid by the colonists would be handed over to the owner of the land on which the colony had been founded. If there were several owners of an area suitable and set aside for colonisation,

If the owners would not give their consent to the chambers' proposal, then the whole matter was to be referred for decision to the ministry of justice, which would commission the appropriate Regierung to decide it.

It may give us pause that small manor farms, that is cultivated land, were also set aside for founding colonies, which really did not agree with the fundamental intentions of the colonisation carried on in South Prussia. It was stressed clearly, however, that only those manor farms could be set aside for this purpose which, because of their excessive distance from larger economic units, were unsuitable for growing grain or rearing cattle on a suitable scale.

Minister Voss was well aware that the settlers arriving from the Reich would be reluctant to settle on abandoned peasant farms among a population foreign to them. Besides, there might arise the danger that the colonists, having received a farm of this kind, would have to perform the manorial services to which the rest of the population living in the village was bound. For the earlier instructions stressed clearly that the colonists received the land in perpetual lease, for which they paid only a rent. Seeing this state of affairs, the General Directory gave an instruction that abandoned peasant farms were to be occupied by the local population, or the abandoned land joined to other peasant farms to enlarge them. It was also possible — according to the instruction — to move peasants from farms lying next to the manor farms to the abandoned farms, and to fill their places with arriving colonists classed as cottagers and smallholders, or else to incorporate the land into the manor farms. In this way an attempt was made on the one hand to create larger peasant farms and on the other to assure the royal domains of a labour force for which the main, indeed the only, means of support would be work on the manor farm.

Similar principles were to be applied in founding colonies on land near the towns. The chambers were to see to the building of rented houses in which artisans, day labourers and Lassbauer (lassyci) would find lodging.

This care to settle free hired labourers on the one hand, and then to create large farms for colonists, bore witness to the far-reaching changes already under way in rural conditions. The feudal economy had at this time begun to outlive itself and slowly, first on the royal estates and then on the nobles' manor farms, to take on the forms of a capitalist economy. The transition to new forms of cultivation, the clearing of forests and the draining of marshes required the settling of a large number of free cottagers, gardeners and smallholders, compelled to sell their labour to the owners of manor farms. And so, although in principle there was constant talk of settling colonist-farmers, at the same time especially many hired labourers were settled, so needed on the manor farms. Colonists were settled mainly on the royal domains, where progressive forms of farming were being introduced, but the Prussian government also influenced the South Prussian nobility to introduce new forms of farming on their manor farms, increasing the areas
wasicki1953/150:
of the manor farms by sowing the fallows, laying out meadows, growing industrial crops. They were also encouraged to abolish common pastures, increase sheep-farming and industrialise the manor farms. Rather generally and cautiously, but at any rate it was stressed, that such changes ought to bring with them "a change in the relations between lords and peasants". These principles were to be put into practice, for example, by the Economic Society of Międzyrzecz, founded in 1802, and the Prussian authorities reckoned with the possibility of extending the network of similar societies over the whole area of South Prussia. Beside the towns, colonies of artisans and day labourers were to arise, needed for work in the productive enterprises developing in this period and relying on free hired labour. It cannot be said that particularly numerous industrial enterprises arose in South Prussia in this period; on the contrary, a gradual decline of those existing until then can be observed, as a result of the competition of other Prussian provinces where manufacture was highly developed, as for example in Silesia; the guidelines of the General Directory, however, amounted only to general principles of colonisation, without taking account in such cases of particular local considerations.

Unlike the earlier instructions issued to the chambers, this one ordered the officials to give the arriving settlers proper care. When, however, it happened that arriving colonists did not wish to settle in the place set aside for them, as was the case with 12 Württemberg families, minister Voss ordered the chambers to leave them to their own fate, without troubling about them further.

From the summer of 1799 the recruiting of colonists for South Prussia was taken in hand by Captain Nothardt. From then on the centralised action gained in strength, and certain fixed principles for it had also by then been worked out. Nothardt presented his proposal and plan for conducting it to the king and the provincial authorities. As the reason for conducting colonisation more vigorously than until then precisely in South Prussia he gave its strategic and economic importance. In the following year, according to the plan drawn up, after the king had approved Nothardt's proposals, the captain was to go to Germany to direct the recruiting of colonists on the spot. At the same time Frederick William II promised to set aside funds for colonisation to the amount of 50 to 60 thousand thalers. In 1800, 445 Württemberg families were settled in South Prussia, and the king aimed to extend the settling activity still further.

Until then the main stress on the king's part had been laid on colonising South Prussia, leaving aside the other provinces formerly part of the nobles' Commonwealth. The motives for this course rested largely on the justification of the whole action laid before the Prussian king by Captain Nothardt. On the same grounds minister Schrötter came forward with a proposal to develop a livelier colonising action in New East Prussia, and mainly in the Płock department. For it formed a prolongation of South Prussia and the link between Silesia and East Prussia. This question evidently raised no doubts, and so the king agreed to extend the colonising action to this region, on the same principles on which colonisation was conducted in the other lands of the new Prussian provinces. In this matter minister Schrötter was to come to an understanding with minister Voss and Capt. Nothardt as to the allocation of colonists among the individual provinces.

Schrötter, in accordance with the king's recommendation, came to an understanding with minister Voss; the principles for settling colonists, however, which were set out in the instructions sent to the chambers, raised serious reservations in his mind. In particular this concerned the day labourers, who, in Schrötter's opinion, were given the best settlement conditions of all the categories of settlers. It could therefore be supposed that the inflow of this category of settlers would be the most numerous, which did not agree with Schrötter's intentions. We have already seen that minister Voss too at first set fairly high property requirements for arriving settlers, precisely in order to stem the inflow into the new province of a poor population which, despite help from the state, was unable to set itself up on the land allotted to it. Only because of an express royal order was the property qualification lowered, and in many cases it was not applied at all when the newcomers came from territories occupied by French troops or forming a theatre of war.

Moreover, the advance of 1,000 thalers for setting up provided in the instruction stood in no proportion to the means brought by the colonist. For these reasons Schrötter considered that the principles relied on in settling colonists in South Prussia could not be applied in New East Prussia. Nor was agreement reached on the distribution of the applying colonists among the individual provinces. Voss was of the opinion that colonists should first of all be directed to South Prussia, and only when the possibility of settlement in that province ceased should they be passed on to New East Prussia. From a conversation with Captain Nothardt minister Schrötter could conclude that he would not only not deal with recruiting settlers for New East Prussia, but on the contrary would put obstacles in the way. In this situation minister Schrötter gave up agreeing and co-ordinating the whole action with minister Voss and Capt. Nothardt and began recruiting colonists on his own account with the help of settlers already living in the province of West Prussia and New East Prussia. They were

The project for the colonisation of New East Prussia that he laid before the king, and his request that suitable funds be set aside for this purpose, received the consent of the king, who granted 200 thousand thalers for carrying on this action. The help intended for colonists was not as high as in South Prussia. It rested on the exact calculation that for the complete setting up of a colonist receiving 3 łany of land on a new farm a sum of 600 thalers was needed, for a 4-łan farm 800 thalers; thus 200 thal. fell to one łan. It was therefore provided that the state's financial help would amount to 300 thalers for those settling on 3 łany, that is the colonist must possess 300 thalers of his own means, on 4 łany 400 thal., on 5 łany 500 thal., and so on. The amount of financial help was thus proportional to the colonist's own means brought in and to the area of land received. Besides financial help, colonists were to be granted, as in South Prussia, travel money and timber for building. The colonist was to take up the land allotted to him within a fixed time and, on pain of losing it, set about bringing it into cultivation.

Schrötter put his plan of recruiting action into effect, and already in 1802 the first Württemberg emissaries came to New East Prussia to find out what the conditions of settlement in the new province were. Volunteers from the left bank of the Rhine also applied to the Prussian legation, asking about the possibility of going to the new province. To spread these conditions Schrötter ordered them to be printed and sent to Frankfurt on the Main. At this time, too, leaflets appeared encouraging settlement in South Prussia and New East Prussia.

The Prussian envoy officiating at Frankfurt on the Main, Formey, did not, however, keep strictly to the instructions he had received and accepted applications for going to New East Prussia from people who could not prove that they had sufficient means. An end to this practice of Formey's was put only

A conversation between a South Prussian colonist and a Swabian peasant], tried to present the condition of the colonists settled in South Prussia in the best possible light. The conversation between the Swabian peasant and the colonist from South Prussia, who came from those parts, begins with the colonist trying to dispel the doubts of the Swabian peasant, who thought that in the new Prussian province there was nothing but hunger, sorrow and dejection. For that was how the situation had been presented to him by those who had returned from there, not having found the promised happiness. The colonist, however, presents the conditions prevailing in South Prussia in an altogether different light. He praises the fertility of the soil, the state's help for settlers, and finally the fact that many colonies had already arisen there, settled mainly by settlers from Germany. To the question why, then, the Prussian government was trying to attract settlers there, and whether the peasants there did not cultivate the land, the newcomer from South Prussia replies that the peasants living in South Prussia are lazy and negligent, because in Polish times they were oppressed by the nobility with labour service. Finally the last revolution that broke out there caused many of them to leave the country, and for this reason new settlers are now needed there. He adds that colonists are settled only on land belonging to the king and are therefore only his subjects, not obliged to the labour service that the peasants sitting on the nobles' and church lands of this province must perform. The colonists are thus free men and all the yield is their property. The Swabian peasants need not fear coming to a province inhabited by a foreign population, since there are already many colonists from Germany there, and besides all the officials speak German. Convinced, the Swabian peasant decides to leave and settle in South Prussia, taking all his property with him. Zimmermann, t. II, s. 37.

The greatest trouble for Schrötter was the question of settling the families classed as Büdner (Büdnerfamilien). For in the colonies being created there was no room for them, because of their fairly numerous inflow despite the restrictions applied, and founding special colonies for this category of settlers seemed unjustified to Schrötter. He therefore turned his attention to the royal manor farms, where he thought there would be the best opportunity of settling them, while at the same time releasing the subjects there from the obligation of labour service (Scharwerk). Until then the obstacle to abolishing this obligation had been the lack of hands for work on the manor farm. Schrötter, wishing to remedy this, ordered the chambers to settle Büdner on the manor farms, in order to assure them a hired labour force. As in South Prussia, so in this province too the lessees of manor farms were to be obliged to settle day labourers at their own cost. In this case the principle that they must possess means of their own of 60 thalers was even departed from, since in Schrötter's opinion too they could not be sent back.

Colonisation in New East Prussia made ever more visible progress, although there was no such express command and care for this action on the part of the king and the General Directory. In 1803 a larger number of colonists was settled in New East Prussia than in the Warsaw department of South Prussia.

The "Reichs-Kolonisten-Werbungs-Büreau" founded by Captain Nothardt at Ohringen near Heilbronn in Württemberg also carried on a lively activity. Frederick William III granted for 1803 a sum of 321,885 thalers for colonisation, stressing that this action should not be checked. The funds set aside for this purpose thus grew more and more. Seeing, however, the very marked progress of this action in New East Prussia, carried on moreover at lower cost, the Prussian king decided to abolish the recruiting office at Ohringen, whose upkeep involved rather high costs. Captain Nothardt was placed at the head of the Kalisz chamber with the special task of supervising the course of the colonising action in all the departments of South Prussia. The recruiting of colonists was entrusted to the Franconian chamber at Ansbach. At the same time, on the king's express order, ministers Voss and Schrötter were to agree together the principles of procedure in settling new settlers. Already before this, however, namely in May 1802, a more detailed instruction on this matter than before had been drawn up for South Prussia, differing fairly considerably from the one issued for the chambers and Capt. Nothardt. For it took account of the points on which minister Schrötter had expressed his reservations.

In the forefront of this new instruction was put the requirement that settlers have professional knowledge useful for farming

The property requirements were by no means given up or lowered; only this small change was introduced, that the colonist had to possess half his means in cash, while the other half he could supply within two to four years; this sum was to be secured by a judicial mortgage on the land received from the state, and its possession had to be proved by credible documents. A horse was counted into the colonist's cash means, at 54 guilders or 84 thal. each. The area of land assigned was decided, as before, by the amount of means possessed. According to these criteria the colonists were divided into six classes.

To the first class were assigned day labourers and cottagers (Tagelöhner und Häusler). The basic livelihood of this category of colonists was to be work on the larger agricultural holdings (ländliche Wirtschaften); it was not, however, explained exactly whether nobles' manor farms or royal estates were meant. In practice they were settled both on the royal domains and beside the larger colonies and near the towns, where they could find employment. This category of settlers was to receive only as much land as was necessary to satisfy their essential needs, on the assumption that the main source of livelihood would be wage work. Its area therefore varied between 4 and 6 morgen, and that again according to the quality of the soil. The means required of this category of settlers amounted to from 50 to 300 guilders (Reichsgeld), or from 27 thal. 12 gr. to 162 thal. 12 gr. Prussian. On settling they were to receive:

1\. 4 to 6 morgen of land in perpetual lease, paying after the free years an appropriate canon.

2\. Ownership of a dwelling house, with the obligation to keep it in proper repair.

3\. Travel money (Meilengeld) at the rate of 2 gr. a mile for each member of the family and each person coming with him.

4\. 3 to 6 free years (Freijahre) according to the kind of land received (land already cultivated, fallows, land requiring clearing).

5\. Reimbursement of the costs of clearing.

6\. The tools needed for the farm.

7\. Livestock according to the amount of land received.

8\. Exemption from the cantons for colonists and their sons.

To the second category were assigned colonists who possessed means of from 300 to 1000 Reichsgeld, or 162 thal. 12 gr. to 541 thal. 16 gr. They were to be settled on farms of 15 to 40 morgen. Besides land they were to receive travel money, 3 to 6 free years and exemption from the cantons.

The third category was formed by colonists who were to be assigned 3 łany (Hufen) of land. The means required to be assigned to this category were to be from 1000 to 2000 Reichsgeld, or 541 thal. 16 gr. to 1083 thal. 8 gr. They were also granted free of charge the necessary amount of timber for building a house and farm buildings, in kind, or cash for buying it. Besides, they received a non-repayable money grant (Gnaden-Geschenk) of 200 thal. and, for a period of 5, 8 or 15 years, an interest-free loan of 600 thal. The free period was to last 6 to 8 years. The colonists were entitled to freedom from the cantons.

The fourth category was formed by colonists whose means amounted to from 2000 to 3000 Reichsgeld, or 1083 thal. 18 gr. to 1625 thal. They were settled on four łany and granted timber for building, a money grant of 200 thal., an interest-free loan of 600 thal., 3—6 free years and freedom from the cantons.

To the fifth category were assigned colonists whose means amounted to from 3000 to 4000 Reichsgeld, or 1625 thal. to 2166 thal. 16 gr. They received 5 łany of land, and besides timber for building, 3 to 6 free years, an interest-free loan of 1400 thal., repayable, however, during the free years, and finally exemption from the cantons.

The sixth and last category of settlers was formed by those for whom an allotment of land of 6 łany was provided. The required means amounted to from 4000 Reichsgeld to 5000 Reichsgeld, or 2166 thal. 16 gr. to 2708 thal. 8 gr. The help provided for them by the state was of the same amount and kind as for the previous group of settlers.

As follows from this, then, the instruction of 1802 differed fairly considerably from the one issued earlier. Financial help was given in principle according to the category of settlers, which again was closely bound up with the amount of land received. It must be admitted that the first category, to which a fairly considerable number of newcomers was assigned — judging from the chamber's reports and the General Directory's interventions in these matters — nevertheless received fairly substantial help. Colonists assigned to the second and even the third group did not, it is true, receive a non-repayable loan for a fixed period, which was in any case closely bound up with the areas of land received, but for them too the benefits provided were fairly considerable.

From the above instruction it follows fairly clearly that the General Directory was concerned on the one hand with creating relatively large rural farms, of 1 to 6 łany, and on the other with supplying hired labour for work on the manor farms.

The figures given in minister Voss's report confirm the principle applied. Of a total of 534 families there were settled in the Poznań department:

As follows from the above list, the largest number were hired labourers, settled directly on the manor farms, in the larger colonies or near the towns, that is where they could more easily find work. Colonists of category IV were few. Colonists assigned to categories V and VI, on the other hand, are entirely lacking. The data cited by Hoffmann, that by 1804 four colonists of groups V and VI had been settled, are therefore not confirmed.

We have no figures for how this matter stood in the other departments, but it may be supposed that it did not depart from the general principles. Thus, although the procedure and principles of colonisation changed fairly substantially compared with the first instructions, and although, contrary to the king's reservations, attempts continued to be made to limit the number of settlers of the first, and even the second, category, it was precisely these colonists who flowed into South Prussia in the greatest numbers. For settling as many hired labourers as possible on the domains was in the king's interest. Minister Schrötter criticised this kind of procedure and the colonisation orders issued for South Prussia, since these categories of settlers, in the opinion — justified, moreover — of the administrator of New East Prussia, showed the strongest tendencies to move beyond the frontiers of the Prussian provinces when they were promised better settlement conditions elsewhere. Already in 1803 the chambers' reports sent to the General Directory very often contain complaints of colonists' secret flight. The cause of this frequent abandonment of both South Prussia and New East Prussia by colonists who had only just arrived was the possibility of moving to Russia. For in this period a very lively colonising action was being carried on in Russia. The appeal of Tsar Alexander I caused many families of colonists, chiefly smallholders, to begin moving to the new lands, where they were undoubtedly given better settlement conditions. The colonists secretly sold the stock allotted to them, so that the chambers had to announce a prohibition on buying these things from colonists without their consent. This announcement was made public in the Gazeta Południowo-Pruska.

It was further explained that inhabitants of South Prussia could be settled only as cottagers, who were to be entitled to the same benefits as newcomers. Requests of colonists of the first category for enlarging their buildings and building barns were to be rejected, and they were even to be allowed to sell part of the land they received, and this both to colonists and to the local peasants. Minister Voss warned the chambers not to accept as colonists newcomers to whom the recruiting offices had refused permission to settle. For he feared that otherwise too many persons would apply who did not possess the required means and who would become only a burden on the provincial authorities, weighing on the fund set aside for colonisation. Frederick William, however, as usual in these matters, did not allow them to be removed from the frontiers of South Prussia.

The legal position of this category of people, however, could not differ, since it rested on the same principles.

After this time he could sell the land, but only after presenting the new buyer to the chamber, which established his qualifications. The colonist could name his successor in case of death, also with the chamber's consent. If he left several successors, the choice of one of them belonged to the chamber.

The colonist was obliged to pay money dues to the state, the amount of which depended on the quantity and quality of the land he held. He paid, then, a rent and a hearth tax (podymne) calculated from the average price of grain. Part of the rent, as a rule ⅛, the colonist delivered in grain to the royal magazines. In the contract he was obliged to keep the dwelling houses and farm buildings in usable condition, but he could not demand free timber for their repair. He was exempt from performing labour services for the domains, but within the colony the settlers were obliged to keep the roads and bridges in order. Besides the hearth tax paid to the state, the colonist was also obliged, after the expiry of the free years, to supply in case of war a horse with a cart, and in peacetime to supply the required carting and forage and to work on fortifications.

The colonies founded formed an independent administrative unit in which authority was exercised by the sołtys (village headman). The authority above the sołtys was the "Amtmann".

It is difficult to give general precise figures for the number of colonists settled in South Prussia. Some light is thrown here only by minister Voss's report, laid before the king. According to it, the number of colonists who arrived up to 1805 was in all 10,295 persons; it is not known, however, whether this covered only settlers in the villages or also in the towns, nor does it appear whether these figures include colonists settled on private estates. The colonists were settled on 62,190 Magdeburg morgen. This figure is given also by other bourgeois historians, German and Polish.

Relying on the list drawn up by the Poznań chamber in 1804, giving both the number of colonies founded and of settlers who arrived, we can state that their number for the Poznań department was 2324 persons in all. It should be supposed that the colonising action in the years 1805—1806 did not increase, but rather weakened, because of the lack of funds and the difficulties the chambers' officials met in settling colonists. Besides, Voss's report sent in 1804 shows many "établissements" not yet occupied but already prepared to receive settlers. Moreover, his report does not show the number of those colonists who, settled in the Poznań chamber, left the land allotted to them and either returned to Germany or moved elsewhere. This was in any case understandable, since Voss was showing the overall expenditure connected with the colonising action and therefore gave figures for all the colonists who arrived and were settled, without mentioning what then became of them.

From A. Pytlak's lists it cannot be concluded whether, as in the Poznań department, part of the colonists were settled on the manor farms as hired labourers. Nor can we establish what area of land was allotted to them. Since, however, the same principles applied in settling colonists, it may be supposed that the situation in the other departments took a similar shape to that in the department of the Poznań chamber. The colonisation of the period of South Prussia might properly be called a Württemberg colonisation. For the great majority of the settlers who arrived came from that part of Germany. After the occupation of the left bank of the Rhine by the revolutionary troops of France the inflow of colonists from those lands increased fairly considerably. There were relatively many colonists from the Hohenzollern provinces, despite the difficulties made at first over settling them. The table cited shows the origin of the colonists settled in the Poznań department up to 1805. (See below.)

The principles and course of colonisation in South Prussia in the years 1793—1806 differ fairly clearly from the colonisation of Polish lands carried on by Frederick II both in Silesia and in West Prussia. Frederician colonisation is well known, since it has received many exhaustive studies, and the work of T. Ladenberger cited at the beginning sums up the results of the research carried on in this direction. It does not therefore seem to us justified to present it again. It is necessary only to show the differences in the principles and course of colonisation in its two periods.

The fundamental aim of Frederician colonisation was to increase the population of the country; the question of the newcomers' usefulness in the province did not play the most important part here. For these reasons the element arriving here had the worst possible reputation, both professionally and morally. In point of farming technique the newcomers stood no higher than the Polish population. Hence the opinions of bourgeois German historians "on the cultural mission of the colonists" remain empty phrases. In the period of colonisation in South Prussia, as we have been able to establish, newcomers wishing to settle on the land were required to have professional training in farming and to possess suitable stock. The colonists were divided into categories according to property criteria, and the state's help was made to depend on the amount of the means brought in.

The colonists of the period of Frederick II's colonising action were in principle allotted small areas of land, so that after the expiry of the free years, unable to live on it under relatively heavy tax obligations, they fell into poverty. The Büdner could earn a living in West Prussia in the Netze district only while fortification works, the building of canals and the like lasted; after these works were finished they no longer had any possibility of supporting themselves by wage work. In South Prussia an attempt was made to create fairly large farms, from at least 20 morgen to 6 łany, which had a chance of surviving and developing further. Day labourers, on the other hand, were settled beside the royal domains, forests, nobles' manor farms and larger colonies or near towns, in order to assure them steady wage work, which was to be the basis of their livelihood. The changes in agriculture, the growing industrialisation of the manor farm, required an increase in the number of hands for work, and that is why the largest number of colonists of this category was settled in South Prussia.

 The origin of the settlers was not everywhere given, so this list is not quite exact as to the number of families of colonists settled. The figures in the list are indicative.

hired labourers were settled. The initiative in winning further settlers and settling them beside the larger colonies was left to the colonists who held considerable areas of land. In the Warta valley near Zagórów there thus arose
wasicki1953/176:
in this period on Prince Hohenlohe's estates the following villages: Sophiental (Olchowo), Ludwigslust (Mały Las), Friedrichsfelde (Tarszewo), Adelshof (Chróściki), the manor farm of Adolfsberg, Ingelfingen (Anielewo), Emilienheim (Michalinów), Augustinhof (Augustynów), Schwentz (Święcia) and the colony of Wrąbczyn.

From the contract of perpetual lease of the land that was concluded it followed that they were free and bound only to very limited services to the manor and certain dues in kind. After the expiry of four free years they were also bound to pay a rent: in two instalments — at Christmas and at St John's — of 30 thalers a year for each Magdeburg łan cleared and cultivated. For the teacher, the sołtys and the cemetery 21 morgen were allotted. The colonists came mostly from the Mark and Pomerania. We have no exact information on how long the German villages and colonies founded there lasted. Breyer reports that already in 1806 two families of colonists asked to be allowed to leave Mały Las and move to East Prussia, and in 1818 forty families from the village of Święcia came forward with the same request. The villages founded thus did not last long.

We also have information that Count Łubieński founded 11 colonies in his starosty of Guzów, settling 167 colonists, for which he was decorated by Frederick William III with the Order of the Red Eagle. Konstanty Milewski, too, owner of the Borszewice estates in the district of Lutomiersk, concluded a contract with 10 colonists from the Netze district and allotted them 10 łany of forest. Attempts by the lessees of royal estates to settle cottager colonists did not succeed, since both the lessees themselves and the settlers, who found worse conditions there, were unwilling about this action because of the considerable money costs. The attempts at settlement ended most often in failure.

2. Urban colonisation

Parallel with the conduct of rural colonisation, efforts were made to settle colonists in the towns. From the first instruction, however, it appeared clearly that what was meant was not to attract specialists for the further development of the manufacturing industry existing in Greater Poland, but only specialists in building, such as bricklayers, carpenters and the like. This by no means means that the settling of other arriving artisans was abandoned, but this came about when a fairly considerable number of newcomers from the left bank of the Rhine flowed into South Prussia.

Already in 1793, immediately after the entry of the Prussian troops, when the action of organising the new new province was in full swing, the chamber in Piotrków came forward with a proposal to settle in the towns colonists from the branch of crafts mentioned above, the lack of whom was particularly felt at that time.

wasicki1953/177:
In the order issued on 16 January 1794 the General Directory promised help and financial support for colonists settled in the towns. This help depended on whether the colonist came from outside the frontiers of the Prussian kingdom or from the Hohenzollern provinces, and finally on whether he settled in royal or private towns. In principle colonists could settle only in those towns where there was a lack of specialists in the branch of craft the colonist practised. According to the instruction, newcomers from outside the Prussian state received: 1) free citizenship, 2) a free licence to carry on a craft, or the right of mastership, 3) a three-year rebate of excise, 4) six years' exemption from the service, that is from payments for the upkeep of the night watchman and the fire-fighting equipment and other town payments and personal burdens such as watch duty and the like, 5) the colonist, together with his sons and the journeymen coming with him, was exempted from the duty of military service. Like the colonists settled in the villages, the town colonists too received travel money at the rate of 2 groschen a head for each mile. Besides, they were granted a special allowance for the transport of their movable property. The state's financial help also took the form of paying the yearly rent of their lodging and partly reimbursing the costs of setting up the workshop and buying tools that could not be brought with them. The order stresses once again that this help is intended exclusively for colonists settling in towns where there is a lack of this category of artisans. They were not forbidden to settle in other towns, but in such cases the state's financial help fell away. They were granted as a benefit only free citizenship, a licence or the right of mastership, and exemption from the cantons. Still greater restrictions were applied to artisans coming from within the Prussian state. They received, it is true, the concessions listed above, but were not exempt from the cantons.

The General Directory, agreeing to the proposals of the South Prussian chambers, recommended that settlers be brought above all to the seats of the provincial colleges, that is Poznań and Piotrków. Newcomers were promised greater financial help in the form of a special payment of 10—15 thalers a year. This applied only to masters and journeymen practising their trade independently.

As to private towns, the General Directory considered that their owners ought in their own interest to strive to settle artisans in them and to build on the empty plots. Colonists in these towns were to be granted the right to build freely on a plot, three years' exemption from all land taxes and obligations to the lord of the town, and finally a year's exemption from paying for lodging. Special credits were to be set aside for building houses.

Such were the first instructions on settling colonists in the towns sent by the General Directory to the chambers in Poznań and Piotrków.

The inflow of settlers to the towns was relatively small compared with the inflow of rural colonists. Like the rural settlers, newcomers to the towns met with many obstacles from the chambers. There were also cases where,

 S. P. Z. vol. III, fol. 9.
wasicki1953/178:
when settlers came to a town, the guilds refused to grant them the right of mastership free of charge, as the order of the General Directory stipulated. The question was settled in such a way that until separate regulations for the guilds were issued on this matter, they would have to grant the right of mastership to those of the newcomers who had held it before. If the applicant did not hold such a right, then all the costs connected with it were to be covered by the chamber from the general fund set aside for colonisation. From the numerous enquiries addressed by the chambers to the General Directory we may conclude that among the newcomers there were some who had left this province still in the time of the nobles' Commonwealth and now wished to return to it. In such cases all the concessions provided for colonists were due to them. If, however, they had left these lands after the partition and now wished to return again, they lost all right to the benefit.

A greater intensity of urban colonisation came during the reign of Frederick William III. More and more often the conditions and concessions for colonists provided by the General Directory's order of January 1794 were made public. In the Gazeta Południowo-Pruska the full text issued by the chamber in Kalisz was published. It would follow from this that the aim now was to attract colonists to the towns of that department. For earlier Poznań and Piotrków had been the object of the central authorities' special care. This did not exclude, however, the fact that colonists settled in other towns, as for example the weavers in Babimost.

Urban colonisation did not make very great progress, the more so since under minister Voss's administration, in accordance with his recommendations, an attempt was made to administer the fund set aside for colonisation very economically. For it was thought that an artisan would find good earnings in his new place. For this reason the time during which the chambers were to pay for the colonist's lodging was shortened. The principle was strictly observed that in the South Prussian towns only those artisans should be settled, and in such numbers, as were indispensably needed by the inhabitants.

When a larger number of artisans than needed wished to settle in them, the help due to them was naturally reduced.

In August 1799 Voss informed the South Prussian chambers that many artisans from the Prussian provinces would try to settle in the new province to improve their condition of life. This did not agree with the real settlement intentions of the General Directory, the more so since these artisans did not possess sufficient means to set up a workshop. The minister therefore considered that the number of this category of colonists should be limited, since the partial financial help granted them by the state would in any case not give the expected results. He therefore ordered the chambers in such cases to acquaint themselves well with the

wasicki1953/179:
means of an artisan wishing to settle in South Prussia, and not to give permission to settle if he did not possess sufficient means. In urban colonisation, then, the same property factors played the decisive part as in rural colonisation. Evidently the chambers did not keep very strictly to the minister's instructions and directions, since in reply to the chambers' numerous enquiries about settling colonists he ordered them to keep strictly to the orders issued earlier. The chambers, however, were concerned mainly with the newcomers from Württemberg, a relatively large number of whom had come to South Prussia, and for them too they tried to obtain increased financial help from the state. To these efforts, however, they received a negative answer from the General Directory, which instructed the chambers that the purpose of the fund set aside for colonisation was help for all the colonists settling, without making particular distinctions. In the particular case of the colonist joiner Baltazar Schiedt, settled in Krotoszyn, the General Directory listed the benefits due to him under the order of January 1794 on this matter.

Those colonists, however, deserved special support who possessed some means, thereby giving a guarantee that after settling they would be able to maintain the workshop they founded by themselves without the state's help. At first the amount of means a colonist should possess to receive the state's financial help was not exactly fixed. Only in 1802 was the amount of means a colonist must possess to obtain permission to settle fixed at 200 thalers. Only this category of persons, then, was entitled to the state's financial help needed for setting up a workshop. All the other colonists were entitled to the benefits listed in the order of 1794, but without financial help. They received a free licence and the right of mastership only after passing the appropriate examination.

As follows from the facts cited above, then, the Prussian authorities did not attach great importance to urban colonisation. This was undoubtedly bound up with the whole policy of the Prussian authorities towards the towns, industry and crafts in the period of South Prussia. The strong development of manufacturing industry in the other Prussian provinces, and especially in Silesia, did not allow the Prussian authorities to settle specialists of this branch in South Prussia, so as not to create dangerous competition for the Prussian provinces. For these reasons, too, urban colonisation was confined to only a small number of building craftsmen. Only the increased inflow of settlers from the lands on the left bank of the Rhine brought about the settlement here of a certain number of weavers, chiefly in Dąbie on the Ner. Unfortunately we cannot give the exact total number of town colonists who arrived and settled in South Prussia. In Voss's reports, tables and lists there was not the slightest mention of it. It must therefore be thought that their number was negligible, since the main stress was laid on rural colonisation.

werner1904/422:
201. Wreschen. (Diocese of Posen I.)

Soon after the beginning of the eighteenth century Evangelicals seem to have lived in the town of Wreschen (Polish Września or Wrzesno). In 1758 they obtained from the lord of the estate, Matthias Lodzia Poniński, the leave to hold religious meetings and to found a school. The Crown Treasurer Prince Adam Poniński renewed this leave in 1760 and furthered, to raise the town by German settlers, the forming of an evangelical local congregation. By a privilege of 1 May 1778 he gave the Evangelicals an orangery house standing in his castle garden for a church, two buildings connected with it for the parson's and the cantor's dwelling, and granted one Culm Hufe of land as parsonage land. The Consistory in Lissa approved the forming of a separate parish in Wreschen in 1779, and the congregation chose Marggraff as its first pastor. The very extensive parish originally included Schwarzenau as well (see there). When a separate parish arose there, Marggraff, it seems, was moved by disagreements with the lords of the estate to go there, and the congregation was then supplied by assistant pastors. The parochial relations were first fully ordered in the time of South Prussia. A district rich in German Hauland lands, with the towns of Peisern and Zagorowo, was lost to the parish in 1817, when those places came to Russia.

In 1822 the church, which had become very dilapidated, was rebuilt from the ground up, for which the lord of the estate Poniński gave generous help; it had massive enclosing walls and a massive tower in the lower storeys. For its further furnishing the Gustav Adolf Verein granted help of 500 Mark in 1883. A new church nevertheless had to be
werner1904/423:
built in the year 1895. It was dedicated on 27 September of the same year by the General Superintendent D. Hesekiel. It cost 67500 Mark. Towards the building sum contributed: the Evangelical Ober-Kirchenrat 3000 Mark, the Gustav-Adolf-Frauenverein in Bremen 1000 Mark, the Provincial Synod from the provincial distress collection of the year 1893 1000 Mark, Gustav-Adolf-Vereine 14000 Mark, besides which a lottery brought 1158.05 Mark.

On 9 November 1879 the congregation kept its centenary jubilee, on which occasion the pastor Schramm published "Nachrichten über die evangelische Kirche in Wreschen" (Notices on the evangelical church in Wreschen).

After the parishes of Miloslaw (see there) and Neßla-Hauland (see there) were branched off, the parish comprises the following localities: Wreschen, Bardo, Biależyce, Biechowo, Bieganowo, Bierzglin, Bierzglinek, Chocicza, Chwalibogowo, Gozdowo, Grzymisławice, Gr. and Kl. Guttowy, Raczanowo, Nehringswalde, Neudorf, Neuvorwerk, Oblaczkowo, Ossowo, Ostrów, Gr. and Kl. Piary, Slomowo, Sokołowo, Soleczno, Zajezierze, Zawodzie, Zerniki, Zieliniec, Gorazdowo, Piastowo, Zafutowo, Tischdorf, Stempocin, Lobenau, Opatówko, Targowa Góra, Racławki, Amilfarowo, Mala Góra, Buchwald, Miecysławowo, Młodziewice, Sokolnik, Galenzewo, Dambrowo, Szamarzewo, with 1821 parishioners. The filial Wilhelmsau belonging to it, set up on 1 June 1892, to which nine other localities belong, counts 336 Evangelicals. In Wilhelmsau stands a Bethaus erected by the Royal Settlement Commission, which was dedicated on 3 June 1892 by the General Superintendent D. Hesekiel.

The pastorate has been held by:

1. Martin August Marggraff, formerly rector in Schmiegel, came here in 1779 and went in 1783 to Schwarzenau (see there).

2. Jonathan Benjamin Krause, born in Liegnitz, was sent here by the Consistory in 1783 as general substitute and died here in 1787.

3. Christian Gottfried Rohrmann, born in Fraustadt, died here as general substitute in 1795.

4. Samuel Gottlieb Schrödt, born in Wollstein, was rector in Schwerzen and was called here as pastor in 1795. He died on 15 November 1818.

5. Johann Gottlob Tiesler, born at Storchnest, became second master and later rector in Rawitsch and was called here in 1819. He died on 18 April 1835.

6. Friedrich Wilhelm Gotthelf Vogel, born at Primkenau in the government district of Liegnitz, entered his office here in 1835. The days of terror which April 1848 brought the
werner1904/424:
German inhabitants of Wreschen forced him to flee with his family, and they brought death to two of his children then lying ill. His early death also seems to have been a consequence of the sufferings he had gone through. He died on 24 December 1849, 41 years old.

7. Rudolf Oswald Heise, born at Reinswalde near Sorau, entered the pastorate in 1850 and laid it down of his own will in 1856.

8. Heinrich August Schiffmann, born in Rügenwalde in Pomerania, became parish curator in 1857 and pastor in 1858. He left his office in 1873.

9. Friedrich Wilhelm Gustav Schramm, born in Jastrow in West Prussia, became assistant preacher in Bromberg (see there) in 1865, parish curator in Ciele (see there) in 1867 and was called here as pastor in 1873. He went in 1883 to Friedeberg in the Neumark as deacon at the town church there.

10. Otto Bock, formerly pastor in Piesske (see there), entered the pastorate in 1884.

On 1 May 1894 an assistant preacher was sent here in the person of the hitherto assistant curate Emil Gellert. When he was called in the same year still to Gogolin, Traugott Schent took his place. The latter was called in 1895 to be pastor of Lindenwald, whereupon Martin Sänger was sent here.

Gnesn. 1775 f. 33);

V p. 120); great-grandson, lastly, of Wojciech Dąmbski, court marshal of the Crown, and of Princess Adelajda Cecylia Radziwiłł, daughter of the chancellor in Lithuania (see vol. I pp. 56—59; vol. IV, table II of the Radziwiłłs; vol. V p. 51.) — Michalina married a second time, Count Stanisław Miączyński, captain in Napoleon's armies and adjutant of Prince Józef Poniatowski (see vol. I pp. 187--189), heir of the estate of Pawłów in the Poznań country. To him she brought as her dowry the Trąbczyn estate, which her grandson, Count Władysław Miączyński, holds today.
zychlinski1891/219: Count Stanisław Adam (11th generation), colonel of the former Polish army, adjutant of Prince Józef Poniatowski, knight of the cross Virtuti militari, heir of Trąbczyn, Wieniec, Brzeź, Dobielewo, Jaronówek, Pawłowo, Dzwonowo, Kolno, Berenbusz and Kamionna, born 24 December 1780, died in Berlin on 22 April 1845. From there his body was taken to the burial chapel of the Miączyńskis at Trąbczyn and buried there. As a young man he joined the ranks of Napoleon's armies, in the guard of the Grand Duke of Berg and Cleves, later king of the Two
zychlinski1891/220:
Sicilies; after which, "in view of his ability", he was appointed by Prince Józef Poniatowski on 2 September supernumerary captain and transferred to the general staff of the army of the Duchy of Warsaw. Having distinguished himself in that post in leading a squadron of the vanguard, he was raised by order of the minister of war of 24 November 1809 to chief of squadron with the rank of lieutenant-colonel and adjutant at the side of Prince Józef. On the occasion of this appointment, confirmed on 11 December of that year by the Duke of Warsaw, King Frederick Augustus of Saxony, and of the disbanding of the so-called "Guides" company, the Prince issued the following [order of the day], most flattering to Stanisław Miączyński:

The Allied Army.

Order of the day. 27 November 1809.

At Headquarters in Kraków.

When the Polish army, on entering Galicia, had as yet freed only a small part of it, the young men of Galicia, crowding beneath their country's standards, already showed sufficiently what spirit moves the inhabitants of this Polish land.

"The hope thus raised was disappointed in nothing; a common striving became the mark of true love of the Fatherland, and the company of Guides that was formed gave, by the praise of all, by its devotion to the good cause of our countrymen, many proofs under my eye that the young men who made it up lacked only the occasion to show themselves worthy of their brothers.

"Since the return of peace does not allow me to employ it longer in this form, it is a pleasure to me, by placing it in the army of the line, to increase there the number of good officers; and from the way of thinking of those who made up the company of Guides one may confidently promise oneself that by zeal in service and exemplary conduct they will always uphold the honour of the corps from which they come.

"To Captain Miączyński, who has commanded the company of Guides until now, I can give no better proof of the satisfaction he has earned than by returning him to my side as Adjutant, with the rank of lieutenant-colonel.

(signed) Józef Prince Poniatowski.

"A true copy of the Original.

Brigadier-General

Chief of the General Staff

Fiszer."

Worn out [printed "Stérauy", for Stérany] by the hardships of the Moscow campaign, Miączyński asked to be discharged. In answer he received the following letter from Prince Józef:

"Warsaw, 13 January 1812.

"Having received the Note in which you, Lieutenant-Colonel, ask to be released from the duties of the service, I have not failed to lay this wish before His Royal Majesty.

"In informing you of this, I hold it my duty to declare to you that, having had occasion during the time you were with me to be convinced of your zeal in fulfilling your duties, I am glad to take this opportunity of doing you the justice owed you in this respect, as I regret that in you I lose a subordinate whose qualities I know how to value.

"With the assurance of true esteem.

"Minister of War. Józef Prince Poniatowski [printed "Poniatowki"]."

"To the Honourable Lieutenant-Colonel Miączyński, knight of the Military Cross, here."

The discharge he asked for was issued, with the rank of colonel, on 25 January 1812; after which Count Stanisław went first to Dresden, and then settled on his wife's estates at Trąbczyn in the Kalisz country. — For already earlier,
zychlinski1891/221:
as a brilliant officer surrounded by the aureole of courage, he had met in the capital a rich and young widow of eminent virtues, Michalina née Prusimska Ostroróg [printed "Prasimskich"], Countess Dąmbska, wife of Józef, daughter of Antoni, starosta of Nieszczewice, and of Maryanna Dąmbska of the Godziemba arms, daughter of the castellan of Kowal (see vol. I p. 59; vol. VII p. 188), and having won her heart, he married her in August 1809. The marriage settlement — by which Michalina née Prusimska, Countess Dąmbska, wife of Józef, assigns to her future husband all the estates named above, while Count Stanisław secures to his future wife, out of the sum of 100,000 złoty of his share after his mother, already received, 90,000 złoty secured on the estates of Count Ignacy Miączyński, starosta of Kamieniopol, and the remaining 10,000 złoty placed on the property of Count Józef Ossoliński, his stepfather, and promises to settle on his wife the rest of his mother's share too after his mother's death, in all a sum of 280,000 złoty — was signed by: Stanisław Count Miączyński; Michalina Dąmbska née Prusimska; in the name of his wife, Teresa née Rafałowicz, by her first marriage Miączyńska, Count Józef Ossoliński; Józef Nowicki, colonel; Adam Broniec; Countess Agnieszka Skarbek née Dąmbska; Walenty Skorochód Majewski, notary; and so on.

The couple lived very happily, now on the Trąbczyn estates in the Kalisz country, now at Pawłowo near Kiszkowo in the Grand Duchy of Posen, where the trees planted by Michalina's hand still form a splendid park. Four sons brightened the evening of the brave Napoleonic veteran's life. When his health failed he went to Berlin for medical advice. There, feeling his strength ebbing, he disposed of his property as follows: to the eldest, Aleksander, he left the Pawłowo estates; to the second, Włodzimierz, then living in exile, capital; to the third, Mieczysław, already the heir of Wieniec in the Kingdom of Poland, he gave, in the form of a sale, the Trąbczyn estates and the village of Szetlewek in the Kalisz country; and lastly to the youngest, Witold, also in the form of a sale, the estate of Brzeź with its appurtenances in the district of Brześć Kujawski. — Count Stanisław's widow ended her life on 19 January 1851 on her estate of Trąbczyn, and was buried there beside her husband. The "Kuryer Warszawski" of the time (no. 65, of 9 March) gave her the following notice: "The late Countess Michalina Miączyńska, having begun the spring of her life in brilliant times in the great world, educated without conceit, beautiful without vanity, had the right to love the bustle of the world, which received her as its ornament; but a mother's feeling showed her another road. Choosing a quiet retreat on her native soil, she spent there a peaceful life, given to the duties of a model wife and model mother. After the loss of her husband the late Mrs Miączyńska redoubled her efforts, for her lofty heart told her to be a mother and to take the place of the dead father. Sparing in her own expenses, sparing in all the pleasures of life, she was generous in holding out a hand to suffering humanity, generous in helping her neighbour. A model citizen, a guardian of the peasants worthy to be followed, a kind neighbour and mistress of her house, she held to the last moments of her life to the principles and virtues that had adorned her from her youth."

1\. Count Aleksander (12th generation), officer of 1831, knight of the golden cross Virtuti militari, heir of the Pawłowo estates near Kiszkowo (8,500 Magdeburg morgen), recognised in the hereditary title of count of the Holy Roman Empire by the Prussian government by ministerial rescript of 5 May 1853, born 9 January 1810; as a young man he joined the national ranks in 1831 and, as a second lieutenant, received for bravery shown in various battles the golden cross Virtuti militari by order of the commander-in-chief of 15 September of that year. Forced to leave the country and go abroad, he wandered long through Germany, Switzerland and France, until at last in 1844 he received leave to return to the Grand Duchy of Posen and settled on the family estate of Pawłowo. In 1847 he married Bronisława Kalkstein of the

 She died at Padua on 2 September 1797, aged 38, and was buried there on 5 September, with a tombstone raised by her husband in the church of St Anthony. Author's note.
zychlinski1891/222:
Koss arms, born 21 March 1825, daughter of Ferdynand and of Paulina Radzimińska, daughter of the voivode's son of Gniezno, with whom he made the marriage contract on 16 November 1847 before the court at Wągrowiec, and whom he lost untimely on 15 August 1858. The death of his beloved wife affected him so painfully that from then on his strength failed more and more. Struck by paralysis, having prepared for death with the great piety that never left him in his life, he fell asleep in peace, surrounded by his children, on 31 October 1869 at Pawłowo, and was buried at Trąbczyn. Of his three children, his daughter Stanisława, born 1848, died 1860, went before him to the grave. Two remained:

† Countess Wanda, born 5 December 1849, married to Gustaw Potworowski of the Dębno arms, son of Gustaw, founder and long-time president of the Polish parliamentary group in Berlin, and of Klementyna née Chłapowska, and grandson of Andrzej and of Ludwika née Żychlińska of the Szeliga arms, heir of the estates of Gola and Stary Gostyń, member for Krobia in the Berlin parliament; she died in the flower of her age and beauty on 9 April 1875 in Berlin, and was laid in the burial chapel of the Potworowskis at Stary Gostyń. Without issue.

Count Władysław [13th generation], born 31 January 1852, heir of the Pawłowo estates by his father, and of the Trąbczyn estates by his uncle Włodzimierz, lieutenant of the reserve of the guard cuirassier regiment in Berlin; having gone through the Sophien-Realschule in Berlin and the agricultural academy at Freiberg, he took possession of the Pawłowo estates, which he sold a few years ago, and moved to the Kingdom of Poland. Since 1877 a member of the Berlin Geographical Society in Berlin ("Gesselschaft [for Gesellschaft] für Erdkunde"), further of the Society of the Friends of Learning in Poznań, and of the heraldic societies "Herold" in Berlin and "Adler" in Vienna; he married, on 7 August 1883, in the court church at Dresden, Helena Potocka of the Piława arms, daughter of Bolesław, lord of Będlewo, Dakowy, Wojnowice etc., and of the late Helena née Countess Kwilecka. The witnesses of the marriage were: Prince Antoni Sułkowski, holder of the entail of Rydzyna; Count Franciszek Kwilecki; Gustaw Potworowski; and Count Maksymilian Mielżyński. — Of this marriage:

Countess Elżbieta Marya Helena Felicya Józefa, born 5 October 1884 at Wrocław.
